# Commentary on Alexandre Kojève, *Introduction à la lecture de Hegel*

Page references are to the Gallimard pagination of 1947, which the scan reproduces; the scan is of a later printing that includes the "Note of the Second Edition" (pp. 436–437). Hegel's paragraphs in the translated sections are located by the standard paragraph numbers of the *Phenomenology* (¶), for orientation only; Kojève himself cites the fourth Hoffmeister edition by page and line. Quotations from Kojève are given in French, followed by an English rendering. Kojève's French terms are rendered consistently: Désir as Desire, Conscience de soi as self-consciousness, Sentiment de soi as self-feeling, reconnaissance as recognition, Maître and Esclave as Master and Slave, angoisse as anguish, négativité-négatrice as negating negativity, supprimer dialectiquement as to overcome dialectically (Hegel's *aufheben*).

Six traps beset this book, and the commentary guards against them throughout. First, Kojève's reading is not Hegel's text: the bracketed glosses and the lectures substitute an atheist, anthropological, labour-centred reading for Hegel's, and Kojève says so openly (p. 38). Claims are therefore attributed to whichever of the two makes them. Second, the "first" fight and the "first" men are not events in prehistory; Kojève puts "premier" in quotation marks because he is isolating an essential structure, not narrating an origin. Third, the end of history does not mean that nothing further happens; it means that the dialectic of recognition has exhausted its possibilities in the universal and homogeneous State. Fourth, Kojève's Desire is not a psychological lack but a "revealed nothingness", an ontological category; its human form is Desire for another Desire, not desire for a thing. Fifth, Kojève's dualism of nature (identity, the given) and man (negativity, action) is his own correction of Hegel's monism, not a report of it. Sixth, the Master is recognised, but unequally and by someone he does not recognise; the impasse lies in that asymmetry, not in an absence of recognition.

The volume opens with two epigraphs from Hegel, the closing words of the Jena lectures of 1806 and a passage from the Heidelberg inaugural address of 1816. The first announces an epoch in which Spirit has "made a leap forward" and a new form of it is emerging, which philosophy must be the first to greet. Placed here, it prefigures Kojève's central thesis: in 1806 history completes itself in the Napoleonic State, and Hegel's philosophy is the self-consciousness of that completion. The second sets courage in the face of truth and faith in the power of Spirit as the first condition of philosophy; man, being Spirit, may deem himself worthy of the highest. Together the epigraphs frame the book as a reading of Hegel as the philosopher of an accomplished history, whose knowledge is a human achievement rather than a revelation.

## Editor's Note

Raymond Queneau apologises for the book's mixed composition and identifies its layers. Its core is the notes he took at Kojève's course at the École pratique des Hautes Études, from January 1933 to May 1939, officially titled "The Religious Philosophy of Hegel" but in fact a commented reading of the *Phenomenology of Spirit*. Kojève revised the notes, but his other duties kept him from writing the promised introduction. Each year is supplemented by the summary printed in the School's *Annuaire*; the first six lectures of 1937–38 and the whole of 1938–39 appear in full from a stenographic record. The opening section reprints Kojève's commented translation of Chapter IV, Section A, published in *Mesures* on 14 January 1939. The appendices add four lectures of 1934–35 on the dialectic of the real and the phenomenological method, two lectures of 1933–34 on death, and a plan of the *Phenomenology* keyed to Hyppolite's translation. All references are to Hoffmeister's fourth edition of 1937. The textual status matters for interpretation: the notes compress and sometimes schematise, whereas the stenographed lectures preserve Kojève's own argument. Queneau's recommended short path through the book, the Introduction, the summary of pages 161–195, and the first two appendices, isolates the book's spine: Desire and recognition, the end of history and the Sage, the dualist ontology of negativity, and finitude.

## By Way of Introduction

The section carries an epigraph from Marx's 1844 manuscripts: Hegel grasps labour as the essence of man, as the essence that proves itself (*das sich bewährende Wesen*). The choice announces the reading. Kojève will render Hegel's *sich bewähren* as "s'avérer", to prove oneself or make good one's claim, and will make labour the site where the Slave's humanity proves itself. A note fixes the typographical convention: the commentary is printed in italics within square brackets, and words joined by hyphens translate a single German term. Kojève's hyphenated compounds ("réalité-essentielle" for *Wesen*, "objet-chosiste" for *Gegenstand*, "élément-constitutif" for *Moment*, "être-donné" for *Sein*) are thus not stylistic mannerisms but a translation device. Each compound builds an interpretation into the rendering: *Sein* becomes the merely "given", which prepares Kojève's opposition between given being and the action that negates it.

The opening bracketed commentary argues that man is self-consciousness and that this is what separates him from the animal, which never rises above self-feeling. Man becomes aware of himself when he first says "I". To understand man through his origin is therefore to understand the origin of the "I" revealed in speech. Kojève places human reality in the revealing word from the outset: self-consciousness is not an inner state but a self that speaks itself. This links the anthropology of Chapter IV to the theory of discourse that the later lectures develop, where the Sage's discourse reveals the totality of being.

Kojève next denies that cognition can explain the birth of the "I". The contemplative subject is lost in its object: «L'homme qui contemple est "absorbé" par ce qu'il contemple» (the man who contemplates is "absorbed" by what he contemplates) (p. 11). Knowledge reveals the object, not the subject. Only Desire, hunger for instance, can call the absorbed subject back to itself. Desire splits the being revealed to itself into an object opposed to a distinct subject. Kojève begins where Hegel's Chapter IV begins, with self-consciousness as Desire (¶167), but cuts it loose from the dialectic of consciousness (Chapters I–III) that leads there, and treats the cognitive chapters as abstractions from it. The target is the whole tradition of the knowing subject from Descartes onward, including Husserl, whom the lectures credit for method but not for this theory of the subject. Kojève's formula is lapidary: «Le Moi (humain) est le Moi d'un — ou du — Désir» (the human I is the I of a — or of the — Desire) (p. 11).

Since self-consciousness presupposes Desire, human reality can arise and endure only within a biological, animal life. Animal Desire is the necessary condition of self-consciousness, but not the sufficient one; by itself it yields only self-feeling. The distinction between necessary and sufficient conditions governs the rest of the argument. It lets Kojève hold together an embodied, finite subject (no human reality without animal life) and a radical difference in kind between man and animal. The later thesis that man is a being who negates nature while remaining rooted in it starts here.

Knowledge leaves man at rest; Desire makes him restless and drives him to act. Action satisfies Desire only by negating its object, destroying or at least transforming it, as eating destroys food. Negation is creative as well as destructive: the eater maintains his own reality by assimilating another. Hence the I of Desire is itself empty: «le Moi du Désir est un vide» (the I of Desire is a void) (p. 12), receiving positive content only from the action that negates the desired non-I. The content of the I is therefore a function of what it negates. If Desire bears on a natural thing, the resulting I is natural, "thing-like", merely alive, and reveals itself only as self-feeling. Two doctrines are seeded here: negativity as the being of man, and the principle that one becomes what one assimilates. The latter drives the whole argument: to become non-natural, Desire must bear on something non-natural.

Self-consciousness therefore requires that Desire bear on a non-natural object, something beyond the given real. The only thing that exceeds the given is Desire itself, which before its satisfaction is «qu'un néant révélé, qu'un vide irréel» (only a revealed nothingness, an unreal void) (p. 12), the presence of the absence of a reality. Desire directed at another Desire, taken as Desire, therefore creates through its satisfaction an I that is itself Desire. Such an I is not a static being identical with itself but becoming: intentional development, conscious progress, the act of transcending the given that it itself is. It is free with respect to the given and historical with respect to itself. The formulation carries Kojève's ontological dualism in embryo: nature is identity, man is the negation of identity, a nothingness that "nihilates" in being. The phrasing, "présence de l'absence", draws on Heidegger's treatment of the nothing; Sartre's *L'Être et le néant* (1943) will take up and radicalise this conception of human negativity.

Human Desire must bear on another Desire, so there must first be a plurality of animal Desires. Man can therefore appear only within a herd, and human reality is social from the start. A herd becomes a society only when each member's Desires bear, or can bear, on the Desires of the others. Kojève's examples are pointed. Between man and woman, Desire is human only if one desires the other's Desire rather than the other's body, that is, desires to be desired, loved, or recognised. Desire for a natural object is human only when mediated by another's Desire for the same object; hence a biologically useless object, a decoration or the enemy's flag, can be desired because others desire it. Kojève concludes: «l'histoire humaine est l'histoire des Désirs désirés» (human history is the history of desired Desires) (p. 13). The mimetic structure of Desire that René Girard will make famous, and Lacan's thesis that desire is the desire of the Other, both derive from this paragraph, which Lacan heard in the course.

Apart from this essential difference, human Desire is analogous to animal Desire. It too seeks satisfaction through negating, transforming, and assimilating action: «L'homme se "nourrit" de Désirs comme l'animal se nourrit de choses réelles» (man "feeds" on Desires as the animal feeds on real things) (p. 13–14). The human I realised through such satisfaction is as much a function of its "food" as the animal body is of its own. The analogy secures the principle stated earlier: because the self is what it assimilates, a self nourished on Desires, which are nothingness, will itself be negativity rather than given being.

For man to be truly human, his human Desire must in fact prevail over his animal Desire. Every Desire is desire for a value, and the animal's supreme value is its own life; all its desires serve self-preservation. Human Desire must therefore override the desire for self-preservation: man proves himself human only by risking his animal life for his human Desire. Kojève glosses "s'avérer" as showing, demonstrating, verifying, and proving oneself. This recovers the sense of Hegel's *sich bewähren*, the term of Marx's epigraph, but relocates the proof in the risk of life before it relocates it in labour. To speak of the origin of self-consciousness is thus necessarily to speak of risking life for a non-vital end.

To desire a Desire is to want to substitute oneself for the value the other Desire desires: «désirer un Désir c'est vouloir se substituer soi-même à la valeur désirée par ce Désir» (to desire a Desire is to wish to put oneself in the place of the value desired by that Desire) (p. 14). Otherwise one would desire the value, not the Desire. To desire another's Desire is therefore to want the other to recognise my value as his value, to recognise me as an autonomous value. All anthropogenic Desire is ultimately a function of the desire for recognition, and the risk of life by which human reality proves itself is a risk undertaken for it. The origin of self-consciousness is thus a fight to the death for recognition. The chain, Desire for Desire, then substitution, then recognition, then risk, then fight, is Kojève's derivation. Hegel reaches recognition from the thesis that self-consciousness finds satisfaction only in another self-consciousness (¶175), but he never construes that satisfaction as desire for the other's desire.

Without this fight to the death for pure prestige, Kojève holds, there would never have been human beings on earth. The claim follows because human being arises only where at least two Desires for recognition confront each other, and each is ready to go to the end, risking its own life and thereby endangering the other's. Their encounter can only be a fight to the death, and only in and through it does human reality engender itself, realise itself, and reveal itself to itself and to others. The phrase "pure prestige" is essential: the fight has no biological stake, and that is precisely why it is anthropogenic. Human reality therefore exists only as recognised reality.

If all the combatants behaved alike, the fight would end in the death of one or both, and neither would yield or recognise the other. Human being would then be impossible. If both die, human reality, which can live only within animal life, disappears. If one dies, the survivor loses the Desire on which his own Desire had to bear to be human, and the dead cannot recognise him. The nascent human multiplicity must therefore contain two essentially different anthropogenic behaviours. The argument is a transcendental one in Kojève's hands: it infers from the fact of human existence the conditions that must have held for it to arise.

Both adversaries must survive, and this is possible only if they behave differently. Kojève locates the difference in freedom: «Par des actes de liberté irréductibles, voire imprévisibles ou "indéductibles"» (through irreducible, even unforeseeable or "non-deducible" acts of freedom) (p. 15), they constitute themselves as unequal in the fight itself. One of them, without being predestined to it, must fear the other, yield, refuse the risk of life, abandon his own desire for recognition, and satisfy the other's. To recognise without being recognised is to recognise the other as one's Master and to make oneself the Master's Slave. Kojève refuses any natural ground for the inequality, whether strength, temperament, or race. Mastery and slavery are self-made through a free act, which makes the Slave responsible for his servitude and able, in principle, to undo it.

At its birth, then, man is never simply man; he is necessarily either Master or Slave: «à son état naissant, l'homme n'est jamais homme tout court» (in its nascent state, man is never simply man) (p. 15). If human reality arises only as social, society is human, at least at its origin, only if it contains an element of mastery and an element of servitude, autonomous and dependent existences. Speaking of the origin of self-consciousness thus means speaking of "the autonomy and dependence of self-consciousness, of Mastery and Servitude", which is Hegel's title for Section A. Kojève has derived Hegel's heading from his own theory of Desire. The consequence is an anthropology with no generic human nature prior to the social relation: the species exists only as divided.

If human being arises only in the fight that ends in the Master–Slave relation, then its progressive realisation and revelation can occur only as a function of that fundamental social relation. If man is nothing other than his becoming, if his being in space is his being in or as time, and if revealed human reality is universal history, then history must be the history of the interaction between Mastery and Servitude: «la "dialectique" historique est la "dialectique" du Maître et de l'Esclave» (historical "dialectic" is the "dialectic" of Master and Slave) (p. 16). But if thesis and antithesis have sense only within their reconciliation in a synthesis, if history has a final term, if man becoming must culminate in man become, if Desire must end in satisfaction, and if the science of man must be definitively and universally true, then the interaction must end in the dialectical overcoming of both Master and Slave. The string of conditionals compresses Kojève's whole reading. It binds the truth of Hegel's science to the end of history: absolute knowledge is possible only if the historical dialectic is closed. The 1937–38 and 1938–39 courses develop exactly this dependence. Kojève's use of "thesis, antithesis, synthesis" here is heuristic; the 1933–34 notes (p. 38) deny that dialectic is a method at all.

Human reality can arise and last only as recognised reality. A human being is truly human, for himself and for others, only when recognised by another, by others, and in the limit by all others. Only when one speaks of recognised human reality can one, in calling it human, «énoncer une vérité au sens propre et fort du terme» (utter a truth in the proper and strong sense of the term) (p. 16), because only then does discourse reveal a reality. Kojève here fuses the ontological and the epistemic: truth is the revelation of reality, and human reality exists only when universally recognised. Universal recognition is thus the condition both of man's full reality and of a true discourse about man, which explains why the Sage can appear only in the universal State. The commentary ends by handing over to Hegel: this is why, in speaking of self-consciousness, one must say what follows.

Hegel's text begins (¶178): self-consciousness exists in and for itself in that, and because, it exists in and for itself for another self-consciousness; that is, it exists only as something recognised («entité-reconnue»). Kojève's preceding commentary has already given this sentence its sense: the being of self-consciousness is its being-recognised. Kojève omits ¶179–184, Hegel's abstract exposition of the "doubling" of self-consciousness and the "pure concept" of mutual recognition, and passes straight to its appearance in experience. The omission is revealing: the speculative structure of recognition, in which each self-consciousness sees itself in the other and returns to itself, is replaced by the genetic story Kojève has just told.

Hegel continues (¶185): this pure concept of recognition, of the doubling of self-consciousness within its unity, must now be considered as its process appears to self-consciousness. Kojève's gloss specifies the standpoint: not to the philosopher who speaks of recognition, but to the self-conscious man who recognises another or makes himself recognised. The distinction between "for us" and "for it", between the philosopher and the consciousness under study, is Hegel's methodological principle; Kojève retains it but gives the "for it" a concrete bearer, the fighting man. The philosopher's standpoint will return at ¶189, where Kojève identifies "for us" with the author and reader who see man from the end of history.

The process will first show the inequality of the two self-consciousnesses, the two men who confront each other for recognition. In Hegel's terms, the middle term, which Kojève glosses as mutual and reciprocal recognition, splits into the two extremes, which as extremes are opposed: one is only recognised, the other only recognising. Kojève explains why: the man who seeks recognition does not at first want to recognise in turn. If he succeeds, recognition will not be mutual; he will be recognised without recognising the one who recognises him. The gloss turns Hegel's logical vocabulary of middle term and extremes, borrowed from the syllogism, into motives. Hegel's inequality follows from the concept's first, one-sided realisation; Kojève's follows from what the combatant wants.

Hegel's ¶186 opens with self-consciousness in its first shape: simple being-for-itself, identical with itself by excluding everything other. Its essence and absolute object is "I", which Kojève glosses as the I isolated from and opposed to everything that is not I. In this immediacy, this given character of its being-for-itself, it is a singular individual, and whatever is other is for it an inessential object marked as negative. Kojève's gloss on immediacy, «non produit par un processus actif créateur» (not produced by an active, creative process) (p. 17), is the key interpretive move: Hegel's "immediate" becomes "given", the opposite of "made". Everything immediate is thereby consigned to nature, and everything mediated to action. The pairing given/created will organise the rest of the commentary and the whole of Kojève's ontology.

The other, however, is also a self-consciousness: one human individual faces another. Appearing immediately, each exists for the other as an ordinary object, as independent shapes of consciousness sunk in the given being of animal life, since the object in its immediate being has been determined as life. Neither has yet carried out for the other the movement of absolute abstraction, which consists in eradicating all immediate being and in being nothing but the purely negative being of self-identical consciousness. Hegel's point is that each is still, for the other, a living thing. Kojève's rendering of *Leben* as "vie-animale" narrows it: Hegel's life is the dialectical concept of Chapter IV's introduction (¶168–173), the fluid universal medium of living shapes, not the animal as a biological kind.

In other words, the two have not yet shown themselves to each other as pure being-for-itself, as self-consciousness. Kojève's gloss sets the scene: when two "first" men meet, each sees in the other only an animal, dangerous and hostile, to be destroyed, not a self-conscious being with autonomous worth. Each is subjectively certain of himself but not of the other, so his certainty lacks truth. Kojève glosses truth as a reality that is objectively, intersubjectively, even universally recognised, and therefore existing and valid. The truth of one's self-certainty would be one's being-for-itself appearing as an independent object, or the object appearing as this pure self-certainty. Kojève's gloss states it plainly: one must rediscover in external, objective reality the idea one has of oneself. Hegel's distinction between certainty and truth thus becomes a distinction between private self-estimation and public recognition. The substitution anticipates the later thesis that truth is a social and historical product.

By the concept of recognition, this is possible only if each carries out for the other the pure abstraction of being-for-itself, as the other does for him, each through his own activity and through that of the other. Hegel's claim is that recognition is a double act: no one can achieve it alone. Kojève's gloss that follows turns the double act into a program. The "first" man already attributes absolute worth to himself and believes himself a man, but his certainty is not yet knowledge; his self-image may be illusory, false, or mad. To become true it must reveal an objective reality, valid not only for itself but for others. He must impose his idea of himself on others and, ideally, on all others, or transform the natural and human world in which he is not recognised into one in which he is. That transformation of a world hostile to a human project into one in accord with it is action. Since the other, if he is or wants to be human, must do the same, the first anthropogenic action necessarily takes the form of «une lutte de pur prestige» (a fight for pure prestige) (p. 18). Kojève's definition of action as the transformation of the world to fit a project unites the fight and labour under one concept, which lets him later treat work as the continuation of the fight by other means.

Hegel's ¶187 states how the pure abstraction of being-for-itself shows itself: by showing that one is the pure negation of one's objective mode of being, bound to no determinate existence, not to the universal singularity of existence as such, not to life. Kojève renders the last phrase as «ne pas être lié à la vie» (not to be bound to life) (p. 18). The showing is a double activity, the other's and one's own. Insofar as it is the other's activity, each seeks the other's death. Insofar as it is one's own, it involves staking one's own life. The relation of the two self-consciousnesses is therefore such that they prove themselves, each for itself and for the other, through a fight of life and death. Hegel derives the fight from the structure of self-manifestation: to show that one is not attached to life, one must put life at stake. Kojève's derivation from Desire and Hegel's derivation from self-presentation converge on the same result, but Hegel's needs no theory of prestige.

Kojève explains "to prove themselves" as turning the purely subjective certainty of one's worth into objective, universally valid, recognised truth. Since truth is the revelation of a reality, and human reality is constituted only in the fight for recognition through the risk of life it involves, the truth of man presupposes the fight to the death. That is why, Hegel continues, the individuals must engage in it: they must raise their self-certainty to truth, in the other and in themselves. Only by risking life is freedom proved, only so is it shown that the essence of self-consciousness is not given being, not its immediate way of appearing, not its immersion in the expanse of life, but that nothing in it is anything but a vanishing moment. The individual who has not risked his life may be recognised as a person, but he has not attained the truth of being recognised as an autonomous self-consciousness. This sentence of Hegel's carries more weight in Kojève than in most readings. The distinction between the person recognised merely in law and the self-consciousness that has proved itself will return in Kojève's reading of the legal person of the Roman world (Chapter VI, A).

Each must therefore aim at the other's death as he risks his own, for the other is worth no more to him than himself. His essence, which Kojève glosses as his recognised human reality and dignity, appears to him as something other, another man who does not recognise him and is independent of him. He is outside himself and must overcome this being-outside-himself. The other is a consciousness existing as given being and entangled in the natural world in many ways; yet he must view his other-being as pure being-for-itself, absolute negativity. Kojève glosses: as long as he is not recognised, the meaning of his life is concentrated in the other, and so he is "outside himself"; yet he wants his worth in himself. He must make himself recognised, but for recognition to satisfy him he must know that the other is human. At first he sees only an animal. To know that it reveals a human reality, he must see the other also wanting recognition, ready to "negate" his animal life. He must therefore provoke the other, force him into a fight to the death for pure prestige, and, not to be killed, he must kill. Kojève adds a step Hegel does not state: the fight is also a test of whether the other is human, since only the other's risk can certify his humanity. Recognition requires a worthy recogniser, and worthiness is itself proved by risk. The same requirement will produce the Master's impasse.

Hegel's ¶188 turns the result against itself: this proof through death abolishes the truth that was meant to come from it, and with it the self-certainty as such. Just as life is the natural positing of consciousness, independence without absolute negativity, so death is the natural negation of consciousness, negation without independence, which therefore lacks the significance recognition requires. Kojève glosses the cases: if both perish, consciousness is abolished, since a dead man is an inanimate body; if one survives, he cannot be recognised by the dead, and his certainty stays subjective. Death does establish that both staked their lives and despised life in themselves and in the other, but not for those who fought. By death they abolish their consciousness, which had been placed in the alien element of natural existence; they abolish themselves. Kojève adds: man is real only in a natural world that is alien to him and that he must negate and transform to realise himself, but outside it he is nothing. The addition marks the boundary of Kojève's dualism: negativity is real only as the negation of a given it cannot do without. There is no pure spirit; man exists only as a nothingness at work within being, and dies with his body.

The two are abolished as extremes seeking to exist for themselves. The essential moment disappears from the play of change, namely the division into extremes with opposite determinations. The middle term collapses into a dead unity, split into dead extremes that merely are and are not opposed. They neither give themselves to nor receive themselves from each other through consciousness; they merely release each other indifferently, as things. Kojève glosses that the dead man is only an unconscious thing from which the living turns away, since he can expect nothing from it. Their deed is abstract negation, not the negation of consciousness, which overcomes in such a way that it preserves and maintains what is overcome and so survives its overcoming. Hegel here gives one of his clearest definitions of *Aufhebung*, and he gives it by contrast with killing.

Kojève's gloss on that sentence defines dialectical overcoming. To overcome dialectically is to abolish while preserving what is abolished, which is sublimated in and by this preserving abolition. What is overcome is annulled in its contingent, meaningless aspect as a given natural entity, the "immediate", and preserved in what is essential and meaningful in it. Mediated by negation, it is raised to a mode of being more comprehensive and more comprehensible than its immediate reality as a merely given, static, positive datum not produced by creative action. The gloss joins *Aufhebung* to action: what is preserved is raised to intelligibility precisely because it has become the result of a negating act. Intelligibility and producedness coincide, which is why Kojève will hold that only human, historical reality is dialectical, and that nature is not (Appendix I).

It is therefore useless for the man of the Fight to kill his adversary. He must overcome him dialectically: leave him life and consciousness and destroy only his autonomy, abolish him only as opposed to and acting against himself. In a word, «il doit l'asservir» (he must enslave him) (p. 21). The gloss applies the definition of *Aufhebung* to the living adversary. Enslavement is the dialectical overcoming of the other: his natural being is preserved, his independence annulled. The Master–Slave relation thus appears as the first *Aufhebung* in human history, and the first social institution.

Hegel's ¶189 draws the lesson: in this experience self-consciousness learns that life is as essential to it as pure self-consciousness. In immediate self-consciousness, the "first" man not yet mediated by contact with the other, the simple I is the absolute object. For us, or in itself, this object, the I, is absolute mediation, whose essential moment is self-maintaining independence. Kojève glosses "for us" as the author and reader of these lines, who see man as he has definitively constituted himself at the end of history through completed social interaction. The gloss is decisive for the whole book. The Hegelian "we", the phenomenological observer, becomes a historical position: the one who stands at the end of history and can see the whole. Phenomenological knowledge is thereby possible only after the fact, which is the thesis the 1938–39 lectures on Chapter VIII will defend. The first experience dissolves the simple unity of the isolated I.

This experience posits a pure self-consciousness, which Kojève glosses as the victor, having abstracted from animal life by risking it, and a consciousness that exists not purely for itself but for another, the spared vanquished, whom Kojève calls «un cadavre vivant» (a living corpse) (p. 22). This second consciousness exists as given being, in the shape of thinghood. Both moments are essential. Since they are at first unequal and opposed, and their reflection into unity has not yet resulted from their action, they exist as two opposed shapes of consciousness: the independent one, whose essence is being-for-itself, and the dependent one, whose essence is life, being for another. The one is the Master, the other the Slave. Kojève adds that the Slave is the adversary who did not go to the end, did not adopt the Masters' principle, conquer or die, and accepted a life granted by another; having preferred servitude to death, he lives as a Slave. "Living corpse" states the Slave's status sharply: in the Master's eyes he died in the fight, and his continued life belongs to the victor. Kojève's gloss "their action" for Hegel's "reflection into unity" also signals that the reconciliation of the two will come through deeds, namely labour and a second fight, not through insight.

Hegel's ¶190 begins: the Master is consciousness existing for itself, no longer merely the concept of it but a real consciousness mediated with itself through another consciousness, one whose essence is to be bound up with given being, with thinghood as such. Kojève glosses the other consciousness as the Slave, who by identifying with his animal life is one with the natural world of things. Refusing to risk his life for pure prestige, he does not rise above the animal and regards himself, and is regarded by the Master, as such. Yet the Slave recognises the Master's human dignity and behaves accordingly. The Master's certainty is thus no longer merely subjective and immediate but objectified and mediated by another's recognition. The Master is already human and mediated, while the Slave remains immediate, natural, "bestial". This is the Master's real gain: his self-image has become a social fact. Kojève's reading already contains the seed of its reversal: the Master's humanity depends on the recognition of someone he classes as an animal.

The Master relates to two moments: to a thing as such, the object of Desire, and to the consciousness whose essence is thinghood, the Slave. Kojève contrasts their attitudes: the Slave, by refusing the risk, binds himself to the things on which he depends; the Master sees them only as means to satisfy his desire and destroys them in doing so. Since the Master, as the concept of self-consciousness, is the immediate relation of being-for-itself, and now also exists as mediation, being-for-itself only through another, he relates immediately to both the thing and the Slave, and mediately to each through the other. He relates to the Slave through independent being, the given: this is the Slave's chain, from which he could not abstract in the fight and which revealed him as dependent. The Master is the power over this being, since he showed in the fight that it counts for him only as negative. Since the Master is the power over given being and given being is the power over the Slave, the Master holds the Slave in subjection in this syllogism, which Kojève calls "real or active". Hegel's logical form, the syllogism with its middle term, is here literal: domination is a relation mediated through nature. The Slave is bound to the Master only because he is bound to life.

The Master also relates to the thing mediately, through the Slave. As self-consciousness, the Slave too relates negatively to the thing and overcomes it, but for him the thing is also independent, so he cannot finish it off by annihilating it, as the Master does in consuming it; he only works on it. Kojève glosses: he prepares it for consumption but does not consume it himself. For the Master, through this mediation, the immediate relation to the thing becomes pure negation of it, that is, enjoyment. Kojève's example: he eats a ready-made dish. What Desire, the isolated man before the Fight face to face with nature, could not achieve, the Master achieves: he gets the better of the thing and satisfies himself in enjoyment. Kojève draws the consequence: only thanks to another's labour is the Master free with respect to nature and satisfied with himself. But he is Master of the Slave only because he first freed himself from nature, his own and the world's, by risking his life in a fight for pure prestige, which has nothing natural about it. Desire failed because of the thing's independence; the Master, having put the Slave between himself and the thing, joins himself only to its dependent side and enjoys it purely, leaving its independent side to the Slave who works on it. The division of the thing into two sides, dependent for the Master and resistant for the Slave, is the hinge of the reversal to come. The Master receives the thing without its resistance and so learns nothing from it; the Slave receives only its resistance and learns everything.

Hegel's ¶191: in these two moments the Master obtains recognition from another consciousness. The Slave posits himself as inessential, both in working on the thing and in his dependence on a determinate existence; in neither can he master given being and reach absolute negation. Here is the moment of recognition in which the other consciousness overcomes itself as being-for-itself and so does to itself what the first does to it. Kojève glosses that the Slave regards himself as a slave, not only the Master regards him so. The other moment of recognition is also present: the Slave's activity is the Master's own, since everything the Slave does is properly the Master's doing. Kojève explains: since the Slave works only to satisfy the Master's desires, it is the Master's desire that acts in and through the Slave. For the Master, being-for-itself alone is essential; he is pure negative power, for which the thing is nothing, and the pure essential activity of the relation. The Slave's activity is inessential. For genuine recognition, a third moment would be needed: that the Master do to himself what he does to the other, and the Slave do to the other what he does to himself. Recognition born of Mastery and Servitude is therefore «une reconnaissance inégale et unilatérale» (an unequal and one-sided recognition) (p. 24). Hegel's three moments state the formal criterion of full recognition: symmetry of what each does to self and other. Kojève's gloss supplies the empirical correlate: the Master does not behave as a Slave, and the Slave does not behave as a Master; «L'Esclave ne risque pas sa vie, et le Maître est oisif» (the Slave does not risk his life, and the Master is idle) (p. 25). Each lacks exactly what the other has, and full recognition will require a single figure who both works and has risked his life, the citizen-soldier of the post-revolutionary State.

Kojève then argues, in a long gloss, that the Master–Slave relation is not recognition properly so called, and examines it from the Master's side. The Slave regards him as Master, so he is recognised in his human reality and dignity. But the recognition is one-sided, because he does not in turn recognise the Slave's humanity; he is recognised by someone he does not recognise. Therein lies the inadequacy, and the tragedy, of his position. He fought and risked his life for recognition and obtained a recognition worthless to him, since he can be satisfied only by recognition from someone he recognises as worthy to recognise him. Kojève calls the Master's attitude «une impasse existentielle» (an existential impasse) (p. 25). He became Master because his Desire bore on another Desire; but having become Master, he must want recognition as Master, which he can get only by making the other his Slave. The Slave, however, is for him an animal or a thing, so he is "recognised" by a thing, and his Desire ultimately bears on a thing, not on a human Desire. The Master has taken a wrong turning: after the fight he is not what he wanted to be, a man recognised by a man. If man can be satisfied only by recognition, the man who behaves as a Master never will be; since man is at first either Master or Slave, the satisfied man will necessarily be the Slave, or rather the one who has been a Slave and has dialectically overcome his servitude. The argument turns Hegel's formal asymmetry into a practical contradiction in the Master's Desire: his Desire is logically self-defeating, since success converts its object from a Desire into a thing. The conclusion, satisfaction belongs to the former Slave, is the thesis on which Kojève's philosophy of history rests.

Hegel's ¶192: the inessential consciousness is for the Master the object that constitutes the truth of his self-certainty, since, Kojève glosses, he can "know" himself as Master only by being recognised as such by the Slave. But this object plainly does not correspond to its concept. Where the Master has fulfilled himself, what has come about for him is quite other than an independent consciousness: a dependent one. He is therefore not certain of being-for-itself as a truth; his truth is the inessential consciousness and its inessential activity. Kojève glosses: «la "vérité" du Maître est l'Esclave ; et son Travail» (the Master's "truth" is the Slave, and his Labour) (p. 26). Others recognise the Master as Master only because he has a Slave, and the Master's life consists in consuming the products of servile labour. Hegel's "truth" of a shape is what it turns out to be when fulfilled; Kojève gives it a sociological content. The Master's identity is not a quality he possesses but the Slave and the Slave's work on which he lives.

Hegel's ¶193: the truth of the independent consciousness is accordingly the servile consciousness. At first it appears outside itself and not as the truth of self-consciousness; Kojève glosses that the Slave recognises human dignity not in himself but in the Master, on whom he depends even for his existence. But just as Mastery showed that its essence is the reverse of what it wants to be, so Servitude will presumably become in its fulfilment the opposite of what it immediately is: as consciousness forced back into itself, it will go into itself and be reversed into true independence. Kojève's gloss states the thesis in its strongest form. The integral man, absolutely free and definitively satisfied, who perfects and completes himself in this satisfaction, will be the Slave who has overcome his servitude. Idle Mastery is a dead end; laborious Servitude is the source of all human, social, and historical progress: «L'Histoire est l'histoire de l'Esclave travailleur» (History is the history of the working Slave) (p. 26). Hegel's word "presumably" (*wohl*) marks a hypothesis to be confirmed by the analysis; Kojève states the result as a thesis in advance. To see it, he says, one must consider the relation from the Slave's point of view.

Hegel's ¶194 begins: we have seen servitude only in relation to mastery, but it is also self-consciousness, and we must consider what it is in and for itself. At first the Master is its essence, so that independent consciousness existing for itself is its truth, which does not yet exist in it. Kojève's gloss identifies the Slave's advantage. The Slave subordinates himself to the Master and so esteems and recognises the value and reality of autonomy, of human freedom, although he does not find it realised in himself but only in the other. The Master, unable to recognise the other who recognises him, is stuck. The Slave has recognised the other from the start, so he need only impose himself on the Master and make himself recognised for mutual recognition to be established, the only kind that can fully and definitively satisfy man. For this the Slave must cease to be a Slave and overcome himself as such; but whereas the Master has no desire, and so no possibility, of overcoming himself as Master, since that would mean becoming a Slave, the Slave has every interest in ceasing to be one. Moreover, the fight that made him a Slave predisposes him to this self-overcoming. Kojève's analysis of the Slave's advantage is structural. Recognition must be mutual; half of it is already in place on the Slave's side; the Master's half can only come from outside him, since he has no motive to change. Historical change is thus asymmetrically driven: only the side with an interest in negating its own condition can move.

Servitude nonetheless has in itself the truth of pure negativity and being-for-itself, because it has experienced this essence in itself. The servile consciousness was afraid not for this or that, not at this or that moment, but for its entire being, for it felt «l'angoisse de la mort, du Maître absolu» (the anguish of death, the absolute Master) (p. 27). In this anguish it has been inwardly dissolved, has trembled through and through, and everything fixed in it has been shaken. This pure universal movement, this absolute liquefaction of everything stable, is the simple essence of self-consciousness, absolute negativity, pure being-for-itself, which thus exists in the servile consciousness. Kojève renders Hegel's *Furcht*, fear, as "angoisse", anguish, and so reads the passage through Heidegger's *Angst*, the fundamental mood that confronts Dasein (existence) with its own nothingness. The rendering makes the Slave's fear an ontological disclosure rather than an emotion about a threat. It also explains how the Slave can have "in himself" the negativity he sees in the Master: death, not the Master, is the true Master, and the Slave has experienced it more fully than the Master who merely risked it.

Kojève's gloss draws the contrast. The Master is fixed in his Mastery: he cannot surpass himself, change, or progress; he must conquer and remain Master, or die; one can kill him but not educate him. Having risked his life to be Master, he holds Mastery as the supreme given value he cannot surpass. The Slave did not want to be a Slave; he became one because he would not risk his life to be Master. In mortal anguish he understood, without realising it, that no given, fixed condition, not even the Master's, can exhaust human existence; he understood the "vanity" of given conditions. He did not bind himself to the Master's condition and does not bind himself to his own. There is nothing fixed in him; he is ready for change, and in his very being he is change, transcendence, transformation, "education"; he is historical becoming from the start. On the one hand he does not identify with what he is and wants to transcend his given state; on the other he has a positive ideal, autonomy, being-for-itself, which he finds embodied in the Master at the origin of his servitude. Kojève's inversion is complete. The Slave's refusal to fight, which seemed a failure of freedom, turns out to be a deeper freedom, a non-attachment to any given condition. The Slave is defined by two features that together make history possible: negativity toward the present and an ideal taken from the other.

The moment of being-for-itself also exists for the servile consciousness, since in the Master being-for-itself is its object. Kojève glosses that the Slave knows what it is to be free, knows he is not, and wants to become so. If the experience of the Fight predisposes the Slave to transcendence, progress, and History, his life of work in the Master's service realises this predisposition. Hegel continues: the servile consciousness is not only this universal dissolution as such; in service it carries out the dissolution in actual reality. In service it overcomes its attachment to natural existence in all its particular moments and works that existence off. Kojève's gloss states the mechanism of liberation. The Master forces the Slave to work, and by working the Slave becomes master of nature. But he became the Master's Slave only because he was first a slave of nature, bound to it by the instinct of self-preservation. By becoming master of nature through labour, he frees himself from his own nature, from the instinct that bound him to nature and made him a Slave; in freeing him from nature, labour therefore frees him from the Master. In the natural, given world the Slave is the Master's slave; in the technical world transformed by his labour he rules, or will one day rule, as absolute Master. That mastery born of labour will be quite different from the Master's "immediate" mastery. The future and History belong not to the warrior Master, who either dies or stays forever identical with himself, but to the working Slave, who by transforming the given world transcends the given and what it determines in himself, and so surpasses the Master, who leaves the given untouched. The anguish of death embodied in the Master is the *sine qua non* of historical progress; only the Slave's labour realises and completes it. The gloss is Kojève's most Marxian passage: technique is the Slave's road to freedom, and the "technical world" replaces nature as the environment in which man is at home. Hegel's text speaks only of working off attachment to natural existence; the notion of a future technical world ruled by the former Slave is Kojève's extrapolation.

Hegel's ¶195: the feeling of absolute power, experienced in the fight and in the details of service, is still only dissolution in itself. Kojève's gloss: without this feeling of power, without anguish and the terror the Master inspires, man would never be a Slave and so could never reach final perfection. But this condition "in itself", objectively real and necessary, does not suffice. Perfection, always self-conscious, can be reached only in and through labour, because only in labour does man become aware of the meaning, value, and necessity of his experience of fearing absolute power. Only after working for the Master does he understand the necessity of the fight and the value of its risk and anguish. Hegel continues: though fear of the lord is the beginning of wisdom, in it consciousness is for itself, but not yet being-for-itself. Kojève glosses: in mortal anguish man grasps his reality, the value of merely living, and so the "seriousness" of existence, but not yet his autonomy, the value and seriousness of his freedom and dignity. Hegel alludes to Psalm 111 and Proverbs 9: fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Kojève retains the allusion without comment, but his reading secularises it throughout: the "Lord" is the human Master and death, and the "wisdom" that begins in fear will end in the Sage of Chapter VIII. Awareness of mortality is thus the first step toward absolute knowledge.

Through labour, however, consciousness comes to itself. It had seemed that the servile consciousness had only the inessential relation to the thing, the moment corresponding to Desire in the Master's consciousness, since in it the thing keeps its independence. Kojève glosses the appearance: it seemed that in labour the Slave is enslaved to nature, to the thing, to raw material, while the Master, who only consumes and enjoys, is perfectly free with regard to it. In fact it is not so. Desire has reserved for itself the pure negating of the object and thus the unmixed feeling of self, but for that very reason its satisfaction is itself only a vanishing, since it lacks the objective side, permanence. Kojève glosses: the Master, not working, produces nothing stable outside himself; he only destroys the Slave's products; his enjoyment remains purely subjective, of interest only to himself, recognisable only by him, without "truth"; it can give pleasure but never complete and definitive satisfaction. Labour, on the other hand, is «un Désir refoulé, un évanouissement arrêté» (a Desire held in check, a vanishing arrested) (p. 29); in other words, it forms and educates. Kojève's rendering of *bilden* as "former-et-éduquer" is itself an interpretation: *Bildung* is both the shaping of a thing and the cultivation of a person, and the double rendering asserts that the two happen in one act. The distinction between pleasure and satisfaction, *Befriedigung*, is Kojève's key to the end of history: pleasure is private and vanishes, satisfaction is recognised and lasts.

Kojève's gloss spells out the formative power of labour. Labour transforms the world and civilises and educates man. The man who wants or has to work must repress the instinct to consume the raw object immediately, and the Slave can work for another only by repressing his own desires. He thus transcends himself in working; he educates, "cultivates", "sublimates" his instincts by repressing them. He does not destroy the thing as given; he postpones its destruction by first transforming it, preparing it for consumption, giving it form. In labour he transforms things and himself at once: he forms things and the world by transforming himself, and he forms himself by transforming things and the world. The vocabulary of repression and sublimation is Freud's, and the parallel is deliberate: labour is civilisation as renunciation. Kojève's formula of reciprocal formation, that one educates oneself by shaping the world and shapes the world by educating oneself, is his gloss on *Bildung* and anticipates the reading of Chapter VI, B, the world of culture.

Hegel continues: the negative relation to the object becomes the object's form and something permanent, precisely because for the worker the object is independent. The negative middle term, the formative activity, is also the singularity or pure being-for-itself of consciousness, which now passes through labour into what lies outside it, into the element of permanence. The working consciousness thus comes to intuit independent being as itself. Kojève glosses: the product of labour is the worker's work, the realisation of his project and idea; it is he who has realised himself in it, and in contemplating it he contemplates himself. Yet this artificial product is as "autonomous", objective, and independent of man as the natural thing. Only through labour, then, does man realise himself objectively as man. Only after producing an artificial object is he really and objectively more and other than a natural being, and only in that product does he truly become aware of his subjective human reality. Through labour, man is a real supernatural being conscious of his reality; working, he is «Esprit "incarné"» ("incarnate" Spirit), historical "World", "objectified" History (p. 30). Hegel's point is that the thing's independence, which frustrated Desire, is what lets labour's result last. Kojève's gloss draws the anthropological conclusion: the product is a mirror that is also a thing, so the worker's self-image acquires the objectivity that the Master's enjoyment lacks. The phrase "Esprit incarné" is Kojève's secular rendering of the Christian incarnation, which he will read throughout as the truth of Hegelian anthropology: God become man is man who makes himself.

A gloss paragraph draws the historical consequences. It is labour that "forms or educates" man out of the animal. The formed, educated man, complete and satisfied by his completion, is therefore necessarily not the Master but the Slave, or at least the one who has passed through Servitude. But there is no Slave without a Master: the Master is «le catalyseur du processus historique, anthropogène» (the catalyst of the historical, anthropogenic process) (p. 30). He does not participate actively in the process, but without his presence it would not be possible. If human history is the history of labour, and labour is historical, social, and human only if carried out against the worker's instinct or immediate interest, then labour must be done in another's service, forced, and driven by the anguish of death. Such labour alone liberates, that is, humanises, the Slave. On one side it creates a real objective world that is non-natural, cultural, historical, human, and only in it does man live a life essentially different from that of the animal and the "primitive" man within nature. On the other side it frees the Slave from the anguish that bound him to given nature and his own innate animality. It is through labour done in anguish in the Master's service that the Slave frees himself from the anguish that enslaved him to the Master. The chemical image of the catalyst is exact: a catalyst makes a reaction possible while remaining unchanged by it. It fixes the Master's historical role, necessary and sterile. The final sentence states the paradox of the whole section: the remedy for anguish comes from labour undertaken in anguish.

Hegel's ¶196 continues: formative activity does not have only the positive significance that the servile consciousness, as pure being-for-itself, becomes in it an existing being for itself. Kojève glosses: labour is something more than the action by which man creates a human technical world as real as the natural world of the animal. Formative activity also has a negative significance, directed against the first moment of servile consciousness, fear. In shaping the thing, its own negativity, its being-for-itself, becomes an object for it only by overcoming the opposite form that exists as given. But this objective negative is precisely the alien essence before which it trembled; now it destroys this alien negative and posits itself as such a negative in the element of permanence, becoming for itself a being-for-itself. In the Master, being-for-itself is another's for the servile consciousness; in fear, it is in the servile consciousness itself; in forming, it becomes its own, and it becomes conscious that it itself exists in and for itself. The form, posited outside, does not become other than the working consciousness, since this form is its pure being-for-itself, which becomes its truth. Kojève glosses: the worker recognises in the world transformed by his labour his own work; he recognises himself there, sees his own human reality, and discovers and reveals to others the objective reality of his humanity, of the idea he had of himself, at first abstract and subjective. Through this rediscovery of itself by itself, the consciousness becomes «sens-ou-volonté propre» (a mind of its own) (p. 32), precisely in labour, where it seemed to be only an alien mind. Hegel's dialectic of the three stages, being-for-itself in the Master, in fear, in labour, traces the interiorisation of negativity from something seen, to something suffered, to something done. Kojève's gloss on recognising oneself in the world makes labour a form of self-recognition that prepares for mutual recognition: the worker first recognises himself in things before others recognise him. The word play on *eigener Sinn*, one's own mind, sets up the counter-concept of obstinacy at the end of the paragraph.

Kojève inserts a gloss: man attains true autonomy, authentic freedom, only after passing through Servitude, only after overcoming the anguish of death by labour done in the service of another who embodies that anguish. Liberating labour is therefore necessarily, at first, the forced labour of a Slave serving an all-powerful Master who holds all real power. The gloss insists on necessity: freedom cannot be reached by a shortcut that bypasses servitude. Kojève will later apply the same logic to the Christian subordination to God, the "sublimated" Master.

Hegel continues: this reflection requires both moments, fear and service as such, and formative education, and both universally. Without the discipline of service and obedience, fear stays formal and does not spread into the conscious actuality of existence. Kojève glosses: it is not enough to have been afraid, even aware of fearing death; one must live according to anguish, which means serving someone who inspires or embodies it, a Master, real and human, or «le Maître "sublimé", — Dieu» (the "sublimated" Master, God) (p. 32). To serve a Master is to obey his laws; without service, anguish cannot transform existence, which then never gets beyond its initial state of anguish. One frees oneself from the enslaving terror of death by serving another, externalising oneself, and joining with others. Without formative education, fear remains inward and mute, and consciousness does not become for itself. Kojève glosses: without labour that transforms the objective world, man cannot really transform himself. If he changes, the change remains inward, subjective, mute, and puts him at odds with the unchanged world and with others who identify with it; such a change turns man into «un fou ou un criminel» (a madman or a criminal) (p. 32), sooner or later destroyed by natural and social reality. Only labour, by finally bringing the objective world into accord with the subjective idea that at first surpasses it, cancels the madness and crime that affect every man who, driven by anguish, tries to surpass a given world in which he cannot be satisfied. The identification of God as the sublimated Master prepares Kojève's reading of Christianity as the Slave's ideology, developed in the later courses. The madman and the criminal are the two failures of inwardness: the one who changes only in thought and the one who acts against the world without transforming it. Both have counterparts in Hegel's Chapter V, in the law of the heart and the madness of self-conceit.

Hegel concludes ¶196: if consciousness shapes things without having undergone the primordial absolute fear, it is only a vain mind of its own. Its form or negativity is not negativity in itself, and its shaping cannot give it consciousness of itself as the essence. If it has endured not absolute fear but only some anxiety, the negative essence has remained external to it, and its substance has not been infected through and through. Since not every content of its natural consciousness has been shaken, it still belongs in itself to determinate being. Its mind of its own, *der eigene Sinn*, is then obstinacy, *Eigensinn*: «une liberté qui séjourne encore à l'intérieur de la Servitude» (a freedom that still dwells within Servitude) (p. 33). The pure form cannot become its essence; spread over particulars, it is not universal formation, not the absolute Concept, but a skill that masters some things, not the universal power and the whole of objective being. Hegel's pun opposes a mind of one's own won through fear to a stubbornness that clings to particular competence. The distinction between skill and universal formation sets up the later contrast between technique that remains within the given world and labour that transforms the whole.

Kojève's closing gloss draws the political consequence. The man who has not felt the anguish of death does not know that the given natural world is hostile to him, tends to kill him, and is essentially unable to satisfy him. He therefore stays fundamentally at one with the given world and wants at most to "reform" it, change its details, without altering its essential features. He will act as a skilful reformist, even a conformist, never as «révolutionnaire véritable» (a true revolutionary) (p. 33). But the given world belongs to the Master, human or divine, and in it he is necessarily a Slave. Only the dialectical, revolutionary overcoming of the world can free and satisfy him, and that presupposes the negation of the given world as a whole, whose origin can only be the absolute terror inspired by the world or by its Master. Man can free himself from an unsatisfying world only if that world in its totality belongs to a Master, real or "sublimated". As long as the Master lives, he remains enslaved to the world he masters; since he transcends it only in risking his life, only his death "realises" his freedom, and if his world perishes, he perishes with it. Only the Slave can transcend the given world, subject to the Master, without perishing; only he can transform the world that forms and fixes him in servitude and create a world he has formed and in which he will be free. He succeeds only through forced, anguished labour in the Master's service. Labour alone does not free him; but by transforming the world, the Slave transforms himself and creates new objective conditions that allow him «de reprendre la Lutte libératrice pour la reconnaissance» (to take up again the liberating Fight for recognition) (p. 34) that he first refused from fear of death. In the end all servile labour realises not the Master's will but the Slave's, unconscious at first, and the Slave succeeds where the Master necessarily fails. The dependent, serving, servile consciousness thus realises and reveals the ideal of autonomous self-consciousness and is its "truth". Hegel's *Eigensinn* becomes, in Kojève's hands, the reformist, and absolute fear becomes the source of revolution. The final thesis corrects any reading of the section as a theory of liberation through work alone: labour prepares a second fight, now undertaken by the former Slave, which Kojève will identify with the French Revolution and the Napoleonic wars. History thus ends not in work but in a fight won by workers, and the universal State that results is the realm of mutual recognition between citizens who both work and are ready to die.

## Course of the 1933–1934 Academic Year

### Preliminary Remarks

#### The Place of the Phenomenology in the "System of Science"

The notes open by tracing three versions of Hegel's system. The Jena draft runs Logic-and-Metaphysics, Philosophy of Nature, Philosophy of Spirit. In 1807, with Logic and Metaphysics identified, the *Phenomenology* serves as introduction, followed by Logic, Nature, and Spirit. The *Encyclopaedia* drops the introduction: Logic, Nature, Spirit, with the *Phenomenology* reduced to a section of the Philosophy of Spirit, and the parallel between Nature and Spirit abandoned. Kojève's point is that the 1807 book occupies a unique position. Only there is the phenomenological description of man the entry to the whole system; later it becomes a regional doctrine. Kojève reads the 1807 arrangement as the authentic one, since it makes the self-understanding of historical man the condition of access to logic.

The Absolute is real neither as essence (Logic) nor as Nature (existence). Nature negates essence and is abstract because it abstracts from Spirit. Only the synthesis is concrete: «l'Homme dans lequel l'essence de l'Absolu est pleinement réalisée et révélée en tant que telle» (Man, in whom the essence of the Absolute is fully realised and revealed as such) (p. 37). Kojève redraws the triad accordingly, with Logic and Nature as two abstract sides that meet in the Philosophy of Spirit. The reading reverses the usual subordination of man to the Absolute: the Absolute is concrete only as man. The later formula "anthropotheism" (p. 47) is already implicit here.

The *Encyclopaedia*'s Philosophy of Spirit divides into subjective spirit (soul, consciousness, spirit: anthropology, phenomenology, psychology), objective spirit (what is realised only in society), and absolute spirit (art, religion, philosophy). It culminates in the philosophy of history, which describes the real becoming of the Absolute. Kojève notes that the *Encyclopaedia*'s "phenomenology" corresponds only to the first two chapters of 1807, consciousness and self-consciousness, while its "psychology" covers the rest. The observation shows how much the 1807 book outgrows the systematic slot later assigned to it: what the *Encyclopaedia* treats as individual psychology, the *Phenomenology* develops as history. Placing the philosophy of history at the summit, rather than absolute spirit's philosophy, is Kojève's own emphasis.

Absolute Philosophy has, strictly, no object, or rather is its own subject. Only the Whole has concrete reality, so philosophy, studying the concrete, studies the Totality. That Totality includes consciousness and absolute philosophy itself, since Hegel has actually realised it. Absolute Philosophy therefore has no object external to it. The argument makes the existence of Hegel's philosophy part of the reality it describes. This self-inclusion is the germ of the later thesis that the Sage's discourse completes being by revealing it: reality is total only when it includes its own complete description.

Kojève calls "dialectical method" a misunderstanding and refers to Appendix I. The triad of thesis, antithesis, synthesis is not a method; dialectic is the proper nature of things themselves (Encyclopaedia §81), not an art external to them. Philosophical method can only be passive contemplation and pure description of the real; absolute knowledge is an apparent inaction, as Hegel said in the Jena lectures of 1801–02. The philosopher's thought is dialectical because it reflects the dialectical real. This is one of Kojève's most influential corrections of the textbook Hegel. It also sets up a tension he will exploit: if the method is pure description, then the dialectic must be found in the real, and Kojève will find it only in human, historical reality, not in nature.

The *Phenomenology* of 1807 can be taken in three ways: as a pedagogical introduction, a secondary aspect; as a subjective introduction, since Hegel himself had to think and write it; or objectively, as the self-awareness of absolute Spirit in and through the book. Historically Spirit has realised itself; it must become aware of itself, and does so by thinking, in Hegel's person, the phenomenology of Spirit, the history of its appearances. The third reading is Kojève's. The book is not about the self-revelation of Spirit; it is that self-revelation. The *Phenomenology* is thus itself a historical event, the last one.

The *Phenomenology* is a phenomenological description «au sens husserlien du mot» (in the Husserlian sense of the word) (p. 38). Its object is man as an "existential phenomenon", man as he appears (*erscheint*) to himself in and through his existence, and the book is his last appearance. A bracket adds that Hegel's phenomenology is distorted by a monist prejudice, oriented toward the Logic: the prejudice that man's being does not differ from nature's. The bracket states Kojève's central departure from Hegel in its most compact form. Kojève accepts the phenomenology and rejects the monist ontology, holding that man's being, negativity, differs in kind from nature's, identity. Appendix I develops the dualism.

There are two tendencies in the *Phenomenology*: ancient monism, which predominates, and Judaeo-Christianity. Hegelian negativity corresponds to the Christian ideas of freedom, individuality, and death. Kojève thus assigns the two sides of his reading to two traditions. Pagan thought gives the identity of being, Christianity gives negativity, and Hegel's achievement is to secularise the Christian side. Kojève's own position radicalises that side against the monist residue.

Hegel's method is Husserl's "ideating abstraction". He considers a concrete man or epoch in order to find in it the possibility, the essence, concept, or idea, that it realises; hence he cites no proper names. The comparison explains a notorious feature of the book: its figures, the Master, the Stoic, the beautiful soul, are types, not portraits. It also governs how Kojève reads the fight "in the beginning": it is an essence abstracted from history, not an event within it.

For Hegel, essence is not independent of existence, so man does not exist outside history. Hegel's phenomenology is therefore "existential" like Heidegger's, and must serve as the basis of an ontology. A bracket adds that the ontology of the Logic is in fact anthropological, and so distorts nature when it interprets it: it is an ontology of man, Spirit, not of nature, despite Hegel's claim to universality. The pairing with Heidegger is Kojève's second interpretive axis beside Husserl. The *Phenomenology* describes existence in order to ground ontology, as *Being and Time* does. The bracket's charge of an unjustified extension of anthropological categories to nature will recur throughout the book.

The *Phenomenology* treats every possible philosophical attitude as an existential attitude. Each rests on a single possibility, so each is false if it claims the whole truth, and true as a moment of absolute philosophy. The formula states the principle of Hegel's history of philosophy in existential terms: doctrines are ways of living, and their truth is partial. It prepares the readings of Stoicism, Scepticism, and the unhappy consciousness as lived attitudes rather than theories.

Whatever Hegel thought of it, the *Phenomenology* is a philosophical anthropology. Its theme is man as human, a real being in history, and its method is phenomenological in the modern sense. It is neither psychology nor ontology. It describes man's integral essence, all human possibilities, cognitive, affective, and active; a given epoch or culture actually realises only one of them. The phrase "independently of what Hegel thought" marks the thesis as Kojève's. Its two negations locate the project: not psychology, because it describes essences rather than facts of mind; not ontology, because it describes man's being rather than being as such.

The title reads: System of Science, First Part, The Phenomenology of Spirit. Kojève glosses: Science equals System equals Philosophy. Scientific philosophy is necessarily systematic, necessary, and complete, not an individual speculation. The system must be circular, and only then is it necessary and complete: circularity is the criterion of absolute truth, the only immanent criterion possible in idealist monism, and perhaps in general. A philosophy implies the totality of the thinkable when one shows that its end point cannot be surpassed without returning to its starting point, wherever that was. The *Phenomenology* is circular in this sense. Circularity replaces correspondence as the criterion of truth. Kojève will tie the criterion to history: the system can close only if history has closed, since an open history would always allow a further step.

The *Phenomenology*'s first title, "Science of the Experience of Consciousness", is glossed: experience (*Erfahrung*) is the path consciousness takes to self-knowledge, to understanding that it is reality itself. The path recalls man's historicity; it is the "interiorising memory" (*Er-innerung*) of completed universal history. Man's historical becoming is a series of active, negating creations; the successive awarenesses of them, the stages of the history of philosophy integrated in the *Phenomenology*, form a series of passive, lived experiences. Kojève separates two series: history is made in action, philosophy remembers it in passive experience. The hyphenated *Er-innerung*, taking into oneself, will return in his reading of the end of Chapter VIII, where Spirit's recollection of its shapes completes knowledge.

A bracket objects that Hegel is not always faithful to his guiding idea. At times historical development appears as the successive realisation in time of an eternal, pre-existing Idea, a pagan notion that contradicts the Judaeo-Christian idea that man is what he becomes. For the Greeks man becomes what he eternally is; pagan morality says "become what you are", Christian morality says "become what you are not yet", a morality of conversion opposed to the Stoic morality of permanence. The contrast between two imperatives will reappear in the 1934–35 course (p. 65), where Kojève proposes "be the opposite of what you are" as the Hegelian commandment. The objection shows Kojève using the Christian strand of Hegel against the pagan strand.

#### Plan and Structure of the Phenomenology

The text has eight chapters; the divisions A, B, C grouping some of them were added later. A (Consciousness) and B (Self-consciousness) follow each other logically, not temporally; they are simultaneous. What develops in history is integral, concrete man, who contains all the elements described in the first five chapters. Temporality appears in each section, but in the first three sections the chapters are not historical, and those sections are simultaneous. The first five chapters describe the constituents of integral man; the last three describe his historical development. The distinction between structural and historical chapters is a standard one, but Kojève's use of it is sharp: the Master–Slave dialectic belongs to the structural part, which is why it can be read as an essence rather than an episode, even while Kojève gives it historical referents.

A, B, and C describe three aspects of consciousness in the broad sense, of man: the in-itself (consciousness in the narrow sense), the for-itself (self-consciousness), and the in-and-for-itself (Reason, the union of the two). In A man opposes himself to the World and is conscious of what is outside. In B he is conscious of his opposition to the world and so of himself; he is isolated from the World, in moral solipsism (Stoicism, Scepticism), and from God (the unhappy consciousness). In C he becomes aware of his interaction with the World and of himself in the World: integral consciousness. The triad is Hegel's, but Kojève's glosses turn it into stages of man's relation to the world: facing it, withdrawing from it, and recognising himself in it. The "isolation" of B anticipates his reading of Stoicism and Scepticism as the Slave's retreat into thought.

In Chapter V, A, man recognises the unity of the universe that includes him, but in a vital rather than spiritual way; he finds himself as man neither in nature nor in God. The world is conceived as an organism, an animal and not Spirit. This is scientific naturalism: man and world are one not because the world is Spirit but because man is nature. In V, B, man acts in the world as a rational animal. In V, C, this ends in absolute individualism, absurd and existentially untenable, a "bestial individualism". Man will reach true self-consciousness, but only in the course of history. Kojève reads Chapter V as the failure of naturalism to understand man. The label "bestial individualism" for Hegel's "spiritual animal kingdom" (V, C) turns Hegel's ironic phrase into a verdict.

Chapters VI and VII run parallel, like Sections A and B but in reversed order. They describe the progress of self-awareness in and through history. Chapter VI presents historical becoming up to Napoleon as a series of active, negating creations; Chapter VII, Religion, describes the series of awarenesses of these creations, of historical epochs, in art, literature, and religion. The distinction between making and becoming aware, stated for the book's title, now structures its second half. Religion becomes the ideology of each epoch, which Kojève's later courses develop (Chapter VII as the "dialectic of historical ideologies").

Chapter VIII: Napoleon completes history and Hegel becomes aware of it: this is absolute knowledge, which will need no further change or completion, «puisqu'il n'y aura plus rien de nouveau dans le Monde» (since there will be nothing new in the World) (p. 41).
