This knowledge describes the totality of the real; it is total and definitive truth, to be developed in the System (the *Encyclopaedia*). To reach it, history had to be completed and its development grasped whole. That awareness is the *Phenomenology*, which "introduces" man into Science. Chapter VIII, representing absolute knowledge within the *Phenomenology*, can only summarise the preceding chapters; at the end, a surpassing leads back to Chapter I, and this circularity proves the totality, the truth, of the whole. The thesis of the end of history appears here in its first form. The phrase "nothing new" must be read with the guard set at the outset: what cannot be new is a new form of human self-understanding, not new events. The link between circularity and the end of history is now explicit.

### Commentary on the Phenomenology

#### A. Consciousness (Section A, Chapters I–III)

Man is taken here in his passive, contemplative attitude as a knowing subject opposed to the known external object: consciousness in the narrow sense, consciousness of the external world. His active attitudes are described in Section B, Chapter IV. The note reaffirms the priority stated in the Introduction: cognition is an abstraction from the whole man, whose concrete being is action.

##### I. Sense-Certainty; or the This and Meaning

Sense-certainty is man reduced to pure sensations. The "This" corresponds in the world to this sensualist cognitive attitude; "meaning" (*das Meinen*) corresponds to the *doxa* of the Greek philosophers. It is the cognitive attitude of naive man, perhaps, in its exclusive form, of the young child and prehistoric man. It is necessary as a moment of all human consciousness, even the philosopher's. The description must show how man rises from it, by negating it, to perception: the immanent dialectic that explains why the primitive and the child become modern men, why the adult is not content with this attitude, and why the philosopher surpasses sensualism. Kojève reads Hegel's untranslatable pun on *meinen*, to mean and to make one's own, through the Greek contrast of opinion and knowledge. He also gives each shape a triple bearer, a stage of the individual, of the species, and of philosophy, which fits his reading of the book as anthropology.

The successive stages have each served as the basis of a complete philosophy: Parmenides, ancient atomism, Protagoras, sensualism generally. Hegel reduces them to their kernel of truth by showing how history surpassed them. The identification of the chapter's moments with named doctrines is Kojève's; Hegel names none, in keeping with the "ideating abstraction" noted above.

The *Phenomenology* is more than a theory of knowledge. Philosophy studies integral man, and Hegel's anthropology is not intellectualist. That the book begins with an analysis of knowledge is, Kojève says, a historical contingency, by Hegel's own admission. Hegel's philosophy is directed against epistemological dualism, of Cartesian origin; it seeks to restore unity against every dualism, starting with the opposition of knowing subject and known object. Kojève's aim is to neutralise the cognitive opening of the book so that Chapter IV can appear as its real beginning. The "admission" he invokes is not documented in the notes.

"The true is the whole." Truth (*Wahrheit*), objective, differs from certainty (*Gewissheit*), subjective. Truth is the totality of reality fully revealing itself to itself: the absolute Idea, the concrete concept. Certainty makes sense only from the standpoint of a subject opposed to an object and forgetting itself in that opposition; it is abstract because it neglects the subject. Certainty is subjective without knowing it; one surpasses it by trying to affirm it, since that introduces the very subject it would exclude. The whole *Phenomenology* describes the transformation of certainty into truth. The definition of certainty as a subjectivity unaware of itself is Kojève's key to the chapter. Asserting "this is" requires someone who says it, and the sayer is what sense-certainty cannot account for.

The first chapter treats naive man, or rather the naive philosopher's reflection on naive man: the sensualist. Sensualism is true in affirming that the real is, false in trying to base all knowledge on sensation alone, which, Hegel will show, involves a contradiction. The distinction between naive man and the naive philosopher tracks Hegel's own layering of the consciousness observed and the observer.

Hegel seeks the elements of knowledge with the minimum of rationality. Since reason is born of negating action, this means a purely passive subject, which is what Bergson will attempt. But for Hegel there are no absolutely non-rational immediate data; there is always a minimum of rationality, of negating action. The only rational categories in sensation are being (*Sein*) and the being-other of the object (*Gegen-stand*, literally what stands against). Below that, where anthropogenic negation ceases, there would be only animal "knowledge", wholly irrational: «le cri inarticulé de la bête» (the inarticulate cry of the beast) (p. 44), which reveals its natural being as self-feeling, not self-consciousness. The contrast with Bergson's "immediate data of consciousness" targets the most influential French philosophy of the day. Kojève's equation of rationality with negation implies that even sensing is a minimal act, which links Chapter I to the theory of Desire.

Sensation reveals only pure, indeterminate being. The truth it contains is that the real is, nothing more. In pure unqualified being, the being of the I is revealed together with that of the real, but consciousness fixed on the world does not notice. The unnoticed co-revelation of the I is what the chapter's dialectic will bring to light: the attempt to hold on to the pure object ends by showing that it depends on the I.

The being of the chapter's first lines is the same as that at the start of the Logic: hidden, unrevealed being, «l'être en puissance d'Aristote» (Aristotle's being in potency) (p. 45). It is, but it is nothing determinate; it is nothing. The comparison with Aristotelian potency is Kojève's: pure being is what could be revealed but is not yet. It anticipates his doctrine that discourse actualises being by revealing it.

Hegel's opening pages summarise the result: the passage from sensation to perception. At this stage being is split into I and object, and by space and time: it is the pure here and now. What is revealed is not being itself but examples of being. Kojève reads Hegel's *Beispiel* strictly: sense-certainty grasps instances, never being as such.

On the sentence stating that sense-certainty says only "it is" of what it knows, Kojève comments that every truth can and must be expressed in words. Truth is the real revealed by knowledge, which is rational and conceptual and therefore expressible in reasonable discourse (*Logos*). Revealed reality equals truth equals concept equals *Logos*. The reality we speak of includes our discourse, since it too is real; to speak of a reality that excludes it, an object without a subject, is to speak abstractly. The object that includes the subject is Spirit, so concrete being is Spirit. This gloss contains Kojève's theory of truth in miniature: the real becomes true when spoken, and the speaking belongs to the real. The definition of Spirit as the object that includes the subject is his most compact statement of what Hegel means by Spirit.

The being in question is also the Cartesian *cogito ergo sum*. Hegel seeks to reduce the dualism of modern philosophy, including Kant and Fichte, which is Cartesian in origin; it is also Fichte's I. The note places Chapter I in a polemic with modern epistemology: the certainty of the "this" is the certainty of the *cogito*, and its dialectic undoes the priority of the isolated subject.

The chapter is planned in three parts: a description of sense-certainty; its dialectic, first of the object (now, then here), then of the I, then of sense-certainty as a whole (now, here); and its transformation into perception. The plan repeats a triad, object, subject, whole, that Kojève finds in each of the first three chapters. It supports his claim that the chapters are parallel.

##### II. Perception; or the Thing and Illusion

The chapter was not commented on; the notes give only its plan. Perception is described, then its dialectic of the object, of the perceiving consciousness, and of the whole, then its transformation into Understanding; a passage in a note criticises the philosophy of common sense. The omission is itself telling: the course moves quickly toward Chapter IV, confirming that the cognitive chapters interest Kojève chiefly as the prelude to Desire.

##### III. Force and the Understanding; Appearance and the Supersensible World

Only some passages were commented. The Understanding distinguishes appearance (*Erscheinung*) from true being, the supersensible world. The object opposed to the subject is kept, as the supersensible world or "the hidden essence of things" (*das Innere*), supposed to exist independently of the subject who thinks it. The inner corresponds to the *mana* of primitive thought, the Platonic Idea, the Leibnizian monad, Newtonian force, vitalist life, and the Kantian thing in itself. The list shows Kojève's way of reading Hegel's shapes as structures that recur across religion, science, and philosophy. What they share is the positing of a real that lies behind appearance and is independent of the subject.

The inner is first the pure being of the real revealed by sensation, the being of Chapter I; it is also a datum for the Understanding beyond sensible consciousness; and the sensible given becomes mere appearance. But appearance does not merely seem; it appears, reveals itself, and reveals what truly is. Being as unfolded by force is appearance. The play on *scheinen* and *erscheinen* carries the chapter's resolution: appearance is not a veil but the manifestation of the real.

The attitude is first that of the magician and the religious man, then of science, then the starting point of philosophy. Only the starting point, since supersensible reality is still conceived as an object opposed to and independent of the subject. At the end of the chapter appears Life, the first notion in which subject and object are not distinguished; Life and the unity of subject and object in general are revealed by Reason, described in Chapter V. The sequence magician, scientist, philosopher reflects Kojève's thesis that each shape has historical bearers. Life is the bridge from Chapter III to Chapter IV, as Hegel's text has it (¶162–165); Kojève postpones its full treatment to Chapter V.

On the object side, the Understanding first meets an empty beyond, the pure negation of sensible appearance; on the subject side, the syllogism. Their interaction yields the "calm realm of laws", Newtonian science. Then comes the critique of this science, dear to Kant: it is only a tautology, as Meyerson also held. The tautology becomes concrete in the unitary idea of Life, which appears to the Understanding become Reason. The reference to Émile Meyerson, whose *Identité et réalité* read science as the reduction of the diverse to the identical, places Hegel's critique of explanation in a contemporary French debate. Koyré, Meyerson's close associate, is in the background.

The beyond is also the universal religious category, religion taken as knowledge, that is, theology. Theology still sees the transcendent, God, as an object opposed to the subject. A theology that distinguishes God from man is not rational and is necessarily a mythology. Science destroys religion but does not understand its symbolic meaning; only absolute philosophy does: «Chaque peuple se vénère lui-même dans les dieux qu'il adore» (each people venerates itself in the gods it worships) (p. 47). Absolute philosophy is Hegel's, and the religion it understands is Christianity, theandry, the humanity of the God Jesus. For the Christian, God becomes man; Hegel interprets that man becomes God at the end of his historical evolution, or rather is God by becoming it through that whole evolution: "anthropotheism". The passage states Kojève's atheist reading of Hegel's religion in its first form. The thesis that a people worships itself in its gods is Feuerbach's; Kojève attributes it to Hegel and makes it the key to Chapter VII. "Anthropotheism" is his coinage for the inversion of the incarnation.

Theology with its transcendent God and beyond, science with its world of primary qualities (Galileo, Descartes), forces (Newton), and laws (Kant), and pre-Hegelian philosophy with its supersensible world opposed to appearances (Kant) are three aspects of the Understanding's partial revelation of the world. All oppose subject and object and forget the subject when they speak of "true reality". A parallel dialectic in Chapter III overcomes their fragmentary, false aspects. Becoming Reason, man identifies subject and object, but by turning the subject, man, into an object, nature. The result is a "materialist" anthropology, a "bestial" existential individualism, and Schelling's naturalist and vitalist monism, in Chapter V. The first identification of subject and object thus fails in the opposite direction: instead of a subject without a world, a world without a subject. Kojève's target in Schelling is the same monism he finds in Hegel himself.

In truth, «Das Uebersinnliche ist die Erscheinung als Erscheinung» (the supersensible is appearance as appearance) (p. 48). The true, absolute, concrete, if one likes "divine" reality is the world revealed, among other ways sensibly, insofar as it reveals itself, among other ways through sensation. But man reveals the world, being. The Absolute is therefore the natural world including the man who senses, perceives, thinks, and speaks of it, finally in the *Phenomenology* and the *Encyclopaedia*, in the System. Hegel's sentence abolishes the two-world scheme; Kojève's gloss makes man the medium of revelation, so that the Absolute is nature plus the discourse that reveals it. The formula anticipates the distinction between being and the revelation of being that Appendix I will ground in the dualism of nature and man.

The plan of Chapter III follows: a description of the Understanding; its dialectic through the unconditioned universal, force (its concept, its action, the play of forces), and the inner (the theological beyond, the realm of laws with its critique of Newtonian science, and the "inverted world" of transcendental dualism); and its transformation into Reason (the idea of Life, Chapter V) and into self-consciousness (Chapter IV). The labels are interpretive: the "inverted world" becomes "transcendental dualism", the realm of laws becomes Newtonian science. The double transformation, into Reason and into self-consciousness, confirms Kojève's view that Chapters IV and V are parallel responses to the Understanding's failure.

#### B. Self-Consciousness (Section B)

##### The Truth of Self-Certainty (Section B, Chapter IV)

Chapters I–III, mainly epistemological, describe consciousness as a cognitive attitude toward an external world; Chapter IV, mainly anthropological, describes self-awareness through Desire and action. The gap between objective truth and subjective certainty partly closes, hence the title, "The Truth of Self-Certainty". Kojève translates: «L'être-révélé de la conscience qui se révèle à elle-même son propre être» (the revealed being of the consciousness that reveals its own being to itself) (p. 49). The translation replaces "truth" with "revealed being", consistent with the equation of truth and revealed reality; the title then describes a being whose being is its self-revelation.

Self-consciousness is certainty and truth: the truth of a certainty and the certainty of a truth. But this still presupposes a distinction of object and subject; self-consciousness here opposes itself to consciousness of something else, and one must distinguish them to speak of self-consciousness at all. The standpoint will be surpassed only when consciousness has become Reason (Chapter V). The note marks the limit of Chapter IV: self-consciousness is still defined against an other, which is why it takes the forms of Desire and struggle.

Chapters I–III parallel Chapter IV. Sensation (Chapter I) corresponds to Desire, "impersonal desire"; perception (Chapter II) to recognition, "desire to be recognised"; the Understanding (Chapter III) to freedom, "desire for freedom", in which the subject opposes not particular beings but the whole external world from which it would free itself. The parallel is Kojève's. It makes each form of Desire the practical counterpart of a form of knowing, and it recasts Stoicism, Scepticism, and the unhappy consciousness as versions of a "desire for freedom" from the world. The 1934–35 course redistributes the correspondences (p. 64), aligning the three cognitive chapters with Desire, fight, and labour, and with Stoicism, Scepticism, and the unhappy consciousness.

Chapter IV is anthropological in dealing with "existence", with desire and action. Hegel is anything but an intellectualist: without creation by negating action there is no contemplation of the given. His anthropology differs fundamentally from the Greek, for which man first knows and recognises himself and then acts. The claim that contemplation presupposes action inverts the classical order of *theoria* and *praxis*. It also answers the objection that the *Phenomenology* begins with knowledge: knowledge is prior in exposition, not in being.

The plan of Chapter IV runs: a description of self-consciousness, compared with the phenomena of Chapters I–III, as the start and end of the chapter's dialectic, with an analysis of Life leading to Chapter V; then its dialectic, in three stages, Desire, "from which anthropogenic action is born"; Lordship and Bondage, "the birth of Man from the Animal", through the fight, the Master, and the Slave; and Freedom, "illusory, abstract", through Stoicism, Scepticism ("Nihilism"), and the unhappy consciousness ("Christianity as an existential, emotional attitude"), subdivided into Judaism, Jesus, and the Christ, and further into contemplative, active, and reflective religion; finally, the transition to Reason, reduced to the chapter's last sentence. The glosses on each title give Kojève's reading at a glance. Scepticism as nihilism and the unhappy consciousness as Christianity are the most contestable identifications; Hegel's text supports the second, not the historical specificity of the first.

Self-knowledge implies an existential distinction between subject and object, emotional and active, and knowledge of their unity. Human life is life in the world, and the world exists "for" man; even when man acts against the world, he acts within it. Man cannot be isolated from the world in fact or in knowledge, yet they must be opposed and distinguished. Their unity is not a given; «elle doit être réalisée par l'action» (it must be realised by action) (p. 50). Desire is the desire to assimilate its object, to make it one's own, to make it oneself: food, sexuality. Originally man sees himself opposed to the outer world, and the opposition is active: it shows itself in desire for the world, a desire to abolish it. The thesis that the unity of man and world is a task rather than a fact separates Kojève from Hegel's speculative identity. It also explains why he reads the whole *Phenomenology* as a history of work and struggle.

The first stage is sensual desire. In its first two paragraphs Hegel speaks of man already aware of himself, but only of his bare existence, abstract being: the pure I of Fichte. It is by actually abolishing the objective reality of the object that man becomes aware of his own concrete subjective reality; the nullity of the other, of nature, gives him certainty of his existence. In Desire he wills the annulment of the object and so, unconsciously at first, the affirmation of himself. Kojève follows Hegel closely here (¶174): self-consciousness is certain of itself only through the removal of the other. The gloss "unconsciously at first" adds the gap between what Desire does and what it knows, which drives the dialectic.

Desire aims at the object in general, not this object: meat, not this piece of meat. Whatever pieces are eaten, Desire persists, and so does its object. "Natural man" is therefore not autonomous: he depends on the external world, cannot abolish it, and so cannot affirm himself in independence, in freedom. The argument restates Hegel's point that Desire reproduces its object as it reproduces itself (¶175), with Kojève's concrete example. The consequence is that Desire bearing on nature can never reach autonomy, which motivates the turn to Desire for another self-consciousness.

###### Independence and Dependence of Self-Consciousness; Lordship and Bondage (Chapter IV, subdivision A): Recognition, or the Doubling of Self-Consciousness

**Ontological description.** The notes distinguish an ontological from an existential description. In the first stage, being is by and for another: negative being. Being-for-itself negates others, but to be for oneself is also to be for others, so in negating the other it negates itself. In the second stage, being is in and for itself: the negation of the other is not absolute; what is negated is not the other but the other's initial position as pure being-for-itself. Man, being free and autonomous, recognises that others are free and autonomous too; conversely, he is free and autonomous only if freely recognised as such by others. The dialectical movement is double, an interaction; it is social, historical man. This is the only place where Kojève treats Hegel's abstract ¶179–184, omitted from the translation. He grasps its essential point: what is overcome in recognition is not the other but his exclusive self-assertion. The pairing of ontological and existential description is Heidegger's distinction between the ontological and the ontic, applied to Hegel.

**Existential description.** This is how the ontological dialectic is lived. Man tries to be recognised as free and autonomous by force; hence the fight to the death, the dialectic of the Master, and the dialectic of the Slave. "By force" names the gap between the ontological structure, which is mutual, and its first realisation, which is violent.

**The fight for life and death.** One starts from man in the state of Desire, who begins to live in a human milieu. Desire persists but changes its object: another man, recognised only as an object and desired as such, for negation and appropriation. Man seeks recognition from others, and simple Desire becomes desire for recognition. Recognition (*Anerkennen*) is an action (*Tun*), not merely a cognition, though not opposed to it: «une action connaissante, une connaissance active» (a knowing action, an active knowing) (p. 52). At first one wants to be recognised without recognising in return. The emphasis on *Tun* follows Hegel, for whom recognition is a "doing" of both sides. Kojève's formula of a knowing action makes recognition the first unity of theory and practice.

To be man is to be held by no determinate existence. Man can negate nature and his own nature, whatever it is; he can negate his empirical animal nature, will his death, risk his life. This is his negative, negating being (*Negativität*): to realise the possibility of negating, and to transcend, by negating it, his given reality, to be more and other than a merely living being. Negativity must be realised, and it is realised in and through action, or as action. The notes here define negativity as a possibility that exists only in its realisation. Man is not a substance with a capacity to negate; he is the negating itself.

If the other's activity also realises this negativity, each seeks the other's death. But killing the other means endangering one's own life, so each accepts his own death, at least as possible. The argument repeats Hegel's ¶187, where the other's deed and one's own deed are the same act.

Negative being is essentially finite: «On ne peut être homme que si l'on peut mourir» (one can be a man only if one can die) (p. 52). But one must die as a man to be a man. Death must be freely accepted; it must be a violent death in combat, not the outcome of a physiological process. The first sentence is Heidegger's being-toward-death. The second departs from Heidegger decisively: human finitude is realised not in anticipating one's own death but in the violent death accepted in struggle. Appendix II, on death, develops this.

If man dies while realising his primitive Desire, the simple desire for a natural reality, he does not negate or free himself; he remains dependent on nature and dies as an animal. The criterion of a human death is its object: dying for a thing is animal; dying for recognition is human.

Man must risk his life to force the other's consciousness; he must engage in a fight for recognition. By risking his life he proves to the other that he is not an animal; by seeking the other's death he proves that he recognises him as a man. The second clause is striking: the attempt to kill is itself a form of recognition, since one fights only with an equal. Hence the necessity of the fight for life and death: «Négativité = Mort = Individualité = Liberté = Histoire» (Negativity = Death = Individuality = Freedom = History) (p. 52); man is mortal, finite, free, a historical individual, and all these concepts are linked. The chain of equations is the programme of Appendix II.

The fight for life and death is not a definitive existential attitude. If man must risk his life to have his personality recognised, it is not as a corpse that he wants to be, or can be, recognised; if he seeks to kill others, it is not by corpses that he can be recognised. Man is neither pure negation (*Negativität*) nor pure position (*Identität*) but a totality (*Totalität*). Pure identity is animal life, natural being; pure negativity is death, absolute nothingness; totality is «néant néantissant dans l'être» (nothingness nihilating within being) (p. 53), man in the world, Spirit. Kojève maps Hegel's three logical categories onto three states: life, death, and the living man who negates. The formula "nihilating nothingness" is Heidegger's *das Nichts nichtet*, which Kojève makes the definition of Spirit.

Man is neither purely vital nor wholly independent of life; he transcends his given existence in and through his very life. Man denies survival: his truth disappears with his animal existence, yet only by negating that existence is he human. The denial of survival makes Kojève's anthropology explicitly atheist and finite. The paradox, that man is human only by negating the life without which he is nothing, restates the result of ¶189.

The dialectical transition from the fight to the Master–Slave relation is stated in capitals: man must stay alive but be or become man. The formula compresses ¶188–189 into a single requirement, which the Master–Slave relation meets in two unequal ways.

**The dialectic of the Master.** After a fight in which neither must die, one is victor and the other vanquished. A parenthesis adds that this dialectic concerns not only relations between individuals, but also Rome and the Barbarians, the Nobility and the Third Estate, and finally, in religious terms, God and man in the Jewish religion. The historical referents show Kojève applying the structure to collective history. The religious referent anticipates his reading of Judaism in the unhappy consciousness as the relation of a Slave to a divine Master.

From the victor's standpoint, the Master is being-for-itself; everything else is a means for him. He recognises himself through the other's recognition but does not recognise that other. He differs from the man of Desire: his consciousness has its own concrete, human content, a relation to another man and to nature; and his I is recognised by another man, so that for the Slave it is an objective reality. The man of Desire is not recognised; nature is the content of his consciousness, so he is himself nature, an animal, existing only for nature. The Master is recognised, but by the Slave's consciousness: he exists for a man, but a man who is only a Slave. The comparison measures the Master's gain against Desire: his selfhood has become objective, but its witness is diminished.

A textual note observes that in the *Phenomenology* Hegel sometimes still uses "concept" (*Begriff*) in the pejorative sense of "mere concept", an abstract notion. The note matters for ¶190, where the Master is "no longer merely the concept" of self-consciousness: "concept" there means the abstract, unrealised form.

**The servile consciousness (dialectic of the Slave).** Independent being (*das selbständige Sein*) means purely natural, biological existence without negativity. The Slave's consciousness is such a being because he prefers to live as a slave rather than die for freedom; he depends on organic life, prefers it, and is it. Kojève reads Hegel's "independent being" in ¶189–190 as nature, which confirms his translation of *Sein* as "given being". The Slave is identified with what he chose.

The Master's consciousness is double: still the immediate consciousness of Desire, yet mediately recognised by the Slave. It remains Desire because the fight begins over a natural object, food or a woman, that the other must recognise as my exclusive property; the object thus becomes possession (*Besitz*). Man fights to assert his recognised, "legitimate" possession, not necessarily to consume it; the fight already relates to another consciousness, so its object differs from that of simple Desire. But if he consumes the object whose possession has been recognised, he consumes as an animal, according to Desire. This is the only passage where Kojève gives the fight a material occasion, and it shifts his account. The fight for "pure prestige" of the Introduction here becomes a fight over property rights, which grounds law and ownership in recognition. The Master's doubleness, human in fighting, animal in consuming, prepares the formula two paragraphs below.

The Master is not true man, only a stage, even an impasse: he will never be satisfied (*befriedigt*) by recognition, since only Slaves recognise him. The Slave will become historical man, true man, and in the end the Philosopher, Hegel, who will understand why and how definitive satisfaction comes through mutual recognition. The line from the Slave to Hegel is Kojève's boldest genealogy: the Sage is the last descendant of the Slave.

The Slave is enslaved to the natural world because he preferred to live; the Master, who risked his life, triumphed over the natural world and so over the Slave. The Master accepted death consciously, the Slave rejected it. The Master therefore behaves as a man toward a Slave who is not properly human: «le Maître a un droit à la Maîtrise» (the Master has a right to Mastery) (p. 54). The claim of right is striking. Mastery is not mere domination; it is justified by the Master's greater humanity at this stage, which explains why the Slave's liberation must pass through his own acceptance of risk.

The Slave depends on life and so on things. Yet his refusal of death is still a human attitude, so his dependence on things is human and negating: he shapes and transforms things. He thus dominates things but also depends on them, as raw materials. This is the negative side of labour: labour enslaves. Hegel will later find its positive side; he neglects it here because he takes the Master's standpoint, and it is through this positive side that the Slave will free himself. The Slave works for the Master, not for himself. Kojève explains the order of Hegel's text (¶190–193 before ¶194–196) by a shift of perspective. The "negative side" of labour, dependence on matter, is what the Master sees; its liberating side is visible only from within.

The Master's relation to things is mediated by the Slave's working consciousness. The Master lives in a technical, historical world humanised by labour, not in a natural one; he no longer depends on it, since the working Slave serves as a protective screen. The image of the screen restates ¶190: the Master touches only the thing's dependent side.

When does nature become a world (*Welt*), a historical world? When there is a Fight, a willed risk of death, the appearance of negativity, which is realised as labour. History is the history of bloody fights for recognition, wars and revolutions, and of the labours that transform nature. The distinction between nature (*Natur*) and world (*Welt*) is Heidegger's, though he does not use it this way; Kojève makes world the product of fight and labour. History has two motors, war and work, which the Introduction had ordered as catalyst and agent.

But the Master fights as a man, for recognition, and consumes as an animal, without having worked. That is his inhumanity: he remains a man of Desire, which he manages to satisfy, and cannot get past this stage because he is idle. «Il peut mourir en homme, mais il ne peut vivre qu'en animal» (he can die as a man, but he can only live as an animal) (p. 55). The formula completes the portrait: the Master's humanity is concentrated in the moment of risk and absent from his daily life.

The man of Desire cannot be recognised by another free man, since the adversary dies or kills him, and recognition is impossible. The Master's attitude is an existential impasse: he does not obtain the recognition he sought, being recognised by an unfree consciousness, and he realises it. The Slave, by contrast, recognises the Master's freedom; he need only free himself by making the Master recognise him to reach true, mutual recognition. The Master's existence is "justified" insofar as, through the Fight, he transforms conscious animals into Slaves who will one day become free men. The notes here state the argument of the Introduction's gloss on ¶191 and ¶194 in brief. The "justification" of the Master is the core of Kojève's historicism: every stage is justified by what it makes possible.

**Dialectic of the servile consciousness.** Its origin is the fear of death. In experiencing the anguish of death (*Furcht*), the Slave experiences pure negativity, his freedom and humanity, the pure nothingness he is in himself, outside the natural world. Hence his awareness of existence in the world, of the finitude of human existence, and of individuality, since only death truly individualises existence: «un autre ne peut pas mourir à ma place» (another cannot die in my place) (p. 55). Mortal anguish also reveals that man is not truly attached to any particular condition of existence. Anguish is a necessary condition of liberation but not sufficient; it is only a possibility of freedom. The notes here gloss *Furcht* with "angoisse" explicitly, confirming the Heideggerian rendering noted in the Introduction. The argument that death individualises because it cannot be delegated is *Being and Time* §47. Kojève grafts Heidegger's analysis of anxiety and death onto Hegel's Slave: the Slave is the one who has understood his finitude.

At first the Slave recognises freedom only in the Master's person, not in himself: he recognises another man's freedom. Serving the Master, he follows another's will, and his consciousness is mediated. He lives according to human anguish, not animal Desire. What matters in service is labour founded on anguish in the Master's service; the Slave is not yet aware of labour's liberating value. The contrast between living "according to anguish" and "according to Desire" separates the Slave from the Master: the Slave's life is organised by his relation to death, the Master's by his appetites.

The Master remains a slave of nature through his Desire. The Slave's labour does not destroy its object, as Desire does; it forms and transforms it, turning *Natur* into *Welt*, the natural universe into a historical world. He thereby frees himself in fact from nature, and through labour also becomes aware of his freedom. The reversal is complete: the Master, free from work, is bound to nature by his Desire; the Slave, bound to work, is freed from nature by it.

This freedom is still only abstract: the Slave does not actually live as a free man, though he has an inner awareness of freedom; he is free only in and for his thought. He believes at first he can stop there, but learns that the attitude is not viable. The experience is described in Chapter IV, B, in three stages: the Stoic attitude, the sceptical or nihilist attitude, and the Christian attitude of the unhappy consciousness. The course thus ends by linking the Slave to the three shapes of Section B as three failed attempts to realise freedom in thought alone. The 1934–35 course takes them up.

### Summary of the 1933–1934 Course

Kojève's report in the School's *Annuaire* presents his lectures as a continuation of Alexandre Koyré's course on Hegel's religious philosophy. Koyré had analysed the texts preceding the *Phenomenology*; Kojève devoted his lectures to the *Phenomenology*, following Koyré's method of interpretation and his guiding ideas. The aim was to bring out Hegel's religious ideas, but the method of the *Phenomenology* does not allow the religious parts to be isolated, so the whole work had to be commented on; only the first three chapters and part of the fourth were covered. The acknowledgement of Koyré is more than courtesy: Koyré's studies of Hegel at Jena, especially of time, shaped Kojève's thesis that Hegel's Spirit is time. The official subject, religion, explains why Kojève's reading is framed from the start as an interpretation of Hegel's theology.

The *Phenomenology* proved to be a philosophical anthropology: a systematic and complete description, phenomenological in the modern Husserlian sense, of man's existential attitudes, undertaken with a view to the ontological analysis of Being as such, the theme of the Logic. With regard to religion, it is neither an objective theology, nor a history of religions, nor a psychology of religious feeling. It describes all the religious attitudes man can adopt while living as a historical being in the spatio-temporal world, which had all been realised by the time the *Phenomenology* appeared. These attitudes are moments *aufgehoben*, suppressed as isolated, but preserved and sublimated in what they have of truth, in the integral attitude of man who has fully realised his essence and fully understood himself: the absolute Philosopher living at the end of history, Hegel, who is what he is only because he wrote the *Phenomenology*, which contains the comprehensive description of these attitudes. The summary presents in public form the theses the notes developed. The claim that all religious attitudes had been realised before 1807 is the end-of-history thesis applied to religion. The last clause makes Hegel's identity depend on his book, which is Kojève's version of the claim that the Sage is his discourse.

In the first four chapters religion appears twice. Toward the middle of Chapter III, Hegel describes it as a cognitive attitude, the Theologian's, characterised by the transcendence of absolute being, God, and by the radical separation and opposition of true, objective being and human, subjective being. At the end of Chapter IV, in the unhappy consciousness, the religious attitude is described as active and emotional: the man who lives and acts in the world believing in the transcendent God of theology. The phenomenological description of the dialectical, immanent, and necessary transformation of these existential attitudes is also a critique of historical theology and religion. The religious attitude has absolute value only as *aufgehoben* in the integral attitude of the Philosopher who possesses absolute knowledge. The summary makes the atheist conclusion explicit while presenting it as the result of description, not of polemic. The double treatment of religion, cognitive in Chapter III and existential in Chapter IV, anticipates the 1934–35 course, which takes up Section B of Chapter IV and ends in the unhappy consciousness.

## Course of the 1934–1935 Academic Year

### Freedom of Self-Consciousness (Chapter IV, subdivision B)

Hegel's introduction to Section B (Hoffmeister pp. 151–152) has three parts: its first three sentences summarise Section A; it states where we stand from the standpoint of absolute knowledge; and it announces the movement of Section B. Kojève notes that the start of IV, B mirrors the start of Chapter III: the Stoic is the counterpart of the scientist and the theologian. Man acquires a concrete I in three ways: by working, as the Slave does; by being recognised by another as an I; and, above all, by recognising another, the Master, as an I. The last clause is the notable one. The Slave's advantage, stated in the Introduction's gloss on ¶194, becomes a source of concrete selfhood: to recognise another as an I is already to know what an I is.

A bracket judges that the passage set off by dashes on Hoffmeister p. 152 concerns Reason and should not appear in the *Phenomenology*. The passage anticipates the unity of thought and being that Chapter V develops. Kojève's editorial severity reflects his view that the book's order is the order of experience, so that an anticipation of Reason in Chapter IV breaks the phenomenological sequence.

**Stoicism.** The Slave becomes aware of his situation and so becomes a Stoic, whose principle is that man is free because he thinks. Comparing Chapter III, Kojève infers that through labour the Slave becomes not only a Stoic but a scientist: «La Physique newtonienne est une physique d'ouvrier, d'ingénieur» (Newtonian physics is a worker's, an engineer's physics) (p. 61). The remark ties the history of science to the social history of labour: the mechanical conception of nature is the Slave's conception, formed by working on matter. Kojève draws on Koyré's history of the Galilean revolution while turning it in a Marxian direction that Koyré himself rejected.

In satisfying his desires, the Stoic enslaves himself to nature; in thinking, he frees himself. He detaches himself from the external world, human and natural: on the throne or in chains, he is equally free, and it matters little what he is in the world or in the State. Hegel's own examples, Marcus Aurelius and Epictetus, are behind the "throne or chains". Kojève's gloss that the Stoic is indifferent to his place in the State makes Stoicism the ideology of a Slave who has given up on changing his condition.

The Stoic Slave no longer has his reality in the Master's will, since he no longer submits to stay alive or works to keep himself in existence. He accepts that the Master may punish him with death; he accepts his own death, «suicide philosophique» (philosophical suicide) (p. 61). He frees himself through this disinterested attitude. The argument gives Stoicism a place in the dialectic of death: the Stoic recovers, in thought, the acceptance of death that the Slave refused in the fight. He becomes, inwardly, a Master.

This is progress over the Slave's existence, since labour frees but also enslaves insofar as it serves to satisfy desires. Stoic freedom is negative, directed against a world and men from which the Stoic disengages; it is abstract, since the Stoic thinks but does not act. His I remains immediate, not mediated; he opposes the world and withdraws into thought, but does not fight the world or the Master to be recognised as free by risking his life. He is free, but abstractly, only in thought, more exactly in his own thought. The distinction between "in thought" and "in his thought" is sharp: the Stoic's freedom is not even universal thought but a private possession. Kojève's criterion of true freedom is now explicit: it must be recognised, and recognition requires risk.

With the Stoic existential attitude, man separates himself from nature; but concrete man must rediscover nature, understand it, and organise it. Kojève points to the bottom of Hoffmeister p. 153. The separation from nature is the positive achievement of Stoicism; the task of reconnecting with it, through science and labour, points ahead to Chapter V and to the technical world of the Introduction.

Hegel's critique of Stoicism: thought opposed to the world is empty. If it has content, it has borrowed it from the external world. The Stoic attitude is therefore provisional and will turn into Scepticism. Kojève notes that Hegel will level analogous criticisms against Kant's moral philosophy. The emptiness objection to Stoic virtue anticipates Hegel's charge of formalism against the categorical imperative in Chapter V, C, and Kojève's pointer places Kant among the Stoics.

This critique appears in naive, non-philosophical consciousness as boredom: Stoic generalities are boring, as Hegel says. Kojève's remark translates a logical defect into a lived one. The existential register of the reading requires that each dialectical failure be felt as well as proved, and boredom is how emptiness is felt.

The summary in the last paragraph: Stoicism is abstract freedom, an illusory independence from the world. The Stoic must acknowledge that his attitude is impossible. What will he do? He will deny the world and society: solipsism, which Hegel calls scepticism. Kojève's equation of scepticism with solipsism is interpretive: ancient scepticism suspended judgement rather than denying the world. The equation lets him read Scepticism as the Slave's inward rejection of the Master's world.

**Scepticism.** Why is scepticism absent from Chapter III? Because it is an emotional attitude, a negation of the natural world. Individuality is sublimated into a moral, existential solipsism equipped with a theoretical complement. The manifold is denied, and only the I remains, the "pure I" revealed by Desire; it is free because it is alone in the world. This is still abstract, and there is still no fight for actual recognition in the real world. Kojève classes Scepticism as existential rather than epistemological: its doubts serve an attitude. The link to the pure I of Desire shows Scepticism reproducing Desire's negation in thought.

The Stoic wants to be free with respect to the world but borrows his moral elements from it. He sees that his freedom is illusory and becomes a Sceptic, or "nihilist". Only the Sceptic realises the Stoic ideal, the abstract freedom of the Understanding, by denying the very existence of the external world. The word "nihilist" brings Hegel's Scepticism into the nineteenth-century Russian and Nietzschean sense, which Kojève exploits below with Dostoevsky.

We are in ancient thought, with the contemplative sage who does not act. The Stoic's ideal is at bottom the Master's attitude, but he does not risk his life in fights for prestige; he does not act. The Sceptic's attitude is negating, like that of the man of Desire and the working Slave. He destroys the very being of the external world, but only mentally, not actively in reality; he too does not act. Kojève places each attitude on the grid of Chapter IV, A: the Stoic imitates the Master without risk, the Sceptic imitates the negation of Desire and labour without effect. Each borrows the form of an earlier act and drops its reality.

The Sceptic realises the ideal of freedom mentally. That freedom was also the aim of the man of Desire and of the Slave, who failed. How does the Sceptic succeed? His negation is purely theoretical, a polemic against science, and implies a "nihilism" that can be realised in theory: one can think the I without thinking the external world, and so destroy the world without destroying oneself, at least in thought. Stoicism, Kojève recalls, is the attitude of the Slave who works but does not fight; it is thought born of labour, not effective action or fight against the Master. The answer to "how does he succeed?" is that he succeeds only where success costs nothing. Thought can separate what reality cannot.

The Understanding will be destroyed by sceptical critique. Yet Scepticism radically affirms the abstract dualism of the Understanding: man opposes the world as nothingness opposes being. For Hegel, man is indeed "other" than the world, nature. He differs radically from it insofar as he is action, «néant qui néantit dans l'être donné de la Nature» (a nothingness that nihilates in the given being of Nature) (p. 63), negating it through fight and labour and realising himself in and by that negation. His activity has human value only insofar as it is thought and conscious, which it is only insofar as it truly negates; and there are degrees of consciousness: sensation, perception, understanding, reason. The passage is Kojève's clearest statement that the Sceptic is right about the difference between man and nature and wrong about its mode. The difference is real, but it exists only as action. Kojève's dualism is thus a dualism of act, not of substance: man is not a second thing beside nature but the negating of nature.

The sceptical attitude is possible only because of the Slave's existence, the action of his labour; but the Stoic must have thought that existence for it to be truly human. And as human, it is first the Sceptic-Nihilist's. The genealogy runs: labour, then Stoic thought of labour, then Scepticism. Scepticism is the reflective form of labour's negativity.

The Stoic's thought is in things, nature and science, and could not deny them without destroying itself. The Sceptic's thought, turned toward itself, can deny them. It thinks one real thing, and that thing is human: in fact, the Slave's labour. The claim that the Sceptic's only object is labour is surprising; Kojève means that the Sceptic's self-directed negation is the thought of negating activity as such, whose real form is work.

Here Hegel equates thought with the infinite. It is the "bad infinite" of mathematics, in which every number is equivalent to zero. The Sceptic's thought is "infinite" because it negates every determination. For Hegel man is not only what he is but what he can be by negating what he is. Scepticism reveals man's negativity, and «c'est ainsi que l'idée de liberté pénètre dans la philosophie» (that is how the idea of freedom enters philosophy) (p. 63). But the Sceptic cannot actually negate his given nature, his servile place in the Master's world, by action in that world, by a fight against the Master for recognition. His negation stays theoretical and mental; he does not get beyond the Understanding and self-consciousness, and that is why he fails. Kojève gives Scepticism an unexpected dignity as the origin of the philosophical idea of freedom. His use of "bad infinite" is also unusual: in Hegel it names an endless progression, which Kojève will later apply to man himself, an open series that death interrupts.

A bracket states the parallel between Chapters I–III, consciousness of the external world, and Chapter IV, self-consciousness, as two aspects of consciousness prior to Reason. Sensation corresponds to Desire (IV, A, 1) and to Stoicism (IV, B, 1), sensualist materialism. Perception, the negation of sensation, corresponds to the Master's fight (IV, A, 2) and to Scepticism (IV, B, 2), the negation of the sensible world. The Understanding, the dualism of sensible and supersensible, corresponds to the Slave's labour (IV, A, 3) and to the unhappy consciousness (IV, B, 3), the dualism of here and beyond. The table revises the correspondences of 1933–34 (p. 49), where perception was paired with recognition and the Understanding with freedom. The new version sets three parallel triads and makes the unhappy consciousness the existential counterpart of the Understanding's two-world scheme, which is the thesis of the course.

Kojève states "Hegel's point of view". Identity is natural being, man's included: everything he has received as a fixed datum, his innate "character". But man can negate nature and his own nature; he can act, negate what he has not done. Negativity is freedom, free or freeing action, the possibility of transcending his nature: what is properly human in man. Totality is man's historicity, his existence in the spatio-temporal world where he fights and works. Man differs from the animal by being a negating being; but he is a synthetic being, a totality, a concrete reality, only insofar as he remembers what he has negated (*Erinnerung*), which implies consciousness in the widest sense. Kojève maps Hegel's logical triad of identity, negativity, and totality onto nature, freedom, and history. Memory is the key to totality: man keeps what he negates by remembering it, which is *Aufhebung* in the element of consciousness. The *Erinnerung* of Chapter VIII is already the model.

Freedom, individuality, and historicity are linked, and their basis is death, man's finitude. Hegel says: «la Liberté, c'est-à-dire la Négativité, c'est-à-dire la Mort» (Freedom, that is, Negativity, that is, Death) (p. 64). It follows that a natural living being does not properly die; it has exhausted its possibilities and rots. Man has infinite possibilities, and that is why he dies. He is a "bad infinite", an open infinite, a cut in an infinite series. Man can potentially transcend death, which is why he imagines immortality and survival, and he does so through historical tradition; but civilisations will also die, and so will humanity. The distinction between dying and perishing inverts the usual picture: the animal ends because it is complete, man dies because he is not. This is Heidegger's distinction between *sterben* and *verenden*, restated through Hegel's bad infinite. The last sentence rules out any collective immortality: history, too, is finite.

A bracket states Kojève's central objection. One should distinguish dialectical, anthropological reality, which involves negativity, from the reality of the natural world, which is not dialectical and remains self-identical; in nature, totality equals identity. But Hegel is a monist. Hence his "circular" conception of truth and his final «escamotage» (spiriting away) of man. History must be circular; it must stop, and only then can true philosophy be realised. The results are that the future is unpredictable and the eternal return impossible, hence the reality of time and history. The stages of history become illusions when true philosophy, Hegel's, is constituted. Ultimately what is true and free is absolute Spirit, not historical man; but this Spirit is nothing other or more than the completed totality of history. This is the densest note of the course. Kojève claims that Hegel's monism, by extending dialectic to nature, forces him to close history and so to dissolve man into Spirit. The results he lists are two-sided: while history is open, the future is unpredictable and time is real; once it closes, its stages look like illusions from the standpoint of the whole. The final sentence rescues man from the "spiriting away": Spirit is nothing but completed history, so the Absolute remains human history seen whole. The 1938–39 lectures return to this tension.

The Sceptic's critique targets the science of the Understanding and its morality, insofar as the Understanding implies and "preserves" sensation while opposing it to the supersensible. The Understanding views objects as isolated from each other, from their surroundings, and from the subject: abstract objects. This is the attitude of "vulgar", "official" science; of the Stoic, who isolates himself from external reality; and of theological morality, which rests on definitive data, moral judgements imposed on man like objects. It is the Aristotelian idea of innate natures, of Master and Slave. Ancient morality demands that man realise a given, eternal ideal in matter: become what you are. Hegel holds this false, since man has no eternal, immutable nature given once for all. The Sceptic denies the principle of pagan morality and so prepares Judaeo-Christianity. The reference to Aristotle's natural slavery (*Politics* I) sharpens Kojève's point: the doctrine of natures is the Master's ideology, and its negation is the Slave's.

A Hegelian morality could command: do not be what you are, be the opposite of what you are; convert, become a "new" man. But Hegel, hostile to moralists, has no moral philosophy, only a philosophy of morality. Its only axiom is that the individual should live according to the mores and customs of his people, as long as they correspond to the spirit of the age, that is, as long as they are "solid" and withstand critique and revolutionary attack. Otherwise he perishes as a criminal or a madman. The Sceptic is already conscious of himself as man opposed to nature and has subjective certainty of his freedom, of his non-natural existence. The axiom of conformity is qualified by a historical test: mores bind only while they hold. Whoever breaks with them before they have lost their solidity perishes, as the Introduction said, as a madman or criminal; whoever breaks with them when they are already hollow becomes a revolutionary. Kojève's historicist ethics is here in outline: success in history is the criterion of right.

The Sceptic fully reveals the negativity of action. What gives action its anthropogenic value is that it negates the given, nature, "innate character". Action is the basis: «l'Homme est action» (Man is action) (p. 65). The formula anticipates the summary's quotation from Hegel, "man's true being is his action" (p. 75, from Chapter V's critique of physiognomy).

Hegel's critique of Scepticism (Hoffmeister pp. 156–158): freedom is not a property but an act. Man is not free once for all; he is absolute dialectical restlessness (*Un-ruhe*). The Sceptic, who does not act, remains within the dualism of consciousness. The hyphenated *Un-ruhe* echoes the "in-quiet" of the Introduction (p. 11). Freedom as act rather than property explains why every stable attitude, Stoic, Sceptic, religious, fails: each tries to possess freedom rather than exercise it.

The sceptical attitude is not viable. The Sceptic remains in the Understanding and in perception, and keeps the distinction of subject and object. He discovers freedom but isolates it, trying to think negativity alone. Negativity isolated leads to nothingness, since it does not exist outside totality; cut off from identity, man outside the world, it is pure nothingness, death. The results are aimless suicide, as in Kirilov, Dostoevsky's character, or else a merely mental, even verbal negation. The Sceptic remains the man of consciousness, isolated from society and nature: pure I equals pure nothingness, "revealed" in existence by suicide. The reference to Kirilov in *Demons*, who kills himself to prove his freedom from God, gives Hegel's Sceptic a modern face. The argument is Kojève's own: negativity without identity is death, so the consistent Sceptic ends in suicide. The logical triad of the previous notes becomes a verdict on nihilism.

The Sceptic negates not a content, a theory, or a morality, but every content, theory, and morality: in Hegel's phrase, "disordered activity in the petty". He contradicts himself, since he does nothing himself and denies in speech everything others do; and he repeats the same negation endlessly, «radotage» (drivel) (p. 66). His life is contradictory; if he goes on living and does not kill himself, his very duration is a contradiction. It is not a truth, a reality in the strong sense: Scepticism is not viable. If he realises this, he becomes the unhappy consciousness. The Sceptic's two options are suicide and chatter. His survival is itself the refutation, which is how the passage to the unhappy consciousness begins.

**The unhappy consciousness.** This is Judaeo-Christian religious consciousness. Hegel has already spoken of it in Chapter III, as the theologian thinking in the manner of the Understanding; here it is taken not as a cognitive but as an emotional attitude, religiosity in general as an existential phenomenon, "the religious soul", especially the Christian one. The identification of the unhappy consciousness with Judaeo-Christianity is standard since Jean Wahl's *Le Malheur de la conscience* (1929), which Kojève's audience knew. What distinguishes his reading is the treatment of religion as a lived attitude, not a doctrine.

The religious man has self-consciousness; he is aware of himself and of his opposition to the world, and isolates himself from it. This isolation is his unhappiness, and he makes it the content of his religious consciousness. He isolates himself because he is still a Slave, living in a hostile world, the Master's, where he is not recognised. He therefore becomes the slave of God. He is now the Master's equal in the sense that both are slaves of God; but he is not really free: this is «égalité dans la servitude» (equality in servitude) (p. 66), without mutual recognition. The "equality in servitude" is Kojève's reading of Christian universalism: all men are equal before God, but as slaves. True equality will require mutual recognition among men.

Its starting point: the Sceptic who lives contradicts himself. Becoming aware of the contradiction, he becomes something else, a religious man, a Christian. He must regard himself as doubled within himself, an empirical I and a negating, free, transcendent I. The contradiction, now conscious and accepted, must disappear. Note that it is the Sceptic who becomes religious. The religious man surpasses the Sceptic because he makes the contradiction livable by accepting both I's; that is why he is unhappy, and why he is a theist. «La religion n'est viable que dans le malheur» (religion is viable only in unhappiness) (p. 67), and it generates and sustains unhappiness. The emphasis that the Sceptic becomes religious reverses a common picture of doubt as the enemy of faith: faith is doubt made livable. Unhappiness is not a side effect but the condition of religion's viability.

The Master–Slave relation is introjected into the religious man, and the relation of God to man is that of Master to servant. As long as he remains a Slave, man must seek a Master. The religious man is still a Slave. The Sceptic denies the Master but remains a Slave; but what is a Slave who remains a Slave without a Master? Chapter VI will show that it is the Bourgeois, who is essentially Christian. "Introjection" is Ferenczi's and Freud's term, used deliberately: the religious man carries the Master–Slave relation within himself. The "Slave without a Master" is one of Kojève's most influential formulas; it defines the bourgeois as someone who serves no one and yet remains servile, working for property instead of for a lord.

Religion brings man out of solipsism, but recreates an imaginary Master, God, because solipsism, lacking any fight, is servile. Religion is thus progress and regression at once: it restores relation to an other, but the other is a Master. The ground of the regression is that the Slave has not fought.

The religious man is Master and Slave at once: master insofar as he is slave, slave insofar as he is master; master of the world, slave of God. In secularised, real form: slave of capital, but of "his" capital. The parenthesis gives the bourgeois form of the unhappy consciousness. Capital, like God, is a Master the bourgeois has made and serves; the phrase "his" capital marks the self-produced character of the servitude. The Marxian theme of alienation is read as the secular unhappy consciousness.

Man is reconciled with himself when he recognises himself as Spirit, surpassing the dualism of the Understanding: as actor in history, citizen of the State. Then he is God: absolute satisfaction. The religious man instead chooses between the two I's; he does not fuse them but chooses the transcendent one. One avowed reason is that the empirical I is mortal; in fact it remains enslaved, unrecognised. In religious consciousness these are two essentially different beings, strangers to each other; then two worlds are opposed, human and divine. In the religious man's eyes the first is null, nothing, compared with the transcendent being: a survival of Scepticism. Suspended between the two worlds, he cannot overcome the contradiction by uniting the opposites through the action of fight and labour. He chooses while remaining passive; he devotes himself to God, opposed to the world. He wants to transcend himself and the world without transforming the world by negating action. The reconciliation formula, "then he is God", states anthropotheism in its political form: the citizen of the final State is the truth of the Christian God. Kojève distinguishes the avowed motive of religious dualism, fear of death, from its real cause, non-recognition, which he develops in the summary.

The religious man is "mistaken", but religion is nonetheless a positive stage. The religious man discovers man's duality and also, in a sense, his unity. Religion ends Chapter IV and opens the next, on Reason, man become "rational". Religion's positive content is the discovery that man is both finite and more than finite; its error is to project the second side outside him.

Kojève sums up what each shape discovers. Stoicism: man is the same on the throne or in chains, not determined, unlike the animal, by his place in the world: "freedom". Scepticism: solipsism, man's uniqueness: "individuality". The religious man discovers "transcendence", but does not understand it, since for him the transcendent is not man but God. In fact transcendence is not "found" in a beyond; it is created by the action that goes beyond (transcends) every given, man's included, through negating action, fight and labour. The three discoveries, freedom, individuality, transcendence, are the three terms Kojève's anthropology needs. His definition of transcendence as the going-beyond performed by action secularises the concept: transcendence is not a place but a deed.

Man's isolation begins with the mistake of the man of Desire who, faced with another man, kills him. The religious man understands that man can escape this existential impasse only by entering into contact with another being; but for him that being is non-human, divine: he "recognises" the other but believes he recognises God. The genealogy traces religious isolation back to the killing in the fight. God is the other that the religious man recognises in place of the men he cannot yet recognise.

From the religious consciousness's inability to synthesise the individual (particular) and the immutable (universal) arises the Trinity. First, the Slave seeks a terrible Master in the beyond because he fears death, which is analogous to the first phase of the fight: Judaism, God the Father. Second, the Logos, the individual God: the Gospel, Jesus. Third, "the unhappy consciousness finds itself in the Immutable": Christianity, the Church, the Holy Spirit. Alternatively: the immutable essence condemning particularity (Judaism); the immutable essence becoming particular (Christianity); and Spirit, in which consciousness finds itself with joy, the passage to the "immanence" of Reason, Chapter V, atheism. The whole passage can also be referred to self-consciousness, to man, rather than to God, which gives Hegel's point of view. A note identifies a sentence on Hoffmeister p. 160 as explanatory. Kojève reads Hegel's three relations of the particular to the unchangeable (¶210) as the persons of the Trinity and as three historical religions. The last clause states his hermeneutic principle: read every statement about God as a statement about man, and one has Hegel's meaning. The third term, Spirit, is thus the end of religion, not its completion.

This chapter is not theology but phenomenology of religious consciousness, in the Husserlian sense. The aim is the union of individuality, the particular, and the absolute, the universal. The first attempt is theandry, the God-man; the synthesis will in fact occur only in the people and the State (Chapters VI–VIII). In theandry the realisation of the union is an object (*Gegenstand*): Christ is not every man but beyond, transcendent. The religious man strives toward a unity he first conceives, in Christ, as outside himself, distant, separated from him in time and space. Religion is purely contemplative; the religious consciousness's knowledge of Christ is imperfect because it involves an opposition: it keeps both the particular and the universal but does not fuse them. The diagnosis is precise: the Christian idea of the God-man is true, but it is held as an object, realised in one man at one time. Its truth will be realised when every man, as citizen, unites particular and universal.

Thought (*Denken*) is born of a negation, that is, of an action, labour. It becomes active itself, "revolutionary", and will finally become purely contemplative when Spirit is realised and history completed. Thought detached from action is "pure thought" (*reines Denken*), the thought of the Understanding, of inactive man. Pure thought cannot reach the individual (Stoicism and its universal concepts); in Scepticism it becomes negating and tends toward action, but it does not create the individual, since its negating "action" is purely mental. Man must act really, in the world and for society; he must realise something trans-individual, universal, trans-subjective. Only then can he live as a man and be "satisfied". The Understanding conceives the universal, general notions; it must be fused with the individual revealed by perception. Kojève gives thought a three-stage history: born of labour, active in revolution, contemplative at the end. The final contemplation is the Sage's, and Kojève distinguishes it sharply from the Understanding's "pure thought": the Sage contemplates after action is complete, the Stoic instead of acting.

The religious man takes the first step in this direction. He maintains both the particular, man, and the universal, God: that is his truth. His imperfection is that he is this in itself, not for itself; Hegel understands it, but he does not. There is therefore no Reason yet; the religious man is not "rational". The distinction between in-itself and for-itself carries the hermeneutic: religion contains the truth without knowing it, and philosophy knows what religion contains.

The religious man begins to act in the world, but for a beyond and through it. He acts for God, not for himself, and his action is, at least in his eyes, God's rather than his own. He therefore does not know that the "kingdom of God" is realised here below, by man, by man's creative, negating action. The secular kingdom of God is the universal State; Kojève's phrase anticipates his reading of the end of history as the realisation of Christian ideals on earth.

**First attitude.** His ideal, Christ, is outside him, so his first attitude (Hoffmeister pp. 162–164) is not action but contemplation of a beyond, of a transcendence. Religious consciousness does not reveal itself to itself; the distant, alien divine individuality reveals itself to man, torn in unhappiness. Pursued empirically, the religious man's contemplative search can end only at God's tomb, in pilgrimages and crusades; but this "reality" in the world will prove illusory, an allusion to the failure of the crusades. The crusades are symbolically a fight, linked to the fight for life and death: a struggle between the soul and God. Becoming religious, man becomes a Slave again, so the fight begins again, this time man's fight against God. It must end in defeat, since this man is religious; but the defeat is not definitive, and man will finally win. Hegel's "grave" (¶217) is read historically as the Holy Sepulchre. Kojève's reading of the crusades as a renewed fight for recognition, against God, is his own; its conclusion, that man will eventually win, is the atheism of the end of history stated as a prophecy.

**Second attitude.** The passage from contemplation to action (pp. 164–167). The religious man's action does not succeed; action will succeed only in the people and the State, as action within society. The religious man acts not as a social individual but as an isolated one. He does not want to realise anything in this world or for others; he wants recognition by God and acts for himself, seeking to realise only his isolated soul in the beyond. He does want to destroy his isolated empirical individuality, but fails here too: the universal always escapes him, and he remains particular, a "particular one". Kojève distinguishes *der Einzelne*, the isolated individual closed in on himself, from *Einzelheit*, singularity, which can contain the universal in potency; the religious man is an *Einzelner*. The distinction prepares Kojève's concept of the individual as the synthesis of particular and universal, realised only in the citizen recognised by the universal State.

After contemplation, the religious man believes he has lost contact with God; he falls back into himself and rediscovers Desire and still servile labour. This is not yet a real synthesis of Master and Slave but a juxtaposition. He is Master and Slave, which means he is still a Slave, «Esclave sans Maître» (a Slave without a Master) (p. 70). He knows he is master of nature, but only because he is the slave of God. His action therefore does not achieve his own unity. The juxtaposition of Master and Slave in one person anticipates the synthesis that Kojève will find in the citizen-soldier; here the two sides coexist without mediation.

The religious man finds himself working as a given fact, because the Lord has commanded it, as with the Slave. He does not know that man works to realise his individuality in this world. The phrase "the Lord" (*le Seigneur*) plays on the double meaning of *Herr*, master and God, which Hegel's text exploits.

Yet the religious man acts in the world, which is a step forward, even though he works only for his transcendent life. He does not know that his action is his own; he believes it effective only through God's will and thanks God for letting him act and for acting through him. God is for him the only true agent. He "sanctifies" himself, for Hegel humanises and frees himself, by acting, in labour and fight, but the action is not his. He wants to annul his individuality, but by working he in fact affirms it, even in giving thanks, since thanksgiving is his act: it is he who performs it. One day he notices the reality of his action, a negating action, since it negates the given for the sake of the beyond, and understands himself as an active individual. Kojève follows ¶222 closely: the thanksgiving that should annul the self is the self's own act. His gloss "sanctify means humanise" applies the principle of reading religious terms as anthropological ones.

Thus certainty becomes truth. Man is no longer only in himself; he is also for himself; he must become in and for himself, which he is as absolute philosopher, Hegel. But one does not pass straight from Chapter IV to Chapter VIII, because religious "action" is not true action, and the liberation remains abstract and intellectual. The remark explains the length of the book: the self-understanding of the religious man is structurally the Sage's, but it lacks the historical action that would make it true.

**Third attitude** (pp. 167–171). There are now two extremes, the religious man's action and God, which must be related. The first stage is ascetic religiosity, monasticism. The religious action has no social scope. How could the action of a being who considers himself nothing have value for him? He decides his action concerns only himself; but then, cut off from society, he discovers himself as an "animal function". Here the Enemy appears, and animal functions become in fact what matters most to the ascetic: a contradictory attitude. The ascetic wants to unite with God, but only thought mediates his destruction of his real, natural being: the mystic. Kojève's reading follows ¶225: the ascetic's obsession with the body he despises makes the body central. The "Enemy" is Hegel's word for the flesh; Kojève's gloss on mysticism makes it the purely mental destruction of nature, a religious Scepticism.

The second stage is the Church (pp. 168–170). It is not a true State, and the community of the faithful is not a true society, because «chacun pour soi et Dieu pour tous» (each for himself and God for all) (p. 71). But the step is considerable. The mediator between particular and universal is now a man, the priest, «le prototype du citoyen» (the prototype of the citizen) (p. 71). The Church is the germ and the schema of the State. The priest is no longer a slave but a servant; yet he is not a citizen, since he is religious: for him the two extremes, transcendent God and sinful man, remain unmediated in the social religious life of the Church. The priest as prototype of the citizen is Kojève's reading of Hegel's "mediator" (¶227–228). The Church anticipates the State in form, a community mediated by a human agent, but not in content, since its end is individual salvation.

There is now an opposition between layman and cleric, representing the empirical individual and the immortal soul. There is no mutual recognition between them, and everything that characterised individual religious life reappears in social life, asceticism as Lent, for instance. The opposition of lay and clergy reproduces the split within the religious man at the level of the community. The absence of recognition is the criterion that marks it as pre-political.

The Church represents the maximum that self-consciousness and the Understanding can reach; beyond lie Reason and Spirit (Chapters V–VIII). The layman's action is null in itself with respect to the beyond. The priest therefore transmits a null action but annuls its sinful character; he removes its individual, particular character, its singularity, and removes the unhappiness. The layman's action becomes universal, trans-individual; it is, however, no longer an action but annulled. The dialectic is precise: the priest universalises the layman's act by cancelling it. Universality is reached at the price of agency, which is why the Church cannot satisfy.

The third stage (pp. 170–171). In the Church man is freed in himself but does not know it, so this is not yet true freedom, which is self-conscious. Besides, absolution comes from God, not from the religious man himself, at least from his standpoint. He does not know that he frees himself; in fact, in the Church, his action has become social, but he believes it has become another's, God's, incarnate in the Church and its priests. «Dieu joue pour le religieux le rôle que joue en réalité la Société» (God plays for the religious man the role that Society plays in reality) (p. 72). His action is realised through the priest's mediation and so is no longer his; and in the priest the action is trans-individual, so not his either. The sentence about God and society is Durkheim's thesis, which Kojève attributes to Hegel's analysis. It gives the key to the whole reading of religion: what the believer ascribes to God is the work of the social whole.

The religious man lives, since he acts; but he does not realise that he acts, and thinks only of his nullity and death. He does not know that the world he lives in is his world, the result of his action; he believes it is God's work, and it remains sin and unhappiness for him.
