The priest consoles him, telling him his action is something positive after all, but this is only a "broken certainty" (Hoffmeister p. 171). The priest says his present unhappiness will be enjoyment in the beyond; but the religious man never has certainty of it, and this bliss is in itself, not for itself. The priest's consolation cannot satisfy because it defers satisfaction to a beyond that is by definition not present. Satisfaction, for Kojève, must be actual and recognised.

Even at the summit, the religious man keeps his traits, unhappiness and isolation, since he believes in a beyond. «Le malheur, l'isolement et la religion forment bloc» (unhappiness, isolation, and religion form a bloc) (p. 72). The thesis of inseparability makes the exit from unhappiness an exit from religion.

Man will now understand that his action is in itself and that his doing and being are the whole of reality. There is no beyond for him any more: he is an atheist. He is no longer isolated with respect to nature; he lives in immanence; he is Reason (Chapter V). This dialectical transformation of the unhappy consciousness, and so of the Understanding, of consciousness and self-consciousness generally, into Reason is described in a single sentence, the last of the chapter. Kojève reads the transition to Reason (¶230–231) as the birth of atheism. Hegel's text says that consciousness becomes certain of being all reality; the equation of this with atheism is Kojève's.

Hegel merely says that one fine day man notices that his imaginary God is in reality himself; he "recognises" himself in God, and his unhappiness ends. He is henceforth the man of Reason, "rational". But this Reason is still abstract; concrete Reason is Spirit. The rational man of Chapter V tries to live "independently" of nature and the State, of history: he is «l'Intellectuel bourgeois» (the bourgeois intellectual) (p. 72). He therefore sinks into nothingness: verbiage, madness, suicide. The identification of Chapter V's shapes with the bourgeois intellectual is Kojève's most polemical application; the three outcomes, verbiage, madness, suicide, roughly match the spiritual animal kingdom, the law of the heart, and the pleasure that ends in necessity and death. The 1935–36 course develops this reading.

A bracket draws a consequence from the transition's brevity. It seems to show that the "conversion" of the religious man to Hegelian atheism, more exactly anthropotheism, is not necessary, and that religion is indefinitely viable. But religious life is a life of unhappiness, without definitive and complete satisfaction. The "passage" is an act of negation, of freedom, and therefore «indéductible» (non-deducible) (p. 73). The same holds for every stage of the *Phenomenology*: Stoicism is surpassed because it is "boring", Scepticism because it is "disquieting" and "sterile", religion because it is inseparable from inner unhappiness. Only one can take pleasure in unhappiness; hence the possibility of an unlimited duration of religion. This bracket makes a claim with large consequences: the transitions of the *Phenomenology* are free acts, not logical deductions. Necessity holds only retrospectively; prospectively, each passage requires a decision. The claim fits the Introduction's "irreducible acts of freedom" in the fight (p. 15) and qualifies the circular necessity of the system: the whole is necessary only once it has been completed.

### Summary of the 1934–1935 Course

Continuing the literal commentary on the *Phenomenology*, the course studied the section on the unhappy, that is, religious, consciousness. The report's word "literal" reflects the course's method of line-by-line reading, which the notes compress.

Religiosity, for Hegel, is characterised by division (*Entzweiung*), the splitting of consciousness into an empirical I, bound to the world and mortal, and a transcendent I, the immortal soul in direct contact with God. The impossibility of overcoming the contradiction (*Widerspruch*) between the two elements of this doubled consciousness is the source of the religious man's unhappiness (*Unglück*, *Schmerz*). Unable to reach unity with himself, he never attains satisfaction (*Befriedigung*), «le but suprême et la justification dernière de l'existence humaine» (the supreme aim and final justification of human existence) (p. 74). Satisfaction is here defined in its full weight. It is the criterion by which every shape of consciousness is judged and the end toward which history moves.

The dualism at the root of religion, and so of unhappiness, has two sources. One is the desire for individual immortality, servile and enslaving fear of death: just as in the fight man becomes his adversary's Slave because he wants to keep his life at any price, so he becomes God's Slave when he tries to escape death by seeking an immortal soul in himself. The other is that man fails to realise his freedom, his true being, in this world. Defeated by fear of death, the Slave has ceded the world to the victorious Master; as long as he does not resolve to fight the Master and conquer the world, he can seek freedom only beyond the world, in the religious transcendent. The Slave seeking freedom in a world dominated by the Master must distinguish his enslaved empirical I from an I supposedly free in the beyond, which is the religious attitude. But the transcendent I is even less free than the servile empirical I, since in his immortal soul the religious man is the Slave of God, the absolute Master. The two sources correspond to the two moments of the Slave's condition: fear of death and non-recognition. The final twist, that the soul is more enslaved than the body, completes the critique: the religious escape from servitude deepens it.

Torn within himself, the religious man cannot realise his freedom, never reaches satisfaction, and remains forever in the unhappiness of Servitude. The word "forever" restates the bracket's conclusion: religion can last indefinitely because unhappiness can.

The texts studied, deliberately equivocal, do not settle whether Hegel's philosophy is atheist. Hegel stresses that he only describes religious consciousness, without raising the question of the truth of its ideas. Yet Hegel himself undoubtedly rejects the idea of a beyond, of God's transcendence. For him the notion that the Absolute lies outside the spatio-temporal world, beyond humanity and history, is precisely what is specific to religion; it opposes theology, even Christian theology, to true philosophy, Hegel's Science, and appears on the existential plane as the religious man's unhappiness. Kojève's public statement is more guarded than the notes: he concedes the texts' equivocation while asserting that Hegel rejects transcendence. The criterion he offers, that transcendence is what distinguishes religion from Science, is textually grounded in Chapter VIII's contrast between the form of representation and the concept.

«L'être vrai de l'Homme est son action» (man's true being is his action), says Hegel (p. 75). Only in action performed as citizen of a State does man realise himself as a free historical individual and so attain satisfaction, which attests the fullness and perfection of his being. Because of the idea of transcendence, the religious man's action is not true action, and the religious society, the Church, is not a true State. He acts, but the aim of his action lies in the beyond, over which he has no hold; its efficacy comes from God, so God acts in him, and his action neither realises his freedom nor satisfies him. Likewise the Church is not a true society or State: its members pursue a transcendent end, salvation, which is strictly individual; in that pursuit no one can help or be helped by another, so there is no genuine social interaction, which alone can bring man to his perfection. The idea of transcendence thus deprives the religious man's individual and social action of all efficacy, and he acknowledges this himself by expecting salvation not from his acts but from divine grace. In acknowledging the inefficacy of his action, the vanity of his being, he acknowledges and accepts the unhappiness that is for him the essence of his existence, and which is as much the source of religiosity as its consequence. The quotation from Hegel comes from Chapter V's critique of physiognomy (¶322), where Hegel opposes deed to face. Kojève makes it the principle of his anthropology. The argument about salvation is precise: salvation is non-transferable, so it cannot ground a community of mutual aid, and hence not a State.

To free himself from unhappiness and reach satisfaction, the realised fullness of his being, man must first abandon the idea of the beyond. He must acknowledge that his true and only reality is his action freely performed here below for here below; he must understand that he is nothing outside his active existence in the world, where he is born, lives, and dies, and where he can reach perfection. And man finally understands it. In doing so he ceases to be the man of self-consciousness culminating in the unhappy consciousness and becomes the man of Reason, which, according to Hegel, «n'a pas de religion» (has no religion) (p. 76). The summary ends on an atheist conclusion that Kojève presents as Hegel's. The claim that Reason "has no religion" is a compression: Chapter V indeed contains no religion, but Hegel's Chapter VII restores religion as a shape of Spirit. Kojève will read that chapter, too, as the history of man's self-worship.

## Course of the 1935–1936 Academic Year

### Reason (Section C, Chapters V–VIII)

#### I. Certainty and Truth of Reason (Section C, Chapter V)

The introduction to Chapter V (Hoffmeister pp. 175–182) is directed against Fichte and his "subjective idealism". The I here is not Hegel's Spirit but Fichte's abstract I. Kojève's heading already signals the reading: Section C covers Chapters V to VIII, so Reason, Spirit, Religion, and absolute knowledge are stages of one development. Chapter V's first shape is a philosophical position, not a historical period, and its target is named.

Hegel's objection to idealism: for idealism to be true, the I would have to be "in itself all reality". At the origin this is false; it becomes true only at the end of the dialectical and historical process set out in Chapter VI. For now the I is only the self-consciousness that emerged at the end of Chapter IV, far from being all reality. For idealism to be true, the I must become all reality and reveal itself as such, and it does so only at the end of history, through man's historical action, fight and labour. Kojève converts idealism's thesis into a result: the identity of I and world is false as a starting point and true as an achievement. The equation of thought and being, which Hegel's absolute knowledge affirms, is thus made to depend on the end of history.

A reminder of what action is: freedom, which is negation, which is mediation. In Fichte there is only an "ought" (*Sollen*), a duty to act, not real action. The chain of equivalences condenses Kojève's anthropology into three words. The charge that Fichte stays with the ought is Hegel's own, from the *Differenzschrift* and *Faith and Knowledge*; Kojève makes it the difference between moralising and making history.

Man forgets the path that led him to Reason, the path described in Chapter IV. So with Fichte: he reveals only the result, not the path and the whole process, and so only a subjective certainty. The idealist who does not account for the road man travelled before reaching idealism is incomprehensible; his claims can only be erroneous, since he does not "justify" his attitude. Justification here means genetic justification: a standpoint is justified only by the history that produced it. This is the *Phenomenology*'s own claim against Schelling's intellectual intuition, shot "as from a pistol", which Kojève extends to Fichte.

The reality attained by Reason in Kant and idealism is "the pure abstraction of reality". Hegel here uses the expressions he used for the I of Desire, because the idealist has forgotten the path: his I is not mediated for himself; it is simple, immediate, pure. This I of subjective idealism cannot be all reality. The echo between the abstract I of idealism and the empty I of Desire (p. 12) is exact in Kojève's reading: the forgetting of mediation returns the I to its starting point.

The Kantian and Fichtean I has two aspects: one goes from unity to multiplicity, the other from multiplicity to unity. On the one side is search, "the restless to and fro"; on the other, "calm unity". For the first, unity is the object, the world; for the second, the object is the I. The note picks out Hegel's description of the categories' application to the manifold (¶235–238). The two directions correspond to the understanding's synthesis and its return to apperception.

The contradiction of subjective idealism is analogous to that of Scepticism, solipsism. Kant gets out of the abstract I only through empiricism. The analogy places idealism in the line of the Slave's ideologies. The reference to empiricism is Hegel's charge that Kantian idealism receives its content from sensation and is therefore an empiricism in disguise.

In the first paragraph of the introduction to Chapter V (Hoffmeister p. 175), Hegel takes stock, summarising Chapter IV, which described the transformation of self-consciousness into Reason, of the unhappy religious man into the rational man. This transformation amounts to the negation of all transcendence and so of all existential and theoretical dualism. The man of Reason is essentially irreligious and atheist. He lives only in himself and thinks only of himself: "individualism", an essentially asocial, apolitical attitude. As a philosopher he therefore imagines subjective idealism: his I is all reality, the world is his representation. Kojève links the metaphysics of idealism to a social type. The phrase "the world is my representation" is Schopenhauer's; Kojève uses it to name the solipsist's creed. The atheism of Reason is the premise; individualism is its first form.

The religious man opposed the I to a transcendent, divine world. Reason identifies the world with the I. But it is still the same abstract I of the religious man, once opposed to the world. Hence the inadequacy of idealism: the world cannot be identical with an I that opposes it. The I must be identified with the world not by thought alone but by historical action, which transforms the world by fight and labour according to the I and so actually identifies them. That action in the world is Spirit (Chapter VI). The argument is Kojève's clearest statement of why idealism fails: it identifies in thought what remains opposed in fact. Spirit is defined as action, not as a substance or a consciousness.

The action that transforms the world can only be collective. But the I of the religious man, and so the "rational" I, is isolated. Hence the "individualism" of Reason and its sterility. The principle that world-transforming action is collective links the anthropology to politics: only a people in a State can make history.

Yet there is progress: having denied transcendence, man no longer flees the world; he bears it. The word "bears" (*supporte*) is apt: Reason accepts the world without yet transforming it.

A textual note on "the middle" (*die Mitte*) at Hoffmeister p. 175: it is the priest of the unhappy consciousness. The past tense "appeared" signals that Hegel is still speaking the language of the religious man of Chapter IV. For Hegel, the middle will be not the priest but the people, not Christ but the State: Spirit. The identification of the mediating term across the book is a characteristic Kojèvian move: priest, Christ, people, and State occupy the same logical position, and the last is the truth of the others.

At the bottom of Hoffmeister p. 175 begins the introduction to Chapter V in the narrow sense. The note marks the division between Hegel's retrospective summary and the account of Reason proper.

Reason is a new attitude toward otherness (*Anderssein*). The rational man no longer denies empirical reality; he accepts it, is interested in it, and observes it (*Beobachtung*). Later, in Chapter VI, he will change the real world, and it is by transforming the world that he will become Spirit. The progression observation, then transformation, then self-understanding, orders Chapters V to VIII. Observation is the first positive relation to the world since Desire.

The religious man had already acted, and socially, in the Church, but as self-consciousness, not as Reason. Man has forgotten this path of action; if he wants to account for his state, he will be an idealist philosopher and take his I for a "thought" rather than a real action in a given world. But the man of Reason, when he does not philosophise, recognises the reality of the world and accepts it without wanting to change it. Moreover, the idealist too must appeal to sensation to obtain a content; he is in fact an empiricist. Kojève divides the man of Reason into two: the philosopher, who is an idealist, and the non-philosopher, who is a realist. Both are passive. The idealist's hidden empiricism shows that his theory misdescribes his practice.

Hegel's phrase "the grave of its truth" (Hoffmeister p. 176) refers to the tomb of Jesus, lost after the crusades: the end of the Middle Ages. Chronologically, Chapter V therefore concerns modern times, even contemporaries: Schelling, Gall, Schlegel. But in principle Hegel describes asocial attitudes, contemplative, active, philosophical, that recur wherever man accepts the natural world, without transcendence or religion, but isolates himself from the social world and is not a citizen. Hegel analyses real history only in Chapters VI and VII. Kojève's double reading, historical reference and structural type, is consistent with his treatment of Chapters I–V as non-historical. The link from the crusades of the unhappy consciousness (p. 69) to modernity fixes Chapter V at the threshold of the modern world.

The world is now of interest to man; he knows he can act in and for it. But he does not transform it; he observes or enjoys it. The two verbs name the two parts of the chapter: observation (V, A) and enjoyment, the first shape of V, B.

Before, the world vanished; now it is permanent, and in this permanence (*Bestehen*) man finds his truth and his presence. The contrast is with the unhappy consciousness, for whom the world was null. Permanence is the property of labour's product in ¶195; the world now has the stability the Slave's work gave it.

The last paragraph of the introduction (Hoffmeister p. 182) announces the process of Reason's realisation described in Chapter V. The plan of the chapter: A, observing Reason (pp. 182–254), the theoretical aspect; B, the actualisation of rational self-consciousness (pp. 255–282), the active aspect; C, individuality real in and for itself (pp. 283–308), the "philosophical" aspect; and the passage to Spirit (pp. 308–312). Kojève's label for C, "philosophical", anticipates his reading of it as the intellectual's attitude.

V, A is the cognitive, theoretical, scientific attitude. After an introduction come the observation of the empirical world, Schelling's vitalism, the "system of nature", the universe as an organism; the observation of the empirical I, empirical psychology and psychological logic; and the observation of the relations between world and I, Gall's phrenology, in fact a critique of every naturalist anthropology, «racisme» (racism) (p. 82). Then comes the passage from the rational observation of the isolated scientist to the active attitude of historical and social man (Chapters VI–VII). The word "racism", written in 1935–36, is pointed: Hegel's critique of phrenology, which reads spirit from bone, becomes a critique of the biological anthropology of Kojève's own day. The reading is justified by Hegel's thesis that spirit is not a thing.

But first, V, B–C analyse the existential, not merely contemplative, attitudes of the rational man isolated from society and indifferent to the State: the "existential individualism" of the bourgeois intellectual (V, B) and its philosophical transpositions (Kant, Fichte; V, C). The division between existential attitudes and their philosophical transpositions repeats the pattern of Chapter IV, where Stoicism and Scepticism were lived attitudes with a theoretical form.

##### A. Observing Reason

Man observes the real, empirical world using sensation, perception, and understanding. These are no longer what they were at the start (Chapters I–III); they are already pervaded by Reason. The situation is nonetheless analogous to the initial one, so the dialectic of Reason will pass through analogous stages. The difference from consciousness in Chapters I–III is the active side of rational knowledge: experiments, one "puts nature to the question". But to describe nature, not yet to transform it: there is no technique. The phrase "put nature to the question", from Bacon, means interrogation under torture. Kojève's qualification, "no technique", marks the line between science that observes and labour that transforms; the Slave's technical world lies beyond Chapter V.

On Hegel's sentence that "the present is rational" (Hoffmeister p. 183): Kojève warns that the rational is an action, a real and rational action. The note preempts a quietist reading. What is rational is not the given as such but what action has made rational.

Man is interested in the world, knows the world is rational, and seeks in it his own infinity, which is realised as life: the totality of the world is a living organism. But the notion of life must be surpassed to reach Spirit. The man of observation looks for himself in nature and finds life, the closest natural analogue to Spirit; the chapter's work is to show the gap.

Observing Reason is not fully realised Reason. It is Reason's inaction, purely passive contemplation, and therefore Reason's unconsciousness: it will not reach Spirit and will stop at the notion of life. It is an abstract reason. The man of Reason does not understand himself as a concrete individual, since observing Reason is the reason of an isolated, asocial individual, «une ombre humaine qui se dégage à peine de la vie purement biologique» (a human shadow barely emerging from purely biological life) (p. 82). The man of observing Reason does not know history and can have only an abstract view of the world; for him the world is only nature (Schelling). The equation of inaction with unconsciousness follows from the Introduction: self-consciousness arises in action. Observing Reason, lacking action, cannot know itself.

Reason is sovereign because the world obeys laws, which are those Reason discovers. But Reason still posits only their signs (*Zeichen*), the words by which it describes the natural world. The distinction between signs and reality anticipates Kojève's theory of the concept as the word that reveals being. Here the word describes without transforming.

A parenthesis on Hoffmeister pp. 183–184 is written from a higher standpoint. The man of Reason acts in nature, not in society, so Reason barely rises above biological knowledge. Observing Reason believes the world interests it for its own sake and that it seeks "the essence of things as things"; it does not understand itself. Here it is Hegel who speaks. Kojève distinguishes the levels of voice in Hegel's text: the consciousness described and the philosopher describing. The discrimination is methodologically important, since many of Hegel's apparently dogmatic statements belong to the observer.

A further parenthesis (Hoffmeister p. 184): here Reason means the Reason of Chapter VIII, realised in Hegel's philosophy, where the being of the thing and the being of man coincide. The philosophy of nature must have the same basis as the philosophy of Spirit. Kojève reports Hegel's monist thesis without endorsing it; his objection, stated in the 1933–34 and 1934–35 notes, is that nature and Spirit have different ontological bases.

On Hoffmeister p. 184: Reason is now, at the start of Chapter V, immediate. It believes itself faced with a raw nature independent of man. It will "act" on this nature by observing it actively, without changing it. The result of the dialectic of V, A will be Reason's awareness of itself, which will be Spirit (Chapter VI). In itself, observing Reason ends in a dead end; the other aspects of Reason, V, B and C, allow the passage to Spirit. The admission that V, A leads nowhere by itself is Kojève's; Hegel's text passes from phrenology to active Reason through the "infinite judgement" that spirit is a bone. Kojève's reading declines to treat that judgement as a real transition.

Hoffmeister pp. 185 ff. are directed against Schelling's philosophy of nature. According to Hegel, Schelling fails to see the category of negativity that he himself discovered in human being. How does life differ from Spirit? The living being is essentially movement, becoming, process, and Hegel says the same of Spirit. But the vital process is not creative, because it does not negate; it ends where it began: «de l'œuf à l'œuf» (from egg to egg) (p. 83). The biological process is circular: no progress, no history. Life culminates in self-feeling, which Hegel pairs with Desire; the animal has no self-consciousness. Life is therefore not Spirit; what separates them is mediation by negating action. The contrast between biological circularity and historical progress is sharp. Yet Hegel's absolute knowledge is also circular. Kojève's answer, developed later, is that history's circle closes once, at the end, while life's repeats.

The essential difference between man and animal, and nature in general: in the biological world, what unites the individual with the universal is the species (*Gattung*); in the human, historical world, it is the people (*Volk*). The species is not an organic whole but an aggregate of isolated individuals without real contact or unity. In the biological realm there are two kinds of individual: the Earth, the universe, and proper singularity, the various animals and plants, with nothing between them. The species does not stand between them or unite them. The people, by contrast, is a true middle term, both an individual and a universe: a universe for its members, an individual for humanity. History does not exist apart from the individuals who make it, whereas the Earth and biological individuals are not on the same plane. Organic nature has no history; it falls directly from the universal to the particular, from life in general to this plant or animal. The argument follows ¶295, where Hegel says organic nature has no history. Kojève's gloss makes the people the logical middle term, the mediation that nature lacks.

Man differs from the animal because he is a citizen (*Bürger*); he can realise himself as man only through a people organised as a State. Mediation is at bottom action in and through society; it is true recognition: man recognises the other as man and is recognised by him as such. Man attains satisfaction in and through another. There is no mediation in the purely natural, vital world, because there is no society in which individuals mutually "recognise" each other's reality and dignity. Outside society, therefore, man is only an animal, the "intellectual beast" of Chapter V, C, a. The chain equates mediation, social action, recognition, and citizenship. The reference to the "spiritual animal kingdom" anticipates the end of the chapter: the intellectual outside the State is still an animal.

##### B. The Actualisation of Rational Self-Consciousness through Itself

This part describes the existential attitudes of man who accepts the given natural world while isolating himself from society and in fact losing interest in the State. It is "existential idealism": each wants recognition but does not recognise the others; each lives in a pseudo-society. In fact he lives in a humanised world, the product of human labour, in a society, if a pseudo-one. The man of Reason lives in society as if he were alone in the world, though he knows he lives in society. This is the stage of Reason, of rational man: «chacun pour soi, et Dieu sait qui pour tous» (each for himself, and God knows who for all) (p. 84). The inversion of the Church's formula (p. 71) is witty and exact: the rational individualist has removed God but kept the structure of isolated salvation.

On Hoffmeister p. 255: the stages of the dialectic of Reason pass again through those of Chapters I–IV. Man must pass from independence, the Master's attitude, to freedom, the Slave's, and finally, at the end of Chapter V, to the citizen's attitude described in Chapter VI. The recapitulation is Hegel's (¶357–359); Kojève maps it onto his three figures, Master, Slave, citizen.

The opening lines of Hoffmeister p. 256 recall Chapter IV. We are at the point where the Slave, successively Stoic, Sceptic, and religious, has become an atheist: no more transcendence or opposition to the given world. He seems to have returned to empirical man, the attitude of Desire, analogous to the Master's. But they are not identical, and this is no dead end. We are dealing not with Masters but with freed Slaves. Remaining Slaves, they keep working: they want to realise their work, a Work; they are not self-sufficient; they want recognition, "fame". The distinction between the Master's Desire and the freed Slave's pursuit of fame is precise: the Slave still works, and his desire for recognition is mediated by a product.

Isolation is the ground of the man of Reason's existence. Hegel calls it "the spiritual animal kingdom" (Hoffmeister p. 285), describing in V, C, a the pseudo-society of "individualists" that is the "Republic of Letters". Kojève identifies the spiritual animal kingdom with the world of letters, a reading shared by many commentators, which he presses into a satire of the intellectual.

The man of Reason in general is one who has not "yet" taken part in social life. He is the Slave who has reached the idea of freedom and has no Master, not even God, but who does not fight as a Master and so is not one. He does not yet take part in the "action" of society; he does not fight in it, for it, or against it. Here Hegel criticises bourgeois individualism and liberalism, attitudes and ideologies of «Esclaves sans Maître» (Slaves without a Master) (p. 85). The formula of 1934–35 is applied to liberalism. The criterion of civic life is fighting in, for, or against society, including revolution.

This man lives in the world but at first does not know it. Hence the experience of the world (*Welterfahrung*), Section A, observing Reason. Purely passive observation does not reveal human life as human, which is action; it grasps and describes biological life, not Spirit. How could it observe Spirit, which is not yet realised? Spirit is realised through negating, creative action in the world. Hence the need for "worldly" experience, active life in the social, historical world (Chapter VI). The argument that Spirit cannot be observed because it is not yet realised is Kojève's; it follows from his thesis that Spirit is action. What does not yet exist cannot be the object of observation.

On Hoffmeister p. 260: this is the man who has not reached satisfaction or even happiness (*Glück*). He follows the chain of impulses arising one from another, as in the dialectic of Desire of Chapter IV; the man of the Renaissance, for example. He is the Slave without a Master, the religious man without God, devoted to pleasure (*Lust*), satisfying his instincts rationally. His counterpart in Chapter VI is the man of the Enlightenment. The distinction between satisfaction and happiness is kept: pleasure yields neither. The historical examples, Renaissance and Enlightenment, give the typological reading a chronology.

Also on p. 260: the man who has lost his social happiness. We are in the domain of sublimated instincts and ideologies. Life has left the "ethical substance", social life, and taken refuge in individuals, who isolate themselves in their instincts and believe they can realise the universal "through themselves". Kojève's reading follows ¶357: the shapes of V, B arise from the loss of ethical life, which Hegel places both before and after it.

"Determination" (*Bestimmung*) has two senses: determination by instincts, and the destination or vocation of man. The pun, which Fichte's *Bestimmung des Menschen* exploits, lets Hegel present the shapes of V, B as both driven and purposive.

Hegel will describe in parallel the process of the sublimation of instincts and the process of the mutual destruction of ideologies. Truth is this destruction, or at least the understanding of this self-destruction. What is true is the coherent whole of all ideologies, that is, their complete description in the *Phenomenology*. Kojève's formula for the book's truth is clear: no ideology is true, but the complete system of their failures is. This is the "true is the whole" applied to worldviews.

Instinct is weaker than Reason and gives way to it: in history, the brigand gives way to the rational merchant. «L'Esprit (Geist) est plus fort que la Nature ; pas seulement plus haut, mais plus fort» (Spirit is stronger than Nature, not only higher but stronger) (p. 86). And Spirit is man, who dominates the world through fight and labour. The example of brigand and merchant, a commonplace of eighteenth-century theories of commerce, illustrates the "sublimation" of instinct. The claim that Spirit is stronger, not just higher, rejects any idealism of values: Spirit wins in fact.

Hegel says (Hoffmeister p. 261) that he will stress the second process, ideologies. He will speak mostly of the individual who has known social life and isolated himself from it, less of the play of instincts in the individual soul, the passage from child to adult. The reason is that the dialectic of ideologies that "sublimate" instincts is a phenomenon of his own time, known and accessible. Chapter V, B–C concerns "the citizen as bourgeois" (*Bürger als Bourgeois*), above all the bourgeois intellectual, who was also the observing Reason of V, A. The phrase *Bürger als Bourgeois*, from Hegel's Jena writings, gives Kojève his key term. The identification of the scientist of V, A with the intellectual of V, B–C unifies the chapter around one type.

V, B treats the dialectic of pleasure (pp. 262–266), sentimentality (pp. 266–274), and virtue (pp. 274–282). The endpoint is the individual who wants to express himself through action; but his action will be individual and isolated, so he will express himself verbally, in literature: he will write books. This is the intellectual bestiary (V, C, a). Then he will want to play legislator (V, C, b). Finally he will try to rest in a purely critical attitude (V, C, c). Then comes the passage to Chapter VI. The sequence, writing books, legislating, criticising, is Kojève's satirical résumé of the intellectual's career. It gives V, C a sociological unity that Hegel's text leaves implicit.

**Pleasure and Necessity** (pp. 262–266). Pleasure is spontaneous: man does not create his happiness but takes it and enjoys it as given. So there is no action, neither the Master's fight nor the Slave's labour. This is Faust's first attitude. The difference between Desire and pleasure is that between rape and "love", pure sexuality and eroticism. Hegel quotes Goethe's *Faust* in this section. Kojève's contrast between Desire and pleasure is blunt: pleasure is Desire civilised by the recognition of the other's consent.

In pleasure, the autonomy of consciousness, of man, is abolished; finally only the animal remains. There is then no difference from Desire: servitude. The life of pleasure brutalises if there is nothing else, no action. Hegel's "necessity" (¶363–365) is the abstract fate that crushes the pleasure-seeker; Kojève reads it as his reversion to animality.

The man of pleasure faces possessions (*Besitz*), not, like the man of Desire, raw immediate realities, mere things. He lives in a society where things are the legal property of men, and treats them accordingly: he buys rather than steals. The note ties the shape to its social setting: pleasure presupposes property and exchange.

What he shares with the man of Desire is that satisfaction is conceived and willed as immediate. The rational man of pleasure wants to enjoy objects transformed by human labour without working, without having transformed the natural object himself. But labour is invested in the thing, which is why one can consume it as a connoisseur rather than as a brute. The observation recovers the Master's position (¶190): the man of pleasure enjoys what others have worked, and his refinement is borrowed from their labour.

His attitude is that of a pseudo-Master: he neither kills nor rapes; he only wants consent to enjoy objects without doing anything, like a Master. But the true Master kills: he fights for satisfaction, recognition. The pseudo-Master has the Master's idleness without his risk.

The ideology of the man of pleasure is a determinist, naturalist anthropology: man is an animal. The ideology fits the practice: whoever lives as an animal theorises man as one. Kojève may have La Mettrie in view.

Hoffmeister pp. 265–266 give the passage to the next shape. One accepts necessity but thinks the I, not nature or the hostile world, is its author. This is the existential subjective idealism of the "needy" man, who fails to live as a pleasure-seeker and wants neither to fight nor to work. Natural "necessity" corresponds to theoretical subjective idealism, social "necessity" to practical subjective idealism. Kojève's pun on *nécessiteux*, needy, makes the transition from necessity to the law of the heart the move of someone who has failed at pleasure and turns his failure into a law.

**The Law of the Heart and the Madness of Self-Conceit** (pp. 266–274). The man with a "tender heart" criticises society. His critique is purely verbal, but it is already an "action", since it is a negation. He is more active, and so more conscious or more "true", than the man of pleasure. He wants to realise himself as an isolated individual, "unique in the world", but believes he has value only through his critique of society. To keep his value he must in fact keep the society he criticises, since it is the critique he cares about. Either he arranges that his critique is not realised, or, if it is, he does not notice and goes on criticising the new society. The critique is purely verbal; he does not want to act. Kojève's analysis of the critic's dependence on what he criticises is his sharpest addition to Hegel. It anticipates his later attacks on intellectuals who need the order they denounce.

How does he differ from the man of pleasure? By chance, his tender heart: he could not realise his pleasure. Essentially, because he opposes something to the given world, to society: a utopia. It is a utopia because he has no need to know the links between his ideal and reality, how the ideal could be realised. He seeks to change neither society nor himself. In fighting the society that determines him, the individual also changes himself: hence the liberating value of revolutionary struggle. He is not a revolutionary. The definition of utopia as an ideal without a theory of its realisation places Kojève in the Marxian critique of utopian socialism. The claim that revolutionary struggle changes the revolutionary restates the Introduction's thesis that one educates oneself by shaping the world.

If, from birth, the individual does not adapt to society, he is a madman or a criminal, and his idea is mad or criminal. If he realises it by transforming the society he "criticises", he transforms himself, and his idea ceases to be mad, since it now corresponds to reality. Utopia, by contrast, ends in madness because it is permanently at odds with the real: this is the existential critique of utopia. The criterion of madness is historical success: an idea is mad until it is realised. The Introduction said the same (p. 32).

The man of the tender heart cannot live his utopian ideal; he lives in fact in society, in and through the very order he criticises. There is a radical internal contradiction, hence madness. He takes the unreal for real and his daily life for unreal. In his isolation he opposes the whole world and is "better" than it: megalomania. Society and the world are bad because I do not like them, because I find no pleasure in them. The man of the tender heart is a failed man of pleasure fleeing into moralising utopia. Hegel's "madness of self-conceit" (*Wahnsinn des Eigendünkels*) is read as the psychology of resentment: moral indignation as sublimated frustration. The genealogy has a Nietzschean ring.

The society in which he lives is made up of individuals like him. When he realises this, he becomes the man of virtue (Hoffmeister pp. 273 ff.). As always, the dialectical passage is an awareness: «comprendre une attitude, c'est la dépasser» (to understand an attitude is to surpass it) (p. 88). The formula states Kojève's general account of transitions within Chapters I–V, where understanding suffices; in Chapter VI, action will be required.

Through his utopian critique the man of the tender heart becomes more real: he finally becomes aware of the reality of society, which is made of individuals like the man of pleasure and the man of the tender heart. He becomes the man of virtue (*Tugend*) and lives in the "way of the world" (*Weltlauf*), the world as it goes. He allies himself not with the order he criticises but with other critics and founds a party. "Virtue" is a party: an unrealised ideal, a phantom society, but already a society, so progress over the tender heart. Kojève's reading of virtue as a party is his own. It lets him treat V, B, c as a satire of the reformist left of his day.

Virtue aims at the "suppression" of individuality (Hoffmeister p. 274). In "Virtue" the "men of heart" unite against the "pleasure-seekers": a party of social reform through moral reform. No fight; no revolution except in words. Hegel's text concerns the ancient and modern moralist who sacrifices individuality to the good; Kojève's political reading is consistent with it but specific.

**Virtue and the Way of the World** (pp. 274–282). There is real interaction between the particular, the individual, and the universal, society and the State; the final aim is their perfect fusion in the citizen. The man of virtue wants to "suppress" individuality, "egoism", by subjecting it to a discipline (*Zucht*). That is his error: he believes the ideal society will result automatically from the "reform" of each individual. In fact the individual realises himself only by realising society and the State through fight and labour. Kojève's objection to moral reform is that it inverts the order of causes: the individual is changed by changing the world, not the world by changing individuals.

The true, dialectical, preserving and sublimating suppression (*Aufhebung*) of particularity, which unites it with universality in the concrete, total individuality of the citizen of the absolute State, is not a personal sacrifice. But such a sacrifice is what Virtue has in view. So the particular is still isolated; he sacrifices himself to an unrealised ideal, his idea of virtue, which he opposes to the real by isolating himself from it. The distinction between *Aufhebung* and sacrifice is crucial. The citizen's individuality is not renounced but fulfilled; the moralist renounces it for an abstraction.

On Hegel's "the true discipline" (Hoffmeister p. 274): it is always, finally, the risk of death in the "revolutionary" fight that conditions victory and human value, which are inseparable: «le révolutionnaire qui échoue est un criminel» (the revolutionary who fails is a criminal) (p. 89). The equation of value with victory is Kojève's historicism in its starkest form. It applies to the revolutionary the criterion applied to the madman: success decides.

To cease being a Slave, man must put himself back in the situation in which he was enslaved, or rather an analogous one: the fight to the death for recognition, this time by society, by the State. The note restates the Introduction's closing thesis (p. 34): liberation requires a second fight.

But the man of virtue can only suppress himself: a kind of suicide, as in Stoicism. The comparison repeats the Stoic's "philosophical suicide" (p. 61): virtue sacrifices the self in thought rather than risking it in reality.

This "Virtue" is, ideally, the existing order itself, rid of its perversions. It is not a truly revolutionary ideal: it denies details and accepts the essential. The distinction between reform and revolution returns from the Introduction (p. 33).

The man of virtue's "socialism" is a pseudo-socialism, a bourgeois individualism for which the individual is a particular, not the citizen who realises himself in a revolutionary social struggle. He gives all value to the particular as he is in his fight against the way of the world; so he must preserve himself as a "fighter" and does not really want to change the given society. He does not want victory, since victory would abolish his reality as a fighter, his value. The ideal remains unreal. Capitalism must be kept so that there will be (always?) a proletariat and a socialist party: "reformist" socialism. The structure is the same as that of the tender heart: the critic needs the criticised. The application to reformist socialism, written in the years of the Popular Front, is Kojève's.

For the man of virtue, human nature is good; one need only enlighten men about the goodness of their nature. But for Hegel there is no "human nature": «l'homme est ce qu'il fait» (man is what he does) (p. 89); he creates himself by action; what is innate in him, his "nature", is the animal. The rejection of human nature is the anthropological premise of Kojève's historicism, and it targets Rousseau's natural goodness.

The man of the way of the world, who accepts the course of things and acts in it, is free with respect to the order he realises and profits from; he can sacrifice everything to it, every ideology and even his life. He is a Master. Everything is for him, not "in itself". He always wins against the man of virtue, whose ideology never changes the course of history. What counts for him is not the idea but concrete action, and it is action that creates human, social, political, historical reality. Only the ideal "perverted" by the man of action becomes reality: Napoleon realises the revolutionary ideal. The way of the world defeats virtue by "perverting" its ideology; but the ideal of virtue is "perverted" by passing "from the nothingness of abstraction to the being of reality", so it is realised, and one can say that virtue has conquered the world. This is Kojève's gloss on ¶390: the way of the world wins because its reality is the individuality that virtue wanted to abolish. The example of Napoleon realising the Revolution anticipates Chapter VI, C.

On condition that it has been transformed into revolutionary action. But such action, being real, belongs to the way of the world, which alone is truly real. The human ideal is realised only in and through the perfect State, as its active citizen. The ideal survives only by being betrayed into reality. Kojève's formula reconciles the moralist and the man of action in the citizen, who has ideals and acts.

##### C. Individuality Which Takes Itself to Be Real in and for Itself

This individuality is the intellectual. Its "doing changes nothing and goes against nothing" (¶394). Its action is turned toward itself and expresses itself: literary activity. It corresponds to religious consciousness, but with a pseudo-transcendent: Art, Science, and the like, trans-social but not otherworldly: the Beautiful, the True, the Good. The identification of V, C with the intellectual rests on Hegel's description of an action that meets no resistance. The analogy with religion is carried through below: the ideal realm of values is the intellectual's beyond.

**The Spiritual Animal Kingdom** (pp. 285–301). The intellectual is an intelligent animal; he simply expresses his innate "nature", his "character", something already existing and "natural", and so animal. His "official", avowed ideology is subjective idealism; but this is an illusion, and the ideology that truly fits his attitude is naturalism. The reversal is typical: the intellectual professes idealism but lives as a naturalist, expressing a given nature rather than transcending it.

The intellectual expresses his "nature", keeps to it, and does not transcend himself. The true, active man transcends himself through fight and labour. When man leaves being, it is a nothingness leaping into nothingness; he vanishes. When he lives humanly, actively, it is «un néant qui néantit dans l'être» (a nothingness that nihilates within being) (p. 90; Hoffmeister p. 287). Nothingness nihilates in true, historical time, according to a true future, not yet existing. Time is nothingness maintaining itself in being by destroying it. Time is Spirit, man. This is the first statement in the course of the thesis that Spirit is time, which the 1938–39 lectures develop. The "future not yet existing" is essential: negation is directed toward what is not yet, so time's primary dimension is the future, as in Heidegger.

A parenthesis adds: this is how the Understanding, not Reason, grasps it. To create history is to fix time in space, the penetration of being by nothingness. In Desire and the action it gives rise to, man understands himself as a present nothingness between the two nothingnesses of past and future, «un néant présent dans l'être» (a nothingness present in being), the true "real presence" of Spirit in the world (p. 91). The "real presence" is the Eucharistic formula, secularised: Spirit is present in the world as the human act. The parenthesis concedes that this formulation belongs to the Understanding, which separates being and nothingness; Reason would grasp their unity.

Man, the real presence of nothingness in being, time, is action, fight and labour, nothing else. The man who knows himself to be nothingness, no survival, hence atheism, is a nothingness nihilating in being. He can attain satisfaction in the present, the satisfaction of the citizen in the State: a citizen who fights and works, the soldier-worker of Napoleon's armies. The soldier-worker unites the Master's risk and the Slave's labour; he is the synthesis the Introduction required. Kojève gives the end of history a concrete figure.

Man is action. His immediate beginning, which is also his aim, is Desire, which gives rise to action, the destruction and negation of the given. Action is revealed by consciousness, and consciousness is realised by action; the two form a bloc. Man is action from the beginning, and at the end, through the *Phenomenology*, he reveals himself, understands himself, as action. The primitive form of action is Desire, still animal; then recognition, human desire for recognition; then fight; then labour; and so on. The given conditions of man's existence are what he has not done (*Nicht-getan-haben*), his "nature". But this is already a human reality, since what he has not done was done by others. The individual's innate nature is thus not purely biological. The interest man takes in this "nature" is human, philosophical; in taking interest in it he takes interest in himself. The concept of *Nicht-getan-haben* is Hegel's (¶402). Kojève's gloss that the given is others' doing turns nature into history: an individual's inheritance is the deposit of past action.

The intellectual, who does not act and so does not create himself, can only take interest in what is in him, his innate "nature". It is human, since he lives in society and has been "educated" (*gebildet*) by the creative action of others. Speaking of his "nature", he will speak of man. But what he says will be false, since he will not understand that «l'être vrai de l'homme est son action» (man's true being is his action). The intellectual's error is not that his subject is inhuman but that he treats a product as a given.

The intellectual's interest is his talent, and his means of action is that talent itself: he shows his talent by his talent. The circularity of talent expressing talent is Hegel's point (¶401): the individual's action only translates his original nature.

The citizen employs the internal means necessary for action, "talent" and "character", and real, objective means. His action is an interaction between the external thing and himself. The intellectual does not act really, and his internal means suffice. The contrast is between action that meets resistance and expression that meets none.

For Hegel, man is what he is only through action; he is action. He is a real object only insofar as he has realised himself through action in the world. The action that realises humanity is the visible transformation of nature by labour. No man realises "his" work; he is the work he has realised. The last sentence inverts ownership: the work is not a possession of the man but his being.

How can one say that man is his work, when the work becomes independent of him, a being, a thing like natural things? The individual and the work must be taken together; their whole is Spirit, man. The individual is more universal than his work and can transcend it. He really does so by creating another work, thereby transcending himself. But he can content himself with a purely subjective, inactive, and so imaginary surpassing: "criticism". He can compare his work with another. Comparing works is the business of the typical intellectual, the literary critic (Schlegel). He finds them all bad and says the least bad are the most sincere, the most honest, the most "disinterested", whatever their content; everything is allowed. Individuals cannot be judged: absolute relativism; all "are right"; one can say and do what one likes, as long as one is "in accord with oneself". One has the right to "express one's nature" in one's work, whatever that nature. The name of Friedrich Schlegel ties the passage to Romantic irony and criticism. The critique of sincerity as a criterion is Hegel's (the "honesty", *Ehrlichkeit*, of ¶412), and Kojève extends it to modern relativism.

For Hegel, the individual judges himself by success. To "be right" he must impose his idea on others, realise it. That is why there are absolute values. Likewise States judge themselves in universal history. True "criticism" is action: one criticises oneself by putting one's idea to work, and others by fighting them to the death. Hegel's *Weltgeschichte ist Weltgericht*, world history is the world's court, stands behind the note. Absolute values exist because history decides, not despite it.

On Hoffmeister p. 290 the problem is posed: how does man transcend his work, which is a being, without destroying it? The citizen's work is a social reality, which also manifests the nature of other individuals. Man is transformed in accomplishing his work; in and through it his innate animal nature is dissolved, and he reaches his truth, becoming truly and really man. The work is a being that others will want to negate, pervert, and destroy as a being like natural being. But man will fight and work to defend it. If he succeeds, he maintains himself in existence as a human reality, Spirit rather than being, mediated by action. The dialectic of the work, exposed to others who transform it, is Hegel's (¶405–410). Kojève adds the defence of the work by fight and labour, which makes it social in the strong sense.

On Hoffmeister p. 292: the work is «un Temps spatialisé» (a spatialised Time) (p. 92). Hegel always opposes space and time, being and becoming, the concept. The definition of the work as spatialised time links the theory of labour to the theory of time just stated: to act is to fix time in space.

When the intellectual launches his work to the public, he could understand himself. He sees himself as an aggregate of contingent elements. But the individual is not a product of chance; he is an active self-synthesis of disparate elements. The individual is his own synthesis, not a collection; Kojève draws the positive lesson the intellectual misses.

Man is his work as duration. The work is perishable, as man is mortal. In the work the intellectual rediscovers death, first forgotten by the man of Reason. But he flees into the imaginary "eternal" universe of the Beautiful, True, and Good, analogous to the beyond, the God of the religious Slave. "The thing itself" (*die Sache selbst*): the intellectual claims to be "disinterested", interested only in "the matter itself"; in fact he is interested only in himself, his isolated particularity. The ideal values are a secularised afterlife, a flight from death. Kojève's reading of the *Sache selbst* as a disguise for self-interest follows ¶415–418, where each claims to care for the matter itself while pursuing his own.

On Hoffmeister p. 294: for the citizen, the "matter itself" is society, the non-transcendent State, at once being and doing, aim to be realised, active realisation, and realised work. Kojève identifies the *Sache selbst* with the State, reading Hegel's transition to Spirit (¶418) as the discovery that the true matter is the common work of all.

Man can transcend his work and be his action only if work and action are social. Social action is the only kind whose product others take up and continue rather than merely consume.

«L'existence humaine est un suicide médiatisé» (human existence is a mediated suicide) (p. 93). Others destroy the individual's work and so the individual himself, and he is those others, society, for which he is ready to sacrifice his life. His work is perverted and destroyed by others, who are himself as member of the people and the State; and this work is himself. To work is therefore to kill oneself mediately: to transcend oneself, to overcome oneself dialectically (*sich selbst aufheben*). The formula is the most arresting of the course. Self-transcendence through work is self-destruction by way of the community: the individual's product is absorbed and transformed by others, and he consents to it as citizen. Appendix II develops the link between finitude and *Aufhebung*.

Intellectuals are differentiated by the "germ" in them, which must pass from potency to act through external manifestation: species (*Gattungen*), as in the animal kingdom: poets, painters, musicians. The Aristotelian vocabulary of potency and act suits a shape that treats talent as a given nature. The comparison with species completes the animal kingdom metaphor.

It is a lie or an imposture (*Betrug*) for the intellectual to claim to sacrifice his selfish, empirical interests to the "absolute" True, Beautiful, and Good. For Hegel these supposed "eternal" values do not exist. What counts is the active negation of a concrete value already realised in time and space. The intellectual negates nothing and so creates nothing; he only manifests his "nature": a "spiritual" animal. Hegel's section ends with "deception" (*Betrug*) all round (¶415–417); Kojève's addition is the denial of eternal values, which follows from his historicism.

What interests him is not his action in or against social reality but the "success" of his work; he wants a "situation", a "rank", a "place" in the given world. He can therefore never sacrifice himself for the True, Beautiful, and Good, for what he thinks his "cause", which is not a "common cause". The ideal universe he opposes to the world is a fiction. What he offers others has no real value, so he deceives them. And the others, in admiring or blaming work and author, deceive him in return, since they do not take them "seriously"; and they deceive themselves, since they believe in the importance of their occupation, the intellectual "elite". «La "République des lettres" est un monde de voleurs volés» (the "Republic of Letters" is a world of robbed robbers) (p. 94). The satire is Kojève's. The phrase "robbed robbers" renders Hegel's mutual deception exactly.

How to get past this point? The intellectual must realise that what matters is the value of the action, not of the thing, and that action is interaction: collective, social, political. He then wants to be recognised by those he judges worthy. He will no longer be the intellectual "above the fray" but an active citizen (Chapter VI). "Above the fray" (*Au-dessus de la mêlée*) is Romain Rolland's pacifist manifesto of 1914. Kojève's allusion names the intellectual's neutrality as a refusal of politics.

But in the intellectual the desire for recognition is still a caricature of the citizen's fight for recognition in a true society. In the pseudo-society of the Republic of Letters it is only a thirst for fame: it is enough to be "known". The contrast between being recognised and being known (*reconnu*, *connu*) is neat: fame is recognition without risk.

The intellectual's action is purely thought. For him collective action, "the doing of all and each", means that his thought must become universal, universally valid. He thus arrives at the moralising idealism of Kant and Fichte, the typical ideology of the intellectual: law-giving Reason. Hegel's phrase *Tun Aller und Jeder* (¶418) names the substance of Spirit; the intellectual transposes it into universal validity. Kojève's transition to Kant's ethics as the intellectual's ideology prepares the next section.

**Law-Giving Reason** (pp. 301–305). Hoffmeister pp. 301–302 are Hegel speaking from his own standpoint, an introduction to the section. The citizen here has overcome his primitive given "nature". The subject is the State, a living pre-revolutionary State, "pre" in the strong sense, and loyal citizens who actively maintain it. The categories are related as intellectual, State, citizen. The customary morality (*Sittlichkeit*) of a living State is opposed both to the intellectual's abstract morality and to the post-revolutionary morality (*Moralität*) of the Hegelian citizen, which is simply awareness of concrete reality. Kojève distinguishes three moralities: the unreflective custom of the ancient citizen, the abstract rules of the moralist, and the conscious acceptance of the post-revolutionary citizen. The last redefines Hegel's *Moralität* in a way Hegel does not: Chapter VI, C treats *Moralität* as the moral view of the world, which Kojève here identifies with the knowledge of the completed State.

Living society is divided into "masses", groups or classes. Hence the necessity and diversity of laws, accepted as data, regarded by the loyal citizen as "natural" realities. This lack of awareness, this immediacy, shows that it is a transitional stage. The loyal citizen understands that laws are not "given" but the result of his own action. To understand it he must negate society by revolutionary action and turn it into a new one. Then the Hegelian citizen accepts society consciously, with full knowledge: his acceptance of the given is mediated by the negating action that created it. The final formula defines post-revolutionary acceptance: one accepts what one has made. It resolves the tension between conformity and revolution in Kojève's ethics.

From "Was sich" (Hoffmeister p. 302) begins the dialectical part. Knowing, law-giving Reason is the loyal citizen of Chapter VI, A who becomes an intellectual, stops acting in order to reflect and reason; more exactly, he becomes one by ceasing to act, fight, and work. Instead of concrete action he seeks to determine good and evil abstractly by thought. This attitude produces first the naive moralist, then the reflective moralist, the philosopher. Kojève identifies the intellectual's origin: a citizen who has withdrawn from action.

The stages of the intellectual's moralism are a naive absolutist morality, Jacobi's subjectivism, and the formalism of Kant and Fichte. One must pass from the first to the second and from the second to the third, ending with Kant in a morality with no content that commands nothing concrete. Hence the absurdity of Fichte's tautology, I = I. Hegel's examples in ¶424–428, "everyone ought to speak the truth" and "love thy neighbour", show that universal rules need qualification and so lose content. Kojève's identification of the stages with Jacobi and Kant is conventional.

What, finally, is Hegel's morality? True moral judgements are those passed by the State, legal morality; States themselves are judged by universal history. For these judgements to make sense, history must be complete. Napoleon and Hegel complete history, which is why Hegel can judge States and individuals. «Est "bon" tout ce qui a préparé Hegel» (everything that prepared Hegel is "good") (p. 95), that is, the formation of the universal Napoleonic Empire (we are in 1807!), which Hegel "understands" in the *Phenomenology*. The claim is deliberately provocative. It follows from Kojève's premises: if value is decided by success and success is final only at the end, then the end judges all that led to it.

What exists, insofar as it exists, is good. Every action, negating what exists, is therefore bad: a sin. But sin can be forgiven, by its success. Success absolves crime, because success is a new reality that exists. To judge success, history must be finished; then one sees what maintains itself in existence, definitive reality. The origin is Christian, Lutheran: every action is a sin; only Hegel, who equals God, can absolve sins by passing the judgement of completed universal history, which equals Christ. Kojève here anticipates his reading of forgiveness at the end of Chapter VI, C, where the "yes of reconciliation" absolves the acting consciousness. The equations Hegel = God and history's judgement = Christ are anthropotheism in its most compressed form.

**Law-Testing Reason** (pp. 306–308). The critical examination of laws is the attitude of the reasoner, the intellectual's last avatar. One looks for laws, moral judgements, and behaviours that are not contradictory. But in the abstract nothing is contradictory; in the concrete everything is. For the reasoner, on one side everything is acceptable; on the other, nothing is. The dilemma restates Hegel's critique of the non-contradiction test (¶430–431): a tautology accepts anything.

The "matter itself", the intellectual's avowed aim, was the Beautiful and the True in the spiritual animal kingdom, the Good in law-giving Reason; here it is no longer an entity but the search for tautology, non-contradiction as the only criterion of "truth". The universal has vanished; one compares particular with particular. The attitude is still abstract and intellectual, and it ends in absolute relativism, as in Pierre Bayle. Bayle, the sceptic of the *Dictionnaire*, typifies the critical reason of the early Enlightenment.

The dialectic runs: in the abstract, property is not contradictory, nor is non-property; in the concrete, non-property is contradictory, and so is property; but the intellectual, living in the abstract, cannot see it. Hegel's example of property (¶430) is kept. Kojève's point is that concrete life is contradictory, so any tautological test either fails everything or passes everything.

«Le Raisonneur est la caricature de Hegel (et Hegel le sait)» (the reasoner is the caricature of Hegel, and Hegel knows it) (p. 96). He replaces action with thought and thinks logically, as Hegel does. But the reasoner thinks abstractly, whereas Hegel thinks concretely and understands that reality is action, a realised contradiction: dialectical, not tautological thought. The essential difference is that Hegel thinks after the end of history, the reasoner before it. Kojève faces the objection that the Sage is also a thinker who has stopped acting. His answer is temporal: contemplation is legitimate only once action is complete. The same act is sterile before the end and wise after it.

**Passage to Chapter VI** (Hoffmeister pp. 308–312). There is a relative justification of the intellectual's attitudes taken in themselves, but the intellectual is always wrong. What is needed is the citizen's loyalty (*Ehrlichkeit*). Intellectuals must end either in tyranny, imposing invalid laws by force, or in anarchy, contradictory laws or no laws at all. Their critiques and attitudes have value only within society and the State; there the moralist's empty formalism receives a content, the reasoner's relativism vanishes, and the philosopher becomes a Sage, with a philosophy of the State. The alternative of tyranny and anarchy anticipates Kojève's reading of the Terror and his later essay on tyranny. The philosopher becoming Sage "in the State" states the political condition of wisdom.

The loyal citizen of VI, A differs from the Slave (IV, A), the religious man (IV, B), and the intellectual (V): his action is mediated by society. But this mediation is immediate, which is its inadequacy. The loyal citizen does not yet know that social laws are his work, the result of his action. He will know it on becoming a reflective citizen of the universal Napoleonic Empire. This reflective citizen, fully conscious of himself and of the natural and social world, is Hegel himself, as author of the *Phenomenology*. The transformation of the loyal citizen into the reflective citizen, exemplarily Hegel, is described in Chapter VI. The "immediate mediation" of the ancient citizen is his unreflective belonging. Kojève's thesis that Hegel is the reflective citizen of the Napoleonic State makes the author of the *Phenomenology* the endpoint of Chapter VI.

#### Introduction to Chapters VI–VIII

The *Phenomenology* can be divided into two parts. The first, Chapters I–V, ignores the historical development of humanity. Hegel analyses elements found in every real man, one of them predominating, and studies man apart from his relations with society, a deliberate abstraction. In Chapter V concrete man appears, but he lives in society while disregarding it, so his real existence is itself somewhat "abstract": that is precisely the intellectual's existence. Real man is always social, political, and historical; he lives and acts within a State, and his acts create history. That history is analysed in its entirety, since for Hegel it is complete, in the second part, Chapters VI–VIII. There Hegel shows how the man who unites all the constituent moments of the first part lives, acts, and understands himself: sensation, perception, understanding; Desire, fight for recognition, labour; and Reason, which lets him reflect on himself and the world. The division confirms the plan of 1933–34 (p. 40). Its novelty is the claim that Chapter V's shapes are "abstract" not by method but by their mode of life.

This man lives in society, and his collective action creates the State and transforms it by successively negating its forms. This transformation of the State, and so of man as citizen, is real universal history, described in Chapter VI, which culminates in Napoleon and his Empire. In creating history man also reveals himself to himself. This successive self-revelation is ideal universal history: the history of religions, art, and literature, analysed in Chapter VII, parallel to Chapter VI, which culminates in Hegel's philosophy. That philosophy is analysed in Chapter VIII, which describes the final period of history: man's complete self-understanding. The division into real and ideal history restates the parallel between Chapters VI and VII and prepares the reading of Chapter VII as the history of ideologies.

#### II. Spirit (Section C, Chapter VI)

The introduction (Hoffmeister pp. 313–316). Subdivision A studies the Master's world, the ancient Greek world. The Master is not only the master of a Slave; he is also a citizen of an aristocratic State, the *polis*, and a member of a Family. The Family is human because its male members fight for recognition and have slaves; they are Masters. Kojève's historical anchoring of Chapter IV's Master in the Greek *polis* is explicit. The Master's humanity at home depends on his mastery abroad and over slaves.

How is ancient society, the State, formed from Families of Masters? By the will of the Tyrant, who "knows" and realises the will of all, the "general will" of the people, against the will of particulars who nonetheless gather behind him. The great statesman turns an unrealised, quasi-animal collective will into the State by his will, which is a tyranny, beyond good and evil. His will is the will of the universal, which destroys the wills of particulars as particulars. These become loyal citizens who realise universal, political aims by particular actions. They are not the Tyrant's slaves; he is not their master but their god. There is no fight to the death between them: some identify with the tyrant, the others are physically eliminated. The Tyrant, the State, embodies the citizens' "general will". This account of state-founding has no counterpart in Hegel's Chapter VI; it draws on the *Jenaer Realphilosophie* of 1805–06, where Hegel describes the founding tyrant, and on Rousseau's general will. The formula "beyond good and evil" places the founder outside morality, since morality presupposes the State he founds. The theme will return in Kojève's *Tyrannie et sagesse*.

The attitude is inadequate precisely because there was no fight for recognition and so no mediation; the citizens submitted "instinctively". Tyranny is transitional: once the State is founded, it sustains itself and no longer needs the Tyrant, who is eliminated. Then comes the rule of laws (described in subdivision A), accepted "loyally", without critical examination or "reflection". For the loyal citizen, laws simply are, or are of divine origin. That is the inadequacy: he accepts tyranny and the aristocratic society that results without a fight. The law is for him a *Nicht-Getan-haben*, something quasi-natural or divine received ready-made, not created by his conscious and voluntary action. Kojève reads Antigone's "unwritten laws" (¶437), which are and no one knows whence, as the mark of unreflective belonging. The inadequacy is the same as the religious man's: what is in fact a human work is taken for a given.

The ancient State is finally an oppression, revealed by the despotism of the Roman emperors, who realise its "truth". It will not withstand the will of people who have reached the notion of freedom, Slaves become Christians. They refuse to fight for the biological person of the Emperor, whose arbitrary will they do not recognise. So ends the ancient world. The mechanism of the fall is a refusal of military service: Christians will not die for a man.

Subdivision B analyses the development of the Christian State, composed of Slaves who have reached the abstract idea of freedom (Understanding). Servile thought culminates in transcendentalist Christian theology and in science, especially Newtonian physics. The dialectic of Chapter IV, B returns: the gap between the reality of slavery and the abstract idea of freedom; Stoicism, Scepticism, Christianity, equality of Master and Slave in servitude; the summit of servile thought, being God's slave; disinterest in society, the intellectual of Chapter V. The claim that Newtonian science and Christian theology are both "servile thought" repeats the 1934–35 remark on engineers' physics (p. 61).

There is nonetheless a Christian society and State. The Masters became Christians, ceased to recognise the Emperors' arbitrary will, and ceased to have slaves. But this "Christian" revolution involved no true fight for recognition; ancient society died a natural, non-violent death. Christian society consists of pseudo-Masters without slaves, the Nobles, and pseudo-Slaves without masters, the Bourgeois, all accepting slavery to God. The account of the transition without a fight is essential to Kojève: because Christianity did not fight, it could not produce satisfaction, which only the French Revolution, a real fight, will achieve.

Subdivision C analyses the contemporary world of 1807, more exactly German idealism, which arises within the Napoleonic Empire. It lies beyond Christianity. Kojève places VI, C, morality and conscience, in the post-revolutionary present, which is disputed: many readers see it as a critique of German moral philosophy, not its apotheosis.

##### A. The True Spirit; Ethical Life

**The Ethical World** (pp. 318–330). Hegel describes the ancient world that frames the active life of the Master-citizen: the State, the *polis*, and the Family. In the ancient State the individual as individual has reality only on the plane of the "divine law", the Family. On the real, political plane of the "human laws" he is a non-particularised individual without value in himself. Kojève's thesis that the ancient citizen has no particularity in public life follows Hegel's contrast of the two laws (¶446–450).

There is a passage from the biological, animal family to the human Family. In paganism the Family opposes the State as the Penates oppose the gods of the city. In the ancient world of the Master, the individual counts as a particular only within the Family. The pursuit of wealth and power for and by the family community makes the Family and family life human. Hegel's point (¶450–451) is that the family's properly ethical action concerns the individual as a whole; Kojève adds the economic pursuit as a humanising element, which Hegel treats as not yet ethical.

Within the Family, real human action goes from particular to particular, the latter taken as a whole. Hence the cult of the dead. The dead man is a completed totality, individualised by death; what is honoured is not the natural, animal particular, the corpse, but a particularity that is, through death, beyond Desire and the here and now, a totality transcending instinct and nature. Society, the State, is interested in the individual's doing (*Tun*); the Family values his being (*Sein*), his mere being, that is, his nothingness and death. The man who does not act is as if dead; insofar as he is a non-citizen, a private person, a particular, he is a shade, a dead man. Dying on a battlefield is a citizen's act; dying in bed completes the individual as family member. The first death is mediated by the consciousness of the one who risks his life; the second by the consciousness of others, the survivors who accompany it with rites. This is the inferiority of the family attitude: there is no self-consciousness. The family's being, as opposed to doing, puts it on the plane of death. The two deaths, the citizen's and the private man's, extend the analysis of human death in the 1933–34 notes (p. 52): a death is human if mediated by consciousness, one's own or others'.

One passes to the plane of being, the divine order: one believes oneself aware of something other than oneself, the dead, the beyond, the divine, the "sacred". The dead has power, though he does not exist or act. The whole of the dead is tradition, everything divine. Spirit is the community (*Gemeinwesen*, common being, common thing or cause); it exists as government of a State. It negates particularity, and its characteristic manifestation here is the army. Through war, the State reminds particulars of their "absolute Master", death, and shakes them out of their "brutishness", their "natural" security.
