In and through war the State constitutes itself as an individuality with respect to other peoples. War is humanising, since it negates: progress through wars. The Family is the State's reservoir of forces, and the State's proper activity, war, negates the Family by killing its members. Hegel's ¶455 on war as the means by which government shakes individuals out of their isolation is the textual base. Kojève's gloss, "progress through wars", draws the historicist consequence, and his phrase "absolute Master" repeats ¶194.

The Family has three relations: husband and wife, parents and children, brother and sister. The first is not human: the mutual "recognition" of man and woman is purely natural, animal sexuality. They realise themselves humanly only through educating the child and working together on the family patrimony. The claim that the conjugal relation is merely natural follows ¶456, where Hegel says husband and wife recognise themselves only in the child.

The second relation is inadequate: the father feels emotion (*Rührung*) watching the growth of the son's consciousness, and the son sees that he owes his "in-itself", his "nature", his "character", to a consciousness other than his own and vanishing. The asymmetry between generations follows ¶456.

The third relation is between brother and sister. They share blood but have no Desire between them, or rather they overcome and negate it, which gives their relation its properly human character. The sister as such reaches the highest presentiment of ethical consciousness; she represents the summit of family existence, and her attitude is the least "natural" of all. Hegel's praise of the sister (¶457) is read by Kojève as the result of repressed desire. Hegel himself says their relation is "unmixed" with desire; Kojève's "or rather they overcome it" introduces a Freudian interpretation.

The feminine plane, limited to the Family, is therefore inferior to the masculine, political plane. The highest feminine attitude is the sister's toward the brother: no biological interest, disinterested love, involving repression, a value attributed to the brother's pure being. It is the purest attitude, freest of "natural" relations; relating to the brother's inactive being, she expects nothing from him, which is why his death changes nothing for her. The claim that the brother's death changes nothing for the sister explains Antigone's devotion to her dead brother: his being, not his doing, was what she valued, and death does not touch being.

The relation is always broken: the brother leaves the Family to live as a citizen under the "human law" of the City; the sister becomes wife and mother and remains under the "divine law". Both overcome and negate the relation, which can only be explained by its having been virtually sexual: it is repressed, then sublimated. Divine law equals value attributed to the particular; human law equals value attributed to the universal, the State. The citizen's action is universal, the family member's particular, "private". The explicit psychoanalytic reading is Kojève's. The equations of the two laws with the two values are his compact summary.

On Hoffmeister p. 328: the dialectical moments of Chapter V are here considered simultaneously as constituents of the ancient citizen. The passage from "Was die Beobachtung" to "was getan wird" summarises Chapter VI. Hegel's recapitulation (¶460) shows the moments of Reason realised in ethical substance.

On Hoffmeister p. 329: a global description of the pagan world, characterised by calm equilibrium and the absence of transcendence. The Hegelian world, VI, C, the Napoleonic Empire, is also "calm" and without a beyond, but after the restlessness (*Unruhe*) and alienation (*Entfremdung*) of the Christian world (VI, B). This equilibrium is the calm of a restlessness; otherwise it would be mere being, like an animal society. Justice, human (the State) and divine (the Family), restores equilibrium immanently: a dynamic, living equilibrium, an overcome disequilibrium. The parallel between the ancient and the final world is central to Kojève: both are without transcendence and at rest, but the final world has passed through alienation. The end of history recovers Greek immanence at a higher level.

The pagan Master is not individualised: neither in his being within the Family, except as dead, nor by his action as citizen, since he is "loyal", not revolutionary or negating, and does not work, does not negate nature. His negating action is directed not against the natural or social universal but against a particular, so it is a crime. Kojève asks us to compare the titles of sections a and b. The claim that every negating act in the pagan world is a crime explains the move from "the ethical world" to "ethical action", which is guilt (*Schuld*).

Within pagan society, negating action is therefore necessarily criminal; so the society, the State, is itself guilty (*Schuld*), and its fate (*Schicksal*), the Family's vengeance, will be its ruin. «Le Monde païen des Maîtres est un Monde tragique» (the pagan world of Masters is a tragic world) (p. 102). The pagan world is tragic because its structure makes action guilty, not because of individual failings.

**Ethical Action** (pp. 330–342). Hoffmeister p. 331 anticipates the end of the pagan world: the despot Emperor who makes the universal, the State, into a particular, his family patrimony; and the Roman Masters, become Slaves without Masters and "legal persons" (*Bürger als Bourgeois*). The emperor who treats the State as family property inverts the ancient order: the particular swallows the universal.

Within pagan law, self-consciousness, man, will act, but will not become individual, since action will be criminal and unconscious. One acts either for the State, universal action, or for the Family, particular action, without fusing them. Despite its "calm", there is conflict in pagan society, a tragic conflict ending in the annihilation of the particular and thereby of the society itself, the pagan State of Masters. The pagan Master's action, on the plane of divine or human law, is always criminal, because he can act on only one plane at a time and the other then seems valueless to him; he negates it in acting, which is a crime. That is tragedy. The analysis follows ¶464–467: action takes one side and so violates the other.

The tragic conflict is not between duty and passion or between two duties. It is a conflict between two planes of existence, one of which the agent considers worthless but others do not. The tragic agent will not be aware of having acted as a criminal; punished, he will feel he undergoes an absolutely unjustifiable "fate", which he accepts without revolt, "without seeking to understand". The rejection of duty versus passion targets the Corneillian model of tragedy. Kojève's reading follows Hegel's *Aesthetics* and the *Phenomenology*'s: tragedy is the collision of two rights.

The pagan Masters lack human particularity to be individualised and so to be satisfied. Their action, dying for the fatherland, realises only universality in them. The Master cannot act as a particular in the State. He has particularity in the Family, but there is no true, anthropogenic, negating action there, only being, pure inactive being, which amounts to nothingness, death. So particularity is "realised" only in death. There is no satisfaction, which exists only in, by, and for the individual, in existence. The Master is "recognised", venerated, by all in his particularity only as dead, an ancestor; only the dead man has individuality, a synthesis of particularity (I, not another) and universality (the recognition of my I's worth by all). The definition of individuality as the synthesis of particularity and universality is Kojève's key to satisfaction. In the ancient world it is achieved only posthumously; in the final State it will be achieved by the living citizen.

The ancient State excludes particularity; particular action will be criminal. Crime is the active opposition of the particular as particular to the given social and political order, the universal. Negating the universal for the sake of particularity is a crime. The definition generalises the tragic crime into a formula that will also fit the revolutionary before his success.

But crime is individualising all the same, since in the death penalty there is a synthesis of universal and particular: it is I, not another, who must be put to death, and this has been decided by all, by society, the State. The State's universal action is concentrated on this particular criminal. Yet there is no satisfaction, since individuality is again realised only in and through death. The thesis that capital punishment individualises the criminal is striking; it makes the executed man a counterpart of the honoured ancestor. Both are recognised as individuals only in death.

The State, excluding particularity, implies suppressing the particular, the family member, that is, his being, since the particular is a natural living being. The essential character of the pagan State is therefore war, the effective destruction of the particular, his death. But war is criminal with respect to the Family, which gives absolute value to the particular, his being, his animal life. The State's essential act is itself a crime from the Family's standpoint.

The State, punishing the criminal, forbids his burial and funeral rites. Individuality is again destroyed: there is no universal recognition, in the funeral rites, of the dead man's particularity. What is punishment for the State is only crime for the Family: the theme of Antigone. Kojève's reading of the *Antigone* as the collision between punishment and burial follows Hegel's (¶470–473).

On Hoffmeister p. 332: the people as a whole of citizens comes into conflict with itself as a whole of Families. The conflict is internal to the people, not between two groups.

On Hoffmeister p. 333: the pagan Master's action is conformist and wants to be. «Le Maître n'est jamais révolutionnaire (tout au plus "anarchiste")» (the Master is never revolutionary, at most "anarchist") (p. 103). The contrast between revolution and anarchy distinguishes negation for a new order from negation of order as such.

Also on p. 333: in the ancient State there is no separation between essence and power (*Wesen* and *Macht*), between citizens and the State's government. The ancient Master cannot exclude himself from the State and cannot be revolutionary; he does not try. Outside the State he is nothing, a dead ancestor. The identity of citizens and power explains why ancient politics admits no opposition: to oppose the State is to cease to be.

His action wants to be loyal. But as human action it can only negate; the Master does not know this. He does not realise his specifically human essence, the negating character of human action; he does not understand himself and is not self-conscious. That is why he is not a true individual. The Master's unconsciousness of his own negativity is the reason he is tragic: he negates without knowing it.

He acts either on the political or on the family plane, and in both cases there is crime. "Ethical life" is essentially crime and guilt (*Verbrechen*, *Schuld*). The pagan's virtues are disguised crimes, as Saint Augustine says; they do not lead to satisfaction. Augustine's *splendida vitia*, the pagan virtues as splendid vices, receives a Hegelian reading: they are crimes because they are one-sided.

The pagan Master's action cannot be revolutionary because he does not work. He does not transcend the natural given by his action, so he has no revolutionary idea that surpasses the social and political given. Objectively, ancient society is founded on slavery. The link between labour and revolutionary imagination is the Introduction's (p. 33): only the one who transforms nature can conceive of transforming society.

The ancient State's own action is criminal: making war. It destroys the citizen's particularity as particularity but does not give him the possibility of living as an individual. That is its crime. War will be the "fate", the "punishment", and finally the ruin of ancient society. The State dies of what defines it.

The ultimate reason for the criminal character of all action in ancient society is the absolute separation of the sexes, which is the ultimate cause of the pagan world's ruin: woman is the particularity of universalities, man the universality of particularities. Kojève promises to return to it. The formulas invert each other: woman stands for the particular within the universal community, man for the universal won by particulars. The separation of the sexes is the "natural" contradiction of the ancient State, a thesis stated below.

The ancient citizen is criminal because he is "loyal". He will suffer the punishment his crime entails, but will not understand why. That is tragedy. Loyalty, uncritical belonging, is the source of guilt: to follow one law blindly is to violate the other.

Every action in the pagan world calls for vengeance. Since the pagan does not know his crime, he cannot avoid it. The typical case is Oedipus: after the act he must recognise it as criminal, which he could not know before. Conscious crime is Antigone's: the State that forbids her brother's burial is criminal in her eyes, for whom her brother's being cannot be destroyed by the criminal character of his action. Hegel distinguishes unconscious and conscious guilt (¶469–470), Oedipus and Antigone. Kojève follows closely.

His tragic fate reveals to the pagan, the Master, the criminal character of his action. Tragedy is the Master's form of self-knowledge: he learns after the fact.

But the Master cannot transcend the pagan world and negate both of its separated planes at once, the exclusively universal State (the idle warrior) and the exclusively particularist Family. The Slave will negate this world. Only one who belongs to neither plane can negate both. The Slave, excluded from the State and from the Family of Masters, is in that position.

What will the pagan Master do? He will lose interest in the State, the universal; he will stop making war and adopt the Slave's particularist ideas, Stoicism, Scepticism, finally Christianity. He will disappear as Master, not in a revolution through the Slave's negating action, but by natural disintegration, like an animal. The passage from the ancient to the Christian State will have revolutionary value, but it will not be a true Revolution. The Master's end mirrors his life: as he lived as an animal (p. 55), he dies as one, by decay rather than defeat.

On Hoffmeister p. 339: the ancient State has a "natural" basis, the people as an ethnic unity. The contradiction within it is also "natural": the separation of the sexes. So when universal and particular fight, citizen and woman, human and divine law, State and Family, the State, destroying the particular, destroys its own root (*Wurzel*) and so itself; and if the particular wins, the State is again destroyed by this criminal activity. In the pagan world there is no mediation between universality, the State, and particularity, the Family. The ancient State is caught: it lives from what it must destroy.

The last paragraph of Hoffmeister p. 339 gives the passage from the ancient City to the Roman Empire. The transition is Hegel's ¶474–476.

On Hoffmeister p. 340: woman is the concrete realisation of crime. The internal enemy of the ancient State is the Family it destroys and the particular it does not recognise, but it cannot do without them. The ancient State perishes through war, the exclusive manifestation of the universal. Hegel's famous phrase on womankind as "the everlasting irony of the community" (¶475) lies behind the note.

One can wage war as a loyal citizen, but also as a criminal: like the intrepid youth (Hoffmeister p. 341) in whom women take pleasure, who makes war a means of realising his particular, even familial, ambitions, and so becomes a despotic head of State, a particular who wants to subject the State, the universal, to his particularity. This perverts the universalist customary morality of the ancient Masters: Alcibiades, Alexander the Great. The historical names are Kojève's; they fit Hegel's description of the youth whom women admire and who turns war to his own ends.

**Legal Status** (pp. 342–346). This concerns the Roman Empire and the advent of Christianity, the passage from VI, A to VI, B. The Roman Empire is not a State properly speaking: it is the patrimony of a particular, the Emperor. Particulars lose interest in the State and put private before public interest. The Masters have stopped making war; they are no longer citizens and so no longer true Masters, since Master equals fight for recognition, which equals war and civic action. The definition "Master = war and civic action" makes mastery a political status, not a psychological trait.

The only product of Roman culture is private law. The Roman State is no longer a "spiritless community", a natural one; it has lost its ethnic character. The State is now a self-conscious unity, in the Emperor's person, and each particular is aware of his private interests, of himself as particular. Hence the victory of particularity, the Family, divine law. The particular here is the legal "person" of the non-citizen bourgeois; he lacks universality. There is no individuality in Rome. The Roman bourgeois opposes to the State the "legal person", the abstract I of the isolated man. The legal person is the abstract I of Stoicism given institutional form. Kojève's point is that the particular's "victory" is empty: he wins private rights and loses his universality.

The Roman State recognises the absolute value of the "person", of particularity, but only as such, not universality within particularity. It recognises no citizens, no true individualities. The recognition of the person is formal: it does not recognise the individual as participant in the universal.

The passage from Empire to Christianity takes up the three stages of the Slave's dialectic in Chapter IV, B. How can Masters accept a Slaves' ideology? They are no longer true Masters but bourgeois, slaves of the Emperor. How could the Stoic's abstract, asocial ideology have social value? Because it corresponds to legal status, to Roman private law of the legal person. And the sceptical solipsist's, denying the reality of the external world? Because there is now private property, the little world that is my creation and escapes all relativism: the realisation of the *solus ipse*. Man reduced to the legal person is an empty, boring content; man reduced to the private owner, the *rentier*, is far from autonomous, since his little world depends on external conditions and their changes. But he does not realise it: he thinks and lives as a "solipsist". The social basis of Stoicism and Scepticism is thus Roman law and property: ideologies correspond to institutions. The link between Hegel's Chapter IV and his account of Rome (¶479–483) is Hegel's own, and Kojève sharpens it in materialist terms.

The "infrastructure" of Christianity: the former Master has in fact become the slave of a despot. He has nothing to lose by adopting the Slave's ideology; on the contrary, by adopting it he becomes, in the only way he can, equal to the Emperor and strips him of his value, since both are slaves of God, equal in servitude. The Christian God is conceived on the model of the Emperor: the "lord of the world" is the only truly real person, but he exists only as recognised by his subjects; so with the Christian God, «qui sera tué par la Révolution française» (who will be killed by the French Revolution) (p. 106). The Marxian word "infrastructure" is deliberate. The thesis that God is modelled on the Emperor and dies with the Revolution completes Kojève's political theology: God lives as long as the Slave's relation to a Master persists.

The Emperor, master of slaves and head of a perverted pseudo-State, is thrown back into private life and debauchery, like his fellow citizens. He is the only link between them. No more people, only dust of particulars, of "legal persons". Hegel's "lord of the world" (¶481) indulges in destructive excess; Kojève stresses that he too is a mere particular.

Likewise God is the only link between the members of the Church, a pseudo-society whose members have no value before him; and he too cannot overcome the sensual desires and "destructive agitation" of the faithful (compare what the Barbarians are for the Emperor). We arrive at the Christian world: recognition of the person, but in transcendence. Now begins the progressive destruction of God's transcendence: «Le Ciel doit descendre sur la Terre» (Heaven must come down to Earth) (p. 107). That is the theme of VI, B. The parallel between Emperor and God, Empire and Church, is systematic. The programme of VI, B, the descent of Heaven to Earth, states the secularisation thesis that Kojève will read into the history from feudalism to Napoleon.

### Summary of the 1935–1936 Course

The course continued the literal commentary, covering Chapter V, Reason, which describes the existential attitudes of the "bourgeois" intellectual, the man who lives in a Christian world but has himself become an atheist, and then Chapter VI, A, on the ancient pagan world. The public summary defines Chapter V's subject in one phrase: the atheist in a Christian world.

The Christian attitude is characterised by isolation from the natural world and from society or the State, a withdrawal into oneself. The Christian pursues a transcendent end, the salvation of his immortal soul, in which he can neither help nor be helped by another; help comes only from beyond, and only there can his end be reached. For reasons Hegel does not give, this Christian may become an atheist: he may abandon the idea of the beyond and replace his transcendent end with one realisable in this world. But in becoming an atheist he becomes a Christian atheist. He now lives here and for here, but still withdrawn into himself, abstaining from any effective interaction with what is not himself, uninterested in social and political activity. He thus becomes an individualist intellectual. The concession "for reasons Hegel does not give" matches the 1934–35 bracket (p. 73) on the non-deducibility of the transition. The "Christian atheist" is Kojève's formula for secular modernity: the content of faith is abandoned, its form of life retained.

This individualism, like the Christian's existential solipsism, is possible only in a society or State that recognises the particular as such, as legal person (*Rechtsperson*) and owner of private property (*Eigentum*), but thereby no longer recognises him as citizen: it excludes him from political life, no longer asks for his life in the State's defence, and makes him the passive subject of a despotic sovereign. This particular who is only particular, no longer a citizen in the proper sense, is the *Bürger als Bourgeois*. He appears in the late Empire, and his history runs to the French Revolution of 1789. In this period the two "bourgeois" ideologies, contrary but complementary, develop and are realised: religious Christianity and atheist or secularised Christianity, which is precisely the intellectual's individualism of Chapter V. The criterion of citizenship is whether the State asks for one's life. The bourgeois is defined by exemption from the risk of death, which makes him a descendant of the Slave.

The intellectual's individualist ideologies rest on the idea, from the Stoic Slave and adopted by Christianity, that man can reach his supreme end, absolute satisfaction, while disregarding social and political action, living in any State and under any conditions. According to Hegel this is impossible, since the individual's satisfaction presupposes the creation of the perfect State, in which all are citizens in the strong sense. That State is born of the Revolution; whoever does not actively contribute to it must experience the inadequacy of his purely "private" ideal. Not being a citizen and so unable to be satisfied in the real social world, the intellectual, like the religious Christian, flees concrete reality into an imaginary world. It is no longer a beyond properly speaking but a secularised beyond: the intellectual universe of the *Sache selbst*, the ideal world of the True, Beautiful, and Good in themselves. Like the religious beyond, it is opposed to and independent of empirical reality. The intellectual's aim, like the religious man's, is the passive manifestation of an abstract absolute value, not its active realisation in the whole concrete world. In pursuing it, seeking immediate contact with absolute value, the atheist intellectual is as isolated as the religious Christian; he can help no one and no one can help him. The parallel between salvation and the intellectual's values is carried through point by point: both are individual, passive, and unshareable.

The passive individualism of the atheist intellectual, the scientist, artist, philosopher, justified by the idea of absolute, eternal, trans-empirical values, is thus a secularisation of the religious Christian's existential solipsism. «L'idéologie du Vrai, du Beau et du Bien est la religion de ceux qui n'en ont pas» (the ideology of the True, the Beautiful, and the Good is the religion of those who have none) (p. 109). It is the ideology of the man who no longer believes in his immortality, or rather has stopped "realising" the idea of his death, and who aspires to absolute satisfaction here below but wants to obtain it immediately, without the effort of negating action needed to transform the natural and social given into a world where the individual's immanent satisfaction becomes really possible. The qualification "has stopped realising the idea of his death" is precise: the intellectual is not immortal in his own eyes, but he lives as if death did not concern him. Kojève's diagnosis is the one Heidegger gives of everyday existence, applied to the cultured class.

Just as the religious Christian can take pleasure in his unhappy consciousness, the atheist Christian can content himself with the pure joy (*Freude*) of intellectual life. But neither can reach definitive satisfaction. The aim of the religious man and the intellectual cannot be man's final aim. So in 1789 active men will come to realise, by negating creation, the abstract ideal of religious and atheist Christianity, transforming the world of bourgeois into a world of citizens, where "bourgeois" ideologies founded on that ideal will have no reason to exist and will finally be replaced by true philosophy, Hegel's Science. The distinction between joy and satisfaction parallels the earlier one between pleasure and satisfaction. The Revolution realises the Christian ideal of equality and freedom, which is why Christianity's truth is political.

The Revolution and the dialectic leading to it are described in Section B of Chapter VI. In Section A, Hegel showed how and why the ancient citizen, the man of the pagan world, ceased to be what he was and became the Roman bourgeois who, by accepting his Slaves' religion, realised the Christian world in which the religious and atheist ideologies of Chapters IV and V develop. The summary joins the structural chapters to the historical ones: the ideologies of IV and V are those of the Christian-bourgeois world whose history VI, B recounts.

## Course of the 1936–1937 Academic Year

### B. Self-Alienated Spirit; Culture (Chapter VI, B)

The introduction (Hoffmeister pp. 346–350). Subdivision B analyses Christian society; in fact it is a phenomenological analysis of the history of France from feudalism to Napoleon. The Christian world ends in the realisation of the idea of freedom, at first abstract, born in the Slave's self-consciousness. This happens through the French Revolution and Napoleon, which are the social, political, and historical realisation of the "abstract" dialectic of Chapter IV, B. The identification of VI, B with French history is Kojève's boldest historical localisation. It makes the Revolution the realisation of what Stoicism, Scepticism, and the unhappy consciousness only thought.

The Christian world consists of pseudo-Masters who have accepted the Slaves' abstract idea of freedom and have thereby become pseudo-Slaves. Pseudo-Slaves and pseudo-Masters, which comes to the same thing, are the bourgeois, the Christian citizens. In post-revolutionary, Napoleonic society (VI, C) there are neither Masters nor Slaves. There are no Masters properly speaking, and in the bloody Revolution the Slave risked his life in a fight for recognition and so ceased to be a Slave. He does not become a Master either, because the freed Slave, now a citizen, goes on working, voluntarily. He works for himself, not for a Master, so he is not a Slave in the proper sense: man works for another only from fear of death, and the citizen has overcome that fear in the revolutionary fight. The argument states precisely how the Revolution overcomes both terms. The citizen has the Master's risk and the Slave's work, but without the Master's idleness or the Slave's fear.

The post-revolutionary State is a conscious, comprehensible reality free of contradiction. The man who takes part in it understands himself completely and lives in accord with himself. He is thus completely satisfied, and satisfied by the mutual recognition of all. Recognition by another has value only if the other is recognised in turn: «seuls, les hommes de 1789 l'ont compris» (only the men of 1789 understood this) (p. 113). The pagan Master fell into an existential impasse by refusing to recognise the one who recognised him, the Slave; hence his tragic situation. The Revolution realised Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity, the recognition of each by all. The Napoleonic State is essentially new. In it the synthetic man is realised, the true citizen, the synthesis of Master and Slave: «le soldat qui travaille et le travailleur qui fait la guerre» (the soldier who works and the worker who makes war) (p. 114). Man thereby reaches complete satisfaction; he realises his individuality, the synthesis of particular and universal, being universally recognised in his irreplaceable particularity, "unique in the world". History therefore stops. It is no longer possible, since the man who made it is satisfied and no longer wants to change or surpass himself. Man can then take up a contemplative attitude and understand himself. He realises absolute philosophy, which replaces religion: Hegel's philosophy, introduced by the *Phenomenology*. This paragraph is the most complete statement so far of the end of history. Every element is defined: the State, the citizen, satisfaction, individuality, and the cessation of history because desire has been met. The inference from satisfaction to the end of history is strict: history is the action of unsatisfied desire, so satisfied desire ends it.

VI, C does not describe the ideal State realised by Napoleon, which has no further interest, but the philosophical and ideological process that prepared Hegel's absolute philosophy. Kojève's reading of VI, C as the genealogy of Hegel's philosophy, running through German moral philosophy, explains why its content is moral rather than political.

«L'Histoire est morte et Hegel en est le fossoyeur» (History is dead and Hegel is its gravedigger) (p. 114), and this equals absolute knowledge. Absolute knowledge is the synthesis of Schelling's philosophy of nature, described in Chapter V, A, a as the bourgeois intellectual's understanding of nature, and of the philosophy of man, of human negating activity, set out in the *Phenomenology* as a whole and in its summary, Chapter VIII. The synthesis is the *Encyclopaedia*, the development of absolute knowledge, described as an existential attitude in Chapter VIII. At the end of history in 1806, which is the sequence of interactions between man and nature, Schelling understands nature and Hegel understands man, history, and realises absolute knowledge. The division of labour between Schelling and Hegel is striking. It concedes to Schelling the philosophy of nature that Kojève elsewhere treats as naturalist, and reserves to Hegel the philosophy of man. The *Encyclopaedia* joins them, which on Kojève's view means that it inherits Schelling's monist error in its treatment of nature.

**Passage from the pagan to the Christian world.** The Christian attitude is servile: fear of death has become a longing for immortality. The Master's Slave is now God's slave. The dualism between the transcendent and real worlds will disappear only with the Revolution. How could the Master become a Christian and accept the abstract idea of freedom? The end of subdivision A explains it. It did not happen through a revolution, since the Slave was not yet ready to risk his life and did not intervene actively. The Slave did not free himself; the Master abandoned his mastery: «Maître sans Esclave = Esclave sans Maître = Chrétien = Bourgeois» (Master without a Slave = Slave without a Master = Christian = Bourgeois) (p. 115). The chain of equations closes the analysis of 1934–35 and 1935–36. The bourgeois arises when the Master's decay meets the Slave's ideology, not through the Slave's victory.

The pagan State is immediate (*unmittelbar*). The warrior, the Master, realises only the universal aspect of man. All have the same will, all warriors resemble one another, and the Tyrant only formulates the will of all. The pagan State excludes the personal I and so individuality, which would preserve that I. The pagan Master's will conforms entirely to the State's universal will; his particularity vanishes in the risk of death in war, since all are equal before death. Equality before death is the only equality of the ancient world, and it is equality in universality alone.

The pagan State has the character of being, of the "natural" and "given"; it is not the pagan's work. It is essentially non-revolutionary and ignores particularity. Hence the conflict between universal and particular, manifested in the opposition of State and Family. The State recognises only the universal in the Master, and only through his particularity does the Master have value in the Family. The two kinds of value are absolutely separated, with no synthesis. The particularity revealed in the Family is passive, a particularity of being, vital and animal. The Master, the pagan citizen, acts only in the fight for life and death, not in labour. If he wants to keep his particularity, he leaves the State and rejects the universal; if he wants to keep his universality as citizen, he must sacrifice his particularity as family member. The pagan is therefore always criminal, either by the State's human law or by the Family's divine law. He cannot be "satisfied"; his destiny is essentially tragic. He speaks of "fate" (*Schicksal*) because he does not know that he is himself at fault, "guilty" (*Schuld*). The note restates the 1935–36 analysis in compact form. The play on *Schicksal* and *Schuld* summarises tragedy: fate is guilt not recognised as one's own.

The contradiction is absolute, a mutual exclusion. The pagan world collapses: the familial and particularist principle triumphs in the form of Christian "individualism". The pagan world is the universal, the Christian world the particular; both are inadequate and both necessary, and their synthesis is the post-revolutionary Napoleonic world. How the passage happens: the pagan State is a military State, and the materially stronger defeats the weaker. Hence the passage from cities to Empire, Alexander and then Rome. Since the Empire can no longer defend itself with its citizens alone, who are too few, it must call on non-citizens. The Masters, recognised by the whole world, stop making war for prestige, the only true war: the *pax romana*. They thereby lose their universal value, equality before death and patriotic sacrifice, and are reduced to their particular value within their families, which differ in wealth and are "selfish". The mechanism is paradoxical: the Masters lose their mastery by succeeding. Universal recognition ends the wars of prestige that made them Masters. The triad of pagan universal, Christian particular, and Napoleonic synthesis is the framework of Kojève's philosophy of history.

From act they become being. Roman law will be private law: security of the body and defence of property. The Greek warrior becomes the Roman bourgeois, who ceases to be a citizen in the pagan sense. The State then has the "right", an explicable possibility, to lose interest in him. The non-warrior pseudo-citizens, interested only in private property, particularity, and not in the universal, are at the mercy of professional soldiers and their chief, the Emperor. The despot in turn regards the State as his private property and his family's. The whole process is unconscious and unwilled. The passage from act to being inverts the Master's origin: he became human by an act and ends as a mere owner. Kojève's insistence that the process is unwilled marks the difference between this transition and a revolution.

Private property is expressed not only in Roman law but in ideologies, which will be the Slave's. The Roman bourgeois can accept them because he is a quasi-slave of the despot. He first becomes a Stoic, uninterested in the external world, then a Sceptic, denying it, then a Christian, seeking refuge in the "other world". «C'est la propriété privée qui est à la base du Christianisme» (it is private property that lies at the basis of Christianity) (p. 116). Because of it the Slave's ideology becomes a social, political, historical reality: the Christian world and its pseudo-States. The thesis is Kojève's materialist rendering of Hegel's ¶479–483. It makes Christianity the ideology of property owners, which will explain its alliance with the bourgeois world down to the Revolution.

A parenthesis notes the Marxist appearance of this process, «mais Marx a supprimé l'Angoisse et la Mort» (but Marx suppressed Anguish and Death) (p. 116). Hegel draws on Gibbon. The two processes, the Master's here and the Slave's in Chapter IV, are entirely independent; the Master's process is immanent and independent of the Slave's action. The Master-Emperor is a being, a natural, given, "hereditary" reality, for the Slave and the quasi-slave bourgeois, although he is in fact their work. So too the transcendent God of Christianity: man creates, "invents" him, but does not notice and accepts him as a datum, a being. The remark on Marx is the book's most explicit statement of its relation to Marxism. Kojève accepts the materialist mechanism but insists that the anthropological core, finitude and the fear of death, is what Marx omitted. The parallel between Emperor and God recurs from 1935–36: both are human works taken for givens.

The Christian world is characterised by the dualism of here and beyond. The Christian is the pagan who has become aware of his inadequacy, but as a Christian he remains in that state, in his unhappiness. He also sees the conflict and lives it, and it is he who prepares the Revolution that will bring the Hegelian, Napoleonic State into existence. The Christian's awareness of inadequacy is the progress over paganism; his remaining in it is his limit.

On Hoffmeister p. 348: the Christian world is a unity of universal and particular, but an insufficient synthesis: there is alienation of spirit (*Entfremdung*). The insufficient unity is purely ideal. Hence the contradiction between the ideal of unity and a reality that is not that unity, where dualism reigns. In the Christian world there is still opposition between the universality of the State and the particularity of families, social classes, and nations. The progressive realisation of the ideal of unity is *Bildung*, "educative formation", carried out in and through labour (compare Chapter IV, A). Kojève links the *Bildung* of VI, B directly to the Slave's formative labour in ¶195–196. The culture of the Christian world is the Slave's labour extended to a civilisation.

The pagan opposition of universal and particular becomes conscious in Christianity, which also brings the ideal of their unity, individuality. There is an opposition between actual (*wirklich*), particularist consciousness and "pure" (*rein*) consciousness turned toward the trans-empirical ideal of the unity of particular and universal. The two consciousnesses, actual and pure, are Hegel's (¶485–486). Kojève's gloss gives the pure one its content: the ideal of individuality.

In the Christian world servitude dominates: the Christian bourgeois isolates himself, neglects the fight, and is uninterested in the external world; hence, as its manifestation, private property. Christian consciousness is a "torn consciousness". It is a world of malcontents and pre-revolutionaries, and also the world of discourse, of language (*Sprache*). For Hegel the transcendent world does not exist, but theology is not nothing, since it has historical value; its reality is that of discourse (*Logos*). The Christian's discourse is that of faith, utopia, the "ideal", and error: it does not reveal what is but creates, in the abstract, an ideal world opposed to the real one. «Le langage naît du mécontentement» (language is born of discontent) (p. 117). Man speaks of the nature that kills him and makes him suffer; he speaks of the State that oppresses him; he does political economy because social reality does not conform to his ideal and does not "satisfy" him, since it does not give his particularity a universally valid value. The thesis that language is born of discontent completes Kojève's theory of discourse. Satisfied man would have nothing to say except the truth; the dissatisfied man speaks to oppose an ideal to the real. The Sage's discourse at the end will be the only one that reveals without opposing.

Man will want to make the reality of his world agree with the ideal expressed in his discourse. The Christian world is the world of intellectuals and ideologues. What is an ideology? It is not a truth (*Wahrheit*), objective truth, nor an error, but something that can become true through the fight and labour that make the world conform to the ideal. The test of fight and labour makes an ideology true or false. At the end of the revolutionary process, what is realised is not the ideology one started from but something different, which is the truth, the "revealed reality", of that ideology. This is Kojève's theory of ideology, and it differs from Marx's. An ideology is not false consciousness but a project whose truth depends on its realisation, and what is realised always differs from what was projected. The formula anticipates his reading of the Revolution as the "perverted" realisation of the Enlightenment.

At the origin there is a Christian ideology, based on an opposition inherited from the Roman world, which implies an ideal: the beyond. The result will be the post-revolutionary world, in which the abstract, imaginary beyond, the ideal, is realised here below. «La "vérité" (réalité révélée) du christianisme n'est plus chrétienne» (the "truth", revealed reality, of Christianity is no longer Christian) (p. 117). The sentence states Kojève's secularisation thesis in its sharpest form: Christianity is true, but its truth is the atheist State.

The Christian awareness of opposition implies discourse and is essentially critical: a critique of the world as a whole, a depreciation of pagan values, of the State, the Family, the body. Critique is the form discourse takes in a world that does not satisfy. The depreciation of pagan values is the Slave's revaluation, which Nietzsche also described, here given a positive historical role.

#### I. The World of Self-Alienated Spirit

The introduction (Hoffmeister p. 350). The fundamental myth of Christianity is the union of the universal, State or God, and the particular, Family or animal man: the incarnation of God, Christ. The Christian's ideal is to imitate Christ, but he cannot become Christ: that is Christianity's internal contradiction. For Hegel it is man who becomes God at the end of history, through the fight and labour that create it: «l'"incarnation", c'est l'Histoire universelle ; la "révélation", c'est la compréhension de cette Histoire par Hegel dans la Phénoménologie» (the "incarnation" is universal history; the "revelation" is Hegel's understanding of that history in the *Phenomenology*) (p. 118). The equation of incarnation with history and revelation with the *Phenomenology* is anthropotheism stated through the two central Christian dogmas. The contradiction of *imitatio Christi*, that one can imitate but not become, is resolved when every citizen realises what Christ symbolised.

Christianity develops through the growing awareness of the conflict until its solution in the post-revolutionary world. The first stage (VI, B, I) is feudalism and absolutism up to nationalism, with the pseudo-synthesis of the Cartesian ego: I am, but I think universal truths. The second (VI, B, II) is the Enlightenment, which empties the transcendent of all content and aims at the "useful", the here below. The third (VI, B, III) is the Revolution of 1789 and the Napoleonic Empire of 1806. In other words: Christianity proper, "Reason" (Cartesian rationalism), and Revolution, whose citizen is the soldier-worker. The Cartesian ego as a pseudo-synthesis of particular and universal is an acute reading: the *cogito* is a particular I that thinks universal truths, but only in thought.

Why "the world of self-alienated spirit"? Because what characterises Christianity is dualism, alienation (*Entfremdung*). The dualism opposes the world of actuality, the real natural and social world, and the world of pure consciousness that man builds for himself in and through his Reason or his Faith, an imaginary world. The Christian feels a stranger in the real world and flees into the imaginary one. Faith is «die Flucht aus der wirklichen Welt» (the flight from the actual world) (¶487). Kojève's *dépaysé*, estranged, renders *entfremdet* in its literal sense of being made foreign.

Chapter IV, B describes Christian faith in the pagan world, a purely subjective Christian attitude. Chapter VI, B describes Christianity as faith realising itself in the Christian world, a social Christian attitude. Chapter VII, C describes Christian doctrine, theology, «qui est une anthropologie qui s'ignore elle-même» (which is an anthropology unaware of itself) (p. 118). The three treatments of Christianity, existential, social, and doctrinal, are distributed across the book. The formula for theology is Feuerbach's.

In the Christian world the philosopher is a particular who reveals only the particular; theology, by contrast, is a collective work through which the State unconsciously reveals itself and the universal. Every particularist philosophy must therefore be completed by a universalist theology. Only Hegel achieves the synthesis of particular and universal, so his philosophy can do without theology. It is therefore no longer philosophy but wisdom (*Sophia*), absolute knowledge. But the opposition of theological faith and philosophical reason in the Christian world is necessary and unavoidable. The claim that theology is collective and philosophy individual is Kojève's. It explains why the Christian world needed both, and why the Sage, whose knowledge is both individual and universal, needs neither.

**Culture (*Bildung*), "educative formation" through labour** (pp. 350–376). The first paragraph of Hoffmeister p. 350 marks the difference between the end of the pagan world (VI, A, c) and the start of the Christian world. Near the bottom of the page, "essence" (*Wesen*) always designates the collectivity, the State. The lexical note fixes a term that recurs throughout VI, B.

In the Christian world the essence is pervaded by self-consciousness: one knows, or thinks one knows, why one lives: one lives for an ideal. That is what is important and new. But note Hegel's phrase "by a self-consciousness": it is the particular who becomes self-conscious, not the universal as such, the State. Hence, as will be seen, the political form adequate to Christianity is absolutism: "L'État c'est moi". The link between Christian self-consciousness and absolutism is Kojève's: the monarch is the particular self-consciousness that claims to be the State.

The Christian believes he can realise and reveal himself "immediately", in his inner self, without passing through the mediation of social action, the action that takes him out of himself. He shuts himself in; the essence stands "over against" him; the State is outside and beyond him, foreign to him. When the particular enters it, he therefore becomes foreign to himself: alienation (*Entfremdung*). The account of alienation is precise: it is not the loss of the self in the world but the experience of the social world as foreign by one who has withdrawn into himself.

In the Christian world "essence" refers to, reveals, and implies the universal element in general. In the pagan world only the State represented the universal; in the Christian world there is also the beyond, the transcendent world, God. The same sentence therefore also means that man is alone before God: I, the particular, am in direct, "immediate" relation with God, the universal, without passing through society, the State, or history. Kojève reads Hegel's sentence doubly, politically and theologically, and the parallel carries his interpretation: the believer's immediate relation to God is the religious form of the bourgeois's withdrawal from the State.

Theologically, God, the spirit of this world, becomes aware of himself as a person independent of the world, but thereby finds himself facing something external: evil. Rationally, man becomes aware of himself as an ego limited to his isolated being; social extension becomes external space, foreign to him. Hence the static, non-dialectical Cartesian dualism of pure thought and matter, space, not mediated by action. Kojève offers a social genealogy of Cartesian dualism: *res extensa* is the social world experienced as foreign by the isolated *res cogitans*.

Hegel's second sentence: the external world is foreign to the Christian, and if he wants to give his self-consciousness objective reality (*Wirklichkeit*), he must renounce himself, alienate his personality. He knows it. The existence (*Dasein*) of the Christian world presupposes and implies these negating actions; it is the result of conscious efforts to realise an ideal opposed to the given "pagan" reality. Although the Christian knows he created this world, he still feels a stranger in it. He must seize it and master it. «Le Monde chrétien est une longue Révolution» (the Christian world is a long Revolution) (p. 120), by which the Christian seeks to establish himself in the world here below that he began by fleeing. The formula is one of Kojève's most suggestive. The Christian world is not stable but a slow revolution whose completion is 1789.

If I create a world, it is in fact mine, so it must become consciously mine: the world of man, who is "master in his own house". «La naissance du Christianisme implique déjà la Révolution de 89» (the birth of Christianity already implies the Revolution of '89) (p. 120). The claim is the teleological form of the secularisation thesis. "Master in his own house" echoes Freud's remark that the ego is not master in its own house, inverted: at the end of history, man will be.

Hegel's third and fourth sentences speak from knowledge the Christian described in the section does not yet have. Then comes the opposition between the start of the Christian dialectic and the end of the pagan one (VI, A, c): the Roman world become Christian and the pagan Roman world. The note distinguishes voices again: Hegel knows the outcome that the consciousness he describes does not.

The Christian is recognised as Christian only because he has made the effort to become one; the pagan is simply pagan, born so, a mere being. What counts for the Christian is the act (*Tun*) by which he becomes Christian, the conscious effort, not his mere animal being. But this effort still aims only to flee the real world and reach the beyond. The Christian does not want to fight to conquer the world. Yet in fact he transforms it, because he works in it, which is also an act. Conversion is the Christian form of self-creation: one is not born Christian. Kojève's point is that effort, even directed at flight, produces a world through labour.

The elements necessary for the constitution of the Christian world are the isolation of the pacifist Roman bourgeois, a private owner living in security without fighting, and the Slave working in anguish and so reaching the Understanding, which can elaborate ideals surpassing given reality, ideals the bourgeois, the former Master, will adopt. The two components, the idle owner and the anxious worker, are the Master and the Slave in their decayed and developed forms.

Just as the bourgeois, when still a Master, created the pagan world in which his security and property were assured, so as bourgeois he will create the Christian world in which he is sure of salvation: he creates the Church, a social reality. Christianity thus ceases to be a pure ideal: the Church, and the State that implies it, realise the ideal conceived by the anxious Worker. Masters and Slaves become bourgeois, Christian bourgeois. «Le Chrétien est un propriétaire angoissé» (the Christian is an anxious owner) (p. 120). The formula combines the two sources of Christianity, property and fear of death, in a single figure.

Hoffmeister p. 351 begins the analysis of *Bildung*. The word first appears in Chapter IV: the Slave's labour in anguish in another's service "educates" (*bildet*) and "forms" his consciousness. The Christian world is one in which labour has positive value, so the ideology of the working Slave triumphs in it. For labour to have value there must be service (*Dienst*): labour and action in general in the service of the Lord, the King, and ultimately God; and labour must be done, as the Slave's was, in anguish before death. Hence *Bildung*: Christian labour aims at the salvation of the soul. It transforms nature and the worker's inner world; the Christian becomes a "cultivated" man (*gebildet*). Hence the predominance of abstract thought and rationalism. Here language, discourse, appears. Within the Christian world there are men who want to live solely in this universe of discourse: the intellectuals of Chapter V. Kojève reconstructs the Christian world from the three conditions of the Slave's formation: labour, service, and fear. Culture is the Slave's education generalised.

To be a Christian, then, it is not enough to be born and to exist; one must make an effort, in the direction of labour (*Arbeit*), of service (*Dienst*), and of anguish (*Furcht*): a triple *Bildung*. This effort can lose itself in chatter: the intellectuals. *Bildung* is only one aspect of estrangement (*Entfremdung*) or alienation (*Entäusserung*). Kojève distinguishes Hegel's two terms: *Entfremdung*, becoming foreign, and *Entäusserung*, externalisation or self-divestment. *Bildung* is their positive face.

On Hoffmeister p. 351: what counts is the energy of the will that sublimates the "natural" self. The degree does not matter; the fact of the effort does. One is born pagan; one becomes Christian by an effort of will, "conversion". The emphasis on effort over achievement is the Christian valuation of intention, which Kojève will contrast with Hegel's valuation of success.

From "Zweck und Inhalt" (p. 351) to "Bleiben hat" (p. 352): in the Christian world individuality has no permanence and cannot maintain itself in the real world, since there is no true individuality, which is that of the post-revolutionary citizen. It is only a "supposed existence" (*gemeintes Dasein*), an imaginary one, an intellectual's "individuality". *Gemeint*, meant or supposed, recalls the *Meinen* of Chapter I: private meaning that the world does not confirm.

On p. 352: the effort of *Bildung* of the individual, the particular, is the *Bildung* of the substance, the universal, itself. The world itself, natural and social, the State, is "formed" by valid individual Christian efforts. The Christian wants to realise himself; unconsciously he realises a world; that is why he feels a stranger in it. The world does not belong to him but to God, the Emperor, kings, feudal lords, and finally capital. The last item in the list completes the series of alien owners: capital is the modern form of the Master.

On Hoffmeister p. 353: "good and bad". The opposition was already noted in Chapter IV as the "torn consciousness". Man's isolation entails a conflict (*Entgegensetzung*) with the non-self, the world; conflict is therefore the essence of the Christian world. It is alienation itself and *Bildung* itself: three aspects of one thing. The conflict exists not only between the here and the beyond but, as will be seen, within each of these worlds. It is conscious: one of the two possibilities must be chosen, since they exclude each other, though each has value only through and against the other. The opposition of good and bad is absolute; no synthesis is possible; the conflict is irreducible. The identity of conflict, alienation, and *Bildung* is the thesis of the section: culture is the working-out of a conflict.

Yet the Christian conflict is no longer tragic, since it is conscious. If man tries to maintain himself within it, the comic arises. Why? Because the conflict is in fact soluble, but man does not know it. Becoming aware of the pagan, tragic, insoluble conflict makes it soluble, Christian; but the Christian believes himself unable to resolve it. This is a remnant of paganism in the Christian world: «la comédie chrétienne (par opposition à la tragédie païenne)» (Christian comedy, as opposed to pagan tragedy) (p. 122). The theory of comedy is Kojève's own. Comedy arises from a soluble conflict treated as insoluble; the Christian is comic because he suffers what he could change. Chapter VII's treatment of comedy follows a different line, and Kojève's use here is analogical.

Good and evil have universal value: everything is both good and bad. One cannot realise the good without realising an equivalent evil, nor destroy "Christian" evil without destroying the Christian good. The intellectual reflects this situation in his universal critical attitude, always finding good in evil and evil in good: «Ici ça devient vraiment comique» (here it becomes really comic) (p. 122). The ambivalence of all values, which Hegel develops in the dialectic of State power and wealth, becomes the intellectual's permanent material.

More exactly, within the Christian world the conflict is in fact insoluble, as in the pagan world. The utopian of Chapter V believes there can be only good; the reformist believes evil can be removed while leaving the good as it is. The solution can only be revolutionary, a fight to the death: the Christian world must be abolished. But that destroys the good, and it is a crime. The Christian who will not commit this crime and yet recognises that the world is "bad" is in a comic situation. The post-revolutionary citizen is neither comic nor tragic. The correction, "more exactly", clarifies the thesis: the conflict is soluble only from outside the Christian world, by revolution. The revolutionary accepts the crime; the Christian refuses it and so remains comic.

On Hoffmeister p. 354: for the Christian the good is, first, immediate, a datum rather than his creation; second, immutable, identical with itself; third, common to all, the universal. The same holds for the good, Reason, in rationalism, which is secularised Christianity. Evil is the particular, change, the new: "vanity" in religious Christianity, the "passions" in seventeenth-century rationalism, "prejudices" and "superstitions" in the eighteenth-century Enlightenment. The three names of evil in three periods show the continuity Kojève sees between religion and rationalism: both locate the good in the immutable and evil in the particular.

This evil, this "vanity", is durable and cannot be eliminated. The Christian good replaces the pagan perfect: a moral category, a "value", replaces an ontological one: the perfect is (being), the good ought to be (becoming). Christianity keeps the ideas of the Roman Empire and of the perfect, in the form of the idea of the good, while knowing that there is also an absolute evil, an omnipresent imperfection. It is thus a critique and even a self-critique, which will become a self-suppression (*Aufhebung*): the French Revolution. The shift from the perfect to the good, from what is to what ought to be, is the Slave's contribution. It introduces the future into ethics and so makes history possible.

Christianity's new idea is sin, something other than pagan guilt (*Schuld*): a sin to be avoided, namely "vanity", which the Christian at first judges "vain". This is the Slave's depreciation of the Master's "glory". When vanity ceases to be vain, sin ceases to be considered sin and Christianity disappears: passing through servile, bourgeois "vanity", the Master's "glory" is sublimated (*aufgehoben*) into the citizen's "dignity". The triad glory, vanity, dignity is one of Kojève's finest. It traces the desire for recognition through three social forms: the Master's glory won by risk, the bourgeois's vanity condemned as sin, and the citizen's dignity universally recognised.

Socially, there is the opposition of State power (*Staatsmacht*), the good, and wealth (*Reichtum*), evil. Wealth, private property, is the basis of Christianity and its world; it is also evil, the enemy of evangelical poverty. This is again Christian self-critique, which will be realised in and through the Revolution. Hegel's pairing of State power and wealth (¶491–494) is read as the Christian world's internal contradiction: it lives on what it condemns.

The State maintains the private property of the particular, the Family, just as God is God for me, for the particular. The State is created by owners and exists for them: feudalism. It is therefore the opposite of itself, namely wealth; but it tends to destroy the wealth that begets and sustains it, just as wealth tends to destroy the State that limits it but which it begot and which defends it. On the other hand wealth, evil, the particular, becomes universal. It is therefore the good, and the State opposed to it is evil. Kojève follows Hegel's reversal (¶494–495): wealth, which gives itself to all, turns out universal; State power, which serves particular owners, turns out particular.

Every activity is thus both good and evil. The Christian believes himself free with respect to both, that is, with respect to objective reality, made up of State and wealth. He knows that good and evil imply each other, so he criticises every act, and unanimity can never be achieved in Christian society. The absence of unanimity is the political consequence of universal ambivalence: every act has its critics.

Every Christian judgement is doubled. It is subjective, particular, since the Christian limits himself to himself: what counts in things is their relation to the particular, to me as a Christian. First, the Christian judges the pagan world; only the fact of judgement is Christian, and the world, State and property, remains pagan; the Christian denies them. Second, the Christian judges State and wealth as both good and evil: everything real here below is imperfect. Third, by this judgement State and wealth become properly Christian; it is as ambivalent that they are realised by action in the Christian, bourgeois world. Kojève follows Hegel's analysis of judgement (¶496–499). The third step is the decisive one: the Christian world is made by the Christian judgement of the pagan world.

State and property are both good and bad, and choosing one or the other is indifferent to the Christian; whoever wants to choose the good cannot choose it here below. It matters little whether the Christian is a citizen or rich. What counts is his attitude, his judgement: he criticises or he does not; he is a nonconformist or a conformist. The good is at first this: to accept the given world, since one believes one can realise one's personal value without transforming the world. Evil is then nonconformism. But this world is bad; so nonconformism is the good. The reversal of conformism and nonconformism anticipates Hegel's reversal of noble and base consciousness.

So there is never unanimity in Christian society; there are always two kinds of Christians, conformists and nonconformists; socially, nobles, bourgeois former Masters, and villeins, bourgeois former Slaves. These judgements are Christian, that is, subjective: the Christian judges whether the world favours his personal, particular aim or not. For Hegel every Christian judgement is in fact both conformist and nonconformist. But for Christianity itself only the conformist judgement is supposed to be recognised; the other is guilty. The social interpretation of Hegel's "noble" and "base" consciousness (*edelmütig*, *niederträchtig*) as nobles and commoners is Kojève's. It gives the dialectic a class content.

Conformism is a remnant of pagan "perfection", from the Master, and of Stoicism, from the Slave. Christianity excludes nonconformism as "low and base"; one must save one's soul in any natural, social, political, or historical conditions, not busy oneself with the world and with "inferior" things like politics and economics. Hence a "noble", conformist consciousness and a "base", nonconformist one. But nobles and villeins are in fact both private owners, anxious and fleeing death. The genealogy of conformism unites Master and Slave in the Christian's political indifference: the Stoic's "on the throne or in chains" becomes Christian quietism.

The Christian noble, a warrior, is only a pseudo-Master: he does not really risk his life, since he believes in the immortality of his soul. He thereby accepts his equality with the Slave, since their immortal souls are equal. The Christian villein, a worker, is only a pseudo-Slave, since there are no true Masters any more. Both are bourgeois, whose State, God, guarantees their life, immortality, and their property, "good works". The argument that belief in immortality annuls the risk of death is central to Kojève's reading of Christianity. The Christian knight cannot be a Master, because he does not believe he can really die.

The dialectic of the Christian world consists in eliminating these pagan survivals, the opposition of nobles and villeins, and in realising bourgeois equality; then the equality and fraternity of the citizens of the post-revolutionary, post-Christian State. Bourgeois equality before God precedes citizens' equality in the State. The first is formal, the second real.

In the Christian world there is always an opposition between the universal, State or God, and the particular, private owner or the here below. The first form of this Christian opposition is the feudal world. Kojève now enters the historical sequence proper.

The feudal lord is a conformist; he lives and acts in the service (*Dienst*) of a given state of affairs. He is heroic: he makes an effort toward a universal value, one recognised by the State. The aspect of service relates the Christian feudal lord to the pagan Master. But unlike the Master-citizen, the lord can make himself independent of the State; he can withdraw to his estates, into private, family life, and the State can likewise separate itself from him. They are distinct: the State is an other for the lord. Like the pagan Slave, the lord serves this other to be paid and recognised by it; in this respect service is servitude. The State recognises the lord only by virtue of service rendered. It is not enough to be born and to exist to be a feudal lord; one must act, make war, to become one. So one can say that the lord, making war, works like the Slave: his labour is war, and killing is his trade. This labour in another's service, in anguish, is by definition *Bildung*, which is already realised and revealed in the feudal world. The lord negates his particularity by serving the State, the universal. He is «le premier Fonctionnaire» (the first civil servant) (p. 125), the first real synthesis of particular and universal, the first sketch of individuality. But it is inadequate. Kojève's reading of the feudal lord as a worker whose work is war, and as the first civil servant, unites the Master's risk and the Slave's service in one figure. This is the first historical approximation of the soldier-worker of the final State.

The feudal State is not a being either; it is "formed" (*gebildet*) by the very effort of the noble-citizen's service. Hence the superiority of the Christian over the pagan State. But the feudal State is inadequate: it is not yet a self (*Selbst*), an I conscious of itself as such. The feudal lord gives the State not his self but his being; he is ready to die for the State, not to live for it: «fonctionnaire de la mort» (a civil servant of death) (p. 125). What others recognise in him is his hereditary office, not his irreplaceable personality. This inadequacy appears in his language, or rather language exists here only in potency, since the lord, the warrior, does not speak and keeps his "noble silence". If he could be supposed to speak to the State, his language would be counsel (*der Rat*), something to which one does not wholly commit oneself; the lord always reserves his self and remains a particular as long as he lives and does not die for the State. Hegel's "heroism of service" (¶503–506) and its "silent" character are Kojève's text. The phrase "civil servant of death" names the inadequacy exactly: the lord's service is concentrated in the moment of sacrifice.

On Hoffmeister p. 361, the passage beginning "Das Fürsichsein" is a note aimed at parliamentarism, English for example, a residue and revival of the feudal State. Here the lords speak a particularist language: they advise the State according to their private interests. Kojève reads Hegel's remark on counsel as a critique of the English constitution, which Hegel indeed attacked in his writing on the Reform Bill (1831).

It is not enough to die on the battlefield as the lord does; one must also live for and through the State. The warrior returning from the battlefield, "the veteran", is dangerous to the State if he thinks only of what he did for it during the war. For the post-revolutionary citizen, the true civil servant, his whole life, not just his death, is a function of the State. The remark about veterans, written in the 1930s, has contemporary resonance. The ideal of a life wholly devoted to the State is Kojève's picture of the final citizen, and anticipates his later career as a French civil servant.

Hoffmeister p. 362: the dialectical passage to absolute monarchy through language, a specifically Christian phenomenon. Language is Christian because it arises from the inner self that the Christian world discovered.

Hoffmeister pp. 362 ff. contain a note on language in general. Language is a synthesis of particular and universal. The spoken "I" expresses a particular I that has universal value as such, since all others understand it in its particularity. This applies only to the perfect language of absolute knowledge, Hegel's own, who reveals himself, while remaining Hegel, as universal man (Spirit); to the language that is the *Phenomenology*. Being precedes its revelation (*Sprache*, *Logos*), but history can be completed only by an awareness of being expressed in language. At the end, the perfect, Napoleonic State is understood by the perfect citizen, Hegel, speaking the perfect language of the *Phenomenology* and the *Encyclopaedia*. Hegel's ¶508 on language as the existence of the self for others is read as a theory of the Sage's discourse. The priority of being over its revelation is Kojève's realism: discourse does not create being but completes it by revealing it.

Hoffmeister p. 363 begins the analysis of the language specific to absolute monarchy. History expresses class struggle; the truly human, anthropogenic fight is a fight for pure prestige. "Vanity" drives the Master to fight for recognition as Master; the same "vanity" is regarded as sin in the Christian world; and "vanity" again grounds the satisfaction of the "definitive" citizen, just as it arose from Desire, animal desire. It is the first and only truly human desire, the desire for recognition. Kojève redefines class struggle as a fight for prestige. This is his decisive correction of Marx: the motive of history is recognition, not economic interest, and economic struggle is its form.

Culture arises from fight and opposition; human culture will be realised in and through class struggle. For language to reach perfection, the opposition between particular and universal must reach its maximum and become conscious. If the opposites determine the opposition, from a certain point the opposition determines the opposites. But only the opposites are ever real; at first the opposition itself is unreal and appears as such only in language. The extremes are real from the start, but the relation between them, the middle term (*Mitte*), exists at first only in the language that expresses it. Where does language have its proper function? First, in the feudal period: in counsel, on the particular side, and in command and law, on the universal side, the State. Third, in its truly specific form, as middle term between opposites, in the language of discussion, which will become the language of the pre-revolutionary intellectual of Chapter V, and which is first "the language of flattery", that of the courtier at Versailles (Hoffmeister p. 364). The thesis that relations exist first only in language is important for Kojève's theory of the concept: discourse mediates before action does. Flattery is the first social form of this mediation.

How does the feudal lord's mute service become the courtier's "speaking" service? The lord represents the principle of particularity as landowner, but is one with the universal through his military service. He is thus double within himself; there is conflict between the private owner's interests and his duty as warrior serving the State, so he begins to speak, to make the contradiction explicit and reveal it in language. Likewise the State is, for him, as particular as he is, in the monarch, and also a military, potentially universal, conquering unit. The State too is double, a contradiction, and it too begins to speak. The contradiction of the State as particular is expressed in language. The feudal State becomes absolute monarchy, where the monarch can say "L'État c'est moi". His courtiers will serve him only by speech, flattery, and his opponents will oppose him only by speech, pamphlets. The derivation of speech from inner contradiction explains why language flourishes in the Christian world: it is the divided consciousness that speaks.

Since the feudal lord is a private owner, the State opposed to him also becomes private property: absolute monarchy. What is new is that the opposition is spoken of; this is already a relation, a link, a synthesis, and that is the relative perfection of this new, still Christian, world. The first form of discourse is the flattery of the courtier at Versailles, and the King too speaks. «Versailles est la première synthèse — purement verbale — entre le Particulier et l'Universel» (Versailles is the first synthesis, purely verbal, between particular and universal) (p. 127). Versailles as a verbal synthesis is Kojève's interpretation of Hegel's "language of flattery" (¶511): the monarch's universality exists in the courtiers' words.

But this synthesis is hereditary; it concerns the monarch's being, not his doing. Moreover, the monarch is recognised only verbally, and not by all but only by Versailles. That is its essential inadequacy, which distinguishes him from Napoleon, «chef de l'État universel et homogène» (head of the universal and homogeneous State) (p. 128), truly recognised by all through the common action of fight and labour of all. The monarch is recognised only by "everybody", the world of Versailles, a tiny minority. The courtiers who tell him what he is do not behave as if he really were; they merely say he is absolute master of all and try to live independently of him, for themselves. The phrase "universal and homogeneous State" appears here for the first time in the book; it will become Kojève's name for the end of history. The contrast between Louis XIV and Napoleon is between recognition in words by a few and recognition in deeds by all.

Versailles is therefore not an actuality (*Wirklichkeit*) but still an "ideal", a "project", which the Revolution will later realise. The courtier at Versailles is the man of pleasure of Chapter V. The identification of the courtier with the man of pleasure localises V, B, a historically.

Versailles is the germ of the post-revolutionary State, and «Louis XIV est le germe de Napoléon» (Louis XIV is the germ of Napoleon) (p. 128). The dialectic of the Christian world must still transform Louis XIV into Napoleon, doubled by Hegel. Louis XIV is absolute monarch only within the Court and with respect to his courtiers. His being depends on them; eventually he will depend on them in fact, as the master depends on servants. The State will thus finally depend on the rich: on property, wealth, and capital, which is evil for the Christian. The Master's dependence on the Slave (¶192) returns as the monarch's dependence on the court. The doubling of Napoleon by Hegel states the thesis that the end of history needs both a man of action and a man who understands.

The State depends on a particular group, and particularity relies on and expresses itself through wealth. The bourgeois wants to be rich to be independent, and for that his wealth must be recognised by the State, which on this plane must be richer than any courtier. So one has a bourgeois State, republic or "constitutional" monarchy, parliamentarism. The monarch is now an empty name, and power belongs to wealth. Kojève reads Hegel's passage from flattery to wealth (¶511–517) as the history from absolutism to constitutional regimes.

The courtier in fact pursues only a private aim, wealth. The nobility neither conforms to the reality of the State nor is conformist; but that is, by definition, "base and vile" consciousness. There are therefore no longer villeins or lords, only bourgeois. What was new in Christianity, the principle of particularity, is now realised. The "truth", revealed reality, of the Christian lord is the bourgeois, the tendency to make particularism prevail. The noble consciousness turns into the base one (¶517–520), which in social terms means the nobility becomes bourgeois.

At the time of the Revolution the true aristocracy had already been eliminated; there were only bourgeois. «La Révolution française apporte la suppression non pas de l'Aristocratie, mais de la Bourgeoisie en tant que telle» (the French Revolution brings the suppression not of the aristocracy but of the bourgeoisie as such) (p. 128), by restoring, in and through Napoleon, the value and reality of the State, the universal.
