This paradoxical thesis is central. The Revolution's enemy is not the nobility, already gone, but the bourgeois principle of particularity; its result is the universal State.

In wealth the bourgeois is governed by laws other than the universalist laws of the State, but by economic laws, which are also universal. Wealth, capital, is for the bourgeois an anonymous universality. Freeing himself from the State through parliamentarism, the bourgeois believed he was freeing himself in his particularity, since he believed wealth suited him. But in fact the State is not "selfish", since it wants as many citizens as possible, whereas wealth rejects those who want to possess it and reduces the number of those who do. Wealth, despite appearances, is hostile to the particular. But its only aim is the particular. Wealth is therefore "in itself overcome"; it abolishes itself. That is the dialectic of the Christian world. The contrast between the State, which multiplies citizens, and capital, which concentrates wealth, is Kojève's economic reading of Hegel. It anticipates Marx's thesis of concentration without adopting Marx's conclusion.

Christian servitude is eliminated through the dialectic of rich and poor bourgeois, the progressive transformation of the poor bourgeois into an intellectual who suppresses servitude in thought, like the Stoic. He differs from the Stoic in being in fact a slave of himself, not of a Master: of God, whom he created without suspecting it, and of wealth, which created him without his realising it. This is sublimated servitude (*auf-gehoben*); its ultimate cause, like that of the other servitude, is the Christian attitude toward death: the Christian denies his finitude, believes in immortality, and refuses to accept his death, as the Slave enslaved himself to save his life. The chain of servitudes, to Master, to God, to capital, has a single root: refusal of death. This is Kojève's deepest thesis about the Christian world.

Wealth has become an object (*Gegenstand*), an external objective reality whose laws the bourgeois undergoes, as the pagan underwent the State's laws and idle man those of nature. But wealth is in fact the bourgeois's work, created by him to oppose the State's universal. Through it he alienates himself and suffers the yoke of his exclusive particularism, just as the Master suffered the yoke of his one-sided universalism. There is no synthesis yet. The symmetry between Master and bourgeois is exact: each is enslaved by the principle he embodies.

Hoffmeister p. 367, last paragraph, and p. 368: the rigidity of economic laws. From "Von jeder" on p. 368 to the end of the first paragraph of p. 369: unlike the Stoic, the bourgeois cannot be indifferent to what is not his self, since wealth is the conscious and voluntary work and the foundation of his self. He cannot declare himself indifferent to the wealth, capital, that enslaves him. The bourgeois's inability to be indifferent is why his servitude drives him to revolt rather than to Stoicism.

Seeing this objectification of wealth, the bourgeois is outraged; all moral values seem false to him. He becomes a Sceptic and nihilist: in Hegel's words, "the purest inequality", "the pure I itself is absolutely disrupted" (Hoffmeister p. 368). The receiver of wealth's gifts, humiliated by dependence (¶517–518), is the source of the "disrupted consciousness".

Poverty is characteristic of the Christian bourgeois State. Even the rich bourgeois is poor, since he possesses only riches, not Wealth. The distinction between riches and Wealth (*des richesses*, *la Richesse*) marks the difference between particular possessions and the universal power of capital, which no one possesses.

Hoffmeister p. 369: the dialectic of the rich man who gives and the poor man who receives. Wealth now links the particular to the universal, no longer the Family or war. The poor man, lacking wealth, is reduced to pure particularity and is therefore pure nothingness. This is the "bottomless depth" (*bodenlose Tiefe*) that opens beneath the rich bourgeois's feet (Hoffmeister p. 370). The poor man is nothing because in the bourgeois world only wealth mediates universality. His nothingness is the abyss that threatens the rich.

Who actually realises "evangelical poverty", in fact and not in intention, which does not count for Hegel? «Le prolétaire du monde bourgeois, non les Apôtres» (the proletarian of the bourgeois world, not the Apostles) (p. 130). This is the revelation of the nothingness of the "creature" proclaimed by Christianity. So it is the poor bourgeois who will speak the most Christian language possible, so Christian that it ceases to be so and becomes atheist, then revolutionary. Since the essence of Christian language is self-critique, its end will be self-suppression. The proletarian as the realisation of Christian poverty is a brilliant reversal: what the Gospel preached as ideal, capitalism produces as fact. The self-suppression of Christianity passes through its most consistent speakers.

Hoffmeister p. 370: there are two types of language. One is conformist, flattery, now "base". The other is nonconformist, the language of disruption (*Sprache der Zerrissenheit*), now "noble", since it corresponds to the reality of the Christian world; it understands and expresses it, reveals it in speech, *Logos*. The reversal of noble and base between flattery and disruption follows ¶520–521: the disrupted consciousness is truer because it tells the truth about a disrupted world.

This new bourgeois world implies a "Republic of Letters", the "intellectual bestiary" of Chapter V, culture. The intellectual who speaks the language of disruption is its spirit; it is abstract culture in the proper sense, pure *Bildung*. It is a "civilised world" that exalts "cultural values". The identification of the spiritual animal kingdom with the Republic of Letters of the eighteenth century gives Chapter V its historical location.

The language of disruption reveals alienation and the inversion of all values. It inverts real, objective values: the State, personified by a monarch who is now only a name, and wealth, seen as the source of evil. The intellectual turns away from both. He also knows that even ideal values, the True, Beautiful, and Good, are at once good and bad. He knows that he is other than what people think of him and other than what he would like to be. The intellectual's self-knowledge is ironic: he knows himself to be what he is not. This is Rameau's nephew's self-description.

The world he lives in is one where all criticise each other and everything is criticised; every day brings an inversion of all values. But the real world is not changed by this language; the critique targets its content, not the world itself. The intellectual Hegel speaks of does not foresee the Revolution, but Hegel knows he is preparing it. The intellectual believes that the middle term uniting the extremes of particular and universal is the Republic of Letters. He believes the "true spirit" is represented by his defiant chatter, "the universal speaking and disrupting judgement". He believes his discourse is invincible and dominates the world. The intellectual's illusion is that talk is mediation. In fact, Kojève says, talk prepares mediation by action, which the intellectual does not intend.

There is still an "honest consciousness" (*das ehrliche Bewusstsein*) in this world. But in reality it does the same thing as the intellectual without being aware of it: by its very existence it destroys the world it verbally recognises as the good. This is the bourgeois proper. The honest consciousness's inconsistency mirrors the intellectual's: one destroys in deed what it praises in word, the other destroys in word what it lives by in deed.

How does the intellectual's discourse appear to the "honest" man? In the person of Diderot's Rameau's Nephew, absolutely frank and sincere, who reveals what he is, namely a lie. His discourse is therefore true and an imposture at once. The imposture (*Betrug*) of Chapter V reappears here. Hegel quotes Diderot's *Le Neveu de Rameau* (in Goethe's translation) throughout ¶521–525. Kojève's point that the Nephew's sincerity is the truthful expression of a lie condenses the paradox.

The "honest" man answers the intellectual with a bare "no", or, if he tries to reason, says the same as the intellectual: "Despite the evil, there is good", a banality that corresponds to the intellectual's dialectic, a "bitter" banality. If he claims one can isolate oneself from the perverted world, the intellectual replies that isolation depends on the very world one wants to leave. If he preaches a "return to nature", he is told it is a utopia. The honest man's two escapes, isolation and return to nature, point to Stoicism and Rousseau; the intellectual refutes both.

The intellectual has already surpassed this bourgeois world in and through his language, but he does not know it. He does not try to overthrow the world his verbal critique has undermined; he reduces himself to the "speaking consciousness", and the world, like the honest man, listens without much emotion. The result is vanity (*Eitelkeit*), the vanity of all things. One notes it and passes to the order of the day. Rameau's Nephew is therefore a clearly conformist attitude, despite its nihilist and sceptical appearance. The conclusion that the nihilist is a conformist extends the analysis of the Sceptic and the man of the tender heart: total verbal negation leaves the world untouched.

Or one tries to escape, not yet by creative, negating, revolutionary action, but by fleeing into a beyond, Christian or secular. Both are in fact Christian, that is, bourgeois, but only the first is religious; the second is atheist. The second will not be discussed again; it is a general attitude that can occur in any society and was described in Chapter V. The two flights, into heaven and into ideal values, repeat the analysis of the 1935–36 summary.

The first, religious aspect is described from "In jener Seite der Rückkehr" (Hoffmeister p. 375). It is the representation of the real, social world in the abstract, in the divine beyond: faith in a kingdom of heaven where individuality is realised and man is recognised in his particularity by the universal, God. The Christian should say of himself and his world what he says of Christ and the kingdom of heaven, since these are in fact the projection into the abstract of the Christian and his bourgeois world. But he cannot say it, since in his own eyes the Christian is not Christ and the real world is not the kingdom of heaven. To be able to say it, he must first transform the real world and himself by the negating, and so creative, action of fight and labour. The kingdom of heaven is the image of the universal State in which each is recognised as an individual. The Christian must make it before he can recognise it as his own.

The Stoic believed he could disregard the world, and would have said any world, had he known another than his own. But there is a world the Christian cannot disregard: the beyond, his ideal realised outside nature. For the secular Christian, the utopian and pseudo-philosopher of Chapter V, the ideal must still be realised within nature, but he neither says nor knows how. The contrast shows the Christian's advantage over the Stoic: he has a positive ideal.

Christian faith is therefore a realism. That is its perfection compared with secular bourgeois utopia; but it is also its inadequacy, since the "reality" it aims at can only be "transcendent", which for Hegel means imaginary, verbal. The claim that faith is a realism is striking: faith holds its ideal to be real, whereas utopia admits that its ideal is not. The believer is right about the reality of the ideal and wrong about its location.

The Christian religion is not religion "in and for itself", which is none other than Hegel's philosophy, absolute knowledge, no longer religion or faith. But it is a true religion, since it acknowledges a transcendence. Paganism, by contrast, is a pseudo-religion; confined to the here below, it is in fact only a cosmology. Christianity implies an unconscious anthropology, since man alone transcends the natural world and himself as natural being; to speak of transcendence is in fact to speak of man. «Le Chrétien parle de l'Homme en croyant parler de Dieu ; mais le Païen, croyant parler de l'Homme (et des dieux) ne parle — en fait — que de la Nature» (the Christian speaks of man believing he speaks of God; but the pagan, believing he speaks of man and gods, in fact speaks only of nature) (p. 132). The asymmetry between pagan and Christian is one of Kojève's sharpest formulations. Transcendence, the religious concept par excellence, is the disguised concept of man's negativity.

The unconscious reflection of the real world in the beyond opposes the Christian's everyday consciousness, and this opposition appears socially, politically, and historically as that of Church and State. The duality of Church and State is the institutional form of the Christian split.

**Faith and Pure Insight** (pp. 376–383). This describes the opposition between faith and Cartesian evidence (*Einsicht*), or Reason in the sense of Chapter V, which are opposed and yet interdependent. If faith is a flight from the world, the flight is determined by the world it criticises and so implies Reason. Christian, Cartesian, bourgeois Reason is essentially critical. Like faith, it reflects the real Christian world, but what it reveals is its internal contradiction, the restlessness (*Unruhe*) of the Idea, negativity, the revolutionary content of Christianity. It is therefore Reason, not faith, that reveals what is specifically Christian in the Christian world. Faith reveals the positive, which remains identical with itself, a natural, non-human being already revealed by the pagan. Reason reveals the negating, specifically human element discovered by Judaeo-Christianity. The inversion is striking: critical reason, not faith, is the true heir of Christianity, because it carries negativity. Kojève reads the Enlightenment as Christianity's own self-realisation.

The first object of Reason's critique is Reason itself. Perpetually critical, it shows itself unstable. To this vanishing instability one opposes a stability that is not only supersensible and otherworldly but also trans-rational: one returns to faith. Faith and Christian, bourgeois Reason of Chapter V engender and destroy each other. The alternation of critique and faith describes the cycle of modern thought; Pascal's return to faith after Cartesian doubt is the model.

Christian Reason is seventeenth-century rationalism; its evidence is that of the Cartesian *cogito*. It tends toward subjective idealism, Berkeley's, which faith opposes. Reason has no content, being purely negative. Faith has a positive content, but raw, "incomprehensible", non-evident: an object. Faith and Reason are thoughts and create only thoughts, "beings of reason"; but the man of faith does not know it and believes God really exists, whereas the man of Reason is self-conscious. The thought of Christian faith is therefore thing-like, hence theology. The man of Reason, pushing his solipsism to the extreme, will declare the world to be his work, or rather the work of thought, of his thought. But he does not understand that one must act, fight and work, to realise thought and create a world. The symmetry is exact: faith has content without self-consciousness, Reason self-consciousness without content. Neither acts.

Hoffmeister pp. 379–382 give the dialectic of faith and Reason in three steps: faith in relation to religion and the world of ideas; faith and Reason in relation to the real world; and faith and Reason in relation to each other. The plan follows Hegel's ¶527–537.

On p. 380, lines 6–9 especially: the world of faith, the beyond, reflects the real world not as it is but as it should be; hence the evolution of the Christian world. The beyond as an image of the ought is the engine of change: the gap between image and reality drives history.

The second paragraph of p. 380 gives the Trinity: the Father is the simple, eternal substance, State power; Christ is the self that sacrifices itself, being for another, wealth; the Holy Spirit is the return of this alienated self into its first simplicity, language. So the Father is the pagan divinity, perfection, preserved in Christianity; Christ is the symbol of the advent of wealth in the world, of the advent of the bourgeois world; the Holy Spirit is the God of the intellectual, of Rameau's Nephew. Kojève follows Hegel's ¶532, which parallels the Trinity with State power, wealth, and their return. His gloss that Christ symbolises wealth, the self that gives itself to all, is audacious but textually grounded in Hegel's description of wealth as "being for others".

The third paragraph of p. 380 treats faith's relations with the real world; the second of p. 381, the relations of faith and Reason (*reine Einsicht*). Faith in the Christian world is a faith one reasons about. The third of p. 381 treats Reason's relation to its own "world", the universe of discourse; p. 382, Reason's relation to the real world. Faith reasoned about is already half Reason, which explains its vulnerability to the Enlightenment.

Rationalisation must become universal (Hoffmeister p. 382): that will be the work of the eighteenth-century Enlightenment. Its critical task will consist mainly in eliminating the idea that man is a "natural", given, "hereditary" being. The critique targets the notion of original, hereditary sin on one side, and the notion of innate genius and talent on the other. The bourgeois intellectual will abolish himself here, becoming a man of action: a revolutionary, then a citizen of the Napoleonic State. The joint target, original sin and innate talent, is well chosen: both make man a given. The intellectual's self-abolition is his becoming a citizen.

The "infinite judgement" (Hoffmeister p. 383) is where the Christian's critical judgement ends, at the close of the real Christian world's development. The infinite judgement negates this world en bloc; it is the absolute nonconformist judgement, the total revolutionary judgement. It is the extreme of "base" consciousness, which thereby abolishes itself and the "noble" consciousness with it. Hegel's "infinite judgement" is the judgement that identifies opposites; Kojève reads it as the total rejection of the existing order. The base consciousness that negates everything abolishes the opposition of noble and base.

On Hoffmeister p. 383, the Enlightenment again: an appeal to all men, to the masses. This is nascent universalism that respects particularity, the beginning of real individuality. The appeal to the masses distinguishes the Enlightenment from the Republic of Letters: its discourse is addressed to all. This universality of address prepares the universality of recognition.

#### II. The Enlightenment

Kojève recalls the alternative. One can accept the world, as the bourgeois intellectual of observing Reason does in Chapter V. Or one can flee, either into heaven, as the religious Christian does in faith, or into an ideal supposed to be worldly, as the "acting" Reason of the Enlightenment does. The Enlightenment is thus the third of three responses to the bourgeois world: acceptance, religious flight, and secular flight toward an ideal that claims to belong to this world.

The Enlightenment's language differs essentially from that of the intellectual of Chapter V, because it prepares the actual Revolution, even though in itself its critique is "empty". It is revolutionary propaganda. The difference between the Republic of Letters and the Enlightenment lies in effect, not content: the same critique, addressed to the masses, becomes a force.

How is this new flight into a secularised "heaven" possible? First, because the bourgeois lives in security in a peaceful world and no longer fears death; he can give up immortality and so every beyond. Second, because he is a city-dweller and nature no longer looks hostile to him, so he need not divinise it as the natural religions of Chapter VII, A did. Third, because he is a citizen and recognised as such, whereas the Slave was excluded from political and social life; he need no longer imagine "a better world" beyond. Each of the three conditions removes a source of religion: fear of death, fear of nature, and exclusion from society. The third is surprising, since Kojève has described the bourgeois as a non-citizen; he means the bourgeois's legal recognition, not full citizenship.

The first paragraph of Hoffmeister p. 383 states the fundamental theme: the interaction of faith and Reason. Both are Christian, abstract forms; they fight and cancel each other in their abstraction. Kojève's reading holds throughout this section that the Enlightenment and faith are two forms of one consciousness, which is Hegel's thesis (¶541–548).

The second paragraph of p. 383 concerns the relation between Reason, here eighteenth-century rationalism, and the real world: the difference between Diderot's rationalism and Descartes's, and between the Diderot of the Enlightenment and his Rameau's Nephew, still purely nihilist. The honest Diderot, as we saw, can say nothing new in reply to the Nephew, who is perfectly self-conscious. But Diderot transcribes the Nephew's language and makes it universal, readable by all. The Nephew stands at the extreme point of individualism and does not care about others; Diderot suffers and wants everyone to hear. If everyone speaks like the Nephew, the world will thereby be changed. «Le Neveu de Rameau universalisé, — c'est l'Aufklärung» (Rameau's Nephew universalised is the Enlightenment) (p. 135). The formula is Kojève's, and it is exact: the Enlightenment adds nothing to the Nephew's critique except its diffusion. Publication turns private nihilism into a public force.

**The Struggle of the Enlightenment against Superstition** (pp. 385–407). The Enlightenment is the propagation (*Verbreitung*) of the Nephew's ideas, and so already a fight for these ideas and therefore against faith and its world. Kojève takes *Verbreitung*, Hegel's word for the spread of pure insight (¶545), as the key to the section.

The first paragraph of Hoffmeister p. 385: the Enlightenment is a social phenomenon, which makes it superior to pagan Scepticism. It gives absolute value to the self of concrete man. It fights the transcendent Christian God, which makes it superior also to bourgeois idealism, which admits transcendence. As pure negation without content of its own, it is an empty "not-A", which will later be filled with a positive content. The three superiorities place the Enlightenment above the Sceptic, the idealist, and, implicitly, the Nephew. Its emptiness is its limit: it knows what it rejects, not what it wants.

The second paragraph of p. 385 gives the Enlightenment's triad: the people, the priests, and the tyrants. The first paragraph of p. 386: the Enlightenment addresses the masses, more exactly their ignorance, to suppress (*aufheben*) it. The triad is Hegel's (¶542): the naive consciousness of the masses, the deceiving priesthood, and the despotism that profits from both. Kojève notes only that the Enlightenment aims at the masses.

The second paragraph of p. 386: Hegel returns to the complementary aspects of the Enlightenment and faith. Reason and faith are identical at bottom. Kojève repeats the thesis because the whole dialectic of the struggle rests on it: the Enlightenment attacks in faith what it itself is.

Hoffmeister pp. 386–388 analyse the Enlightenment's victory. It happens without a fight; it is a "quiet expansion" (Hoffmeister p. 387), spread by propaganda alone. When one notices the extent of the "disease", it is too late. The "Trinity" of the True, Beautiful, and Good has quietly settled beside the Christian God, and "one fine morning" it elbows its comrade and, crash, he falls: a quotation from *Rameau's Nephew*. Hegel's image of the infection that spreads unnoticed (¶545) and Diderot's image of the idol that topples one morning are joined. Kojève's point is that the old order dies of contagion, not of assault, which his reading of the Revolution will stress.

The first paragraph of Hoffmeister p. 388: there was nonetheless a fight. The Enlightenment is verbalism, but this verbalism is a kind of negating action. The man of the Enlightenment is an agitator, a propagandist; there too is secularised Christianity: he is an "apostle". The concession qualifies Kojève's earlier strictures on verbal critique. Propaganda is speech that acts, since it changes those who hear it.

The second paragraph of p. 388 and what follows concern propaganda. Through propaganda every ideology becomes something other than it is; it becomes impure and mendacious. The Enlightenment is a lie because it reveals a lie, that of faith, concretely realised in and through the bourgeois world. The propaganda-Reason of the Enlightenment is perverted because it imagines it is fighting something other than itself. But Christian Reason and faith are one. To safeguard itself, "enlightened" Reason must slander faith. Hegel's charge that the Enlightenment misrepresents faith (¶549–553) becomes a general theory of propaganda: to fight what one is, one must distort it.

At the end of Hoffmeister p. 389: dialectical, active negation is "for itself", consciously, what "in itself", unconsciously, is its other, position; it is synthesis, totality. Every revolutionary action is therefore also self-negating. But the revolutionary does not want to commit suicide, even if he is willing to pass for a murderer. So he wants to pass for other than he is: he places himself, or imagines he places himself, outside society, so as not to be dragged down in its ruin, and to do so he slanders society. Slander is the force of propaganda: to decry society is in fact to adhere to it. The revolutionary is therefore a liar. But he forms one body with society as its slanderer; in and through him society slanders itself; it is itself a lie, and even a conscious lie. Slander is the sign of the existing society's weakness, not of the weakness of revolutionary propaganda. It will disappear only through the suppression of the slandered, society, not of the slanderer, the revolutionary. Slander will have no hold on the new, post-revolutionary society. To "slander" it would be to say that it does not differ from the old one. That is partly true, since the present implies the past, though not the future. The so-called slander would then only tell the truth, and so it would be powerless, since truth reveals what is and negates nothing. The "slander" would not be propaganda at all but a contribution to a better understanding of the new society, and so its affirmation and reinforcement. This long note is a small theory of revolutionary speech. The revolutionary must misrepresent society because he belongs to what he negates; his lie is the society's own self-denunciation. The claim that criticism of the final society would be true but harmless follows from the end of history: once no future can differ from the present, critique becomes description.

The man of propaganda proper, who does not act, is estranged (*entfremdet*): he imagines he is already other than he is, whereas he could only become so by action. The analogy with the Christian holds: the Christian too believes himself estranged, but after his discontent with society he flees toward a transcendence with positive content. The Enlightenment's critique of faith and society is at first without positive content: the transcendent is replaced by nothing. The positive idea forms in action. The positive content of this critique will be, after the Revolution, the observation that man and society, now in conformity, agree. Before critique and propaganda, man conforms to his pagan world without knowing it. Critique, propaganda, and Revolution oppose him consciously to his Christian, bourgeois world. After the Revolution he conforms again, but now he is a "conformist", conscious and satisfied to be so. The revolutionary, active negation of society by fight, which is also a negation of oneself as determined by the old society, thus ends in the reconciliation of transformed man with himself and with transformed society, which equals the State, which equals the historical world. The triad of unconscious conformity, conscious opposition, and conscious conformity is Kojève's scheme of history in miniature. It also redefines the end of history as a return to conformity, now chosen.

Hoffmeister pp. 390–396: the Enlightenment disfigures faith, and faith does not recognise itself in its critique; how faith answers. Kojève passes over Hegel's detailed analysis of the three charges against faith, concerning its object, its ground, and its practice (¶553–565).

The paragraph on Hoffmeister p. 396 begins the Enlightenment's positive doctrine. At first it was only negating; this is the passage from propaganda-Reason to revolutionary action. It has three parts: deism, sensualism, and "utilitarianism". The three positive doctrines are Hegel's (¶557–561): the absolute being as empty, sense-certainty as the truth of the finite, and utility as the relation between them.

Deism, from the last line of Hoffmeister p. 396: the absolute essence, the "supreme being", becomes a void, a "vacuum" (p. 397). This is the maximal sublimation of the Christian idea of transcendence: the divine beyond is so "other" than the natural world that it is no longer anything at all. Hence a reversal and the beginning of immanentism: deism is already in fact atheism. We will see later that the truth of the Enlightenment is atheism, or more exactly anthropotheism. For Hegel accepts the pagan idea of a realised and total perfection, but this perfection is the presence (*Gegenwart*), the "real presence", of Spirit in the world, this "Spirit" being "total" man after the end of history, or better the integrated totality, in and through Hegel's thought, of human history. The claim that deism is atheism is standard; Kojève's addition is the positive sense of anthropotheism. The pagan idea of perfection returns in the completed totality of history, which is the one thing that is perfect because nothing can be added to it.

Sensualism, the paragraph on Hoffmeister p. 397, is the necessary complement of deism. It differs from the "sensualism" of Chapter I in that man here has passed through all the experiences of the beyond before returning to the "sensation" of the real, whereas there he had not yet surpassed the sensible real. The distinction between first and second immediacy is Hegelian: the Enlightenment's return to the senses is mediated by the whole history of transcendence.

Utilitarianism, the paragraph on Hoffmeister p. 398: everything is for man, who is the measure of all things. The Enlightenment has a double attitude toward sensible things: they exist in themselves, and they are for something else, for human consciousness. This is analogous to the dialectic of good and evil, an abstract transposition of it into the opposition of being-in-itself and being-for-another: everything is at once end and means, as everything was for the believing Christian both good and evil. For the Enlightenment everything must serve some purpose, a secularisation of the Christian category of service. At the same time the autonomy and absolute value of each thing appear. Everything serves everything; each thing serves the universe and the universe serves each thing, so every thing is also an end in itself. Compare the dialectic of wealth, which is nothing in itself, gives itself to the first comer, and yet dominates everything (Hoffmeister pp. 398–399). We are indeed in the Christian, bourgeois world. The paradox follows that each thing is an absolute end. At the same time the Enlightenment regards every judgement as relative, hence instability. This "utilitarianism" is the ideological expression of the rich bourgeois and of the man of pleasure of Chapter V; compare the naturalist anthropology of phrenology (V, A, c). Everything that exists exists for me, for my pleasure. This "egoism" needs a complement, which will be bourgeois altruism, socialism, and "harmonism" (Hoffmeister p. 399). In these bourgeois conceptions one has a "being of all and each", not a "doing of all and each" as in the post-revolutionary State: cohabitation, not interaction. The Enlightenment is unconscious of its truth, hence its flatness and ridiculousness. It is Hegel who knows that it prepares the Revolution, action; it does not know it itself and so does not say it. The analysis of utility as the secularisation of service is Kojève's; it links the Enlightenment to the feudal *Dienst*. The distinction between the being of all and the doing of all separates the liberal harmony of interests from the citizens' common work. Utilitarian society coexists; the final State acts together.

Hoffmeister pp. 400–407 treat the interaction of the Enlightenment and faith. The first paragraph of p. 400 shows how the Enlightenment appears to faith: as flatness. Faith's charge of shallowness against the Enlightenment is Hegel's; Kojève accepts it as true of the Enlightenment's self-understanding.

The second paragraph of p. 400: the right (*Recht*) of the Enlightenment, its right to exist and to triumph over faith, which is its truth. The divine right of faith is opposed to the purely human right of the Enlightenment. In paganism the one is the right of the dead, of the Family, the other the right of the living, of the State; the one is the right to be properly buried, the other the right of the living to bury the dead, or rather, very exactly, the right of the dead to bury their own dead. For when faith is dead, the Enlightenment is no less so: it dies burying faith, since it lived only by its critique. After the French Revolution, however, the Enlightenment is resurrected by and in Hegel's philosophy, and with it faith too, in what both have that is true. The Enlightenment and faith become "immortal" in and through Hegel's philosophy. But in this "resurrection" it is human right that wins and is absolute: «ce n'est pas Dieu qui devient homme, mais l'Homme qui devient Dieu» (it is not God who becomes man, but man who becomes God) (p. 139). The allusion to Matthew 8:22, "let the dead bury their dead", is turned against the Enlightenment. Its death with faith, and their joint resurrection in Hegel, repeat the Christian narrative in the history of ideas.

The right of faith is the right of being; that of the Enlightenment is the right of doing, which negates being. So the Enlightenment will triumph over faith. The divine right of faith is also the right of pure thought, a right to "eternal" thought. In abolishing it, the Enlightenment commits an injustice (*Unrecht*). But this injustice is human right: the right to injustice. Human action is always criminal, because negating, here too. The formula "right to injustice" condenses Kojève's ethics of action: to act is to violate a given right, and the violation becomes right only by success.

**The Truth of the Enlightenment** (pp. 407–413). Otherness (*Anderssein*) is what lies beyond thought, the real, concrete world. Man now relates his Reason to otherness, to the real world, so the Enlightenment returns to reality. But not to reality as it exists in its given structure; the "enlightened" man of Reason is no longer obliged to accept it. The world is for him formless matter, a pure thought or a "pure" thing, and he can do with it what he likes. Distinctions within the world are no longer accepted as given; human activity introduces them into the world voluntarily and consciously, and destroys them too. Yet the Enlightenment's thought is still subjective, and the real world is still a beyond for it. Not yet having become true action, fight and labour, it is not always different from faith, since it is still estranged from itself. Man does not yet know that his "absolute essence", God or his innate "nature", is identical with the "movement of consciousness", that is, with himself as he creates himself through the action of fight and labour in the course of history. The world as formless matter awaiting human form is the premise of the Revolution: nothing in it is sacred or fixed. Kojève's gloss on the "absolute essence" as the movement of self-creation states his anthropotheism once more.

After the Enlightenment's victory there is a fight within the Enlightenment itself, and this split proves its victory, since it shows that the opposing party has been completely crushed. The internal duality of Christianity is now expressed in two different systems: deism, which becomes idealism, and sensualism, which becomes materialism. They differ only in two different starting points of *Bildung*; otherwise they are completely identical. The observation that a victorious party splits is Hegel's (¶575), and Kojève's parenthetical agreement suggests he has contemporary parties in mind. The identity of idealism and materialism is Hegel's thesis about "pure essence" and "pure matter" (¶577).

"Pure matter" accounts no better for the richness of nature than "pure spirit" for the richness of history. Neither party of the Enlightenment managed to surpass Cartesian metaphysics, to understand that in itself being, space, and thought, time, are identical. In truth they are not identical; they become so only in the course of history. It is through action that thought becomes real being and being is thought. Only then does "thought is thinghood, or thinghood is thought" hold (Hoffmeister p. 410). That is the "truth" and "synthesis" of deism become idealism and of sensualism become materialism. In the Enlightenment, Christian dualism has become evident in the irreducible opposition of idealism and materialism, and that is all. Kojève corrects Hegel's sentence: thought and thinghood are identical only as a result of history. The equation of being with space and thought with time is the first statement in the book of the thesis the 1938–39 lectures develop: the concept is time.

There remains the third aspect of the Enlightenment, "utilitarianism", which contains its truth properly speaking. A thought has value only if put to work: that is what the utility dear to "enlightened" Reason shows. Reason has three adversaries who call it "flat and petty": faith; "aestheticism" or sentimentality (*Empfindsamkeit*); and "abstraction calling itself speculation", that is, bourgeois pseudo-philosophy. But this is not yet absolute truth, since man thinks he must be useful to what already is; it is not yet active negativity. His idea of himself does not yet encroach on social reality, which still has the form of an object. Man still lives in a world that is not his own, the pre-revolutionary world. He wants to use what exists, not to create what is useful to him by the action of fight and labour. The Revolution will do that. «L'Homme "éclairé" qui commence à agir, c'est le Révolutionnaire de 1789» (the "enlightened" man who begins to act is the revolutionary of 1789) (p. 141). Utility is the truth of the Enlightenment because it measures thought by its effects; it falls short because it measures effects against the given world. The step from using the world to making it is the step to revolution.

#### III. Absolute Freedom and Terror

The attempt to realise the Christian ideal on earth is the French Revolution. Kojève's one-sentence thesis joins the secularisation reading to the political history: 1789 is Christianity made worldly.

The introduction (Hoffmeister p. 413): in utility, consciousness, man, has found its concept (*Begriff*). But it is still an object and an unattained end (*Zweck*). That is why there is no satisfaction, no objective, social realisation of the subject, the particular. Kojève recalls the terms: being-in-itself is man's natural being; being-for-itself is the idea man has of himself; being-for-another is social existence. The revolutionary transformation of society comes not through labour but through the fight for recognition. Man must no longer conform to the object, which was utilitarianism properly speaking, but destroy and transform it. This transformation had taken place "in itself", imperceptibly and unconsciously; now, in absolute freedom, it takes place consciously and voluntarily. The distinction between labour and fight as modes of transformation matters: labour transformed nature and the Slave; the Revolution transforms society, and requires risk.

Hegel does not speak of the fall of the Ancien Régime. It is already dead here, killed by the Enlightenment's propaganda; now it is only being buried. «Une grande Révolution est toujours non-sanglante à son début» (a great Revolution is always bloodless at its beginning) (p. 141); there is not even a fight. The Ancien Régime dies of disease, by contagion (Hoffmeister p. 387), not by murder, and the disease is the Enlightenment's propaganda. Now the corpse is buried: this is the world of absolute freedom. What is there now? No more conformism, since there is nothing left to conform to. Nothing real separates man any longer from satisfaction, but he is still far from it. There is liberation from a given that no longer exists, but not yet creation of a new real world. Man is in total emptiness: that is "absolute freedom". The thesis that great revolutions begin without bloodshed is a historical generalisation Kojève offers on his own account. It locates the violence of revolution not in the overthrow of the old order but in the attempt to build the new one.

On Hoffmeister pp. 413–414: the reality of the "given", pre-revolutionary world has vanished. There remains only a semblance (*Schein*) of world and State. The real Christian-bourgeois world and the Christian-bourgeois ideology no longer exist, except in the consciousnesses that justify and regret, or condemn, this vanished world and ideology. There is no longer a community, only isolated men, particulars. The State exists only in the particulars' ideas, their projects for a constitution. These are reduced to their inner, non-objective reality, their "revolutionary consciousnesses"; they are "pure metaphysics"; they can think and say anything. There is no world any more, only an unstructured object, the empty place for a world. Being-for-another has taken refuge in being-for-itself, in the self; but the self is now no different from the I and corresponds to no objective, social, political human reality. Each can want to turn his personal ideas into political reality without passing for a madman or a criminal; each can say "L'État c'est moi" in proposing "his" constitution. The self-consciousness's knowledge can turn into a dialectical "movement", a social, political, historical process; each one's subjective certainty can become truth for all, all without fight, effort, or the destruction of a given. That is absolute freedom. The condition of absolute freedom is precisely the one in which the madman and the criminal of the Introduction would be vindicated: when there is no order, every private idea is a candidate for reality. Kojève's image of the empty place for a world is striking.

Hoffmeister p. 414 to p. 417 describe the dialectic of the libertarian period at the start of the Revolution, an ideology that is only an illusion: absolute freedom is pure nothingness, which equals death. The equation of absolute freedom with death was prepared by the Sceptic's negativity, which isolated led to suicide (p. 65).

There is an immanent inadequacy in this attitude: there is no fight, no risk of life, so action is immediate, not mediated by the nothingness of death. The Ancien Régime having died without a fight, the man of absolute freedom believes that "the action of all and each", which creates the post-revolutionary State, can also be carried out without a bloody fight, that this action can be "immediate". On Hoffmeister p. 415: all classes (*Stände*) have disappeared, man is a particular in the strong sense, and he believes he can represent humanity in general as such, a serious illusion. The diagnosis is the one Kojève applies throughout: every immediacy is an unpaid debt to death. The revolutionaries believed the new State could be made as easily as the old one fell.

This ideology of absolute freedom is indeed the "heaven come down to earth" that "enlightened" Reason dreamed of (Hoffmeister p. 413). In fact it is a void that annihilates itself. The realisation and revelation of this self-annihilation of absolute freedom is the Terror (*Schrecken*), mediation by death. The phrase "heaven come down to earth" is Hegel's (¶581); Kojève had announced it as the theme of VI, B (p. 107). The Terror is its truth: the earthly heaven, as long as it is only a void, is death.

On Hoffmeister p. 416: this is the revolutionary government of the period of absolute freedom, which appears to be a dictatorship, since any particular can want to say "L'État c'est moi". No one opposes this government. It comes to power without a fight; everything it says will be law (*Gesetz*), everything it does an act of State (*Staatsaktion*). But it is not a dictatorship, precisely because nothing opposes it; it is constituted in a void. It leaves no traces in objective reality, and in fact no one obeys it. It can accomplish no real, positive work. There is no successful action, and therefore no true, real freedom. The paradox that a government without opposition cannot be a dictatorship follows from Kojève's theory of action: power exists only where it meets and overcomes resistance.

Hoffmeister p. 416 to p. 417: what should have been done then, and what Napoleon will later do, is a post-revolutionary corporative State, the hereditary social classes having been destroyed. Hegel's text (¶588) says absolute freedom cannot tolerate division into "spiritual masses"; Kojève reads it as prescribing a re-articulation of society in non-hereditary corporations, which he attributes to Napoleon. The word "corporative", in 1937, is loaded; Kojève uses it in Hegel's sense of estates open to merit.

On Hoffmeister p. 417: any revolutionary government wants to realise absolute freedom; then it becomes in fact dictatorial: it is "the fury of disappearing" (*die Furie des Verschwindens*), the fury of annihilation, the Terror (*Schrecken*). Hegel's phrase (¶589) names the only work absolute freedom can do: destruction.

The last paragraph of Hoffmeister p. 417 to p. 419 describes the dialectic of the Terror. The government wants to realise freedom and suppresses "absolute" freedom, but thereby prepares the realisation of true freedom. "Absolute" freedom is a nothingness: it is not, which is why its "realisation" or revelation is only death and nothingness. The Terror's double effect, suppressing false freedom and preparing true freedom, gives it a necessary place in the dialectic.

In the state of absolute freedom each wants to become dictator and impose his particular will on all. Anyone can become one, but he is then only a pseudo-dictator, since the other wills remain particular and so impenetrable to his. The idea of dictatorship is abstract; to realise it the particular wills must actually be suppressed, by death and the Terror. For there is no universal will any more, only particular beings, who can be reached only in their biological existence, not in their works or actions, since they do nothing, they only "oppose". Such a process could end only in the extermination of all members of society and the suicide of the pseudo-dictator himself. «La Terreur n'est en fait que le suicide de la Société même» (the Terror is in fact only the suicide of society itself) (p. 143). Hegel's point that the only work of absolute freedom is death, "the coldest, flattest death" (¶590), is read as the logic of a government that faces only particular wills. Because citizens produce nothing, they can be reached only in their bodies.

The realisation of absolute freedom takes place through a fight of factions. There the Slave, or the bourgeois former Slave, finally frees himself, since this is for him the fight (*Kampf*), the bloody fight for recognition he needed to integrate into his being the element of mastery, of freedom. The revolutionary government is the victorious faction, and its final fall is as necessary as that of the other factions, which are particulars. For the post-revolutionary government cannot be a party government, a government of only a part of the whole: it must abolish itself or be abolished. But as long as it is revolutionary it must be a party government and so act by Terror. This is Kojève's central claim about the Revolution: the Terror is the Slave's fight for recognition, the risk of death he refused at the origin. The theory of party government that must abolish itself anticipates his later reflections on revolutionary dictatorship.

Through the Terror man becomes aware of what he really is: nothingness. "The terror of death is the intuition of this its negative essence", the essence of freedom (Hoffmeister p. 419). Only after this experience does man become truly "rational" and want to realise a society, a State, in which freedom is truly possible. Until this moment of the Terror, man, still a Slave, still separates soul from body; he is still Christian. Through the Terror he understands that to want to realise abstract, "absolute" freedom is to want his death, and he then understands that he wants to live, body and soul, here below, since that alone truly interests him and can satisfy him. The Terror, "the fear of its absolute master, death" (Hoffmeister p. 420), disposes particular consciousnesses to accept a State in which they can realise themselves in a divided and limited way, and yet be truly and really free. Hegel's phrase repeats ¶194, "the fear of the absolute master, death": the Terror reenacts the Slave's origin, but now the Slave has faced death. Kojève's reading that the Terror ends the separation of soul and body makes the Revolution the end of Christian dualism in lived experience.

Once more: it is through the Terror that slavery ends, and with it the Master–Slave relation itself, and so Christianity. Henceforth man will seek satisfaction on this earth and within a State. There will be no absolute freedom in it, except for the chief, Napoleon; even his freedom, one can say, is limited by reality; yet the chief of the post-revolutionary State is fully "satisfied" by his action, since the reality that limits it is entirely his own work. The claim that only Napoleon is fully free and satisfied is qualified in the next section: all citizens are potentially so.

The paragraph on Hoffmeister p. 420, from "Der Geist wäre" to "konnte": there is no going back. Despite appearances the post-revolutionary State is radically different from pre-revolutionary States. At line 22, "Aber": there is no return because this State presupposes absolute freedom, which it destroys only to realise its nothingness. Hegel's rejection of a return to the old order (¶593–594) is read as the irreversibility of history: the Restoration cannot restore.

The Revolution, the revolutionary, is a function neither of natural instincts nor of a given aim, which would then depend on the given world and not be revolutionary. The revolutionary acts consciously not to establish an ideal world but to destroy the given world, and he knows it. And it is he who will rebuild a new world from nothing. There is thus a self that creates itself from a world reduced to nothing. There is no true creation without prior destruction of the given: action equals negating negativity. The thesis that the revolutionary aims at destruction, not at an ideal, distinguishes him from the utopian of Chapter V. Creation *ex nihilo* is the secularised divine attribute that the revolutionary appropriates.

Absolute freedom is therefore the highest and last *Bildung*, which reveals to man his nothingness, without positivist "compensation": "the meaningless death, the pure terror of the negative" (Hoffmeister p. 421). And the State that follows will be the summit of negativity, its "dialectical reversal" into absolute positivity. The phrase "without positivist compensation" rules out any consoling reading of the Terror. The final State is negativity turned into positivity: a world wholly made by negation, which therefore no longer needs to negate.

#### C. Spirit Certain of Itself; Morality

Subdivision C of Chapter VI treats the post-revolutionary State, the Napoleonic Empire of 1806. We are at the end of history. The dialectic culminates here in the advent of Hegel himself, more exactly of the *Phenomenology*. Chapter VIII will treat the *Phenomenology*, summarise it from a higher standpoint, and show how and why its whole is the basis of the absolute knowledge realised and revealed in the second part of the System of Science, the *Encyclopaedia*. The historical localisation of VI, C in 1806 is Kojève's; most readers place its shapes within German moral philosophy without dating them to the Empire.

"Spirit certain of itself" is ultimately Hegel himself, his philosophical System, the *Phenomenology* plus the *Encyclopaedia*, which is no longer the search for wisdom but wisdom itself, absolute knowledge. Here subjective certainty (*Gewissheit*) coincides with objective truth (*Wahrheit*), reality revealed by language. But a truth is truly true, universally and necessarily, "eternally", valid, only if the reality it reveals is wholly completed, everything possible having actually been realised, and so "perfect", without possibility of extension or change. This "total", "definitive" reality is the Napoleonic Empire. For Hegel in 1806 it is a universal and homogeneous State: it unites the whole of humanity, at least the part that counts historically, and "suppresses" (*aufhebt*) within itself all "specific differences" (*Besonderheit*): nations, social classes, families. Christianity too being "suppressed", there is no longer a dualism of Church and State. So wars and revolutions are henceforth impossible. That is, this State will change no more and will remain eternally identical with itself. Man is formed by the State in which he lives and acts, so man will not change either. And nature, without negativity, is in any case "completed" from all eternity. Consequently the science that correctly and completely describes the Napoleonic world will remain always and wholly valid. It will be absolute knowledge, the final term of all philosophical inquiry. This knowledge is Spirit certain of itself. Here the argument of the whole book is set out in one chain. Absolute truth requires a completed reality; completed reality is a State that cannot change; such a State is universal, since no external war is possible, and homogeneous, since no internal revolution is. The qualification "at least the part that counts historically" concedes that the universality is not yet actual. The claim that nature is completed from all eternity keeps the dualism: only human reality needed to end.

Ultimately this State no longer changes because all its citizens are "satisfied" (*befriedigt*). I am fully and definitively "satisfied" when my exclusively personal personality is "recognised", in its reality and value, its "dignity", by all, on condition that I myself "recognise" the reality and value of those who are to "recognise" me. To be "satisfied" is to be «"unique au monde et (néanmoins) universellement valable"» ("unique in the world and nonetheless universally valid") (p. 146). That is what is realised for the citizen of the universal and homogeneous State. On the one hand, thanks to its universality, I am "recognised" there by all men, who are all my peers. On the other, thanks to its homogeneity, it is really I who am "recognised", not my family, social class, or nation, "I" as "representative" of a rich or illustrious family, a propertied or governing class, a powerful or civilised nation. The particular, I, relates directly to the universal, the State, without screens formed by the "specific differences", families, classes, nations. In the post-revolutionary world individuality is thus realised for the first time. To be an individual, man properly speaking, is to be "satisfied", no longer to want, and therefore no longer to be able, to "transcend" oneself, to become other than one is. To understand oneself is then to understand integral, definitive, "perfect" man. That is what Hegel does in and through his System. The paragraph states Kojève's concept of satisfaction with precision. The two attributes of the final State correspond to the two sides of individuality: universality to recognition by all, homogeneity to recognition of oneself rather than one's group. The last step, from no longer wanting to no longer being able to transcend oneself, grounds the end of history in desire: capacity for change depends on the wish for it.

Admittedly, only the chief of the universal and homogeneous State, Napoleon, is really "satisfied", recognised by all in his personal reality and value. He alone is therefore truly free, more than all chiefs before him, who were always "limited" by the "specific differences" of families, classes, and nations. But all citizens are "satisfied" potentially, since each can become this chief, whose personal, "particular" action is at the same time universal, State action, the action of all (*Tun Aller und Jeder*). For there is no longer heredity, an "inhuman", "natural", "pagan" element. Each can therefore actualise his desire for recognition, on condition that he accept, as the element of mastery, the risk of death that competition, political struggle, implies in this State, a risk that guarantees the "seriousness" of candidates; and on condition that he has first taken part in the constructive activity of society, the collective labour that maintains the State in reality, the element of servitude or service, which guarantees the candidates' "competence". The citizen's "satisfaction" is therefore the result of the synthesis in him of the warrior-Master and the worker-Slave. What is new in this State is that all are, on occasion, warriors, through conscription, and all take part in social labour. As for the Sage, Hegel, he is content to understand: the State and its chief, the warrior and working citizen, and finally himself, first through the *Phenomenology*, at whose end he finds himself as result, final term, and integration of the historical process of humanity. This Sage, who reveals through "knowledge" the reality incarnated in Napoleon, is the incarnation of absolute Spirit; he is therefore, if one likes, the incarnate God the Christians dreamed of. «Le Christ véritable, réel = Napoléon-Jésus + Hegel-Logos» (the true, real Christ equals Napoleon-Jesus plus Hegel-Logos) (p. 147); the incarnation thus takes place not in the middle but at the end of time. The concession that only the chief is actually satisfied is important: universal satisfaction is potential, secured by open access to the summit. The two conditions of access, risk and labour, reproduce the Master and the Slave within the career of every citizen. The division of the incarnation between Napoleon and Hegel, deed and word, is Kojève's most famous formula. It locates the incarnation at the end of history, as its completion rather than its turning point.

The subtitle reads "Morality". Morality (*Moralität*) is "reflective morality", as opposed to ethical life (*Sittlichkeit*), "customary morality" (VI, A). The pagan Master underwent his State's moral law, custom, as idle man undergoes the laws of nature. Customary morality, a style of life, is accepted as a "given", a "divine command" or, which is already better, a "legacy of the ancestors". It is collective and unconscious of its motives and reason for being. Reflective morality, by contrast, is "invented" by man, who knows that he promulgates it. It is therefore "individual", "mine" if one likes, but supposed to be universally valid. This "philosophical" morality develops within the Napoleonic State, in fact in Germany: Kant, the Romantics (Novalis), and so on, and it ends in Hegel's implicit and definitive morality. The dialectic of this morality from Kant to Hegel is described in VI, C. The contrast between custom and reflective morality follows Hegel's distinction. Kojève's localisation of reflective morality "within the Napoleonic State, in fact in Germany" is his interpretive choice; Hegel's text does not date the moral view of the world.

This subdivision therefore does not speak explicitly of the Napoleonic State, of Napoleon, or of the post-revolutionary citizen. It concerns less the post-revolutionary world than the ideologies that develop in it and that culminate in the Hegelian idea. But Hegel has already spoken briefly of this world at the end of the previous subdivision. He will speak of it incidentally in the analyses of VI, C, answering Napoleon's German critics. And he speaks of it in the short introduction to VI, C. Kojève concedes that his reading goes beyond the explicit text, and names the passages that support it.

The introduction (Hoffmeister pp. 423–424). Here Hegel speaks of the citizen of the universal and homogeneous, Napoleonic State, the fully and definitively "satisfied" man. In reality he means Napoleon, the only one "satisfied" in act, and Hegel himself, also fully "satisfied" by having understood Napoleon. Napoleon acts but does not understand himself; Hegel understands him: "revelation" equals Napoleon plus Hegel. The division between the one who acts and the one who understands is the premise of the whole reading of VI, C and VIII.

Hoffmeister p. 423, lines 1–3, concern the Greek pagan world; lines 3–4 the Roman world; lines 4–9 the Christian world up to Napoleon; line 9 onward and p. 424, the world of post-revolutionary man. Hegel's retrospective sentences (¶596) summarise VI, A and VI, B; Kojève assigns each clause to its period.

Man thinks of the world what the world is, and the world is what man thinks of it. Man himself really conforms to the idea he has of himself. The State is a knowledge (*Wissen*). Man has become God. Napoleon has made all recognise his "vanity", and the State is the revelation and realisation of this "vanity"; in Napoleon vanity is therefore no longer "vain", no longer a sin. The chain of equations describes the end of alienation: thought, world, and self coincide. The fate of vanity, from sin to recognised dignity, completes the triad glory, vanity, dignity of p. 123.

Moreover, man, Napoleon, conforms to the State he created. He is a citizen: he serves his own work; he knows what he does and does only what he knows; there is absolute coincidence of will and knowledge. Napoleon rises above being but does not flee it; he is "really present" in the world, in the State (end of the first paragraph of Hoffmeister p. 424). The coincidence of will and knowledge defines the post-revolutionary agent. "Real presence" returns from 1935–36 (p. 91): the Eucharistic formula now designates Napoleon's presence in his State.

The paragraph on Hoffmeister p. 424: Napoleon is the absolutely free and perfectly satisfied man; he knows he is free; he proves it to himself and others. Kojève follows Hegel's description of the self-certain spirit whose knowledge of itself is its freedom.

But note the word "seems" (*scheint*) on Hoffmeister p. 423: Napoleon does not know that satisfaction comes ultimately from knowledge, not action, though knowledge presupposes action. It is therefore Hegel who is absolutely satisfied. Truth has two aspects, real and ideal. Satisfaction lies not in the being that reveals itself but in the revelation of being. «La Wahrheit, — c'est Napoléon révélé par Hegel, c'est Hegel révélant Napoléon» (the truth is Napoleon revealed by Hegel, Hegel revealing Napoleon) (p. 148). The priority of knowledge over action in satisfaction reverses the anthropology of the Introduction, where satisfaction came from recognition won by fight and labour. Kojève reconciles the two by making knowledge the completion of action: action makes the world, knowledge makes it one's own.

The text of VI, C now follows, in which Hegel speaks of German philosophy from Kant to himself. As always, it is divided into three paragraphs corresponding to the three stages of the real dialectical process described: first, Kant and Fichte as ideologues of "absolute freedom"; second, the self-suppression of Kant's and Fichte's philosophy, ending in a philosophical anarchy recalling the anarchy that preceded the Terror; third, conscience (*das Gewissen*) as Jacobi, the beautiful soul (*die schöne Seele*) as Novalis and Schelling, and evil and its forgiveness (*das Böse und seine Verzeihung*) as Hegel, who by his implicit morality legitimates the revolutionary crime and the completion of the Revolution, and so of history, by Napoleon. The assignment of names to shapes is Kojève's. The identification of "evil and its forgiveness" with Napoleon and Hegel is his most original reading of VI, C.

**The Moral View of the World** (pp. 424–434). This is Kant. Only his anthropology, implied in his morality, and his "moralism" are discussed. Kant is the ideologue of the Revolution, through his critique of utility. But Kant regards nature as independent of human action, a remnant of pagan cosmology and of Christianity. This dualism of man and nature is a remnant of servility toward nature: Kant, living in the pre-revolutionary world, is still a Slave. He does not take account of the interaction of man and nature; he does not understand the labour that transforms the world. Nor has he understood the necessity of a Napoleon, or that man must realise a State to perfect himself and reach satisfaction. The reading of Kant as the Revolution's ideologue is common since Heine and Marx. Kojève's charge is that Kant's separation of freedom from nature is servile: it leaves nature as a given Master.

For Kant satisfaction is a postulate, that is, a faith. He reaches only the "hope" of satisfaction: Kant is the philosopher of hope, a specifically Christian category. Kant postulates guarantors: the immortality of the soul and the existence of God. Kantian man ultimately seeks happiness (*Glück*), given in and through a beyond, not satisfaction. He thus ends in the Christian solution itself. He starts from man's autonomy, homologous to absolute freedom, and ends in man's servitude. Hence an internal contradiction. Kant's third question, "what may I hope?", is read as the mark of his Christianity. The contrast between happiness, received, and satisfaction, achieved, is Kojève's key to the difference between Kant and Hegel.

**Dissemblance** (pp. 434–444). This is the self-suppression of Kantianism. Kantian man cannot take himself seriously, nor the real and complete fulfilment of duty, nor therefore duty itself. He is the ideologue of absolute freedom, which ends in ideological and existential nothingness. Hegel's philosophy would come next, but Romanticism intervenes between Kant and Hegel. Hegel's "dissemblance" (*Verstellung*) exposes the moral consciousness's shifting between positions (¶616–631). Kojève's parallel with absolute freedom makes Kant's morality the ideological counterpart of the Revolution's first phase.

**Conscience; the Beautiful Soul; Evil and its Forgiveness** (pp. 444–472). The Hegelian "forgiveness" (*Verzeihung*) is preceded by Jacobi's conscience and the beautiful soul of Novalis and the Romantics. This is the process of transforming a theist anthropology, Kant's, into an anthropotheist one, Hegel's. The Romantic is the Kantian who has understood himself: he can no longer speak of God without hypocrisy (*Heuchelei*). He should be an atheist but cannot bring himself to it. For the Romantics the perfect man is the one who lives in accord with himself. Hence an immanent contradiction, theoretical and existential. The Romantic stands at the threshold of atheism, and his hypocrisy is his refusal to cross it.

"Living in accord with oneself" is conscience (*das Gewissen*), moral consciousness. Man is the only moral value; he is "justified" as soon as he acts "according to his conscience", whatever it is. But this is inadequate; this anthropology is not viable and is not Hegel's. It lacks mediation by the action of fight and labour. The Romantic has his truth in immediacy, in inaction: that is his error. He transcends being by "the elevation of his soul", but this negation, to be viable, must be realised in being, in nature and the State, by the action that transforms the given. Labour transforms error into truth, and fight transforms crime into virtue; compare the Preface's passage on the true and the false (Hoffmeister pp. 33–34). Crime and madness, which negate being, have value and "remain", as overcome, only if they justify themselves, that is, if they realise a State in which they are recognised as virtue and truth and are no longer considered crime and madness. The pair of formulas, labour turns error into truth and fight turns crime into virtue, completes Kojève's theory of justification by success. Every new truth begins as an error and every new order as a crime.

**Conscience** (Hoffmeister p. 445 to p. 456). Kantian man has not yet become aware of post-revolutionary reality; the man of conscience, Jacobi, is the first to do so. But this consciousness is immediate. It is not mediated by action; it is pure imagination; it is not yet a doing of all and each. One accepts the Revolution but takes no active part in it. This is the attitude of the post-revolutionary intellectual, the Romantic. The identification of the man of conscience with Jacobi is conventional.

The Romantic sees the freedom acquired by the Revolution, the result of labour and fight, but he accepts only the result, not the means, bloody fight and the labour of all. He ignores the prehistory of this freedom and does not see the effort that led to it. He would like to "enjoy the freedom" won by others, as the man of pleasure of Chapter V enjoys the products of others' labour. The comparison with the man of pleasure is exact: the Romantic stands to the Revolution as the pleasure-seeker to labour.

The difference from the pre-revolutionary intellectual of the bestiary (V, C, a) is that the post-revolutionary intellectual has understood that he himself is the supreme value. But his autonomy is revealed not by action but by immediate, subjective conviction, one's own conviction (*eigene Überzeugung*), dependent on nothing but oneself. So the Romantic lives in accord with his own convictions, whatever they are; that is all he wants (Hoffmeister p. 449). Romantic man wants to be "recognised", and in this he is right; but he is wrong to want it "immediately", without effort, without the action of fight and labour. He does not want to fight. When he sees that others do not recognise his convictions as the True, Good, and Beautiful, he is content that others recognise that they are convictions, or his convictions, always admitted alongside others and sometimes true, good, or beautiful. But these convictions are finally not negations of the given, nor even independent of it; on the contrary, they are functions of it, of the individual's instincts or of family, social, and national traditions, "drives and inclinations" (Hoffmeister p. 452). The Romantic intellectual therefore does not realise his ideal. If his convictions are "revolutionary", he does not act; if they are "conformist", he depends on the given; in any case he does nothing for them or according to them. The argument that convictions are functions of the given is Hegel's (¶643–645): conviction, as mere form, can take any content, and that content comes from nature and circumstance.

The intellectual chooses the subterfuge of hypocrisy and denies his failure. He contents himself with tolerance toward his convictions and all others, except "intolerant" ones. This is the pacifist ideology of conscience: political and economic liberalism. The Romantics chatter about the public good while businessmen act according to their private interests. This society is essentially pre-revolutionary, by its extreme particularism and its destruction of Christianity. In the Church's pseudo-society the principle "each for himself, God for all" reigned. God has now been removed, but the principle remains: each for himself in real life, and the Romantic chatters for all. The identification of the ethics of conscience with liberalism is Kojève's political reading. The phrase "essentially pre-revolutionary" implies that liberal society, even after 1789, has not completed the Revolution.

The ideology that reveals this society holds that the universal, truth, the State, emerges from the "free play" of convictions and economic forces. But this play remains a game, and no one takes it seriously: one can reach neither truth, nor universal knowledge, nor a universal State. The target is the liberal theory of the market of ideas and interests. Kojève's objection is that play produces no universal.

The ideal is absolute self-sufficiency (Hoffmeister p. 455), but it is not realised; one believes it can be reached "immediately". The ideal of autarky is the Romantic's version of the Master's independence, pursued without risk.

**The beautiful soul** (Hoffmeister p. 456 to p. 462). The post-revolutionary Romantic is not yet satisfied: he is not universally recognised in his "uniqueness", his genius. Either he imposes his convictions, acts, ceases to be a revolutionary intellectual, and becomes a citizen: Napoleon. Or he does not want to act, and even has the convictions needed not to act. It is enough for him to "express himself" without encroaching on others' convictions. His means is language. In the society where the Romantic lives, one can say anything; everything is "tolerated", and almost everything is found "interesting", even crime and madness. The alternative, Napoleon or the beautiful soul, frames VI, C: the one who acts on his conviction becomes the Emperor; the one who does not becomes a poet.

This man believes he can be "satisfied" by words, words accepted, "recognised", by society. He thereby believes himself universally accepted and satisfied. He must therefore lead a purely literary existence. The beautiful soul repeats the intellectual's substitution of fame for recognition, now in its purest form.

The difference from the intellectual of the bestiary (V, C, a): he no longer flees himself; on the contrary, he describes himself and complacently reveals himself to all. He flees the world, not himself, the only self he knows and cares about. This is man's last flight from the world: refuge in himself, "the ivory tower". The phrase "ivory tower", from Sainte-Beuve, names the Romantic's retreat.

The summit of Romantic expression will be the novel of a novel, the book of a book. There is an analogy with the *Phenomenology*, which explains how the *Phenomenology* itself is possible; but the latter has a real content, man as agent of history. Kojève acknowledges the formal kinship between the self-reflexive Romantic work and the *Phenomenology*, and locates the difference in content: Hegel's reflexivity comprehends history, the Romantic's only itself.

This man is, first, a thought that thinks itself, the pagan, Aristotelian God, and so already anthropotheism; but he settles for little in identifying himself with a pagan divinity, whereas Hegel wants to be Christ. Second, he creates a world from nothing solely in order to be "recognised", the Christian God who creates the world to "reveal" himself in it; except that the Romantic's "world" is only a novel. The two divine attributes, self-thinking thought and creation for the sake of revelation, are the Aristotelian and Christian Gods. The beautiful soul has both, but only in imagination. «Hegel veut être Christ» (Hegel wants to be Christ) (p. 152): the God who acts in history rather than thinks himself.

Romantic imagination, creator of fictional, "marvellous" worlds, culminates in Novalis, as the political action that creates a real world culminates in Napoleon. But even Novalis does not take his "divinity" seriously, whereas Napoleon will be effectively "the God who appears" (*der erscheinende Gott*, Hoffmeister p. 472). The poet is only ever recognised by the few, by a "chapel", not even a Church; Napoleon, by contrast, imposes himself effectively on all. The poet who reduces himself to himself finally exhausts himself and annihilates himself in his own nothingness. This is "absolute untruth" (Hoffmeister p. 461), the lie pushed to the extreme that annihilates itself. This sublimated and vanishing Romantic is the beautiful soul, which equals the Christian unhappy consciousness that has lost its God. The parallel between Novalis and Napoleon is the axis of Kojève's reading of VI, C: imagination and action, the chapel and the Empire. The beautiful soul as the unhappy consciousness without God makes Romanticism the last form of Christianity.

The Romantic poet wanted to be God, and he was right to want it, but he did not know how. He annihilates himself in madness or suicide (Hoffmeister p. 462). It is a "beautiful death", but a death nonetheless: a total and definitive failure. Hegel's beautiful soul "wastes away in yearning" (¶658); Kojève reads it biographically, thinking of Novalis's early death and Hölderlin's madness. The concession "he was right to want it" is striking: the goal is correct, the method wrong.

**Evil and its forgiveness** (Hoffmeister p. 462 to p. 472). Evil is the Revolution and its realiser, Napoleon. Forgiveness is the justification of the Revolution and of Napoleon by Hegel in and through the *Phenomenology*. The theme is Napoleon and German philosophy: Kant and Fichte (Hoffmeister pp. 463–465), the Romantic poet (pp. 465–469), and Hegel (pp. 469–472) facing Napoleon. The identification of the acting consciousness that confesses its evil with Napoleon is Kojève's boldest reading. Hegel's text concerns two abstract figures, the acting and the judging consciousness; Kojève gives them historical names.

From the Christian standpoint Napoleon realises vanity; he is therefore the incarnation of sin, the Antichrist. He is the first who dared to attribute absolute, universal value effectively to human particularity. For Kant and Fichte he is evil (*das Böse*), the amoral being par excellence. For the liberal and tolerant Romantic he is a traitor who "betrays" the Revolution. For the "divine" poet he is only a hypocrite. The judgements reproduce the judging consciousness's charges in ¶660–664: evil and hypocrisy.

For Napoleon there is universally valid morality only for others; he himself is "beyond good and evil", and so, if one likes, a "hypocrite". But Kantian morality has no right to judge him so. Nor, in the name of Romantic judgement, can one accuse Napoleon of egoism and crime, since every action is egoistic and criminal as long as it has not succeeded, and Napoleon has succeeded. Moreover, Napoleon's opponents do not act against him or destroy him; their judgement is therefore pure vanity, chatter. They are pure inactivity, that is, a being, and so a nothingness. If Germany, and so German philosophy, refuses to "recognise" Napoleon, it will disappear as a people; the nations (*Besonderheit*) that want to oppose the universal Empire (*Allgemeinheit*) will be annihilated.
