Hegel's analysis of the judging consciousness's hypocrisy (¶664–666), which judges without acting, is turned into a political warning to Germany. The judgement that the inactive judge is "a being, and so a nothingness" applies the ontology of negativity: whoever does not act does not exist humanly.

But Hegel recognises Napoleon and reveals him to Germany. He believes he can save Germany through his *Phenomenology* and preserve it in sublimated form (*aufgehoben*) within the Napoleonic Empire. The claim that the *Phenomenology* was meant to save Germany by reconciling it with Napoleon is Kojève's speculation. The "forgiveness" of ¶670 becomes Hegel's recognition of Napoleon.

One finally arrives at a duality: the realiser and the revealer, Napoleon and Hegel, universal action and absolute knowledge. On one side there is consciousness (*Bewusstsein*), on the other self-consciousness (*Selbstbewusstsein*). The two sides of the book's first two sections, consciousness and self-consciousness, return here as two persons.

Napoleon is turned toward the external social and natural world; he understands it, since he acts successfully. But he does not understand himself; he does not know that he is God. Hegel is turned toward Napoleon; but Napoleon is a man, man "perfected" by the total integration of history; to understand him is to understand man, to understand oneself. By understanding, which equals justifying, Napoleon, Hegel therefore completes his self-consciousness. That is how he becomes a Sage, an "accomplished" philosopher. If Napoleon is the revealed God (*der erscheinende Gott*), it is Hegel who reveals him. Absolute Spirit is the fullness of consciousness and self-consciousness, the real natural world including the universal and homogeneous State realised by Napoleon and revealed by Hegel. The argument that understanding Napoleon is self-understanding follows from Napoleon's being the completed man: Hegel understands himself by understanding the one in whom humanity is complete. "The God who appears", the last words of Chapter VI (¶671), is read as Napoleon.

Yet Hegel and Napoleon are two different men; consciousness and self-consciousness are therefore still separated. And Hegel does not like dualism. Is the final dyad to be abolished? This could be done, "and even then!", if Napoleon "recognised" Hegel as Hegel recognised Napoleon. Did Hegel expect in 1806 to be called by Napoleon to Paris, to become the philosopher, the Sage, of the universal and homogeneous State, who would explain, justify, and perhaps direct Napoleon's activity? Since Plato the thing has always tempted great philosophers. But the text of the *Phenomenology* that concerns it (Hoffmeister pp. 471–472) is, deliberately perhaps, obscure. «Quoi qu'il en soit, — l'Histoire est terminée» (in any case, history is finished) (p. 154). The speculation about Hegel's hope of a call to Paris is Kojève's, and he marks it as such. The allusion to Plato's journeys to Syracuse anticipates Kojève's debate with Leo Strauss on tyranny and wisdom. The closing sentence detaches the end of history from the unresolved duality: whether or not the Sage is recognised by the Emperor, history is complete.

### Summary of the 1936–1937 Course

The course studied Sections B and C of Chapter VI, devoted to the dialectical development of the Christian world from its origins to Hegel. The summary covers both sections, although the notes show that VI, C was treated in outline.

Hegel sees the origin and foundation of Christianity in the idea of individuality, discovered by the Slave and unknown in the world of the pagan Masters. Individuality is a synthesis of particular and universal: absolute or universal value realised in and through a particular being, and the particular being obtaining as such an absolute, universally recognised value. Only this synthesis, realised as human existence, can give man definitive satisfaction. It makes useless and impossible any flight (*Flucht*) into a beyond (*Jenseits*), in faith or artistic imagination, as well as any genuine surpassing of the given world through the negating effort of fight and labour that creates a new real world. The man who realises individuality therefore perfects and completes historical development. The definition of individuality ties satisfaction and the end of history together: where individuality is real, there is neither flight nor transcendence.

Christianity presupposes, implies, and reveals this idea or ideal of individuality. But at first the Christian Slave, who discovers this ideal because, having no universal or social value, he can attribute value only to his isolated, particular personality, remains subject to the Master's pagan cosmologism, or "naturalism", and universalism; the Master attributed "universal" value to himself as citizen living in a given world. Placing the axiological accent on the universal, the Slave therefore represents (*vor-stellt*) individuality as resulting not from the universalisation of the particular, the deification of man, but from the particularisation of the universal, the incarnation of God. And if his personal value is no longer determined by the place (*topos*) he occupies by birth in the given natural cosmos, he sees this value not in the creation of a human world that would exist only through and for him, but in the aspiration to a "place" in the divine cosmos, also given, since independent of human will. The inversion of incarnation and deification is the key to Kojève's reading of Christianity: the same synthesis, read from the universal downward, is theology; read from the particular upward, it is anthropology.

Christianity is thus at first a religion. The individualist anthropology enters the world in the form of a personalist theology: man begins by saying of God, his Master, what he wants, at first unconsciously, to be himself and what he will finally want and be able to say of himself. As long as man understands himself through the Christian religion, he will see in his proud desire to assign absolute or universally recognised value to his autonomous, purely human particularity not an ideal to realise for self-satisfaction here below, but an evil to repress for salvation in the beyond, granted by the Lord's grace. Discovering pride as the basis and motive of human existence, the Christian religion sees in it the fundamental sin, which it sets out to suppress, and interprets this pride as vain vanity. As long as the world is dominated by the Christian religion, man will not satisfy his pride by realising in the world the ideal of individuality, which is nonetheless the source and essential content of Christianity. To realise Christianity by realising in the empirical world the anthropological ideal of individuality, one must therefore suppress the Christian religion and theology, purifying the new anthropology of the remnants of the Master's pagan cosmology and axiology, and so freeing the Slave from the remnants of his servitude. The thesis that pride is both Christianity's discovery and its condemned sin gives the dialectic its engine: Christianity knows the truth about man and forbids him to realise it.

As long as the Slave depended on the pagan Master who dominated the world, he did not share the universal value of the citizen and could not have his personal value universally recognised. Through his faith in God, the absolute Master before whom all men are equal in absolute servitude, the Slave freed himself from dependence on the human Master. But living in this faith, he does not yet dare attribute to his human particularity the value the Master refused him. Having no real Master any more, he remains a Slave in and for himself; he is his own Slave, believing himself the Slave of a God of whom he is in truth the author. Being thus his own Slave, he can free himself and realise his Christian ideal only by freeing himself from himself, by surpassing himself, ceasing to be what he is. But he is what he is in and through his Christian faith in an absolute Master. It is therefore from this faith, from the Christian religion and the world it dominates, that he must free himself: from this Slave's religion which, by creating a world in which he is enslaved because he enslaves himself, makes him a Slave, and which preserves in his servitude the paganism of the vanished Master. The self-enslavement thesis is the summary's core. The Slave without a Master is his own Master and his own Slave, and his liberation is necessarily a liberation from himself.

Freeing himself progressively from his servitude, the Christian Slave gradually eliminates pagan theology from his religion and becomes more and more conscious of his anthropological ideal of autonomous individuality. He realises this ideal by committing, knowingly and voluntarily, the Christian sin of pride; thereby pride is overcome (*aufgehoben*) as such, and, ceasing to be vain vanity, it maintains itself in its truth (*Wahrheit*) or revealed essential reality. The conscious commission of the sin of pride is the Revolution. Pride becomes dignity by being realised.

This process of the revealing realisation of human individuality is described in Sections B and C of Chapter VI. We learn there, first, that Napoleon realises the ideal of individuality by having the absolute value of his particularity recognised by a world he created, from the revolutionary nothingness, for the sake of that universal recognition; and second, that Hegel reveals this realisation of individuality to men by rethinking history in the *Phenomenology*. The reality of Napoleon revealed by Hegel is "the God who appears", the real and living God appearing to men in the world he created to be recognised in it. And it is his revelation by Hegel that transforms the myth of Christian faith (*Glauben*) into truth or absolute knowledge (*absolutes Wissen*). The summary ends by restating the division of the incarnation between Napoleon and Hegel in public form. Its last sentence states the programme of the next two courses: the relation of faith and absolute knowledge, Chapters VII and VIII.

## Course of the 1937–1938 Academic Year

### Summary of the First Six Chapters of the Phenomenology of Spirit

The text of the first three lectures of 1937–38 is given in full. Kojève begins by placing the two remaining chapters. Chapter VII is titled "Religion", Chapter VIII "Absolute Knowledge". Absolute knowledge is nothing other than the complete system of Hegel's philosophy or "Science", later set out in the *Encyclopaedia*. Chapter VIII therefore does not develop its content; it treats this knowledge as a kind of "faculty". It shows what this knowledge must be, and what the man endowed with a knowledge able to reveal completely and adequately the totality of existing being must be. In particular, it shows the difference between this philosophical absolute knowledge and another knowledge that also claims to be absolute: the knowledge implied in Christian revelation and the theology derived from it. One of Chapter VIII's main themes is thus the comparison between Hegel's "Science" and the Christian religion. To understand both and their relation, one must consider their genesis. The change of register is noticeable: the notes' compressed glosses give way to continuous exposition. Kojève frames the last two chapters around the rivalry between two claims to absolute knowledge, revelation and Science, which anticipates his reading of Chapter VIII as secularised theology.

The genesis of Christianity, the "absolute religion", from the most "primitive" religion is described in Chapter VII. As for the genesis of Hegel's philosophy, the whole *Phenomenology*, and in particular Chapters I–VI, is nothing but its description, culminating in the production of the *Phenomenology* itself, which describes this genesis and so makes it possible by understanding its possibility. Chapters I–VI also complete the analysis of the genesis of the Christian religion given in Chapter VII. For Hegel, «pour employer le langage marxiste» (to use Marxist language) (p. 161), religion is only an ideological superstructure born and existing only as a function of a real infrastructure. This infrastructure, supporting both religion and philosophy, is the whole of the human actions carried out in the course of universal history, in and through which man created a series of specifically human worlds essentially different from the natural world. These social worlds are reflected in religious and philosophical ideologies. And absolute knowledge, which reveals the totality of being, can therefore be realised only at the end of history, in the last world created by man. To understand what absolute knowledge is, one must therefore understand the whole of universal history, which Hegel did in Chapter VI. The explicit borrowing of Marx's base and superstructure is attributed to Hegel. The self-referential claim, that the *Phenomenology* makes its own genesis possible by understanding it, restates the circularity criterion of 1933–34.

To understand the edifice of universal history and the process of its construction, one must know its materials, which are men. Man is quite other than a brick. Men are not only the bricks but the masons who build and the architects who conceive the plan, which is itself elaborated progressively in the course of construction. And even as "brick", man changes during construction, as do the mason and the architect. Nonetheless there is something in every man that makes him able to take part, passively or actively, in universal history: the necessary and sufficient conditions for the beginning of the history that ends in absolute knowledge. Hegel studies them in the first four chapters. The building image is carefully qualified: history has no prior plan, and its materials change as it is built. The first four chapters give the conditions of history, not a stage within it, which confirms the structural reading of the Master–Slave dialectic.

Man is also the one for whom the edifice is built: he lives in it, sees and understands it, describes and criticises it. There is a whole category of men who do not take an active part in the construction and are content to live in the building and talk about it. These men who live "above the fray", talking about things they do not create by their action, are the intellectuals, producers of intellectuals' ideologies, which they take, and pass off, for philosophy. Hegel describes and criticises these ideologies in Chapter V. The intellectual is defined by his position in the building: he inhabits without constructing. Rolland's phrase returns from 1935–36.

The whole *Phenomenology*, summarised in Chapter VIII, must therefore answer the question: what is absolute knowledge and how is it possible? That is: what must man and his historical development be for an individual who «par hasard porte le nom de Hegel» (happens by chance to bear the name Hegel) (p. 163) to find himself, at a certain moment of that development, in possession of an absolute knowledge, one that reveals not a particular and momentary aspect of being, mistaken for its totality, but being in its integral whole as it is in and for itself? In its Cartesian form, the *Phenomenology* must answer the question of the philosopher who believes himself able to reach definitive truth: "I think, therefore I am; but what am I?" The phrase "by chance" is deliberate: the individual is contingent, the position necessary. Kojève's reframing of the book as an answer to Descartes's second question gives the lectures their thread.

Descartes's answer, "I am a thinking thing", does not satisfy Hegel. Certainly, he must have said to himself, I am a thinking being. But what interests me above all is that I am a philosopher able to reveal definitive truth, endowed with absolute, universally and eternally valid knowledge. If all men are thinking beings, I alone, for the moment at least, possess this knowledge. In answering "a thinking being", I therefore understand nothing, or very little, in myself. The objection is precise: Descartes's answer names what the philosopher shares with everyone and so cannot explain what distinguishes him.

I am not only a thinking being; I am the bearer of an absolute knowledge, now incarnated in me, Hegel. So I am, first of all, Hegel. What is this Hegel? First, a man of flesh and blood who knows himself to be so. Then, this man does not hover in a void. He sits on a chair, at a table, writing with a pen on paper. He knows these objects did not fall from the sky; they are products of what is called human labour. He knows this labour takes place in a human world, within a nature of which he is himself a part. And this world is present to his mind as he writes to answer his "what am I?". He hears noises from afar, and knows they are cannon shots, and that cannons too are products of labour, made for a fight to the death between men. More: he knows they are the shots fired by Napoleon's cannon at the battle of Jena. He knows that he lives in a world where Napoleon acts. That is something Descartes, Plato, and so many other philosophers did not and could not know. The scene of Hegel writing at Jena while Napoleon's guns fire is Kojève's most famous image. It dramatises the thesis that self-knowledge includes one's material and historical situation: the table stands for labour, the cannon for the fight, and Napoleon for their completion. The biographical fact that Hegel finished the *Phenomenology* as the battle was fought (October 1806) gives the image its force.

Is that why Hegel reaches the absolute knowledge his predecessors sought in vain? Perhaps. But why Hegel and not one of his contemporaries, who all knew there was a man named Napoleon? Did they really know what Napoleon was? To understand Napoleon is to understand him as the one who perfects, by realising it, the ideal of the French Revolution, which requires understanding the ideology of the Enlightenment, and in general to understand him in terms of the whole prior historical development, the whole of universal history. Almost none of Hegel's contemporaries posed this problem, and none but Hegel solved it. Hegel alone could accept and justify Napoleon's existence, that is, "deduce" it from the first principles of his philosophy, his anthropology, his conception of history. The others had to condemn Napoleon, and so to condemn historical reality, and by that very fact their systems are condemned by that reality. The principle that philosophies are judged by their ability to justify reality applies Kojève's historicism to the history of philosophy. The contemporaries who condemned Napoleon, Kant's heirs and the Romantics of VI, C, lose by the verdict of history.

Would Hegel not be this Hegel, the thinker endowed with absolute knowledge, because he lives in Napoleon's time and is alone in understanding him? That, Kojève says, is exactly what Hegel says in the *Phenomenology*. The two conditions, historical and personal, are joined; the next paragraph separates them.

Absolute knowledge became objectively possible because in and through Napoleon the real process of historical development, in which man created new worlds and transformed himself by creating them, reached its end. To reveal this world is therefore to reveal the world, being in the completed totality of its spatio-temporal existence. Subjectively, absolute knowledge became possible because a man named Hegel was able to understand the world in which he lived and to understand himself as living in and understanding it. Like each of his contemporaries, Hegel was a microcosm, integrating in his particular being the completed totality of the spatio-temporal realisation of universal being. But he alone understood himself as this integrity and gave a correct and complete answer to the Cartesian "what am I?". Understanding himself through the understanding of the whole anthropogenic process ending in Napoleon and his contemporaries, and understanding this process through his self-understanding, Hegel made the completed whole of the real universal process enter his particular consciousness, and this consciousness was penetrated by it. It thus became as total and universal as the process it reveals in understanding itself. This fully self-conscious consciousness is absolute knowledge, which, developed in discourse, forms the content of absolute philosophy or Science, the *Encyclopaedia*, containing the sum of all possible knowledge. The distinction between objective and subjective conditions of absolute knowledge is the core of the lecture. The microcosm thesis explains why self-understanding can be total: each man at the end of history contains the whole, and the Sage is the one who knows it.

Descartes's philosophy is inadequate because his answer to "what am I?" was inadequate from the start. Certainly Descartes could not realise Hegel's absolute philosophy: history was not complete in his time. Even had he understood himself fully, he would have grasped only part of human reality, and a system founded on this self-understanding would necessarily be inadequate and false insofar as it claims, as every system must, to be total. But beyond that, Descartes, for reasons Hegel explains, went about it badly. His answer, "I am a thinking being", was not only too summary but false because one-sided. Two defects are distinguished: an unavoidable one, due to history's incompleteness, and an avoidable one, the one-sidedness that the next paragraphs analyse.

Starting from "I think", Descartes fixed his attention only on "think", completely neglecting the "I". Yet this I is essential. For man, and so the philosopher, is not only consciousness but, above all, self-consciousness. Man is not only a being who thinks, who reveals being by the *Logos*, a discourse formed of meaningful words. He also reveals, again by discourse, the being that reveals being, the being he himself is, the revealing being he opposes to revealed being, giving it the name I, Self (*Ich*, *Selbst*). The critique of Descartes for neglecting the "I" is Kojève's. Descartes's *cogito* is in fact concerned with the I, but as a thinking substance; Kojève's point is that Descartes did not ask what kind of being says "I", which is the question of Desire.

There is no human existence without consciousness of the external world. But for truly human existence that can become philosophical existence, there must also be self-consciousness; and for that there must be the self, the specifically human something that man reveals, that reveals itself, when he says "I". The link between self-consciousness and philosophical existence underlies the whole argument: philosophy is the fullest form of saying "I".

Before analysing the "I think", before proceeding to the Kantian theory of knowledge, of the relation between conscious subject and conceived object, one must ask what this "subject" is that reveals itself in and through the I of "I think". One must ask when, why, and how man is led to say "I". The priority of the question of the subject over the theory of knowledge restates the 1933–34 thesis (p. 44) that the *Phenomenology* is anthropology before epistemology.

Self-consciousness presupposes consciousness: a revelation of being by speech, if only by the single word "being" (*Sein*); a revelation of a being that will later be called "objective, external, non-human being", "world", "nature", but which for the moment is still neutral, since there is not yet self-consciousness and so no opposition of subject and object, I and not-I, human and natural. The neutral being revealed by the first word is the being of sense-certainty, prior to the subject–object split.

The most elementary form of consciousness is studied in Chapter I as "sense-certainty". What matters is that from this consciousness there is no way to reach self-consciousness. One must start from something other than the contemplative knowledge of being, its passive revelation, which leaves it as it is in itself, independent of the knowledge that reveals it. This is Kojève's reason for treating Chapters I–III as leading nowhere by themselves: contemplation cannot generate a self.

A man who contemplates a thing attentively, who wants to see it as it is, is "absorbed" by it. He forgets himself and thinks only of the thing, neither of his contemplation nor still less of himself, his "I". The more conscious he is of the thing, the less conscious of himself. He may speak of the thing, but never of himself: the word "I" will not appear in his discourse. For it to appear there must be something other than purely passive contemplation. That something, for Hegel, is Desire (*Begierde*), of which he speaks at the start of Chapter IV. The paragraph restates p. 11 of the Introduction in fuller form. The criterion is linguistic: the absorbed contemplator's discourse has no first person.

When man feels a desire, when he is hungry and wants to eat, and becomes aware of it, he necessarily becomes aware of himself. Desire always reveals itself as my desire, and to reveal it one must use the word "I". However absorbed he is in contemplating the thing, the moment the desire for it arises he is "called back to himself". He sees that besides the thing there is his contemplation, and he, who is not the thing. The thing appears to him as an "object" (*Gegen-stand*), an external reality not in him, not him, a not-I. The hyphenated *Gegen-stand*, what stands against, marks the moment desire makes the thing into an object.

So it is not purely cognitive, passive contemplation that underlies self-consciousness, truly human existence, and ultimately philosophical existence, but Desire. Hence, parenthetically, human existence is possible only where there is biological, animal life (*Leben*), since there is no Desire without life. The parenthesis restates the necessary condition of p. 11.

What is Desire, hunger for instance, if not the desire to transform the contemplated thing by an action, to abolish it in its being that has no relation to mine, to negate it in its independence, and to assimilate it to me, make it mine, absorb it in and through my I? For there to be self-consciousness and philosophy, there must be in man not only positive, passive contemplation that merely reveals being, but negating Desire and so action that transforms given being. The human I must be an I of Desire: an active, negating I that transforms being and creates a new being by destroying the given. Kojève links the anthropological claim directly to the possibility of philosophy: a philosophy of self-consciousness presupposes a negating subject.

What is the I of Desire, of the hungry man, if not a void avid for content, a void that wants to fill itself with what is full, to fill itself by emptying the full, and, once filled, to put itself in the place of the full, occupying with its fullness the void formed by the abolition of the full that was not its own? If true, absolute philosophy is not, like Kantian and pre-Kantian philosophy, a philosophy of consciousness, but a philosophy of self-consciousness, conscious of itself, accounting for and justifying itself, knowing itself to be absolute and revealing itself as such to itself, then the philosopher, and man, must be at the root of his being not only passive and positive contemplation but active, negating Desire. To be so he cannot be a being that is, eternally identical with itself and self-sufficient. «L'homme doit être un vide, un néant, qui n'est pas néant pur, reines Nichts, mais quelque chose qui est dans la mesure où il anéantit l'Être» (man must be a void, a nothingness, which is not pure nothingness but something that is to the extent that it annihilates being) (p. 167), to realise itself at being's expense and nihilate in being. Man is negating action that transforms given being and transforms itself in transforming it. Man is what he is only insofar as he becomes it; his true being (*Sein*) is becoming (*Werden*), time, history, and he becomes, he is history, only in and through the negating action of fight and labour: the labour that will finally produce the table on which Hegel writes the *Phenomenology*, and the fight that will ultimately be the battle of Jena whose noise he hears as he writes. That is why, in answering "what am I?", Hegel had to take account of both the table and the noise. The distinction between pure nothingness (*reines Nichts*, Hegel's term from the Logic) and the nothingness that nihilates in being is the ontological core of the lectures. It separates Kojève's man from both being and pure nothing: man is the negating of being, which exists only as long as there is being to negate.

There is no human existence without consciousness and self-consciousness, without revelation of being by speech and without the Desire that reveals and creates the I. Within the *Phenomenology*, a phenomenological anthropology, the elementary possibility of revealing given being by speech, implied in sense-certainty, and the destructive or negating action of given being born of Desire are two irreducible data that it presupposes as premises. But these premises do not suffice. Kojève now sets out the premises of the *Phenomenology* explicitly, an axiomatic reconstruction original to these lectures.

The analysis of Desire's constitutive role shows why human existence is possible only on the basis of animal existence: a stone or plant, lacking Desire, never reaches self-consciousness and philosophy. But the animal does not either. Animal Desire is a necessary but not sufficient condition. Animal Desire and the action it gives rise to negate the natural given; in modifying it and making it its own, the animal rises above it. For Hegel the animal, eating the plant, realises and reveals its superiority over it. But feeding on plants, it depends on them and does not truly surpass them. The void or I revealed by biological Desire is filled by biological action only with natural content. The I, or pseudo-I, realised by satisfying it is as natural as its object. The animal rises above nature negated in its Desire only to fall back into it by satisfying that Desire. It reaches only self-feeling (*Selbstgefühl*), not self-consciousness; it cannot speak of itself or say "I", because it does not truly transcend itself as given, as body; it does not rise above itself to return to itself; it has no distance from itself to contemplate itself. The account of the animal's lack of self-distance explains self-feeling: the animal feels itself but cannot view itself, because nothing in it stands apart from its body.

For there to be self-consciousness and philosophy, there must be transcendence of self with respect to self as given. For Hegel this is possible only if Desire bears not on a given being but on a non-being. To desire being is to fill oneself with given being and to enslave oneself to it. To desire non-being is to free oneself from being, to realise one's autonomy, one's freedom. To be anthropogenic, Desire must therefore bear on a non-being, another Desire, another avid void, another I. For Desire is absence of being (to be hungry is to lack food): a nothingness nihilating in being, not a being that is. The argument that to desire a being is to be enslaved to it is the deepest ground of the theory: freedom requires an object that is not a given. Only another Desire qualifies.

The action aimed at satisfying an animal Desire bearing on an existing thing never realises a human, self-conscious I. Desire is human, or rather "humanising", "anthropogenic", only if directed at another Desire. To be human, man must act not to subdue a thing but to subdue another Desire, for the thing. The man who desires a thing humanly acts not so much to seize it as to make another recognise his right, as it will later be called, to it, to be recognised as its owner, and ultimately to make the other recognise his superiority over the other. Only the Desire for such recognition (*Anerkennung*), and the action arising from it, creates, realises, and reveals a human, non-biological I. The link between recognition and property, noted in 1933–34 (p. 53), is now built into the definition of human desire: to desire humanly is to claim a right.

The *Phenomenology* must therefore admit a third irreducible premise: the existence of several Desires that can desire each other, each wanting to negate, assimilate, make its own, and subdue the other Desire as Desire. This plurality is as "non-deducible" as Desire itself. Admitting it, one can already foresee, understand, or "deduce" what human existence will be. The plurality of desires is a premise because nothing in one Desire implies another. Kojève's anthropology is thus irreducibly social from its axioms.

If self-consciousness and man in general are ultimately nothing but Desire seeking satisfaction by being recognised by another Desire in its exclusive right to satisfaction, then man can realise and reveal himself fully, satisfy himself definitively, only through universal recognition. And if there is a plurality of such Desires for universal recognition, the action they give rise to can only be, at first at least, a fight for life and death (*Kampf auf Leben und Tod*): a fight, because each will want to subdue the other, all others, by negating, destructive action; for life and death, because the Desire bearing on a Desire bearing on a Desire exceeds the biological given, so that the action it gives rise to is not limited by it. Man will risk his biological life to satisfy his non-biological Desire. And Hegel says that the being unable to endanger its life for ends not immediately vital, unable to risk its life in a fight for recognition, a fight for pure prestige, is not truly human. The reasoning from Desire to universal recognition is new in its compactness: since Desire claims an exclusive right, only recognition by all can satisfy it.

Human, historical, self-conscious existence is therefore possible only where there are, or at least have been, bloody fights, wars of prestige. It was one of these fights whose noises Hegel heard as he finished the *Phenomenology*. Jena is thus the last in the series that began with the first fight.

The three premises do not suffice to explain the battle of Jena. If all men were as described, every fight for prestige would end in the death of at least one adversary. Finally only one man would remain in the world, and, for Hegel, he would no longer be human, since human reality is nothing but the recognition of one man by another. The argument is that of the Introduction (p. 15), now put as the insufficiency of three premises.

To explain Jena, and the history it completes, a fourth and last irreducible premise is needed. The fight must end with both adversaries alive, which requires that one yield to the other and submit, recognising him without being recognised. The fight must end in the victory of the one ready to go to the end over the one who, facing death, cannot rise above his biological instinct of preservation, identity. In Hegel's language, there must be a victor who becomes the Master of the vanquished, or a vanquished who becomes the Slave of the victor. The existence of a difference between Master and Slave, or more exactly the possibility of a difference between future Master and future Slave, is the fourth and last premise. Kojève glosses the instinct of preservation as "identity", the logical category of nature. The Slave is the one whom identity holds.

The vanquished has subordinated his human desire for recognition to the biological desire to preserve his life, which determines and reveals, to him and to the victor, his inferiority. The victor has risked his life for a non-vital end, which determines and reveals, to him and to the vanquished, his superiority over biological life and so over the vanquished. The difference between Master and Slave is thus realised in the existence of victor and vanquished and recognised by both. The difference is both real and recognised: an institution, not merely a fact.

The Master's superiority over nature, founded on the risk of life, is realised through the Slave's labour, which interposes itself between Master and nature. The Slave transforms the given conditions of existence to fit the Master's demands. Nature transformed by the Slave's labour serves the Master without his having to serve it in turn. The enslaving side of interaction with nature falls to the Slave: by enslaving him and forcing him to work, the Master enslaves nature and realises his freedom in nature. The Master's existence can remain exclusively warlike: he fights but does not work. The Slave's existence is reduced to labour (*Arbeit*) performed in the Master's service (*Dienst*): he works but does not fight. For Hegel only action performed in another's service is labour in the proper sense, an essentially human and humanising action. The being that acts to satisfy its own instincts, always natural as such, does not rise above nature; it remains a natural being, an animal. But acting to satisfy an instinct that is not mine, I act according to what is not, for me, instinct; I act according to an idea, a non-biological end. This transformation of nature according to a non-material idea is labour in the proper sense: labour that creates a non-natural, technical, humanised world, adapted to the human Desire of a being that has proved and realised its superiority over nature by risking its life for the non-biological end of recognition. Only this labour could finally produce the table on which Hegel wrote the *Phenomenology*, part of the content of the I he analysed in answering "what am I?". The definition of labour as action for another's instinct is Kojève's most precise account of why servile labour humanises. To serve is to act for an idea, the Master's desire, rather than for one's own instinct; hence the Slave's labour is the first action guided by a concept.

Admitting these four premises, first, the revelation of given being by speech; second, a Desire engendering negating action that transforms given being; third, several Desires that can desire each other; fourth, the possibility of a difference between the Desires of future Masters and of future Slaves, one understands the possibility of a historical process, a history which is, as a whole, the history of the fights and labour that ended in Napoleon's wars and in the table on which Hegel wrote the *Phenomenology* to understand both. Conversely, to explain the possibility of the *Phenomenology*, written on a table and explaining Napoleon's wars, one must suppose the four premises. A footnote adds that one might try to deduce the first premise from the other three: speech, the *Logos* that reveals being, is born in and of the Slave's self-consciousness through labour. The fourth premise postulates the act of freedom, since nothing predisposes the future Master to mastery or the future Slave to servitude; each can freely create himself as Master or Slave. What is given is not the difference between Master and Slave but the free act that creates it; and the free act is by definition "non-deducible", so this is indeed an absolute premise. All one can say is that without the primordial free act that creates mastery and servitude, history and philosophy could not exist; and this act presupposes a plurality of mutually desiring Desires. The four premises are the lectures' most systematic contribution. The footnote reduces them further: speech may derive from labour, and the fourth premise is an act of freedom, not a fact. The irreducible core is Desire, its plurality, and a free act.

In sum: man was born, and history began, with the first fight ending in the appearance of a Master and a Slave. At his origin, man is always either Master or Slave, and there is true man only where there is a Master and a Slave: «il faut, pour le moins, être deux pour être humain» (one must at least be two to be human) (p. 172). Universal history, the history of the interaction between men and with nature, is the history of the interaction between warlike Masters and working Slaves. History therefore stops when the difference, the opposition, between Master and Slave disappears: when the Master ceases to be Master because he no longer has a Slave, and the Slave ceases to be Slave because he no longer has a Master, without becoming Master in turn, since he will have no Slave. For Hegel this completion of history through the dialectical overcoming (*Aufheben*) of Master and Slave is realised in and through Napoleon's wars, in particular the battle of Jena. The presence of the battle in Hegel's consciousness is therefore of capital importance: it is because Hegel hears its noise that he can know that history is ending or has ended, that his conception of the world is total, and his knowledge absolute. The formula for the end of history, no Master because no Slave, no Slave because no Master, is exact. It defines the final State negatively, by the disappearance of the founding relation.

But to know he is the thinker able to realise absolute Science, he must know that Napoleon's wars realise the dialectical synthesis of Master and Slave. For that he must know, on the one hand, the essence (*Wesen*) of Master and Slave, and on the other, how and why the history that began with the "first" fight for prestige ended in Napoleon's wars. The analysis of the essential character of the Master–Slave opposition, the moving principle of history, is in Chapter IV; the analysis of the historical process itself is in Chapter VI. The division of labour between Chapters IV and VI, essence and history, organises the rest of the lecture.

History, the universal human process that conditioned the advent of Hegel, a process that thinker must understand in a phenomenology before realising absolute knowledge in the System of Science, is therefore nothing but the history of the dialectical, that is, active, relation between mastery and servitude. History will therefore end when the synthesis of Master and Slave is realised: integral man, the citizen of the universal and homogeneous State created by Napoleon. "Dialectical, that is, active" repeats the thesis that dialectic is a feature of action, not of method.

This conception makes sense of the division of history into three great periods, of very unequal length. If history begins with the fight after which a Master dominates a Slave, the first period must be one in which human existence is wholly determined by the Master's existence; in it mastery reveals its essence by realising its existential possibilities through action. But if history is a dialectic of mastery and servitude, servitude too must reveal itself fully by realising itself through action, so a second period must follow, in which human existence is determined by servile existence. Finally, if the end of history is the synthesis of mastery and servitude and the understanding of that synthesis, these two periods must be followed by a third, in which a neutralised, synthetic human existence reveals itself to itself by actively realising its own possibilities, which this time include the possibility of understanding itself fully, definitively, perfectly. The three periods, pagan, Christian, and post-revolutionary, correspond to VI, A, B, and C. The inference from the dialectic to the periodisation is presented as deduction; the "very unequal durations" concede that the third period is brief.

Hegel analyses these three periods in Chapter VI. But to write it, to understand history, it is not enough to know that history has three periods; one must know what each is and understand the why and how of each one's development and of the passage from one to another. For that one must know the essential reality (*Wesen*) of mastery and servitude, the two principles whose interaction realises the process, and this analysis of the Master and the Slave as such is in Section B of Chapter IV. Kojève's reference to "Section B" is a slip: the analysis of Master and Slave is in Section A of Chapter IV, as his own commentary shows.

Kojève begins with the Master. The Master is the man who went to the end in a fight for prestige, who risked his life to be recognised in his absolute superiority by another man. He preferred to his real, natural, biological life something ideal, spiritual, non-biological: being recognised (*anerkannt*) in and by a consciousness, bearing the name "Master", being called "Master". He thus "proved" (*bewährt*), realised, and revealed his superiority over biological existence, his own, over the natural world in general, and over everything that knows itself and that he knows to be bound up with that world, notably the Slave. This superiority, at first purely ideal, consisting in the mental fact of being recognised and knowing oneself recognised as Master by the Slave, is realised and materialised through the Slave's labour. The Master who could force the Slave to recognise him can also force him to work for him and hand over the result. The Master no longer needs to make efforts to satisfy his natural desires; the enslaving side of this satisfaction has passed to the Slave. Dominating the working Slave, the Master dominates nature and lives in it as Master. To maintain oneself in nature without fighting it is to live in enjoyment (*Genuss*), and enjoyment obtained without effort is pleasure (*Lust*). The Masters' life, insofar as it is not bloody fighting for prestige with other men, is a life of pleasure. Kojève's gloss that the Master prefers "a name", being called Master, stresses the ideality of recognition: the Master dies for a word. The distinction between enjoyment and pleasure fixes his life outside war.

At first sight the Master seems to realise the summit of human existence, being fully satisfied in and by his real existence, because he is. In fact he is not. What does this man want to be, if not a Master? He risked his life to become and be Master, not to live in pleasure. What he wanted in engaging the fight was to be recognised by another, by another who is like him, another man. But at the end of the fight he is recognised only by a Slave. To be a man he wanted to be recognised by another man; but if to be a man is to be a Master, the Slave is not a man, and being recognised by a Slave is not being recognised by a man. He would have to be recognised by another Master, which is impossible, since by definition the Master prefers death to servile recognition of another's superiority. The Master never achieves the end for which he risks his life. He can be satisfied only in and through death, his own or his adversary's. But one cannot be satisfied by what is, by what one is, in and through death: «Car la mort n'est pas, le mort n'est pas» (for death is not, the dead man is not) (p. 174). What is, what lives, is only a Slave. Was it worth risking one's life to know oneself recognised by a Slave? Obviously not. So as long as the Master does not become brutalised in his pleasure, as soon as he realises his true aim and the motive of his warlike actions, he will never be satisfied by what is, by what he is. The argument is the Introduction's (p. 25), stated with greater force. The logical point is sharp: recognition by a Master is impossible because Masters do not yield, and recognition by a Slave is worthless because Slaves are not men.

Mastery is therefore an existential impasse. The Master can either brutalise himself in pleasure or die as Master on the battlefield, but he cannot live consciously knowing himself satisfied by what he is. Only conscious satisfaction (*Befriedigung*) can complete history, since only the man who knows himself satisfied by what he is no longer seeks to surpass himself, what he is and what is, through the action that transforms nature and creates history. If history is to end and absolute knowledge to be possible, only the Slave can do it, by reaching satisfaction. That is why Hegel says the "truth", revealed reality, of the Master is the Slave. The human ideal born in the Master can be realised and revealed, become truth (*Wahrheit*), only in and through slavery. The two outcomes, brutish pleasure and heroic death, exhaust the Master's options. The requirement that satisfaction be conscious links the end of history to self-knowledge.

To stop and understand oneself, one must be satisfied; for that one must cease to be a Slave; but to cease to be a Slave one must have been one. Since there is a Slave only where there is a Master, mastery, though an impasse, is "justified" as a necessary stage of the historical existence leading to Hegel's absolute Science. The Master appears only to beget the Slave who "overcomes" (*aufhebt*) him as Master, thereby overcoming himself as Slave. It is this overcome Slave who will be satisfied by what he is and will understand himself as satisfied in and through Hegel's philosophy, in the *Phenomenology*. The Master is only the "catalyst" of the history that will be realised, completed, and revealed by the Slave or former Slave become citizen. The catalyst of the Introduction (p. 30) returns. The claim that one must have been a Slave to cease being one gives servitude a retrospective necessity.

Let us see first what the Slave is at his beginnings, the Master's Slave, not yet satisfied by the citizenship that realises and reveals his freedom. The transition marks the Slave's two advantages to come: his experience of death and his labour.

Man became a Slave because he feared death. On the one hand this fear (*Furcht*) reveals his dependence on nature and so justifies his dependence on the Master, who dominates nature. On the other hand, for Hegel, the same fear has a positive value that conditions the Slave's superiority over the Master. «À travers la peur animale de la mort (Angst) l'Esclave a éprouvé la Terreur ou l'angoisse (Furcht) du Néant, de son néant» (through the animal fear of death, *Angst*, the Slave experienced the terror or anguish, *Furcht*, of Nothingness, of his nothingness) (p. 175). He glimpsed himself as nothingness and understood that his whole existence was only a death "overcome", "suppressed" (*aufgehoben*), a nothingness maintained in being. The deep basis of Hegelian anthropology is the idea that man is not a being that is, in eternal identity with itself in space, but a nothingness that nihilates as time in spatial being, by negating that being: by negating or transforming the given from an idea or ideal that is not yet, that is still nothingness, a "project"; by the negation called action (*Tat*) of fight and labour (*Kampf* and *Arbeit*). The Slave who, through the fear of death, grasps the human nothingness at the bottom of his natural being understands himself and man better than the Master. From the "first" fight the Slave has an intuition of human reality, and that is the deep reason why it is he, not the Master, who will finally complete history by revealing the truth about man in Hegel's Science. The terminology deserves notice. Kojève here assigns *Angst* to animal fear and *Furcht* to the anguish of nothingness, the reverse of Heidegger's distinction, in which fear (*Furcht*) has a determinate object and anxiety (*Angst*) discloses the nothing. Hegel's text uses *Furcht*, which is why Kojève attaches the ontological sense to it; the result is a Heideggerian content under inverted labels. The definition of the project as an idea "that is not yet, that is still nothingness" links the theory of time to the theory of action: the future is present in action as the project it realises.

Thanks again to the Master, the Slave has another advantage, due to the fact that he works, and works in another's service (*Dienst*). To work for another is to act against the instincts that drive man to satisfy his own needs. No instinct forces the Slave to work for the Master; he does it from fear of the Master. But this fear differs from what he felt in the fight: the danger is no longer immediate; the Slave only knows the Master can kill him; he does not see him in murderous posture. The Slave working for the Master represses his instincts according to an idea, a concept. That is precisely what makes his activity specifically human, labour (*Arbeit*). Acting, he negates, transforms the given, nature, his own nature, according to an idea, according to what is not in the biological sense, the idea of a Master, an essentially social, human, historical notion. To be able to transform the natural given according to a non-natural idea is to possess a technique, and the idea that engenders a technique is a scientific concept; to possess scientific concepts is to be endowed with the Understanding (*Verstand*), the faculty of abstract notions. A footnote specifies that for Hegel the concept (*Begriff*) and Understanding are born of the Slave's labour, whereas sense-certainty is an irreducible datum; but one might try to deduce all human knowledge from labour. The distinction between the fear in the fight and the fear in service is new and precise. The first is immediate terror; the second is mediated by knowledge, so it can govern conduct over time. The derivation of the concept from mediated fear is the most compressed statement of Kojève's genealogy of reason.

Understanding, abstract thought, science, technique, and the arts therefore originate in the Slave's forced labour. It is the Slave, not the Master, who realises everything related to them: notably Newtonian physics, which so impressed Kant, the physics of force and law, which for Hegel are ultimately the victor's force in the fight for prestige and the Master's law recognised by the Slave. The claim that force and law in physics are sublimated forms of the Master's force and law is Kojève's boldest genealogy of science. It reads Chapter III's "force" and "law" as projections of the social relation of Chapter IV.

But that is not all the advantage labour brings. It will also open the way to freedom, or more exactly to liberation. The distinction between freedom and liberation marks the Slave's freedom as a process.

The Master realised his freedom by overcoming his life instinct in the fight. Working for another, the Slave also overcomes his instincts, and, rising thereby to thought, science, and technique, transforming nature according to an idea, he too comes to dominate nature and his own "nature", the very nature that dominated him in the fight and made him the Master's Slave. By labour the Slave reaches the result the Master reached by risking his life: he no longer depends on the given natural conditions of existence; he modifies them from the idea he has of himself. Becoming aware of this, he becomes aware of his freedom (*Freiheit*), his autonomy (*Selbständigkeit*). Using the thought born of his labour, he forms the abstract notion of the freedom that the same labour has realised in him. The parallel between risk and labour as two routes to freedom from nature is the key to the synthesis: each achieves in its own way what the other achieves.

In the Slave proper, this notion of freedom does not yet correspond to a true reality. He frees himself mentally only through forced labour, because he is a Master's Slave, and he remains that Slave. He frees himself, so to speak, only to be freely a Slave, more a Slave than before he formed the idea of freedom. But what is the Slave's inadequacy is at the same time his perfection: because he is not really free, he has an idea of freedom, unrealised, which can be realised by the conscious and voluntary transformation of given existence, the active abolition of servitude. The Master, by contrast, is free; his idea of freedom is not abstract, so it is not an idea in the proper sense, an ideal to be realised. That is why the Master never gets beyond the freedom realised in him and its inadequacy. Progress in realising freedom can only be made by the Slave, who starts from an unrealised ideal. And because he has an ideal, an abstract idea, progress in realising freedom can end in an understanding of freedom, in the birth of the absolute Idea (*absolute Idee*) of human freedom revealed in absolute knowledge. The thesis that the Slave's lack is his advantage is precise: only the one who lacks freedom can conceive it as an ideal. The absolute Idea, the culmination of Hegel's Logic, is here the Idea of human freedom, an anthropological reading of the Logic's summit.

In general, only the Slave can make progress, go beyond the given, in particular the given he himself is. On the one hand, possessing the idea of freedom and not being free, he is driven to transform the given social conditions of his existence, to make historical progress. Further, and this is the important point, this progress has a meaning for him that it does not and cannot have for the Master. The Master's freedom, engendered in the fight, is an impasse: to realise it he must have it recognised by a Slave, must turn the one who recognises it into a Slave. My freedom ceases to be a dream, an illusion, an abstract ideal only insofar as it is universally recognised by those I recognise as worthy to recognise it. That is precisely what the Master can never obtain. His freedom is recognised, so it is real; but only by Slaves, so it is inadequate in its reality and cannot satisfy the one who realises it. As long as it remains a Master's freedom it cannot be otherwise. The Slave's freedom, by contrast, recognised at first by no one but himself, and so purely abstract, can end by realising itself and realising itself perfectly. For the Slave recognises the human reality and dignity of the Master. He need only impose his freedom on the Master to reach the definitive satisfaction given by mutual recognition, and so stop the historical process. The definition of real freedom as recognition by those one recognises as worthy is the criterion for the whole book. It shows that the Slave already holds half of mutual recognition.

To do so he must fight the Master, cease to be a Slave, overcome his fear of death. He must become other than he is. Unlike the warrior-Master, who will always remain what he already is, a Master, the working Slave can change, and does change, thanks to his labour. The Master's fixity and the Slave's changeability repeat the Introduction's gloss on ¶194 (p. 27).

The Master's human action reduces to the risk of life, and the risk of life is everywhere and always the same. What counts is the fact of risk; it matters little whether a stone axe or a machine gun is involved. It is not the fight as such, the risk of life, but labour that one day produces a machine gun instead of an axe. The purely warlike attitude of the Master does not vary through the centuries, so it cannot produce historical change. Without the Slave's labour the "first" fight would repeat indefinitely: nothing would change in it; it would change nothing in the Master; nothing would change in man, by man, or for man; the world would remain identical with itself, nature and not a historical, human world. The image of the axe and the machine gun is one of Kojève's most memorable. It locates the source of historical change in technique: war changes because its instruments change, and they change through labour.

The situation created by labour is quite different. The man who works transforms given nature. If he repeats his act, he repeats it under other conditions, so his act itself will be other. After making the first axe, man can use it to make a second, which will thereby be other and better. Production transforms the means of production; the modification of the means simplifies production; and so on. Where there is labour there is necessarily change, progress, historical evolution. A footnote adds that the manufactured object embodies an idea, a "project", independent of the material here and now, which is why such objects are "exchanged"; hence the birth of an "economic" world, specifically human, where money, capital, interest, wages, and so on appear. The self-amplifying character of labour, tools making better tools, is the engine of history. "Means of production" is Marx's term. The footnote grounds exchange in the ideality of the product: because the object embodies a project, it can circulate apart from its maker.

What changes through labour is not only the natural world but, above all, man himself. At first man depends on the given natural conditions of his existence. He can rise above them by risking his life in a fight for prestige, but in this risk he negates the whole of these conditions, always the same; he negates them en bloc without modifying them, and this negation is always the same. The freedom he creates in and through it does not depend on the particular forms of the given. Only by rising above the given conditions through the negation performed in labour does man remain in contact with the concrete, which differs in space and time. That is why he changes himself in transforming the world. The contrast between negation en bloc and negation in detail is decisive. Risk negates the given abstractly; labour negates it concretely, and only concrete negation produces a history, since only it varies with circumstances.

The schema of historical development is as follows. At the start, the future Master and future Slave are both determined by a given, natural world independent of them; they are not yet truly human, historical beings. Then, by risking his life, the Master rises above given nature, his given animal "nature", and becomes a human being who creates himself in and through his conscious negating action. Then he forces the Slave to work. The Slave changes the real given world; he too rises above nature, his animal "nature", since he makes it other than it is. Certainly the Slave, like the Master and man in general, is determined by the real world. But since this world has been changed, he changes himself. And since it is he who changed the world, it is he who changes himself, whereas the Master changes only through the Slave. The historical process, the historical becoming of the human being, is therefore the work of the working Slave, not of the warrior Master. Without the Master there would have been no history, but only because without him there would have been no Slave and so no labour. A footnote qualifies the claim: animals too have (pseudo-)techniques; the first spider changed the world by weaving the first web. It would be better to say that the world changes essentially, and becomes human, through "exchange", which is possible only through labour that realises a "project". The footnote is a significant self-correction. Technique alone does not distinguish man, since animals modify their environment; exchange, founded on the ideality of the project, does. Kojève thus moves the criterion of the human from production to exchange, closer to Marx's analysis of the commodity.

Once again, thanks to his labour the Slave can change and become other than he is, and ultimately cease to be a Slave. Labour is *Bildung* in the double sense of the word: it forms and transforms the world, humanises it, adapts it better to man; and it transforms, forms, educates man, humanises him, makes him conform more closely to the idea he has of himself, which is at first only an abstract idea, an ideal. If at the start, in the given world, the Slave had a fearful "nature" and had to submit to the Master, the strong, it does not follow that it will always be so. Thanks to his labour he can become other, and the world can become other. That is what actually happened, as universal history and finally the French Revolution and Napoleon show. The double sense of *Bildung* was stated in the Introduction (p. 29). Here it grounds the claim that the Slave's "nature" is not fixed.

This creative education of man by labour creates history, human time. «Le Travail est Temps» (labour is time) (p. 180), and that is why it is necessarily in time: it takes time. The Slave's transformation, which will let him overcome his terror, his fear of the Master, by overcoming the anguish of death, is long and painful. At first the Slave who has risen through labour to the abstract idea of his freedom does not manage to realise it, because he does not yet dare act for its realisation, fight the Master and risk his life in a fight for freedom. The equation of labour and time is a step toward the 1938–39 thesis that the concept is time. It makes the duration of history the duration of the Slave's education.

Before realising freedom, the Slave imagines a series of ideologies by which he tries to justify himself and his servitude and to reconcile the ideal of freedom with the fact of slavery. The ideologies of Chapter IV, B are now defined as justifications of inaction.

The first is Stoicism. The Slave tries to persuade himself that he is actually free by the mere fact of knowing himself free, having the abstract idea of freedom. The real conditions of existence would not matter at all: it matters little whether one is Roman emperor or slave, rich or poor, sick or healthy; it suffices to have the idea of freedom, of autonomy, of absolute independence from all given conditions of existence. Hence, parenthetically, the modern variant of Stoicism discussed in Chapter V: freedom is identified with freedom of thought; a State is called free when one can speak freely in it; as long as that freedom is safeguarded, there is nothing to change in the State. The "modern variant" is liberalism reduced to freedom of expression. Kojève's parenthesis identifies it as Stoicism: a freedom that leaves the real order untouched.

Hegel's critique, or rather his explanation of why man did not stop at this Stoic solution, apparently so satisfying, may seem unconvincing and odd. Hegel says man abandons Stoicism because, as a Stoic, he is bored. The Stoic ideology was invented to justify the Slave's inaction, his refusal to fight to realise his libertarian ideal. It prevents man from acting and obliges him to content himself with talk. And, says Hegel, all discourse that remains discourse ends by boring man. Kojève anticipates the objection that boredom is a trivial motive for a world-historical transition, and answers it next.

This objection, or explanation, is simplistic only at first sight. In fact it has a deep metaphysical basis. Man is not a being that is; he is a nothingness that nihilates through the negation of being, and the negation of being is action. That is why Hegel says "man's true being is his action". Not to act is therefore not to be as a truly human being; it is to be as given, natural being (*Sein*); it is to decline, to become brutish. This metaphysical truth reveals itself to man in the phenomenon of boredom: the man who, like the thing, the animal, or the angel, remains identical with himself, does not negate or negate himself, that is, does not act, is bored. «Et ce n'est que l'Homme qui peut s'ennuyer» (and only man can be bored) (p. 181). Hegel mentions boredom only in passing, of the Stoic's edifying generalities (¶200); the metaphysics of boredom is Kojève's. Boredom is the lived experience of one's own negativity idling. The angel, which remains identical with itself, is placed with the thing and the animal: only a finite, negating being can be bored. Heidegger's remark on profound boredom in *What Is Metaphysics?* (1929) stands in the background.

It is boredom caused by Stoic chatter that forced man to seek something else. Man can be satisfied only by action. To act is to transform the real, and to transform the real is to negate the given. For the Slave, to act effectively would be to negate servitude, the Master, and so to risk his life in a fight against him. The Slave does not yet dare. Boredom pushing him to action, he contents himself with activating his thought, as it were; he makes it negate the given. The Stoic Slave becomes the sceptic-nihilist Slave. Scepticism is the Slave's thought made active without becoming action.

This new attitude culminates in solipsism: the value and even the reality of everything that is not I is denied, and the purely abstract, verbal character of this negation is compensated by its universality and radicalism. The compensation of verbal negation by universality is the Sceptic's substitute for real negation: he denies everything because he cannot change anything.

Man does not manage to hold himself in this sceptic-nihilist attitude, because he contradicts himself by his very existence: how and why live when one denies the value and being of the world and other men? To take the nihilist seriously is to commit suicide, to cease acting completely and so to cease living. But the radical Sceptic does not interest Hegel, since by definition he disappears by suicide, ceases to be, and so ceases to be a human being, an agent of historical development. Only the nihilist who remains alive is interesting. The dismissal of the consistent nihilist is characteristic: philosophy of history concerns only those who survive. Kirilov, cited in 1934–35, is excluded by his consistency.

The living nihilist must eventually notice the contradiction his existence implies. In general it is the awareness of a contradiction that moves human, historical development. To become aware of a contradiction is necessarily to want to remove it. But one can in fact remove the contradiction of a given existence only by modifying that existence, transforming it by action. For the Slave, to transform his existence is again to fight the Master, which he does not want to do. So he tries to justify this contradiction of sceptical existence, which is ultimately the Stoic, servile contradiction between the idea or ideal of freedom and the reality of servitude, by a new ideology. This third and last ideology of the Slave is the Christian one. The general principle, that awareness of contradiction moves history, is Kojève's version of dialectic: contradiction drives change only when it is felt, and it is removed only by action.

The Slave now does not deny that his existence is contradictory, but tries to justify it by saying it is necessary and inevitable, that all existence implies a contradiction. To this end he imagines an "other world" beyond (*Jenseits*) the natural, sensible world. Here below he is a Slave and does nothing to free himself. But he is right, since in this world everything is servitude, and the Master is as much a slave as he. Freedom is not an empty word, an abstract idea, an unrealisable ideal, as in Stoicism and Scepticism; it is real, real in the beyond. There is no need to fight the Master, since one is already free insofar as one participates in the beyond, freed by it, by its intervention in the sensible world. No need to fight for recognition by the Master, since one is recognised by a God. No need to fight to free oneself in this world, which is as vain and worthless for the Christian as for the Sceptic. No need to fight or act, since in the beyond, the only world that really counts, one is already freed and the Master's equal in the servitude of God. One can therefore maintain the Stoic attitude, but this time with good reason, and without boredom, since now one does not remain eternally the same: one changes and must change, must always surpass oneself to rise above oneself as given in the real empirical world, to reach the transcendent world, the beyond that remains inaccessible. Without fight or effort the Christian thus realises the Slave's ideal: he obtains, in and through God, equality with the Master; inequality is only a mirage, like the whole sensible world where servitude and mastery reign. The analysis explains why Christianity succeeded where Stoicism failed: it gives the Slave a reason for inaction and a task of perpetual self-transcendence that cures boredom. The inaccessibility of the beyond keeps the negativity at work without ever satisfying it.

A solution of genius, Hegel will say, and no wonder man could for centuries believe himself "satisfied" by this pious reward for his labour. But, Hegel adds, all this is too good, too simple, too easy to be true. What made man a Slave was his refusal to risk his life. He will not cease to be one as long as he is not ready to risk his life in a fight against the Master, as long as he does not accept the idea of his death. «Une libération sans Lutte sanglante est donc métaphysiquement impossible» (a liberation without bloody fight is therefore metaphysically impossible) (p. 182). And this metaphysical impossibility is revealed in Christian ideology itself. The thesis that liberation requires bloodshed is the political consequence of the ontology: freedom is the acceptance of death, and one proves that acceptance only in risking death.

The Christian Slave can affirm his equality with the Master only by admitting another world and a transcendent God. But this God is necessarily a Master, and an absolute one. The Christian frees himself from the human Master only to enslave himself to the divine Master. He frees himself, at least in idea, from the human Master; but having no Master he does not cease to be a Slave. He is a Slave without a Master, a Slave in himself, the pure essence of servitude. And this "absolute" servitude engenders an equally absolute Master. He is the Master's equal before God, so only in absolute servitude. He remains a servant, the servant of a Master for whose glory and pleasure he works. And this new Master is such that the new Christian Slave is even more a slave than the pagan Slave. The "Slave without a Master" as "the pure essence of servitude" is the formula of 1934–35 raised to a metaphysical claim. Servitude without an external Master produces an absolute one.

If the Slave accepts this new divine Master, he does so for the same reason he accepted the human Master: fear of death. He accepted, or produced, his first servitude as the price of his biological life; he accepts, or produces, the second as the price of his eternal life. The ultimate motive of the ideology of "two worlds" and of the duality of human existence is the servile desire for life at any cost, sublimated into the desire for eternal life. Christianity is born, ultimately, of the Slave's anguish before nothingness, his nothingness, that is, for Hegel, of the impossibility of bearing the necessary condition of human existence, the condition of death, of finitude. A footnote: there is no human, conscious, speaking, free existence without fight implying the risk of life, and so without death, without essential finitude: «L'homme "immortel" — c'est un "cercle carré"» (the "immortal" man is a "square circle") (p. 183). The footnote is the most concise statement of Kojève's atheism: immortality contradicts the concept of man, since man is defined by the capacity to die for recognition.

Consequently, to remove the inadequacy of Christian ideology, to free oneself from the absolute Master and from the beyond, to realise freedom and live in the world as an autonomous, free human being, is possible only on condition of accepting the idea of death, and so atheism. The whole development of the Christian world is nothing but a march toward the atheist awareness of the essential finitude of human existence. Only thus, only by "overcoming" Christian theology, will man cease definitively to be a Slave and realise the idea of freedom that, remaining an abstract idea, an ideal, engendered Christianity. The equation of atheism with the acceptance of death is the thesis the 1938–39 lectures and Appendix II develop. The Christian world's history is read as the education of mankind to finitude.

This is achieved in and through the French Revolution, which completes the development of the Christian world and inaugurates the third historical world, in which realised freedom will finally be conceived (*begriffen*) by philosophy: by German philosophy and finally Hegel. For a revolution really to overcome Christianity, the Christian ideal must first be realised in the form of a world. For an ideology to be surpassed, man must first experience its realisation in the real world where he lives. The question is therefore how the pagan world of mastery could become a Christian world of servitude without a fight between Masters and Slaves, without a revolution properly speaking. For in that case the Slave would have become the free worker who fights and risks his life; he would cease to be a Slave and could not realise an essentially servile Christian world. The principle that an ideology must be realised before it can be surpassed explains why Christianity had to become a world, and why that world had to arise without a revolution.

Hegel solves this problem in Section A of Chapter VI. The lecture now returns to the ancient world.

In the *Phenomenology* Hegel does not speak of the genesis of the pagan State, so it is studied as already formed. The omission contrasts with the 1935–36 account of the founding Tyrant (p. 99), which Kojève took from Hegel's Jena manuscripts.

The essential character of the pagan State and society is determined by its being a State, a society, of Masters. The pagan State recognised only Masters as citizens. Only the one who makes war is a citizen, and only the citizen makes war. Labour is assigned to Slaves, who are on the margins of society and State. The State as a whole is thus a Master-State, seeing the meaning of its existence not in its labour but in its prestige, in the wars of prestige it wages to have its autonomy and supremacy recognised by other States, by all other States. The State as Master reproduces the individual Master's structure: it seeks recognition by war and lives on others' labour.

For Hegel it follows that the pagan State of warlike and idle Masters can recognise, have recognised, or realise only the universal element of human existence; the particular element remains on the margins of society and State. The conclusion prepares the second reading of history, as a dialectic of particular and universal.

This opposition of particularity and universality (*Einzelheit*, *Allgemeinheit*) is fundamental in Hegel. If history can be interpreted as a dialectic of mastery and servitude, it can also be understood as a dialectic of particular and universal in human existence. The two interpretations complement each other, since mastery corresponds to universality and servitude to particularity. The equation of Master with universal and Slave with particular joins Kojève's social reading to Hegel's logical categories. Mastery is universal because risk is the same for all; servitude is particular because labour varies with circumstance.

Man seeks recognition (*Anerkennung*) from the start. He is not content to attribute a value to himself; he wants this particular value of his to be recognised by all, universally. Desire for recognition already contains the synthesis of particular and universal as its aim.

In other words, man can be truly "satisfied", and history can stop, only in and through the formation of a society, a State, in which the strictly particular, personal, individual value of each is recognised as such, in its very particularity, by all, by the universality embodied in the State as such; and in which the universal value of the State is recognised and realised by the particular as particular, by all particulars. A footnote adds that the particular who realises a universal value is no longer a particular: he is an individual, the citizen of the universal and homogeneous State, a synthesis of particular and universal.
