Likewise the universal, the State, realised by the particular is individualised: it is the State-Individual or Individual-State, incarnate in the person of the universal chief, Napoleon, and revealed by the Sage, Hegel. Such a State, such a synthesis of particularity and universality, is possible only after the "overcoming" of the opposition of Master and Slave, the synthesis of particular and universal being also a synthesis of mastery and servitude. The footnote's "State-Individual" is an important addition: the final State is itself an individual, since it is realised in and recognised through one person. The chief is the point where State and individual coincide.

As long as Master opposes Slave, the synthesis of particular and universal cannot be realised and human existence will never be satisfied. Not only because the Slave is not universally recognised, and not only because the Master himself does not reach truly universal recognition, since he does not recognise some of those who recognise him, the Slaves. The synthesis is impossible because the Master realises and has recognised only the universal element in man, while the Slave reduces his existence to a purely particular value. The third reason is the deepest: each side of the opposition realises only one of the two elements needed for individuality.

The Master constitutes his human value by risking his life, and this risk is everywhere, always, and for all the same. The man who risks his life differs in nothing, by the mere fact of having risked it, from all others who have done so. Human value constituted by the fight is essentially universal, "impersonal". That is why the State of Masters, which recognises a man only by his risking his life for the State in a war of prestige, recognises only the purely universal element in man, in the citizen. The citizen of this State is any citizen; as recognised by the State he does not differ from others; he is an anonymous warrior, not Mr So-and-so. Even the head of State is only a representative of the State, of the universal, not an individual properly speaking; in his activity he is a function of the State, not the State a function of his personal, particular will. In short, the head of the Greek city-state is not a "dictator" in the modern, Christian, Romantic sense. He is not a Napoleon who creates a State by his personal will in order to realise and have his individuality recognised. The pagan chief accepts a given State, and his own value, his very reality, is only a function of that State, of the universal element of existence. That is why the Master, the pagan, is never "satisfied"; only the individual could be. The anonymous warrior is Kojève's figure for ancient universality. The contrast with Napoleon clarifies what the modern "dictator" adds: a State created by and for one individual's recognition.

The Slave's existence is limited to the purely particular element. Human value constituted by labour is essentially particular, "personal". The formative education (*Bildung*) of the worker by labour depends on the concrete conditions in which labour is carried out, which vary in space and change in time as a function of labour itself. It is ultimately through labour that differences among men are constituted, that "particularities", "personalities", are formed. It is also the working Slave, not the warrior Master, who becomes aware of his "personality" and imagines the "individualist" ideologies in which absolute value is attributed to particularity, to "personality", and not to universality, to the State as such and to the citizen as citizen. The thesis that personality is a product of labour, because labour varies with conditions while risk does not, is one of the lectures' most original claims. It explains why individualism is a Slave's ideology.

But what is recognised universally, by others, by the State, by mastery as such, is not the labour or the "personality" of the worker but at most the impersonal product of labour. As long as the Slave works while remaining a Slave, as long as he does not risk his life or fight to impose his personal value on the State, as long as he does not intervene actively in social life, his particular value remains purely subjective: he alone recognises it. His value is therefore only particular; the synthesis of particular and universal, individuality, is realised in the Slave as little as in the Master. That is why, once again, the synthesis of particularity and universality in individuality, which alone can truly "satisfy" man, can be realised only in and through a synthetic "overcoming" of mastery and servitude. The recognition of the product rather than the producer is an anticipation of Marx's analysis of alienation, which Kojève draws from Hegel.

Returning to the pagan State of warlike, non-working Masters: this State, like every State, is interested in and recognises only the action of its citizens, which here reduces to warlike action. It recognises in the citizen only the universal aspect of human existence. Yet the particular element is not and cannot be entirely excluded. The Master is not only master of slaves and warrior-citizen; he is also necessarily a member of a Family, and to the Family belongs, for the pagan Master, the particular aspect of his existence. The principle that the State recognises only action anticipates the definition of the final State as the recognition of individual action.

Within his Family man is not any Master, citizen, or warrior; he is father, husband, son, and this father, this husband, a "particular". But his particularity recognised in and by the Family is not truly human. For the non-working pagan Master, human, humanising action reduces to the warlike action of the fight, and there is no fight, no risk of life, within the Family. It is therefore not human action (*Tat*) that is recognised by and in the Family, but only being (*Sein*), static-given being, the biological existence of the man, father, husband, son, brother. The analysis restates the 1935–36 reading of VI, A with sharper terms.

To attribute absolute value to a being not for what it does, its acts, but simply because it is, by the mere fact of its being, is to love it. One can therefore also say that it is love that is realised in and through the ancient Family. Since love does not depend on the acts of the beloved, it cannot be stopped even by his death. Loving a man in his inaction, one considers him as if he were dead. Death therefore changes nothing in love, in the value attributed in and by the Family. That is why love and the cult of the dead have their place in the pagan Family. The definition of love as valuing being rather than doing is Kojève's; it explains the Family's cult of the dead. Its corollary, that to love someone is to treat him as if dead, is striking.

The particular and particularist Family is thus a necessary complement of the universal and universalist pagan State. But the pagan Master is as little "satisfied" by his family life as by his existence as citizen. In and through the State his human existence is realised and recognised, but it is not really his; it is not he who is recognised. The Family recognises his personal, particular existence, but that existence, essentially inactive, is not truly human. The double failure is exact: the State recognises the human but not the person; the Family recognises the person but not the human.

Where the human actions of fight and labour are not synthesised in a single human being, man is never fully "satisfied". The realisation and recognition of purely universal action in the State satisfy man as little as the realisation and recognition of his personal, particular being in the Family. The general principle joins the two analyses: satisfaction requires one being who both fights and works.

In principle a synthesis of the familial particular and the State universal could satisfy man. But such a synthesis is absolutely impossible in the pagan world, since Family and State exclude each other and man cannot do without either. For the Family the supreme value is being, natural being, the biological life of its member; what the State demands of this member is precisely the risk of his life, his death for the universal cause. To fulfil the citizen's duty is therefore necessarily to violate the Family's law, and conversely. The mutual exclusion follows from their opposite relations to death: the Family preserves life, the State demands its sacrifice.

In the pagan world this conflict is inevitable and without issue. Man cannot renounce the Family, since he cannot renounce the particularity of his being; nor the State, since he cannot renounce the universality of his action. So he is always necessarily criminal, either toward the State or toward the Family. That is what makes pagan life tragic. The tragic structure of VI, A is here derived from the two irrenounceable sides of human existence.

Like the hero of ancient tragedy, the pagan world of warrior-Masters finds itself in an inevitable conflict without issue, which necessarily ends in death, the complete ruin of that world. Hegel represents the development of this tragedy as follows. The pagan world as tragic hero is Kojève's image for the whole of VI, A.

Ultimately the pagan world perishes because it excludes labour. But the immediate agent of its ruin is, curiously, Woman. For Woman represents the familial principle, the principle of particularity hostile to society as such, whose victory means the ruin of the State, of the universal properly speaking. The two causes, ultimate and immediate, are distinguished: the exclusion of labour is the reason, Woman the agent. The distinction is Kojève's way of reconciling his materialist thesis with Hegel's text on womankind.

On the one hand, Woman acts on the young man, who is not yet completely detached from the Family, who has not yet completely subordinated his particularity to the universality of the State. On the other hand, precisely because the State is a warrior State, it is the young man, the young military hero, who must finally take power in it. Once in power, this young hero, Alexander the Great, asserts his familial, still feminine particularity. He tends to turn the State into his private property, his family patrimony, and the citizens into his own subjects. And he succeeds. Alexander returns from 1935–36 (p. 104) as the type of the young hero through whom particularity captures the State.

Why? Again because the pagan State excludes labour. The only human value being that realised in fight and risk of life, the State's life must necessarily be warlike; the pagan State is a human State only insofar as it wages perpetual wars of prestige. But the laws of war, of brute force, are such that the strongest State must gradually swallow the weaker ones, and the victorious city gradually turns into an Empire, the Roman Empire. The mechanism of empire formation is the one stated in the 1936–37 notes (p. 115): prestige war selects the strongest.

The inhabitants of the mother city, the Masters properly speaking, are too few to defend the Empire. The Emperor must resort to mercenaries. At once the citizens are no longer obliged to make war, and gradually they no longer do. They thereby can no longer resist the Emperor's particularism, which "overcomes" them as citizens and turns them into "particulars" belonging to his patrimony, "private persons". The citizens' loss of military obligation is the hinge of the ancient world's decline in Kojève's account.

In sum, the former citizens become the sovereign's slaves, and they become so because they already are. To be a Master is to fight, to risk one's life; citizens who no longer make war cease to be Masters, and that is why they become slaves of the Roman Emperor. That is also why they accept their slaves' ideology: Stoicism first, then Scepticism, and finally Christianity. The phrase "because they already are" states the priority of the existential fact over the political status: the Masters were already Slaves before the Emperor enslaved them.

Here is the solution of the problem: the Masters accepted their Slaves' ideology. The pagan man of mastery became the Christian man of servitude without a fight, without a revolution properly speaking, because the Masters themselves became Slaves, or more precisely pseudo-Slaves, or, if one likes, pseudo-Masters. They are no longer true Masters, since they no longer risk their lives; nor true Slaves, since they do not work in another's service. They are Slaves without Masters, pseudo-Slaves. And ceasing to be true Masters, they end by having no true Slaves: they free them, and the Slaves thus become Slaves without Masters, pseudo-Masters. The opposition of mastery and servitude is thus "overcome", but not because the Slaves have become true Masters. The unification takes place in pseudo-mastery, which is in fact a pseudo-servitude, a servitude without Masters. The resolution is a false synthesis: the opposition disappears not by being overcome but by both terms decaying into one. The true synthesis will require the Revolution.

This Slave without a Master, this Master without a Slave, is what Hegel calls the Bourgeois, the private owner. It is by becoming a private owner that the Greek Master, citizen of the city, becomes the peaceful Roman bourgeois, subject of the Emperor, who is himself only a bourgeois, a private owner whose patrimony is the Empire. And it is through private property that the Slaves' manumission takes place: they become owners, bourgeois, like their former masters. Hegel's word is *Bürger* in the *Jenaer Realphilosophie*; Kojève attributes the concept of the bourgeois to the *Phenomenology*, where it is implicit in the analysis of legal status.

Unlike the Greek city, the Roman Empire is therefore a bourgeois world, and it is as such that it finally becomes a Christian world. The thesis that Rome became Christian because it was bourgeois reverses the usual order of explanation.

The bourgeois world elaborates private law, for Hegel Rome's only original creation. The fundamental notion of Roman legal thought, the "legal person" (*rechtliche Persönlichkeit*), corresponds to the Stoic conception of human existence and to the principle of familial particularism. Like the Family, private law attaches absolute value to the mere being of man, independent of his actions. And as in the Stoic conception, the value attributed to the "person" does not depend on the concrete conditions of existence: everywhere and always one is a "legal person", and all are equally so. It is the bourgeois State founded on the idea of private law that is the real basis of Stoicism, taken not as an abstract idea but as a social, historical reality. The legal person unites two earlier elements: the Family's valuation of being and the Stoic's indifference to circumstance. Kojève's thesis that Roman law is the social reality of Stoicism repeats the 1935–36 reading (p. 105).

The same holds for nihilist Scepticism: private property (*Eigentum*) is its real basis and its social, historical reality. The nihilist Scepticism of the solipsist Slave, who attributes value and true being only to himself, is found again in the private owner, who subordinates everything, the State included, to the absolute value of his own property. If the only reality of particularist, so-called "individualist" ideologies is private property, it is only in a bourgeois world dominated by the idea of such property that these ideologies can become real social forces. Scepticism's social form is the owner who treats the State as a means to his property. The claim that individualist ideologies become real only in a property-based world is Kojève's materialism.

The same bourgeois essence of the Roman Empire explains its transformation into a Christian world, which makes the reality of Christianity possible and turns the Christian idea and ideal into a social and historical reality. The explanation follows.

To be truly human, the bourgeois, who in principle does not fight or risk his life, must work, like the Slave. But unlike the Slave, having no Master, he need not work in another's service; he believes he works for himself. In Hegel's conception, labour can be truly labour, a specifically human action, only if it is carried out according to an idea (a "project"), something other than the given, and in particular than the given the worker himself is. So the Slave could work sustained by the idea of the Master, of mastery, of service (*Dienst*). One can also, and this is Hegel's definitive solution, work sustained by the idea of the community, the State: one can and must work for the State. But the bourgeois can do neither. He no longer has a Master to serve by working, and he does not yet have a State, since the bourgeois world is only an agglomeration of private owners isolated from one another, without true community. The dilemma is precise: human labour requires an idea other than oneself, and the bourgeois has lost the Master without gaining the State.

The bourgeois's problem seems insoluble: he must work for another and can work only for himself. In fact man solves it, again through the bourgeois principle of private property. The bourgeois does not work for another; nor does he work for himself as a biological entity. He works for himself as a "legal person", as private owner: he works for property as such, that is, property become money: «il travaille pour le Capital» (he works for Capital) (p. 191). Capital is the solution: an idea, other than the biological self, for which the bourgeois can work while believing he works for himself.

In other words, bourgeois labour presupposes and conditions a renunciation (*Entsagung*), an abnegation of human existence. Man transcends himself, surpasses himself, projects himself far from himself by projecting himself onto the idea of private property, of capital, which, though the owner's work, becomes independent of him and enslaves him as the Master enslaved the Slave, with the difference that the enslavement is now conscious and freely accepted by the worker. A parenthesis notes that for Hegel, as for Marx, the central phenomenon of the bourgeois world is not the enslavement of the worker, the poor bourgeois, by the rich bourgeois, but the enslavement of both by capital. In any case bourgeois existence presupposes, engenders, and nourishes abnegation. And it is precisely this abnegation that is reflected in dualist Christian ideology, giving it a new, specific, non-pagan content. The same Christian dualism is found in bourgeois existence: the opposition between the "legal person", the private owner, and the man of flesh and blood; the existence of an ideal transcendent world, represented in reality by money, capital, to which man is supposed to devote his actions and sacrifice his sensible, biological desires. This is the lectures' fullest statement of the parallel between Christianity and capitalism, which recalls Max Weber's thesis on the Protestant ethic without citing it. The parenthesis on Marx is historically important: Kojève reads Marx's theory of capital as the domination of both classes by an impersonal power, not primarily as class exploitation.

The structure of the Christian beyond is formed in the image of the relations realised in the Roman Empire between the Emperor and his subjects, relations which have the same origin as Christian ideology: the refusal of death, the desire for animal life, being, sublimated in Christianity into a desire for immortality, "eternal life". If the pagan Master accepts his Slave's Christian ideology, which makes him a servant of the absolute Master, the King of Heaven, God, it is because, having ceased to risk his life and become a peaceful bourgeois, he sees himself cease to be a citizen able to satisfy himself by political activity. He sees himself a passive subject of a despot-Emperor. Like the Slave, he has nothing to lose and everything to gain by imagining a transcendent world where all are equal before an all-powerful, truly universal Master, who moreover recognises the absolute value of each particular as such. The Emperor as model for God returns from 1935–36 (p. 106).

That is how and why the pagan world of Masters became a bourgeois Christian world. The paragraph closes the account of the transition.

In contrast to paganism, the religion of Masters, of warrior-citizens who gave true value only to universality, to what is valid for all and always, Christianity, the religion of Slaves or more exactly of subject-bourgeois, attributes absolute value to particularity, to the here and now. This change appears clearly in the myth of God's incarnation in Jesus Christ and in the idea that God has a direct, immediate relation with each man taken in isolation, without passing through the universal, social and political, element of human existence. The incarnation, God in one particular man, is read as the religious form of the valuation of particularity.

Christianity is thus first a particularist, familial, and servile reaction against the pagan universalism of Master-citizens. But it is more than that. It also implies the idea of a synthesis of particular and universal, and so of mastery and servitude: the idea of individuality, of the realisation of universal values and realities in and by the particular and the universal recognition of the particular's value, which alone can give man supreme and definitive satisfaction (*Befriedigung*). Christianity's double character, reaction and synthesis, explains why it is both the Slave's religion and the source of the final ideal.

In other words, Christianity finds the solution to the pagan tragedy. That is why, since Christ's coming, there is no longer true tragedy, no longer inevitable and truly irresolvable conflict. The thesis that Christianity ends tragedy agrees with the 1936–37 notes (p. 122), where the Christian conflict is comic rather than tragic.

The whole problem now is to realise the Christian idea of individuality, and the history of the Christian world is nothing but the history of that realisation. Kojève's definition of the Christian world by its task links VI, B to the ideal it realises.

For Hegel, the Christian anthropological ideal, which he accepts in full, can be realised only by "overcoming" Christian theology. The Christian can really become what he wants to be only by becoming a man without God, or, if one likes, a Man-God. He must realise in himself what he at first believed realised in his God. «Pour être réellement Chrétien, il doit lui-même devenir Christ» (to be really Christian, he must himself become Christ) (p. 192). The formula condenses anthropotheism in Christian terms. It explains Kojève's earlier remark that Hegel wants to be Christ (p. 152).

According to the Christian religion, individuality, the synthesis of particular and universal, takes place only in and through the beyond, after man's death. The deferral of synthesis to the afterlife is the Christian form of the "not yet".

This conception makes sense only if man is presupposed immortal. But for Hegel immortality is incompatible with the very essence of the human being and so with Christian anthropology itself. The claim that immortality contradicts Christian anthropology is Kojève's: the Christian idea of individuality presupposes a being who can die, since only such a being has a self to be recognised.

The human ideal can be realised only if it can be realised by a mortal man who knows himself to be so. The Christian synthesis must take place not in the beyond after death but here below during man's life. That means the transcendent universal, God, who recognises the particular, must be replaced by a universal immanent in the world, and for Hegel this can only be the State. What is supposed to be realised by God in the kingdom of heaven must be realised in and through the State, in the earthly kingdom. That is why Hegel says the "absolute" State he has in view, Napoleon's Empire, is the realisation of the Christian kingdom of heaven. The substitution of the State for God as universal recognising power is the political theology of the lectures. Kojève attributes to Hegel the statement that Napoleon's Empire is the kingdom of heaven realised; Hegel's text speaks of heaven transplanted to earth (¶581), in the context of absolute freedom.

The history of the Christian world is therefore the history of the progressive realisation of this ideal State, in which man will finally be "satisfied" by realising himself as individuality, the synthesis of universal and particular, Master and Slave, fight and labour. But to realise it man must turn his eyes from the beyond, fix them on the here below, and act solely for it; he must eliminate the Christian idea of transcendence. The development of the Christian world is therefore double: on one side the real development, which prepares the social and political conditions for the "absolute" State; on the other the ideal development, which eliminates the transcendent ideal and brings heaven down to earth, as Hegel says. The two developments, real and ideal, anticipate the next paragraphs: the bourgeois prepares the conditions, the intellectual eliminates transcendence.

The ideal development, destructive of Christian theology, is the work of the intellectual. Hegel is much interested in the phenomenon of the Christian or bourgeois intellectual, discussing it in VI, B and devoting the whole of Chapter V to it. A footnote adds that the intellectual of Chapter V, the man who lives in society and a State while believing or pretending to be "alone in the world", appears at every stage of the bourgeois world; but in describing him Hegel has his contemporaries chiefly in view. The footnote reconciles the typological and historical readings of Chapter V.

This intellectual can subsist only in the Christian bourgeois world, where one can be neither Master, having no slaves, nor fight, without thereby becoming a Slave. But the bourgeois intellectual is still something other than the bourgeois proper. If, like the bourgeois, the non-Master, he is essentially peaceful and does not fight, he differs from the bourgeois in not working either. He thus lacks the essential character of the Slave as much as that of the Master. The intellectual is defined by a double absence: neither fight nor labour.

Not being a Slave, the intellectual can free himself from the essentially servile aspect of Christianity, its theological, transcendent element. Not being a Master, he can maintain the element of the particular, the "individualist" ideology of Christian anthropology. Being neither Master nor Slave, he can, in this nothingness, this absence of all given determination, in a sense "realise" the sought-for synthesis of mastery and servitude: he can conceive it. But being neither Master nor Slave, abstaining from all labour and all fight, he cannot really realise the synthesis he discovers: without fight and labour the synthesis conceived by the intellectual remains purely verbal. The paradox is elegant: the intellectual's emptiness is what lets him conceive the synthesis, and the same emptiness prevents him from realising it. This gives the Enlightenment its double role.

What matters is realisation, since only the reality of the synthesis can "satisfy" man, complete history, and prove absolute Science. The ideal process must therefore rejoin the real process; social and historical conditions must be such that the intellectual's ideology can be realised. That is what happens at the French Revolution, in which the immanent idea of individuality, elaborated by the intellectuals of the Enlightenment, is realised in and through the fight of the working bourgeois, first revolutionaries and then citizens of the universal and homogeneous State, the Napoleonic Empire. The Revolution is the meeting of the two processes: the intellectual's idea and the bourgeois's action.

The realisation of the Christian idea, secularised by the intellectual and thus made realisable, is not possible without fight, social war, risk of life, for "metaphysical" reasons. The idea to be realised being the idea of a synthesis of mastery and servitude, it can be realised only if the servile element of labour joins the element of the fight for life and death that characterises the Master. The working bourgeois, to become the "satisfied" citizen of the "absolute" State, must become a warrior: he must introduce death into his existence, consciously and voluntarily risking his life while knowing himself mortal. But in the bourgeois world there are no Masters. The fight in question cannot be a class struggle properly speaking, a war between Masters and Slaves. The bourgeois is neither Slave nor Master; being the slave of capital, he is his own Slave. It is from himself that he must free himself. That is why the liberating risk of life takes the form not of risk on the battlefield but of the risk created by Robespierre's Terror. The working bourgeois become revolutionary himself creates the situation that introduces the element of death into him. Only through the Terror is the idea of the final synthesis, which definitively "satisfies" man, realised. This is the lectures' most precise account of the Terror's necessity. Since the bourgeois has no external Master, his liberation must be self-inflicted: the Terror is the bourgeois's fight to the death with himself. The claim that it cannot be class struggle "properly speaking" distinguishes Kojève from Marx: the decisive fight of modernity is not between classes but within the bourgeois.

The State in which this "satisfaction" is reached is born in the Terror. For the author of the *Phenomenology* it is Napoleon's Empire. And Napoleon himself is the integrally "satisfied" man who, in and through his definitive satisfaction, completes the course of the historical development of humanity. He is the human individual in the proper and strong sense, since it is through him, this particular, that the truly universal "common cause" is realised, and since this particular is recognised in his very particularity by all, universally. What he lacks is only self-consciousness: he is the perfect man, but he does not yet know it, and that is why in him alone man is not fully "satisfied". He cannot say of himself everything Kojève has just said of him. The distinction between being satisfied and knowing oneself satisfied, stated in the 1936–37 notes (p. 148), is repeated. Napoleon's lack is the Sage's task.

«Or, je l'ai dit parce que je l'ai lu dans la PhG» (now, I said it because I read it in the *Phenomenology*) (p. 195). Hegel, the author of the *Phenomenology*, is therefore in a sense Napoleon's self-consciousness. Since the perfect man, fully "satisfied" by what he is, can only be a man who knows what he is, who is fully self-conscious, it is Napoleon's existence as revealed to all in and through the *Phenomenology* that is the realised ideal of human existence. Kojève's first-person remark places his own lecturing in the chain of revelation: he says what he read in Hegel, who said what Napoleon was.

That is why the Christian period (VI, B), culminating in Napoleon, must be completed by a third historical period, a very short one (VI, C), that of German philosophy, culminating in Hegel as author of the *Phenomenology*. The third period is defined not by new political forms but by the self-understanding of the completed State.

The phenomenon that completes historical development and so makes absolute Science possible is the "conception" (*Begreifen*) of Napoleon by Hegel. This dyad, formed by Napoleon and Hegel, is perfect man, fully and definitively "satisfied" by what he is and by what he knows himself to be. It is the realisation of the ideal revealed by the myth of Jesus Christ, the Man-God. That is why Hegel ends Chapter VI with the words "Es ist der erscheinende Gott", "it is God revealed", the real, true Christ. The dyad replaces the individual Man-God of Christianity: the perfect man is two men, deed and word. The residual duality, noted in 1936–37 (p. 153), is here accepted as the form of completion.

Having said this, Hegel is obliged to settle accounts with the Christian, theological interpretation of the idea of Christ. He must speak of the relation between his philosophy, the *Phenomenology*, and Christian theology. He must say what this theology really is. That is the central theme of Chapter VII. The summary ends by announcing the task of the next lectures: to show that theology is an anthropology unaware of itself.

### Interpretation of the General Introduction to Chapter VII (Hoffmeister pp. 473–480)

This section gives the full text of the fourth and fifth lectures of 1937–38. After six chapters, Kojève observes, one is surprised to find a seventh titled "Religion". Hegel has already spoken of religion several times, and Chapter VI has already brought us to the end of history, to Napoleon and to Hegel himself. Hegel will warn, in the third section of Chapter VII, that the sequence of chapters is not temporal. Chapters VI and VII are parallel and complementary: VI analyses historical development proper, VII the religions formed in its course. But there is a displacement. VI, A treats the Greco-Roman world, VI, B the Christian world from its origin to the Revolution, and VI, C the post-revolutionary world in which German philosophy develops. VII, A is devoted to natural religion, the "primitive" religions that preceded, at least logically, the Greco-Roman one; VII, B treats Greco-Roman religion; VII, C treats Christianity, ending with the definitive elaboration of Protestant theology. The reason is that Chapter VI concerned the social and political side of human existence, the relation of the particular to the State, and so began with Greece, where for Hegel the first State properly speaking, the first human society in the strong sense, was formed. Religion, however, reflects not only man's relation to the State but also his relation to nature, the milieu in which he lived before the State existed. That pre-State religion is VII, A, which has no equivalent in Chapter VI. VII, B and VII, C correspond roughly to VI, A and VI, B. VI, C has no equivalent in VII because the post-revolutionary period, being post-Christian, is post-religious in general: philosophy, German philosophy, takes the place of religion there, and Hegel's Science, in which it culminates, is called to replace every kind of religion in human existence once and for all. The explanation of the displacement is Kojève's. Its last step carries weight: the absence of a religious counterpart to VI, C is the textual sign that history ends in the replacement of religion by Science.

Kojève turns to the other question: why a special chapter on religion when Hegel has already discussed it? The first part of the introduction to Chapter VII answers it, and the general answer is in its first sentence. The lecture proceeds by close reading, translating each sentence and interpreting it.

Kojève translates the sentence (Hoffmeister p. 473): religion, as consciousness of the absolute essential reality in general, has also appeared in the shapes considered so far, which are distinguished as consciousness (Chapters I–III), self-consciousness (IV), Reason (V), and Spirit (VI); but only from the standpoint of consciousness that becomes conscious of the absolute essential reality, not the absolute essential reality in and for itself, not the self-consciousness of Spirit. Kojève's bracketed chapter numbers turn Hegel's abstract terms into references to the book's sections. His rendering of *Bewusstsein* as "consciousness-external" (*Conscience-extérieure*) builds his interpretation into the translation: consciousness is always consciousness of something outside.

The passage, Kojève says, is deliberately equivocal. It is one of those that the "right" Hegelians could cite in support of their theist interpretation. "Deliberately" attributes to Hegel a strategy of concealment, a claim Kojève repeats (p. 75) and one that anticipates the attention to esoteric writing in his later correspondent Leo Strauss.

The theist interpretation, itself "heretical", supposes that "absolute essence" and "Spirit" here mean God. The passage would then say: so far we have spoken of man's attitude toward God, the way man becomes conscious of the divine; but not yet of God himself, of the way God becomes conscious of himself in and through religion, independently of his revelation to men. The passage would imply a God, a Spirit other than the human, who reveals himself to himself through the religions he engenders in human consciousness in the course of history, and Chapter VII would interpret these self-revelations. The theist reading is stated fairly before being rejected. Kojève's parenthesis "itself heretical" notes that even the theist reading is not orthodox, since it makes God's self-consciousness depend on human religion.

But this theist interpretation is absolutely impossible. If the *Phenomenology* has a meaning, the Spirit in question is nothing other than the human spirit: there is no Spirit outside the world, and Spirit in the world is man, humanity, universal history. The argument is not textual but global: the theist reading contradicts the sense of the whole book. Kojève's "if the *Phenomenology* has a meaning" makes his atheist reading a condition of the book's coherence.

Starting from there, another interpretation must be given. The step is brief; the next paragraphs supply it.

What is the absolute essential reality for the author of the *Phenomenology*? What is truly real is not nature, the natural world other than man, since the real world in fact includes man; conversely, man outside the world is only an abstraction. Reality is therefore the world that includes man, man who lives in the world. What is the essential reality of this real, its essence, its "entelechy", its "idea"? It is man, insofar as he is something other than the world while able to exist only in the world. Man is the essential reality of the existing real: for Hegel, as for every Judaeo-Christian thinker, this is an axiom to be accepted without discussion: "Spirit is higher than nature", he says somewhere. But the absolute essential reality is not the human individual, the "particular", since isolated man exists as little as man-outside-the-world or world-without-man. The essential reality of the real is humanity taken in its spatio-temporal whole: what Hegel calls objective spirit, world spirit, spirit of a people, but also history, or more concretely the State, the State as State, society as such. The identification of the absolute *Wesen* with humanity as a whole, and concretely with the State, is the key move of the lecture. The admission that the superiority of spirit over nature is an axiom, not a result, is candid: Kojève's anthropology rests on a Judaeo-Christian premise it does not demonstrate.

Hegel says that this essential reality was considered until now "from the standpoint of consciousness". Consciousness is consciousness of external reality, of the not-I opposed to the I, of the conceived object opposed to the knowing subject. So it concerned the attitude of the human individual, the particular, toward man as such taken as the essential reality of the real in general, this reality being for him something external, autonomous, and opposed. In fact this absolute essential reality, the "entelechy" of the whole real, is also the "entelechy" of each human individual. The State is only an integration of citizens, and each citizen is what he is only by participating in the State. But as long as man does not realise this, as long as the reality of the State and of political life does not reveal it explicitly, man opposes himself to the State and sees in it an independent, autonomous entity. He is thus in the attitude of consciousness. One can say: so far it was a question of the attitudes that the individual who opposes himself to humanity, the totality, the State, takes toward them. The reading of "standpoint of consciousness" as the individual's estrangement from the State is Kojève's. It makes religious consciousness a form of political alienation.

But for the man of consciousness the essential reality is not only the State. He also opposes the world to the I and sees it as an autonomous entity. The essential reality of this world will therefore itself be an autonomous reality opposed to him, and so a divine essential reality. For him the absolute essence is God, or more generally the divine. The divine arises from a double estrangement: from the State and from the world. Both appear as external, and their essence as a transcendent power.

Consequently, in speaking of the essential reality from the standpoint of consciousness, as in Chapters III and IV, Hegel had to speak of man's attitude toward his God, of religion; of the attitude of the man who opposes and distinguishes himself from God. He was therefore indeed speaking of religion in the widest sense. The conclusion restates the reference to Chapters III and IV.

The first part of the theist interpretation was therefore correct, but "religion" and "absolute essence" must be taken in an atheist's sense. The second part of the sentence must be read in the same atheist sense. It concerns the absolute essential reality "in and for itself": man as such, collective man living in the world, the world spirit, the spirit of a people, ultimately the State. But no longer from the standpoint of consciousness, of the individual who opposes the State and sees it from outside: it concerns the self-consciousness of Spirit. In Chapter VII the task is to show and understand how Spirit understands itself as such, not only through the attitudes of individuals toward it. For Hegel this self-understanding of Spirit, of the spirit of a people, takes place in and through religion, in the widest sense. Chapter VII will therefore concern the content of religious knowledge, theology. The atheist reading keeps the structure of the theist one and changes its referent: the self-consciousness of Spirit is the self-understanding of a people through its religion.

For Hegel, man understands himself as an isolated individual in and through philosophy. All pre-Hegelian philosophy was in this sense a philosophy of consciousness, studying and revealing on the one hand the subject opposed to the object, the human individual opposed to the natural world, and on the other the autonomous object external to the subject. Man as one with the world, real, collective, historical man, or the State, reveals himself to himself in and through religion. That is why pre-Hegelian philosophy of consciousness must necessarily be completed by a religion. Conversely every religion engenders its philosophical complement, since in religion essence is interpreted as non-human, external to man; the religious man who wants to understand himself must understand himself as opposed to essence, as consciousness, and so through a pre-Hegelian philosophy. The complementarity of philosophy and religion, individual and collective self-understanding, repeats the 1936–37 notes (p. 118). It explains why the history of philosophy and the history of religion are two halves of one history.

Only when the State becomes such that the opposition of particular and universal is "overcome" in it can the opposition of philosophy and religion disappear. When the State is a "doing of all and each", a universal integration of particular actions in which each one's action is that of all and conversely, man will see that the absolute essential reality is also his own. At once it will cease to be opposed to him and cease to be divine. He will know it not through a theology but through an anthropology, which will also reveal his own essential reality: it will replace not only religion but philosophy. This synthesis of philosophy and religion, made possible by the reality of the "absolute" State, is Hegel's Science, in particular the *Phenomenology*, which is the "self-consciousness of Spirit" in the proper sense of the sentence under discussion. The dependence of the end of religion on a political fact, the State in which each one's action is everyone's, is the core of Kojève's thesis. God ceases to be divine when the State ceases to be alien.

This self-consciousness is the absolute knowledge described in Chapter VIII. The development described in Chapter VII explains the genesis of this knowledge, which, being the synthesis of particular and universal, arises as much from the earlier philosophies discussed in the first six chapters as from the religions described in Chapter VII. Absolute knowledge has two ancestors, philosophy and religion; Chapters I–VI trace the first, Chapter VII the second.

The atheist interpretation is the only one compatible with the whole *Phenomenology*. One need only read Chapter VII to reject the theist one. Hegel speaks there of religion, but in a very broad sense. Speaking of Greco-Roman "religion", he speaks much less of pagan theology than of ancient art: sculpture, epic, tragedy, and even comedy. «Dire que c'est Dieu qui se révèle lui-même à lui-même et prend conscience-de-soi en se révélant aux Grecs par Lysistrata par exemple, — c'est tout de même choquer par trop le bon sens» (to say that it is God who reveals himself to himself and becomes self-conscious by revealing himself to the Greeks through *Lysistrata*, for example, is really too great an offence to common sense) (p. 200). The argument from Aristophanes is Kojève's wittiest. It is also a real argument: the inclusion of comedy in the "art-religion" shows that Hegel's concept of religion is the concept of a people's self-representation.

The content of Chapter VII fits the atheist interpretation well. It concerns the general process of the development of unconscious, symbolic, mythical anthropology: man speaking of himself while believing he speaks of something else. It concerns myth in the proper sense, which in our terminology is as much art as theology. Religion and art, primitive and ancient, revealed to man his universal, social, political reality, while the particular, "private" reality of the individual was revealed to him in and through philosophy in the narrow sense. For Hegel, it will therefore be as impossible in the post-revolutionary State to write a tragedy or build a beautiful building as to create a religion or a philosophy of consciousness. The parenthesis on the end of art is a strong claim: tragedy and monumental architecture are forms of collective self-representation that the transparent final State no longer needs. It anticipates Kojève's later remarks on post-historical man.

To remove all doubt, Kojève cites a text roughly contemporary with the *Phenomenology* in which Hegel expresses himself much more clearly: the Jena lectures of 1803–04 (Lasson–Hoffmeister, vol. XIX, p. 232). Kojève translates: the absolute spirit of a people is the absolute universal element that absorbs all particular consciousnesses; it is the simple, living, unique absolute substance, which must also be active and oppose itself to itself as consciousness. As an acting people, it passes into the product of its action; insofar as this common work of all is produced by them as consciousnesses, they constitute themselves in it as an external entity. But this external entity is their action; it is only what they have made of it. In this externality of themselves they contemplate themselves as a people, and this work is their own spirit. «Ils produisent (erzeugen) cet Esprit ; mais ils le vénèrent (verehren) comme une entité-qui-existe-comme-un-être-donné» (they produce this spirit, but they venerate it as an entity existing as a given being) (p. 201). And this spirit is indeed for itself, since the activity by which they produce it is their self-overcoming, and this self-overcoming is the universal spirit existing for itself. The Jena text is Kojève's strongest evidence. It states in Hegel's own words the thesis that a people produces its spirit and then worships it as given, which is the whole atheist reading in one sentence.

The meaning is clear. The people acts, and in and through this collective action creates itself as a State, an organised people, real as a people. But the product of the action detaches itself from the action and the agent and becomes for him an external, autonomous reality, part of the real world in which the agents live and act. When the agent stops acting and tries to understand what he has done, he necessarily becomes consciousness, conscious of an external entity. Necessarily, because only action links I and not-I; in contemplation being is always a given, autonomous not-I. So the man who contemplates the State, the people, understands them as autonomous entities: "they venerate it as a static given being existing for itself". And this understanding of the people as people takes a mythical form and is expressed in art or theology. The explanation of religion's origin is precise: alienation arises when the agent turns contemplator. The principle that only action unites I and not-I explains why contemplation always produces an external object, and so why every contemplative self-understanding of a collective work is religious.

Hegel says the same clearly in the *System der Sittlichkeit* (1802?; vol. VII, p. 467): "The universality that has absolutely united particularity to itself is the divinity of the people. And this same universality, contemplated in the ideal form of particularity, is the God of the people: this God is the ideal way of contemplating the people." The second text states the identity of God and people directly. Kojève's two citations from the Jena writings make his reading a philological argument, not only a systematic one.

After stating the theme of Chapter VII in the first sentence, Hegel quickly reviews the religious themes of the six preceding chapters. We have seen that they concerned the attitude of the human individual toward the absolute essential reality, which he regards as something other than himself. The transition introduces Hegel's retrospective summary, which Kojève reads paragraph by paragraph.

The notion of essence first appeared in Chapter III, "Force and the Understanding", concerning the Understanding and "vulgar" science, notably Newtonian physics. Kojève translates Hegel's summary (Hoffmeister p. 473): consciousness, as Understanding, already becomes consciousness of the supersensible, of the inner of objective existence; but the supersensible, the eternal, whatever name it is given, is without a personal self (*selbstlos*); it is only the universal, still far from being Spirit that knows itself as Spirit. The page reference in Kojève's text reads "p. 435", a misprint for p. 473; several references in this lecture carry similar misprints. *Selbstlos*, without self, marks the limit of the Understanding's God: an impersonal principle, not yet a person.

Through his labour the Slave rose to the Understanding, the creator of abstract notions. Transforming the world himself according to an idea, he is led to believe that the world too is moved by an ideal, supersensible motive. Behind the sensible phenomenon the man of the Understanding sees the essence, the supersensible essential reality: the "idea" or "essence" of the thing, its "entelechy", its inner. But the Slave, who works according to the Master's will and executes the Master's orders, lives in a world that is not yet his. That is why it does not occur to him that he is the entelechy of the world, the supersensible essence maintaining itself in sensible reality. The essence of the world he discovers seems to him as transcendent, autonomous, and independent of him as the world itself, dominated by the Master. The essence is not only above the sensible world; it is also super-human. The genealogy of transcendence from labour for another is Kojève's most striking argument here. The Slave projects the structure of his own labour, action guided by an idea, onto the world, but because the world belongs to another, he assigns the idea to another too.

The Slave arrives at a transcendentalist conception of essence because this essence is for him the essence of a world belonging to another, the Master. This origin is reflected in the content of the notion. In a word, the essence is a kind of all-powerful Master: a God who creates or at least dominates the world. So Newtonian physics of forces and laws has as its necessary complement a transcendentalist theology, just as conversely this theology engenders a "mechanist" interpretation of the world: «Ce n'est donc pas par hasard que Newton était aussi théologien» (it is therefore not by chance that Newton was also a theologian) (p. 203). The remark on Newton, whose theological writings were then largely unpublished, links mechanism and voluntarist theology, a connection that historians of science, Koyré among them, were exploring.

Yet the Understanding alone does not reach theology proper. It only constitutes the conceptual frameworks within which the properly theological content will be placed, and this content must come from elsewhere. For the Understanding, essence is the essence of the natural world, the not-I; so it will also be a not-I, not a supersensible I, not a self-conscious essential reality, not Spirit. The distinction between the framework and the content of theology prepares the role of Chapter IV.

But everything theology will say of Spirit, of the divine Spirit transcendent to man, an irresistible force and an implacable law for him, will fit into the still empty frameworks formed by the notion of the transcendent supersensible elaborated by the Slave's Understanding. In Chapter III Hegel described the typical attitude of the human individual toward the essence he opposes to himself, insofar as this attitude is purely cognitive and contemplative: the frameworks of all theology understood as knowledge. The divine attributes "irresistible force" and "implacable law" repeat Chapter III's force and law, now as attributes of God.

But to fill these frameworks with theological content and turn abstract essence into a self-conscious divine Spirit, one needs something besides the Understanding and the cognitive or contemplative attitude generally. To understand the origin of theology one must analyse not only the thought, the notion, but also the feeling of transcendence. The analysis of the particular's cognitive attitude toward essence must be completed by an analysis of his emotional attitude; one must discover not only the frameworks of all theological thought but also those of all religious psychology. Hegel did this in Chapter IV. The division of theology into cognitive framework and emotional content is Kojève's systematisation of the two retrospective sentences.

Kojève translates Hegel's summary of Chapter IV (Hoffmeister p. 473): self-consciousness, which had its completion in the shape of the unhappy consciousness, was only the pain of Spirit striving again toward objectivity but not reaching it; the union of particular self-consciousness with its immutable essence, toward which it strives, therefore remains a beyond for it. Kojève renders *Gegenständlichkeit* as "objectivité-chosiste", thing-like objectivity: the unhappy consciousness wants to become a thing in the world, to be real and recognised.

The unhappy consciousness is Christian consciousness, the psychology of the Christian, for Hegel the most perfect type of the religious man. What does the Christian want? Like every man, he wants to objectify himself, to realise his ideal, which, as long as it is unrealised, reveals itself to him in the feeling of insufficiency, of pain (*Schmerz*). But as long as he remains religious he does not succeed; or, if one prefers, he remains religious as long as he does not succeed. What is it to realise and objectify one's ideal, if not to have it recognised by others, by all others? It is to realise individuality, the synthesis of particular and universal. And that is precisely the individuality the Christian seeks in his religious feeling. If he imagines a divinity and relates to a God, an absolute external reality, it is because he wants to be recognised by him, recognised by the universal in his most particular particularity. But he does not succeed. The inversion "he remains religious as long as he does not succeed" makes religion the form of unsatisfied desire for recognition. God is the universal recogniser the Christian cannot find on earth.

Man imagines God because he wants to objectify himself, and he imagines a transcendent God because he cannot objectify himself in the world. But to want to realise individuality through union with a transcendent God is to realise it in the transcendent, in the beyond of the world and of oneself as consciousness living in the world. It is to renounce realising the ideal here below, and so to be and know oneself unhappy in this world. The chain is exact: failure in the world, projection beyond it, renunciation of the world, unhappiness.

The religious emotional attitude is born of the pain caused by the experience of the impossibility of realising oneself in the world, and it engenders and nourishes this feeling. This nostalgia, projected into the beyond, fills the Understanding's frameworks of transcendence with theological content, placing in them the image of a personal God, a self-conscious reality, a Spirit which is in fact only the projection into the beyond of the religious consciousness's unhappiness. The formula "God is the projection of unhappiness" is Kojève's version of Feuerbach, sharpened by the theory of recognition: God is the image of the recogniser one lacks.

To nourish and cultivate nostalgia, the painful feeling of the insufficiency of lived reality, is to be in the religious, even Christian, attitude; conversely, to adopt this attitude is to nourish unhappiness and nostalgia. To escape religious psychology is therefore to suppress the unhappiness of consciousness, the feeling of insufficiency. One can do so either by realising a real world in which man would be truly "satisfied", or by abolishing transcendence by an abstract act and accommodating the ideal to reality. The first solution is carried out in and through the French Revolution, which made Hegel's absolute atheist science possible. The second is that of the bourgeois intellectual, whom Hegel discussed in Chapter V. The two exits from religion, revolution and accommodation, distinguish Hegel's atheism from the intellectual's.

Hegel's text on the second (cited as "p. 373", a misprint for p. 473): the immediate existence of Reason, which for us has emerged from this pain of the unhappy consciousness, and its proper shapes, have no religion, because their self-consciousness knows itself or seeks itself in immediate real presence. The quotation is the one summarised at the end of the 1934–35 course (p. 76).

"The immediate existence of Reason" is the intellectual of Chapter V. His existence is "immediate" because not mediated by the effort of labour and fight, which alone can really transform the world. The intellectual finds, or rather seeks, himself in the "immediate" present: it is not after death, not in the beyond, that he wants to be "satisfied", but here and now. He is therefore not religious: he lacks the thought and feeling of transcendence, and also the feeling of unhappiness. The gloss on "immediate" as "unmediated by labour and fight" fixes its sense throughout the lectures.

Yet he is not truly "satisfied", precisely because of the "immediacy" of his attitude. He leaves the world as it is and is content to enjoy it, where the religious man pined away. If the depreciation of the given real characterises the religious attitude, the positive appreciation of the given is typical of the artistic attitude. The given world, ceasing to be regarded as evil, can only be regarded as beautiful. The intellectual can therefore reach at most joy (*Freude*), the pure joy of the inactive and peaceful artist, which is quite other than satisfaction (*Befriedigung*), the true satisfaction of the successful revolutionary. Moreover, the man who delights in the joy of pure knowledge or artistic contemplation can remain an intellectual or artist forever, as the man who delights in unhappiness can remain religious or Christian forever. The opposition of joy and satisfaction completes the typology: pleasure (the man of pleasure), joy (the intellectual), happiness (the Kantian), and satisfaction (the citizen). The claim that both the intellectual and the religious man can persist indefinitely repeats the 1934–35 thesis that transitions are free acts.

Kojève does not insist. The intellectual, being essentially areligious or atheist, no longer appears in Chapter VII. It suffices to note that besides the subjective, theological, religious attitude there is an areligious, aesthetic, pre-revolutionary attitude that has nothing to do with Hegel's post-revolutionary atheism. The distinction between two atheisms, aesthetic and revolutionary, protects Hegel's atheism from being confused with the Enlightenment's or the Romantics'.

In the next three paragraphs (Hoffmeister pp. 473–474), Hegel summarises the three sections of Chapter VI. In Chapters III and IV the question was the cognitive and emotional attitude of the isolated man toward the universal conceived as a transcendent God. In Chapter VI it is the role this conception, religion proper, plays in the historical development of humanity. Here too it is not, as in Chapter VII, the content of theological doctrines that is at issue, but the relations between these doctrines and particulars, insofar as they determine the course of the global historical development integrating their actions. The distinction between religion's historical role (VI) and its doctrinal content (VII) clarifies why religion is treated twice.

Having already summarised Chapter VI, Kojève will not comment on Hegel's summary: the text, extremely condensed, is almost incomprehensible, and explaining it would mean redoing the summary. He only translates it. The summary of VI, A, the pagan world (Hoffmeister p. 473 to p. 474): in the world of customary morality we saw a religion, the religion of the underworld: faith in the unknown, terrifying night of fate and in the Eumenides of the departed spirit. This night is pure negativity in the form of universality, and the Eumenides the same negativity in the form of particularity. In this latter form the absolute essence is a personal self and really present, since the self exists in no other way. But this particular self is the particular ghost, the dead ancestor, which has universality, fate, as separated from itself. The ghost is a "this" overcome and so a universal self, but its negative significance has not yet turned into this positive one, so the overcome self still means immediately a "this" and one without essential reality. Fate, being without self, remains the unconscious night that reaches neither differentiation nor the clarity of self-knowledge. Kojève's bracketed gloss identifies the ghost as the dead ancestor, consistent with his reading of the Family's cult of the dead in VI, A.

The fate (*Schicksal*) of paganism is Christianity, the religion of the Christian bourgeois world, of which Hegel speaks in the next paragraph (cited as p. 477, a misprint for p. 474). Kojève translates: this faith in the nothingness of necessity and in the underworld becomes faith in heaven, because the departed self must unite with its universality, unfold in it what it contains, and so become clear to itself. But we have seen this kingdom of faith unfold its content only in the element of thought, without the concept, and so sink into its fate, the religion of the Enlightenment. In this religion the supersensible beyond of the Understanding is constituted again, but so that self-consciousness stands, satisfied, in the here below and sees in the empty supersensible beyond, which can no more be known than feared, neither a self nor a power. The phrase "without the concept" names the defect of Christian faith: it has the content of absolute knowledge in the form of representation. Kojève's translation of *befriedigt* as "satisfied" for the Enlightenment's self-consciousness is literal, though he denies the Enlightenment true satisfaction.

The fate of Christianity is atheism, Hegel's anthropotheism, reached by way of the religion of the Enlightenment, deism. The frameworks of transcendentalist theology, elaborated by the Understanding and filled with positive content by the unhappy consciousness, are emptied again by eighteenth-century critique. And when the Enlightenment's ideology is realised by the French Revolution, these frameworks themselves, already empty, the very notion of transcendence, are abolished. Man is now an atheist; he knows that he, not God, is the essential reality of the world. The three stages, framework, filling, emptying, give a concise history of theism: the Understanding builds the frame, Christianity fills it, the Enlightenment empties it, the Revolution removes it.

At first post-revolutionary man is not yet aware of his atheism. With Kant, Fichte, and others, he still speaks of God. But in fact he is interested only in himself, and his "theology" is essentially contradictory and impossible. Of this religion or pseudo-religion of morality, post-revolutionary German philosophy, Hegel speaks in the next paragraph. The thesis that Kant's religion is already atheism in disguise was stated in 1936–37 (p. 149).

Kojève translates (Hoffmeister p. 474): in the religion of morality the situation is restored in which the absolute essential reality is a positive content; but this content is united with the negativity of the Enlightenment. It is a being that is equally taken back into the self and remains enclosed there, a differentiated content whose parts are negated as immediately as they are posited. The fate in which this contradictory dialectical movement sinks is the self that has become conscious of itself as the fate of essentiality and actuality. Hegel's formula for the moral world-view's instability, positing and negating in turn, recalls the "dissemblance" of VI, C, b.

In post-revolutionary German philosophies man is already put in God's place, but this new atheist conception of man is still introduced into Christian theist frameworks. Hence a perpetual contradiction, the negation of what has been posited and the positing of what has been negated. The fate of this unconscious atheism is Hegel's radical and conscious atheism, or more exactly his anthropotheism, his deification of man, who finally, after the French Revolution and thanks to Napoleon, can rightly say of himself everything he wrongly attributed to the various nonexistent gods, or gods existing only in the half-conscious thought of the men who created history by their action. The fate of the pseudo-religion of the post-revolutionary German philosophers, and of all religions in general, is the self, the human personal I, which knows itself to be, and is, "the fate of essentiality and actuality". The words "rightly" and "wrongly" state the thesis of anthropotheism with its precondition: man could not rightly claim divinity before Napoleon, since before the end of history he had not yet become what the gods symbolised.

This atheism will be proclaimed in Chapter VIII, the conclusion of the *Phenomenology*. In Chapter VII Hegel will review all the theological ideas integrated into his anthropology. This summary of the religious parts of the six chapters is the first part of the introduction to Chapter VII (pp. 473–474); in the second and third parts Hegel sets out the essential features of the theologies he will analyse. The plan of the lecture is thereby stated.

Hegel's atheist Science is the "self-knowing Spirit" in the proper and strong sense: in and through it Spirit, meaning the human spirit, since there is no other, as this same Science shows, understands itself. But in a broader sense religion, theology, is also self-knowledge, since in believing he speaks of God, man in fact speaks only of himself. One can therefore say that the Spirit manifested in religions, the Spirit theologies speak of, is also a self-knowing Spirit; theology is a self-consciousness of Spirit. The two senses, strict and broad, allow Kojève to read Hegel's phrase "self-knowing Spirit" as applying to religion without conceding theism.

Hegel says this in the first sentence of the second part of the introduction (Hoffmeister p. 474): in religion, self-knowing Spirit is immediately its own pure self-consciousness. The sentence is short and Kojève translates it without insertion.

In and through theology or theologies, Spirit, meaning human spirit, becomes conscious of itself. Yet theology is not philosophy, still less Hegel's Science. The self-consciousness that appears in theologies is still inadequate, and Hegel indicates this inadequacy by the sacramental word "immediate": in theology Spirit is already self-consciousness, but only "immediately". Instead of "immediate" one can say "in itself" (*an sich*), as opposed to "for itself" (*für sich*) or "in and for itself". In theology Spirit is self-conscious "in itself", not "for itself": it becomes self-conscious only in fact, because in fact there is no Spirit other than the human. And "in itself" also means "for us": it is we, Hegel and his readers, who know that all theology is in fact only anthropology. The equation of "in itself" with "for us" is Hegel's methodological principle; Kojève identifies "us" as Hegel and his readers, as he did in the Introduction (p. 21).

The man who does theology does not know it; he believes he speaks of God, a Spirit other than the human. His self-consciousness is therefore not self-consciousness "for itself"; for him it is only consciousness, conscious of an entity external to man, a beyond, a transcendent, extra-mundane, super-human divinity. The religious man's self-consciousness takes the form of consciousness of an other.

That is what characterises every theology whatever: "in itself" and "for us" it is always man-in-the-world becoming conscious of himself; "for itself", for this man, it is something other than man and the world he lives in. The general definition of theology follows.

Hegel says this in the next sentence (Hoffmeister p. 474 to p. 475): the shapes of Spirit considered, the true Spirit, self-alienated Spirit, and Spirit certain of itself, together constitute Spirit in consciousness, which, opposing itself to its world, does not recognise itself in it. The sentence names the three sections of Chapter VI.

The true Spirit is paganism; self-alienated Spirit is Christianity; Spirit certain of itself is the pseudo-religion of post-revolutionary German philosophy and Protestant theology: Kant, Fichte, Jacobi, the Romantics, and Schleiermacher too. Wherever there is theo-logy there is misunderstanding on man's side: man living in the world becomes conscious of himself unconsciously, as it were, believing he becomes conscious of an extra-mundane, super-human spiritual being. The whole of the theologies man has imagined in the course of history constitutes Spirit in its consciousness, Spirit that in fact becomes self-conscious while believing it becomes conscious of something other than itself. This Spirit opposes itself to the real world and to the Spirit in that world, man, and does not recognise itself there. Chapter VII will concern this Spirit: anthropology presented in the form of theology. The hyphenated "théo-logie", discourse about God, underlines that what is at issue is a kind of discourse, not its object. Schleiermacher's inclusion extends the critique to liberal Protestant theology.

In morality, however, in the still theological philosophy and already philosophical theology of Hegel's immediate German precursors, the transformation of theology into anthropology is already announced, and Hegel's conscious atheist anthropology is only the necessary result of the dialectical development of this third great period. So in Chapter VII Hegel no longer speaks of this German pseudo-religion, but he says a few words about it in the introduction. Kojève translates (Hoffmeister p. 475): in conscience Spirit subjects its objective world, its representation and determinate concepts, and is now self-consciousness at home with itself. In it Spirit, represented as object, has for itself the significance of universal Spirit containing all essential and objective reality; but not in the form of free objective reality, of nature appearing independently. Insofar as Spirit is the object of its consciousness it has a shape, the form of being; but since in religion consciousness is posited as self-consciousness, the shape of Spirit is perfectly transparent to itself, and the objective reality it contains is enclosed and overcome in it, as when we say "all reality": it is universal thought reality. The passage places the moral conscience at the threshold of absolute knowledge: Spirit is transparent to itself, but its reality is only thought.

The Romantic poets, Schelling, Jacobi, Kant himself, in fact divinised man: for them he is the supreme value, absolutely autonomous; they are therefore in fact atheists. Likewise Schleiermacher's Protestant theology is already atheism: for him God has meaning and reality only insofar as he reveals himself in and through man, and religion is reduced to religious psychology. One is very close to Hegelian atheism or anthropotheism. Yet all these thinkers continued to speak of God. Why? Hegel has just said: because they could not identify the man they spoke of with real, conscious man living in the world. They spoke of the "soul", "Spirit", the "knowing subject", not of living, real, tangible man. Like all bourgeois intellectuals, they opposed "ideal" man, living in and through his reasoning, to real man, living in and through his action in the world. They were therefore still Christians: they split man in two and fled the real. And this idealist dualism necessarily takes a theist form: soul opposed to body, the empirical world opposed to a "pure", supersensible Spirit, a God. The explanation of why the idealists kept God is Kojève's key argument: theism survives wherever the real, acting man is separated from an ideal self. God is the name of the ideal self when it is not recognised as one's own.

Man attributes supreme value to himself, but does not yet dare attribute it to himself as living, that is, acting, in the concrete world; he does not dare accept this world as an ideal. He attributes value to what is extra-mundane, purely mental in him. He flees the world, flees himself as "worldly", and in this flight necessarily finds a super-human God to whom he attributes the values he in fact wanted to attribute to himself. The verb "dare" repeats the Slave's lack of courage: the idealist, like the Slave, does not dare.

It is therefore ultimately the refusal, servile in origin, to accept the real world, the desire to flee into the extra-mundane ideal, that is the basis of every religion, every theo-logy. The dualism between the ideal, the image I form of myself, and the reality I am, underlies the dualism between the world and man-in-the-world on the one side and God and the beyond on the other. This is Kojève's most general definition of religion: the projection of the gap between self-image and reality. Its servile origin ties it to the Master–Slave dialectic.

Hegel studies the objectification of this dualism by theological thought in Chapter VII. He tries to show how the development of religions gradually eliminates this dualism and ends in post-revolutionary atheism, which finally equates the human ideal and human reality by realising the ideal in the world. Then Spirit-in-the-world, human Spirit, becomes Spirit simply; then God ceases to be a super-human being and man himself becomes God, in and through Hegel's Science. The formula "Spirit-in-the-world becomes Spirit simply" states anthropotheism in Hegel's own vocabulary.

Hegel says this in the next passage (Hoffmeister p. 475). Kojève translates: since in religion the determination of Spirit's consciousness proper does not have the form of free otherness, Spirit's existence is distinguished from its self-consciousness, and its proper reality falls outside religion. There is only one Spirit of both, but its consciousness does not embrace both at once, and religion appears as only a part of the existence and activity of Spirit, the other part being life in its objectively real world. Since we now know, after the analyses of Chapter VI, that Spirit in its world and Spirit conscious of itself as Spirit, Spirit in religion, are one and the same, the perfection (*Vollendung*) of religion consists in the two becoming equal: not only that the objective reality of Spirit be embraced by religion, but that Spirit as self-conscious become objectively real to itself and the object of its consciousness. Kojève's bracket, "after the analyses of Chapter VI", places the knowledge of the identity of the two Spirits after the historical chapter, as his reading requires.

Religion is born of dualism, of the gap between ideal and reality, between the idea man has of himself, his self, and his conscious life in the empirical world, his existence (*Dasein*). As long as the gap remains there will always be a tendency to project the ideal outside the world: there will always be religion, theism, theology. Conversely, every religion reflects this dualism: in religious thought, theology, which always opposes the divine to the worldly and human; and in religious reality itself. Religion never encompasses the whole of human existence: «il n'y a jamais de théo-cratie véritable» (there is never true theocracy) (p. 212). Religious existence runs alongside existence in the concrete world, and the religious man is always more or less a monk, detached "from the world", "from the age". The claim that true theocracy is impossible follows from the structure of religion: a religion that encompassed the whole of existence would have no beyond and would cease to be religion.

Since the dualism at the basis of religion, and engendered by it, is ultimately illusory, the unrealised ideal and its transposition into God not existing, it cannot last forever, for then it would be real: religion is therefore a transient phenomenon. When the ideal is realised, the dualism disappears and with it religion and theism. The ideal is realised in and through revolutionary negating action. So every true, fully successful revolution necessarily entails atheism. Conversely, only when man ceases to project the ideal into the beyond can he want to realise it by action in the world, to make a revolution: conscious atheism necessarily leads to revolution. «Théisme et Révolution s'excluent donc mutuellement» (theism and revolution therefore exclude each other) (p. 213), and every attempt at synthesis can lead only to a misunderstanding, revealed as such as soon as one moves to action proper. But one must not forget that the Revolution realises the very ideal that religion projects into the beyond. The Revolution realises religion in the world, but does so by "overcoming" it as religion. And religion "overcome" as religion or theology by its realisation in the world is absolute Science.
