The argument that an illusion cannot last forever, since what lasts forever is real, is a characteristic Kojèvian inference from ontology to history. The mutual exclusion of theism and revolution was a live political thesis in the 1930s, when Christian socialism and Catholic revolutionary movements sought a synthesis. Kojève's answer is that the synthesis is a misunderstanding, yet the revolution is religion realised.

For Hegel this concerns the Christian religion, its realisation by the Revolution of 1789, and its "sublimation" in Hegel's Science. The Revolution is preceded by eighteenth-century atheism, in which the nothingness of God was revealed to man through the emptiness of deist theology or pseudo-theology. It is therefore an atheist man who triggers revolutionary action. But this action realises the Christian ideal. This realisation transforms the ideal into truth (*Wahrheit*), the revelation of a reality, into absolute Science. Hegel's Science therefore reveals nothing but the complete reality of the Christian idea. But once realised in the world, this idea ceases to be Christian, theist, religious, since the divine Spirit realised in the world is no longer divine but human. «Et c'est là le fond même de la Science absolue de Hegel» (and that is the very foundation of Hegel's absolute Science) (p. 213). The paradox, an atheist revolution realising the Christian ideal, is the historical form of anthropotheism. Hegel's Science is Christian in content and atheist in form.

That is what Hegel says in the last three lines of the passage cited. The aim of religious development is the integral realisation of religion, the Christian religion: man must be "embraced" (*befasst*) by religion in his objective reality, as humanity living in the world, as universal State. But, Hegel adds, this means atheism, since at that moment man will be and understand himself as objective and real Spirit; he will say of himself what he previously said of his God. In short, the "completion" (*Vollendung*) of religion is its "overcoming" (*Aufhebung*) as religion in and through Hegel's anthropological Science. Kojève remarks that this passage is no longer equivocal: "Spirit in religion", God, and "Spirit in its world", man or humanity, are "the same" (*dasselbe*). The identity of *Vollendung* and *Aufhebung* is the formula of the whole lecture. Kojève's claim that *dasselbe* removes the equivocation is his strongest textual point.

These ideas are developed further in the passage that ends the second part of the introduction (Hoffmeister p. 475 to p. 476). Kojève translates: insofar as in religion Spirit represents itself to itself, it is consciousness, and the objective reality enclosed in religion is the shape and garment (*Kleid*) of Spirit's representation. But in this representation objective reality does not obtain its full right, to be not only garment but free, autonomous existence. Conversely, because it lacks completion in itself, this reality is a determinate shape that does not attain what it should represent, self-conscious Spirit. For Spirit's shape to express Spirit itself, it would have to be nothing but this Spirit, and Spirit would have to appear to itself, be objectively real, as it is in its essence. Only so would what may seem the opposite demand also be met, that the object of Spirit's consciousness have the form of free objective reality; for only the being that is its own object as absolute Spirit is as much a free objective reality for itself as it remains self-conscious in that reality. The image of the garment names religion's relation to reality: it clothes Spirit without being its body.

As long as man becomes conscious of himself unconsciously, as it were, doing anthropology in the form of theology, speaking of himself while believing he speaks of God, he will never understand himself fully and completely; he will never know what Spirit really is. On the one hand, in theology he does not understand his own real existence in the world; if he assimilates himself to God, he must conceive himself as able and obliged to live outside the world. On the other hand, and for that reason, Spirit appears to him in an imperfect, perishable, material form. The Spirit one opposes to the world and to concrete man, conceiving it as a transcendent God, is not total: it is a reality opposed to another reality, and so a particular reality, a being beside other beings. The God of theology is always an "ideal", a more or less complete "abstraction". To give divine Spirit the fullness of being one must place it in the world and conceive it as the "entelechy" of the world. But to conceive it so is to conceive it as worldly Spirit, human Spirit, no longer as God. In short, the man who seeks to understand himself fully and completely as Spirit can be satisfied only by an atheist anthropology. That is why the fate of every theology, of every religion, is ultimately atheism. The argument that a transcendent God is a particular being beside others is Hegel's critique of the "bad infinite" applied to theology: an infinite opposed to the finite is itself finite. Kojève draws the atheist consequence Hegel draws only implicitly.

This passage contains the technical term Hegel uses for theology: *Vor-stellung*, re-presentation. In theism man becomes conscious of himself, but in the mode of representation: he projects himself outside himself, "places himself before himself" (*stellt sich vor*), and, no longer recognising himself in this projection, believes he is facing a transcendent God. So Hegel can say that the only difference between his Science and Christian theology is that the latter is a representation (*Vorstellung*) while his Science is a concept (*Begriff*), a developed concept. «Il suffit de dire de l'Homme tout ce que le chrétien dit de son Dieu, pour avoir l'anthropologie athée qui est à la base de la Science de Hegel» (it suffices to say of man everything the Christian says of his God to have the atheist anthropology at the basis of Hegel's Science) (p. 215). The hyphenated *Vor-stellung*, placing before, and *be-greifen*, grasping, carry the argument: to conceive is to take back what one had projected. The last sentence is the most concise formula of Kojève's reading of Hegel.

Having indicated the essential features of the phenomenon to be described in Chapter VII, theology, and marked the endpoint of its dialectical development, the history of religious doctrines, Hegel moves to the third and last part of the introduction: placing Chapter VII within the whole of the *Phenomenology* and indicating its internal structure. The transition is Kojève's.

Kojève translates (Hoffmeister p. 476 to p. 477): since self-consciousness is at first distinguished from consciousness proper, religion from Spirit in its world, from Spirit's existence, this existence consists in the whole of Spirit insofar as its moments present themselves as separating from one another, each for itself. The moments are consciousness (Chapters I–III), self-consciousness (IV), Reason (V), and Spirit (VI), namely Spirit as immediate, not yet consciousness of Spirit. Their integrated totality constitutes Spirit in its worldly existence as such. Spirit as Spirit contains the shapes considered so far in their general determinations, these four moments. Religion presupposes the complete course of these moments and is their simple totality, their absolute self. Moreover, the course of these moments should not be represented, in relation to religion, as taking place in time. Only the whole Spirit is in time, and only the shapes that are shapes of the whole Spirit as whole present themselves in a series. For only the whole has objective reality proper, and so the form of pure freedom toward the other, which expresses itself as time. The moments of Spirit, consciousness, self-consciousness, Reason, and Spirit, have no empirical existence separately, since they are only moments. As Spirit was distinguished from its moments, their particular determination must be distinguished from the moments themselves: each moment differentiates itself again into a process and takes shape differently, as sense-certainty was distinguished from perception within consciousness. These aspects separate in time and belong to a specific whole. For Spirit descends from its universality to particularity through determination: determination, the middle term, is consciousness, self-consciousness, and so on; particularity is constituted by the shapes of these moments, which therefore represent Spirit in its particularity, its objective reality, and are distinguished in time, but so that each following shape preserves in itself those that precede. The passage (¶679–680) is Hegel's own statement of the logical and temporal structure of the book, which Kojève's reading of Chapters I–V as structural and VI–VIII as historical depends on. The definition of time as "the form of pure freedom toward the other" belonging only to the whole is important for his later lectures on time.

The text first teaches something that goes without saying. The sequence of sections, consciousness (Chapters I–III), self-consciousness (IV), Reason (V), and Spirit (VI), is not temporal. The sequence of phenomena within each section, however, unfolds in time: sensation (I) precedes perception (II), which precedes the Understanding (III). But the Understanding, vulgar science and so on, is posterior to the fight and labour described in Chapter IV. Likewise the intellectual of Chapter V is found only in the Christian world analysed in VI, B, and so is posterior to the pagan world of VI, A. But the sequence of sections A, B, C of Chapter VI corresponds to the course of historical development: Greek city, Roman Empire, feudalism, absolutism, Revolution, Napoleon, German philosophy, Hegel. And the temporal series sensation, perception, Understanding corresponds not only to the development of the isolated individual but also to the evolution of humanity analysed in Chapter VI. The reading gives a double chronology: within sections the order is temporal, between sections it is logical, and Chapter VI's order is historical. The Understanding comes after labour in time though before it in the book, which confirms Kojève's genealogy of science from servile labour.

Religion presupposes, in the logical, not temporal, sense, the whole of the "moments" described in the six preceding chapters. That can only mean: it is concrete, real man who is religious and does theology, not a "pure" consciousness, a "pure" Desire, a "pure" action, but man-conscious-of-himself-in-his-active-life-in-the-world. Hegel says that religion logically presupposes the whole of this life in the world, that is, history. Religion is always an ideology, an ideal "superstructure" founded on the "infrastructure" of real, active history realised as fight and labour. Religion is only the "absolute self" of this reality: in and through theology man becomes conscious of real humanity, the people, the State, social, political, historical reality. A people must first constitute itself by action in order then to contemplate itself, unconsciously, in a religion, in its God. The Marxian vocabulary returns explicitly. The priority of action over religion is the materialist thesis: the people exists before its god.

But on the other hand, only by becoming conscious of itself is a people truly a people and not an animal "society". It becomes conscious of itself in religion. So only in and through religion is the people constituted as a human individuality, at least as long as religion is not replaced by Hegelian Science. The correction qualifies the materialism: religion is not merely a reflection, since it constitutes the people as human. The relation between infrastructure and superstructure is reciprocal.

Hegel says this in the following passage (Hoffmeister p. 477 to p. 478). Kojève translates: religion is the completion of Spirit, to which its particular moments, consciousness, self-consciousness, Reason, and Spirit, return as to their ground; and these moments together constitute the existing objective reality of the whole Spirit, which exists only as the movement that differentiates its aspects and returns into itself from them. The becoming of religion as such is contained in the movement of the universal moments. The whole Spirit, the Spirit of religion, is the movement by which Spirit proceeds from its immediacy to the knowledge of what it is in itself, and reaches the point where the shape in which it appears to its consciousness perfectly equals its essence and it contemplates itself as it is. In this becoming Spirit is itself in the determinate shapes that constitute its differences, and each determinate religion has a determinate objectively real Spirit. The determinate shape of a religion selects, for its real Spirit, from the shapes of each moment the one that corresponds to it; the single determination of the religion penetrates all aspects of its real existence and stamps them with a common seal. The idea that each religion "selects" corresponding shapes from all the moments gives Kojève the basis for his reading of religions as total visions of a society.

Religious development is only a "moment" of real, active historical development, and it is this real process, the infrastructure, that determines the particular forms of the religions. The aim of religious development is atheist philosophy, in which Spirit contemplates itself as it really is: "er sich anschaue wie er ist". The stages of this perfect self-understanding are represented by the different religions, each corresponding to a society, a determinate Spirit: "einen bestimmten Geist". A religion, a theology, reflects the specific characters of the real Spirit, the spirit of a people; it is therefore indeed a projection into the beyond of the character of an already formed social reality. But on the other hand, the people constitutes itself as a homogeneous unity only by having elaborated a religion common to all its members. Christianity, for instance, results from the real transformations that formed the bourgeois world in the Roman Empire; without that Empire Christianity would have remained «une simple secte galiléenne» (a mere Galilean sect) (p. 219). But the new social unity, the Christian world, was constituted only because there was projection into the Christian religion. The example of Christianity illustrates the reciprocal relation: the Empire made Christianity possible, and Christianity made the Christian world a unity.

According to what Hegel has just said, the analysis of religious development in Chapter VII should pass through the same stages as the analysis of real development in Chapter VI. In fact the parallelism is not maintained, and Hegel now explains why. The transition restates the problem of the displacement raised at the start of the lecture.

Kojève translates (Hoffmeister p. 478 to p. 479): the shapes presented so far are now arranged differently from the way they appeared in their series. In the series considered, each moment deepened itself into a whole in its own principle, and knowing was the depth or Spirit in which these moments, which have no subsistence in themselves, had their substance. Now this substance has come to the surface; it is the depth of Spirit certain of itself, which does not allow the particular principle to isolate itself and make itself a whole. Gathering all the moments and holding them together, this substance advances in the total richness of its real Spirit, and all its determinate moments receive in common the same determination, that of the whole. This Spirit certain of itself and its movement are the true objective reality and the being in and for itself of these moments. The single series so far marked its turns by knots, but from these knots continued as a single line; now it is, so to speak, broken at these knots, the universal moments, and decomposed into several lines, which unite symmetrically, gathered into a single bundle, so that the analogous differences in which each specific line took shape coincide. These differences must be understood only as moments of becoming, not as parts of a static whole. In real Spirit they are attributes of its substance; in religion they are only predicates of the subject. In itself, or for us, all forms are in Spirit and in each Spirit; but what matters in Spirit's reality is the choice of the determination that exists for it in its consciousness, in which it knows its self is expressed, the shape in which it knows its essence lies. The image of the series broken at its knots and rebound into a bundle describes the method of Chapter VII: each religion gathers the moments of all the earlier chapters under one determination. The distinction between attributes of a substance and predicates of a subject is Spinozist in vocabulary; Kojève uses it next.

In the previous chapters Hegel analysed the constituents of the human being one after another: sensation, perception, Understanding, Desire, and so on. But all these elements are real only in concrete man, and concrete man exists only within society, the people, the State. The people becomes conscious of itself, unconsciously, in its religion. It is therefore theology that reflects human reality, not sense experience, physics, psychology, and so on. Each theology gives a global vision of human reality, in which the "attributes of the substance", the substance being society as such (people, State), appear in the form of "predicates" attributed to the "subject", God. The different religions are thus stages in the becoming of humanity's self-consciousness, not fragments of it to be added together into a whole. Each religion is a total vision of human reality, and there is becoming of religion only because there is becoming of that reality. The claim that theology, not psychology or physics, reflects human reality is striking: it gives religion a cognitive privilege over the sciences, as the only form of knowledge that grasps society as a whole.

Yet if "in itself or for us" each religion reflects the totality, it is not so for those who profess it. Each given religion emphasises one "moment" more than the others, which presupposes and conditions the real predominance of that element in the historical life of the people who hold it. The actual totality is therefore an integration of the "moments" partially actualised in the different religions. One can say, after all, that complete self-consciousness is a sum or integration of the partial becomings-conscious that take place in and through religions. The two statements, each religion is total and the totality is a sum of religions, are reconciled by the distinction between "for us" and "for them".

We know, moreover, that perfect self-consciousness is areligious, atheist: man then knows that it is himself he becomes conscious of, not God. The partial becomings-conscious are theological: man partially becomes conscious of his human reality by imagining a particular form of divinity. The restatement prepares Hegel's next sentence.

Hegel has already insisted on this difference but returns to it (Hoffmeister p. 479). Kojève translates: the difference between real Spirit and Spirit that knows itself as Spirit, between itself as consciousness and itself as self-consciousness, is overcome in the Spirit that knows itself according to its truth: its consciousness and self-consciousness are equalised. The sentence states the goal: consciousness and self-consciousness coincide in absolute knowledge.

"The Spirit that knows itself in its truth", or revealed reality, is the Hegelian Spirit of absolute knowledge treated in Chapter VIII. In Chapter VII the concern is the Spirit that knows itself in and through religion. Kojève translates Hegel's contrast (Hoffmeister p. 479 to p. 480): since religion here exists only immediately, the difference is not yet taken back into Spirit; only the mere concept of religion is posited. In it the essence is self-consciousness that is all truth for itself and contains all reality in it. This self-consciousness, as consciousness, has itself for object. Spirit that knows itself only immediately is for itself Spirit in the form of immediacy, and the determination of the shape in which it appears to itself is that of being. This being is filled not by sensation or manifold matter or other one-sided moments, aims, and determinations, but by Spirit, and is known to itself as all truth and reality. But this filling is not equal to its shape; Spirit as essence is not equal to its consciousness. Spirit is real only as absolute Spirit, insofar as it exists for itself in its truth as it is in its self-certainty, or insofar as the extremes into which it divides as consciousness exist for one another in the shape of Spirit. The shape Spirit takes as object of its consciousness remains filled by its certainty as by a substance, and this content prevents the object from sinking to pure objectivity, the form of self-consciousness's negativity. The immediate unity of Spirit with itself is the basis, or pure consciousness, within which consciousness divides. Enclosed in its pure self-consciousness, Spirit in religion does not exist as the creator of a nature as such; what it produces in this movement are its own shapes as spirits, which together form the completeness of its manifestation; and this movement is the becoming of its perfect reality through its particular aspects, its imperfect realities. Kojève inserts "God" as a gloss on "being": the immediate self-knowledge of Spirit represents itself as a being, that is, as God.

Religion is "immediate" in Chapter VII: it is religion in the proper sense, theology. Theology is the "immediate" form of "Science": anthropology not mediated by the negation of God, which presupposes mediation by the nothingness of death, realised in and through Robespierre's Terror. "Science" not mediated by negation is non-dialectical, pre-Hegelian philosophy. It is "positive" in that it substantialises Spirit, understanding it as a being, a given being, in fact natural and non-human but conceived here as a divine, all-powerful, eternal being identical with itself. Spirit conceived as such a being is God. "Immediate" philosophy is therefore theology and not anthropology. The link between the negation of God and the Terror is Kojève's boldest: atheism is mediated by the experience of death, and the Terror is where that experience was had collectively. The definition of God as Spirit conceived as given being connects theology with the naturalism Kojève attributes to Hegel's monism.

God is therefore a being, but a spiritual being: materialised Spirit. And this Spirit, says Hegel, creates not nature, the sensible world, but spiritual shapes, "shapes as spirits", that is, gods. In other words, as a religious being, man or human Spirit creates not natural forms and laws, not real, empirical worlds, but theologies, myths with anthropological content and theological form. The formula "anthropological content, theological form" summarises the whole reading of Chapter VII.

The becoming of this god-creating Spirit, the development of religious thought, the logico-temporal sequence of the theologies elaborated in history, is what Hegel will describe in Chapter VII. In the passage that ends the introduction he indicates its general structure: section A on primitive, prehistoric religion, which he calls natural religion; section B on "art-religion", Greco-Roman religion; and section C on "absolute religion", Christianity. "Logico-temporal" names the double order of Chapter VII: its sequence is both a logical progression and a history.

Kojève translates the final passage (Hoffmeister p. 480): the first reality of Spirit in religion is the mere concept of religion itself, religion as immediate and so natural; in it Spirit knows itself as its object in a natural, immediate shape. The second is necessarily that in which Spirit knows itself in the shape of overcome naturalness, the self; it is therefore art-religion, since the shape rises to the form of the self through the productive activity of consciousness, which thereby contemplates in its object its own action, the self. The third overcomes the one-sidedness of the first two: the self is as much immediate as immediacy is self. If in the first Spirit is in the form of consciousness and in the second in that of self-consciousness, in the third it is in the form of their union; it has the shape of being in and for itself, and insofar as it is represented as it is in and for itself, it is revealed religion. But although in revealed religion Spirit has reached its true shape, this shape and representation are the unsurmounted side from which Spirit must pass into the concept, to dissolve completely in it the form of objectivity, in the concept that contains its opposite in itself. At that moment, and this is the absolute knowledge of Chapter VIII, Spirit has grasped its own concept as "we", Hegel and his readers, have just grasped it; and the shape of this Spirit, the element of its existence, insofar as it is concept, is this Spirit itself. The three religions correspond to consciousness, self-consciousness, and their union, the triad of Chapters I–III, IV, and V. Art-religion, where consciousness contemplates its own productive action, is the religion of labour in Kojève's sense, as the plan in the appendix confirms.

This last "shape" of Spirit, which is itself Spirit, is the Sage in his empirical existence: «c'est Hegel» (it is Hegel) (p. 224). The lecture ends with the identification that Chapter VIII will justify: the concept existing as a man. The Sage is the shape of Spirit that is Spirit itself, the incarnation of the concept in a particular empirical individual.

### A. Natural Religion (Hoffmeister pp. 481–489)

#### Interpretation of the Introduction to Section A of Chapter VII (Hoffmeister pp. 481–483)

The sixth lecture of 1937–38, given in full, opens with a remark on the text's scope. This new introduction is still quite general, less an introduction to Section A than to the whole chapter; Hegel takes up the ideas of the general introduction just commented on, but more simply and clearly. Kojève's reading of the section's introduction as a second general introduction explains why he treats it at length and the natural religions themselves only in notes.

Hegel first fixes again the phenomenon to be studied, religion or theology. Kojève translates (Hoffmeister p. 481): Spirit that knows Spirit is consciousness of itself and exists for itself in the form of the objective; it is, and is at the same time being-for-itself. It is for itself, the side of self-consciousness, as opposed to the side of its consciousness, of relating to itself as object. In its consciousness lies opposition and so the determinateness of the shape in which Spirit appears to itself and knows itself. The consideration of religion concerns only this shape, since its shapeless essence, its pure concept, has already emerged. Kojève's bracketed "at the end of Chapter VI" places the pure concept of Spirit there, which he interprets next.

In self-consciousness the knowing subject relates to itself as a known object. Self-consciousness is necessarily also consciousness of something outside consciousness, which here is consciousness itself. In self-consciousness the I I become conscious of is necessarily also an object (*Gegen-stand*), a thing set before me, which I contemplate as a static, given being, identical with itself, unchanged by being known. The description sets up the problem: how can the subject be an object for itself?

All this is incontestable; no philosopher has described self-consciousness differently from Hegel's first sentence. Divergences begin only with the explanation: how and why the subject can relate to itself as to an object. Kojève distinguishes description from explanation, as in phenomenology generally: the phenomenon is agreed, its ground disputed.

Hegel's explanation is familiar. In self-consciousness man relates to himself as object. For self-consciousness to be a truth, the revelation of a reality, man must really be an object; he must first really objectify himself. He does so by action (*Tat*, *Tun*) and only by action: by the negating action of labour, which creates the human world of technique, as objective and real as the natural world; and by the negating action of the fight, which creates the social, political, historical human world, equally real and objective. The technical and historical world is man's work and would not exist without him. In becoming conscious of this world one becomes conscious of a human reality, and of a reality (*Wirklichkeit*) because this world is as real, as much a being, as the natural world. The explanation joins the theory of self-consciousness to the theory of labour: one becomes an object to oneself only by making objects.

Only by becoming conscious of his objective work, the product of his action that maintains itself in reality, can man become conscious of himself and reach a truth in the proper sense. The conclusion follows: self-knowledge is knowledge of one's works.

Hegel said this in so many words in Chapter V (Hoffmeister pp. 287–288). Kojève translates: human activity (*Handeln*) is precisely the becoming of Spirit as consciousness; what this consciousness is in itself it knows from its reality; so the individual cannot know what he is until he has brought himself to reality through activity (*Tun*). The passage comes from the spiritual animal kingdom (¶401), which Kojève read in 1935–36 as a critique of the intellectual.

For self-consciousness, for man to relate to himself as object, he must first realise and objectify himself by action. The cited text might suggest that man acts only to know himself, that he exists before acting. In fact he cannot become self-conscious before objectifying action, because there is nothing in him to be known. Before action he is only Desire (*Begierde*) or pure I (*reines Ich*), a void that becomes something knowable only by actively negating what is and what is not himself, being, the given. «Car l'Homme est son activité ; il n'existe pas en dehors de son œuvre» (for man is his activity; he does not exist outside his work) (p. 227). That is why he can become self-conscious only by relating to himself as object, to his work, the product of his action. The correction is important: action is not a means to self-knowledge of a pre-existing self; it produces the self that will be known.

Hegel says this in another passage of Chapter V (Hoffmeister p. 246). Kojève translates: the true being (*Sein*) of man is rather his deed (*Tat*); in it individuality is real; in action individuality presents itself as the negative essence that is only insofar as it overcomes being. The quotation is the one cited from the physiognomy section (¶322) in 1934–35 (p. 75).

Man exists only insofar as he "overcomes dialectically" being, the given. This overcoming, which preserves the overcome by sublimating it, is the deed, the human action of fight and labour, which transforms, negates, or overcomes the given as given but preserves it as a being produced by man, and so "sublimates" it by conscious and voluntary overcoming. Man's work is more human, more "spiritual", than the raw material. In this work, this sublimated, humanised being, man realises himself, and only in becoming conscious of it does he truly become conscious of what he really, objectively is, «car il n'est rien d'autre ni de plus que ce qu'est son œuvre» (for he is nothing other or more than his work is) (p. 227). The gloss applies *Aufhebung* to labour: the product preserves the material as humanised. The equation of man with his work is the strongest form of the thesis.

This action, carried out, objectified in its work, and conscious of itself in it, is what Hegel calls Spirit. "Spirit that knows Spirit" is Spirit, man, who knows he is action conscious of itself in and through its work. Man knows this through Hegel's Science. The "Spirit that knows Spirit" of the first line is therefore Hegel, or more exactly the *Phenomenology*, or more exactly still the absolute knowledge that results from it. In the second sentence Hegel speaks of the man of absolute knowledge, who places himself on the side of self-consciousness as opposed to consciousness, through which he relates to himself as an external object. The definition of Spirit as action conscious of itself in its work is Kojève's most compact. The identification of the first line's subject with Hegel follows from it.

Man knows he is action and that the object he relates to is his work. He knows this object is really himself, that he knows himself in knowing the object. Only thus, in and through Hegel's Science, is man truly self-consciousness. Self-consciousness proper is reserved for the Sage.

Before becoming Hegel or Hegelian man, man is only consciousness. In becoming conscious of the object, the world he lives in, he does not know he becomes conscious of himself, because he does not know that he is his action, that he is in his work, that the work is he. Not knowing it, he believes the work or object is a fixed and stable being independent of him, an entity opposed to him (*Entgegengesetztes*). This object is thus for him a "determinateness of shape" (*Bestimmtheit der Gestalt*): a determinate, fixed, immutable entity, a plastic, concrete form. Recognising himself in the work in this way, he understands himself as a determinateness and a shape: man is then for himself a fixed given thing with determinate, stable qualities. That is what Hegel says in the third sentence. The consequence is important: whoever misrecognises his work as a thing misrecognises himself as a thing. Religious consciousness reifies both God and man.

In the first part of the fourth sentence Hegel says that this is precisely how man understands himself in religion or theo-logy. He contemplates himself in his work without knowing it is his; so the work is for him a shape, a being, an immutable divine being given once for all, not an action or its product. And he himself, facing this being, is also a being: «un Homme-chose en rapport fixe et donné une fois pour toutes avec le Dieu-chose» (a thing-man in a fixed relation, given once for all, with the thing-God) (p. 228). The pair "thing-man" and "thing-God" names religion's double reification.

The second part of the fourth sentence says that Chapter VII will speak only of the shape (*Gestalt*), the plastic external form of Spirit, Spirit as it appears in theology; as for the shapeless essence (*ungestaltetes Wesen*), the pure concept of Spirit, we already know it. We know it because it was constituted at the end of Chapter VI, where Hegel appeared, that is, Spirit as it appears in and through Hegel's Science. The claim that Hegel himself appeared at the end of Chapter VI rests on the reading of "evil and forgiveness" in 1936–37.

What does this mean? Hegel's Science is absolute knowledge, in which Spirit reveals itself to itself as it is. If this Science is the fullness of the revelation of Spirit, the theological revelation must be less perfect and its analysis should precede that of Hegel's Science. Yet Chapter VII comes after the end of Chapter VI, where this Science has already appeared. There seems to be a contradiction. Kojève raises the objection his reading invites: if Hegel's Science appears at the end of VI, why is religion analysed afterwards?

In fact there is none. Hegel's Science as a whole is analysed under the name of absolute knowledge in Chapter VIII, so the analysis of theological knowledge precedes it. To remove all trace of contradiction one need only say that what appeared at the end of Chapter VI is only a part, or rather an aspect, of Hegel's Science, which must be completed by the aspect constituted in the analysis of religious knowledge in Chapter VII to form the whole of absolute knowledge. The solution divides Hegel's Science into two aspects, which the next paragraphs identify.

Hegel indicates this himself in saying "pure concept": what appeared at the end of VI is only the abstract notion of Hegel's Science and of the Spirit revealed through it. The concept proper, the concrete concept, appears only in Chapter VIII, and its concreteness comes from the concreteness of the shape that appears in Chapter VII. «Le "Begriff" du Chapitre VIII, c'est le "reiner Begriff" du Chapitre VI, plus la "Gestalt" du Chapitre VII» (the "concept" of Chapter VIII is the "pure concept" of Chapter VI plus the "shape" of Chapter VII) (p. 229). The formula is a clear structural thesis about the book's last three chapters. It matches Hegel's statement in Chapter VIII that absolute knowledge unites the beautiful soul and revealed religion (¶794–797).

For Hegel Spirit is human Spirit. The abstract notion of Spirit is the notion of abstract Spirit, of abstract man. Abstract man, nonexistent in reality and existing only in thought for the abstract thinker, is the isolated particular opposed to the universal: the community, the people, the State, humanity in its spatio-temporal whole, history. Pre-Hegelian philosophy, as opposed to religion or theology, deals with this abstract man. What appeared at the end of Chapter VI is indeed Hegel, but Hegel as the last of the philosophers, still opposed to religion and so necessarily requiring a theological complement: the particularist side, the *Einzelheit* side, of Hegel's Science. This must be completed by a universalist side, the *Allgemeinheit* side, to form the "totalitarianism" of absolute knowledge. The word *totalitarisme*, used in 1938, means here only the totality of absolute knowledge, though its political resonance in that year is hard to miss. The division of Hegel into the last philosopher and the first Sage is a precise interpretation of the transition from VI to VIII.

This knowledge is absolute only because the particular side is linked in it to the universal side, which thereby ceases to be a theology and becomes a universalist anthropology, completing particularist philosophy and so accounting for the whole of Spirit as human Spirit. Only thus is Hegel not only the last representative of philosophy opposed to religion but the first thinker, the Sage, who replaces religion with Science instead of opposing it. In Chapter VII Hegel will show how and why theology finally becomes an atheist anthropology, one that remains as universal and concrete as the theology from which it came. Chapter VI showed the origin of the particularist aspect of Science; Chapter VII will show the origin of the universalist side. That is why Chapter VIII does not follow immediately on Chapter VI. Chapter VI ends with Hegel's interpretation of Napoleon, the most concrete and real of men, since he is the first realisation of individuality. But at the end of Chapter VI Hegel's Science accounts only for the particularist aspect of Napoleon's individuality. It shows that Napoleon and the State are one, but in their particularist aspect: Napoleon as creator of the State, the State as the realisation of his particularity. It does not yet show that Napoleon is what he is, the Emperor, only through the State he created. The distinction between Napoleon as creator of the State and as its creature names the missing half: the universal side of the individual.

Or rather, Hegel indicates it by declaring that Napoleon is a God, the "revealed God". But at the end of Chapter VI this remains inexact, since one does not yet know what God is; the absolute essence itself appears only in Chapter VII. If Napoleon is the fully revealed God, he is the integration of all the gods revealed to man in history, and one can account for him only by saying of him everything men have said of their gods. At the end of Chapter VII, in Protestant Christianity, the God-man reveals himself as the community of believers (*Gemeinde*). Only one step then remains: to say that this community is the State, not the Church, the State of Napoleon. In saying it Hegel accounts for concrete man and reaches the concrete concept (*Begriff*) of Spirit; only then is his knowledge truly absolute. At that moment Spirit ceases to be a shape opposed to consciousness and becomes concept, since man knows, through Hegel's thought, that his reality is his conscious and voluntary work, the State realised by Napoleon's action. The step from the Protestant community to the Napoleonic State is the decisive move of Kojève's reading of the end of Chapter VII. Hegel's text identifies the risen Christ with the spirit of the community (¶781–787); the substitution of State for Church is Kojève's.

As long as the State does not know it, Hegel's Science not yet being part of public education in the Napoleonic Empire, as long as the State has not understood that it is the objective reality of Spirit, man will not see his own work in the objectification of Spirit. The State will be for him an autonomous, external reality, and Spirit will be understood as a quasi-natural given. This understanding of Spirit takes place in theology, and only of it will Hegel speak in Chapter VII. The parenthesis about public education is characteristic irony: the end of history awaits the State's adoption of the *Phenomenology* as official doctrine, a condition the Empire did not meet.

Though in theology Spirit has for man the form of a being, this being is not purely natural. Spirit, though extra-human, remains Spirit, and this existing Spirit is called God. The knowledge of Chapter VII is neither vulgar science of nature nor pre-Hegelian philosophical anthropology: it is a theo-logy, a science of Spirit conceived as divine being. The definition of God as "existing Spirit" places theology between physics and philosophy.

Hegel explains this in the next sentence (Hoffmeister p. 481). Kojève translates: the difference between consciousness and self-consciousness falls at the same time within the latter. The shape of religion, God, does not contain the existence of Spirit either as nature free from thought or as thought free from existence; it is existence preserved in thinking, and a thought that is there for itself as existence. The insertion "that is, God" makes the translation an interpretation.

Pre-Hegelian philosophy of consciousness deals only with the isolated particular. Speaking of him, it must speak of the universal to which he is opposed; but this universal is nature, not the State, something absolutely inhuman. Man is considered only in passive opposition to nature; active, transformative contact through labour is neglected. So conceived, man becomes an absolutely non-natural being, without real contact with or power over nature. The diagnosis explains the Cartesian dualism of 1936–37 (p. 119): a philosophy that ignores labour cannot connect mind and world.

Descartes represents this standpoint most clearly, and Hegel has him in mind; but all pre-Hegelian philosophy is more or less Cartesian here. It opposes isolated man reduced to pure, unreal thought to the real universe reduced to thoughtless being, and seeks in vain the link between thoughtless extension and extensionless thought. In vain, since the real link, the negating and so creative action of fight and labour, is wholly unknown to it. The thesis that action is the missing link between *res cogitans* and *res extensa* is Kojève's answer to the mind–body problem: it is solved by labour, not by a theory of substance.

Religion deals with neither this extension nor this thought; it is neither Newtonian physics nor pre-Hegelian philosophy. Its object is Spirit: "existence preserved in thought, and a thought that has existence for itself". For us, for Hegel, this Spirit is real, concrete man in the whole of his conscious creative activity, universal history and the State. For the religious man it is an autonomous entity different from man. That is what the first words indicate: in religion there is a distinction (*Unterschied*) between consciousness and self-consciousness. In its conception of man religion keeps the standpoint of consciousness, which is why pre-Hegelian philosophy can accommodate religion and cannot exist without it. Man here is a particular needing an external universal complement: for philosophy, nature; for religion, God. The symmetry completes the thesis that philosophy and religion need each other, each supplying the universal the other lacks.

That is the whole difference. In religion the opposition of consciousness and self-consciousness is located within self-consciousness. The religious man finds the opposition of particular and universal within himself; the universal is not wholly outside him or inhuman; it is spiritual, Spirit; it is God, not nature. The inner location of the universal distinguishes God from nature.

The religious man distinguishes himself from himself within himself: he opposes consciousness of his isolated, intimate being to consciousness of his being as attached to the universal. This universal, attached to man, is a quasi-human Spirit, yet non-human since opposed to man: in a word, God. God is the religious man's universal side, experienced as other.

Attached to the human particular, the universal is spiritual: thought, self-consciousness, free action. But opposed to the particular and not his work, it is external, given, static: a being. This spiritual being, Spirit existing as a being, is God. The two attributes of God, spirituality and givenness, derive from the two sides of the religious man's relation to his universal: it is his, and it is not his work.

Spirit conceived as being is necessarily a "determinate shape", with a fixed character given once for all, and each religion differs by the form its God takes. Kojève translates Hegel (Hoffmeister p. 481): one religion differs from another by the determinateness of the shape in which Spirit knows itself in it; but this presentation does not exhaust a real religion. The series of religions presents only the different aspects of a single religion, and indeed of each, and the representations that seem to distinguish one real religion from another are found in each. The unity of religion across its forms is Hegel's thesis (¶684).

Hegel repeats what he said in the general introduction (Kojève writes "to Chapter VIII", a slip for Chapter VII). In religion man unconsciously becomes conscious of concrete man, who implies all the constituents of the human being; so there is properly only one religion. Religions differ only by emphasis: in each, one element is stressed and the others remain quasi-unconscious, and the stressed element corresponds to the element of human existence realised most particularly in the historical world or State that engenders the religion. The theory of emphasis unites the unity and plurality of religions and ties each emphasis to a social reality.

At bottom there is only one religion on earth; yet the differences of emphasis are real, and there are several religions. Unity and plurality are reconciled only by becoming: there is a development of religion, whose stages we call religions. Becoming reconciles one and many, Hegel's general solution applied to religion.

Kojève translates Hegel's explanation (Hoffmeister pp. 481–482): the difference must also be considered as a difference of religion. Since Spirit is in the distinction of its consciousness and self-consciousness, the movement aims to overcome this distinction and give the object of consciousness the form of self-consciousness. It is not overcome merely because God is represented as self-consciousness; the represented self is not the real self. For the self truly to belong to the shape, it must be posited there by the activity (*Tun*) of self-consciousness, and the lower determination must show itself overcome by the higher. The represented ceases to be alien only because the self has produced it and so contemplates its determination as its own. Hegel's condition, that the self must be posited by the activity of self-consciousness, is the textual ground for Kojève's reading: God becomes self only when man knows he made him.

This passage confirms Kojève's overall interpretation. There is a real development of religion because religion finally abolishes itself and becomes atheist anthropology, which requires that the notion of God be transformed in history. The aim is the abolition of transcendence: understanding Spirit as human. For this man must understand that he created God, and so must first form an idea of God resembling his idea of himself: theological development is progressive anthropomorphisation. He must also recognise surpassed religious forms as his work, the "idols" he invented before becoming conscious of the "true" God. This development is only the ideological reflection of real, active historical development. The second mechanism is ironic: each religion teaches its believers that earlier gods were human inventions, preparing the same verdict on itself.

The final result is Hegel's atheist anthropology. The anthropomorphisation of God culminates in the idea of Christ; then comes the understanding that this idea is a product of the human mind; man then recognises himself in Christ and understands that he should have said of himself all he said of his God. Hegel says it: man contemplates himself in "objective Spirit", once conceived as divine, when he understands that this Spirit is the State, his work, and he understands it through Hegel's philosophy of the State, a Science that recognises the perfect State and is, or should be, recognised by it. The phrase "is, or should be" repeats the ironic condition of p. 231.

In the next sentence Hegel specifies the character of religious development (Hoffmeister p. 482). Kojève translates: through this activity the lower determination has vanished, since activity is negative, carried out at the expense of another. Where it is still present it has receded into inessentiality; where the lower still dominates while the higher is present, the higher stands beside it without self (*selbstlos*). The sentence describes how religions contain one another in subordinate form.

All development is creative, and all creation is negating action on the given. When a new religion appears, the previous ones are "overcome": the stressing of a new aspect happens only by negating the stressing of the others. In a given religion earlier emphases are preserved without essential value; later emphases are already present, but accessorily. This is *Aufhebung* applied to the history of religions.

This holds, parenthetically, for Hegel's Science in relation to Christianity. Christian theology stresses the individuality of absolute Spirit: God is a person, and a divine-human person. The aspect stressed in Hegel's Science, the human side of Spirit, is thus already present, but accessory: in Jesus Christ man is only a temporary support of God. In Hegel, even if there is anthropotheism, man's being God, a transcendent Spirit, no longer has essential value. What characterises man is no longer the possibility of fleeing the world into a beyond but the possibility of maintaining himself in the world by subjecting it to himself. The parenthesis corrects a possible misreading of anthropotheism: man's divinity lies not in transcendence but in mastery of the world.

The next sentence only specifies what has been said (Hoffmeister p. 482). Kojève translates: although the representations within a religion present the complete movement of the forms of religion, each religion's character is determined by the particular union of consciousness and self-consciousness, by self-consciousness having grasped the determination of the object, appropriated it by its activity, and known it as essential. The key word is "activity": self-consciousness appropriates by doing.

In each religion the believer knows that the stressed aspect is essential (*wesentlich*) because in empirical reality he has just realised by action the constituent of his existence of which he becomes conscious as his God's essential character. It is his because produced by him, and real because inserted into the real world; it is there that he is truly human, since "man's true being is his action". Man attributes a character to his God in theology because he has realised it in his world by action. This is the materialist theory of religion stated precisely: theology follows practice.

Hegel says so explicitly (Hoffmeister p. 482). Kojève translates: the truth of faith in a determinate God shows itself in the fact that the real Spirit, the people having the religion, is constituted like the shape in which it contemplates itself. So the incarnation of God in the pre-Christian Oriental religion has no truth, because its real Spirit lacks this reconciliation of particular and universal. Kojève's brackets gloss the reconciliation in political terms: the universal is God for religion and the State for Hegel.

Truth (*Wahrheit*) is the revelation of a reality in the strong sense. There is truth in a religion only insofar as the idea implied in its theology has been realised in the world where it prevails. This definition of religious truth as realisation is the principle of the whole reading.

So Christian theology is not a truth as long as the Christian world has not realised the idea of individuality, the fusion of particular and universal, of real man and Spirit. A parenthesis adds that this apparently harmless remark contains the whole Hegelian critique of Christianity. Christianity becomes true only when the Christian idea of individuality is realised in this world; but a realised ideal ceases to be an ideal. Man stops projecting it into the beyond and thinking it theologically; instead of fleeing the world he recognises himself in it. When Christianity is realised in the post-revolutionary world, it ceases to be a religion; becoming a truth, it becomes Hegel's atheist anthropology. The paradox is the one stated in the previous lecture: Christianity's truth is its end as religion.

Finally (Hoffmeister pp. 482–483) Hegel explains how Chapter VII will study the religions. Kojève translates: this is not the place to show how the completeness of the other determinations is contained in a particular one. The higher form placed under a lower loses its significance for self-conscious Spirit and belongs to it only superficially, to its representation. The higher form must be considered where it is the principle of a specific religion and is proved true (*bewährt*) by its real Spirit. The principle of method is to treat each form where it dominates.

This marks the difference between a phenomenology and a history of religions. The historian describes a religion as it appeared to its believers; the phenomenologist describes only its essential character, placing it in the whole of religious development to show its role. To aid understanding he "idealises" the stages, taking a religion not as it was but as it should have been had it fully understood itself and fulfilled its historical mission. For this he must connect each religion with the world that engendered it: Chapter VII can be written and understood only after Chapter VI. The method is idealising abstraction applied to religions, and it makes Hegel's philosophy of religion depend on his philosophy of history.

**The Luminous Essence** (*Das Lichtwesen*, Hoffmeister pp. 483–484). The notes return to compressed form. This is the Indo-Iranian religion of light, and also, Kojève adds, the "mana" of primitives, unknown to Hegel. The first paragraph of p. 483 summarises the ontological side of Hegel's system and introduces the section. Man here is a pure I: Desire is still empty and man has not yet acted. He becomes conscious of natural being as something given and unmodifiable, and so of an aspect of himself, but this self is only Desire, something natural. Yet this being is "filled with Spirit"; it is humanised and has the form of a Lord (*Herr*). Man becomes conscious of the divine because there is in him an unsatisfied Desire, satisfied desire vanishing. The Lord here is the future Master before the fight, the man of Desire of the introduction to Chapter IV. There are no Slaves yet in this society: a society where one is hungry and wants to make love, with feasts and orgies. The identification of Hegel's first religion with the stage of Desire begins the mapping of Section A onto Chapter IV. The reference to mana, from the ethnology of Kojève's day, extends Hegel's scheme to material he did not know.

The divinised being here is "the shape of shapelessness" (Hoffmeister p. 484): pure light and darkness, the symbol of empty Desire, the dark I, facing nature, light. Their interaction is symbolised by life-giving light, since only being can satisfy Desire, and devouring fire, since Desire destroys the given. The religion's essential character is the sublime, the majestic, everything concentrated in the "measureless" given. This conformist element of majesty will subsist in all religions but become inessential. The reading of light and darkness as nature and Desire is Kojève's; the persistence of majesty illustrates the law of emphasis just stated.

This religion becomes "totemism" (last paragraph of p. 484) by the dispersion of light into plants and so on. Being in its concrete existence is now venerated: the stage of Desire's natural satisfaction, no longer of Desire unsatisfied. The transition from unsatisfied to satisfied Desire orders the first two stages.

**Plant and Animal** (*Die Pflanze und das Tier*, Hoffmeister pp. 485–486). This is totemism. It corresponds to the fight for life and death (IV, A), but to the fight itself, not the victory that realises mastery: its biological aspect. It is a religion of killing: one kills the totem animal, sacrifices the god. It is the religion of peoples who fight to the death, not to victory; they do not know how to make slaves. It is "natural", plant and animal, without social content, and there is no State. The identification of Hegel's animal religion, the hostile spirits of peoples (¶689), with the fight before enslavement makes Section A a replay of the genesis of man in Chapter IV.

The second paragraph gives the passage to the religion of labour, still natural: it concerns the man who works, turned toward nature, not the man for whom one works, the Master. The distinction anticipates the next stage.

**The Artificer** (*Der Werkmeister*, Hoffmeister pp. 486–489). This is Egyptian religion. What is divinised is the labour of the man who cannot do otherwise than work, labour conditioned by the most urgent need, working not to starve. It is a peasant's religion more than an artisan's. One works for oneself as an animal, not for a human Master: the religion of the future Slave. It is necessary, forced labour without being servile: great effort for a mediocre result. The distinction between forced and servile labour matters: nature forces, but no Master commands.

Man does not merely work; he sanctifies his labour, in an attitude corresponding to the Understanding. Hegel thinks of the Egyptian religion of the pyramid and the obelisk, things that do not exist in nature and so symbolise labour: rational labour realising what exists only in the human mind. The straight line, which is useful (the lever), is sanctified; the tool must be simple. Labour is sanctified only as long as there is no Master; under a Master it is no longer a "natural" instinct but a function of human recognition. The link between geometry and labour applies Kojève's genealogy of the Understanding to Egyptian monuments. The claim about Masters explains why later religions do not worship labour.

To give the dead eternal life, the corpse is placed inside a product of rational labour, the pyramid. The obelisk is a sundial: the cult of light of section a is here mediated by labour. The reading links the first and third stages: light is now measured by a human artefact.

These three stages are progress in religion toward Christianity, but also toward atheism, since each humanises God further. At each step man is superior to the god of the previous stage. Each time man works for a god he surpasses him, until he works consciously for himself, in the perfect State. The thesis restates the lecture's argument in the notes' terms.

The last paragraph gives the passage to Greek religion: man wants to inhabit the pyramid while alive, to enjoy the products of rational labour. At the artificer's stage man still works for another, the god, and is not satisfied; but it is not properly human labour, since not mediated by a Master: bee-like labour, without "service". Yet the world is transformed by this labour, and man begins to work for another. There is a passage from the religion of the artisan, centred on the producer, to the religion of the artist, oriented toward the consumer. The symbol of the passage is the Sphinx, but the Sphinx that speaks: myth and prayer. The producer and consumer religions map the Slave's and the Master's relations to the product. The speaking Sphinx is Hegel's image for the emergence of language from the half-animal form.

### B. The Art-Religion (Hoffmeister pp. 490–520)

The introduction (Hoffmeister pp. 490–492). Man will now speak of the gods, mythology, and to the gods, prayer. Religion is no longer natural: man speaks, and the god resembles man; the divine shape takes human appearance. Recalling labour: at first the raw material dominates and the form is only in potency; at the end the human form is in act. At Hoffmeister p. 490 man has become a "spiritual worker" (*geistiger Arbeiter*), who in fact speaks of himself while believing he speaks of the gods. The section heading gives the pages as 490–420, a misprint for 490–520. The vocabulary of potency and act describes the stone becoming a human shape; the "intellectual worker" is a worker who does not labour with his hands.

How does the passage happen? Because the real Greek world differs from the Egyptian. The world in which man can speak without working is not that of gathering (A, a), of hunting (A, b), or of pure agriculture (A, c). It is the world of "true Spirit" of VI, A: the Greek city, here especially Athens, in VI, A especially Sparta. Man, the Master, no longer works with his hands; he lives on the Slaves' labour and has no direct contact with nature. The art-religion is the religion of Masters, who reveal themselves to themselves in it unconsciously. Within agrarian society a class of Masters forms that lives on agricultural products without producing them. It is the world of recognition: the fight aims not at killing but at victory, and there are Slaves who have recognised the Masters and work, in terror and for another. The identification of the three natural religions with gathering, hunting, and agriculture is Kojève's economic anthropology; the contrast of Athens and Sparta, art-religion and ethical life, is apt.

Section B is also divided into a, b, c: Desire, fight, labour, as in A. But these are no longer natural; men now live in cities, and Desire, fight, and labour are specifically human, man here being only a Master. The repetition of the triad at a higher level structures Kojève's reading of the chapter.

Why a religion of art? The Master is recognised only by slavery, and what distinguishes him is leisure. He not only may not work, he must not; yet he must do something: the arts. He "works" without working, an "intellectual worker". He must, morally (Aristotle), and he cannot do otherwise, since he does not know how to work. The beautiful is what gives pleasure without pain; to enjoy the world without effort is to live "as an artist". The Master finds the Slave's products, which cost him nothing, beautiful and appreciates them as an aesthete; they are detached from the effort of production and so from the producer. His religion divinises being as beauty while forgetting that beauty is a human work. Temples are still built, but what counts is their beauty and the man who appreciates it. The theory of art as the Master's relation to the Slave's product is Kojève's. Its definition of the beautiful has an Epicurean ring; the reference to Aristotle is to the doctrine of leisure (*scholē*) in the *Politics*.

The State appears with the Greek city. Before, in Egypt, there is only its appearance, since a society founded on castes is still natural, the division itself imposed by nature: peasants, smiths, and shoemakers exist because earth, iron, and leather differ. The hive too divides labour. The division into Masters and servants, classes, is human: there is a State only where there are classes. Greek religion is an art-religion because it is a class religion, the Masters', who become aware of the beauty of the Slave's work. But class division rests on a natural remainder, the Slave working for the Master's natural needs, which is why every class tends to harden into a caste through heredity. The distinction between caste and class is Kojève's sociology of the State: castes follow the natural division of materials, classes the human division of risk. The tendency of classes to become castes anticipates the thesis that the final State abolishes heredity (p. 146).

The Master either brutalises himself in pleasure or "works" without working, in art; but the world that results is illusory, the fictitious world of art and letters. The alternative repeats the Master's impasse (p. 174).

For there to be religion, man must transcend himself: man and citizen must not coincide; there must be opposition between man and his world; man must be a rebel. In a youthful writing Hegel said that "happy peoples have no religion", and so thought the Greeks were not religious; in the *Phenomenology* he no longer thinks them a "happy" people. The quotation, from the Tübingen and Bern fragments, marks a development in Hegel's view of Greece: the *Phenomenology* finds discontent even in the city.

For an art-religion the Master must become aware of the insufficiency of the ethical world he lives in. Not the Slave, who is outside the State, while religion expresses the State. The unsatisfied man is the idle Master, and it is his religion. The Master's discontent, not the Slave's, generates the art-religion, which is why it is a religion of beauty rather than salvation.

There are two religions in paganism: the family religion (see VI, A, a), and the official religion, born of the citizen's discontent. How can there be a synthesis of universal and particular, when the city casts back into nature by ostracism whoever would impose his particularity on the State? Through enjoyment (*Genuss*) of the products of another's labour. This aesthetic enjoyment can give joy (*Freude*) but not satisfaction (*Befriedigung*), since the mediating action, labour, is not that of the one who rejoices. The reading of ostracism as the city's expulsion of particularity is apt. The distinction between joy and satisfaction returns (p. 206), now grounded in labour: satisfaction requires that one's own action mediate.

Man, not satisfied by the work of art, will think it was made for another, a god. What essence of the ethical world is revealed in the art-religion? Hegel answers by summarising VI, A (Hoffmeister p. 491). Its dialectic ends in "Spirit subjectively certain of itself", here the slave-owner. Then (Hoffmeister pp. 491–492) the Master becomes an aesthete. The aesthete is subjectively certain of himself, but not recognised as such by the mass or by other aesthetes: that is his dissatisfaction. He mourns his world; he is an "émigré". He flees it because he does not dare change it to fit his aesthetic ideal, and so aspires to a religion. The word "émigré", from a Russian émigré lecturing in Paris in 1938, is pointed: the aesthete mourns a lost world he dares not change.

At the first paragraph of p. 492, absolute art appears: art is religion and religion is art; at the second, Spirit will later surpass art. The three paragraphs of B have these themes: a, man wants recognition without fighting or working: plastic arts and poetry, the abstract work of art; b, fight without labour and without risk of life, for recognition: sport, the living work of art; c, labour within the fight for recognition, but not physical labour, building a non-natural world without physical effort: literature, the "world" of fiction, epic, tragedy, comedy, the spiritual work of art. Mapping the three works of art onto Desire, fight, and labour, with sport as fight without risk, is Kojève's most ingenious schematisation of VII, B.

**The Abstract Work of Art** (Hoffmeister pp. 493–501). The paragraph has three unmarked stages: the statue, representational plastic art, corresponding to A, a (the artist venerates nature and believes in beauty as a kind of mana) and to the epic (B, c, 1), static description; the hymn or chorus, lyric poetry, the fight in its most general form, purely verbal interaction, communion by speech alone; and the cult, where interaction is more real, action is distributed among participants, symbolic fight, the building of the temple. The cult cannot cover the whole of real life; the totality of human existence is not sanctified. Paragraph b presents sport as intermediate between symbolic cultic fight and real fight.

First stage (Hoffmeister pp. 493–495). Three questions: what is art, what theology corresponds to it, what is the artist. First, the statue. In it the artist does not reconcile being and action; it is only the image of what is immobile, already accomplished, in man. The temple surrounds it: one represents the universal, the other the particular; a real relation and a real gap, corresponding to the disharmony between the Master's private life and his life as citizen. The Greek temple is more "rational", more "atheist", than earlier forms: it has the shape of a house. But the Master forgets the Slave's effort and believes the natural cosmos already rational, and so the human body too. He is mistaken and eventually notices: the temple, no longer simple like the pyramid, is complicated by irrationality, irrational ratios. Only labour "rationalises" nature by humanising it. The irrational ratios allude to the Greek discovery of incommensurables, which Kojève reads as the Master's discovery that nature is not already rational.

Second, the god who dwells in the statue. There is a passage to anthropomorphism: the neediness (*Bedürftigkeit*) of animal life is removed; the Master no longer depends on nature and has leisure. The struggle of Olympians and Titans symbolises man's struggle with nature, which is in reality labour. The Titanomachy as the mythic form of labour is Kojève's allegorical reading: the Olympians' victory over natural powers represents a victory the Slaves in fact won.

Third, the artist is recognised only through the mute statue, so his activity is not recognised: the insufficiency of plastic art. He has the work recognised, not its production or consumption. His joy is "abstract", not human, since man is not being but action. What is truly human is the production and consumption of works of art, not the works. The anthropology of action is here applied consistently to aesthetics.

Second stage (Hoffmeister pp. 495–498). The word appears, with two aspects: its empirical existence (*Dasein*), sound, and its non-natural existence, meaning. Through language subjectivity is recognised by all, but immediately, which is its insufficiency. Human existence is not reduced to language, and man recognised only through his language is not integral man. The poet differs from integral man; poetry is the soul, not soul and body. This partial existence in poetic language tends to present itself as other than me, on another plane: poetry tends toward the divine, the religious hymn (Hoffmeister p. 496). The poet's god has his activity within himself, pure and immediate: not a creator but the "perfect", self-sufficient god, the gods of Epicurus. To the hymn as existence corresponds prayer (*Andacht*) as inwardness. The dialectic resumes at p. 498: poetry, like time, is fleeting, without permanence (*Bestehen*). The comparison with Epicurus's gods, inactive in the intermundia, fits the lyric god. The ephemerality of poetry anticipates the thesis that only labour gives permanence.

An interpolated note (Hoffmeister pp. 496–498) concerns the oracle. In the hymn the poet speaks to and of the gods; in the oracle the god speaks to and of man. Its dialectical link is natural religion. The oracle is the first form of language, *Logos*, on earth, but not yet truly human language, having no universal content. At the end of p. 496: the man who first speaks a human language with universal content is isolated and not understood; he feels himself a particular and believes himself "inspired". This language always reveals the given and only the given, even the "revolutionary" oracle; only the user's attitude changes. The oracle is either incomprehensible or reveals the given, and then it is banal, conformist. Pages 497–498 treat Socrates and his daimon, and the sentence "Das Höhere als beide" (p. 498) expresses Hegel's "morality". The reading of the "inspired" speaker as the first, isolated speaker of universal truth is a genealogy of prophecy. The dilemma of the oracle, incomprehensible or banal, applies to all speech that is not action. The "morality" is the one sketched in 1934–35: follow the customs of one's people insofar as they are solid (p. 65).

Third stage (Hoffmeister pp. 498–501). The cult is the synthesis of statue and hymn. There is religion and cult only where there is flight, non-satisfaction through action. In the cult, since there is action, though symbolic, transcendence is attenuated: the god takes part in it, and there is interaction between man and God. Its three elements are mystical prayer (Desire), sacrifice (fight), and building of the temple (labour). The triad repeats Desire, fight, labour a third time.

First (Hoffmeister pp. 498–499): the cult is born of the hymn, not of plastic art. An element in every cult but not essential to it is the mystical, originating in prayer; separated from the official cult, it gives the mysteries. The mystic is an activist. The poet shows the desired object without wanting to consume it: an act, but failed. Mysticism is active in structure, since the object is abolished and identified with the subject, but in the imaginary. The poet who becomes a mystic wants to go beyond joy and identify with the object, but still will not abolish it; so he fails, refusing to commit the "crime" of abolishing the object. The crime of Desire will be symbolic, and so will the purification. The mystic as an activist of the imaginary is Kojève's characterisation; the "crime" of Desire recalls the Introduction: to desire is to negate, and the mystic negates only in imagination.

Second (Hoffmeister pp. 499–501): action, first internal, becomes manifest but remains symbolic; ritual brings man back to himself, but not as he lives in the real world. Sacrifice reflects the fight: the Master sacrifices his life for the State, but the pagan State returns less than he gives. In the cult he sacrifices symbolically objects that belong to him, hoping to reach the union of particular and universal he misses as citizen. As the real world is full of being, the divine world has no room for a new divine; part of the divine must be abolished to sanctify man: that is sacrifice, where the victim is identified with a god. Sacrifice brings enjoyment (*Genuss*), the common eating of the animal; but it has no morrow, like poetry, since it involves no labour. The Master thus experiences his insufficiency in the cult. The theory of sacrifice as making room for man in a full divine world is Kojève's: one sacrifices not to feed the god but to displace part of him with the human.

Third (paragraph on p. 501): labour is introduced symbolically into the cult, completed by the ritual building of the temple. This labour abolishes transcendence, and in the temple the people manifests its own glory, "its own wealth and adornment" (last line of the paragraph). The people worshipping its own wealth in its temple is the Jena thesis of p. 201 applied to the art-religion.

**The Living Work of Art** (Hoffmeister pp. 502–506). The first paragraph of p. 502 is the only allusion to Judaism, which Hegel does not treat in the *Phenomenology*; it is only a note. Judaism is the synthesis of the three elements of VII, A and so the perfection of natural religion (compare the youthful writings, Nohl's edition). It is not a religion of Masters. The opposition of Jew and Gentile seems analogous to Greek and barbarian, but is not, since the Jewish State is not recognised as a State; the Jew lives in a pre-political world, and his religion is a nature religion. If he is a warrior, he must establish a totemic link with his God; but he fails to impose himself as a warrior people and returns to the mana-god, the abstract One. Yet if the people is defeated, its God still triumphs, since he willed the defeat: the defeat is at bottom the people's victory over itself. The Jewish people also builds a temple; the totem-God is also an artisan-God, a demiurge: a mana-God acting in labour, a paradoxical synthesis. As a natural religion it is inferior to Greek religion, already human since artistic, but superior insofar as Greek religion is only a religion of limited, self-identical Masters. The biblical God, one and without rival, can change without becoming less; the pagan gods must remain "perfect" or be debased. The biblical God ends as a perfection that becomes, incomprehensible to abstract reason; he becomes the Christian God and maintains himself so as long as history lasts. The note is Kojève's construction, drawing on Hegel's harsh early treatment of Judaism in *The Spirit of Christianity and its Fate*. Kojève's reading is more nuanced: a people that reads defeat as its God's will turns defeat into self-overcoming, and a God who can change prepares the historical God of Christianity. The claim that the Jewish State was "not recognised as a State" repeats Hegel's early schema and is historically contestable.

Again three stages: the mysteries (the Bacchanal), the athlete (the festival), literary language (Pindar), after a short introduction on the passage from public cult to mysteries. The plan follows Hegel's ¶718–726.

The mysteries (Hoffmeister pp. 503–504). The citizen–State relation shows itself in the mysteries, a synthesis of public cult (sacrifice) and the mystical element. This element takes a new form: the god is now an object not only of contemplation but of Desire (*Begierde*), which leads to destruction, the Bacchanals. The Greek mysteries are the first, naive attempt to divinise man. An interpolated note (Hoffmeister p. 503) is directed against rationalist philosophers from Kant to Schelling: to understand history as the becoming of truth is Hegelianism; the others err in believing they can reach truth by reason alone. The note, Kojève says, refutes the alleged "panlogism" of Hegel. The remark is a significant interpretive claim: Hegel does not deduce truth from reason but reads it from history, against a standard charge from the nineteenth century on.

The next two paragraphs (Hoffmeister pp. 503–504): man becomes human when he stops desiring a thing and desires a desire. The "first" Desire is repressed in the fight, and man ceases to be an animal.
