This sublimation appears first in plastic art, lyric poetry, and mysticism, where the desired object is no longer real, and in mysticism even its idea disappears. The man who will not lose himself in mystical union returns to the material basis of his Desire: the orgiastic cult of the mysteries, in which he becomes hunger (Eleusis) and sexuality (Dionysus) again, without regression, since self-consciousness is kept. The orgy integrates the active elements the official cult excluded, but it too is punctual and ephemeral. One can no more live in a perpetual orgy than spend one's life in a temple; the content, human existence, overflows the religious form. Man goes beyond the orgy because he wants to realise his bodily life integrally, not dissolve it. The pagan mysteries are mysteries of bread and wine, not yet of flesh and blood; the cult of the athlete makes the transition. The formula "bread and wine, not yet flesh and blood" is Hegel's (¶724), anticipating the Eucharist. The criterion that a form of life must be livable in its totality recurs throughout.

The athlete (Hoffmeister pp. 504–505). The mysteries of the higher gods are the Olympic games, the religious festival. The athlete represents the essence of the art-religion: the Master's ideal, recognised without crime, and a god become flesh. The cult of the games is the festival man gives in his own honour. The athlete is "an animated, living work of art" (Hoffmeister p. 505). For the first time man can live integrally in a "religious" world, the sporting world; one does not live among statues or in a temple. What is missing is Spirit: the athlete does not speak; there is no *Logos*, only flesh. "Recognised without crime", without killing, defines sport as the fight for recognition without risk of death. The athlete's silence is the limit the next stage removes.

Literary language (last paragraph). The athlete is silent, but the dithyrambic poet, Pindar, speaks of him. This is the passage from art-religion proper to literary religion. Pindar's victory odes are the literary form of the athletic cult.

**The Spiritual Work of Art** (Hoffmeister pp. 506–520). The sporting world is a human world one can live in; it even seems perfect, since it has a "world champion", a man universally recognised in his particularity after a fight. But the sporting fight lacks seriousness, since there is no risk of life, and man is recognised only in his body. So there is no integral individuality and no true satisfaction. The "world champion" as a parody of the universally recognised individual is Kojève's wittiest image: sport lacks both risk and speech.

The new world is a literary world, lacking objective reality. Man flees the real world by building it, so it is religious; and every religion entails a literature, first sacred, then profane, always claiming supreme value. Every literature creates a world. The pagan literary world is born with epic, lives in tragedy, and dies as comedy: epic gives the framework, tragedy the actor acting within it, comedy the result of his action. There is no introduction, since the last paragraph of b serves as one: literature is born of the mysteries, the orgy, and sport. That literature creates a world, a fictitious one, makes it the counterpart of labour: it builds a world without effort and so without reality.

The epic (Hoffmeister pp. 506–509). First paragraph: the first union of peoples into a nation for a common aim, the Trojan War. This unity exists only by exclusion, union against; it does not flow from the world's "essence"; there is no universal State, no Empire. Second paragraph: the epic world is total; one can live in it. But there is a supreme command (*Oberbefehl*), not a supreme government (*Oberherrschaft*), reflected in the pantheon. It is the stage of sensation, not yet perception (tragedy) or Understanding (comedy). There is no single hero or actor; when he appears he will destroy this union in tragedy, and the conflict of universal and particular, latent in the "sacred union", will become open. The phrase *union sacrée*, the French wartime coalition of 1914, names the epic unity: a coalition against an external enemy that suspends internal conflict. The correspondence of epic, tragedy, and comedy with sensation, perception, and Understanding extends the parallel of the first chapters.

Third paragraph: this world reveals itself through the epic, whose "syllogism" has three terms: the extreme of universality, the world of the gods; the middle, particularity, the people in its heroes; and the extreme of singularity, the singer. The people, acting and individualised through its heroes, mediates between Olympus and the singer. The singer creates this world rather than reproducing it: no "realism". The gods act, which is new: in art man became conscious of himself as being; in literature, as action. The syllogism is Hegel's (¶729); Kojève's addition is that literature, unlike plastic art, represents action, a step toward self-knowledge as action.

Fourth paragraph: the epic hero's action. "Synthetic" (Hoffmeister p. 508) here means "juxtaposed", since there is no true synthesis yet. The action destroys the nation's calm pseudo-synthesis and shows its contradiction: the victor is neither a State presiding over the coalition nor any one nation but the "united nations". Then either the victory is abolished, or the nations are, by integrating them into an Empire; in both cases the epic world ends. The phrase "united nations", in 1938, is striking in retrospect: a victorious alliance must dissolve or become a single State.

Fifth paragraph: the epic conflict appears in the divine world too. It is comic to see the gods forget their eternal nature in their quarrels: why fight if no victory could change their nature? It is a game without result. Kojève sketches two series: silence of the animal and the athlete, literature, absolute knowledge; isolated particularity, nation, Empire. The nation realises itself by "overcoming" itself in the Empire. The first Empire is Alexander's, the first tragic hero, the actor; he fails because he tries to realise the Empire in a world of Masters, not of citizens, as Napoleon will. The two series place literature between the athlete's silence and the Sage's discourse, and the nation between the particular and the Empire. Alexander as the first tragic hero, failing where Napoleon succeeds, returns from 1935–36 (p. 104).

Tragedy (Hoffmeister pp. 509–517). Aeschylus's *Oresteia* underlies the analysis (compare VI, A, a–b). A new character appears: the actor. Tragedy shows the conflict of particular and universal in the world of pagan Masters, an insoluble conflict. After the epic victory the coalition dissolves and each people closes on itself; the universal fragments but survives, since each people and each man finds in himself the contradiction of universal action and particularist activity. In the epic world it seemed external and removable; in the tragic world it becomes necessary and essential. "Necessity" (*Notwendigkeit*) here means fate, the Empire into which the nations will be integrated. The reading of tragic necessity as the coming Empire is Kojève's historical interpretation of fate.

Just before tragedy, the epic syllogism had: imperial fate, represented by the gods; the heroic people; and the rhapsode, who sees the Empire coming and announces it, thereby excluding himself from the nation and annihilating himself. In tragedy the actor appears, in whom the two extremes are actualised: the author who understands fate must become active. The actor sees the solution but cannot realise it, or he would be Alexander. His action is of course imaginary. The summit of art will be comedy, where the actor acts exactly as man acts in everyday life; then art abolishes itself and one passes to real life. The epic hero was mute and the rhapsode spoke for him; the tragic hero speaks, and the actor speaks for him wearing his mask. In epic one must know what happens; in tragedy, what is said. Foreign, epic war needs no speeches; civil, tragic war does. The contrast of foreign and civil war as settings of epic and tragedy is Kojève's. The claim that comedy is art's summit because it coincides with everyday life anticipates his reading of the end of art.

Hoffmeister p. 511: tragedy has three constituents, the chorus, the actor, and the spectators. Its first condition is that the people, the chorus, is passive: the action is not its own. It watches the two heroes go to their ruin without intervening, sees the conflict but no solution, and laments. It is the most tragic figure of the tragedy, and so is the author insofar as he sides with it. The chorus knows the end will be tragic and still makes the hero act: the hero is a scapegoat, as in mystical religion. But this is not serious; the actor is not killed, and finally the hero loses his tragic quality and becomes comic. There can be only two actors, no third, since there is no middle term to resolve the conflict; hence a single tragic author, Aeschylus. The chorus as the most tragic figure reflects the people's passivity in the Masters' world. The inference from two actors to "a single tragic author" is a striking judgement: Sophocles's third actor already signals the middle term that dissolves tragedy.

Recalling VI, A, a–b: the society of Masters is self-contradictory, and actualising it by action makes it disappear. Such action within a closed world is criminal, notably civil war, the crime par excellence. The polytheism of epic becomes in tragedy a dualism: the superior gods of the city and the infernal gods of the Family, Apollo, Zeus, and Athena against the Erinyes. (Compare vol. VII, p. 385, Hegel's first essay on tragedy, in the essay on natural law.) The sacrifice of Iphigenia shows the contradiction of State and Family. The murder of Agamemnon abolishes the principle of kingship, the State, and the Family takes its whole place; Aegisthus is not a king. By destroying the Family, killing his mother, Orestes wants to restore kingship to his father by becoming king, Agamemnon then being a king's father and so king. Orestes will be killed by the infernal gods; there is no solution. Aeschylus disavows Agamemnon: the "domestication" of the Erinyes transforms tragedy into comedy. Kojève's statement that Orestes "will be killed" departs from Aeschylus, where Orestes is acquitted; he means that within the tragic logic Orestes is doomed, and that the acquittal already belongs to comedy.

Hamlet is an intellectual's tragedy; the only modern tragedies, *Hamlet* and *Faust*, are tragedies of intellectuals. But this bourgeois or Christian tragedy is a tragedy of inaction, whereas the pagan Master's is one of action. The intellectual can be tragic because, not working, he resembles the Master; but he does not fight either, and so resembles the Slave: he is a bourgeois, a Slave without a Master. Hence either a tragedy of inaction or a comedy of peaceful, even pacifist, idleness. The distinction between tragedies of action and of inaction is Kojève's contribution to the theory of modern tragedy: Hamlet's hesitation is tragic only because he has the Master's leisure.

Hoffmeister p. 514, last line: the key word is imposture (*Betrug*), hypocrisy. The Master believes and wants others to believe that he is wholly Master and that his mastery exhausts the human essence. This error becomes a fraud, since the task is not to eliminate the particular before the universal but to unite them; a Master's life excluding particularity is impossible. Tragedy reveals that in his universalist action the Master acts as a particular, since his "character" is a particular nature, different from the Slave's and the Woman's, and so limited. The Master who claims the universal has as much particularity in him as the one who openly sides with the Family. He can avoid neither tragedy nor its imposture. The Master's ideal is not viable: one can only die as a Master. The Master who claims to live as Master is an impostor playing a tragic "role". Tragedy cannot subsist as such; it must give way to comedy and then the novel. The pun on hypocrisy, from Greek *hypokritēs*, actor, is Hegel's (¶742). The conclusion restates the Master's impasse in theatrical terms.

Aeschylus's solution is peace, the State's inactivity, or foreign war, which would return to epic: the transformation of a warrior State of Masters into a bourgeois "democracy", comedy. The end of the *Oresteia* parallels the end of Aristophanes's *Peace*: Aristophanes is a bourgeois already, nostalgic for past mastery; Aeschylus a Master still, nostalgic for the coming bourgeoisie. The chiasmus places each poet on one side of the transition, looking toward the other.

Hoffmeister p. 515, last line: another result of tragedy is the depopulation of heaven. Only Zeus remains, and he is already the god of the hearth. The Erinyes have in fact triumphed over Apollo and Athena, and their peace treaty abolishes the gods of the city. Yet it is also Athena's victory, since the Erinyes become citizens, which is already comic. The tragic hero is a bourgeois who has put on the mask and takes it off afterward; there is no real life of the Master, only a role, a game, which becomes conscious and avowed in comedy. The Erinyes settled in Athens as Eumenides are read as the city's domestication of the Family's gods and so as the beginning of comedy. That the Master's life is only a role is the most radical form of Kojève's critique of mastery.

Comedy (Hoffmeister pp. 517–520). The comic or bourgeois world is homogeneous: no absolute conflict, no flight from the world. A homogeneous world is a world without God, and this new atheism is what comedy brings. Art as religion abolishes itself, and so does the art-religion; the gods, claiming to be absolute, become comic. But to laugh at the gods man must still believe in a God; he is not yet truly atheist. The equation of homogeneity with atheism anticipates the final State: a world without internal conflict needs no beyond. Comic atheism is a first, unconscious atheism.

The bourgeois, in his Greek beginnings and later as intellectual, is ironic; but he must then become serious and "want to be something proper" (*etwas Rechtes sein will*, Hoffmeister p. 517). The theme of comic action is the realisation of the particular as particular. Man does not forget the universal that appeared in tragedy and attempts a synthesis; if not yet a true one, it is the one-sided elaboration of the particular with a view to the future synthesis. There is therefore no comic satisfaction; the ironic bourgeois remains religious and keeps an art and a literature. Comedy as the elaboration of particularity prepares the synthesis the final State will realise.

The gods die in comedy, but this death still has religious value, since comedy was part of Athenian religious life; the theology that will emerge is that of the crucified God. For the bourgeois, nature is only what lets him persevere in his natural being, eating and drinking; comedy completes the death of natural religion: art kills nature. The bourgeois seeks truth: Socrates's dialectic destroys everything by relativism, critical irony, and the use of empty, abstract notions of the beautiful and the good. The result of comedy is the self-deification of the private man: the bourgeois who has forgotten mastery, rejoices in well-being, lives within the Family, and believes he exhausts all existential possibilities. But there is no satisfaction, since the completed religion of the bourgeois, Protestantism, completes the unhappy consciousness without abolishing it. The link between the death of the gods in comedy and the crucified God is Kojève's boldest bridge between VII, B and VII, C. Socrates's place in comedy follows Hegel's association of Aristophanes's *Clouds* with Socratic dialectic. "Persevere in his being" is Spinoza's *conatus*, applied to the bourgeois.

### C. The Revealed Religion (Hoffmeister pp. 521–548)

The introduction (Hoffmeister pp. 521–525). Curiously, comedy comes just before Christianity. The "levity" (*Leichtsinn*) of comedy asserts that "the self is the absolute essence", God. The first religion, natural religion, is God without man; the first atheism, comedy, is man without God; Christianity is God who becomes man; the second and last atheism, Hegel's Science, is man who becomes God. In comedy paganism abolishes itself, and art too, since paganism is a religion of art; art reaches real life, and this same real life, bourgeois life, gave birth to Christianity. Comedy, having shown that profane life is possible, abolishes itself as comedy; there remains the bourgeois who takes himself seriously and lives the life comedy showed him: the Christian bourgeois, who will produce Christian theology. The four-term scheme is one of Kojève's most memorable formulas: Christianity is the mediation between two atheisms.

The paragraph on p. 521 ("Dieser Satz") summarises Chapter VI. In the world of comedy bourgeois well-being is complemented by the unhappy consciousness, which produces Christianity. There is a reversal of values, a renewal of theism, but no return to natural religion or to the transcendence of the luminous essence. The Christian theologian who speaks of God knows he also speaks of himself. The atheism of comedy was unconscious; the theologian is half-conscious, since atheism is only in germ in his theology of the God-man. The Christian God is no longer a natural being but a self, a person: humanised, but not yet openly identified with man. The degrees of consciousness of atheism, unconscious in comedy, half-conscious in theology, conscious in Hegel, give the chapter its thread.

Private property, the legal person of Roman law, and Jewish monotheism are three parallel phenomena that fuse in the Christian bourgeois world, and Stoicism, Scepticism, and the unhappy consciousness are the three ideologies expressing it. The unhappy consciousness is nostalgia for the universal, the lost State. The bourgeois reduced to his private property, capital, mourns the loss of the real world, the State, and constructs in thought a transcendent world. The three converging sources of Christianity, economic, legal, and religious, summarise the year's lectures. The definition of the unhappy consciousness as nostalgia for the lost State is the political core of Kojève's reading.

The great news Christianity brings is the "hard saying": God is dead (Hoffmeister p. 523). The bourgeois tries to make a religion of this conclusion of the pagan world, but at first does not take its meaning seriously. Theism properly speaking perishes with the pagan world, and art with it: "the works of the Muse lack the power of Spirit" (Hoffmeister p. 523). «Le Christianisme, — c'est le devenir de l'athéisme» (Christianity is the becoming of atheism) (p. 256). Hegel's "hard saying that God himself is dead" (¶752) is the key to Christianity here, and Kojève's formula states his whole reading.

Christian theology develops in three stages: the idea of the God-man (Neoplatonism, Jesus Christ); the Gospel narrative and Saint Paul; and post-evangelical theology and the Church (Catholicism, then Protestantism, then atheism). The sequence ending in atheism makes Protestantism the penultimate stage.

The God-man (Hoffmeister pp. 525–527). "The self is the absolute essence", says the atheist bourgeois of comedy. But he soon notices that the particular detached from the universal has no value, and becomes "unhappy". The universalist formula returns, but there is no longer a real universal, a State; so the universal he thinks of is transcendent: God. The Christian formula synthesises primitive, naturalist mana-theism, the first universalism, and comic bourgeois atheism, the first particularism, without regression. God will be universal only because incarnate in a particular man, Jesus, only as a self: an individual God. The idea of the individual appears first in Roman law, but the legal person is abstract and empty; it is first made concrete in the Christian notion of the divine person, supposed to be realised in Jesus Christ. The synthesis of mana and comedy is Kojève's most economical account of the incarnation: universal God plus particular man. The line from the Roman legal person to the divine person is standard in the history of the concept of person.

For the Christian the individual is not an ideal to be realised; it already exists, in the beyond: the risen, transcendent Christ. There is a substantialisation of the idea of the individual. What the Christian says of Jesus Christ is absolutely true, provided it is referred to the human spirit. Man must have "a real mother", a body, "and a transcendent father", a transcendent idea, a project to realise by fight and labour. The reading of the virgin birth, real mother and transcendent father, as body and project is Kojève's boldest demythologisation, following Hegel's own reading (¶755).

In the first paragraph of p. 526 Hegel is thinking of Neoplatonism. The birth of Christ in question is not the Gospel's but the birth of Christian theology, whose parents are, ideologically, Neoplatonism, and really, Roman law and Empire. Neoplatonism is an abortive sketch of Christianity, too theist, too pagan. It goes beyond comedy and knows an infinite God, but not that he has become man; its God is absolutely transcendent, the One of which one cannot even say it exists. The Neoplatonist hovers in the abstract and could never create a Church; Neoplatonism remained a sect of intellectuals, a mystical *Schwärmerei*. The next paragraph (pp. 526–527) gives the passage to Christianity: Neoplatonism disappears because it does not correspond to social reality; the Roman bourgeois does not recognise himself in Plotinus. The paragraph on p. 527 concerns Jesus: atheism is virtually reached, since God equals man, but one must become aware of it, which the development of Christianity and its theology will do. The identification of Neoplatonism in ¶754–755 is Kojève's; the social criterion, that a theology fails when no class recognises itself in it, is his too.

The Gospel, the Apostles, and Saint Paul (Hoffmeister pp. 527–532). Again three stages: Christ; the evangelical community; the community after Christ, the genesis of theology and the Church.

The Christ of the Gospel (Hoffmeister pp. 527–529). Hegel uses here for the Christian God the same terms he applied in the Preface to human Spirit realising itself through history. Christianity is therefore a symbolic and imperfect expression of Hegelian absolute Spirit, which theology substantialises into a representation, placed before, projected outside man. Christianity is "revealed" because it reveals the identity of God and man, to be taken literally. An interpolated note (Hoffmeister pp. 528–529) says that the first Christian is Jesus, the first man who knows this identity (compare vol. XX, p. 268). In Christianity the idea of God culminates, and this culmination is also its degradation, its abolition: a dialectical reversal, in the sensible, material character of the man identified with God. The observation about the Preface's vocabulary is textually sound; "Jesus the first Christian" is Kojève's inversion: Jesus did not preach Christ but knew the identity of God and man.

The Christianity of the Apostles (Hoffmeister pp. 529–530). The Apostles, seeing this man who says he is God and believing him, recognise him as such. The God to whom a determinate man is identified is not just any God but the Jewish God, synthesis of natural religion's elements (universal One, warrior or totem God, demiurge) and of the pagan idea of perfection. And the man must be integral man, who has realised all existential possibilities and become aware of them: for the Christian, Jesus; for Hegel, the dyad Napoleon–Hegel. Divinity here is recognised status, the theory of recognition applied to Christology. The parallel with the dyad repeats p. 195.

The Christ of the first community (Hoffmeister pp. 530–532). The Church. Jesus was not mad in saying he was God, since he created a sect that accepted him as God, and the sect became a Church, a real world in which man lives. The Christian idea, born in the pagan world, developed into theology in the Christian world, created by the negating action of those who believed in Jesus. Through the Church the idea of Christ realises itself and creates the Christian world. At the last line of p. 530: the Church is nothing other than the risen Christ; it realises the idea of the resurrection. The paragraph on p. 531 and the next form a note on how the theological and Hegelian interpretations of Christianity are identical and different. The criterion of madness returns from the Introduction (p. 32): an idea is mad until realised, and Jesus's claim was realised in the Church. The Church as risen Christ follows Hegel's identification of the resurrection with the spirit of the community (¶763).

Theology and the Church (Hoffmeister pp. 532–546). The introduction (pp. 532–533): the truth of Christianity is neither the believer's inwardness (*Innerlichkeit*), against Schleiermacher, nor objective theology; it is the dialectical movement by which there is a "real self", Christians of flesh and blood recognised as such, living in a real Christian world, who are "subject", knowing that they are its authors. The truth of Christianity is the Christian community, the Church. An interpolated note (p. 532) condemns every attempt to return to "evangelical simplicity". The analysis has three stages: Christian abstract thought, theology, especially the Trinity and Christ-Logos; the relations of God, man, and world, Christian morality; and the Church's understanding of itself, Christian "politics" (Paulinism, Catholicism, Protestantism). Through theology the Church becomes conscious of itself as a world and of man as its member. The rejection of both inwardness and dogma in favour of the community prepares the substitution of State for Church. The note against evangelical simplicity applies Hegel's historicism: one cannot go back behind a completed development.

Christian theology (Hoffmeister pp. 533–535). The dogma of the Trinity implies the whole of Christian metaphysics. Hegel states its truth and so sets out his own metaphysics and the trinitarian, "dialectical" structure of being: essence (*Wesen*), being-for-itself (*Fürsichsein*), being-for-itself-in-the-other (*Fürsichsein im Andern*), that is, Father, Son, and the Holy Spirit returning to itself, which is history closing and completing itself. An interpolated note (p. 534) says that neither non-dialectical philosophers nor theologians who think in representation rather than concept can understand this structure. Another (p. 535) justifies Hegel's atheist interpretation of the Trinity: just as primitive evangelical thought cannot be opposed to theology, theology cannot be opposed to Hegel's Science. The identification of the Spirit with completed history is Kojève's. The second note's argument is precise: Hegel's Science develops theology as legitimately as theology developed the Gospel.

Christian morality (Hoffmeister pp. 535–542). The introduction (pp. 535–536): Hegel interprets the dogma of creation and the relation of Creator and creature, and criticises Christian morality: the opposition of God and world is such that God must die, and the tension within the Trinity is irresolvable. Under these conditions one cannot tell people "love one another". For Hegel love is mutual recognition, to which the fight for prestige, the duel, is opposed. In love conflicts are inessential; differences do not become radical oppositions; where there is no love, conflicts sharpen until all is destroyed. But one cannot begin with love: the Master–Slave conflict is essential and primitive. Love exists only between equals, and absolute equality arises only in the perfect, universal and homogeneous State in which history ends. As long as history lasts, existence is in fight and labour, not love. There are only false forms of love: natural love, pre-human, in the Family; and Christian love-charity, between human beings as human. Charity has value only because there were Masters and Slaves and still are oppositions; it presupposes inequality and cannot occur between equals, though it will not admit it. It disregards social distinctions but leaves them intact, transposing equality to the beyond: men are brothers "in Jesus Christ", all Slaves of an absolute Master. It must be completed by humility, contempt for others tempered by contempt for oneself. Charity is insufficient, since it maintains social differences; but it is also an ideal, realised only through the fight and the abolition of classes in the final State. Love will then have nothing Christian about it: there is no room for "charity" where man is "satisfied". The analysis of charity as presupposing inequality is Kojève's sharpest critique of Christian ethics. Love as mutual recognition is the Jena Hegel's concept; placing it at the end of history follows from Kojève's premises.

Again three stages: creation and fall; good and evil and their conflict; the Christian solution, death and resurrection. Creation and fall (Hoffmeister pp. 536–537). The first paragraph concerns the creation of the world, the second that of man. The tension between man and world is negating Desire, which is crime. Original sin properly interpreted is at p. 536, last line ("Wie dieses einzelne Selbst"); its Christian expression at p. 537 ("Der Mensch wird"). Paradise is the "garden of animals"; the paradisal state is still natural, animal; sin, the crime of Desire, humanises. The reading of the fall as humanisation follows Hegel (¶775–776), and completes the anthropology: man is born by the negating act of Desire.

Good and evil (Hoffmeister pp. 537–539). Fallen man is essentially evil, sinful, criminal; facing real evil, dogma presents the ideal of the good, Christ. An interpolated note (pp. 537–538) is directed against Schelling as disciple of Jakob Böhme: evil is not prior to man; evil is man, and man is "evil". At p. 538 ("Das Gute und das Böse"), the incarnation: Jesus is the ideal meant to resolve the pagan, tragic conflict. The Christian knows from the start the essential importance of labour and conceives through it an ideal that can resolve the idle Master's conflict. At p. 539 ("Die andere Seite"), the devil, recalling Böhme. At p. 539 ("Die Entfremdung"), the opposition of Jesus and devil is that of universalist and particularist tendencies; man is the middle term, individuality. The conflict is not hopeless: it is not the pagan conflict of two gods but of God and the devil, a "comic" situation. The bourgeois pseudo-tragedy of duty against "passion" is analogous: soluble, and so comic, since passion can be subordinated to duty; true tragedy is a conflict of two duties. The thesis that evil is man, against Böhme's theodicy, locates evil in negativity. The comparison of Christ against the devil with duty against passion repeats 1935–36 (p. 103).

The Christian solution (Hoffmeister pp. 539–542). Christianity admits a struggle between two separate, autonomous principles, good and evil, which has no meaning. The compromise: since evil cannot and must not wholly abolish good, good must abolish itself as opposed to evil, and likewise evil. The true solution: through labour the particular universalises itself, and through fight and risk of life the universal, the State, recognises the particular. There are two struggles: the pagan one, which annihilates the enemy, and the "dialectical" one, which overcomes him by preserving and sublimating him. The real Christian struggle is that of opposed tendencies in the bourgeois world (compare wealth and State in VI, B), not Jesus against the devil, which is only an anticipatory allegory: in thought a solution can be conceived from the start, since thought meets no resistance, but the real solution takes eighteen centuries. The life and death of Christ symbolise the real course of history: Christ sacrifices his particularity, Jesus, to realise the universal, the Logos, and the universal, God, recognises this particularity, man, which is God himself, Christ. Christ works, as a carpenter; he sacrifices his life, which is fight and risk. Yet he does not fight properly, since he remains a Slave, dying on the cross. And Christ also reveals the final atheism, the death of God. He rises as real man, as community, Church, the prototype of the Napoleonic Empire. Christianity has two insufficiencies: Christ remains transcendent, and the Church has a "mystical body" distinct from its reality; only in the final State do ideal and reality coincide completely. These propositions are nonetheless "true" in Christianity. An interpolated note (pp. 540–542) again targets Schelling as Böhme's disciple. The reading of Christ as carpenter and martyr, uniting labour and risk yet dying a Slave, is Kojève's typology of the passion. "Eighteen centuries" measures the delay between conceiving the synthesis and realising it. The Church as "prototype of the Napoleonic Empire" completes the substitution announced on p. 231.

The Church (Hoffmeister pp. 542–546). The introduction (pp. 542–543): the Church elaborates a dogma such that removing the idea of God and transcendence yields Hegel's Science. Again three stages: faith, Saint Paul, leading to Protestantism; the Eucharist, Catholicism, leading to atheism; Christianity as universal religion, leading to absolute knowledge. The lineages are Kojève's; Catholicism's leading to atheism, through the "real presence", anticipates the note below.

Faith (Hoffmeister pp. 543–544). The pagan who becomes Christian becomes "evil", sinful; in fact he only becomes conscious of what he already was. The early Christians expected an imminent end of the world, but history continued and the Roman State became Christian, so Christian existence in a Christian world had to be justified. This existence negates evangelical theology, and a new theology is elaborated: justification by faith (Paul), the Eucharist (Catholicism), the universal Church. On this theology the Christian has value as Christian and the Church as Church. The empirical fact, Adam–Jesus, becomes a notion, a knowledge; their reality is abolished: what matters is the consciousness of sin, not sin (Adam), and faith in the Saviour, not the Saviour. With Paul there is, as it were, a second killing of Jesus. At p. 543 ("Wenn also") is Paul's dialectical theology, which identifies good and evil: sin prepares the incarnation; God gives man the Law so that sin, and so redemption, become possible (compare Romans: sin is replaced by the feeling of sin, which engenders faith). For Paul salvation is immediate, without effort or works: conversion. That is his error, since then Jesus's life has no meaning, only his death and resurrection. In reality the transformation of sin into salvation takes time; between them lies an act of freedom, an active life imitating Christ. If salvation comes from God, it is grace, which deprives the Christian of value of his own and, coming from the timeless Logos, transcends history. If it comes from man, then neither did Adam damn nor Jesus save. So Kant will say Jesus is merely an exemplary man, as the young Hegel also said (compare Nohl); or else all Christians are Jesuses. Paul holds a cooperation of grace and conversion, which are in reality incompatible. It is not enough to be conscious of sin and converted; one must live as a Christian. Faith without works is nothing; what saves is faith realised, the world actually transformed into Church. Salvation must be mediated by works and history, and so Paul gives way to Catholicism. The "second killing of Jesus", replacing the life with the doctrine, is Kojève's provocation. His resolution of the dilemma of grace and freedom is historical: salvation is the transformation of the world by works over time.

The Eucharist (Hoffmeister pp. 544–546). What counts now is Christ's life, his acts, works. At p. 544 ("Außer dieser Unmittelbarkeit"): the summit of Catholic dogma, the Eucharist, symbol of Christ in the Church, of his death and resurrection in the real world, "dying and rising daily in it" (last line of p. 544). The Christian is saved only by communion, and so by the Church, by his Christian life in a Christian world. At p. 545 ("Dasjenige"): the Eucharist also symbolises the transformation of particular into universal and universal into particular, and in this sense the dogma is absolutely true. But it is only a symbol, which is the insufficiency of Christianity in general, culminating in Catholicism. In fact the real presence (*Gegenwart*) of Spirit in the world is neither Jesus Christ nor Christ in the Eucharist but man's historical life in the natural world. The reinterpretation of the real presence as history completes a motif running through the book (pp. 91, 150). Kojève's preference here for Catholicism over Protestantism is notable: the Eucharist symbolises the unity of particular and universal as a daily act.

The universal Church (Hoffmeister p. 546). The Catholic Church is in principle universal, but the Napoleonic Empire will realise this universality; and it will encompass the whole of man's life, whereas the Church sanctifies only parts of it: man cannot live his whole life in a church. The criterion of total livability returns: the Church, like the temple and the orgy, covers only part of life; the State covers the whole.

The general conclusion of Chapter VII (Hoffmeister pp. 546–548) gives a general critique of religion and Christianity, of the idea of the transcendence of Spirit, and the passage to the absolute knowledge of Chapter VIII. The notes stop there; the 1938–39 lectures begin with Chapter VIII.

### Summary of the 1937–1938 Course

The year's lectures explained Chapter VII, "Religion", in which Hegel studies the structure and development of theological doctrines. For Hegel the real object of religious thought is man himself: all theology is necessarily an anthropology. The supersensible or transcendent entity, Spirit, is in reality nothing other than the negating, that is creative, action man realises in the given world. As long as man is religious he does not realise this: he thinks as a theologian, substantialising and externalising the concept (*Begriff*) of Spirit by representing it (*vorstellen*) as a being existing outside man and independently of his action. Speaking in fact of himself, the religious man believes he speaks of a God. The public summary states the atheist reading without hedging.

This lack of self-consciousness, this imaginative projection of human content into the beyond (*Vor-stellung*), distinguishes religious, theological thought from philosophical, anthropological thought. The two necessarily coexist, opposing, engendering, and completing each other. Pre-Hegelian philosophy deals consciously with man, but reveals him by isolating him from his natural and social world; only the particular man (*Einzelner*) who shuts himself in himself can elaborate a "philosophical" anthropology. Theology, by contrast, reveals without knowing it the universal aspect of human existence: the State, society, the people, and man as their member. As long as history continues and the perfect State is not realised, the opposition of the two standpoints is inevitable. The man who cannot satisfy himself by action in his world takes refuge in abstract intelligence and becomes conscious of himself in a "philosophical" anthropology reflecting the particularist tendency. In his universalist tendency the same man cannot recognise the world as his work: universal reality seems to exist outside him, and the universal ideal beyond him, so he becomes conscious of them, and of himself as part of the world, in theological myth. The particularist subjectivism of philosophy will always be complemented and combated by the universalist objectivism of theology. The summary states in careful form the thesis that philosophy and theology are the particular and universal halves of an unreconciled self-understanding.

Theology is therefore the unconscious reflection of the social and historical world in which the theologian lives and of the ideal forming in it. The study of a religion lets us understand the essential character of the world that accepts it; and since theology also reflects the social and political ideal that tends to be realised by transforming the given, its study lets us understand that world's development. That is why the study of real historical development in Chapter VI must be completed by that of theological thought in Chapter VII. The double function of theology, reflecting the present and anticipating the ideal, qualifies the materialist reading: religion is not only a reflection but a guide.

The existential ideal is elaborated and realised progressively: each stage of its elaboration is marked by a determinate theology, and each stage of its realisation by the historical world that accepts it. In its perfection the ideal is the idea of individuality, satisfaction through the real, active synthesis of the particularist and universalist tendencies. It first appears as the Christian notion of the divine individuality of Christ, the God-man. It is realised through the French Revolution, which completes the Christian world in the real and symbolic person of the Man-God Napoleon, at once creator-chief of the perfect State and citizen contributing actively to its indefinite maintenance. The real opposition of particular and universal being abolished, the ideal conflict between philosophical anthropology and religious theology disappears too. Hegel, revealing man to himself by speaking of his Napoleonic realisation, reveals him in both aspects. His doctrine is both "philosophical" and "theological", and being both it is neither: not pre-Hegelian philosophy, since it does not operate with an abstract Spirit distinct from natural and social reality and action; not theology, since theology places a real and concrete Spirit outside man and the world. Hegel's doctrine is absolute knowledge (*absolutes Wissen*), which completes and overcomes (*aufhebt*) both developments, revealing the perfect man realised at the end of history and presupposing his real existence. Napoleon as both creator-chief and citizen maintaining the State "indefinitely" matters: the final State is meant to last. "Both, and so neither" defines absolute knowledge by its double overcoming.

The perfect man, fully and definitively satisfied, being the realisation of the Christian idea of individuality, his revelation by absolute knowledge has the same content as Christian theology, minus transcendence. «Il suffit de dire de l'Homme tout ce que le Chrétien dit de son Dieu pour passer de la Théologie absolue ou chrétienne à la philosophie absolue ou Science de Hegel» (it suffices to say of man everything the Christian says of his God to pass from absolute or Christian theology to absolute philosophy or Hegel's Science) (p. 267). This passage is possible thanks to Napoleon, as Chapter VI showed. Chapter VII shows why and how the most primitive theology was transformed into the Christian doctrine, which differs from Hegel's only in form: Christian theology reveals nothing but the Hegelian concept of individuality, but in the form of the representation (*Vor-stellung*) of theandry. The summary ends with the formula of p. 215 and with "theandry", the union of God and man, the content Christianity and Hegel share. The next course turns to Chapter VIII, where the form of the concept replaces that of representation.

## Course of the 1938–1939 Academic Year

The sixth part of the book reproduces the whole of the last course, from stenographic notes, in full text. The change in textual status matters: what follows is Kojève's own continuous argument, not Queneau's compressed notes, and it includes his most personal reflections on the scope and limits of Hegel's claims.

### First Lecture: Introduction: Philosophy and Wisdom

In the first seven chapters, Kojève begins, Hegel spoke of philosophy; in Chapter VIII he speaks of something else. "Philosophy" is taken in its precise, narrow sense: "philo-sophy", love of wisdom, the aspiration to wisdom, as opposed to *Sophia*, wisdom itself. Chapter VIII speaks not of the philosopher but of the Sage, since "absolute knowledge" (*das absolute Wissen*) is nothing other than wisdom, opposed to philosophy, to theology, and to vulgar science. Before interpreting the chapter, Kojève will say something about wisdom and its relations with philosophy. The etymological distinction frames the whole course. Absolute knowledge is not a higher philosophy but the end of philosophy, the possession of what philosophy desired.

All philosophers agree on the definition of the Sage, which fits in a sentence: the Sage is the man capable of answering in an intelligible, even satisfying, way all the questions that can be asked him about his acts, and answering so that the whole of his answers forms a coherent discourse. Or, what comes to the same: the Sage is the man fully and perfectly self-conscious. The definition is Kojève's formalisation, not a quotation. Its merit is that it is operational: wisdom is tested by questioning, which ties it to Socratic dialogue.

It suffices to grasp the meaning of this definition to understand why Plato could deny that the ideal can be realised. Starting from any act, washing or paying taxes, a series of "whys" leads quickly, "vertically", to the relation of soul and body, individual and State, finite and infinite, death and immortality, God and the world, and finally to knowledge itself, the coherent, meaningful language in which we ask and answer. One soon faces the whole of the so-called philosophical or "metaphysical" questions. The example of washing or paying taxes is deliberately banal: any act, pursued far enough, opens onto the whole.

Starting from the same banal act and progressing "horizontally", one will end, less quickly, by going round all the sciences taught in modern universities, and perhaps discover others not yet in existence. To answer all questions about any act is ultimately to answer all possible questions: to realise the encyclopaedia of possible knowledge. To be perfectly self-conscious is to possess, at least virtually, encyclopaedic knowledge in the strong sense. The vertical and horizontal directions correspond to metaphysics and the sciences; their union is the encyclopaedia. The inference from self-consciousness to omniscience is the key step: whoever fully understands himself understands everything his acts involve.

Hegel, defining the Sage, the man of absolute knowledge, as the perfectly self-conscious, that is, at least potentially omniscient, man, nonetheless had the unheard-of audacity to affirm that he had realised wisdom in his own person. Kojève's "unheard-of audacity" states the claim at its full strength, before examining it.

Usually the Sage is presented under another, apparently more accessible, aspect. The Stoics, for whom the idea of the Sage is central and who, against Plato, affirmed its possibility and even its reality, define him as the man perfectly satisfied by what he is. The Sage would be the man who wants and desires nothing, who wants to change nothing in himself or outside himself, and so does not act. He simply is and does not become; he remains identical with himself and is satisfied in this identity. The Stoic definition by satisfaction is the second of the three definitions Kojève will set out. The description of the Sage as one who does not act and does not become anticipates his own account of the end of history: post-historical man no longer negates.

For Hegel this second definition is only a paraphrase of the first, by perfect self-knowledge, and he accepts both because he identifies them. Kojève will not demonstrate this, since the demonstration is the whole of the first seven chapters. He notes only that the claim that perfect satisfaction implies full self-consciousness is more acceptable than the inverse claim that the perfectly self-conscious man is necessarily satisfied by what he becomes conscious of. To demonstrate the first, it suffices to say: since one can be satisfied only by knowing that one is, by becoming conscious of one's satisfaction, perfect satisfaction implies absolute self-consciousness. But Kojève does not insist, knowing that we "moderns" are much too "romantic" to be convinced by "easy", that is, evident, arguments. The asymmetry between the two implications is carefully stated: satisfaction implies self-consciousness more obviously than self-consciousness implies satisfaction. The remark about "romantic" moderns anticipates the admission, made in the footnote, that evidence does not compel conviction.

He appeals instead to psychological experience. However satisfied we believe ourselves, it suffices that someone ask us "why" about our satisfaction and we cannot answer for the satisfaction to vanish as if by enchantment, even if the sensation of pleasure, happiness, joy, or well-being resists the test for a while. One can make the experiment oneself, or read Plato's *Ion*, where a man who believed himself satisfied by what he is ceases to be, solely because he cannot justify his satisfaction by answering Socrates's questions. The scene is quite convincing. A footnote qualifies at once. Plato convinces those who read and understand his dialogue, but they are few, and fewer still understand him; the scene can convince only those who are willing to be convinced. The same holds for the "easy" argument: it is evident, but convincing only to those ready to yield to evidence. We moderns are romantic enough to distinguish theoretical evidence from existential conviction. In general, everything said is truly convincing only to those who place the supreme existential value in self-consciousness, and they are convinced in advance: for them satisfaction and self-consciousness are two aspects of one thing, whereas for common mortals the identification is not obvious; they separate the two and, preferring satisfaction, think it far more accessible than omniscience. The *Ion* example is apt: the rhapsode's contentment dissolves under questioning. The footnote is one of the most important passages in the book. Kojève concedes that the Hegelian identification of satisfaction and self-consciousness convinces only those who already hold self-consciousness as the supreme value. The concession reappears below as the thesis that Hegel's ideal is valid only for the philosopher.

In general one tends to underestimate the difficulties of satisfaction and overestimate those of omniscience. So thinkers who believe in the myth of easy satisfaction, invented by moralists, and who keep the ideal of the Sage knowing it is extremely hard to realise, have in view neither omniscience, which they think inaccessible, nor satisfaction, which they think too easy, but a third definition: they identify wisdom with moral perfection. The Sage would be the morally perfect man. The third definition, by moral perfection, completes the triad. The phrase "the myth of easy satisfaction" targets moralists who think contentment a matter of attitude.

Hegel believes he can show that the third definition is equivalent to the second and so to the first. Kojève thinks it cannot seriously be contested that the perfect man is satisfied by what he is. Even Christians must affirm it as soon as they identify holiness with perfection, rather than, as they usually do, with a minimal imperfection, a minimum of sin, or with a maximal consciousness of imperfection and sin. Whoever speaks of moral perfection necessarily also speaks of satisfaction with what one is. The remark on Christian holiness is precise: Christianity usually defines sanctity by sin, minimal or maximally acknowledged, which is why it cannot identify perfection and satisfaction.

To see why, reflect on the concept of moral perfection, abstracting from its content, about which opinions differ. Either the concept has no meaning, or it means a human existence that serves as a model for all men, the final aim and motive of their actions being conformity to it. If the Sage realises moral perfection, his existence serves as a model to himself and others: he wants to resemble himself indefinitely, and others want to resemble him. That amounts to saying he is satisfied by what he is: subjectively, since nothing in him drives him to surpass himself, change, negate, or refuse what he already is; and objectively, by universal "recognition", since no one would want to force him to change the state that satisfies him. The derivation of satisfaction from perfection through the notion of a model is elegant. Objective satisfaction is recognition: others want to be like him and so do not want to change him.

Kojève has said that the concept of moral perfection has meaning only if universally valid, accepted as a model by all. This may seem contestable, since we are accustomed to speaking of several irreducible existential types, several essentially different moralities. He has no intention of contesting this pluralism, this ethical relativism. He means only that under these conditions it no longer makes sense to speak of perfection, since the concept of "perfection" becomes strictly identical with that of "subjective satisfaction". To affirm a plurality of existential or moral types is to affirm that recognition by all is not implied in the ideal of perfection realisable within each type; it suffices to believe oneself perfect to be perfect, and to believe oneself perfect is to be satisfied by what one is; and conversely. Only by affirming a single type of moral perfection does one complete the concept of subjective satisfaction with that of objective satisfaction, satisfaction by universal recognition. But even then the truly perfect man is satisfied by what he is. It is only the inverse claim that seems debatable: it seems one can be satisfied without wanting or being able to serve as a model for all. The treatment of pluralism is striking: Kojève does not refute it but shows that it empties the concept of perfection. His refusal to contest relativism is itself a philosophical position: he leaves the choice open.

Kojève cannot reproduce Hegel's demonstration that the satisfied man is morally perfect, a model for all. He recalls only that Hegel shows that man can be satisfied only by being universally recognised, so that man can be satisfied only by being perfect, and is perfect only by being satisfied. He reaches this by identifying man with self-consciousness. Here again the argument convinces only those willing to be convinced by reasoning. Hegel shows only that the first definition of the Sage, by self-consciousness, coincides with the definitions by satisfaction and by moral perfection. But he demonstrates nothing to one who denies the first definition, that the Sage must be self-conscious; the only thing Hegel can say is that nothing can be demonstrated to those who deny it. Nor does he show that the satisfied man is actually taken as a model by all; he shows only what is evident from the start, that the fully satisfied and perfectly self-conscious man serves as a morally perfect model for all who place the supreme existential value in self-consciousness, those who by definition accept the ideal he realises. The concession is decisive: Hegel's argument proves the equivalence of the three definitions within the premise of self-consciousness, but cannot establish the premise.

At first sight Hegel's argument is a simple tautology, and he too seems to have an irreducible pluralism depriving the concept of perfection of meaning. But Hegel would not accept this interpretation. He would say his concept of perfection is valid, since universally valid, like every concept; for those who reject it have no concept at all. The reply attributed to Hegel is powerful: whoever rejects self-consciousness as the supreme value rejects conceptual discourse, and so has nothing to oppose to Hegel's concept.

Discussing the second definition, Kojève promised to return to an analogous situation, and does so now. For Hegel the three definitions are rigorously equivalent. The Sage is the perfectly self-conscious man, fully satisfied by what he is, realising moral perfection, a model to himself and all others, with the important restriction: to all those for whom he exists, who understand him, who know that he is and what he is. The Sage is therefore universally recognised: there is only one type of wisdom. In affirming this one meets the contrary thesis of existential pluralism or relativism. How does Hegel demonstrate his thesis? Only by starting from the first definition as an axiom. The demonstration is simple. Suppose the Sage perfectly self-conscious; perfect self-consciousness equals omniscience; the Sage's knowledge is total and reveals the totality of being. Since being obeys the principle of identity with itself, there is only one totality of being, and so only one knowledge that reveals it wholly. There is therefore only one possible type of conscious wisdom. The restriction "to all those for whom he exists" is important: universal recognition means recognition by those who understand. The argument for the uniqueness of wisdom from the uniqueness of being is clean: there is one whole, so one complete knowledge of it.

If the ideal of self-conscious wisdom is unique, the Sage who realises it also realises moral perfection and is therefore satisfied by what he is. It suffices to suppose that the Sage is fully self-conscious to affirm that in wisdom, necessarily unique, self-consciousness, subjective satisfaction, and objective perfection coincide completely. To reach Hegel's triple definition it suffices to suppose that man is self-consciousness in his "essence" and his very existence, that he differs from the animal and the thing by self-consciousness and by it alone. From this supposition the triple definition can indeed be deduced. The whole edifice rests on one anthropological premise: man is self-consciousness.

Once more, the deduction, given in the first seven chapters, will not be reproduced; but Kojève declares it irrefutable. After reading these chapters one sees that it suffices to define man by self-consciousness to conclude necessarily that there must be an ideal of the Sage, that there can be only one type of Sage, and that the Sage answers the triple definition. At least, so Hegel would have said. But looking more closely, one sees that Hegel presupposes a little more than the mere fact of self-consciousness: he supposes that self-consciousness tends naturally, spontaneously, to extend itself throughout the whole domain of reality given to man and in man. The dialectical movement of the *Phenomenology* always follows this scheme: a situation A has formed, and Hegel describes it; he then says that, this situation given, the man who realises it must necessarily become conscious of it; finally he shows how the situation changes through this becoming-conscious and turns into a new situation B; and so on. But this becoming-conscious may be much less necessary, natural, and universal than Hegel thinks. It may be that normally man, even self-conscious, resists the extension of his consciousness, tends to shut himself up in it, and to reject into the unconscious, the automatic, whatever exceeds the field already conscious. If so, the dialectical movement that ends in the ideal and reality of wisdom ceases to be necessary. For it to reach its term, at each dialectical turn there must actually be a self-consciousness tending to extend itself over the new reality, and nothing proves that such a self-consciousness must necessarily be there when needed. The analysis of the *Phenomenology*'s method is Kojève's most important critical contribution. Each transition presupposes someone who becomes conscious of the new situation; if no one does, the dialectic stalls. This is the ground of his 1934–35 claim that transitions are free acts (p. 73).

For the deductions of the *Phenomenology* to be valid, one must therefore suppose not only a self-consciousness but a self-consciousness that always tends to extend itself as far as possible. This supplementary condition is very important. For the moment Kojève says only that discussion can bear only on the premises of the *Phenomenology*, not on its deductions. Personally, having accepted the premises, one can make no objection to the conclusions Hegel draws; at least he has heard of no serious objection of this kind. Accepting the starting point, one necessarily arrives at the final result, the concept of the Sage in its triple definition. The division between premises and deductions is Kojève's methodological stance throughout: he accepts the logic and questions the anthropology.

But the final result of the *Phenomenology* has a double aspect. Hegel deduces the triple ideal of the Sage, and he affirms that this ideal is realised, by himself, the author of the deduction. The deductions can demonstrate only the ideal possibility of the Sage, not his real possibility, still less his reality. Plato, who starts from the same supposition as Hegel (man equals self-consciousness), recognises that the Sage is the necessary ideal of thought and discourse, but denies that man can realise it, meaning real man, living in a real world during the limited time between birth and death. The distinction between ideal and real possibility makes the question of the Sage a question of fact.

Since this is a question of reality, of fact, Platonic scepticism can be refuted by Hegel only by showing a fact. Kojève will return to the reality of the Sage; for now he develops the "theoretical" difficulties. A fact can be refuted only by a fact: the existence of a Sage. Hegel's claim to be one is the only possible refutation of Plato.

One can raise not only the question of fact but the question of right: one can doubt the Plato–Hegel starting point, the identification of man with self-consciousness and the claim that self-consciousness always tends to extend itself. The deduction is not hypothetical, since self-consciousness is not an arbitrary axiom but an indisputable fact. But it can be interpreted differently. One can deny that self-consciousness reveals the "essence" of man; or, more simply, say either that self-consciousness is a kind of disease that man must and can overcome, or that beside conscious men there are unconscious men who are nonetheless equally, if differently, human. In doing so one denies the universality of wisdom and contests the identity of the three definitions. The two alternatives, self-consciousness as disease and unconscious humanity, are real positions in the history of thought. Kojève gives them next.

This denial is not his invention; it has actually been made. One need only think of the Hindu thinkers who say that man approaches perfection-satisfaction in dreamless sleep, that it is realised in the absolute night of the Brahmins' "fourth state" (*turīya*), or in the Buddhists' Nirvana, the extinction of all consciousness. More generally, of all those who seek perfection-satisfaction in absolute silence, excluding even monologue or dialogue with God. One may think also of the ideal Nietzsche called "Chinese", the ideal of the "citizen", in a non-Hegelian sense, wholly "brutalised" in and by the security of his well-being (*The Gay Science*, book I, § 24). Finally, of the ideal of "salvation" through unconscious erotic or aesthetic ecstasy, musical for instance. The examples cover mysticism, the Last Man, and aesthetic rapture. The reference to Nietzsche's "Chinese" ideal, the comfortable, unthinking citizen, anticipates Kojève's later discussions of post-historical man, which he will describe in terms close to Nietzsche's Last Man.

There is no doubt that men have been satisfied in unconsciousness, since they have voluntarily remained identical with themselves until death. And one can say, if one likes, that they realised a "moral perfection", since there were men who took them as models. The word is then used improperly, since the universality of the ideal plays no role. Nietzsche seriously considered that the "Chinese" ideal might become universal, which does not seem absurd; it is possible, if not opposed, and then one could speak of a satisfied perfection in the proper sense. The admission that the "Chinese" ideal could become universal is prophetic in the context of Kojève's later thought, where the end of history is sometimes described as the triumph of such comfort.

These are facts opposed to Hegel, and he can answer nothing. At most he can oppose to the facts of unconscious "Sages" the fact of the conscious Sage. And if this fact did not exist? In any case Hegel cannot, by definition, refute or "convert" the unconscious "Sage". He can refute him only by speech, and in beginning to speak or listen, this "Sage" already accepts the Hegelian ideal. If he really is what he is, an unconscious "Sage", he will refuse all discussion, and then he can be "refuted" only as one "refutes" a fact, a thing, or a beast: by destroying him physically. The conclusion is stark: against the silent there is no argument, only force. The remark is less a threat than a statement of the limit of discourse, the point at which dialectic becomes fight.

Hegel could say that the unconscious "Sage" is not truly human, but that would be an arbitrary definition. Hegelian wisdom is a necessary ideal only for a determinate type of human being, the man who places the supreme value in self-consciousness, and only this man can realise it. «L'idéal platono-hégélien de Sagesse ne vaut que pour le Philosophe» (the Platonic-Hegelian ideal of wisdom is valid only for the philosopher) (p. 279). The conclusion restricts the scope of Hegel's system: it is universal for philosophers, not for all men. This is Kojève's most significant qualification of Hegel.

This clarifies the precision mentioned earlier, that Hegel presupposes not only that man is essentially self-conscious but that his self-consciousness tends naturally and necessarily to extend itself. It means simply that Hegel presupposes the existence of the philosopher. For the dialectic of the *Phenomenology* to reach its term, the idea and realisation of wisdom, there must be at each dialectical turn a philosopher ready to become conscious of the newly constituted reality. It is the philosopher alone who wants at all costs to know where he stands, to realise what he is, who does not go further before having done so. The others, though self-conscious, shut themselves up in what they have already become conscious of and remain impervious to new facts in and outside themselves. For them "the more it changes, the more it is the same thing"; they "remain faithful to their principles"; for them "a war is always a war" and "all dictatorships are equal". It is not by themselves but only through the philosopher that they realise, reluctantly, an essential change of "situation", of the world they live in and so of themselves. The political examples, "a war is always a war", "all dictatorships are equal", written in 1938–39, are pointed: the philosopher is the one who sees what is new in a situation, the non-philosopher the one who assimilates it to old categories. The philosopher is the agent of historical self-consciousness.

The man the *Phenomenology* has in view, who necessarily arrives at the Platonic-Hegelian ideal of the Sage and is supposed one day to realise it, is not simply man. It is only the philosopher. The restriction completes the argument: the *Phenomenology* is the autobiography of the philosopher.

This lets one specify the notion of philosophy. If philo-sophy is love of wisdom, if being a philosopher means wanting to become a Sage, the Sage the philosopher wants to become is necessarily the Platonic-Hegelian Sage, the perfect and satisfied man essentially and completely conscious of his perfection and satisfaction. Philosophy can be nothing but a form of self-consciousness. Whereas the sciences, mathematics for instance, relate to the real that gives them content, meaning, through space-time, philosophy relates to the real only through self-consciousness. Without this pivot, "metaphysical" speculations are as "formal", empty, meaningless, as pure mathematics. Philosophy that is more than a "game of the mind", comparable to a card game, implies and presupposes the ideal of wisdom understood as full and perfect self-consciousness. The comparison of philosophy without self-consciousness to pure mathematics and card games is severe: metaphysics has meaning only as the philosopher's self-understanding. The position is close to existential philosophy and distant from analytical metaphysics.

Kojève now compares the philosopher and the Sage. First: if wisdom is the art of answering all questions that can be asked about human existence, philosophy is the art of asking them; the philosopher is the man who always ends by asking himself a question he can no longer answer. When he wants at all costs to answer it, he ceases to be a philosopher without becoming a Sage, answering either with something that contradicts the rest of his discourse or by appeal to an incomprehensible, ineffable "un-conscious". The two failures of the philosopher, contradiction and appeal to the ineffable, correspond to dogmatism and mysticism.

Second: if the Sage is satisfied by what he is, the philosopher is conscious of his non-satisfaction; he is essentially a malcontent, which does not necessarily mean unhappy, and he is malcontent as a philosopher solely because he does not know himself satisfied. If one wants to be malicious, one can say the philosopher is malcontent because he does not know what he wants; to be just, one must say the same thing, with the stress on "know". He has desires like everyone, but their satisfaction does not satisfy him as a philosopher as long as he does not understand them, integrate them into the coherent discourse that reveals his existence, justify them, usually but not necessarily morally. That is why the ideal of unconscious "wisdom" or "satisfaction" does not exist for the philosopher: the mere fact of not understanding his well-being, pleasure, joy, happiness, or ecstasy would already make him malcontent. If conscious satisfaction is expressed in identity with oneself, consciousness of non-satisfaction provokes and reveals change: the philosopher is the man who essentially changes, consciously, who wants to become other than he is, solely because he does not know himself satisfied. Since self-consciousness is expressed in discourse (*Logos*), and a discourse revealing a change is called dialectical, every philosopher is necessarily a dialectician. A footnote adds that his dialectic, by the first definition of wisdom, can ultimately be reduced to a series of questions about his existence and answers. The play on "ne sait pas ce qu'il veut", malice and justice using the same words with different stress, is elegant. The derivation of dialectic from the philosopher's dissatisfaction makes dialectic existential before it is logical: a discourse of self-transformation.

Third: if the Sage is a model to himself and others, meaning philosophers who tend toward the ideal he realises, the philosopher is, so to speak, a negative model: he reveals his existence only to show that one must not be like him, that man wants to be not a philosopher but a Sage. The philosopher changes knowing what not to be and what to become; in his changes he makes progress. A footnote argues that if "progress" has meaning only in relation to conscious change, every conscious change is necessarily progress, since self-consciousness implies memory and every change in its domain is an extension of it. And progress cannot be defined otherwise than by saying there is progress from A to B if one can understand A from B without being able to understand B from A. The definition of progress in the footnote is one of Kojève's most precise: an asymmetry of understanding. The later stage understands the earlier, not conversely. It grounds the claim that the history of self-consciousness is necessarily progressive.

The philosopher's dialectical discourse, revealing his change, reveals a progress, and since every revealed progress has pedagogical value, every philosophy is necessarily, as Plato saw, a pedagogical dialectic or dialectical pedagogy, starting from the first question about the existence of the one who asks it and ending, at least in principle, in wisdom, the answer, at least virtual, to all possible questions. The *Phenomenology* itself is such a pedagogy: it leads the reader from sense-certainty to absolute knowledge.

That a man has decided to read the *Phenomenology* proves he loves philosophy; that he understands it proves he is a philosopher, since in reading and understanding it he actually increases his self-consciousness. Being a philosopher, he is interested in himself and uninterested in those who are not philosophers, who on principle refuse to read the *Phenomenology* and so to extend their self-consciousness. Abandoning them to their fate and returning to himself, the philosopher learns from the *Phenomenology* that, as a philosopher, he is a "lover of wisdom" as defined in and by this book: he wants to become a Sage, a perfectly self-conscious man, fully satisfied by this self-consciousness, and so a model to all his "colleagues". Seeing in the Sage the human ideal in general, the philosopher attributes to himself as philosopher a human value beyond compare, since for him only the philosopher can become a Sage. The irony about "colleagues" and the philosopher's self-estimation is characteristic. The passage describes the readership of the *Phenomenology* as a self-selecting elite.

The whole question reduces to whether the philosopher can really hope to become a Sage. Hegel says yes, claiming to have reached wisdom in and through the *Phenomenology*; Plato says no. To decide, one must understand what the two attitudes mean: the acceptance of the ideal of wisdom together with the denial of its realisation (the case of Plato), and the affirmation of a man who says he is a Sage (the case of Hegel). The lecture ends by posing the dilemma the next lecture will analyse.

### Second Lecture: Introduction: Philosophy and Wisdom (Continued and Concluded)

The result so far: philosophy has meaning only as the road to wisdom, or at least guided by the ideal of the Sage; conversely, acceptance of this ideal leads necessarily to philosophy as a means of reaching or at least orienting oneself toward it. On the definition of the Sage and the philosopher, Plato, who marks the beginning of classical philosophy, agrees with Hegel, who marks its end. The only fundamental divergence possible on the Sage is between Hegel and Plato: accepting the ideal and its Platonic-Hegelian definition, one can either affirm or deny the possibility of realising wisdom, of actually becoming a Sage after having been a philosopher. Plato and Hegel as the beginning and end of classical philosophy frame the history of philosophy as a single enterprise.

One can, like Plato, deny the possibility of realising wisdom. But then either the ideal of the Sage is never and nowhere realised, and the philosopher is simply mad, claiming or wanting to be what cannot be, and, which is worse, what he knows to be impossible; or he is not mad, and his ideal is or will be realised and his definition of the Sage is or will be a truth. But since by definition it cannot be realised by man in time, it is or will be realised by a being other than man, outside time. We all know such a being is called God. So if one denies with Plato the possibility of the human Sage, one must either deny philosophy or affirm the existence of God. The dilemma is Kojève's: Platonism is either madness or theology. The criterion of madness, wanting what one knows impossible, recalls the Introduction's definition (p. 32).

Suppose God exists. Truth reveals what is and remains eternally identical with itself; it reveals a being that remains identical with itself. By definition the man who remains eternally a philosopher always changes, and since the world includes changing man, the world as a whole changes. Human discourse contains truth only insofar as it reveals a being other than man and the world; it is true only insofar as it reveals God, the only perfect being, satisfied and conscious of himself and his perfect satisfaction. All philosophical progress is therefore in fact theo-logical, not anthropo-logical. Wisdom for man means not perfect self-consciousness but perfect knowledge of God. The argument is precise: if truth is eternal and man changes, truth must be about something other than man.

The Plato–Hegel opposition is therefore not an opposition within philosophy but between philosophy and theology, and ultimately between wisdom and religion. Subjectively: the philosopher hopes to reach wisdom, which for him is self-consciousness, by a continuous process of dialectical pedagogy in which each step is conditioned only by the preceding ones; the religious man can hope to reach wisdom, knowledge of God, only by a sudden leap, "conversion", conditioned at least partly by an element external to the process, "revelation" or "grace". Objectively: the philosopher's knowledge can reveal itself as absolute or total only by revealing itself as circular, returning to its starting point; the religious man's knowledge is absolute or total without being circular. Its circle is closed only by a "singular point" that interrupts the line: God. God is a particular being, essentially different from the world and man, yet absolute and total. Knowledge is total as soon as it includes perfect knowledge of God, and the rest, concerning man and the world, can be partial, open, non-circular. For the atheist philosopher, by contrast, circularity is the only guarantee of totality, of the absolute truth of knowledge. Passing to empirical reality: since the Sage's knowledge reveals only man-in-the-world, the reality that turns this total and circular knowledge into truth is the universal and homogeneous State, free of internal contradictions, class struggles, and so on; the philosopher can therefore reach absolute knowledge only after this State is realised, after the end of history. For the religious man, the universal and homogeneous reality that proves his total knowledge true is God, supposed universal and homogeneous at every moment of history; he can reach absolute knowledge at any moment, under any conditions, provided God reveals himself to him. The image of the circle closed by a singular point is a brilliant formalisation of the difference between theology and absolute knowledge. It explains why the philosopher must wait for the end of history and the believer need not: God is a permanent universal and homogeneous reality, the final State a historical one.

A footnote illustrates from the history of philosophy that denying the possibility of the Sage turns philosophy into theology, and denying God necessarily affirms the possibility that man will one day realise wisdom. Plato, denying it, saw that his dialectical discourse had meaning only if theological, referred in the end to the transcendent One-Good; the wisdom it leads to is, according to the Seventh Letter, a "conversion" ending in silent contemplation of God.
