Aristotle, wanting to eliminate the transcendent Good while maintaining the absolute value of discourse, immediately affirmed the possibility of wisdom on earth. Descartes denies the possibility of wisdom by defining man by error (whereas Hegel defines him as the being who abolishes error by action) and must introduce a transcendent God from the start: not the circularity of the system but the direct relation of its parts to the singular total being guarantees its truth. Spinoza, wanting to eliminate the transcendent element of Cartesianism, develops his system in a book entitled *Ethics*, treating human wisdom. Kant, discovering the transcendental, believes he can do without the transcendent, or, what is the same, avoid the alternative by supposing an infinite or indefinite philosophical progress. But this was an illusion: he does not need God in each of the two parts of his system, but cannot do without him to unite them; he abandons the "System" and connects the two Critiques by a third, knowing the link has the value not of a truth but of an "as if"; one need only turn the third Critique into the third part of the System for the System to become theological. The footnote is a compact history of philosophy organised by Kojève's criterion. The reading of Kant, whose third Critique unites the first two only "as if", is sharp: Kant's system is either incomplete or theological.

In the last analysis there are three possible existential attitudes, and only three. First, one can deny the Platonic-Hegelian ideal of the Sage, deny that the supreme value lies in self-consciousness. Deciding so, one decides against all philosophy, and more: the decision ultimately deprives all human discourse of meaning. In its radical form this attitude ends in absolute silence. The first attitude is the silence of the unconscious "Sage" of the first lecture.

So: first, rejecting the ideal of wisdom, one decides against all meaningful discourse for absolute silence or for a "language" without meaning, mathematical, musical, and so on. Second, accepting the ideal but denying that man can realise it, one opts for a meaningful discourse relating to a reality essentially other than mine: theology against philosophy. Third, one can opt for philosophy, but then one must admit the possibility of one day realising the ideal of wisdom. Hegel opts for the third with full knowledge, and in the *Phenomenology* tries to prove it the only possible one. The inclusion of mathematics and music among "languages without meaning" follows from Kojève's definition of meaning as reference through self-consciousness: they are formal.

In fact he does not succeed. He cannot refute those who aspire to an existential ideal excluding self-consciousness, or at least its indefinite extension. As for theology, he manages only to show that the religious man's existence is necessarily unhappy. But since he himself says that the religious man is satisfied by his unhappiness, he cannot refute him either, except by appealing again to the extension of self-consciousness; and this no longer interests the religious man once he believes he has reached full knowledge of God. The *Phenomenology* shows only that the ideal of the Sage as it defines it is the necessary ideal of philosophy, of every man who places the supreme value in self-consciousness. The admission that Hegel does not succeed is unusually candid from a commentator who presents the system as irrefutable in its deductions. It repeats the 1934–35 remark that one can take pleasure in unhappiness (p. 73).

This restriction is no objection to the *Phenomenology*. Hegel wrote it to answer "what am I?", and the man who asks this, who wants to become self-conscious before living and acting further, is by definition a philosopher. To answer "what am I?" is necessarily to speak of the philosopher. The man of the *Phenomenology* is not simply man but the philosopher, or rather the various human types appear in it only insofar as they are integrated in the person of the philosopher analysing himself, Hegel asking "what am I?". No wonder, then, that Hegel manages to show the reader, himself a philosopher, that the man described tends ever more consciously toward the ideal of wisdom and finally realises it. The man who gives a complete answer to "what am I?" is by definition a Sage: answering in the strong sense, one answers not "I am a philosopher" but "I am a Sage". A footnote adds that the discourse of the man who knows himself a Sage is no longer the *Phenomenology*, still a philosophy, but the completed Science, the *Encyclopaedia*. The integration of all human types in the philosopher's person restates the microcosm thesis (p. 164). The distinction between the *Phenomenology* as philosophy and the *Encyclopaedia* as wisdom is precise.

The answer to the question posed in the *Phenomenology* is thus at the same time the proof of the reality of wisdom, and so a refutation in fact of Plato and of theo-logy in general. The whole question is whether the answer given by the whole work, or its first seven chapters, is really total, an answer to all possible questions about human existence. Hegel believes he demonstrates totality by circularity. The factual refutation of Plato is the existence of a complete answer.

This idea of circularity is, if one likes, the only original element Hegel brought. His definition of philosophy and wisdom is that of all philosophers. The claim that wisdom is realisable was made by Aristotle; the Stoics even claimed it had been realised; and it is more than probable that some Epicureans spoke of the Sage in the first person. But none of these thinkers gave a sufficient criterion for identifying the Sage. In practice one was always content with the fact of satisfaction, subjective (immobility, absence of desires) or objective (identity with oneself, conscious agreement with oneself, usually presented ethically). One never managed to show that the aspirant to wisdom actually realised the fullness of self-consciousness, and without this aspect the ideal has no meaning. The claim that circularity is Hegel's only original contribution is Kojève's provocative simplification. The point is that Hegel supplied a criterion for wisdom that earlier claimants lacked.

Hegel is, Kojève believes, the first to have found an answer, not the answer, to whether one's self-knowledge, and so knowledge in general, is total, unsurpassable, unmodifiable, universally and definitively valid, absolutely true. For him the answer is given by the circularity of knowledge: the Sage's absolute knowledge is circular, and every circular knowledge, of which only one is possible, is the Sage's absolute knowledge. Asking any question, one arrives sooner or later, after a series of answers and questions, at one of the questions within the circular knowledge the Sage possesses. Starting from it and progressing logically, one necessarily arrives back at the starting point, and sees that one has exhausted all possible questions and answers. One has a total answer: each part of the circular knowledge has as its answer the whole of this knowledge, which, being circular, is the whole of all knowledge. The qualification "an answer, not the answer" marks Kojève's reserve. The description of circularity as a practical test, any question leads into the circle, which then returns to its start, makes the criterion operational.

It is known that Hegel held his knowledge circular and circularity the necessary and sufficient condition of absolute truth. But one usually forgets, and learns only from the *Phenomenology*, that the conception of circularity, like every Hegelian conception, has a double aspect: an ideal or abstract aspect and a real, concrete, "existential" aspect, and only their union constitutes what Hegel calls the concept (*Begriff*). The real aspect of the "circularity" of wisdom is the "circular" existence of the Sage. In the Sage's absolute knowledge each question is its own answer, but only by passing through the totality of questions and answers forming the system. Likewise in his existence the Sage remains identical with himself, enclosed in himself, but he remains identical with himself because he passes through the totality of others, and is enclosed in himself because he encloses in himself the totality of others. According to the *Phenomenology*, this means simply that only a citizen of the universal and homogeneous State can be a Sage, the State of the "doing of all and each", where each is only through and for the whole and the whole through and for each. The parallel between logical circularity and social circularity is Kojève's most original thesis in these lectures. The Sage's self-identity through others mirrors the answer that returns to itself through all questions.

The Sage's absolute knowledge, realising perfect self-consciousness, answers "what am I?". The Sage's real existence must therefore be "circular", he must be a citizen of the universal and homogeneous State, for the knowledge revealing this existence to be circular, an absolute truth. Only the citizen of the perfect State can realise absolute knowledge. Conversely, since Hegel supposes that every man is a philosopher, made to become conscious of what he is (at least he is interested only in such men), a citizen of the perfect State always ends by understanding himself in and through a circular, absolute knowledge. The converse depends on the premise just criticised, that every man is a philosopher.

This conception has an important consequence: for Hegel wisdom can be realised only at the end of history, since, according to the *Phenomenology*, the State in question necessarily marks the end of the history of humanity, meaning self-conscious humanity or humanity aspiring to self-consciousness. This too is universally known: one always knew that for Hegel the advent of wisdom completes history (which is banal, since if one knows everything there is no way left to progress or change, for the philosopher, for whom alone this problem exists), and also that the advent is possible only at the end of history. One knows it, but does not always understand why, and one does not understand it as long as one does not know that the Sage must be a citizen of the universal, that is, non-expandable, and homogeneous, that is, non-transformable, State. And one does not know this until one has understood that this State is nothing other than the real basis, the "infrastructure", of the circularity of the absolute system: the citizen realises as active citizen the circularity he reveals by his system as contemplative Sage. The glosses "universal = non-expandable" and "homogeneous = non-transformable" are the clearest definitions of the two attributes in the book. The State is universal because it cannot grow, homogeneous because it cannot change internally.

A footnote draws the consequence for Hegel's attitude toward Plato. For Hegel, Plato was right to deny the possibility of the Sage, since Plato's "ideal" State, which only reflects the real State of his time, is not universal and homogeneous; its citizen is not "circular", nor is his knowledge. When one tried to affirm the possibility of the Sage within this imperfect State, one had to transform the ideal itself, arriving at the caricature of the Stoic and Sceptic "Sage", who, as the *Phenomenology* shows, is not self-conscious. As soon as such a "Sage" becomes self-conscious, he sees that he does not realise perfection, even that he cannot, and, becoming Christian, thinks perfection realised outside the world, by God. The "Sage" become Christian thus rediscovers the Platonic, theological conception, but more consciously than Plato: he knows he cannot be a Sage because the State he lives in is not perfect. He can then have the idea of a perfect State and try to realise it, and when he does he becomes, ceasing to be Platonic and Christian, Hegelian; more exactly, he will be Hegel, the real Sage, the successful Aristotelian, Stoic, and Sceptic. «Si l'on veut, c'est encore du Platon : la philosophie hégélienne est une théo-logie ; seulement son Dieu est le Sage» (if one likes, it is still Plato: Hegelian philosophy is a theo-logy, only its God is the Sage) (p. 289). The footnote justifies Plato historically: his denial of the Sage was true of his world. The final sentence is one of Kojève's most memorable: Hegel's philosophy is a theology whose God is the Sage.

What is our attitude toward all this? There are three possibilities and only three. The first can be eliminated without discussion: first, because it is strictly speaking indisputable, and second, because the very fact of our study of the *Phenomenology* proves that silent satisfaction does not tempt us overmuch. The only serious dilemma for us is Plato or Hegel, theo-logy or philo-sophy. The play on "indiscutable", both unquestionable and not open to discussion, is exact: silence cannot be argued with.

We face a fact: a visibly sane man named Hegel claims to have realised wisdom. Before deciding for or against philosophy or theology, for or against the impossibility of wisdom, one must see whether Hegel was right to claim he is a Sage, whether he has not already, by his very being, settled the question. For this one must see whether the present state of things corresponds to what Hegel calls the perfect State and the end of history, and whether Hegel's knowledge is really circular. The two criteria, political and logical, organise the rest of the lecture.

The answer to the first seems very easy: the perfect State? Without doubt we are far from it. But writing in 1806, Hegel too knew that the State was not yet realised in act in all its perfection. He claimed only the presence in the world of its germ and the existence of the necessary and sufficient conditions for its flourishing. Can we deny with certainty the presence of such a germ and such conditions in our world? And even if we wanted to, we could not settle the question of Hegelian wisdom, since we cannot affirm, from attempts already made, that the State in question is impossible in principle. If it is possible, wisdom is too. Then there is no need to abandon philosophy and flee into any religion whatever, no need to subordinate my self-consciousness to a consciousness of what I am not: God, or some inhuman perfection, aesthetic or other, or race, people, or nation. The list of alternatives to self-consciousness, God, aesthetic perfection, race, people, nation, written in 1938–39, is political: it names the religions of the age, including fascist nationalism and racism. "Attempts already made" may allude discreetly to the Soviet experiment.

What does it mean for us that Hegel's perfect State is not yet realised? Under these conditions Hegel's philosophy, notably the anthropology of the *Phenomenology*, ceases to be a truth, since it does not reveal a reality. But it is not necessarily an error; it would be one only if the universal and homogeneous State could be shown impossible, which it cannot. What is neither an error nor a truth is an idea, or an ideal. This idea can become truth only by negating action, which, by destroying the world that does not correspond to the idea, will create through that very destruction the world that conforms to the ideal. One can accept the anthropology of the *Phenomenology*, knowing that its perfect man, the Sage, is not yet realised, only on condition of wanting to act for the realisation of the Hegelian State indispensable to his existence, or at least of accepting and "justifying" such action if it is carried out by someone somewhere. This is the political core of Kojève's Hegelianism. Hegel's philosophy is neither true nor false but a project, which becomes true only if realised by revolutionary action. The phrase "by someone somewhere", in 1938–39, is often read as pointing toward the Soviet Union, whose action Kojève would then be declaring himself willing to justify. Accepting Hegel means taking a political side.

This does not dispense us from studying the second criterion, circularity, which is infinitely more important. The first concerns a question of fact, essentially uncertain; the second concerns a logical, rational analysis in which no divergence of opinion is possible. If Hegel's system is effectively circular, we must conclude that, despite appearances and perhaps common sense, history is completed and the State in which the system could be realised is the perfect State. That is what Hegel himself did: after Napoleon's fall he declared that the Prussian State, which he otherwise detested, was the definitive or perfect State. He could not do otherwise, being convinced of his system's circularity. The logical criterion overrides the factual: if the system is circular, history is over whatever the appearances. The remark on the Prussian State, which Hegel "detested", is a generous reading of Hegel's later political philosophy: he was forced by his logic to find the end of history where he was.

The whole question for us reduces to this: if the *Phenomenology* is effectively circular, we must accept it en bloc with all that follows; if not, we must treat it as a hypothetico-deductive whole and verify each hypothesis and deduction one by one. A footnote adds that it is not enough for the *Phenomenology* to be circular; the Logic, or the *Encyclopaedia*, must be too, and, much more important, so must the system as a whole, the *Phenomenology* together with the *Encyclopaedia*. «Or c'est précisément là que la non-circularité du système de Hegel est parfaitement évidente» (and it is precisely there that the non-circularity of Hegel's system is perfectly evident) (p. 291); but he can say this only in passing and without demonstrating it. The footnote is momentous: Kojève declares Hegel's system as a whole not circular, and so not absolute knowledge by its own criterion. The failure lies in the relation between the *Phenomenology* and the *Encyclopaedia*, which is the point at which the anthropology meets the philosophy of nature, where Kojève's dualism has always located Hegel's error.

One must therefore begin by studying the *Phenomenology* from the standpoint of its circularity. But first one must know what the requirement of circularity means, and understand why absolute, truly true truth can only be circular. The discussion of these two preliminary questions will occupy the year's course. The lecture announces the programme: the analysis of Chapter VIII as the theory of circular knowledge, which Kojève will link to time.

### Third Lecture: Interpretation of the Introduction to Chapter VIII (Hoffmeister pp. 549–550)

Chapter VIII follows immediately on the chapter about religion or theology, the knowledge of the religious man, who realises perfection without self-consciousness. Between the Christian religious man and the Hegelian Sage, Hegel himself, the man perfect and satisfied by the completion of his self-consciousness, there is nothing: no intermediate type of existence is possible; the compromises of every kind have long been eliminated. Man is now satisfied only by absolute knowledge, and the whole question is whether this knowledge is for him, as for Hegel, perfect self-knowledge, or, as for the religious man, knowledge of an absolute other than himself, God. The claim that nothing lies between Christian and Sage reduces the final alternative to two terms, as the second lecture's three attitudes reduced to two once silence was set aside.

In both cases the content (*Inhalt*) of knowledge is the same; how could it be otherwise, since knowledge is absolute, total? The difference lies only in the form (*Form*). For both it is being itself that reveals itself to itself in and as absolute knowledge in its self-enclosed circularity. But for the religious man the totality of being is outside him, though he is within it; total being is other than he, and the absolute knowledge by which it reveals itself is other than human knowledge; it is this other being that understands itself in absolute knowledge, and the religious man understands it only through his own knowledge. The religious man has self-knowledge too, but it is absolute only by passing through the other being's absolute self-knowledge; he is absolutely self-conscious only insofar as he is himself in and through the Other. Christian, theological knowledge is absolute, but it is not a self-knowledge (*Sich-selbst-Wissen*), not the knowledge that the knowing man realises the completed totality he reveals, that the knowing I is the known I. The identity of content and difference of form is Hegel's thesis (¶797–798). Kojève's formula makes the difference a matter of reference: the same knowledge referred to God or to oneself.

The Sage, by contrast, refers everything to himself, without losing his dignity as Sage or forgetting that his knowledge is absolute knowledge, the knowledge. If he refers everything to himself, it is because he reduces himself to his total knowledge and is thus himself the whole, while remaining himself. He refers to himself strictly the same total content the religious man refers to his God: to himself in his total reality as citizen of the universal and homogeneous State, and in his ideal totality as possessor of absolute knowledge. The Sage's "self" is not the private ego but the self reduced to total knowledge; the double totality, real (citizen) and ideal (knower), repeats the two criteria of the second lecture.

The opposition is clear, and there is nothing between the two extremes. Since the working Slave divided the world between his Master and himself, annulling by his labour the autonomous reality of inhuman nature; or, in other words, since Judaeo-Christian man divided Parmenides's sphere between himself and his God (who, for us, is made in his image, and who, for him, is the image after which he was made); since this total division, man can no longer project his knowledge onto a natural reality and prove it true, as the pagan philosopher did, by the circular movement of the stars. He must refer it either to himself or to God, and cannot refer it to both, since only one absolute is possible. The image of Parmenides's sphere divided between man and God is Kojève's most compact history of metaphysics. Pagan thought found its circle in the heavens; Judaeo-Christian thought must find it in man or God. The chiasmus "made in his image / the image after which he was made" states Feuerbach's inversion.

Both extreme attitudes are realised: one by Hegel's anthropo-logy, the other by the elaboration of Christian theo-logy. They are evidently irreconcilable, and neither can be surpassed. One can pass from one to the other only by a sudden leap, since there is no possible transition, nothing between them. To be in one is to decide against the other; to reject one is to settle in the other. The decision is absolutely unique and as simple as possible: to decide for oneself, against God, or for God, against oneself. «Et il n'y a pas de "raison" de la décision autre que la décision elle-même» (and there is no "reason" for the decision other than the decision itself) (p. 293). The decisionism is Kojève's own, and he immediately marks it as such. It anticipates the existentialist reception of his reading, and it states in its sharpest form the thesis of the 1934–35 notes that transitions are free acts.

Of course, in presenting things so, Kojève departs from the text of the *Phenomenology*. For Hegel too the two attitudes are ultimately the only possible ones, and he knows they exclude each other. But for him there is more than juxtaposition: there is hierarchy; the Sage is "above" the religious man. And if Hegel knows that the passage from one to the other can only be sudden, a total reversal, he believes it necessary: the man who has become Christian must necessarily end by becoming a Sage. The explicit distinction between his own view and Hegel's is important: Kojève accepts the alternative and rejects its necessity.

There is hierarchy only for the philosopher, the one who admits from the start the superiority of Hegelian wisdom, that knowledge, even absolute, is a value only if it is self-knowledge (*Sich-selbst-Wissen*). A footnote adds that for the religious man there is no hierarchy: the atheist Sage's knowledge is not a lesser knowledge but no knowledge at all, a total and absolute error. As Saint Paul put it, the knowledge of the Sage and of the religious man stand to each other as folly and truth, not, as for the Sage, as successive stages of the revealing realisation of one and the same truth, the Sage's. The reference is to 1 Corinthians 1–3, where the wisdom of the world is folly to God. The footnote shows that the hierarchy is asymmetrical: each side sees the other as error.

Likewise the passage from religion to wisdom is necessary only for the philosopher, the one who seeks self-consciousness from the start, who is ready to extend indefinitely his self-consciousness, the domain of being whose knowledge reveals itself to him as self-knowledge. The restriction repeats the first lecture's conclusion about the scope of Hegel's ideal.

To be convinced, one need only recall the text at the end of Chapter VII (Hoffmeister p. 546), truly unique of its kind, whose content was to be demonstrated by its form. There Hegel summarised Christian theological doctrine as definitively constituted at the end of the evolution of the "absolute" religion. Instead of "God" he says "Spirit". The form is such that reading "divine Spirit" yields an absolutely correct summary of Christian theology, and reading "human Spirit" a correct summary of Hegel's anthropology. By the very form of the text Hegel shows that man finally established an idea of God that could, unmodified, be applied to man. Christian theism turns into Hegelian anthropotheism as soon as one abolishes the idea of the transcendence of being, as soon as the speaker refers what he says to himself and sees in it not knowledge of what he is not, a transcendent God, but self-knowledge. The observation about the double reading of ¶787 is one of Kojève's most persuasive textual arguments: the text is written so as to be read both ways.

The text is very impressive, and convincing. But Hegel nowhere says why man must abandon transcendence and end by referring theological knowledge to himself. The passage from theo-logy to anthropo-logy is undoubtedly possible, since Hegel carried it out himself; but one does not see why it is necessary. It is necessary only for Hegel, or for the philosopher in general. The distinction between possibility and necessity is the critical axis of the lecture.

Neither in Chapter VII nor in Chapter VIII does Hegel say a word about the why and how of the passage from the transcendence to the immanence of knowledge, and he does not explain it elsewhere either. The claim is strong: the decisive transition of the system is unargued.

For Hegel the passage from the religious man's transcendentalism to the citizen's and Sage's immanentism is not direct. Between them is the pseudo-transcendentalism or pseudo-immanentism of the intellectual, who refers his existence and knowledge to the True, the Beautiful, and the Good "in themselves", to the "matter itself" (*Sache selbst*). Like the religious man's supreme value, God, these values are "transcendent" in that they exist independently of him, of his real existence and its external natural and social conditions, so that the isolated particular can reach them directly. But they are also "immanent", like the citizen's and Sage's values, in that man reaches them in his lifetime, without really transcending himself, without ceasing to be man living in the natural and social world. Their immanence preserves the intellectual from "conversion", the "monastery", the "feeling of sin", the impossibility of taking pleasure in "worldly" life, since the True, Good, and Beautiful are still values of "this world". Their transcendence, by contrast, prevents him from acting as revolutionary or citizen: not outside the world, these values are nonetheless something other than it, and one need not realise anything in the world to "realise" them. The analysis of the intellectual's values as at once transcendent and immanent explains his double immunity: to religious conversion and to political action. It restates the 1935–36 summary (p. 109).

The passage from the religious man to the intellectual is described at the end of Chapter IV, from the intellectual to the citizen at the end of Chapter V. But Hegel explains the necessity of these transitions as little as that from theology to wisdom at the end of Chapter VII. The intellectual at the end of Chapter V, content to "understand everything" while remaining "above the fray", is as unassailable as the "anti-worldly" religious man at the end of Chapter IV and the transcendentalist theologian at the end of Chapter VII. At the end of Chapter IV Hegel says the religious man must end by understanding that the world he lives in is his world, and so accept it. But this is necessary only for one who wants at all costs to account for his real "worldly" existence, and the religious man can remain indifferent to it indefinitely. The religious man becomes an intellectual only by becoming at least a little of a philosopher, and one does not see why he must. Likewise Hegel rightly notes that the intellectual "above the fray" who claims to understand everything does not in fact understand himself, never managing to explain his own standpoint. But here too the objection holds only for one who will not be content with the pseudo-philosophy of "eternal" trans-personal values, and nothing says man cannot indefinitely remain unshocked by the absurdity of what he calls "impartial objectivity". Finally, it is by no means necessary to refer the totality of knowledge to oneself; one can be content indefinitely with theological absolute knowledge. The critique generalises: all three decisive transitions of the book, IV to V, V to VI, VII to VIII, require a philosopher's will to self-understanding. The phrase "impartial objectivity" targets the academic ideal of detachment.

In any case Hegel's conception is clear: in theological knowledge the knowing subject and the known object are outside each other; in the Sage's absolute knowledge they coincide. A footnote addresses an objection: religion too knows a coincidence of subject and object, the "mystical union" of man and God. But Kojève believes mysticism has nothing to do with religion and theology. That it is often attached to religion proves nothing, since art, obviously something else, is too; and religion is always more or less hostile to mysticism. What matters is that mystical union takes place necessarily in silence; the God the mystic unites with is always in principle ineffable. The mystic's perfection thus belongs to the "unconscious" perfections eliminated at the outset; mysticism excludes all knowledge, both consciousness and self-consciousness. There is no mystical knowledge in the sense in which there is philosophical or religious knowledge. In fact the mystic usually speaks of his "ineffable" God, but then either, remaining orthodox, he develops a theological knowledge no different from the transcendentalist theology of the end of Chapter VII, which does not account for the lived experience of union; or, wanting to account for it, he develops a "heterodox", atheist, anthropotheist theology approaching the absolute knowledge of Chapter VIII. One may say, if one likes, that Hegelian knowledge is nothing but the absolute self-consciousness of the mystical experience of the union of knowing subject and known object. But it makes no sense to call Hegel a "mystic", since his knowledge is essentially rational, "logical", expressed in discourse, *Logos*. Returning to the theme of his introduction, Kojève distinguishes three types of absolute satisfaction: the mystic's irrational, mute satisfaction (as which Hegel speaks of *Andacht* in Chapter VII); and speaking satisfaction, which is either religious, if one is satisfied by speaking of a being one is not, or Hegelian, if one is satisfied only by speaking of oneself. The footnote is a significant contribution: mysticism is excluded from religion and assimilated to silence, yet Hegel's knowledge is described as the rational self-consciousness of what mysticism experiences. The three satisfactions, mute, religious, and Hegelian, map the three attitudes of the second lecture. The claim that heterodox mysticism tends toward anthropotheism has Meister Eckhart and Böhme in the background.

This is the result Hegel reaches at the end of Chapter VII: Christian theological knowledge is absolute, total and definitive in content; but it refers to a universal reality other than mine. The second step is to refer this knowledge, already total and absolute, to oneself. Hegel says this in the first part of the short introduction to Chapter VIII, summarising the result of Chapter VII. The formulation "the second step" makes absolute knowledge a change of reference rather than of content.

Kojève translates (Hoffmeister p. 549): the Spirit of the revealed religion has not yet overcome its consciousness as such; or, what is the same, its real self-consciousness is not the object of its consciousness. Spirit itself and the moments distinguished in it fall within representation (*Vorstellung*) and the form of objectivity. The content of representation is absolute Spirit, and it is only a matter of overcoming (*Aufheben*) this mere form; or rather, since this form belongs to consciousness as such, its truth must already have emerged in the shapes of consciousness. The final clause is the one Kojève will reconstruct: the truth of the theological form must already have appeared in the earlier shapes.

The Christian theologian's knowledge, absolute as it is, is the summit of consciousness, of consciousness of the external, and does not account for "real self-consciousness", real man knowing what he is. It is consciousness of the external, not self-consciousness. One need only turn consciousness into self-consciousness, transcendence into immanence, to reach the Sage's absolute knowledge, the summit of self-consciousness. Of course the Sage can perform this transformation only because he is "absolute", total and definitive in his own conscious reality, which he can be only as citizen of the "absolute", universal and homogeneous State. The parenthesis ties the epistemic transformation to its political condition.

In the last sentence of the passage Hegel says that this transformation of theo-logy into wisdom is necessary and has already taken place in the concrete shapes of consciousness studied in the first seven chapters. He has in view the man described at the end of Chapter VI: Napoleon, the Napoleonic citizen, Hegel himself as citizen of the Empire, supposed universal and homogeneous and considered as already realised in principle. This man is the truth, the revealed reality, of the theological "form", since it is he who realises the perfection the theologian speaks of, which in the theologian is only an abstract idea, since God, supposed to realise it, does not exist. The reading of "the shapes of consciousness" as the end of Chapter VI is Kojève's; it makes the Napoleonic citizen the truth of Christian theology.

Kojève reconstructs Hegel's reasoning. The "form" in question, Christian theology, is actually elaborated: it is a psychological fact, a real idea as idea. Either it corresponds to an objective reality (*Wirklichkeit*) or not. In the first case there is a reality in the world that realises the Christian's idea of God, and evidently it can only be human reality. In the second, the absolute idea is an "abstract" ideal. But Hegel presupposes that every idea conceived by man necessarily tends to be realised, and can and must be realised if not absolutely false. So the Christian idea should produce a new type of human existence. But the circularity of the *Phenomenology* proves that its analyses exhaust all existential possibilities; so the Christian idea must already be realised. One need only look among the existences described in the *Phenomenology* for the one corresponding to this idea, and one finds the Napoleonic citizen, or, if one prefers, Hegel himself. The reconstruction exposes two premises: that every idea tends to be realised, and that the *Phenomenology* is circular. The argument is valid, but both premises are strong, and the second is the one Kojève doubts (p. 291).

Starting from the fact of Christian theology and presupposing the circularity of the *Phenomenology*, Hegel deduces the necessity of the realisation of the Christian idea by man-in-the-world. This idea is therefore a truth (*Wahrheit*) in that it corresponds to an objective reality, precisely the man of 1806. But this is not enough, since truth is not only reality but reality revealed by speech, self-conscious reality. To affirm the truth of the theological "form" is to affirm the existence not only of the "absolute" citizen but of the self-conscious citizen, the "absolute" citizen become philosopher, or rather, since he is absolute, become Sage: it is to affirm or presuppose the existence of Hegel himself. That is what Kojève said in his introduction: the passage from Christian theo-logy to Hegelian anthropo-logy is necessary only for and through the philosopher, here Hegel himself. «Or, rien ne prouve que l'avènement de ce Philosophe soit nécessaire» (but nothing proves that the advent of this philosopher is necessary) (p. 298). Nothing proves that the citizen of the perfect State cannot remain relatively unconscious and so maintain religion, Christian theology, regarding the State not as his own work but as God's. This is the lecture's most important critical thesis. The end of history could be realised without the Sage: a perfect State whose citizens think it God's work. Wisdom is contingent on the existence of a philosopher, and nothing in the system guarantees him.

In any case, this first part of the introduction, summarising the reasoning of Chapter VII, shows how the Sage and his absolute knowledge differ from the religious man and his absolute religion or theology: the Sage by opposition to the religious man. In the second part, indicating the subject of Chapter VIII, Hegel speaks of the Sage or of absolute knowledge considered in itself. Kojève translates (Hoffmeister pp. 549–550): this overcoming of the object of consciousness is not to be taken one-sidedly as the object's showing itself as returning into the self. More precisely, it is such that on the one hand the object as such presents itself to the self as vanishing, and on the other, and rather, it is the externalisation of self-consciousness that posits thinghood; and this externalisation has not only a negative but a positive significance, not only for us or in itself but for self-consciousness itself. The negative of the object, its self-overcoming, has a positive significance for self-consciousness: self-consciousness knows the nullity (*Nichtigkeit*) of the object, on the one hand by externalising itself, since in this externalisation it posits itself as object, or, by the inseparable unity of being-for-itself, posits the object as itself; on the other hand, it has equally overcome and taken back into itself this externalisation and objectivity, and so is at home with itself (*bei sich*) in its otherness. The passage (¶788) is the densest of the introduction. Kojève's translation of *Entäußerung* as "alienation-or-externalisation" keeps both senses.

To reach absolute knowledge one must "overcome" the opposition between its object and its subject, the man who possesses it: one must refer absolute, total and definitive knowledge to oneself. Hegel has just explained what this means. First, it is neither solipsism nor "idealism" nor any subjectivism: "the object does not return into the self". The Sage who refers the totality of his knowledge to himself does not claim to be the totality of being taken in his isolated particularity, his inner, purely subjective intimacy. It is not my I, neither the abstract I (*Ich*) nor the personal self (*Selbst*), not my thought, nor anything of the kind, that is the whole. The rejection of subjective idealism is emphatic: absolute knowledge is not the ego's absorption of the world.

For knowledge to be absolute, for subject and object to coincide, says Hegel, the object must have manifested itself to consciousness as vanishing. This sentence has first a theological meaning. In Christianity religion abolishes itself as religion; so Hegel interprets the Gospel narrative: Christian theology is the theology of God dead as God. Christianity is already an unconscious, even symbolic, atheism. Absolute knowledge only becomes conscious of this atheism or anthropotheism and expresses it rationally through the concept (*Begriff* = *Logos*). The object "vanishing" is the dead God: the theological reading of ¶788 links it to the "hard saying" of ¶752.

One cannot "abolish" religion in any of its forms; one can abolish it definitively only in its Christian form. When one abolishes a God "from outside", one can only replace him with another God; for God to disappear completely, he must abolish himself, and it is precisely the Christian God who abolishes himself as God to become man. The Sage's atheism cannot arise from just any theology; it arises from Christian theology and only from it. More exactly, it is not atheism but anthropotheism, and Hegelian anthropotheism presupposes Christian theology, since it applies to man the Christian idea of God. The thesis that only a self-abolishing God can be definitively abolished is a precise argument for the Christian origin of modern atheism: external critique produces new idols; only the incarnation empties heaven from within.

We know that religion only projects into the beyond the social reality in which it arises. So the Sage is possible only after the realisation of the historical world in which the Christian religion could form and perfect itself. The historical condition follows from the theological one.

But one need not pass through Hegel's anthropology to reach this result; it can be drawn directly from the text by referring the word "object" (*Gegenstand*) to the real universe, the natural and human or social world. In the social world, man's "external object" is another man. In Chapter IV Hegel showed that it is useless for a man to abolish another completely, to kill him, since the dead man is of no interest. A footnote adds that this non-dialectical abolition would be the equivalent of atheism, of bourgeois comedy, not of the anthropotheism of the Hegelian citizen. What can count is only the other's self-abolition, and the man who "abolishes" himself before another submits to him as a Slave to his Master. For there to be absolute knowledge, the object must "abolish" itself, and on the social plane this means there must be servitude and all that follows: the Master–Slave dialectic, the whole historical evolution of humanity as described in the *Phenomenology*. The Sage is possible only in the State that completes this evolution, where all citizens "abolish" themselves, so that none is any longer for another an external object (*Gegen-stand*), where there are no longer mutually exclusive particular interests. The social reading of the object's "vanishing" is Kojève's most ingenious interpretation of ¶788. The object that must abolish itself is the other man, who does so first as Slave and finally as citizen. The footnote distinguishes killing God (comic atheism) from God's self-abolition (anthropotheism), parallel to killing the adversary and enslaving him.

Likewise, referring the sentence to the natural world, one sees that wisdom is possible only in a world that lends itself to man's technical action, where the desert, wild beasts, bad weather, and so on bend to human will. The natural condition of wisdom is the technical mastery of nature.

In general, absolute knowledge, wisdom, presupposes the total success of man's negating action. It is possible only in a universal and homogeneous State, where no man is external to another and no social opposition remains unabolished; and within a nature tamed by man's labour, which, no longer opposing man, is no longer alien to him. If in absolute knowledge the Sage can rightfully affirm the identity of being as such with the being he himself is, it is because he experiences that conflicts within the State are definitively abolished and that there is no longer evident opposition between him and the world, social and natural. Before this experience (*Erfahrung*), the affirmation of the identity of subject and object can only be gratuitous. The word *Erfahrung* recalls the first title of the *Phenomenology*, "Science of the Experience of Consciousness": absolute knowledge is the last experience, of a reconciled world.

Even this is not enough. It is not enough to know that the world and the State lend themselves to real identification with us, to note, with Kant, the "transcendental chance" that lets us apply our abstract knowledge to real being and so dominate it. One must also recognise what Kant forgets and Hegel says: that "thinghood is posited by the externalisation of self-consciousness". There is not transcendental chance, not given identity, but active identification, conscious and voluntary, realised by man himself in his social struggles and labour. The phrase "transcendental chance" refers to Kant's acknowledgement, in the third Critique, of the contingent fit of nature to our understanding. Kojève's answer replaces the lucky fit with a made one: the world fits because man shaped it.

From the theological standpoint, the sentence means that saying a God does not exist is not enough to abolish him definitively. One must also, as Hume well said, understand why his existence was affirmed, the why and how of his creation by human thought. Wisdom can be realised only after religion has been destroyed by its anthropological interpretation, as in Chapter VII. One must understand that man creates his gods by projecting himself, as ideal, into the beyond. The reference is to Hume's *Natural History of Religion*. The principle, that an illusion is overcome only when its genesis is understood, is the method of Chapter VII.

In general, one must know that being in its totality is not reduced to given being; that it also includes a being created by self-conscious man, who externalises or alienates himself (*sich entäußert*) through action, realising outside himself the ideas he forges within. Only by knowing himself as successful negating action can man reach wisdom and affirm in absolute knowledge his identity with being as a whole. Only by understanding himself as he did in and through the *Phenomenology* can the philosopher become a Sage. The thesis that being includes created being is the ontological core of Kojève's reading: totality is nature plus history.

But to become a Sage, man must understand himself so. It is not enough to be creative action, a working citizen of the perfect State; one must know it, become self-conscious. Hegel expresses this by saying that the object's self-abolition and its positing by the subject must exist not only "in itself" or "for us" but for self-consciousness itself. The distinction between being and knowing oneself to be recurs: the citizen is the Sage in itself, the Sage is the citizen for himself.

To reach absolute knowledge it is not enough to be a "philosopher" in the usual sense, reasoning from something one is not; nor is it enough to be integral man. One must reason about the integral man one is. As Hegel says, man must "overcome" and take back into himself the externalisation or external object "realised" by the action of fight and labour. The two insufficiencies, the philosopher without reality and the citizen without self-knowledge, meet only in the Sage.

It is a matter not of the object's returning (*Zurückkehren*) into the subject but of the subject's taking back (*Zurücknehmen*) the object posited by the subject, says Hegel. The Sage's identification with the object of his knowledge is active in that it implies and presupposes the action of fight and labour by which man actually abolished the opposition between himself and the natural and social world, between subject and object. «La quiétude satisfaite de la Sagesse contemplative n'est possible QU'APRÈS l'effort victorieux du Travail et de la Lutte» (the satisfied quiet of contemplative wisdom is possible ONLY AFTER the victorious effort of labour and fight) (p. 302). But wisdom must ultimately result from this effort. Man creates an external world by action only to "take it back" into himself by comprehending contemplation. One transforms the natural world by labour to understand it, and makes oneself by fight a citizen of the perfect State to understand oneself. In short, the perfect State, and so the whole of history, are there only so that the philosopher can reach wisdom by writing a Book ("Bible") containing absolute knowledge. The distinction between *Zurückkehren* and *Zurücknehmen* is precise: the object does not come back of itself; it is retrieved by the one who made it. The final sentence is one of the most striking in the book: history exists for the sake of a book. It reverses the primacy of action that dominated the earlier courses and recalls Mallarmé's dictum that the world exists to end in a book. Kojève's quotation marks around "Bible" mark the book as the secular scripture of the end of history.

The State is certainly necessary, and not only, as was thought before Hegel, to maintain the Sage's body: it is necessary for the Sage as Sage, to engender wisdom. But the Sage and his wisdom are the final justification of the State and of history. The State must be homogeneous and universal for the sake of the homogeneity and universality of the knowledge that develops in it, and the Sage knows this. He knows that the "absolute" State is ultimately only a means to self-conscious satisfaction through true identification with the totality of being in absolute knowledge. The second part of the introduction thus gives an analysis of the real, existential conditions of absolute knowledge, a summary analysis of the Sage; but it can equally be read as an analysis of the formal structure of absolute knowledge itself. Since absolute knowledge will be treated again, Kojève passes to the third part. The subordination of the State to wisdom is explicit: the State is a means, the Sage the end. The inversion of Marx, for whom philosophy is realised in and abolished by the social order, is complete: here the social order is realised in and justified by philosophy.

In the first part Hegel spoke of the religious man and his theological knowledge in opposition to the Sage; in the second, of the Sage in relation to his wisdom; in the third, he will speak of the Sage in relation to the philosopher, of the becoming of wisdom from philosophical knowledge. This last part also indicates the subject of the first part of the chapter itself. Kojève translates (Hoffmeister p. 550): all this is the movement of consciousness, and consciousness in it is the totality of its moments. Consciousness must equally relate to the object according to the totality of its determinations and have grasped it according to each. This totality of determinations makes the object in itself a spiritual essence, and it becomes so in truth for consciousness through grasping (*Auffassen*) each determination as the self, through the spiritual relation to them just mentioned. The tripartite plan, religious man, Sage, philosopher, organises Kojève's reading of the introduction.

The passage concerns absolute knowledge, characterised above all by its "totality" (*Totalität*), a word that recurs three times in eight lines. To say knowledge is absolute, universally and definitively valid, is to say it is total, implying at least virtually all possible determinations of knowing and being, subject and object. Hegel will say later that this totality reveals itself by its circularity. The word count is a characteristic piece of Kojève's close reading.

In the first sentence Hegel says that the dialectical movement described in the preceding passage constitutes the totality of the moments of consciousness. The Sage is integral man, who integrates in his existence all man's existential possibilities. He can integrate them only after they have been realised one by one in history. As the integration of the process of man's historical advent, the Sage completes this process and can appear only at its end. Only because he integrates the totality of existential possibilities is his self-consciousness absolute knowledge. The microcosm thesis of the first 1937–38 lecture (p. 164) returns as the reading of the first sentence.

In the second sentence Hegel says that integrating in one's existence the totality of existential possibilities is not enough for actual wisdom, absolute knowledge. This integration, virtual wisdom, is found in every citizen of the absolute State. But only the citizen-philosopher can realise actual wisdom, since to actualise it one must become conscious of the totality one integrates. Since man is always man-in-the-world, to become conscious of the totality in oneself as subject is also to become conscious of the totality of the world, the object. Only by becoming conscious of this double totality does one recognise its absolute homogeneity, the fundamental identity of subject and object, of man-in-the-world and world-including-man. Absolute knowledge, being total, is as much self-knowledge as science of the world. Only in and through this identification, effected in absolute knowledge by the Sage, is the homogeneous totality of being Spirit, being real and conscious of its reality. The distinction between virtual wisdom in every citizen and actual wisdom in the citizen-philosopher restates the thesis that the Sage is contingent on a philosopher. The definition of Spirit as being conscious of its reality completes the equation of the second part.

Just as integral man was realised gradually in history, integral knowledge has a history too: the history of philosophy, of man's attempts to understand the world and himself in it. The stages of existential evolution and of philosophical evolution are two complementary aspects of one evolution, the double evolution Hegel described in the first seven chapters. The parallel between history and the history of philosophy is the 1933–34 thesis (p. 39) restated.

The Sage is on the one hand the man or citizen who becomes self-conscious, and on the other the philosopher who reaches his goal. To become self-conscious one must become conscious of one's becoming, the integral and integrated becoming of man Hegel described in the *Phenomenology*. The citizen is fully self-conscious only insofar as he has read, or written, the *Phenomenology*, as Kojève has read it so far, in its anthropological or "existential" aspect. But the philosopher becoming Sage must also integrate his becoming as philosopher by becoming conscious of it: he must become conscious of the becoming or history of philosophy. He too must read or write the *Phenomenology*, but under the aspect so far neglected, its "metaphysical" aspect, or, as Hegel says here, from the standpoint "of the relation of consciousness to the determinations of the object, to be understood as so many determinations of the I". In the text of the *Phenomenology* the two standpoints are united and cannot actually be dissociated; but in principle the philosophical attitude presupposes the existential one. That is why the *Phenomenology* should be read twice: once as Kojève has done so far, up to the end of Chapter VII, as the genetic phenomenology of active man; and a second time on its metaphysical plane, from the first chapter to the last, as the genetic phenomenology of the philosopher, or more exactly of the Sage. This is what Hegel indicates in saying that to reach absolute knowledge one must take up one by one the philosophical stages described in Chapters I–VII. He does so himself in the first part of Chapter VIII, a summary of the first seven chapters under their second, metaphysical aspect, hitherto neglected in Kojève's interpretation, to which the next lecture is devoted. The admission that his reading has so far neglected the metaphysical aspect is important. Kojève's anthropological reading, dominant for five years, is now presented as the first of two readings, with the metaphysical one to follow. The priority of the existential over the philosophical ("the philosophical attitude presupposes the existential") nonetheless keeps his anthropology as the ground.

### Fourth Lecture: Interpretation of the First Part of Chapter VIII (Hoffmeister pp. 550, l. 11 – 559, l. 9)

The text of the last chapter can be divided into three parts. The first, about six pages, treats the philosopher; the second, five pages, the Sage; the third, three pages, wisdom or, as Hegel says, "Science" (*Wissenschaft*). In the first, the road leading to wisdom; in the second, the real, existential support of wisdom, the man who develops Science; in the third, this knowledge itself, independently of the road and of its real conditions. One can also say that the first part treats the Sage and his wisdom as the global and definitive result of humanity's temporal evolution; the second treats this result apart from its origin, isolating the last moment of time, the Sage's existence, from the whole temporal extent; and the third relates this last moment of time to eternity, the Sage who completes history to wisdom or absolute knowledge, which, being eternal, is eternity. In Hegel's own terms: the first part treats consciousness (*Bewusstsein*), the second absolute knowledge (*das absolute Wissen*), the third Science (*Wissenschaft*): the philosopher, the Sage who realises wisdom, and wisdom itself. The tripartite division is Kojève's. Its mapping onto time, the last moment of time, and eternity announces the theme of the following lectures: the relation of concept and time.

According to Chapter VIII, the whole of the first seven chapters, the *Phenomenology* proper, is an analysis of consciousness, consciousness of the external, as Hegel also says in the Preface and elsewhere. The term must be taken in the widest sense. In calling the first three chapters "consciousness" in the narrow sense, as opposed to the fourth, "self-consciousness", and the fifth, "Reason", Hegel means only that throughout the book there is consciousness of the external, a distinction between object and subject, between man and the world he lives in. Self-consciousness here is self-consciousness within consciousness in the wide sense: man becomes conscious of himself knowing, or believing he knows, that he lives in a world external to him. The same holds for Reason, Spirit, and Religion. The claim that all seven chapters are "consciousness" in the wide sense follows Hegel's title "shapes of consciousness" (*Gestaltungen des Bewusstseins*).

The generic term for all the phenomena of the *Phenomenology* is therefore consciousness. Where there is consciousness of the external, there is the external itself: where there is *Bewusstsein*, there is *Gegen-stand*, the object opposed to the consciousness relating to it. There are necessarily two parallel planes, that of consciousness and that of the object. Being in its real totality has two aspects, different but complementary, opposed but related: one that reveals the totality, and one revealed by the first. In its first aspect the totality of being is man-in-the-world, man taken in his spatio-temporal totality, humanity in the whole of its history; in its second, it is the world-where-man-lives, nature. If the totality of being exists as evolution or "movement", there are necessarily two parallel evolutions, of man and of the world, of consciousness and of the object. A footnote adds: taken in isolation, abstractly, independently of man, nature is space, not time; it does not evolve. But the real world implies man, and man is time, movement, evolution; so the world that implies man evolves too. Man peoples it with houses, automobiles, and so on, which are as "natural" as the stars and yet change and essentially modify the world's aspect. The footnote states Kojève's dualism in its most compact form: nature is space, man is time. The example of houses and automobiles makes the point concrete: the world evolves only through human works.

But, as Hegel will repeat in the short introduction to the summary in Chapter VIII, the *Phenomenology* treats neither the totality of being as totality nor its natural aspect. It treats man and man only: consciousness, not the object of consciousness. A footnote explains that this is precisely why the *Phenomenology* differs from the "Philosophy of Spirit" of the *Encyclopaedia*: it is a phenomenology, not the Science. In the Science, man is studied as part of the totality of being, as an integral part of nature, in his conscious reality, his real history. In the *Phenomenology* one speaks of man abstracting from the world, of abstract, even unreal, man; of consciousness without the object to which it relates, so of the abstract notion of consciousness, its ideal possibilities: ideal existential, social, and political types, not their concrete realisation in history; and ideal types of relation to the object, philosophical, religious, or aesthetic possibilities, not their realisations in the history of philosophy, religion, and art. The footnote significantly qualifies Kojève's historical reading: the *Phenomenology* describes ideal types, not historical realisations. The concrete history belongs to the *Encyclopaedia*. The qualification fits the "ideating abstraction" of 1933–34 (p. 39).

Unquestionably the *Phenomenology* treats consciousness and not its object. Yet it has two superposed or parallel planes. If there is evolution in it, it can only be that of consciousness, but this evolution is itself necessarily double, since consciousness has two aspects, different but complementary. Human consciousness reveals not only the unconscious, natural aspect of being but the totality of being, and so also itself, since it is part of that totality. It is both consciousness of the external and self-consciousness. A footnote adds that this too must be taken broadly: all the phenomena of the *Phenomenology*, not only those of Chapter IV, are at once consciousness and self-consciousness, and all self-consciousness in it is self-consciousness within consciousness: man becomes self-conscious as opposed to the world he lives in. The doubling of consciousness into consciousness of the world and of itself grounds the two readings.

The *Phenomenology* is written so that every, or almost every, sentence refers to both aspects at once. One can read the first seven chapters from end to end as a description of self-consciousness, of the ways man understands himself: the anthropological interpretation, which is that of Kojève's course. One can also read them as a description of consciousness of the external, of the ways man becomes conscious of the world and of being in general: the metaphysical interpretation, which Kojève has not discussed and which Hegel summarises in Chapter VIII. The explicit statement that the anthropological reading is one of two is important for assessing the whole book: Kojève knowingly chose one plane.

What does this mean for the idea of the Sage and of Science? First the anthropological plane. "The true being of man is his action." Man creates himself by the negating action of the given and, after each creative stage, becomes conscious of what he has created, of what he is after becoming it. Knowledge of man can therefore be absolute, definitive, only when negating action definitively ceases, when man is fully "reconciled" with the given and "satisfied" in and by it. Hegel claims that when he wrote the *Phenomenology* this action had already ceased, and that the phenomena studied exhaust all possible negating-creative actions. He also shows that each creative negation negates a given resulting from all previous creative negations. The man who lives at the end of history thus realises human existence in its absolute fullness: his being implies all human possibilities. He is the citizen of the absolute State, practically Napoleon. But being this citizen is not enough to be a Sage. The Sage is the citizen fully conscious of what he is. If the citizen integrates in his active existence the totality of existential possibilities, the Sage integrates in his absolute knowledge the totality of the becomings-conscious of these possibilities, the partial becomings-conscious of partial realisations described in the *Phenomenology*. One becomes a Sage by writing, or reading, a *Phenomenology* containing the complete list of partial becomings-conscious. At the end of Chapter VII man is fully self-conscious in the strong sense: he knows all that he is, and he actually is all that man can be. The anthropological route to wisdom is stated in its clearest form: the Sage integrates in knowledge what the citizen integrates in existence.

Yet to be a Sage it is not enough to have written or read the *Phenomenology* in its anthropological aspect. The Sage's Science is true: it reveals reality. What is real is man-in-the-world; man without the world is as nonexistent an abstraction as the world without man. One could have existed without the other, but the Sage need not concern himself with what could or should have been; he must understand what is. What is is nature peopled by human beings, men living in a nature that gives them birth and kills them. The Sage's knowledge, revealing being in its concrete reality, reveals neither man alone nor the world alone; Science reveals man and the world. One can as well say the world reveals itself through the Sage as that the Sage reveals himself through the revelation of the world. More correctly, the totality of real being reveals itself to itself and by itself as the absolute "System of Science". In the language of the *Phenomenology*: in Science, consciousness, knowledge of the world, coincides with self-consciousness, self-knowledge. To become fully conscious of the real world is also to become fully conscious of oneself, since the I is implied in the world, a "worldly" reality acting on it and undergoing the counterblow; conversely, to become conscious of oneself as real is to become conscious of the world in which the I is realised. The remark "one could have existed without the other" concedes that nature without man is possible, which is Kojève's dualism: man depends on nature, not nature on man. The phrase "a nature that gives them birth and kills them" grounds finitude in nature.

But this coincidence of self-consciousness and consciousness is possible only when both are total. From the whole's being necessarily identical with itself it does not follow that one part is identical with another. Every self-consciousness has a consciousness of the external as its necessary complement; but as long as self-consciousness is not total, the corresponding consciousness is necessarily a perspective: it reveals one aspect of real being, not being in its reality, the totality of its aspects. One can see that a perspective is only one among others only by surpassing it, placing oneself in another. Whoever is placed in his own perspective, "solidary" with it, necessarily sees in it not a perspective but a total vision of reality. He believes he possesses "Science", which is to say he possesses an "ideology". To have an ideology is precisely to affirm that the natural and social world is as it appears from a particular point of view, this point of view not being the integrity of all possible points of view. A footnote remarks that Hegel's idea of absolute knowledge is represented in modern mathematical physics by the universal "tensor", which represents the real not in a single privileged coordinate system but in all at once. The definition of ideology as a perspective mistaken for the whole is Kojève's clearest. It generalises the 1936–37 theory of ideology (p. 117). The footnote on the tensor, from relativity theory, is a striking analogy: absolute knowledge is invariant under change of perspective because it contains all perspectives.

Every partial theory with which man is solidary is necessarily an "ideology", having for him the value of a total, "objective" theory. My perspective, individual or collective, necessarily engenders an ideology as long as my theory of the world is not the theory of the world, not implying all possible theories. The inclusion of collective perspectives extends the concept to class and national ideologies.

The suppression of the opposition between consciousness and self-consciousness is thus possible only after the total integration of each. Each stage of self-consciousness has a stage of consciousness as its complement. The integration must be double, so the *Phenomenology* must be written, or read, in both aspects. Only when one has integrated all man's partial self-revelations and in parallel all his partial revelations of the world does self-consciousness coincide with consciousness and knowledge become total and absolute. Before this, consciousness is always opposed to self-consciousness; the philosopher, developing his partial or relative knowledge, always speaks sooner or later of an object, a being other than himself. A footnote notes a difficulty within the *Phenomenology* itself: on the last, obscure page of Chapter VI Hegel still opposes Napoleon, representing consciousness, to himself, representing self-consciousness, and seems still to have expected a kind of "official" recognition of his philosophy by Napoleon; yet the last line speaks of the "revealed God", this God being man, so there would no longer be an object. This is not very clear but unimportant for now. The footnote returns to the dyad problem of 1936–37 (p. 153). Kojève leaves it unresolved.

What characterises the situation before Science is thus the separation of consciousness and self-consciousness, and when one possesses Science one sees that this separation is the infallible sign of the relativity of knowledge, of its incomplete, open, provisional, in short philosophical, character. The philosopher, like the Sage, believes his knowledge total; but the fact that he still distinguishes man and world, self-consciousness and consciousness, proves that his knowledge is only one possible perspective, relating partially revealed man to a partial revelation of the world. Such partial knowledge can and must be surpassed. A footnote identifies this separation with "philosophy of reflection" (*Reflexionsphilosophie*). Every philosophy properly speaking is a philosophy of reflection; Hegel's is not, and so is no longer a philosophy but Science. The philosopher of reflection reflects *on* being, placing himself, or believing he places himself, outside it; he never manages to explain himself, since he excludes himself from his reflection; he reflects on the being he wants to reveal instead of being the being he reveals by his very existence. Philosophy of reflection is always abstract: one eliminates from being the one who describes it, and so describes only an abstraction, since real being implies its describer. On the existential plane the philosopher of reflection is always more or less a Stoic, more or less the intellectual of the last paragraph of Chapter V, "above the fray". The critique of *Reflexionsphilosophie* is Hegel's, from the Jena essays against Kant, Jacobi, and Fichte. Kojève's addition is the existential diagnosis: the reflective philosopher is the Stoic intellectual, who excludes himself from what he describes.

Philosophy is therefore surmounted and Science attained when self-consciousness coincides with consciousness. This coincidence is effected by integrating all the partial revelations of the moments of both aspects of consciousness described in the *Phenomenology*, in the consciousness of the author and reader of the first seven chapters, written and read on both planes. To pass from philosophy to Science in Chapter VIII, Hegel need only summarise the preceding chapters, which he does in the first part, but the summary bears on the metaphysical plane. This justifies Kojève's method of interpretation. At this point one should reread the seven chapters, read so far in their anthropological aspect, in their metaphysical aspect, and continue with Chapter VIII after this recapitulation. The claim that the metaphysical summary "justifies" the anthropological reading is subtle: since Hegel himself separates the metaphysical recapitulation, the anthropological reading can stand as the first of the two.

Kojève will therefore not read the summary contained in the first part. But the part has a short introduction and conclusion in which Hegel speaks about the summary rather than summarising, and these Kojève will translate and interpret. The decision to skip the summary of ¶789–796 is methodologically consistent but leaves the metaphysical reading unexecuted, which the next lectures partly supply through the theory of time.

Kojève translates the first two sentences of the introduction (Hoffmeister p. 550): on the one hand the object is immediate being (*Sein*), a thing as such, corresponding to immediate consciousness, sensation. On the other it is a becoming-other than itself, its relation (*Verhältnis*) or being-for-another, and being-for-itself, determinateness (*Bestimmtheit*), corresponding to perception. Finally it is essence or universal, corresponding to the Understanding. As a whole the object is the syllogism, the movement of the universal through determination to particularity, and the inverse movement from particularity to the universal through particularity as overcome, determination. The passage (¶789) sets out the three aspects of the object that correspond to the three forms of consciousness.

Hegel speaks here of the object of consciousness, not of consciousness reflecting on itself; of the world, not of man. It is "metaphysics", not "anthropology". The distinction confirms the plane.

Consciousness reveals the object. Consciousness has three aspects: immediate or sensible consciousness, sensation; perception; and the Understanding. The object must therefore also have three aspects. The inference from the aspects of consciousness to the aspects of being follows from the principle that real revelation reveals real features.

The most elementary form of consciousness is sensation, always particular: an isolated here and now, without relation to what it is not or to itself; there is no true relation between what senses and what is sensed. Sensation is "something" but not a "thing"; it is a "thing as such" (*Ding überhaupt*), which is what it is without opposing or depending on anything else. Since sensation reveals the object, being, there must be an aspect of being corresponding to it. Indeed, to be is always to be here and now; to be is always to be "something"; to be is always to be what one was before becoming something else, independently of there being something else, without relation to what one is and is not; to be is always already to be, before one's determination to being and before the determination of being by its internal and external relations. The anaphora "être, c'est toujours..." sets out the particular aspect of being: its bare thereness. Kojève reads Hegel's categories as ontological, not merely epistemic.

But sensation is only a moment of consciousness, artificially isolated, since in fact it is always integrated in a perception. Perception is something determinate, essentially relation: between perceiver and perceived, between the thing and its qualities, and among the qualities. Since perception is, inserting itself in being by revealing it, being itself has an aspect corresponding to perception. To be is also always to be something determinate, this or that thing; to exist for oneself by opposing everything one is not, excluding it, and thereby to exist for and through the other, in the relation of the same one is to the other one is not; to be is to be determined by this relation, to be the relation; so to relate to oneself, to distinguish what one is from what one is, and at the same time to be all that one is; to be other while being oneself, to become other than one is. To be is not only to be "something" but a "thing" that is always determinate and specific, not only isolated or one within oneself, but specified: like certain other things and other than the others. The second anaphora gives the specific aspect: being as relation and determination. The phrase "to become other than one is" already introduces becoming into being through relation.

But real consciousness is never only sensation and perception; it is always also Understanding. When I perceive this table, I do not perceive that it is a table; my perception does not reveal that it is a realisation of "the table". Yet the real table is not only a "thing" with a perceptible form but a "table", a determinate thing corresponding to the word "table". There are not only sensations and perceptions on earth; there are also meaningful words, concepts. The word or concept, leaving the specific content of the perceptible thing intact, separates it from the here and now of sensation of this thing's being. THIS table is here and now; this TABLE can be later and elsewhere; THE table is always and nowhere. Yet the word "table" corresponding to the table is perceived and sensed here and now: while being a "concept", it is a "thing" and "something", just like the table to which it corresponds. The word-concept is as things are; it too is part of being. So real being is also, in one of its aspects, concept. To be is therefore also to be universal: to be more and other than one is here and now, more and other than one is in one's specific determination. The table example is the first statement of Kojève's theory of the concept, which the next lectures develop: the concept detaches the essence of a thing from its here and now. The typography, THIS table, this TABLE, THE table, shows the three aspects at a glance. The claim that the word is itself a thing, part of being, prepares the thesis that the concept is real only as spoken discourse in time.

All real consciousness is a whole formed by the sensation of the PARTICULAR, the perception of the SPECIFIC, and the understanding of the UNIVERSAL; and this whole is a dialectical movement that integrates particular sensations by specifying them in perceptions that the Understanding universalises, or, inversely, makes the universal Understanding, specified by perception, penetrate into sensible particularity. Since real consciousness reveals real being, real being is itself this whole formed by this trinitarian dialectical movement. Being is really such as it forms itself in and through the negating or creative action of human labour; and this labour starts from a UNIVERSAL concept, which it SPECIFIES by its perceptible material realisation, and so inserts into the PARTICULAR here and now of sensation.
