Conversely, being is really such as it reveals itself through consciousness, which starts from the PARTICULAR of sensation to reach the UNIVERSAL of the Understanding by passing through the SPECIFIC of perception. The symmetry is elegant: labour goes from universal to particular (realising a concept in a thing), knowledge from particular to universal (grasping a thing through a concept). The two movements together form the syllogism of ¶789. Labour thus appears as the inverse of cognition, the concept made thing.

Consciousness reveals these three aspects of being, and "philosophy of reflection" reveals the three aspects of consciousness itself. For Hegel the task is now to abolish the opposition between consciousness and its object: consciousness must understand that it is itself the same being as its object. For this it suffices to discover the integral unity of the three aspects of the object and see that it coincides with the integral unity of the three aspects of consciousness. Consciousness must know that it is its object in each aspect and so in their totality. Hegel says this (Hoffmeister p. 550): it is according to these three determinations that consciousness must know the object as itself. The coincidence is structural: the same trinitarian form in knower and known.

But, as said, the *Phenomenology* does not describe being in its complete totality; that will be the theme of Science itself, in the *Encyclopaedia*. The first seven chapters show the opposition of consciousness and object and describe only consciousness; their metaphysical aspect describes consciousness as revealing the object, not the object itself as revealed. It is only a matter of understanding how the identification of consciousness and object that characterises Science could arise, which means reviewing all the stages of the revelation of the object by a consciousness that still feels opposed to it. And insofar as it believes itself opposed to the object, it really is opposed to it as consciousness: as real subject, as man. To understand the advent of Science one must also review the stages or possibilities of human existence. But in the summary they are reviewed only in their metaphysical aspect: not the existential attitudes as existential, but only the cognitive element implied in each: not the aspects of being revealed, but the cognitive attitudes themselves as revelations of the aspects of being. The distinction between reviewing attitudes and reviewing what they reveal is fine but important: the summary is a history of forms of knowing, not of the known.

Hegel says this now (Hoffmeister p. 550). Kojève translates: it is not knowledge as pure conceptual comprehension of the object that is at issue in the *Phenomenology*; this knowledge is to be shown in its becoming, in its moments, only in the aspect belonging to consciousness as such, and the moments of the concept proper, pure knowledge, in the form of shapes of consciousness. The sentence (¶789) restricts the *Phenomenology* to the becoming of knowledge.

Each recalled stage is thus a particular form of the opposition between consciousness and object. In them the object is not total revealed being, Spirit or *Logos*, since only part of the totality is revealed in each stage, and the revealed part does not coincide with the revealing part. Only the Sage, integrating all possible cognitive attitudes, only this total integration, abolishes in Science the "philosophical" opposition of knowing subject and known object. The argument locates the opposition in partiality: each stage reveals a part, and a part revealed by another part cannot coincide with it.

Hegel says this in the next sentence (Hoffmeister p. 550). Kojève translates: consequently, in consciousness as such, as studied in the first seven chapters, the object does not yet appear as the spiritual essence just expressed by us in Chapter VIII, speaking from the standpoint of absolute knowledge. The attitude (*Verhalten*) of consciousness toward the object is neither its consideration in this totality, which makes it spiritual, nor in its pure conceptual form, but on the one hand a shape of consciousness, on the other a number (*Anzahl*) of such shapes, which we gather together in the *Phenomenology* and in which the totality of the moments of the object and of the attitude of consciousness can be shown only as dissolved into its moments. Kojève's brackets repeatedly identify "we" with the standpoint of absolute knowledge.

To pass from philosophy to wisdom one must therefore integrate all possible philosophies. One can do so only by having really integrated all existential possibilities and having become conscious of this integration. But to do it effectively one must also integrate philosophies as philosophies: the cognitive elements implied in all existential attitudes, all aspects of conscious existence as turned toward the object and not reflected upon itself. All these necessary stages of the progressive revelation of the object have already been described in the first seven chapters. To integrate them, which allows the passage from philosophy to wisdom, it suffices to review them once more, observing that they complete one another without contradiction and so form a whole closed on itself, from which nothing can be removed and to which nothing can be added. The criterion "nothing can be removed or added" is the circularity criterion restated as completeness.

Hegel says this in the sentence ending the introduction (Hoffmeister p. 550). Kojève translates: consequently, for this aspect of the grasping (*Erfassen*) of the object as it exists in the shape of consciousness, it suffices to recall the earlier shapes already met with in the first seven chapters. The sentence justifies the summary's brevity.

Then comes the text of the first part, which Kojève does not comment on. He says only this. When Hegel spoke of sensation, perception, and Understanding, he did not have in view only the phenomena of the first three chapters. These three forms of consciousness recur, sublimated, in all existential attitudes, or more exactly in all their cognitive aspects. Every existential attitude is conscious, and since all consciousness is sensation, perception, and Understanding, every existential attitude is a specific form of the revelation of being by these three; and since these revelations are real, being itself is actually as it appears in them. So Hegel summarises not only the three chapters titled sense-certainty, perception, and Understanding, but the whole of the seven phenomenological chapters. The claim that the triad recurs, sublimated, in every attitude matches the structure of Hegel's summary (¶789–796), which runs through observing Reason, the beautiful soul, and so on under the three headings.

Moreover, each existential stage is already an integration of the previous ones, and so of their cognitive aspects. The last stage will therefore be an integration of all stages in general, and totality is not yet reached only because the integration this last stage represents is still opposed to the elements it integrates. In the last stage all aspects of being are already revealed, and revealed in their unity; being is revealed in its totality; the content of the knowledge reached is total, absolute, absolutely true. But by excluding itself from its own content, the knowledge of this stage still opposes itself to it. Being is now a revealed totality, but one still detached from its revelation; REVEALED being is total but still opposed to the being that REVEALS it. This being, total and yet opposed to something, is the transcendent God of Christian theology. This theology is by definition the last stage of "reflection" on Spirit. To pass from there to Science, which is revealed being or Spirit, it suffices to abolish this element of transcendence. One must identify oneself with the Christian God; one must know and be able to say that the total being Christian theology speaks of is in reality the very man who speaks of it. The formula "total and yet opposed" is a precise definition of the transcendent God: a totality minus its knower. The step to Science is to add the knower to the totality, which abolishes transcendence.

Hegel says this in the short conclusion of his summary. In the summary he showed again how and why man, becoming a Sage, manages to abolish the *Theos* of theo-logy and so pass to "Logic" simply, to his own discursive thought (*Logos*) understood as "the thought of God before the creation of the world". He showed how man finally manages to be and to know himself to be God: the creating and revealing God of Christian theology, the absolute trinitarian God who contains in himself the totality of being and its revelation. The quotation "God's thought before the creation of the world" is Hegel's description of the Logic in the introduction to the *Science of Logic*. Kojève reads it anthropotheistically: the Logic is man's thought, and "before creation" means independently of the particular world.

In the conclusion Hegel first says (Hoffmeister pp. 555–556), in Kojève's translation: what in religion was content, the form of representation of an other, is here the self's own activity (*Tun*). The concept binds things so that the content is the self's own activity; for this concept is the knowledge that the self's activity within itself is the whole of essentiality and of empirical existence; the knowledge of this subject as substance and of substance as this knowledge of the subject's activity. Hegel's formula, subject as substance and substance as subject, echoes the Preface's programme (¶17), which Kojève reads here as the identity of man and being.

At first sight this is extremely simple. One need only read a manual of Christian theology, Kojève stresses Christian, in which God is indeed a total and infinite being, and say after reading it: the being in question is myself. Simple indeed. Yet even today this seems an absurdity, an unparalleled "enormity", and we call mad whoever affirms it openly. It is extremely hard to affirm seriously, and millennia of philosophical thought passed before a Hegel dared to say it. First, it was not easy to reach the concept of the Christian God; then, having reached it, it was not easy to identify with it and apply it to oneself. Hegel tells us that this is possible only for the citizen of the universal and homogeneous State. Only this citizen, the man who has actually realised the trinitarian totality of existence by the circularity of the movement that starts from the particular and returns to it after rising to the universal through the specific, can affirm it without being mad, as a Sage, revealing a reality, stating an absolute truth. The criterion of madness is decisive: the same sentence, "I am God", is madness in any other world and wisdom in the final State. Kojève's circle of existence, particular, specific, universal, particular, maps the syllogism onto the citizen's life.

To do so it is not enough to believe in oneself as one believes in God. Just as religion is religion, and not a strictly "private" "emotional state", only insofar as it is a theo-logy, wisdom is wisdom, and not "megalomania", only insofar as it is a Logic. One can reach this Logic only after writing the *Phenomenology*, after integrating, by understanding them, all possible attitudes of self-consciousness and consciousness. «Mais cette simple intégration de ce qui a déjà été suffit pour réaliser ce qui n'a encore jamais existé, à savoir la Sagesse» (but this simple integration of what has already been suffices to realise what has never yet existed, namely wisdom) (p. 319). The parallel between religion and theology on the one hand, wisdom and Logic on the other, gives a criterion distinguishing wisdom from megalomania: articulated discourse. The last sentence is paradoxical and precise: wisdom is new, but it adds nothing except the gathering of the old.

Hegel says this in the sentence ending the conclusion (Hoffmeister p. 556). Kojève translates: what we have added here, in the preceding summary, is only, on the one hand, the gathering of the particular and isolated moments, each of which represents in principle the life of the whole Spirit; on the other, the holding fast (*Festhalten*) of the concept in the form of the concept, the concept whose content would result from the moments mentioned, and would already result, independently of this summary, but only in the form of a shape of consciousness. Hegel's "holding fast of the concept in the form of the concept" names what absolute knowledge adds: not content, but form.

The "shape of consciousness" resulting from this integration is wisdom or, as Hegel says, "absolute knowledge": if one likes, the Sage taken as the empty "vessel" of wisdom. The summary makes him fit to be filled; the Science developed in the *Encyclopaedia* will fill him. The image of the Sage as an empty vessel is striking: the *Phenomenology* produces the wise man, the *Encyclopaedia* his wisdom. It repeats the distinction between the *Phenomenology* as philosophy and the *Encyclopaedia* as Science (p. 287).

The summary in the first part of Chapter VIII has shown how the Sage arises from the philosophical evolution of humanity; it shows the Sage in his relations with philosophy or philosophers. In the second part Hegel will describe the Sage himself, the man who, while identifying himself with the totality of being, nonetheless has a particular, isolated reality, since the Sage too is "Mr So-and-so"; but in his wisdom taken as Science he is as universal and infinite as the being his Science reveals. In the third and last part Hegel will speak of this Science, which he was preparing to set out in the second part of his "System of THE Science", a part never written and replaced by the "Encyclopaedia OF THE Philosophical Sciences". The capitals mark a shift noted with irony: from "the Science" in the singular to "the philosophical sciences" in the plural, from a system to an encyclopaedia. The remark that the Sage is "Mr So-and-so" states the problem of the next lecture: how a particular man can be the bearer of universal knowledge.

### Fifth Lecture: Interpretation of the Second Part of Chapter VIII (Hoffmeister pp. 556, l. 10 – 561, l. 27)

In the first part Hegel summarised the "metaphysical" content of the first seven chapters. This summary, or rather integration, abolishes the opposition of subject and object found in each of the integrated elements. Knowledge is no longer reflection on being, so no longer philosophy; it is absolute: being itself reveals itself in and as this knowledge, and this self-revelation of being is Science (*Wissenschaft*). But this total Science, revealing being as such, appears within being as a particular reality. This objective reality (*Wirklichkeit*), this empirical existence (*Dasein*) of Science, is the Sage, whom Hegel calls "absolute knowledge". "Das absolute Wissen" is the man possessing absolute knowledge, as "self-consciousness" is the self-conscious man and "conscience" (*das Gewissen*) the man endowed with moral conscience. The lexical rule is one of Kojève's most useful: Hegel's abstract nouns name human types. "Absolute knowledge" names the Sage, not a disembodied content.

One must therefore distinguish the Sage in flesh and blood from wisdom, the real, living "vessel" of Science from Science itself. Hegel made this distinction in the conclusion of the first part, between knowledge as concept (*Begriff*), Science, and knowledge as "shape of consciousness" (*Gestalt des Bewusstseins*), real man, the Sage; and he said the Sage is constituted before Science. This means the following. Each existential attitude described in the *Phenomenology* is a real integration of all earlier attitudes, so the last is a complete integration of all possible attitudes; and each attitude is conscious, so that self-consciousness widens with each; the last attitude realises the fullness of self-consciousness. This real existence fully conscious of itself, this self-consciousness fully realised in empirical existence, is the Sage, absolute knowledge as a shape of consciousness. So the Sage appears at the end of the first seven chapters as their result. But as such he is still opposed to the world, still a shape of consciousness of the external. To abolish this opposition he must integrate not only the totality of existential attitudes, conscious of themselves, but the totality of cognitive attitudes, conscious of thinghood, of the object; he does so by rethinking the *Phenomenology* in its metaphysical aspect, writing the summary in the first part of Chapter VIII. Before the summary there is the Sage as shape of consciousness, as man-in-the-world; after it, wisdom, Science as concept, which "comprehends" the totality of being. Or: before the summary, before the *Phenomenology* itself, there is the man capable of writing the *Phenomenology*, Hegel as its author; after it, the man capable of writing the *Logic*, or rather writing it, or better still the *Logic* itself, Science. The summary ends by distinguishing these two aspects of realised wisdom, the Sage and Science. It showed how and why the Sage completes humanity's real historical evolution and Science its ideal, philosophical or metaphysical evolution. The sequence, author of the *Phenomenology*, author of the *Logic*, the *Logic* itself, marks three degrees of the Sage's identification with his work. The Sage precedes Science as the producer precedes the product.

The first part of Chapter VIII thus treats the historical and metaphysical genesis of the Sage and of Science; the second part treats the Sage himself; the third, Science as it was to be set out in the second part of the System, which Hegel did not write. The second part has three sections. In the first Hegel develops the concept of the Sage, what the Sage is as generator of Science. In the second he speaks of the Sage's reality: first in objective reality (*Wirklichkeit*), real space or the world; then in time (*Zeit*); finally in objectively real time, temporal objective reality, history. In the third he speaks of the Sage's activity, the actualisation of his real being described in the second section and so the realisation of his concept described in the first. This activity is precisely the production of Science, the subject of the third part of Chapter VIII, set out in the *Logic*. Kojève will interpret the first section and the first step of the second. The plan divides ¶797–808 in Kojève's way. The progression space, time, history anticipates the next lecture's "Note on Eternity, Time, and the Concept".

Kojève translates the first sentence (Hoffmeister p. 556): this last shape of Spirit, Spirit that gives its complete and true content at the same time the form of the self, and thereby realises its concept while remaining within its concept in this realisation, is absolute knowledge. It is Spirit that knows itself in the shape of Spirit, or conceptually comprehending knowledge (*begreifendes Wissen*). The definition (¶798) is the one Kojève will read as describing the Sage.

"Absolute knowledge" is not wisdom but the Sage: the man in flesh and blood who realises wisdom or Science by his action. Hegel calls it a "shape of Spirit", a concrete form like those studied in the preceding chapters. A line earlier, at the end of the first part, he said "shape of consciousness"; so it is still a realisation of consciousness of the external, a real man living in the world, for whom there is still an external world, an objective reality different from his subjective reality, the self. But this shape is the last, says Hegel: it cannot be surpassed by a shape of consciousness. The result of the Sage's activity, the reality he produces that surpasses his given reality, is Science; and Science is no longer subjective or objective, no longer a particular subjective reality opposed to a universal objective being; it is this being as revealed in its real totality. Being-revealed-to-itself-in-the-totality-of-its-reality, self-conscious objective reality or objectively real self-consciousness, is Spirit. So, while being as real man a shape of consciousness, the Sage is, as participant in Science, a shape of Spirit, and to be a shape of Spirit is to be Spirit itself, since Science reveals the totality of being, and total revealed being is Spirit itself, not merely a shape of it. Hence Hegel can define absolute knowledge, the Sage generating Science, as "Spirit that gives its complete and true content the form of the self". The oscillation between "shape of consciousness" and "shape of Spirit" is resolved by the double nature of the Sage: man in the world and participant in Science. The argument that the last shape cannot be surpassed because its product is Science, which is no longer a shape, is precise.

Insofar as the Sage is distinguished from Science, he is a human individual, a self. So Science is also his Science, in a double sense: a knowledge belonging to him, his work or the result of his action; and a knowledge that reveals him to himself, whose content he is, a self-consciousness. The double possessive, "his" as author and as subject matter, states the Sage's relation to Science.

But, says Hegel, this content of knowledge is the complete and true content of Spirit. The Sage realises in his concrete reality the integrity of self-conscious human existence; his content, being total, is *the* content. And it is "true", revealed in its reality and realised in its revelation. The Sage thinks everything thinkable, and when the Sage lives, everything thinkable is already actually realised; the totality of his knowledge is thus proved true by the totality of realisation. His knowledge is therefore *the* knowledge, and the content of this knowledge that he himself is, is content in general, the content of Spirit. As Hegel says, the Sage is "Spirit that realises its concept and remains within its concept in this realisation". In and through the Sage, Spirit realises its concept, which "comprehends" everything, in the double sense of containing and knowing; and in realising its concept through the Sage, Spirit remains within its concept, since if the Sage's being, like every man's, is his action, the action is now that of producing Science, the concept that comprehends everything, the concept of the being that is Spirit. Insofar as the Sage coincides with his Science, he coincides with *the* Science, and being the Science, he is Spirit. Hegel can therefore say the Sage is "Spirit that knows itself in the shape of Spirit". The Sage is a self, a shape; but he knows that the content of this self is the revealed or comprehended totality of being, so that this content, his, is the content of Spirit; he knows that the shape he is is the shape of Spirit. Since he is and knows it, one can say that Spirit knows itself as shape in and through the Sage. The Sage is nothing but "conceptually comprehending knowledge": the knowledge that comprehends everything because it contains everything, and contains everything because it comprehends everything. The play on *comprendre*, to contain and to understand, is Hegel's *begreifen* and Kojève's key: the Sage contains everything because history is complete and he integrates it, and knows everything because he contains it. The claim that everything thinkable is already realised when the Sage lives is the end-of-history thesis applied to knowledge.

In the next sentence Hegel specifies the definition (Hoffmeister p. 556). Kojève translates: truth is not only in itself perfectly identical with certainty; it also has the shape of self-certainty, the form of knowledge of itself in its very empirical existence, for knowing Spirit. The sentence (¶798) adds that the identity is known.

In the Sage, truth (*Wahrheit*), the comprehending revelation of objective reality, coincides with certainty (*Gewissheit*), the subjective certainty or knowledge the Sage has of himself. On the one hand, the Sage actually realises, by his concrete and active existence, the idea he has of himself, the "ideal" he is supposed to realise; on the other, his self-consciousness is total, a consciousness of the totality of being. And the Sage knows it. In him truth has the shape of self-certainty: he knows he is the real totality he reveals by his knowledge. As Hegel says, truth has an empirical existence (*Dasein*), since it is the real Sage, a man of flesh and blood, who realises absolute knowledge, and this absolute knowledge exists for this real Sage as self-knowledge. The coincidence of truth and certainty closes the gap opened in Chapter I, where certainty was subjective and truth objective.

We already know that it is only because it is self-knowledge that the Sage's absolute knowledge differs from the Christian religious man's. Hegel recalls this in the next two sentences (Hoffmeister p. 556), in Kojève's translation: truth, that is, Science, is the same content that in religion is still not identical with its certainty; this identity consists in the content, God, having received in Science the shape of the self, meaning human. Kojève's bracketed "meaning: human" makes the anthropotheist reading explicit in the translation.

In theological knowledge, truth reveals a reality essentially other than that of knowledge and its empirical support: God is something other than the theologian and theology. In the Sage's knowledge, the object of knowledge, knowledge itself, and the subject who possesses it are one. Hegel says this *coincidentia oppositorum* occurs because "the content has received the form of the self". The content of theological knowledge is God; so the Sage is the man who could and did identify himself with God, in the sense that he refers the totality of his knowledge not to a being partly other than himself but to the being he himself is, this being being all being. The Latin phrase is Nicholas of Cusa's, the coincidence of opposites that defines God; Kojève transfers it to the Sage.

Of course, this is not a *unio mystica*, and the term God is only a metaphor: there is no being to which the Sage unites, since he is total being; and he is "God" only in the sense that the totality of his knowledge, the totality of truth, is only a development of "I am who I am" (*sum qui sum*): he actually is all that is, he says it, and he is all that he says. In other words, his being is his knowledge of his being: he is the revelation of being because he is revealed being. The knowledge he has of his being is his very being: he is knowledge, and it is by being knowledge that he is what he is, the Sage. The appropriation of Exodus 3:14 is Kojève's boldest stroke: the Sage's self-knowledge is the divine name, humanised. The explicit statement that "God" is a metaphor guards against a mystical reading, consistently with the third lecture's footnote.

Hegel says this in the next two sentences (Hoffmeister p. 556). Kojève translates: what has thereby become the element of empirical existence, the form of objectivity for consciousness, is essence itself, the concept. Spirit, appearing to consciousness in this element, or, what is the same here, produced by it in this element, is Science. The sentence (¶798) states that the concept itself has become the object of consciousness.

Science is produced by the Sage, and the Sage is its producer. Insofar as the Sage is an empirical existence, a real man, he is still a consciousness facing an object. But for the Sage this object is no longer the world or nature but his Science, the concept. He lives and acts, but lives only by Science and acts only for Science. And since he lives and acts as a real man, the product of his active existence, Science or the concept, also has an empirical existence: if the Sage is a man of flesh and blood, Science is a discourse (*Logos*) actually uttered or a book ("Bible"). This book is produced by the Sage, and at the same time it "appears" to him as an object, an external thing. But its content is the Sage himself. The being that produces itself and reveals itself to itself is Spirit, and Spirit existing empirically in the form of discourse, *Logos*, concept, is Science, set out in a book. The Sage's object is his book: this is the new form of the object after the abolition of the world's externality. The book is at once a thing in the world and the Sage's self-revelation, which is why it can be the empirical existence of Spirit.

The Sage identifies himself with this Science, which reveals the totality of being, so he identifies himself with this totality: his self is a universal self; he realises in his personal existence the conscious integrity of being. But the Sage's knowledge is his in a double sense: his work, and a revelation of the being he himself is. While universal, his self remains his: a self, the self of a concrete man named Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. The full name is a characteristic emphasis: universality is realised in one man with a name.

Hegel says this in the next sentence (Hoffmeister p. 556). Kojève translates: the nature, moments, and movement of this knowledge thus result from the preceding analysis in such a way that this knowledge is the pure being-for-itself of self-consciousness. This absolute knowledge, the Sage, is the I that is this I and no other, and that is just as immediately mediated, an overcome or universal I. Hegel's formula (¶799), "this I and no other" yet "universal", states the synthesis of particular and universal that defines the individual.

Particularity is not annihilated but dialectically overcome in universal Science, in the Sage: it is preserved in what is essential in it and sublimated in that essence. It is not a matter, as in theological mysticism, which vainly tries to account for the *unio mystica*, of uniting with a given totality essentially different from the particularity I am, renouncing one's particularity or personality, drowning in the Absolute. The Sage ceases to be a particularity (*Einzelheit*) because he becomes universal himself, while remaining what he is, a particular. His particularity and personality are preserved in his totality: he remains a man, this man, G. W. F. Hegel. He reduces himself to his knowledge, and his knowledge is universal; but it is still his knowledge, which no one but he could realise. The contrast with mystical self-loss is sharp: the Sage keeps his name. This is the Sage as individual in the strong sense, universally valid and unique.

This is possible only in Hegelian absolute knowledge, that is, atheist, anthropotheist, or "egotheist". Theological knowledge, whose content is an absolute being other than man, annuls human individuality instead of overcoming it by preserving and sublimating it. The Sage is a synthesis of particular and universal, a true "individuality", only because his knowledge has as content the same I that he himself is. The coinage "egotheist" is Kojève's most provocative term, and it is exact: the Sage's God is his own I made universal. The contrast between annulling and overcoming individuality is the argument against theology on the terrain of the individual.

Hegel expresses this as follows (Hoffmeister p. 556). Kojève translates: this I has a content that it distinguishes from itself, since it is pure negativity, the act of dividing itself in two: it is consciousness. But in its very distinction this content is the I, since it is the movement of self-overcoming, the same pure negativity that the I is. In the content as distinguished, the I is reflected into itself; the content is conceptually comprehended only because the I is at home with itself (*bei sich*) in its otherness. The definition of the I as pure negativity that divides itself in two unites Kojève's anthropology with Hegel's logic.

The Sage's I is a consciousness opposed to an object: the Sage distinguishes himself from his Science, and Science distinguishes itself from its object. There are thus three distinct things: the Sage, his Book, and the real world that includes both. Everything takes place here below, within empirical existence. The Sage remains a man and so continues to express by his existence the very essence of the human being, negativity; that is why he continues to oppose himself to a not-I, an object that, not being he, must be abolished by him if he is to realise himself. But the abolition of the object, and so of the opposition between I and object, now takes place no longer through action, which "negates" only a particular object and so can never abolish objectivity as such, the opposition of subject and object in general, but through Science itself, which, revealing the totality of being, abolishes within this revealed totality all existing oppositions, notably that of subject and object. The Sage's Science is itself negating, and indeed negating negativity as such, since it abolishes not the object but the very opposition of subject and object. Negativity is man, the I; so Science is I, the Sage who creates it. Objectifying itself as Science, the Sage's I "remains at home with itself in this otherness". The distinction is important: action negates particular objects, Science negates objectivity itself. The Sage's negativity survives the end of history as knowledge. The triad Sage, Book, world is the final structure of reality.

If Science is the Sage and the Sage Science, Science must have the same essence as man: it must be dialectical movement, creative becoming proceeding by negations. That is what it is, as Hegel says in the sentence ending the first section (Hoffmeister pp. 556–557). Kojève translates: giving a more precise idea of this content, one can say it is nothing but the movement just mentioned, since this content is Spirit that runs through itself as Spirit, doing so for itself, and can do so because in its very objectivity it has the shape of the concept. The inference from the Sage's essence to Science's essence makes the Logic a movement, not a table of categories.

Now comes the second section, in which Hegel speaks of the reality of the Sage defined in the first, in three steps: the Sage in objective reality; the Sage in time; the Sage in objectively real time, history. The introduction begins (Hoffmeister p. 557), in Kojève's translation: as for the empirical existence of this concept, Science does not appear in time and in objective reality before Spirit has arrived at this consciousness of itself. As Spirit that knows what it is, Spirit does not exist before, and exists nowhere else than where it exists after the completion of the work of mastering its imperfect shape, procuring for its consciousness the shape of its essence, and so equalising its self-consciousness with its consciousness. Hegel's "not before" (¶800) is the textual basis of the thesis that Science appears only at the end of history.

Hegel says here what we have long known. In time and objective reality, in history, Science cannot appear at just any moment. Before man can develop Science he must define himself as Hegel has just done in the first section, which means he must have written the first seven chapters of the *Phenomenology*, which he can do only as citizen of the universal and homogeneous State that completes history and is thus the "completion of Spirit" (*Vollendung des Geistes*) Hegel speaks of. Total Science can result only from a total effort of man, the whole collective human effort realised by the completed evolution of universal history. Only then is the coincidence of self-consciousness and consciousness that Science proclaims true as theory, because only then is it real. The equation of "Vollendung des Geistes" with the final State is Kojève's gloss.

Before the accomplishment of the total historical effort, absolute knowledge is not possible, precisely because the total or absolute reality it is supposed to reveal does not yet exist. In the real world before the end of history there can be no Sage, and so no objectively real knowledge, no book containing Science. The conclusion is strict: the Book can exist only at the end.

Hegel says this in the sentence ending the introduction (Hoffmeister p. 557). Kojève translates: Spirit existing in and for itself, differentiated into its moments, not yet integrated by the synthetic comprehension that is Science, is knowledge existing for itself, conceptual comprehension as such, which has not yet reached substance; it is not in itself absolute knowledge. The sentence (¶800) distinguishes the concept without substance from the concept that has integrated its moments.

The "absolute knowledge" that is "in itself" is the Sage. Before his advent Science exists only as a mere possibility. It exists as possibility because being is always total and always has the form of the concept, since one day it will actually be revealed in its totality by knowledge. But Science will be real as Science only when it can insert itself as Science into the real totality of being, which it does in the form of the book written by the Sage. This book, and so the Sage, are the objective reality (*Wirklichkeit*) of absolute Science. Only when Science has become real as Science in the form of the book is real being really revealed to itself by itself, and only then is it really Spirit. The claim that being "always has the form of the concept" because it will one day be revealed is a retrospective possibility: being is conceivable because it will be conceived. Spirit is real only from the moment of the Book.

To speak of Spirit is to speak of Science; and to speak of Science is to speak of its objective reality, the Sage as acting, writing the book, in the real world. That is the subject of the first step of the second section. The equation, Spirit equals Science equals Sage writing, ties the ontology to a scene of writing, as the Jena scene of the first 1937–38 lecture did.

In the first step Hegel first says (Hoffmeister p. 557), in Kojève's translation: in objective reality the knowing substance is there before its form, before the conceptual shape of substance. The sentence (¶801) sets the order: substance before concept.

This sentence has a double meaning, anthropological and theological, and anthropologically it can be referred either to historical man or to the Sage. In the *Phenomenology* "substance" usually means community, people, State, as opposed on the one hand to the isolated individual, the particular, and on the other to the man who reflects on the community or State and reveals them in speech. Here it is "knowing substance", what Hegel later called "objective spirit": the civilisation or collective culture of a people, in the widest sense. The "form" or "conceptual shape" is philosophy as the attempt to understand culture, to reflect not on the community itself but on its culture. Hegel says substance precedes its form. He thus says of the collective what he said in Chapter V of the individual: man must first realise himself objectively and only then can become conscious of what he is. Like the individual, the collective or people must first create itself as a historical entity by its action, and only then can a philosophy come to reveal the essence of this new collective human reality, understand the sense and significance of its culture. In other words, Hegel rejects every kind of "revelation" in philosophy. Nothing can come from God, from any extra-worldly, extra-human, non-temporal reality. It is the creative temporal action of humanity, history, that creates the reality philosophy reveals. So to understand this reality fully, to reach perfect philosophy or "Science", is to understand human reality in the whole of its creative becoming, the total meaning of history. The gloss on "knowing substance" as objective spirit and collective culture is consistent with Kojève's reading of "substance" as the State. The rejection of revelation in philosophy is his thesis in its most direct form: philosophy follows history.

If one refers "conceptual shape" to Science, the sentence says that Science presupposes the completed totality of historical evolution. Science receives nothing from outside and creates nothing itself; it only reveals what is, being in its spatial and temporal totality. That is why the Sage's knowledge is his and his alone. Like every man he is heir to his past, and since Science only reveals this past, which is his, it reveals man himself to himself. The claim that Science creates nothing matches the first 1933–34 remark that the philosophical method is pure description (p. 38).

Finally, one can see in "knowing substance" the conscious or anthropomorphic entity opposed to the human individual and to man in general: God. Then the sentence means that "God", the theology that speaks of him, exists before the concept, before philosophy and so before Science. For Hegel a religion, or rather a theology, also reveals the collective culture it belongs to, but without knowing it, externalising the content it reveals, substantialising it. This "substance" is precisely the God of the theology in question. The conceptual shape of collective culture is philosophy. Hegel thus says that theology necessarily existed before philosophy, which ultimately means that Christian theology precedes Science. Religion can exist without philosophy, but philosophy cannot appear without a religion. There is first the action that creates culture; then the theological revelation of this culture, which speaks of it while believing it speaks of a transcendent God; and only then the philosophical revelation of culture, which contents itself, all in all, with referring to man the content that the corresponding theology wrongly refers to a God. The three-stage sequence, action, theology, philosophy, is Kojève's genealogy of knowledge. Its claim that philosophy always follows a religion and redirects its content to man is the general form of anthropotheism.

In the next two sentences (Hoffmeister p. 557) Hegel develops the idea. Kojève translates: substance is the undeveloped in-itself, the ground and concept in their still immobile simplicity; so it is inwardness, the self of Spirit that is not yet there as self. What is there is there as the still undeveloped simple and as the immediate: the object of representing consciousness as such. The sentence (¶801) describes the priority of undeveloped content over its form.

What first appears in objective reality is the material content of culture, raw, undivided, undifferentiated, cultural reality, and also immediate, unreflected, unexplained. This content first presents itself to "externalising consciousness" in the form of an object. Human reality represented in the form of an object is a so-called divine reality. The definition of the divine as human reality in the form of an object is the lecture's most compact formula for religion.

Once more: philosophy, and so Science, appear in objective reality in third place: preceded by the symbolic revelation of human reality in theology, which itself presupposes the creation of human reality by temporal historical action. Certain consequences follow concerning the character of philosophy and Science on one side, and of real cultural life and its theological transposition on the other, which Hegel draws in the passage ending the first step. The transition announces the comparison of richness and clarity.

He first says (Hoffmeister p. 557), in Kojève's translation: for this reason philosophical knowledge at first has only a poor object, compared with which substance and its theological consciousness are richer. It is poorer because it is spiritual consciousness, for which what exists in itself exists only insofar as it is being for the self and being of the self, that is, concept. The sentence (¶801) grants theology an initial advantage in richness.

At first, real cultural or historical life and its theological transposition are always richer than the philosophy this life engenders. Philosophy never reveals the totality of the life that gives rise to it, and reveals less of it than the corresponding theology. Hegel explains why. I understand philosophically, conceptually, only what exists for me, what is my being. At first, and as long as historical evolution lasts, the collective life of the people is always richer than the private life of the isolated particular who is the philosopher. The philosopher, who by his philosophy reveals only himself, since all philosophy is always self-consciousness and only self-consciousness, reveals less than the theologian, who represents, symbolically it is true, the self-consciousness of the community as such, and so less than this community is. Only the citizen of the universal and homogeneous State, where the opposition of particular and universal is abolished, can reveal the totality of human reality by revealing only himself. Only this citizen's philosophy can be total, which is why it is Science or wisdom and no longer philo-sophy. The argument explains why philosophy lags behind theology: the philosopher is a particular, and his life is poorer than his people's. The final State removes the gap because private life then coincides with public life.

Yet if philosophy is always less "rich" than the corresponding historical reality and its religion, it is "clearer" than they. Culture itself is without consciousness in general; theology believes it speaks of something other than man and his culture, so it is without self-consciousness. Only self-consciousness is truly revealing, since only the self can be revealed. Hegel says this in the next sentence (Hoffmeister p. 557). Kojève translates: the manifestness that substance has in this theological consciousness is in fact hiddenness, since substance there is static being still without self; what is manifest to itself is only the certainty of itself. The paradox, theology's revelation is concealment, reverses the Christian claim: the revealed religion hides what it reveals, since it does not know that it speaks of man.

We now understand how the passage from philosophy to Science occurs in historical objective reality. Hegel speaks of it next (Hoffmeister p. 557). Kojève translates: at first only the abstract moments of substance belong to philosophical self-consciousness. But insofar as these moments, as pure movements, progress by moving themselves, philosophical self-consciousness enriches itself until it has taken from religious consciousness the whole of substance, absorbed into itself the whole edifice of its essentialities, and, since this negative attitude toward objectivity is equally positive, a positing, produced substance out of itself and so restored it for consciousness, now the Sage's. Kojève's numbered brackets mark three stages: taking from religion, absorbing, reproducing.

Being "poorer" than the historical reality it reveals, each philosophy is "abstract": each reveals certain moments of reality, but none realises that these moments do not exist in the isolated state in which they appear in it. But in the course of history philosophical self-consciousness becomes richer and richer, as the life of the particular becomes richer, approaching collective or "universal" life. At the end of history, in the universal and homogeneous State, collective or "public" life, cultural, social, political, coincides completely with "personal" life, which thus ceases to be purely "private". The philosophical self-consciousness of the citizen of this final State reveals the totality of real cultural and political life. At once the surplus a theology could reveal no longer exists: the religious man no longer has a reason to be, and so he disappears. But this destruction of objectivity (*Gegenständlichkeit*), of divine reality, is at the same time the positing of human reality; the same reality is negated as divine and posited as human. At this moment the philosopher is a Sage, and philosophy is wisdom or Science. This Science recreates human reality for consciousness, so human reality is again an object; indeed, history described in a book is as much an object for consciousness as real history itself. But this object, consciously created by man, the scholar, is no longer thing-like, external, transcendent: it is the immanent object of knowledge, the concept. This "construction" or "deduction" of human reality takes place in and through the *Phenomenology*; it is in and through the *Phenomenology* that the philosopher becomes a Sage. And the human reality consciously constructed in it can no longer be referred to anything other than the man who constructs it: the absolute knowledge of this revelation cannot be theo-logy. It will be "Logic" simply, Science properly speaking, the second part of the System of which the *Phenomenology* is the first. The account of religion's disappearance is economical: religion reveals the surplus of collective life over private life, and when the surplus vanishes, religion has nothing left to reveal. The dying away of religion is a consequence of the coincidence of public and private life in the final State. The distinction between the thing-like object and the immanent object, the concept, completes the distinction between *Vorstellung* and *Begriff*.

This Science reveals completely the totality of objective reality. Between reality and Science there is now only one difference: in reality the whole precedes the parts, whereas in Science the parts precede the whole. Hegel says this (Hoffmeister pp. 557–558). Kojève translates: in the concept that knows itself as concept, in Science, the moments present themselves before the fulfilled whole whose becoming is their movement; in consciousness, naive and religious, the whole exists before the moments, but as a whole not comprehended by the concept. The inversion of whole and parts (¶801) is the formal difference between reality and knowledge.

Reality is analytic, Science synthetic. Consciousness, naive, theological, or philosophical, is always faced with a whole, a complete and undivided real life that it does not at first understand; it understands and reveals it only by decomposing it, so each revelation is abstract. That is why in theology, for the religious man, the total "hidden" reality, the creating God, is prior to its revealing development in and through creation, a development that never exhausts the hidden divine whole. Science, by contrast, constructs the whole from its moments, moments disengaged from the whole and revealed one by one by philosophy in the course of history. Unlike theology, it knows that the whole is nothing but the integration of its moments. These moments are worldly, human, temporal, so for Science the whole is too. The totality of being revealed by Science is not God but the totality of being that is the same being as the being of the one who reveals it; the Sage's consciousness of the external is therefore also a self-consciousness. The contrast between the theological *Deus absconditus*, a whole never exhausted by its manifestations, and the Science that knows the whole as the sum of its moments is precise. It makes transcendence the surplus of an unanalysed whole over its known parts.

In the *Phenomenology* Hegel constructs integral history from the constituent elements of human reality, and within this history the successive theologies. He shows that these theologies are human works and so that the being they reveal can only be human being. In creating Science, the *Phenomenology* necessarily destroys all theology and all philosophy, and also all science in the current sense, Newtonian physics in particular, Hegel's *bête noire*. The inclusion of Newtonian physics among the casualties of Science is characteristic: Hegel's hostility to mechanism, which Kojève attributes to the Master's physics (p. 61), makes vulgar science one more partial perspective overcome.

The step devoted to the objective reality of the Sage and of Science is over. It always concerned a before and an after; to understand the objective reality of Science is to understand its temporal reality. That is why Hegel will speak, in the second step, of the relation between the Sage, with his knowledge, and time. The transition leads directly to the sixth lecture, the "Note on Eternity, Time, and the Concept", the philosophical centre of the book.

### Sixth Lecture: Note on Eternity, Time, and the Concept (cf. Hoffmeister p. 558, ll. 3–4)

As soon as one speaks of the appearance of Science in the concrete reality of the historical world, one must speak of a before and an after, of a becoming, and so of time. To ask about the relation between Science and objective reality is to ask about the relation between Science and time, which Hegel does in the second step of the second section of the second part of Chapter VIII. The title "Note" is modest; the three lectures it spans are the philosophical centre of the book, where Kojève sets out his interpretation of the concept as time.

The problem is far from new; one can say it has arisen since philosophy has existed. All philosophies have sought, and usually claimed to have found, truth or at least truths. Truth in the proper sense is supposed to be neither modifiable nor deniable: it is valid "universally and necessarily", not subject to change; it is eternal or non-temporal. On the other hand, there is no doubt that it is found at a certain moment of time and exists in time, since it exists through and for man, who lives in the world. As soon as one raises the problem of truth, even partial, one raises the problem of time, or more particularly of the relation between time and the eternal or the non-temporal. This is the problem Hegel poses and solves in the step in question. The formulation of the problem, truth is eternal yet appears in time, is the classical problem of the historicity of truth, which Kojève makes the criterion for classifying all philosophies.

With Hegel, one can call the coherent whole of conceptual knowledge that claims truth the concept (*Begriff*); indeed truth is always a "concept" in the broad sense, a coherent whole of meaningful words. The problem can then be put as the question of the relations between the concept and time. The definition of the concept as a coherent whole of meaningful words anchors it in discourse, which will be decisive: discourse takes time.

Hegel answers in the first words of the step, and rather unexpectedly: «Die Zeit ist der Begriff selbst, der da ist» ("Time is the concept itself that is there", in empirical existence) (Hoffmeister p. 558). In writing this strange sentence Hegel weighed his words, since he had already said exactly the same in the Preface (Hoffmeister p. 38): "As for time, it is the empirically existing concept itself." The sentence is clear, and at the same time rather incomprehensible. To understand it better Kojève will briefly review the solutions proposed before Hegel by Plato and Aristotle, Spinoza, and Kant, in lectures VI to VIII. The double attestation, in the Preface (¶46) and Chapter VIII (¶801), establishes that the identification of time and concept is a considered thesis. Kojève's typology is a way of making it intelligible by contrast.

The task is to establish a relation, positive or negative, between the concept and time. There is evidently a very limited number of possibilities, which Kojève sets out in formulas. C symbolises the concept: not this or that concept but the concept, the integration of all concepts, the complete system of concepts, the "idea of ideas", the Idea in the Hegelian (Logic) and Kantian sense. T designates time or temporal reality; E its opposite, eternity, non-temporal reality in the positive sense; E′ the "eternal" as opposed to eternity (as this table is without being being, the concept can be conceived as eternal without being eternity: it "participates" in eternity, it is an eternal function of eternity, but eternity itself is something other than the concept); and T′ the "temporal", distinguished from time itself as the eternal is from eternity. The possibilities are: I, C = E; II, C = E′, relating either to E (a, outside T; b, in T) or to T; III, C = T; IV, C = T′. The symbolic table is Kojève's most schematic device. The distinction between eternity and the eternal, time and the temporal, allows a clean classification.

The formulas read as follows. First possibility: the concept is eternity. It then relates to nothing: not to time, evidently, and not to eternity, since it is eternity. This is Parmenides's position, but since the Parmenidean standpoint, fully developed and truly understood, is known only through Spinoza, Kojève will discuss Spinoza under it. Third possibility: the concept is time, and so relates neither to eternity nor to time: Hegel's position. Possibilities 1 and 3, being identifications, cannot be subdivided. Possibility 2 divides in two, the first of which has two variants, giving three types of philosophy, among which all philosophies other than those of Parmenides–Spinoza and Hegel can be distributed. A footnote draws the consequence: since this problem expresses the essential content of all philosophy, there are only five irreducible philosophical types: an impossible type (1, Parmenides–Spinoza); three relatively possible but insufficient types (2, Plato, Aristotle, Kant); and a true type, «qu'il s'agit d'ailleurs de développer, de réaliser ; car personnellement je crois que ce n'est pas encore fait (Hegel et Heidegger représentent cette possibilité 3)» (which, moreover, has still to be developed and realised; for personally I believe this has not yet been done; Hegel and Heidegger represent this possibility 3) (p. 338). The footnote is among the most important in the book. Kojève declares that the true philosophy, the identification of concept and time, has not yet been achieved, which contradicts any literal reading of Hegel's claim to wisdom. He also places Heidegger beside Hegel as the representative of possibility III, confirming the Heideggerian inspiration of his reading of time.

There is also possibility 4: the concept is temporal. But this is no longer a philosophical possibility, since this sceptical type of thought makes all philosophy impossible by denying the very idea of truth: the concept, being temporal, changes essentially, so there is no definitive and so no true knowledge in the proper sense. Possibility 3, by contrast, is compatible with the idea of truth, since if everything in time, everything temporal, always changes, time itself does not change. The distinction between the temporal, which changes, and time, which does not, saves Hegel's position from relativism. It is an elegant argument: identifying the concept with time rather than with the temporal secures its permanence.

Possibility 2 divides in two. Being eternal, and not eternity, the concept relates to something other than itself. Hence two variants: the ancient or pagan, according to which the eternal concept relates to eternity, clearly formulated by Plato and Aristotle, who agree on this point; and the modern or Judaeo-Christian, clearly formulated by Kant: the eternal concept relates to time. The first variant implies two possible types: the eternal concept relating to eternity outside time (Plato), and relating to eternity in time (Aristotle). A footnote adds that the modern variant cannot be subdivided in the same way, since there can be no time in eternity. Some Christian philosophers affirmed it, explicitly or implicitly; but either they made meaningless puns or, without realising it, they realised the Hegelian or atheist type of philosophy. The division of possibility II into pagan and Judaeo-Christian variants maps the history of philosophy onto the history of religion. The footnote's charge that Christian theories of time in eternity are either wordplay or disguised Hegelianism is characteristic.

The universe of ideas, the idea of ideas, is in Plato what Hegel calls concept (*Begriff*), or in the Logic, Idea. The world of phenomena is what Hegel calls empirical existence (*Dasein*). For simplicity, speak of "concept" and "existence". Existence is essentially change, a temporal entity; and there is change only in existence, so existence is not only temporal but time itself. The concept, by contrast, does not change, essentially; it is essentially something other than temporal and other than time. One would be tempted to say with Parmenides and Spinoza that it is eternity. But Plato does not say this, since he believes he has discovered that the concept, the *Logos*, the word or meaningful discourse, relates to something other than the concept itself, the word. «C'est ici le point où il faut attaquer Platon, et les philosophes platonisants, de Platon à Kant, si l'on veut éviter les conséquences anthropologiques désagréables que leurs philosophies impliquent» (this is the point at which one must attack Plato and the Platonising philosophers, from Plato to Kant, if one wants to avoid the unpleasant anthropological consequences their philosophies imply) (p. 339). So the concept is not eternity; it is only eternal, and one must pose the problem of the relations between the eternal concept on the one hand and time and eternity on the other. The parenthesis identifies the target of Kojève's critique precisely: the referential theory of the concept, the claim that the concept relates to something other than itself. The "unpleasant anthropological consequences" are the denial of human freedom and history, which the lecture will show.

First, a fact Plato does not ignore: real, empirically existing man utters meaningful discourse. So concepts, and the integral concept, subsist in time while being by definition eternal, essentially other than time; they are in change but, not changing, necessarily other than change. If one symbolises temporal existence, man-in-the-world, by a line, the concept must be represented by a singular point on it, essentially other than the other points (fig. 1). For Plato the concept relates to something other than itself; this is where Plato criticised Parmenides–Spinoza, and where Hegel criticises Plato and all other philosophers, since for Hegel, as for Parmenides–Spinoza, the concept relates to nothing but itself. Being eternal, the concept must relate to eternity, says Plato (Aristotle follows him; Kant opposes him, saying the eternal concept relates to time). But eternity can only be outside time, says Plato (Aristotle denies this, discovering eternity in time). The schema must be completed (fig. 2). The diagrams, reproduced in the book, translate the positions into geometry: a line for time, points for concepts, a circle for eternity. Kojève's alignment of Hegel with Parmenides–Spinoza against Plato, on the non-referential concept, is the key to the lecture.

Further: the appearance of concepts, even of the concept, in existence is not a unique phenomenon; the concept can appear at any moment of time, so the line symbolising existence implies several eternal singular points (fig. 3). By definition eternity, the entity to which the concept relates, is always the same, and so is the concept's relation to it. At every instant of time the same relation to one and the same extra-temporal entity is possible. To symbolise Plato's conception the schema must be modified (fig. 4). The step from one to many singular points and back to a single relation prepares the circle.

One thus finds the schema of the metaphysics of the *Timaeus*: a circular time, whose circularity, and that of what is temporal in it, is determined by the relation of what is in time to what is outside time. And at the same time one finds the famous "central point" that a Christian theology, which for Kojève is a variant of Platonism, must necessarily introduce into the Hegelian circle symbolising absolute or circular knowledge. The circle can symbolise the totality of knowledge: both the knowledge relating to man-in-the-world, temporal, and the knowledge relating to what lies outside it. This "central point", which appears necessarily as soon as the concept is interpreted as a relation to something other than itself, as soon as transcendence enters knowledge, has been called God. This theist schema has nothing specifically Christian about it, since it has been drawn from Plato's conception. A footnote adds that it is the schema of all monotheist knowledge, of all knowledge that recognises one transcendent; and every philosophy recognises a transcendence, except the acosmism of Parmenides–Spinoza and Hegel's atheism. The return of the circle with a central point from the second lecture (p. 286) ties the analysis of time to the analysis of theology: God is the point to which the eternal concept refers. The claim that Christian theology is a variant of Platonism is Kojève's.

So say the "central point" is God, which one can do since for Plato the One-Good (*to hen agathon*) symbolised by the point is also *theos*. The name matters little; one must see what the thing means, and so make the drawing more precise. The identification of the Platonic Good with God follows the tradition of Christian Platonism.

First, simplify. The concept can repeat itself in time, but its repetition does not change it or its relation to eternity; it modifies nothing. One can suppress all the circle's radii but one (fig. 5), but one, since the presence of the concept in time is of capital importance: the point on the circumference symbolises human knowledge taking place in time. Now see what the radius symbolises. The single radius represents the one relation that matters: human knowledge at a point in time referring to eternity.

The radius symbolises the relation between the eternal concept and eternity or the eternal entity; this relation is also non-temporal or eternal. Yet it is clearly a relation in the strong sense, between two different things, so it is "extended", in space, since there is no time in it; hence the dotted line, distinguished from the solid temporal line. But the relation is double (fig. 6). On the one hand the eternal concept situated in time, the word, rises by its meaning to the entity revealed by this meaning; on the other hand this entity descends through the meaning to the word, which it creates as word from its changing sonorous, phonetic reality. Without the word, eternity would not be represented in time and so would not be accessible to man; without eternity, the word would have no meaning and would not raise man above time and change; there would be no truth for man. Taking a concept as an example: the word "dog" reveals the essence of the dog, and without this word this essence would not be revealed to man; but it is the essence of the dog that realises the meaning of the word; it is the dog that makes it possible to develop the word "dog" into a judgement: "the dog is a four-legged animal covered with hair", and so on. In general one goes from the word to the thing and comes back from the thing to the word, and only this double relation constitutes truth, the revelation of reality, the concept in the proper sense. This double relation exhausts truth or the concept: the eternal concept relates only to eternity, and eternity reveals itself exclusively through the concept. Though in time, they are without relation to time and the temporal. The dog example appears here for the first time; the next lecture will return to it. The double movement, word to thing and thing to word, is the referential theory Kojève will reject.

The double, even circular, relation of the eternal concept and eternity therefore cuts the temporal circle. Change as change remains inaccessible to the concept: there is no truth in the temporal, neither before the concept nor after it. Through the concept one can rise from the temporal to eternity and then fall back into the temporal, but after the fall one is exactly what one was before. To live in the concept, in truth, one must live outside time in the eternal circle. The eternal circle of absolute knowledge, though in time, is without relation to time, and the whole of knowledge is absolute only insofar as it implies an eternal circle relating solely to eternity. Plato's conception of absolute knowledge must be represented as in fig. 7, which is the schema of theo-logical knowledge; the circle with a central point was only a graphic variant of it. The image of rising to eternity and falling back unchanged states the Platonic conception of contemplation: it transforms nothing in time.

The difference between the theological and the Hegelian atheist system thus goes back very far. In metaphysical language, one has a theist system properly speaking, frankly transcendentalist and monotheist, as soon as one defines the concept, absolute knowledge, as an eternal entity relating to eternity, the latter being outside time. The genealogy of theism from the referential concept is Kojève's central thesis in this lecture: theology follows from a theory of meaning.

What does this mean for the temporal world of phenomena? Knowledge of this world and of man in it is symbolised by the large circle. Suppress the small circle of the eternal concept (fig. 8). Two interpretations are then possible. First, one can say the arc has fixed, definitive, uncrossable limits (fig. 9). This is the schema of knowledge Kojève called "mystical" in the broad sense. By suppressing God in a given theological system one can thus arrive at a mystical system, in which one can speak of everything except God, who is essentially ineffable; if radical, one will say one cannot even say of God that he is God, at most that he is ineffable; and the ineffable being can reveal itself through anything, "ecstasy", music, and so on, except speech. A footnote notes that in Plato the mystical tendency is very clear: the One-Good "reveals" itself in and through silent contemplation. As for other things, temporal entities, one can say everything; knowledge of them can in principle be total and definitive, since time is limited and can be exhausted by discourse. But in saying all one can say of temporal reality, worldly and human, one reaches its limit, that is, of this beyond; and the observation of its presence proves one cannot be content with discourse, even total. One is obliged to surpass discourse by a "mystical", "ecstatic", "algorithmic", "sonorous" or other silence. The inclusion of the "algorithmic" among the silences is striking: mathematics, like music and ecstasy, is a non-discursive language, which recalls the second lecture (p. 285).

Second, one can say that after suppressing the small circle, the arc of the large circle is without limits, its two "last" points lying on the removed small circle (fig. 8). This is the schema of sceptical or relative knowledge, of the absence of true knowledge in the strong sense. Knowledge relates to time, to change; but time now being without limits, change never stops. There is no eternal or definitive knowledge: no *epistēmē*, only *doxa*. Even here one can say the circle is closed, positing the ideal of Hegelian absolute, circular knowledge (fig. 11); but this ideal remains forever an ideal: the circle of real knowledge is never actually closed (fig. 10). This is the optimistic form of scepticism: the scepticism of the eternal "why", of humanity "that is always learning", marching tirelessly like one man toward a goal it will never reach. Truth remains "white", according to the definition of the Devil in "The Well of Saint Clare". It is also the "eternal task" (*ewige Aufgabe*) of Kantian criticism. In both variants of sceptical knowledge, philosophy as the road that actually leads to wisdom is evidently impossible. The allusion to Anatole France's *Le Puits de Sainte Claire*, where the Devil describes truth as white because it contains all colours or none, is characteristic of Kojève's literary range. The "optimistic scepticism" of infinite progress targets both Kant and the positivist ideal of science.

Conversely, by introducing the eternal concept, discursive truth, into a given mystical or sceptical system, one always obtains a theo-logical system, even if the term God does not explicitly appear. In that case truth would necessarily reveal a being situated outside time, outside the world and man. The converse completes the classification: any eternal concept brings God with it.

Once more, what does the theological system, neither mystical nor sceptical, mean for knowledge of the temporal world? In principle one can say everything of the world and man; the knowledge relating to them is total. But knowledge relating to time and the temporal remains in itself relative: it is *doxa*. Only by relating it as a whole to eternal knowledge relating to eternity can one say something definitive of the temporal. The theological system grants total but relative knowledge of the world, absolute only through God.

Take the world. In theological language in the narrow sense, events in the world, and the world itself, are contingent; there is no absolute knowledge of them. But if, per impossibile, one knew God's designs and creative will, one could have a true science of the world. In symbolic theological language, there is science of the world only insofar as it implies geometrical elements. Kant showed that to transform algorithm into discourse one must relate it either to time or to space; here, relating it to time being excluded by definition, one can relate it only to space, a space outside time in this conception. And one can indeed speak of geometry: "the circle" is also a meaningful word, and one can say what it is, as opposed, for instance, to a non-spatialised integral, expressible only by an algorithm. So the theological system can produce a real geometry, a geometrical physics, and nothing else. This physics can tell us that the earth is round, but not why it attracts heavy objects, since the force of attraction, like every force, is essentially temporal as well as spatial; and so it cannot say what the earth is as Earth, the planet on which trees grow and man lives. The thesis that theological knowledge yields only geometry, not dynamics, links Platonism to Cartesian physics. The phrase "the planet on which trees grow and man lives" marks what geometry cannot say: the living world.

As for man himself, the situation is the same. There is true science of him only insofar as he is related to eternity. I can demonstrate God's existence: an eternal truth. But I cannot in the same way demonstrate my existence, except by conceiving myself as an eternal idea in God. Of myself in my temporal or worldly existence I can know nothing. More: it is precisely absolute knowledge related to eternity that makes absolute knowledge of the temporal impossible. Take Christian theology. What really matters to the Christian is to know whether he is saved or damned as a result of his worldly or temporal existence. But the analysis of the eternal concept revealing God shows that one cannot know it, can never know it. If the Christian does not want to be "mystical", to renounce discourse completely, he must necessarily be sceptical about his temporal existence; he may do what he likes, he will not have the certainty of acting rightly. A footnote adds that the Christian admits God's decision conforms to human reason. The example of salvation is well chosen: the Christian has certain knowledge of God and none of himself. This is the anthropological consequence of theism.

In short, in the theological system there is absolute knowledge in and through consciousness (*Bewusstsein*), but not in and through self-consciousness (*Selbstbewusstsein*). The formula condenses the lecture: theology knows the other absolutely and the self not at all.

Finally, one can present the theological system in its anthropological aspect by explaining what the idea of human freedom means in it, which is the idea of man himself, since without freedom man is only an animal. Freedom need not be defined here; a footnote adds that in fact either the word has no meaning or it is the negativity Hegel speaks of, which a Descartes and a Kant have in view without saying so. We all have "an idea of what it is", even if we cannot define it, and this suffices to say the following. The free act is situated, so to speak, outside the line of temporal evolution. The here and now, represented by a point on the line, is determined by the past, which through it also determines the future. The here and now of the free act, by contrast, is inexplicable from its past, not fixed by it. The being endowed with freedom, while in space-time, must be able to detach itself from the here and now, rise above it, take a position toward it. But the free act relates to the here and now; it occurs under given conditions. The content of the here and now must be preserved while being detached from the here and now. What preserves the content of a perception while detaching it from the here and now of sensation is precisely the concept or meaningful word: this table is bound to the here and now, but the meaning of the words "this table" is everywhere and always. That is why everyone agrees that only a speaking being can be free. A footnote adds that Hegel reverses this, saying only a free being can speak, but he too maintains the close connection between language and freedom. The link between freedom and the concept, both detach content from the here and now, is one of Kojève's deepest theses. It unites the theory of the concept with the theory of negativity: to speak is already to negate the given.

As for Plato, who believes virtue can be taught through dialectic, through discourse, the free act is evidently of the same nature as the act of conceptual knowledge: two complementary aspects of one thing. The unity of virtue and knowledge in Plato confirms the link.

For Plato the concept is eternal, relates to eternity, and eternity is outside time. Applying this definition to the free act yields the following result. Just as the concept does not relate to temporal reality, where *doxa* reigns, the free act too is impossible in this reality. In the free act man relates to something outside time. As Plato says in his well-known myth, the soul chooses its destiny before birth. There is choice, so freedom; but the choice takes place outside temporal existence, which is absolutely determined in its evolution. In his myth Plato adopts metempsychosis: the choice can be repeated and choices differ. But this hypothesis fits the Platonic system badly, since the non-temporal admits no variations. So one soon arrives at the Gnostic and Christian conception of a single choice fixed by the relation between extra-temporal eternity, God, and the free agent: the idea of the Angel who decides once for all, outside time properly speaking, for or against God, becoming a "virtuous" Angel or an Angel forever "fallen", the Devil. A footnote adds that this conception also appears in the dogma of original sin: in Adam integral man decides freely once for all; the act is in time but does not relate to time; it relates to God's eternal commandment, God being outside time. As for man's freedom properly speaking, it is the stumbling block of every theology, especially Christian theology; even if divine election is a cooperation with man, which is already rather "heretical", human acts are judged by God en bloc, so freedom remains a single act outside time, related to eternity. The myth of Er (*Republic* X) is read as the necessary consequence of the Platonic theory of the concept: if truth is outside time, so is freedom.
