The Angel who decides once for all is the figure of freedom in theology, which reappears in Kant's intelligible character.

In general this conception cannot explain temporal existence as such, as history. History is always a comedy here, not a tragedy: the tragic is before or after, in any case outside temporal life; this life realises a programme fixed in advance and so has no sense or value in itself. The characterisation of history as comedy repeats the 1936–37 theory (p. 122): a conflict resolved in advance is comic.

In sum: every system of theo-logical absolute knowledge sees in the concept an eternal entity relating to eternity, and conversely this conception, once developed, necessarily leads to theological knowledge. If, as in Plato, eternity is outside time, the system is rigorously monotheist and radically transcendentalist: God's being is essentially other than the being of the one who speaks of it, and this divine being is absolutely one and unique, eternally identical with itself, excluding all change. With regard to the natural world, the system gives a purely geometrical theory, which can at most operate with the notion of purely incorporeal "movement", as Descartes does, but not with the notion of force: it admits a kinematics or phoronomy but excludes dynamics, and so does not explain biological phenomena, in which time is constitutive. With regard to the human world, it explains at most "angelic" existence but deprives historical life, man's temporal existence, of all sense and value. The summary closes the analysis of Plato with a triple verdict: geometry without dynamics, no biology, no history. Descartes appears as Plato's heir in physics.

### Seventh Lecture: Note on Eternity, Time, and the Concept (Continued)

Having discussed the Platonic conception, possibility II, 1, a, at length, Kojève passes to Aristotle, possibility II, 1, b. Aristotle saw Plato's difficulties and made a great discovery. The numbering follows the table of the previous lecture.

Like Plato, Aristotle defines the concept as eternal, as a relation to something else, and this something else is for him, as for Plato, not time but eternity: there is *epistēmē* only in the cosmos where there are ideas, eternal entities having eternity as their *topos*. But Aristotle saw what Plato seems not to have seen: that eternity is not outside time but in time; at least there is something eternal in time. Plato reasoned: all real dogs change; the concept "dog" remains identical with itself; so it must relate to an eternity outside real dogs, outside time. This eternity is the "idea" of dog and ultimately the Idea of ideas. Aristotle answered: certainly the concept "dog" relates to eternity, but eternity subsists in time, since if real dogs change, *the* real dog, the species "dog", does not change. The species being eternal while in time, it is possible to relate the concept to eternity in time. There is thus absolute knowledge of the temporal world insofar as it implies eternity. Plato forgot that in Heraclitus's river there are permanent eddies: first of all animals and plants. The eternal or immutable axis of the "eddies" is the *telos* or entelechy, which appears, in relation to the concept, as the Idea of the "eddy". But there are also the planets and finally the cosmos. Aristotle therefore says that time itself is eternal: it is circular, as in Hegel (footnote), but the circle is traversed eternally, whereas in Hegel the traversal is unique (footnote). The cosmos has the same structure as the animal; the Aristotelian system gives an explanation of life and a biologistic conception of the world. The image of permanent eddies in Heraclitus's river is Kojève's most memorable rendering of Aristotelian form. The two footnotes fix the difference with Hegel precisely: both hold time circular, but Aristotle's circle repeats and Hegel's is traversed once.

Theologically speaking, the conception that relates the eternal concept to eternity in time amounts to polytheism. Aristotle is too far from the totemic mentality to affirm that animals and plants are gods, but when he says the planets are gods he is much more in accord with his system than Plato. In the end the difference is not very important: mono- or poly-theism, in both cases the knowledge is theo-logical. The cosmic revolution repeats eternally, and only because there is eternal repetition is there absolute knowledge of the cosmos. It is one and the same eternity that manifests itself in and through the eternal return of time: there is a supreme god, God properly speaking, who maintains the cosmos in its identity and so makes conceptual knowledge possible. This divine eternity, while manifesting itself through the course of time, differs essentially from everything in time. Man can, at a pinch, also speak of himself, as species, when he speaks of God. But between him as historical individual and the eternal God he speaks of the difference is essential. It is still, as in Plato, an absolute knowledge of consciousness, not of self-consciousness, since the species has no self-consciousness, no self or personal I; it says at most "we", not "I". The observation that the species says "we" but not "I" is sharp: Aristotle's knowledge of man is knowledge of the species, which has no self-consciousness.

The Aristotelian system thus explains man's biological existence, not his truly human, historical existence, which is seen better on the anthropological plane, in the problem of freedom. Certainly Aristotle speaks of freedom, but everyone does, even Spinoza. If one does not play on words and has in view the true notion of freedom, made explicit in the Hegelian conception of the *Phenomenology*, one must say Aristotle's system is incompatible with it. This system excludes by definition a creator God, since eternity-in-time means eternity of the world, return, eternal return. Where there is no room for God's creative action, there is still less room for man's: man undergoes history but does not create it; he is not free in time. Here Aristotle does not go beyond Plato. But his system is even less acceptable, since it excludes even the transcendent free act. Eternity being in time and the eternal concept relating to eternity in time, every possibility of leaving time is excluded: one is outside time only by being in time. A temporal existence one could choose outside time would be conceptually unknowable, since it would not be eternal in time, whereas the concept can relate only to an eternity in time. In short, insofar as man changes, he does not know; not knowing, he is not free, by definition; and insofar as he knows, he does not change and so is not free either, in the normal sense. The dilemma is well put: in Aristotle knowledge and change exclude each other, so freedom, which requires both, is impossible. The link between creation and freedom anticipates Kojève's claim that human freedom is the secularised divine creation.

For Aristotle as for Plato one can have absolute knowledge of man only by relating man to eternity. The individual soul is too small to be known, says Plato in the *Republic*; to know it one must see it writ large, contemplate the city. For Aristotle Plato's eternal State is only a utopia; in fact all States change and sooner or later perish, so there is no absolute political knowledge relating to one possible form of the State. But fortunately there is a closed cycle in the transformation of States, eternally repeated, which can be understood conceptually, and in speaking of it one can grasp the different States and man himself through concepts. Certainly; but if so, history has nothing to do with what we call "history" today, and in this history man is anything but free. The cycle of constitutions (*Politics* V) is Aristotle's eternity in political time. Kojève's point is that cyclic history is not history in the modern sense, which requires unrepeatable novelty.

The Aristotelian variant of the Platonic system, replacing geometry by biology, thus explains man as animal but not as free historical individual; it does not even explain him, as Plato did, as fallen angel. The comparison completes the pagan variants: Plato explains the angel, Aristotle the animal, neither the historical man.

Beside the great philosophies there have always been more or less barbarous or barbarised theories. The Platonic-Aristotelian notion of the concept has been barbarised too, either by a vulgar and absurd negation or by a disfiguring acceptance. The vulgar negation says that the concept, far from being eternal, is as temporal as anything else existing in time: possibility 4, which Kojève will not discuss since it abolishes the very idea of true knowledge. It is scepticism or relativism, which Plato denounced as "sophistry", Kant criticised as "empiricism", and Husserl has recently denounced again as "psychologism". The lineage sophistry, empiricism, psychologism places Husserl's *Logical Investigations* in the line of the defence of the concept's eternity.

The disfiguring acceptance, no less absurd though less evidently so, continues to say the concept is eternal but, while eternal, in time, which means, one says, that it relates to what is in time, to the temporal (not to time but to the temporal), and relating to it, relates to it in time, existing in time before the temporal properly speaking. This is the well-known notion of the *a priori* or "innate idea" preceding experience. Against this "apriorism", which Kant called "dogmatism", is directed the famous first sentence of the Introduction to the *Critique of Pure Reason*: there is no doubt, Kant says roughly, that in time experience, temporal reality, always precedes the concept that appears in time as my knowledge. There is indeed no possible doubt. Vulgar apriorism starts from a supposed fact only to arrive at a truly untenable conception, both on the epistemological plane and on the anthropological, where it becomes the famous "free will". One need only develop this apriorism a little to arrive at scepticism or relativism, at Kant, or at a return to Plato and Aristotle. The reading of innate ideas as a temporal priority of the concept, which Kant rejects in the first sentence of the Introduction, is apt. "Free will" as the anthropological form of apriorism, a choice prior to experience, is a quick but suggestive link.

Before discussing Kant, Kojève mentions another solution, Spinoza's. As he said, Spinoza's system is the perfect incarnation of the absurd, which is why, when one tries to "realise" his thought, one feels the same vertigo as before a paradox of formal logic or set theory. The comparison with the paradoxes of set theory, Russell's and Cantor's, is apt: a totality that contains itself.

Curiously, absolute error or absurdity is, and must be, as "circular" as truth. So Spinoza's and Parmenides's absolute knowledge must be symbolised by a closed circle, without a central point (fig. 1). If Spinoza says the concept is eternity while Hegel affirms it is time, they have in common that the concept is not a relation, or relates only to itself. Being and conceptual thought are one and the same, said Parmenides; thought, the concept, is the attribute of substance, which does not differ from its attribute, says Spinoza. In both cases, Parmenides–Spinoza and Hegel, there is no "reflection" on being: being itself reflects on itself in and through, or better as, the concept. Absolute knowledge reflecting the totality of being is as closed on itself, as "circular", as being itself in its totality: there is nothing outside this knowledge, as there is nothing outside being. But there is an essential difference: the being-concept of Parmenides–Spinoza is eternity, Hegel's is time. Spinozist absolute knowledge must therefore also be eternity and exclude time: one needs no time to realise it; the *Ethics* must be thought, written, and read «en un clin d'œil» (in the twinkling of an eye) (p. 352). That is the absurdity of the thing; Plotinus, however, accepts the consequence. The phrase "in the twinkling of an eye" is the book's most famous objection to Spinoza: a system of eternity cannot be written in time. The shared circle of Spinoza and Hegel is the formal kinship Kojève insists on.

Plato already denounced this absurdity in the *Parmenides*. If being is really one, the One, excluding all diversity and so all change, if it is eternity annulling time, one could not speak of it, Plato remarks: discourse would have to be as one as the being it reveals and could not go beyond the single word "one". And even then; at bottom it is always a question of time. Discourse would have to be non-temporal, and without time man cannot utter even a single word. If being is one, or, what comes to the same, if the concept is eternity, "absolute knowledge" reduces for man to absolute silence. A footnote adds that Plato accepts this: the One is ineffable. The argument that a single word takes time is the decisive point: discourse is temporal in its very utterance.

For man, that is: for the speaking being who lives in time, needs time to live and to speak, to think conceptually. As we have seen, the concept as such is not, or does not seem to be, necessarily bound to time. The universe of concepts or ideas can be conceived as a universe of discourse: an eternal discourse in which all elements coexist, as Plotinus says. There seem to be non-temporal relations among concepts: all Euclid's theorems exist simultaneously in the whole of his axioms, as Plotinus insists. A footnote adds that there are also, as Descartes rightly remarked, non-temporal motions. There would thus be a non-temporal discourse. The idea of the Spinozist system is therefore not absurd: it is simply the idea of absolute knowledge. What is absurd is that this system is supposed to be made by a man, who in fact needed time to make it. In Plotinus this system belongs to the eternal Intelligence; or the system can exist outside time, but there is no access to it from temporal existence. The Spinozist system is Hegel's *Logic*, for which there would not and could not be a *Phenomenology* leading to it; or Descartes's system, to which one could not accede by a *Discourse on Method*. The *Ethics* is made according to a method one cannot account for in human language: it explains everything except the possibility for a man living in time to write it. And if the *Phenomenology* explains why the *Logic* appears at a particular moment of history and not at another, the *Ethics* demonstrates the impossibility of its own appearance at any moment of time. In short, the *Ethics* could have been written, if true, only by God himself, and, be it noted, by a God not incarnate. The formula that Spinoza's system is Hegel's *Logic* without a *Phenomenology* is the crux: what the *Phenomenology* adds is the account of how a man in time can reach the timeless system. Without it, the system has no author.

The difference between Spinoza and Hegel can be put this way: Hegel becomes God by thinking or writing the *Logic*; or, if one likes, it is in becoming God that he writes or thinks it. Spinoza, by contrast, must be God from all eternity to be able to write or think his *Ethics*. If a being that becomes God in time can be called "God" only on condition of using the term as a metaphor, a correct one, the being that is God always is God in the proper and strong sense. To be a Spinozist is therefore effectively to replace God the Father, without a Son, by Spinoza, while maintaining divine transcendence in all its rigour: Spinoza is the transcendent God who speaks to humans, but speaks to them as eternal God. «Et ceci est, évidemment, le comble de l'absurdité : prendre Spinoza au sérieux, c'est effectivement être — ou devenir — fou» (and this is obviously the height of absurdity: to take Spinoza seriously is effectively to be, or become, mad) (p. 354). The contrast between becoming God in time and being God eternally is the lecture's sharpest formulation. "God the Father without a Son" names Spinozism as a theology without incarnation, which is why it cannot be human.

Spinoza, like Hegel, identifies man, the Sage, with God. It seems one could say in both cases either that there is nothing but God or that there is nothing but man. In fact the two statements are not identical; the first is accepted by Spinoza, only the second expresses Hegel's thought. That is what Hegel means in saying that Spinoza's system is not a pantheism but an acosmism: the universe or totality of being reduced to God alone, a God without world and without men. And to say this is to say that everything that is change, becoming, time does not exist for Science; if it is in fact discussed in the *Ethics*, one does not know how or why these things appear there. Hegel's characterisation of Spinozism as acosmism, not atheism, is from the *Encyclopaedia* (§ 50) and the *Lectures on the History of Philosophy*. Kojève's inversion, Spinoza says "only God", Hegel "only man", marks the difference between acosmism and anthropotheism.

Using the symbolic circles, the difference between Hegel's and Spinoza's systems can be represented as follows. Start from the symbol of the theist system, in its pure form Plato's, but symbolising possibility 2 in general (fig. 2). For Aristotle several small circles must be inscribed in the large one to symbolise the relation of eternity and time (fig. 3); but these circles should nest, and in the end one would find the Platonic symbol with a single small circle: every truly coherent theism is a monotheism. For Kant the same symbol serves, but the small circle must be dotted, to show that Kant's theology has only the value of "as if" (fig. 4). In short, the symbol of the theist system holds for every system that defines the concept as an eternal entity related to something other than itself, whether this other is eternity in time, outside time, or time itself. Returning to Spinoza: starting from the theist system, Hegel suppresses the small circle, reduced beforehand by his predecessors to a singular point (fig. 5); Spinoza, by contrast, suppresses the large circle (fig. 6). The second set of diagrams, reproduced in the book, summarises the whole typology. Hegel removes God and keeps the world; Spinoza removes the world and keeps God.

The symbol is therefore the same in both cases: a closed homogeneous circle. This is important, since it shows that it suffices to deny that the concept is a relation to something other than itself to posit the ideal of absolute, circular knowledge. If the concept relates to another reality, an isolated concept can be proved true by adequation with this autonomous reality: there are partial evidences, even partial truths. But if the concept is revealed being itself, it can prove itself true only by itself; the demonstration no longer differs from what is to be demonstrated. This means that truth is a "system", as Hegel says. The word "system" is not found in Spinoza, but the thing is. Apart from Parmenides, he is the only philosopher who understood that the principle of all or nothing holds for knowledge: either one knows everything or one knows nothing, since only in seeing that one knows everything does one see, know, that one truly knows something. That is why the study of Spinoza is so instructive despite the absurdity of his standpoint. Spinoza posits the idea of total, "systematic", "circular" knowledge; only his system is impossible in time. «Et tout l'effort de Hegel consiste à créer un Système spinoziste pouvant être écrit par un homme vivant dans un Monde historique» (and Hegel's whole effort consists in creating a Spinozist system that can be written by a man living in a historical world) (p. 356). That is why, while admitting with Spinoza that the concept is not a relation, Hegel identifies it not with eternity but with time (see the Preface, Hoffmeister pp. 19 ff.). The sentence defining Hegel's project as a temporalised Spinozism is one of Kojève's most influential formulations. It explains the derivation of the circularity criterion from the non-referential concept: without an external referent, truth can only be the self-confirmation of a complete system.

The symbols of the two systems are identical; they differ only by their provenance, which one does not see in the drawing: suppression of the small or the large circle. This corresponds to reality. One understands that a temporal knowledge can finally encompass the totality of becoming; one does not understand how an eternal knowledge could absorb everything in time, for the simple reason that it would absorb us ourselves. It would be the absolute knowledge of consciousness that had completely absorbed self-consciousness, which is evidently absurd. Kojève stops; to know what the identification of the concept with eternity means, one must read the whole *Ethics*. He returns to Kant. The asymmetry, temporal knowledge can encompass becoming, eternal knowledge cannot absorb the knower, is the final argument against Spinoza.

Kant agrees with Plato and Aristotle, against Parmenides–Spinoza and Hegel, that the concept is an eternal entity related to something other than itself; only he relates this eternal concept not to eternity but to time. One can say Kant defines the concept as a relation precisely because he sees the impossibility of Spinozism, as Plato did to avoid the impossibility of Eleaticism. He may not have read Spinoza, but in the "Transcendental Deduction of the Categories" and the "Schematism" he says why the Spinozist conception of knowledge is impossible: it is impossible because for us, for man, "the concept without intuition is empty". The parallel between Plato's reaction to Parmenides and Kant's to Spinoza is Kojève's.

The Parmenidean-Spinozist (and Hegelian) concept, which is not related to a being other than itself but is being revealing itself to itself, is called in Kant the "transcendental I" or the "transcendental synthesis of apperception". "Transcendental" means in Kant what makes experience possible. Experience is essentially temporal, and everything temporal belongs to the domain of experience; so "transcendental" means what makes the temporal as temporal possible. Kant says the transcendental entity is "before" time or "outside" time; the transcendental is therefore "eternal", or, as Kant says, *a priori*: it precedes "the temporal taken as temporal". To say there is *epistēmē*, absolute knowledge, truly true truth, is to say there are universally and necessarily valid concepts, valid at every moment of time and excluding time from themselves, never modifiable: *a priori*, transcendental, eternal concepts. The identification of the transcendental unity of apperception with the Parmenidean-Spinozist concept is Kojève's striking thesis: Kant's "I think" is Spinoza's God.

The eternal concept, like every eternal entity, is not eternal in and by itself; it is eternal by its provenance from eternity, by its origin. The origin of the eternal concept is the "transcendental I" or "transcendental synthesis". This I or synthesis is therefore not eternal; it is eternity. Kant's transcendental self-consciousness is the substance of Parmenides conceived as a spiritual subject, that is, God: the real eternity that reveals itself to itself in and through the concept; the source of all being revealed by the concept and of all conceptual revelation of being; the eternal source of all temporal being. The argument turns on the distinction between the eternal and eternity: categories are eternal, the transcendental I is eternity.

But, says Kant, we humans can say of the transcendental I that it is and that it is one, and that is all we can say of it. Kant accepts Plato's critique of Parmenides: if the concept is eternity, absolute knowledge reduces to the single word *hen* or *on*, and no discourse is possible. Strictly, one cannot even say the transcendental I is and is one, since, as will be seen, the categories of being and quantity cannot be applied here. At most one can say it is "something" and not nothing; but one cannot say it is a thing with such and such qualities; and this being of which one can only say that it is, is a being (*Sein*) that, as Hegel will say, does not differ from nothing (*Nichts*). The link to the opening of Hegel's Logic, pure being equals nothing, is Kojève's: the transcendental I is Hegel's pure being.

The Parmenidean-Spinozist system is therefore impossible, says Kant. The unity of self-conscious essential eternity has twelve aspects, the famous twelve category-concepts. These twelve aspects of eternity are evidently eternal: they "precede" everything in time; they are valid at every moment of time and, excluding time, cannot change; they are *a priori*. The error or illusion of Parmenides–Spinoza was to believe that the eternal that comes from eternity reveals it by determining it, qualifying it; for them the category-concepts are attributes of the One that is and can be attributed to it. A footnote adds that for Plotinus they cannot be attributed to the One, but can be to the One-that-is, the second hypostasis, Intelligence or the intelligible cosmos. For Kant this is not so. The reading of Spinoza's attributes as categories applied to God is Kojève's. The Plotinian distinction between the One and the One-that-is maps onto the Kantian distinction between the unknowable I and the categories.

It is not so because it is impossible, and at the end of § 16 of the second edition of the *Critique of Pure Reason* Kant explains why. A determination of eternity by the eternal category-concepts would be possible only by an Understanding "through whose self-consciousness all the manifold would at the same time be given", or by an Understanding whose representations' objects exist by the mere fact of these representations: a divine or "archetypal" Understanding. The being that, thinking itself, thinks everything thinkable, and creates the objects thought by the mere act of thinking them, is God. Spinoza was right to call God Parmenides's *hen-on* that coincides with the concept revealing it; but he was wrong to forget that only God can apply this concept to himself. For us, who are not God, to apply our concept to God is to relate the concept to something other than itself; and the concept that is a relation in the proper sense, a relation to something else, is at most eternal, not eternity. Either the very basis of Spinozism is false (the concept is not eternity), or, if the concept is eternity, only God can do Spinozism. To affirm that one is not God and write the *Ethics* is not to know what one is doing, to do something one cannot account for, something "absurd". The appeal to the intuitive understanding of § 16 is precise: Kant's archetypal intellect is Spinoza's God, and its unavailability to us is the refutation of Spinozism.

But in principle, according to Kant, God could write the *Ethics*. The whole question is whether a man, Spinoza, cannot be God. For Kant this is impossible, since man can draw nothing from the content of his self-consciousness: taken in itself, the human I is a point without content, an empty vessel, and the manifold content must be given to it (*gegeben*), must come from elsewhere. Or, what comes to the same: it is not enough for man to think for there to be true knowledge; the object man thinks must also exist, and exist independently of his act of thinking it. As Kant says, human consciousness necessarily has two constituents: concept (*Begriff*) and intuition (*Anschauung*), the latter presenting a manifold content given to man and not produced by him, from him, or in him. The "empty vessel" returns from the fourth lecture (p. 320), where the Sage was the empty vessel to be filled by the *Encyclopaedia*. The contrast is instructive: for Kant the human I remains empty and must receive; for Hegel it is filled by history.

The concept of a being that is not God is therefore a relation: it can be eternal, but it is not eternity. That is why Spinozism is "absurd": «Il est absurde parce que Spinoza n'est pas Dieu» (it is absurd because Spinoza is not God) (p. 359). The conclusion is one of Kojève's wittiest sentences.

But there remains the conception of Plato–Aristotle, which admits that the human concept is a relation, but a relation to eternity and not to time. Eternity or God implies the manifold in its own unity and itself creates the manifold it reveals through the concept. This manifold, being the eternal development of eternity within itself, is itself eternity: the manifold universe of ideas-concepts, which has nothing to do with the space-time world. But it is eternity itself that develops into this universe; it is not our concept, only eternal, that produces it. This universe is given to us, and our concept relates to it. Our absolute knowledge is not God's knowledge of himself but our knowledge of God, of a God essentially different from us, transcendent: a theo-logical knowledge in the proper sense, the relation of the eternal concept to eternity, not to time. The reconstruction presents Platonism as a theory of a given intelligible manifold, to which Kant's critique will apply.

According to Kant this too is impossible, for the simple reason that the relation of the eternal to eternity must itself be eternal or non-temporal, whereas our knowledge is not only in time but, more seriously, itself temporal: we need time to think. In principle, says Kant, there can be a non-spatio-temporal intuition; in principle one can apply the category-concepts to any given manifold; a non-divine being could in principle develop an absolute knowledge revealing the non-spatio-temporal universe of Platonic ideas. But the non-divine being called man cannot. If Spinozism is possible only for God, Platonism is possible only for a non-divine intelligence other than human intelligence, an "angelic" intelligence for instance. For, once more, and it is an irreducible and inexplicable fact according to Kant (cf. the end of § 21), for us humans the given manifold is always given in spatio-temporal form. The triad God, angel, man, each with its possible knowledge, is a clear summary: Spinoza is for God, Plato for angels, Kant for men.

We can think only on condition that a manifold is given to us. But this manifold must be, as a whole and in each of its elements; so the one and unique being of Parmenides must differentiate itself into a manifold being. For us the identical can be diverse only on condition of being space or being in space: two identical geometrical points can differ only by their positions in space, and space is nothing but the infinite whole of points rigorously identical in their intrinsic character, which is the absence of all "character", and nonetheless different from one another. But for there to be knowledge the diverse must be identified: every act of knowing is a synthesis, says Kant, introducing unity into the given manifold. And for us the diverse can be identical only in time or as time. A footnote explains: to identify point A with point B is to make it pass from A to B; in general, to identify two different things is to say that it is one and the same thing that has changed; and time is only the infinite whole of all identifications of the diverse, of all changes whatever. The definitions are the lecture's most original philosophical content: space is the diversity of the identical, time the identity of the diverse. They ground Kojève's thesis that knowledge, as synthesis, is essentially temporal.

So for us knowledge, the identification of the diverse, can take place only in time, since the identification of the diverse is already time. One always knew that the human concept appears at some moment of time and that man needs time to think. But Kant was the first to see that this is not accidental but essential to man. The world in which man thinks is necessarily a temporal world. And if actual human thought relates to what is in time, Kant's analysis shows that it is time that makes the actual exercise of thought possible: we can use our eternal concepts only by relating them to time as such, by "schematising" them, as Kant says. A footnote adds: it is not enough, as Plato or Descartes do, to geometrise physics; one would also have to geometrise the thought of the philosopher who performs this geometrisation, exclude time from this thought itself, which is impossible. The ideal of the "universal tensor" of modern relativistic physics is the ideal of a non-temporal knowledge: all content would be given simultaneously in this formula; but even if this tensor is possible, it is only an algorithm, not a discourse; all discursive thought necessarily develops in time, since the attribution of a predicate to a subject is already a temporal act. The footnote qualifies the fourth lecture's tensor analogy (p. 310): the tensor is timeless because it is not discourse. The claim that predication is a temporal act is the decisive argument for the temporality of the concept: "S is P" identifies the diverse, which is change.

So the "transcendental I" that is only self-consciousness is Spinoza's God, of which we can say nothing; the transcendental I that is the source of category-concepts relating to a non-spatio-temporal, eternal manifold is the I as pre-Kantian, Platonic-Aristotelian philosophy conceived it, and this I is not human, since it is supposed to be able to think outside time. Only the transcendental I that is the origin of schematised categories, concepts relating to time, is the human transcendental I, which makes actual human thought possible. The three I's, God's, the angel's, and man's, complete the typology.

Human thought takes place in time and is a temporal phenomenon; as such it is purely empirical, a *doxa*. But for the eternal concept to be applicable to the temporal, the concept must first be "schematised", applied to time as such. This application takes place "before" time or "outside" time; it is *a priori*, unmodifiable, always valid. Absolute knowledge is therefore the whole of the relations between the eternal concept and time: the whole of the "synthetic principles", Kant's ontology. Kojève's reading of the Analytic of Principles as absolute knowledge of the relation between concept and time is a precise identification of what is absolute in Kant.

What does the Kantian conception give for the world and for man? In the natural world, time is represented by motion. The temporalised concept relates to real motion, and what makes the temporalised concept possible, the "schematism", the relation to time "prior" to time, corresponds to what makes real motion really possible: force. To say that the eternal concept relates to time is, among other things, to state a dynamic conception of matter and the world, a physics of forces. Kantian philosophy will necessarily rediscover Newtonian physics; conversely, if the world is as Newton's physics says, one must accept Kant's philosophy as a given truth. The correspondence between schematism and force is Kojève's: the Kantian relation of concept to time is the philosophical form of Newtonian dynamics.

But even setting aside that the Newtonian world is as uninhabitable for man as Plato's geometrical world, one can point to an insufficiency in the Kantian-Newtonian conception of the purely natural world. The impossibility of relating the concept to eternity means in the end the impossibility of an absolute geometrical knowledge of the world: one denies the notion of cosmos, of the eternal or static structure of the natural universe, and so cannot explain the existence of eternal structures in the world; in particular one cannot explain, as Aristotle does, the biological species. In general one does not explain purely spatial structure: one explains by force the motion of the planets, but not the structure of the solar system. And the impossibility is absolute: that in the real world laws apply to stable entities is, for Kant, a "transcendental chance". One can say it is so, and that is all one can say. The "transcendental chance" returns from the third lecture (p. 303). The insufficiency is precise: Kant explains motion but not form.

Certainly Kant develops a theory of the living being in the third Critique. But this theory holds only in the mode of "as if", the third Critique having no equivalent in the "system"; a footnote explains that this is precisely because knowledge properly speaking starts from the relation between concept and time, not between concept and eternity. And what holds for the animal in particular holds for the animal in general, the cosmos: here too the cosmology, Leibnizian moreover, has only a "regulative" value. The same holds for God: God being eternity, no knowledge relating to God is possible. The reading repeats the second lecture's remark on the third Critique (p. 285).

In sum, if Kantian knowledge is closed, total and definitive or absolute, one finds the theist or Platonic schema of two circles (fig. 2). But since the concept does not relate to eternity, the small circle remains forever purely hypothetical (fig. 4). Suppressing it, one obtains not Hegel's single closed circle (fig. 5) but the open circle without fixed limits of scepticism (fig. 7). The eternal concept being related to time, no absolute adequation is possible; at most the eternal infinity of time can fully fill the frames of the eternal category-concepts. Thought, which is in time, never gets there. That is why Kant says absolute knowledge is an "infinite task" (*unendliche Aufgabe*). The two positions of Kant, hypothetical theology or infinite task, are the two faces of criticism: the as-if God and endless science.

What does the Kantian conception mean on the anthropological plane? The concept is eternal but relates to time. If the concept is eternal, there is in man something that places him outside time: freedom, the "transcendental I" taken as "practical reason" or "pure will". If there is a relation of the concept to time, there is also application of the pure will to temporal reality. But insofar as there is an *a priori* concept, which here means an act of freedom, the relation to time takes place "before" time. The act of freedom, while relating to time, is therefore outside time: the famous "choice of the intelligible character". This choice is not temporal, but it determines the whole of man's temporal existence, in which there is therefore no freedom. The intelligible character (*Critique of Pure Reason*, Third Antinomy; *Religion within the Limits*) is the Kantian form of the Platonic prenatal choice.

One thus finds again Plato's myth. Only in Plato the concept relates to eternity, in Kant to time, and this difference means that the "transcendental choice" is made not, as in Plato, with a view to what man is, or "was", outside time, but with a view to what he is, or "will be", in time. In Plato it is an affirmation, in Kant a negation: there, becoming in time what one is eternally; here, not being eternally what one has become in time; there, acceptance of eternal nature, here, negation of temporal nature. Or again: there, the freedom of the Angel who adheres to God or separates from him; here, the freedom of fallen man who disowns his sin in a single extra-temporal act. A footnote adds that this is how the Christian act must be conceived: having to be compatible with eternal divine grace, it must be "transcendental". The contrast between Platonic affirmation and Kantian negation is fine: Kant introduces negativity into freedom, though outside time. This is why Kojève places Kant in the modern, Judaeo-Christian variant.

Here, as in the description of the natural world, there is progress; but there as here, there is an irreducible insufficiency. Man as historical being remains inexplicable: one understands neither the world of concrete things in which he lives nor the history he creates by temporal free acts. The verdict on Kant parallels the verdict on Plato and Aristotle.

The result is this. Possibility I is excluded, since man cannot realise it. Possibility IV is excluded too, since it abolishes the very idea of truth in the proper sense. Possibility II gives partial explanations, but in none of its three variants does it account for history, for man as free creator in time; in any case, if in the Kantian or "criticist" variant one can at a pinch speak of an infinite historical evolution, it is impossible to reach absolute knowledge of history and so of historical man. Consequently, if philosophy wants to reach absolute knowledge of man as we now conceive him, it must accept possibility III. That is what Hegel did in saying that the concept is time. It remains to see what this means. The conclusion is reached by elimination: only the identification of concept and time allows absolute knowledge of historical, free man. The eighth lecture will develop what this identification means.

### Eighth Lecture: Note on Eternity, Time, and the Concept (Continued and Concluded)

With Hegel we pass to the third possibility, the identification of the concept with time. At the dawn of philosophy Parmenides identified the concept with eternity, so time had nothing to do with the concept, with absolute knowledge, *epistēmē*, or truth, nor with man, insofar as man, bearer of the concept, is the empirical existence of knowledge in the temporal world; and this temporal existence of the concept is inexplicable from Parmenides's standpoint, as from Spinoza's. With Plato man's existence becomes necessary for knowledge: true knowledge, the concept, is now a relation, so absolute knowledge necessarily implies two elements, one of which can at a pinch be called "man". But the concept is eternal and relates to eternity outside time; the eternal is not eternity, and the eternal concept is already, so to speak, closer to time than the Parmenidean-Spinozist one; yet, not being eternity, it relates to eternity, and this eternity has nothing to do with time. Only with Aristotle does time enter absolute knowledge: the eternity to which the concept relates is now in time, but time enters absolute knowledge only insofar as time itself is eternal ("eternal return"). Kant is the first to break with this pagan conception and take account, in metaphysics itself, of the pre-philosophical Judaeo-Christian anthropology of the Bible and the Epistle to the Romans, the anthropology of historical man endowed with an immortal "soul": for Kant the concept, while remaining eternal, relates to time taken as time. The recapitulation is a history of the progressive approach of concept to time, in which each step corresponds to a stage in the understanding of man. The reference to Romans places Paul's anthropology of the divided, historical self behind Kant.

Only one possibility remains to go further in bringing concept and time together, avoiding the difficulties of the earlier conceptions: to identify them. Hegel does this, and it is his great discovery, which makes him a great philosopher, of the rank of Plato, Aristotle, and Kant. He is the first to identify concept and time, and, curiously, he says so in so many words, whereas in the other philosophers one would seek in vain the explicit formulas Kojève used in his schematic exposition. He said it in the Preface, in the paradoxical sentence already cited, and repeats it verbatim in Chapter VIII. The observation that Hegel alone states his principle explicitly, whereas the formulas for Plato, Aristotle, and Kant are Kojève's reconstructions, is a fair acknowledgement of the constructed character of the typology.

This sentence marks an extremely important date in the history of philosophy. Setting aside Parmenides–Spinoza, there are two great periods: from Plato to Kant, and the one that begins with Hegel. Kojève has said, without being able to demonstrate it, that philosophers who do not identify concept and time cannot account for history, for the existence of the man each of us believes himself to be, the free historical individual. The periodisation, Plato to Kant and Hegel onward, makes Hegel the founder of modern philosophy in Kojève's sense. The admission "without being able to demonstrate it" is candid.

Hegel's reform therefore aimed chiefly to account for the fact of history. On its phenomenological plane, Hegel's philosophy or "Science" describes the existence of man who sees himself living in a world where he knows himself a free and historical individual. On its metaphysical plane, it tells us what the world must be for man to appear to himself so. On the ontological plane, it asks what being itself must be to exist as such a world. And Hegel answers that this is possible only if the real concept, being revealed to itself by an empirically existing discourse, is time. The three planes, phenomenological, metaphysical, and ontological, organise Kojève's later project; they are the three levels of analysis of Appendix I.

The whole of Hegel's philosophy can therefore be summed up in the sentence: "Time is the concept itself that is there in empirical existence", in real space or the world. But reading the sentence is not enough to know what Hegelian philosophy is, as saying that the eternal concept relates to time is not enough to know Kant's. These condensed formulas must be developed, and to develop a formula fully is to reconstruct the whole philosophy in question, supposing its author made no error in developing it. The qualification "supposing its author made no error" anticipates the error Kojève will find.

It is out of the question to reconstruct Hegel's whole philosophy from the identification of empirically existing concept and time. Kojève will make only some very general remarks, analogous to those he made about the other conceptions. The modesty is methodological: the lecture gives the principle and its first consequences.

Hegel's philosophy aims to account for the fact of history. One can conclude that the time he identifies with the concept is historical time, the time in which human history unfolds, or better, the time that realises itself not as the motion of the stars but as universal history. A footnote adds that to identify time and concept is to understand history as the history of the human discourse that reveals being; and indeed for Hegel real time, universal history, is ultimately the history of philosophy. The footnote states a surprising consequence: history is ultimately the history of philosophy, which follows from the identification of time with the concept.

In the *Phenomenology* Hegel is very radical. He says at the end of the penultimate paragraph and the start of the last (Hoffmeister p. 563) that nature is space, whereas time is history. There is no natural, cosmic time; there is time only insofar as there is history, human existence, speaking existence. Man, who in the course of history reveals being by his discourse, is the "empirically existing concept" (*der daseiende Begriff*), and time is nothing but this concept. Without man, nature would be space and space only. Only man is in time, and time does not exist outside man: man is time and time is man, the "concept that is there in the spatial empirical existence of nature". The reading of ¶807–808, where Hegel speaks of nature as the externalisation of Spirit in space and of history as its externalisation in time, grounds Kojève's dualism textually. The equation "man is time" is the lecture's thesis.

In his other writings Hegel is less radical and admits a cosmic time; but in doing so he identifies cosmic and historical time. Two footnotes follow. It may be impossible to do without time in nature, since biological life is probably an essentially temporal phenomenon. And «C'est là, à mon avis, son erreur de base» (that, in my opinion, is his basic error) (p. 366): if life is a temporal phenomenon, biological time certainly has a different structure from historical or human time; the whole question is how these two times coexist, and they probably coexist with a cosmic or physical time differing from both in structure. The footnote locates Hegel's "basic error" precisely: the identification of cosmic and historical time, which is the monism Kojève has rejected since 1933–34 (p. 38). The suggestion that there are three times, cosmic, biological, and historical, with different structures, is Kojève's own programme.

This matters little for the moment. If Hegel identifies the two times, admitting only one, one can apply to historical time, which alone interests us, everything he says of time in general. Curiously, the decisive text on time is in the "Philosophy of Nature" of the Jena *Realphilosophie*. This text was translated and commented by Koyré in an article born of his course on Hegel's early writings: «article décisif, qui est la source et la base de mon interprétation de la PhG» (a decisive article, which is the source and basis of my interpretation of the *Phenomenology*) (p. 367). Kojève will reproduce briefly its main results. The acknowledgement of Koyré's "Hegel à Iéna" (1934) as the source of his whole interpretation is the most important bibliographical statement in the book. It confirms the 1933–34 summary's credit to Koyré (p. 57).

The text shows that the time Hegel has in view is what is for us historical time, not biological or cosmic, since it is characterised by the primacy of the future. In the time considered by pre-Hegelian philosophy, the movement went from past to future through the present. In the time Hegel speaks of, the movement arises in the future and goes toward the present through the past: future, past, present, (future). This is the specific structure of properly human, historical time. A footnote adds that the time in which the present has primacy may be cosmic or physical time, whereas biological time would be characterised by the primacy of the past; the physical or cosmic object seems a mere presence (*Gegenwart*), the fundamental biological phenomenon is probably memory in the broad sense, and the specifically human phenomenon is without doubt the project. It may also be that the cosmic and biological forms of time exist as time only in relation to man, to historical time. The structure future–past–present is Koyré's reading of the Jena text, and it recalls Heidegger's ecstatic temporality in *Being and Time* §65, where the future has primacy. The footnote's triad, presence, memory, project, assigns a dimension to each kind of time.

Consider the phenomenological, or anthropological, projection of this metaphysical analysis of time; a footnote adds that on the ontological plane one would have to study the relations between thesis = identity, antithesis = negativity, and synthesis = totality, but he will not. The movement engendered by the future is the movement born of Desire: specifically human, creative Desire, bearing on an entity that does not exist and has not existed in the real natural world. Only then can one say the movement is engendered by the future, since the future is precisely what is not yet and has not already been. Desire can bear on an absolutely non-existent entity only if it bears on another Desire as Desire. Desire is the presence of an absence: I am thirsty because there is an absence of water in me; it is the presence of a future in the present, the future act of drinking. To desire to drink is to desire something that is, water, and so to act according to the present. But to act according to the desire of a desire is to act according to what is not yet, according to the future. The being that acts so is in a time where the future has primacy, and conversely the future can really have primacy only if there is in the real spatial world a being capable of acting so. The link between Desire and future joins the Introduction's anthropology to the theory of time: human Desire is the future present in the world. The distinction between desiring water and desiring a desire is the difference between animal and historical time.

In Chapter IV Hegel shows that Desire bearing on another Desire is necessarily the desire for recognition, which, opposing Master and Slave, engenders and moves history, as long as it is not definitively abolished by satisfaction. So, in realising itself, the time in which the future has primacy engenders history, which lasts as long as this time lasts; and this time lasts only as long as history lasts, as long as human acts are performed for the sake of social recognition. The mutual dependence of historical time and the desire for recognition implies that when desire is satisfied, historical time ends: the end of history is the end of time in the human sense.

If Desire is the presence of an absence, it is not, as such, an empirical reality; it does not exist positively in the natural, spatial present. It is rather like a gap or "hole" in space, a void, a nothingness; and it is, so to speak, in this "hole" that the purely temporal future comes to lodge in the spatial present. Desire relating to Desire relates to nothing; to "realise" it is to realise nothing. By relating only to the future, one reaches no reality and is not really in motion. On the other hand, if one affirms or accepts the present spatial real, one desires nothing, does not relate to the future, does not go beyond the present, and so does not move either. To realise itself, Desire must relate to a reality, but cannot relate to it positively; it must relate to it negatively. Desire is necessarily the desire to negate the given real or present, and its reality comes from the negation of the given reality. A footnote explains: the desire to drink is an absence of water, but its quality, thirst, is determined not by the absence as such but by its being an absence of water, and this desire is realised by the "negation" of real water in drinking. The negated real is the real that has ceased to be: the past real, the real past. Desire determined by the future appears in the present as a reality, as satisfied Desire, only on condition of having negated a real, a past. The way the past has been negatively formed according to the future determines the quality of the real present. Only the present so determined by future and past is a human or historical present. In general, historical movement arises from the future and passes through the past to realise itself in the present or as temporal present. The time Hegel has in view is human or historical time: the time of conscious and voluntary action that realises in the present a project for the future, formed from knowledge of the past. The image of Desire as a "hole" in space is Kojève's most famous metaphor for negativity, and it is Sartre's too, who will make the "hole in being" a central image of *Being and Nothingness*. The derivation of the three dimensions of time from the structure of negating Desire is the lecture's core: future (the desired non-being), past (the negated real), present (the realisation).

Two footnotes illustrate. First: a moment is called "historical" when the action performed in it is performed according to the agent's idea of the future, a project: one decides a future war, and so acts according to the future. But for the moment to be truly "historical" there must be change: the decision must be negating in relation to the given. In deciding for the future war one decides against the reigning peace, and by the decision for war one turns peace into the past. The present historical act, triggered by the idea of the future, is determined by the past it creates: if the peace is secure and honourable, the negation that relegates it to the past is the act of a madman or a criminal; if it is humiliating, its negation is an act worthy of a statesman. The example of war and peace, given in 1939, is pointed: the value of a decision for war depends on the peace it destroys. The criterion of madness and crime returns (p. 32).

The second footnote takes the famous anecdote of the Rubicon as an example of a "historical moment". What is in the present properly speaking? A man walks at night beside a small river: something extremely banal, nothing "historical". Even if the man were Caesar, the event would be nothing historical if Caesar walked so merely because of some insomnia. The moment is historical because the night walker is thinking of a coup d'état, civil war, the conquest of Rome, and world domination; and, note, because he has the project of doing so, since all this is still in the future. The event would not be "historical" if there were not a real presence (*Gegenwart*) of the future in the real world, first in Caesar's brain. The present is "historical" only because it involves a relation to the future, or more exactly because it is a function of the future: Caesar walking because he is thinking of the future. That is the sense in which one can speak of a primacy of the future in historical time. But this is not enough. Suppose the walker were a Roman adolescent "dreaming" of world domination, or a clinical "megalomaniac" constructing a "project" otherwise identical to Caesar's. The walk at once ceases to be a "historical event". It is historical only because it is Caesar who, walking, thinks of his project, or "decides", turning a "hypothesis" without precise relation to real time into a concrete "project for the future". Why? Because Caesar has the possibility, but not the certainty, since then there would be no future properly speaking and no true project, of realising his plans. This possibility is assured to him by his whole past, and his past alone: the whole of the actions of fight and labour performed in presents according to the project, the future. It is this past that distinguishes the "project" from a mere "dream" or "utopia". There is therefore a "historical moment" only where the present organises itself according to the future, on condition that the future enters the present not immediately (*unmittelbar*, the case of utopia) but mediated (*vermittelt*) by the past, by action already accomplished. The Rubicon footnote is one of the most celebrated passages of the book. It distinguishes project from dream by the mediation of the past: what makes Caesar's walk historical is his history of action. The distinction between immediate and mediated future gives Hegel's logical terms a precise temporal meaning.

It is historical time, then, and Hegel says this "time is the concept itself that exists empirically". Leave aside for the moment the term "concept". Hegel says time is an X, something, that exists empirically. This can be deduced from the very analysis of the Hegelian notion of historical time. Time in which the future has primacy can realise itself, can exist, only on condition of negating or annihilating. For there to be time there must be something other than time: first of all space, the place of rest, as it were. So no time without space: time is something that is in space. A footnote recalls that Desire, time, was called a "hole", and for there to be a hole there must be a space in which it exists. Time is the negation of space, of diversity; but if it is something and not nothing, it is because it is the negation of space. One can really negate only what really exists, what resists; and the space that resists is full: extended matter, real space, the natural world. Time must therefore exist in a world: it is something that "ist da", as Hegel says, that is there in a space, in empirical space, a sensible space or natural world. Time annihilates this world by making it sink at every instant into the nothingness of the past. But time is nothing but this annihilation of the world, and if there were no real world to be annihilated, time would be pure nothingness: there would be no time. The time that is, is therefore something that "exists empirically", in a real space or spatial world. The dependence of time on space is Kojève's ontological dualism in its most precise form: negativity (time) exists only as the negation of identity (space); without nature, man is nothing.

We have seen that the presence of time, in which the future has primacy, in the real world is called Desire bearing on another Desire, and that this Desire is specifically human, the action realising it being man's very being. The real presence of time in the world is therefore called man. «Le Temps est l'Homme, et l'Homme est le Temps» (time is man, and man is time) (p. 370). The equation is the conclusion of the argument from Desire.

In the *Phenomenology* Hegel does not say so explicitly, since he avoids the word "man" there. But in the Jena lectures he says: "Geist ist Zeit", "Spirit is time". And "Spirit" means in Hegel, especially here, "human spirit" or man, more particularly collective man, the people or State, and ultimately integral man, humanity in the totality of its spatio-temporal existence, the totality of universal history. The Jena formula "Geist ist Zeit" is Kojève's strongest textual support; it is also the source of Heidegger's discussion of Hegel's concept of time in *Being and Time* §82, which Kojève does not mention.

Time, historical time with the rhythm future–past–present, is therefore man in his integral empirical, spatial reality: time is the history-of-man-in-the-world. Without man there would be no time in the world; nature that did not harbour man would be only a real space, a footnote adds, four-dimensional. Certainly the animal too has desires and acts according to them, negating the real: it eats and drinks as man does. But the animal's desires are natural; they bear on what is and are determined by it; the negating action they give rise to cannot negate essentially, cannot change the essence of what is. As a whole, in its reality, being is not modified by these "natural" desires; it does not change essentially according to them; it remains identical with itself and so is space, not time. An animal certainly transforms the aspect of the natural world it lives in, but it dies and returns to the earth what it took from it; and since its offspring repeat it identically, the changes it makes in the world are repeated too. As a whole nature remains what it is. A footnote adds: if there is time here, it is biological time, Aristotle's circular time, eternity in time, the time in which everything changes to remain the same. Man, by contrast, transforms the world essentially by the negating action of his fights and labour, an action born of non-natural human Desire bearing on another Desire, on something that does not really exist in the natural world. A second footnote: the olive tree of the time of Pericles is "the same" olive tree as in the time of Venizelos; but the Greece of Pericles is a past that never becomes a present again, and Venizelos represents in relation to Pericles a future that has never yet been a past. Only man creates and destroys essentially. Natural reality implies time only if it implies a human reality. Man creates and destroys essentially according to the idea he forms of the future, and the idea of the future appears in the real present in the form of a Desire bearing on another Desire, a desire for social recognition. The action born of this Desire engenders history. There is time only where there is history. The olive tree footnote is one of Kojève's finest illustrations: nature repeats, history does not. The reference to Venizelos, the Greek statesman who died in 1936, is contemporary. The distinction between the animal that "returns to the earth what it took" and man who transforms essentially is the difference between metabolism and history.

So "die Zeit ist der daseiende Begriff selbst" means: time is man-in-the-world and his real history. But Hegel also says "Geist ist Zeit": man is time. We have just seen what this means: man is Desire bearing on another Desire, desire for recognition, negating action performed to satisfy it, bloody fight for prestige, the Master–Slave relation, labour, historical evolution that ends in the universal and homogeneous State and in absolute knowledge revealing integral man realised in and by this State. In short, to say man is time is to say everything Hegel says of man in the *Phenomenology*; and it is also to say that the existing universe, and being itself, must be such that man so conceived is possible and can realise himself. The sentence identifying Spirit and time thus sums up the whole of Hegel's philosophy, as the other schematic formulas sum up those of Plato, Aristotle, and so on. The chain of equations recapitulates the whole course from the Introduction to Chapter VIII: the identification of Spirit and time contains Kojève's reading in nuce.

But in the schematic formulas it was a question of the concept, and Hegel says not only "Geist ist Zeit" but also "die Zeit ist der Begriff der da ist". These are two ways of saying the same thing. If man is time, and time is the "empirically existing concept", man is the "empirically existing concept". And he is: being the only speaking being in the world, he is the incarnate *Logos*, the *Logos* become flesh and so existing as an empirical reality in the natural world. Man is the empirical existence (*Dasein*) of the concept, and the "empirically existing concept" is man. To say time is the "empirically existing concept" is therefore to say time is man, provided man is conceived as Hegel does in the *Phenomenology*. Everything Hegel says of man in the *Phenomenology* holds of time, and conversely everything one can say of the "appearance" (*Erscheinung*) or "phenomenology" of time, of Spirit, in the world, Hegel says in the *Phenomenology*. The identification of man with the *Logos* become flesh (John 1:14) is anthropotheism in its Johannine form: the incarnation is the existence of discourse in nature.

To understand the paradoxical identification of time and concept, one must therefore know the whole of the *Phenomenology*: on the one hand, that the time in question is human or historical time, where the future determines the present through the past; on the other, how Hegel defines the concept. A footnote adds that the Hegelian concept is identified with Hegelian time; one cannot identify the pre-Hegelian concept with pre-Hegelian time, nor the Hegelian concept with pre-Hegelian time, nor the pre-Hegelian concept with Hegelian time. The footnote's combinatorics is a warning against simplification: both terms of the identification must be understood in Hegel's sense.

It remains to recall briefly what the concept is for Hegel. In Chapter VII Hegel said that all conceptual comprehension (*Begreifen*) is equivalent to a murder. Kojève recalls what he had in view. The claim that comprehension is murder is Kojève's reading of the Preface's "tremendous power of the negative" (¶32), which he attributes loosely to Chapter VII.

As long as meaning (or essence, concept, *Logos*, idea) is incarnate in an empirically existing entity, this meaning or essence, and this entity, live. As long as, for example, the meaning or essence "dog" is incarnate in a sensible entity, it lives: it is the real, living dog that runs, drinks, and eats. But when the meaning "dog" passes into the word "dog", becomes an abstract concept different from the sensible reality it reveals by its meaning, the meaning dies: the word "dog" does not run, drink, or eat; in it the meaning ceases to live, it dies. That is why conceptual comprehension of empirical reality is equivalent to a murder. Hegel knows well that one need not kill a dog to understand it by its concept, to name or define it, nor wait until it actually dies to do so; a footnote notes, however, that conceptual or "scientific" comprehension of the dog in fact leads sooner or later to its dissection. But, says Hegel, if the dog were not mortal, essentially finite or limited in duration, one could not detach its concept from it, make the meaning incarnate in the real dog pass into the non-living word; into the meaningful word, the abstract concept, which exists not in the dog, which realises it, but in the man who thinks it, in something other than the sensible reality the concept reveals by its meaning. The concept "dog" that is my concept, other than the living dog and relating to it as an external reality, is possible only if the dog is essentially mortal, if it dies or annihilates itself at every instant of its existence. This dog that annihilates itself at every instant is precisely the dog that lasts in time, that ceases at every instant to live or exist in the present to annihilate itself in the past, as past. If the dog were eternal, existing outside time or without time, the concept "dog" would never be detached from the dog itself. The empirical existence of the concept "dog" would be the living dog, not the word "dog", thought or spoken. There would be no discourse (*Logos*) in the world; and since empirically existing discourse is only man, actually speaking, there would be no man in the world. The word-concept detaches itself from the sensible here and now, but it can do so only because the here and now, spatial being, is temporal, annihilates itself in the past. And the real that disappears into the past maintains itself, as non-real, in the present in the form of the word-concept. «L'Univers du Discours (le Monde des Idées) est l'arc-en-ciel permanent qui se forme au-dessus d'une cataracte : et la cataracte, — c'est le réel temporel qui s'anéantit dans le néant du Passé» (the universe of discourse, the world of ideas, is the permanent rainbow that forms above a waterfall; and the waterfall is the temporal real annihilating itself in the nothingness of the past) (p. 374). The theory of the concept as the "murder" of the thing is Kojève's most influential contribution to twentieth-century French thought: Blanchot's "the word gives me the being, but deprived of being" and Lacan's "the symbol manifests itself first of all as the murder of the thing" derive from it. The image of the rainbow over the waterfall is the lecture's most beautiful: the concept is the permanence produced by ceaseless disappearance.

A footnote compares Aristotle: for him there is a concept "dog" only because there is an eternal real dog, the species "dog", always present; for Hegel there is a concept "dog" only because the real dog is a temporal entity, essentially finite or "mortal", annihilating itself at every instant, and the concept is the permanent maintenance of this annihilation of the spatial real, which annihilation is nothing but time. For Hegel too the concept maintains itself, "eternally" if one likes, but in the sense of "as long as time lasts". But for him it is only the concept "dog" that maintains itself (the concept, the temporal annihilation of the real dog, which lasts as long as time lasts, since time is this annihilation as such), whereas for Aristotle it is the real dog that maintains itself, eternally in the strict sense, since there is eternal return, at least as species. That is why Hegel explains what Aristotle cannot: the maintenance, in and by man, of the concept of an animal belonging to an extinct species, even without fossil remains. The extinct-species argument is an elegant refutation of Aristotle: concepts outlive their referents, which Aristotelian realism cannot explain.

Another footnote: Kant already saw that conceptual knowledge implies memory, and Hegel maintains this idea, Platonic in the last analysis. For Hegel too, *Er-innerung*, the internalisation of the objective real in and through the concept that reveals it but is in me, is also *Erinnerung*, remembrance. And there is memory only where there is time, where the present real annihilates itself by becoming the unreal past. In general, in his theory of the concept Hegel only specifies, and so transforms, the Kantian theory of schematism. For Kant the concepts, categories, apply to given being (*Sein*) because time serves them as "schema", intermediary or "mediation" (*Vermittlung*, in Hegel). But this mediation is purely passive: time is contemplation, intuition. In Hegel, by contrast, the mediation is active: it is the deed (*Tat*, *Tun*), the negating action of the given, the activity of fight and labour. This negation of the given (*Sein*), of the "present", is historical time, and historical time is this active negation. For Hegel as for Kant, it is time that allows the application of the concept to being; but in Hegel this mediating time of conceptual thought is "materialised": it is a movement (*Bewegung*), a dialectical movement, active, so negating, so transforming the given, so creating the new. If man can understand, reveal, being by the concept, it is because he transforms given being according to this concept, which is then a project, and makes it conform. The transformation of given being according to the concept-project is precisely conscious and voluntary action, the doing (*Tun*) that is labour and fight. For Kant being conforms to the concept, and mediation by time only allows passing from one to the other without modifying either; that is why Kant cannot explain this conformity, which is for him a given, a chance (*transzendentale Zufälligkeit*). Hegel, by contrast, explains this conformity, which for him is a process of conformation, by his dialectical ontology: being becomes conformed to the concept, at the end of history, through the completed totality of negating action that transforms being according to this same concept. In Kant, time is "schema" and passive "intuition"; in Hegel it is "movement" and conscious and voluntary "action". Consequently the concept or *a priori* is in Kant a "notion" that lets man conform to given being, whereas in Hegel the *a priori* concept is a "project" that lets man transform given being and make it conform. The footnote contains the most precise statement of Kojève's relation to Kant: Hegel's concept is Kant's schematised category made active. The formula "the concept is a project" resolves the "transcendental chance" (p. 303): being conforms to the concept because action has made it conform.

Certainly the real lasts in time as real. But because it lasts in time, it is its own memory: at every instant it realises its essence or meaning, which is to say that it realises in the present what remains of it after its annihilation in the past; and this something that remains and that it re-realises is its concept. At the moment the present real sinks into the past, its meaning (essence) detaches itself from its reality (existence); and there appears the possibility of retaining this meaning outside reality by passing it into the word. This word reveals the meaning of the real that realises in the present its own past, this same past that maintains itself "eternally" in the word-concept. In short, the concept can have an empirical existence in the world, which is nothing but human existence, only if the world is temporal, only if time has an empirical existence in the world. That is why one can say time is the empirically existing concept. The formula "the real is its own memory" gives the concept a ground in the real's temporal self-maintenance.

A long footnote gives the ontological version. On the ontological plane this "metaphysical" observation means that being must have a trinitarian structure, being "synthesis" or "totality" uniting "thesis" or "identity" and "antithesis" or "negativity", this presence in existing being of the negation of being being precisely time. To understand the identification of concept and time, form the concept of being, of the totality of what is. What is the difference between this concept "being" and being itself? In content they are identical, since no "abstraction" has been made. And yet, despite Parmenides, the concept "being" is not being, otherwise there would be no discourse; the concept would not be *Logos*. What distinguishes being from the concept "being" is only the being of being itself: being is as being, but is not in the concept "being", while being "present" in it by its content, as the meaning of the concept "being". One obtains the concept "being" by subtracting being from being: being minus being equals the concept "being", not nothing or zero, since the negation of A is not nothing but "not-A", something. This apparently paradoxical, even "impossible", subtraction of being from being is in reality something quite "ordinary": it takes place literally "at every instant" and is called time. For it is time that at every instant takes from being, the totality of what is in the present, its being, by making it pass into the past, where being is not, or is no longer. But for there to be time there must "be" a past (the pure or eternal present is not time): the past and the being that has sunk into it are not nothing; they are "something". One is something only in the present. To be something, the past and past being must maintain themselves in the present while ceasing to be present. And the presence of past being is the concept "being", being from which being has been taken without turning it into pure nothing. The concept "being" is, if one likes, the "memory" of being, in the double sense: it is being that "remembers", and it "remembers" its being. At the level at which we are, one does not usually speak of "memory"; the memory in view is called "time", or more exactly "temporality", that general medium of being in which, "besides" the present, there is something else: the past, and the future, of which he will not speak here. So if there is a concept "being", it is because being is temporal, and one can say the concept is time, the coexistence of present and past. It is evident that being "conforms" to the concept "being", since the latter is being itself minus being; one can say that being is the being of the concept "being", which is why being that is in the present can be "conceived" or revealed by the concept; or more exactly, being is conceived "at every instant" of its being; or again, being is not only being but also truth, the adequation of concept and being. This is simple. The whole question is where error comes from. For it to be possible, the concept must be detached from being and opposed to it. It is man who does this; more exactly, man is the concept detached from being, or better still, he is the act of detaching the concept from being. He does it by negating negativity, by action, and here the future, the pro-ject, intervenes. This detachment is equivalent to an inadequation (the deep sense of *errare humanum est*), and one must negate or act again to arrive at conformity between the concept (= project) and being (made to conform to the project by action). For man the adequation of being and concept is therefore a process (*Bewegung*), and truth (*Wahrheit*) is a result. Only this "result of the process" deserves the name of discursive "truth", since only this process is *Logos* or discourse: being, before its negation by man, does not speak, since it is the concept detached from being that is in the word or *Logos*, or as word-*logos*. Hegel says all this in a passage of the Preface that gives the key to his whole system (Hoffmeister pp. 29–30); see Appendix II. The footnote is the densest page of the book. "Being minus being equals the concept being" is its formula: the concept is being without its being, which is what time does to the present at every instant.
