The theory of error as man's detachment of concept from being, and of truth as the result of action that re-establishes conformity, completes the account: *errare humanum est* in the strong sense that to be human is to err, since man is the gap between concept and being. The reference to the Preface's passage on the power of the negative (¶32) and to Appendix II marks where the theory of death will be developed.

So there is no concept in the world as long as there is no empirically existing time in it. The empirical existence of time in the world is human Desire, bearing on Desire as Desire. So no conceptual comprehension without Desire. Desire is realised by negating action, and human Desire by the action of the fight to the death for pure prestige. This fight is realised by the Master's victory over the Slave and by the Slave's labour in the Master's service. It is the Slave's labour that realises the Master's Desire by satisfying it. So, as Hegel says expressly in Chapter IV, no concept without labour: thought (*Denken*) and Understanding (*Verstand*), the conceptual comprehension of the world, are born of the Slave's labour. The chain from Desire to concept through fight and labour closes the circle begun in the Introduction.

We now understand why. It is labour, and labour alone, that transforms the world essentially, creating truly new realities. If there were only animals on earth, Aristotle would be right: the concept would be incarnate in the eternal species, eternally identical with itself, and would not exist, as Plato claimed, outside time and the world. But one would then not understand how the concept could exist outside the species, in the temporal world in the form of a word; one would not understand how man could exist, this being who is not a dog, for instance, and in whom the meaning "dog" nonetheless exists as much as in the dog, since there is in him the word-concept "dog". For this to be possible, the being revealed by the concept must be essentially temporal, finite, having a beginning and an end in time. It is not the natural object, not even the animal or plant, but only the product of human labour that is essentially temporal. Human labour temporalises the spatial natural world; so it is labour that engenders the concept existing in the natural world while being other than this world; labour that engenders man in this world, that transforms the purely natural world into a technical world inhabited by man, a historical world. The thesis that only the product of labour is essentially temporal, having a beginning and an end, grounds the concept in labour: the artefact is the first thing whose essence exists before its existence (as project) and outlives it (as concept).

Only the world transformed by human labour reveals itself in and by the concept existing empirically in the world without being the world. «Le Concept est donc le Travail, et le Travail est le Concept» (the concept is therefore labour, and labour is the concept) (p. 377). And if, as Marx rightly remarks, labour is for Hegel "the essence of man" (*das Wesen des Menschen*), one can also say that for Hegel the essence of man is the concept. That is why Hegel says not only that time is the concept but that it is Spirit. If labour temporalises space, the existence of labour in the world is the existence of time in this world; and if man is the concept and the concept is labour, man and the concept are also time. The return of Marx's phrase from the Introduction's epigraph (p. 9) closes the book's arc: "Hegel grasps labour as the essence of man" becomes "the concept is labour".

If so, one must say first that there is conceptual comprehension only where there is an essentially temporal, historical reality, and second that only historical or temporal existence can reveal itself through the concept; in other words, conceptual comprehension is necessarily dialectical. A footnote explains that "dialectical" comprehension is nothing but the historical or temporal comprehension of the real. Dialectic reveals the trinitarian structure of being: in and through its dialectic the real reveals itself not *sub specie aeternitatis*, outside time or as eternally identical with itself, but as a present situated between past and future, as a *Bewegung*, a creative movement, or as a result that is a project and a project that is a result, a result born of the project and a project engendered by a result; in a word, the real reveals itself in its dialectical truth as a synthesis (see Appendix I). The footnote defines dialectic by time: the dialectical is the historical, and synthesis is the present between past and future.

If so, and if nature is only space and not time, one would have to conclude that there is no conceptual comprehension of nature. One would understand in the strong sense only where there is time; one would truly understand only history. In any case it is only history that one can and must understand dialectically. «Il faudrait le dire. Mais Hegel ne le dit pas. Et c'est là, je crois, son erreur de base» (one would have to say it. But Hegel does not say it. And that, I believe, is his basic error) (p. 378). The conclusion repeats the earlier footnote's charge: Hegel's basic error is to extend dialectic, and so the concept, to nature.

First, there is a hesitation in Hegel. On the one hand he says nature is only space. On the other he sees that biological life is a temporal phenomenon; hence the idea that life (*Leben*) is a manifestation of Spirit (*Geist*). But Hegel also sees, and is the first to say explicitly, that truly human existence is possible only through the negation of life: as we know, the risk of life in the fight for prestige is constitutive of man. Hence an opposition of life and Spirit. But if this opposition exists, life is not historical; there is no biological dialectic, and so no conceptual comprehension of life. The hesitation is precise: if life is Spirit, man's negation of life is incoherent; if life is opposed to Spirit, it cannot be understood dialectically.

Yet Hegel affirms this comprehension. He imagines, following Schelling, a dialectical biology and sets it out in the *Phenomenology* (Chapter V, A, a). Certainly he denies the conceptual or dialectical comprehension of non-vital reality, but this only leads him to say that the real world is a living being. «D'où sa philosophie absurde de la Nature, sa critique insensée de Newton, et sa propre physique "magique" qui a discrédité son Système au XIXe siècle» (hence his absurd philosophy of nature, his senseless critique of Newton, and his own "magical" physics that discredited his system in the nineteenth century) (p. 378). The verdict is harsh and explicit. It explains Kojève's own neglect of the philosophy of nature: he considers it the discredited part of the system.

There is more. Dialectical comprehension applies only to historical reality, created by labour according to a project. To affirm, as Hegel does, that all comprehension is dialectical and the natural world comprehensible is to affirm that this world is the work of a demiurge, a creator God conceived in the image of working man. And that is what Hegel says in the *Logic*, in saying that his *Logic*, his ontology, is "the thought of God before the creation of the world". It would follow that Hegel understands the world because the world is created according to the concept Hegel has. We are in full paradox: Hegelian anthropotheism ceases to be an image; Hegel is actually God, creator God and eternal God. But a man cannot affirm, without being mad, that he created the world. If the thought revealed in the *Logic* is the thought that created the world, it is certainly not Hegel's thought; it is the thought of a creator other than Hegel, other than man in general: God's. And the *Logic*, despite its title, is not simply logic; like Spinoza's *Ethics*, it is theo-logy, logic, thought, or discourse of God. The argument turns Kojève's critique into a reductio: the dialectic of nature makes Hegel a Spinoza, which is madness, or a theologian, which contradicts his atheism. The comparison with the *Ethics* recalls the seventh lecture.

A footnote says: personally Kojève does not believe this consequence necessary. He sees no objection to saying that the natural world escapes conceptual comprehension. This would mean only that the existence of nature reveals itself through mathematical algorithm, for instance, and not through concepts, meaningful words. Modern physics arrives at this result: one cannot speak of physical reality without contradictions; as soon as one passes from algorithm to verbal description, one contradicts oneself (corpuscles and waves, for instance). There would thus be no discourse revealing physical or natural reality, which, as Galileo already sensed, would reveal itself to man only through the articulated silence of the algorithm. One understands conceptually or dialectically, one can speak of, physical matter only insofar as it is the "raw material" of a product of human labour. And raw material itself is not molecules or electrons but wood, stone, and so on, things which, if not living, exist at least at the scale of life and of man as living being. It seems the algorithm, being non-temporal, does not reveal life; but dialectic does not either. It may therefore be necessary to combine Plato's conception, for the mathematical or geometrical substructure of the world, with Aristotle's, for its biological structure, and Kant's, for its physical or dynamic structure, reserving Hegelian dialectic for man and history. The footnote is Kojève's positive philosophy of nature, and it is striking. Nature is revealed by the "articulated silence of the algorithm"; wave–particle duality shows that physics cannot be put into consistent words. The proposed division of labour, Plato for geometry, Aristotle for life, Kant for dynamics, Hegel for history, turns the typology of the previous lectures into an ontological pluralism. It is the fullest statement of the dualism that runs through the whole book.

But leave the natural world. Hegel made immense philosophical progress in identifying concept and time, since in so doing, in discovering dialectical knowledge, he found the means to establish a phenomenology, a metaphysics, and an ontology of history, of man as we conceive him today and as he is in reality. The concession limits the achievement to the human domain, where Kojève holds it valid.

Now for the decisive consequence of this discovery for man. The concept is time, in the strong sense of a time in which there is a future in the strong sense, a future that will never become either present or past. Man is the empirical existence of the concept in the world, so the empirical existence in the world of a future that will never become present. This future is for man his death, his own future that will never become his present; and the only reality or presence of this future is the knowledge man has in the present of his future death. So if man is concept and the concept is time, if man is an essentially temporal being, man is essentially mortal; and he is concept, absolute knowledge or incarnate wisdom, only if he knows it. «Le Logos ne devient chair, ne devient Homme, qu'à condition de vouloir et pouvoir mourir» (the *Logos* becomes flesh, becomes man, only on condition of willing and being able to die) (p. 379). The consequence is the culmination of the lecture: the future that never becomes present is death, and the concept exists only in a mortal being who knows he will die. This is *Being and Time* §§46–53 inscribed in Hegel's theory of the concept. The final sentence rewrites John 1:14 as a theory of finitude.

This makes us understand why possibility III, adopted by Hegel, appears so late in the history of philosophy. To deny that the concept is eternal, to say it is time, is to deny that man is immortal or eternal, at least insofar as he thinks, insofar as he is truly human. And man accepts his death only in the last extremity; so it is also only in its last extremity that philosophy accepted possibility III. A footnote adds that the expression "anthropotheism" is thus only a metaphor: circular, dialectical absolute knowledge reveals finite or mortal being; this being is not divine; it is indeed human being; but man can know it as his only on condition of knowing himself mortal. The explanation of the lateness of Hegel's discovery by the human refusal of death gives the history of philosophy an existential motive. The footnote on anthropotheism as metaphor, confirming the fifth lecture (p. 326), is the correct reading of the whole: man is "God" only in knowing himself mortal.

"Alles Endliche ist dies, sich selbst aufzuheben", says Hegel in the *Encyclopaedia*: all that is finite is this, to overcome itself. Only finite being overcomes itself dialectically. If the concept is time, if conceptual comprehension is dialectical, the existence of the concept, and so of being revealed by the concept, is essentially finite. History itself must therefore be essentially finite; collective man, humanity, must die as the human individual dies; universal history must have a definitive end. The quotation from the *Encyclopaedia* (§ 81, Addition) grounds the finitude of history in the finitude of the dialectical. The claim that humanity must die is the collective form of being-toward-death, stated earlier (p. 64).

We know that for Hegel this end of history is marked by the advent of Science in the form of a book, the appearance in the world of the Sage or absolute knowledge. This absolute knowledge, being the last moment of time, a moment without future, is no longer a temporal moment. If absolute knowledge becomes in time, or better as time or history, the knowledge that has become is no longer temporal or historical: it is eternal, or, if one likes, it is eternity revealed to itself; it is the substance of Parmenides–Spinoza that reveals itself through a discourse, and not through silence, precisely because it is the result of a historical becoming; «il est l'Éternité engendrée par le Temps» (it is eternity engendered by time) (p. 380). This is what Hegel will explain in the text of the second step of the second section of the second part of Chapter VIII. The conclusion reconciles Hegel with Spinoza at the end: absolute knowledge is Spinoza's substance, but reached through time and so speakable. "Eternity engendered by time" is the formula that resolves the problem posed at the start of the sixth lecture: truth is eternal because it is the result of a completed history.

### Ninth Lecture: Interpretation of the Second Part of Chapter VIII (Continued)

Kojève resumes the reading of Chapter VIII where he left off at the end of the fifth lecture: the second section of the second part, devoted to the analysis of the Sage's existence in the world. This analysis of the Sage's empirical existence (*Dasein*) proceeds in three steps. In the first, already begun, Hegel spoke of the Sage's relation to objective reality (*Wirklichkeit*); in the second he speaks of the relations between the Sage and time; in the third he will situate the Sage in objectively real time, history. Hegel proceeds by abstraction. In fact objective reality and time cannot be separated: objective reality is temporal, and time is possible only insofar as it is objectively real. But for the needs of analysis Hegel separates them: he spoke of objective reality without speaking of time, and now speaks of time distinguished from objective reality, abstract time, the notion of time. The return to the text after the three lectures on time frames what follows as the application of the theory.

Hegel gives the definition of time in the first sentence of the second step (Hoffmeister p. 558). Kojève translates: time is the concept itself that is there, in empirical existence, and that presents itself (*vorstellt*) to consciousness as empty intuition (*Anschauung*). He has commented at length on the first words. The first part of the sentence refers, as he said, to time in general, including real time or history, of which Hegel will speak in the third step. But the second part indicates that here Hegel speaks of abstract time. Time here is "empty intuition": the time Kant speaks of, and philosophers in general; time taken in isolation, "abstracting from" what is in time; the empty "vessel" that in fact contains temporal reality but is considered as this empty vessel. And this time, Hegel says, "presents itself to consciousness": it presents itself as something outside consciousness. It is THE time, which is not, or not only, MY time: cosmic time, in which man participates but which he does not create. It is also the notion of time that is in me, as opposed to time itself, which is also outside me. The "empty intuition" is Kant's form of inner sense. Kojève's reading of the second half of the sentence as describing abstract time prepares the paradox that follows.

Hegel identifies time and concept, so to speak of abstract time is also to speak of the abstract concept, and he says so here: time, meaning abstract time, is the concept itself, taken as an empty entity presenting itself to consciousness from outside. This is the ordinary conception of the concept: the "subjective" concept that is or can be separated from its real content, the empty vase containing reality, and also the concept that exists outside me, independently of me. Time is interpreted as the concept is: if the concept is opposed to reality, if knowledge is a relation, time is itself opposed to reality, and conversely. As soon as one distinguishes between concept and reality, one must also distinguish between the concept and man: if the dog is something other than the concept "dog", this concept is something other than my concept of the dog; the concept is a more or less Platonic "idea", a non-real entity, a void filled by an entity other than itself, presenting itself to consciousness from outside. And since time and concept are in fact one, whatever one says of the concept one must say of time, which is what is generally done. The parallel between the referential concept and objective time is the application of the sixth lecture's typology: philosophies that separate concept from reality also separate time from man.

But in the sentence Hegel does not say, as Kojève does, "abstract time"; he says "time" simply. It seems that for him time in general, real time itself or history, is "an empty intuition that presents itself to consciousness". And that is what he in fact thinks, as the sequel shows. At first sight the sentence contradicts everything Kojève has said about time in the *Phenomenology*. In fact it does not, and to see this one need only develop the elliptical sentence a little. In developing it, as Hegel does himself in what follows, an essential aspect of the Hegelian conception of time appears, which Kojève only evoked earlier and must now analyse more closely. The apparent contradiction is real: Hegel calls time an "empty intuition" immediately after identifying it with the concept. Kojève's resolution follows.

According to Hegel, pre-Hegelian philosophy, which opposes the concept, and so time, to reality, is not an accidental error. When it appears on earth, it is not even an error at all: it is true, for its time. For concept and reality do not coincide from the start; they coincide only at the end. It is by labour that man abolishes the initial opposition between himself and the natural world, and by his fights that the particular abolishes the initial opposition between himself and the universal, the social and political world. As long as the effort of labour and fight is not completed, the opposition remains real. As long as this is so, man is right to say that concept and thing are not one; and as long as this is so, time does not coincide with reality either and is external to man. The historical justification of pre-Hegelian philosophy is the most generous statement of Kojève's historicism: the philosophies of separation were true while the separation was real.

Pre-Hegelian philosophy is not false, but it becomes so, only in, through, and for absolute knowledge, for which the concept, and time, coincides with the real, or better, which is this coincidence. But absolute knowledge, universal and homogeneous, can appear only in a reality that is likewise so: it presupposes the homogeneity and universality of the State, of the human world, and the "abolition" of the opposition between this world and the natural world. This happens when human Desire is fully and definitively satisfied. There is then no more negating action: man is reconciled with the given world, which is now the result of his wholly accomplished effort, and with what he himself is in and through this world. But Desire and the action born of it are the manifestation of human or historical time, time properly speaking. The man reconciled with what he is no longer goes beyond the given real; he ceases to create history, ceases to be time. And if the universal and homogeneous State and the Science that reveals it complete history, they also complete time. The argument is precise: time is the manifestation of Desire; satisfied Desire ends time. The end of history is literally the end of time.

At the moment when the concept, and so time, coincides with objective reality and ceases to be external to man, time ceases to be historical or human time, time in the proper sense. Concept and time coincide in, through, and for absolute knowledge or the Sage. The Sage certainly appears in time, but his advent "at the end of times" marks the end of time. For the result of his temporal action, Science, is no longer time: Science is eternity revealing itself to itself. The phrase "at the end of times" is eschatological: the Sage is the last event.

As long as time lasts, as long as there is truly time, time and the concept are therefore necessarily abstract. And pre-Hegelian philosophy, which affirms this, is therefore true not only for its time but for all time: it remains true until the advent of absolute knowledge, until the end of history, until the end of time as such. The formula "true for all time" is paradoxical and exact: the separation of concept and reality is true as long as there is time.

In other words, when time ceases to be abstract, it ceases to be time. Human or historical time, time properly speaking, is necessarily and essentially abstract. It is abstract, first, in being opposed to objective reality. As long as man opposes himself to nature, which is for him objective reality, nature is space and not time; time is only in and through man; it is, if one likes, subjective. And when man "abolishes" his opposition with nature, he abolishes time too. Second, time is abstract in being external to man. As long as man has not realised the universal and homogeneous State, the particular differs from the universal, and the particular's time, MY time, is not time in general: the social and political future is not my future; «je meurs avant la fin de l'Histoire, et je nais après son commencement» (I die before the end of history, and I am born after its beginning) (p. 384). But when the opposition of particular and universal is abolished, history stops and time is abolished too. The two senses of "abstract", opposed to nature and external to the individual, correspond to labour and fight. The sentence about dying before the end and being born after the beginning states the individual's finitude within historical time.

Time is man himself; to abolish time is therefore also to abolish man. "Man's true being is his action", that is, successful action; man is the objective result of his action. The result of the action of the Sage, the integral and perfect man who completes the becoming of human reality, is Science. But the empirical existence (*Dasein*) of Science is not man; it is the Book. It is not man, not the Sage in flesh and blood, but the Book that is the appearance (*Erscheinung*) of Science in the world, this appearance being absolute knowledge. The step from "abolishing time" to "abolishing man" is the most radical consequence of the theory. The Book, not the Sage, is the final existence of Spirit.

Certainly the objective result of action always detaches itself from the agent and survives him. But as long as this result is not total or perfect, universal and homogeneous (non-expandable and free of contradictions), it has a future of its own, since it changes and perishes. It is not only in time but is time: it is historical or truly human. That is why the result of a man's action is always realised in and through, or better as, a new human action. The result of the Sage's action, by contrast, is perfect. It does not change and cannot be surpassed: in short, it has no future properly speaking. This result is therefore not a historical event properly speaking, not a true moment of time; and to say so is to say it is no longer a human reality. Once more, the empirical existence of Science in the world is not man but the Book. The glosses "universal = non-expandable" and "homogeneous = free of contradictions" repeat the second lecture's definitions (p. 288). Every imperfect result provokes new action; the perfect result provokes none.

Certainly this existence is "empirical" and so has a duration: the Book lasts too; it deteriorates, is reprinted, and so on. But the *n*th edition differs in nothing from the first: nothing can be modified or added. While changing, the Book remains identical with itself. The time in which it lasts is therefore natural or cosmic, not historical or human. Certainly the Book, to be a Book and not bound blackened paper, must be read and understood by men. But successive readers change nothing in the Book. And if to read the Book man must live, be born, develop, and die, his life, reduced essentially to this reading, creates nothing new. For, let us not forget, the universal and homogeneous State being there and Desire fully satisfied, there is no more fight or labour; history is over; there is nothing more to do; and one is man only insofar as one reads and understands the Book that reveals everything that has been and could be done. «L'avenir de Paul qui n'a pas encore lu le Livre n'est que le passé de Pierre qui l'a déjà lu» (the future of Paul, who has not yet read the Book, is only the past of Peter, who has already read it) (p. 385). The time in which man-reader-of-the-Book lasts is therefore Aristotle's cyclical or biological time, not linear, historical, Hegelian time. The description of post-historical life as reading the Book is Kojève's most extreme image. Its consequence is explicit: post-historical man lives in cyclical, biological time; he is no longer human in the strong sense. The sentence about Paul and Peter is the formula of post-historical repetition.

Once more: to realise absolute knowledge in the form of a Book, to make the integral concept coincide with the real taken as a whole, to annul the difference between the real and time and so abolish the externality of time in relation to man, is to abolish time itself; and so to abolish man himself as a free, temporal individual. Time is the concept that is man, historical man, the man of Desire, the man not satisfied by what is and what he is, the man who transforms the given by fight and labour. That is why time is always and essentially "abstract", external to the natural reality that is objective in relation to man, and external to man himself. The chain of identifications closes: the Book's completion is man's abolition.

This is what Hegel says in the sentence of which Kojève cited only the beginning, stopping at a semicolon (Hoffmeister p. 558). Kojève translates: time is the concept itself that is there and presents itself to consciousness as empty intuition. For this reason Spirit necessarily appears in time, and it appears in time as long as it has not grasped its pure concept, that is, has not annulled (*tilgt*) time. Time is the pure external self intuited and not grasped by the self; it is the concept only intuited. When the concept grasps itself, it overcomes its temporal form, conceives the intuition, and is conceived and conceiving intuition. The sentence (¶801) is the textual basis for the "annulment of time", which Kojève reads literally.

In the Jena lectures Hegel said "Geist ist Zeit", "Spirit is time". Here he says "der Geist erscheint in der Zeit", "Spirit appears in time". Has he changed his mind? Kojève thinks not; it is, he believes, a simple terminological difference. There, *Geist* meant *Volksgeist*, Spirit in the process of becoming. Here it is Spirit become, completed and perfect, revealing itself to itself in and through, or as, absolute Science (*Wissenschaft*), or, as Hegel says, "that has grasped its concept". Or again: there "Geist" meant "man", whereas here the word refers to a Book. The reconciliation of the two formulas by a shift in the reference of *Geist*, from man to Book, is ingenious. It is also a reading that stakes much on the Book.

The Book that results from the Sage's activity, actualising absolute knowledge as the empirical existence of Science, is certainly not a purely natural entity, like a stone. It has a meaning; it is a discourse; it is an entity that reveals its meaning itself to itself. On the one hand, the Book is a spiritual entity, and since its content is total, since it reveals only its own content, one must say it is integral Spirit, *der Geist*. On the other hand, the Book is certainly not a human being. It reveals its content without modifying it; it has no Desire, is not an action. Remaining eternally identical with itself, it has no true future, so it is not time. And since its eternal content relates only to itself, it is not only eternal but eternity. The Book is thus the realisation of possibility I of the sixth lecture: the concept as eternity. The Parmenidean-Spinozist ideal is realised at the end of history in a Book.

But the Book is the result of the activity of the Sage, who, as man and citizen of the perfect State, integrates the whole historical evolution of humanity. So this history itself is in the end only the history of the Book, or more exactly of the evolution of knowledge leading to it; and this history of the Book is time. If "Geist" means Spirit completed or existing empirically as a Book, which detaches itself from integral man or the Sage after his fall into the absolute past, after the end of history, one can no longer say Spirit is time: one must say it is eternity. But Parmenides and Spinoza were wrong to believe that eternity can be revealed by discourse without time. Plato was wrong to believe eternity independent of time, and Aristotle mistaken in saying eternity exists in time as eternity. Kant too was mistaken in thinking eternity ontologically precedes time. No, says Hegel: eternity, revealed by discourse, is the result of time; «elle est le Temps qui est mort d'une mort pour ainsi dire naturelle» (it is time that has died a death one might call natural) (p. 387). Only this eternity, which presupposes time and results from it, being its integration, can be revealed by human speech. It does not exist in time as eternity, since as long as time lasts, it is time that exists and not eternity. But eternity, or integral Spirit, appears in time. For the Book is written at a determinate moment of time, and can be written only at the last moment, since it proceeds from the totality of time; which means it is already, potentially, in the first moment of time. It is this virtual presence of integral Spirit in time (the presence of the end of time in its very beginning and throughout its duration; or again, the essential finitude of time) that Hegel calls "the appearance of Spirit in time". And this "appearance", which is time, is nothing but man in his temporal evolution, precisely what Hegel called "Geist" in the Jena lectures. In this acceptation one must indeed say "Geist ist Zeit". The rectification of all four earlier positions in one paragraph is the lecture's philosophical summit: eternity is neither prior, outside, within, nor identical with time, but its result. "Time that has died a natural death" is the image of the end of history. The "virtual presence of the end in the beginning" is Kojève's reading of teleology as finitude.

As Hegel says, then, "Spirit appears in time as long as it has not grasped its concept, that is, annulled time". This annulment takes place, at the last moment of time, in and through Science. In and for Science object and subject coincide; man speaks only of himself; it is self-consciousness, not consciousness of the external. The man who no longer relates to an object opposed to him no longer needs to negate in order to maintain himself in existence while preserving his identity with himself. And the man who no longer negates has no true future, since he accepts the given present forever. He is no longer Hegelian or historical time. This man is the citizen of the perfect State, fully and definitively satisfied by it. Nothing changes or can change any more in this universal and homogeneous State. There is no more history; the future there is a past that has already been; life there is therefore purely biological. There is no longer man properly speaking. The human, Spirit, has taken refuge, after the definitive end of historical man, in the Book, which is therefore no longer time but eternity. The phrase "life there is purely biological" is the most explicit statement in the book of what post-historical existence means. Kojève's 1962 note to the second edition, on post-historical animality, develops it.

A footnote draws the full consequence. The fact that at the end of time the word-concept (*Logos*) detaches itself from man and exists empirically no longer as a human reality but as a Book reveals man's essential finitude. It is not only this or that man who dies: man dies as such. «La fin de l'Histoire est la mort de l'Homme proprement dit» (the end of history is the death of man properly speaking) (p. 388). After this death there remain, first, living bodies having human form but deprived of Spirit, of time or creative power; and second, a Spirit that exists empirically, but in the form of an inorganic, non-living reality: a Book that, not even animal life, has nothing more to do with time. The relation between the Sage and his Book is thus rigorously analogous to that between man and his death. My death is indeed mine, not another's; but it is mine only in the future, since one can say "I shall die" but not "I am dead". So with the Book: it is my work, not another's, and it is about me; but I am in the Book, I am this Book, only as long as I write or publish it, as long as it is still a future, a project. Once published, the Book detaches itself from me; it ceases to be me, as my body ceases to be me after my death. Death is as impersonal and eternal, as inhuman, as the Spirit fully realised in and through the Book. This footnote is one of the most consequential in twentieth-century French philosophy. "The death of man" anticipates Foucault's formula in *Les Mots et les choses* (1966) by nearly three decades. The analogy of Sage and Book with man and death is exact and grim: the Book is the Sage's corpse, the impersonal remainder of a finished life. "I shall die" but not "I am dead" is the Heideggerian mineness of death applied to authorship.

One can therefore say, as Hegel does in the text cited, that time is the concept "only intuited" (*angeschaut*), not "conceived" (*begriffen*). Intuition is the contemplation of something outside the one who contemplates: a state of consciousness of the external, not of self-consciousness. There is time only where there is *Bewusstsein*, consciousness of the external, human existence in the proper sense, the existence of a being that opposes itself radically to the natural world and transforms it essentially in order to "abolish" this opposition. At the very moment it succeeds, consciousness becomes self-consciousness, subject coincides with object, Science appears on earth, and time is annulled by the annulment of Desire and of historical or human action. The equation of time with consciousness of the external completes the analysis: time is the gap between man and world, and it closes when the gap closes.

In the passage ending the paragraph Hegel develops his idea (Hoffmeister p. 558). Kojève translates: time therefore appears as the destiny and necessity of Spirit that is not completed in itself: the necessity of enriching the share self-consciousness has in consciousness, of setting in dialectical motion the immediacy of the in-itself, the form in which substance is in consciousness; or conversely, taking the in-itself as the inner, the necessity of realising and revealing what is at first only inner, of delivering it to the certainty of itself. The passage (¶802) names time "the destiny and necessity of incomplete Spirit".

It is always the same thing. Time is history, and history is essentially finite. History is the progressive transformation of consciousness into self-consciousness, and so, in the end, the history of philosophy. But this history of philosophy presupposes history in the ordinary sense, whose course "sets the in-itself in motion" and "realises and reveals what is at first only inner". The essential transformation of nature and the objective realisation of the subjective idea take place only through the action of fight and labour. As long as man fights and works, there is history, there is time, and Spirit is nowhere else than in time, where it exists as these fights and labours of man. But when history is "completed" (*vollendet*), when man has realised everything, history stops definitively and time is annulled; man dies or disappears as historical man, and Spirit subsists as Spirit that no longer changes and so is eternity. The double history, real history and the history of philosophy, is restated with the priority of the first.

Now come the applications of this conception of the relation between eternity, time, and concept (Hoffmeister p. 558). Kojève translates: for this reason one must say that nothing is known that is not in experience (*Erfahrung*), or, as one also says to express the same thing, that is not present as felt truth, as an eternal revealed inwardly, as a sacred object of belief, and so on, according to the various customary expressions. For experience is precisely the fact that the content, which is Spirit, exists in itself, is substance and so object of consciousness. The sentence (¶802) links experience, feeling, inner revelation, and faith as forms of knowing an object given.

This is evidently a paraphrase of the beginning of the Introduction to the *Critique of Pure Reason*. In time, says Kant, the real precedes knowledge. Hegel accepts this: as long as the concept is time, it relates to something other than itself, and in this relation the thing is before the concept. But Hegel takes "experience" (*Erfahrung*) in a very broad sense, including religious experience. In the sentence he also says: for eternity to be revealed, there must first be time. In time the concept is outside the real, so it must be the same for the concept of Spirit: it must be conceived as external to real Spirit. Spirit external to its concept, external to man, is God. So as long as time lasts, until the advent of Science, Spirit reveals itself to man in the form of theological knowledge. As long as history lasts there is necessarily religion, and, if one likes, God. But the ultimate cause and deep reason for the existence of religion, and of God, is implied in the very nature of time or history, of man. «Ce n'est pas Dieu qui crée l'Homme avant le Temps ; c'est l'Homme qui crée ses Dieux au cours de l'Histoire» (it is not God who creates man before time; it is man who creates his gods in the course of history) (p. 390). Experience, religious or other, "is the fact that Spirit exists as an object of consciousness". The opposition between knowledge and the real is precisely man, since man is the empirical existence of the revelation of the world, which, while in the world, is something other than the natural world it reveals. And this consciousness reaches knowledge only by relating to an object. For man to know himself he must first objectify himself, externalise himself, become a world: "man must first realise and objectify himself by action before he can know himself". Man's objectivity is precisely the existence of his labours and fights, of history, which is time. As long as time lasts, as long as there is history, the object remains external to the subject, and man does not recognise himself in his objective works; the historical world he created appears to him as a world created by something other than himself: by a Spirit, certainly, but not his own, a divine Spirit. That is why there is necessarily religion, and God, as long as there is man, history, and time. The derivation of religion from the structure of time is the lecture's theory of religion: God is the externality of man's works to man, which lasts as long as history lasts. Religion is necessary, not accidental, during history.

Religion is therefore an epiphenomenon of human labour, an essentially historical phenomenon. Even in its theological appearance Spirit is essentially a becoming. There is no revealed God outside history. Or again, eternity can be a truth, a reality revealed by human discourse, only if it is the result of a becoming, of time. Hegelian "absolute Spirit" is therefore not "God" in the normal sense: this Spirit is its own becoming, revealed in its integrity by speech and so transformed into truth; and the becoming that Spirit is, is time or man, human history. "Epiphenomenon of labour" is the most materialist formula in the book. It restates the 1937–38 thesis that religion is a superstructure (p. 161).

Hegel says this in the next sentence (Hoffmeister p. 558). Kojève translates: this substance that is Spirit is the becoming of itself, becoming for itself what it is in itself; and only as this becoming reflecting itself into itself is it in itself in truth Spirit. The sentence (¶802) defines Spirit as its own becoming.

The becoming of Spirit that is history, the historical becoming of humanity, is nothing but the becoming of Science, which is "absolute Spirit", Spirit become, completed or perfect and revealed to itself by itself. It is still man, if one likes, but dead man, or, if one prefers, man become God. «Certes, un "Dieu" qui s'est constitué dans le Temps ou en tant que Temps, à partir de l'Homme, n'est pas vraiment Dieu. Mais l'Homme qui est devenu "Dieu" n'est pas non plus vraiment un Homme» (certainly a "God" constituted in time or as time, from man, is not really God; but the man who has become "God" is no longer really a man either) (p. 391). In any case history is for Hegel the becoming of "absolute Spirit", of Spirit perfectly revealed and fully realised in and through Science; history is therefore the becoming of Science, the history of philosophy. The double negation, neither truly God nor truly man, states the ambiguity of anthropotheism at the end of history: the result is neither.

Hegel says this in effect (Hoffmeister p. 558). Kojève translates: Spirit is in itself the dialectical movement that is knowledge: the transformation of the in-itself into for-itself, of substance into subject, of the object of consciousness into object of self-consciousness, into an object that is equally overcome, into concept. The sentence (¶802) restates the Preface's programme, substance as subject.

This movement, which is time or history, ultimately the history of human knowledge or philosophy, is, Hegel adds, a circular movement; Science, which reveals it as completed, must be circular too (Hoffmeister p. 558). Kojève translates: the movement is the circle that returns into itself, presupposes its beginning, and reaches (*erreicht*) it only at the end. The sentence (¶802) is the textual source of the circle.

Hegel's time, historical or human time, is therefore a circle, and it differs from Aristotelian or biological time only in not being cyclical: «le cercle hégélien ne peut être parcouru qu'une seule fois» (the Hegelian circle can be traversed only once) (p. 391). The distinction between circular and cyclical, stated in the seventh lecture's footnotes (p. 349), is the key to the difference between Hegel and Aristotle.

The circular "dialectical movement" is time, history. History is the opposition between man and the natural world. The beginning of the "movement" is what is not in movement: the absence of opposition between man and world, or, what is the same, the absence of man. Hegel says "the circle presupposes its beginning": time presupposes space; man presupposes the world; the identity of man and world is before man. This identity is the world's unrevealed identity, hidden or mute because it does not yet include man. This origin of man does not exist for man, since being-for-man is being-revealed-by-the-concept, and as soon as there is revelation of being there is already man revealing it by his discourse. And man is action, the opposition between man and world, precisely the "dialectical movement" or time. Human time therefore has a beginning in the world: history begins in an already existing natural world. But history is the history of human action, and this action is the "dialectical overcoming" of the opposition between man and world; and the "overcoming" of the opposition is the "overcoming" of man himself, of history, and so of human time. The end of the "movement" is therefore also identity, like its beginning. Only at the end, identity is revealed by the concept. The movement, history, which is ultimately the process of the revelation of being by discourse, therefore "reaches" its beginning only at the end: only at the end of history does the identity of man and world exist for man, as revealed by human discourse. History that has begun therefore necessarily has an end, and this end is the discursive revelation of its beginning. (This "beginning" being, as we know, anthropogenic Desire, the "end" is the understanding of this Desire, as set out in the *Phenomenology*.) But if the beginning of man, history, and time exists for man only at the end of time and history, this end is no longer a new beginning, either for man or of man, but truly his end. The revealed identity of man and world abolishes the Desire that is precisely the beginning of history, man, and time. The circle of time can be traversed only once; history is completed but does not begin again; man dies and is not resurrected, at least as man. A footnote gives the ontological reason: the uniqueness of the circle comes from the fact that being, including man, includes antithesis or negativity. Biological life proceeds by positions; history proceeds by negations; so it is impossible to redo history, since every historical progress is a negation of what is and has been. History progresses as long as there is an actualised possibility of negation; when there is none, it stops definitively. The derivation of the circle's uniqueness is precise: the end reveals the beginning (Desire) and so abolishes it, so there can be no second round. The distinction between life by positions and history by negations grounds the difference between cyclical and circular time. "The end is the understanding of Desire as set out in the *Phenomenology*": the book ends by understanding what began history.

But while not cyclical, time is necessarily circular: at the end one reaches the identity of the beginning. Without this identity, without the natural world, history could not have begun; and it is completed only with the re-establishment of this identity, and then it is necessarily completed. One returns finally to the point of departure: the nothingness of man. The phrase "the nothingness of man" as the end is stark: the circle returns to a world without man.

Science, which reveals the integrated totality of man, the completed course of history, must therefore be circular too. And this circularity is the only criterion of its absolute truth, its perfect adequation to the totality of reality. If the human real is a becoming, none of its partial or "instantaneous" revelations is true in the strong sense: the real being "abolished" each time by action, the concept that correctly reveals it at one moment will cease to be true at another. Only the whole of the "movement", the integrated whole of history, man, and time, does not change; only the totality of becoming remains eternally identical with itself, and so only the revelation of this totality is truly true. The argument for circularity as criterion is the clearest in the book: partial truths about a changing reality become false; only the whole of change is changeless.

Science must therefore be circular, and only circular Science is completed or absolute Science. The advent of this Science is thus the proof of the end of man, history, and time. When human discourse, starting from any point and progressing necessarily, in conformity with logical necessity, returns to its starting point, one sees that the totality of discourse is exhausted. And the exhaustion of discourse is also the exhaustion of history, of man and time. The equation of the exhaustion of discourse with the exhaustion of history is the formal version of the end of history: when everything has been said, nothing more remains to be done.

Like time, history, and man, Science is therefore circular. But if the historical circle is traversed only once, the circle of Science is a cycle that repeats eternally; a footnote explains that in Science there is no more negativity: absolute knowledge does not modify the being it reveals, since it arises only when man is satisfied by what he is and so no longer acts. There is a possibility of repeating Science, and this repetition is even necessary. The content of Science relates only to itself: the Book is its own content. The content of the Book is fully revealed only at the end of the Book. But since this content is the Book itself, the answer given at the end to the question of what the content is can be nothing but the whole Book. So, having reached the end, one must reread, or rethink, the Book; and this cycle repeats eternally. A footnote: in the *Logic* being finally reveals itself as the Idea; the final answer to "what is being?" is "being is the Idea". But if one asks "what is the Idea?", one must answer: "it is being that is nothing, that is, it is essence, and so on". In other words, one must reread the whole *Logic*. The contrast between the circle traversed once (history) and the cycle repeated eternally (Science) completes the theory of post-historical time. The *Logic* footnote illustrates concretely: the last category sends one back to the first.

Science is therefore not only circular but cyclical. In a cycle the future is always also a past; there is therefore no true future, no time properly speaking, no human or historical time. If one wants to say the dialectical movement of Science is time, one must say it is cyclical time, time without primacy of the future, time that is eternity: in short, Aristotle's biological time. That is why the empirical existence of Science is not historical man but a paper Book, a natural entity. Certainly the Book must be read and understood by men to be a Book and not paper. But the man who reads it no longer creates anything, nor does he change himself; he is no longer time with the primacy of the future, or history; he is not man in the strong sense. This man too is a quasi-natural or cyclical being: «c'est un animal raisonnable, qui change et se reproduit tout en restant éternellement identique à lui-même» (he is a rational animal, who changes and reproduces himself while remaining eternally identical with himself) (p. 394). And it is this "rational animal" that is "absolute Spirit", Spirit become or completed; that is, dead. The designation of post-historical man as "rational animal" reverses the history of the definition: Aristotle's definition of man becomes the definition of what remains after man. "Absolute Spirit … that is, dead" is the lecture's most provocative identification.

What follows is a kind of conclusion. Hegel first summarises what he has said about the relation between Spirit, or being revealed by the concept, and time (Hoffmeister pp. 558–559). Kojève translates: insofar as Spirit is necessarily this differentiation within itself, its totality, intuited, stands over against (*gegenüber*) its simple self-consciousness. And since this totality is what is differentiated, it is differentiated into its pure intuited concept, which is time, and into its content, which is the in-itself. Substance as subject has in itself a necessity, at first inner, to present (*darzustellen*) itself in itself as it is in itself, as Spirit. Only the completed objective presentation (*Darstellung*) is at the same time the reflection of substance, its becoming into the self. This text brings nothing new; everything Kojève has said can serve as its commentary, so he only translates it. The restraint is methodological: the conclusion restates.

The same holds for the next sentence, in which Hegel says in so many words that Science can appear only at the end of history, that there is absolute truth only if history has an end, which means, if man is essentially mortal. Kojève translates this famous sentence (Hoffmeister p. 559): consequently, as long as Spirit has not completed itself in itself, as world-historical Spirit, it cannot reach its completion as self-conscious, that is, philosophical, Spirit. The "world spirit" (*Weltgeist*) is the history of humanity; "self-conscious Spirit" is Science. The gloss "which means: if man is essentially mortal" ties the end of history once more to finitude.

Finally, in a closing note (Hoffmeister p. 559), Hegel writes what Kojève has already said about religion or theology in commenting the passage on experience. Kojève translates: in time, the content of Christian religion therefore expresses what human Spirit is before Hegelian Science; but the latter alone is the true knowledge Spirit has of itself. As long as time, history, and man last, revealed being is conceived as a transcendent or divine Spirit. The abolition of Spirit's transcendence, which entails the abolition of theology, marks the end of time, history, and man. But only at the end of time is reality revealed, does truth appear. For in reality or truth, Spirit-eternity is the result of time and history: «il est l'Homme mort, et non un Dieu ressuscité» (it is dead man, and not a resurrected God) (p. 395). That is why the reality of eternal or absolute Spirit is not a transcendent God living in heaven but a Book written by a man living in the natural world. The final sentence is the lecture's conclusion and one of the most striking in the book. The Christian narrative of death and resurrection is inverted: absolute Spirit is the death of man that does not rise. Its reality is a Book, a thing among things in nature.

### Tenth Lecture: Interpretation of the Second Part of Chapter VIII (Continued and Concluded)

Kojève passes to the third and last step of the second section of the second part of Chapter VIII. The second part treats the Sage; its second section analyses his appearance in the real world, in three steps. In the first Hegel spoke of the relation between the Sage, incarnate Science ("absolute knowledge"), and objective reality considered independently of time. In the second, of the relation between the Sage, or absolute knowledge, and time: absolute knowledge appears at the last moment of time; the advent of Science in the world completes time, that is, history, since Hegel's time is essentially human or historical time; and Science itself is no longer an essentially temporal phenomenon, since completed Science is eternity revealed to itself. But the separation of objective reality and time is purely artificial; objective reality is essentially temporal, and time is necessarily real, even objectively real. To analyse the relations between the Sage and the real world, one must unite the analyses of the first two steps and speak of temporal reality or real time, which Hegel does in the third. For Hegel, at least in the *Phenomenology*, time is human or historical time; so temporal reality or real time is for him not nature enduring as cosmos or organic life, but history and history alone. The recapitulation frames the third step as the synthesis of the first two: thesis, reality; antithesis, time; synthesis, history.

In the first sentence indicating the theme of the third step, Hegel speaks only of *Geschichte*, history (Hoffmeister p. 559). Kojève translates: the dialectical movement that consists in Spirit's act of bringing forth from itself (*von sich hervorzutreiben*) the form of its knowledge is the labour that Spirit accomplishes as objectively real history. In the first, thetic step it was a question of "objective reality"; in the second, antithetic, of "time"; in the third, synthetic, there should be a question of "real time", but Hegel says "real history". The terms "time" and "history" are therefore rigorously equivalent. The Sage appears not within a nature enduring in cosmic or biological time but within "real history", a "world" essentially historical, and the advent of Science can be understood only in and through history. The equivalence of time and history is read off the text's structure, the synthesis the triad demands. The word "labour" (*Arbeit*) in Hegel's sentence (¶803) supports Kojève's reading of history as labour.

The sentence confirms that for Hegel the history of humanity reduces in the last analysis to the history of philosophy. The "labour accomplished by Spirit, by humanity, in the course of history" consists in the production of a knowledge (*Wissen*), the knowledge Spirit, man, has of itself. Historical progress is in the last analysis a progress of self-consciousness, a philosophical progress, ending in "absolute knowledge", the fullness of self-consciousness, the Sage or integral man who expresses his total self-consciousness in and through Science. Certainly history is a synthesis of objective reality and time, which means that philosophy, which is nothing but history understood, presupposes on the one hand a nature independent of time and so of man, and on the other time itself, the man of Desire and action. No philosophy without nature and without historical action in the strong sense, carried out within nature. But for Hegel objective reality and time, nature and history (the action of fight and labour), are only constituent elements (*Momente*) of true reality, which is knowledge, the discourse that reveals the world and historical man, and so philosophy. Man properly speaking, truly real as man, is therefore the philosopher. The natural man, the animal of the species *Homo sapiens*, and the man of historical action, of fight and labour, are only the necessary conditions of the truly human reality that is man's philosophical existence. There is a nature so that man can fight and work; but man fights and works only in order to be able to speak of what he does, to become self-conscious as the being who has done what he did by fighting and working. Self-consciousness and philosophy are one and the same thing. Man therefore fights and works in order to be able to become a philosopher, or more exactly to be able to satisfy himself as philosopher, to become a Sage and produce Science. The teleology is stated at its most extreme: nature exists for history, history for philosophy. This is the logic of the third lecture's "the State exists so that the Sage can write a Book" (p. 302), now stated as Hegel's view before Kojève criticises it.

The non-philosopher does not suspect this. Fighting and working, he believes he pursues other ends; but he believes so precisely because he is not a philosopher, not truly self-conscious: he does not know what he is, what he does, or why. In fact, even without realising it, man tends to become a philosopher. But only those who tend toward it consciously are philosophers. And for those who understand history, and do not merely create or undergo it, for philosophers, history as a whole is a history of philosophy, which will evidently stop at the very moment when wisdom appears and "overcomes" philosophy. The statement "man tends to become a philosopher even without realising it" is the thesis Kojève is about to contest.

This is clear and, at first sight, convincing. But one can doubt it, and Kojève has already formulated his doubts in the first two lectures. There he said that the identification of history with the history of philosophy is required as soon as one makes the hypothesis that self-consciousness necessarily tends to extend itself as far as possible, that man always becomes fully conscious of the modifications created in him by the transformations of the external world, natural and social or historical. «Mais je ne pense pas personnellement que cette hypothèse soit vraie : je pense que l'Homme n'est pas naturellement Philosophe» (but I do not personally think this hypothesis is true: I think that man is not naturally a philosopher) (p. 398). He believes that incessant efforts are needed to widen self-consciousness, which naturally tends to keep its limits fixed, and that man could very well not make these efforts. In any case the anthropological analyses of the *Phenomenology* do not allow the hypothesis to be advanced. One can note the fact of the philosopher's existence but cannot explain it; one cannot "deduce" philosophical existence from human existence as it appears in the *Phenomenology*. The explicit rejection of the hypothesis, in the first person, is the lecture's central critical statement. It repeats the first lecture's objection (p. 275) and makes it Kojève's own position: the philosopher is a contingent fact, not a deducible necessity.

For Hegel this has no importance, since he has the fact at his disposal. He writes at the end of history and notes that in fact there have always been philosophers to become conscious of the historical facts created by men and of the modifications of man engendered by them. (The question becomes important only for those who do not think they live at the moment when history is already completed.) Hegel can therefore say that history is in fact always conscious of itself, a history of philosophy; and, having noted this fact, he can say that man as such is in the last analysis a philosopher, that human self-consciousness necessarily tends to extend itself ever further. The parenthesis is decisive: Kojève places himself among those who do not think they live at the end of history. The whole critique follows from this refusal to assume the end.

Hegel says this in a passage of the Introduction to the *Phenomenology* (Hoffmeister p. 69; the text prints "p. 59", a misprint). Kojève translates: the goal is imposed on knowledge with as much necessity as the progression; it lies where knowledge no longer needs to go beyond itself, where it finds itself, and where the concept corresponds to the object and the object to the concept. The progress toward this goal therefore cannot be halted on the way, and satisfaction can be found at no earlier station. If self-consciousness is philosophy and its progressive extension the history of philosophy, this history necessarily stops when any new extension becomes impossible; conversely, it cannot stop earlier, since philosophy cannot be satisfied by a self-consciousness still capable of extension. For Hegel the impossibility of extending self-consciousness is guaranteed and revealed by the circularity of the knowledge that expresses it; but this does not matter now. Note only that for Hegel the tendency to go beyond limits that are visibly limits characterises self-consciousness as such. The passage (Introduction, ¶80) is the textual locus of the premise Kojève contests. Its claim that satisfaction cannot be found at any earlier station is precisely what the unphilosophical attitudes deny.

The schema of historical evolution would then be as follows. Man acts and so transforms the given world. Living in this world, he is himself transformed by this transformation: he undergoes its counterblow. Being transformed, he necessarily becomes conscious of his transformation. Becoming self-conscious, he notes that he is still in disagreement with the given world, even transformed, that the idea he has of himself independently of his existence in the world (*Begriff*) differs from his reality in the world (*Gegenstand*). He therefore acts again, to transform the given world further and make it conform to him. And the game necessarily continues as long as man does not note a perfect agreement between himself and the world, between concept and object. At that moment history, action, stops definitively, and the philosopher has reached his goal, wisdom, since it is now impossible, action being abolished, to change oneself and so to go beyond the consciousness one already has of oneself. That is what Hegel means in the passage cited. The schema, action, becoming conscious, action, is the engine of history in Kojève's reading, stated cleanly before its critique.

But this reasoning is correct only if every man of action is a philosopher and every philosopher a man of action. If the man who acts does not philosophise, or the philosopher does not act, the reasoning no longer holds. Suppose the man who has acted does not become self-conscious after acting. Mistaken about himself, he may well not see the inadequacy of his action, not notice the gap still remaining between idea-ideal and reality. He will then stop acting and halt before reaching the true, unsurpassable end of history; on this hypothesis there will never be wisdom on earth. Conversely, if the philosopher does not act, he cannot transform the world; he will not change himself; history will again stop before its absolute term; and the philosopher will never become a Sage. The critique identifies two failure modes: action without self-consciousness and self-consciousness without action. Either can halt history short of its end.

Once more Hegel can appeal to the fact of the Sage that he himself is. But can he really explain it? Kojève doubts it. «Et je doute donc qu'il soit le Sage achevant l'Histoire, car c'est précisément la capacité de s'expliquer soi-même qui caractérise la Sagesse» (and I therefore doubt that he is the Sage who completes history, since it is precisely the capacity to explain oneself that characterises wisdom) (p. 400). The conclusion is devastating: by the first lecture's definition of the Sage, one who can answer every question about himself, Hegel fails, since he cannot explain his own existence as philosopher. Kojève here denies Hegel the title of Sage.

Kojève thinks Hegel has no right to affirm that consciousness that does not extend itself indefinitely is not human consciousness. Yet he affirms it in a passage where he opposes to the animal that merely lives not the being that becomes conscious of its life but the being capable of extending its consciousness indefinitely: to the animal Hegel opposes not self-conscious man but the philosopher (Hoffmeister p. 69). Kojève translates: what is limited to a natural, animal life cannot by itself go beyond its immediate, given existence; it is driven beyond it by another, and this being torn out and thrown out is its death. Consciousness, by contrast, is for itself its own concept; it is therefore immediately the going beyond the limited, and so beyond itself, since this limited belongs to it. For consciousness the beyond is posited together with the particular, if only beside the limited, as in spatial intuition. Consciousness therefore suffers from itself this violence (*Gewalt*) of spoiling limited satisfaction. The passage (¶80) states that self-transcendence is essential to consciousness, which is the premise at issue.

The animal has, if one likes, a kind of "self-consciousness", which Hegel calls self-feeling (*Selbstgefühl*). But this animal "consciousness" cannot extend itself. If the animal changes, goes beyond itself, its "self-consciousness" is annulled instead of extended: it becomes nothing, dies or disappears by becoming another animal; biological evolution is not a history. That is why for Hegel the animal has no self-consciousness but only self-feeling. The self-consciousness that characterises man is necessarily one that always extends or transcends itself, and Hegel says so in the second part of the passage cited. The parenthesis "biological evolution is not a history" is an important precision: the species that changes becomes another species rather than a changed self.

In this passage Hegel has in view the same schema of historical evolution: action, becoming conscious, action. Under these conditions history is indeed a history of philosophy and must necessarily progress until philosophy becomes wisdom. Certainly Hegel is aware of the difficulty of any extension of self-consciousness. He speaks of "violence" (*Gewalt*): one must do oneself "violence" to acknowledge that one is no longer what one was. But according to Hegel the man who cannot do himself this violence is not a human being in the strong sense. This claim seems paradoxical, and Hegel himself must restrict it. He must admit that there are self-conscious beings whom everyone calls men and who nonetheless refuse to extend the consciousness they already have of themselves. The "violence" of self-transformation connects to the fight: self-knowledge, like freedom, requires overcoming resistance.

Kojève translates Hegel's next sentences (Hoffmeister pp. 69–70): in experiencing this violence, fear (*Angst*) may recoil from truth and seek to preserve what is threatened with loss. But it can find no rest, unless it wants to stop in thoughtless inertia (*gedankenloser Trägheit*); for thought troubles thoughtlessness and its restlessness disturbs inertia. Or fear of change may consolidate itself as sentimentality (*Empfindsamkeit*), which assures us that everything is good in its kind; but this assurance too suffers violence from Reason, which finds that something is not good precisely because it is a kind and not an individual unique in its kind. Or fear (*Furcht*) of truth may hide itself, for itself and others, behind the illusion that it is precisely ardent zeal for truth that makes it so hard, indeed impossible, to find any truth other than the sole truth of vanity (*Eitelkeit*), always being cleverer than any idea one draws from oneself or others. This vanity, which can frustrate every universal truth and return from it into itself, which feeds on its own understanding that always manages to dissolve all ideas and find, in place of all objective content, only the dry and sterile abstract I, is a satisfaction that must be left to itself, since it flees the universal and seeks only being-for-itself. Hegel's three refusals (¶80) are Kojève's material for his critique.

Hegel recognises here three essentially non-philosophical attitudes, three typical cases in which man refuses to change objectively or subjectively and so to extend his self-consciousness beyond given limits. First, "thoughtless inertia": the "brute" who at most undergoes history as a stone "undergoes" the laws of its fall. He is incapable of accepting, consciously and voluntarily, a change, notably the change that may mean his death; but he cannot refuse it consciously and voluntarily either. So when the case arises, he is led to death as the beast is led to the slaughterhouse. That, for Hegel, characterises the animal. But while being very severe with this "thoughtless inertia", can one really affirm that the man who brutalises himself in this intellectual laziness ceases completely to be a man? The question challenges Hegel's equation of non-philosophy with animality. The brute undergoes death as an animal does, yet remains human.

And one must not forget that the opposite of this inert and indolent man, the man of action who protests, retorts, tries to change what displeases him, is not what one generally means by "philosopher". It is rather the "blond brute", the "blonde Bestie" of which Nietzsche spoke with nostalgia: the man who really transforms the world by his action and so, by counterblow, transforms himself; but nothing says he becomes conscious of his own transformation or will accept the words of one who tells him he has changed. A footnote adds: experience shows, for example, that the men who made a Revolution do not stay in power, precisely because they continue to remain, or to believe they remain, as they were before the Revolution: nonconformists. In short, the man of action is not by definition a philosopher. By Hegel's definition the "blond beast" is no less a brute than the inert, passive, conformist brute. But evidently one is worth more than the other, and this proves that we are dealing with a human reality, since purely natural reality has no degrees of value; it is absolutely homogeneous in this respect. The "blond beast" is from Nietzsche's *Genealogy of Morals* (I, 11). The footnote on revolutionaries who lose power because they remain nonconformists is a sharp observation, written in 1939 after the Moscow trials. The argument that degrees of value prove humanity, since nature has none, is Kojève's refutation of Hegel's reduction of the non-philosopher to the animal.

As for the philosopher: is it not characteristic that it is precisely he who, in the eyes of the "vulgar", is supposed to have the attitude of "sentimentality" (*Empfindsamkeit*) Hegel speaks of? For what Hegel has in view is also the attitude of "to understand all is to forgive all", which means to justify and accept everything. It is the famous "objectivity" expected of the scholar and especially of the "philosopher", who is also supposed to be there to say "the more it changes, the more it stays the same". Certainly one can and must say that this "philosopher" is only a caricature, a "sophist". Without doubt the philosopher can and must understand everything without "forgiving" anything. But one must not forget that those who do not "forgive" do not always "understand" either. And experience shows that without the intervention of men who act without understanding, the philosophical desire to change everything that can, and so must, be changed generally remains ineffective. One can answer, with Aristotle, that man also uses beasts to realise his ends. But the answer does not seem very convincing, if only because the "beasts" in question do not always obey and can sometimes "protest". The passage is one of Kojève's most personal: the philosopher needs men of action who do not understand, and those men are not tools. The allusion to Aristotle's natural slaves returns to the Master–Slave theme: the "beasts" who protest are the revolutionary masses. The maxim *tout comprendre, c'est tout pardonner* names the philosopher's temptation.

Where one would like to agree with Hegel is where he speaks of "vanity" (*Eitelkeit*), of what is called "individualism". The man who sees in everything that happens only the "emotions" he experiences; the man who wants only to cultivate his I, which he believes "personal" but which, isolated and shut in on itself, is in fact empty and abstract, strictly like the I of every other "individualist"; the apolitical and asocial man of false transcendence, who believes himself "above the fray" and is content to observe others' changes and conflicts in order to take blissful pleasure in repeatedly noting his own permanent agreement with himself: this man of the "spiritual animal kingdom" does seem to deserve the name "learned or intellectual beast" Hegel gives him. But despite, or rather because of, the disgust he inspires, one must still say that this is only a metaphor. The concession is qualified immediately: even the intellectual individualist, whom Kojève detests, is not an animal. "Because of the disgust he inspires" is the key: disgust is a human reaction to a human failing.

Finally, and this is the gravest objection, there is the religious man, who according to Hegel is not self-conscious either, since he always speaks of an I essentially other than his own. It is certainly not by chance that Hegel does not mention him in his list. A footnote adds that Hegel could have: the religious man, fixing his self-consciousness, in the form of a consciousness of the external, on a God eternally identical with himself, is also opposed to every essential change in human life; he is always opposed to social revolution and never accepts the changes it brings, at least as religious. He does not mention him because it is visibly impossible to speak here of animal existence, even metaphorically. The religious man is the strongest counter-example: a being clearly human, even spiritually elevated, who refuses to extend self-consciousness. Hegel's silence about him is, for Kojève, telling.

Without doubt whoever is, or believes himself, a philosopher must know himself infinitely superior to the religious man who is only religious, not to speak of the others. For the philosopher alone can understand and express the true meaning of what the others are content to do or undergo. In general, a man, individual or collective, is superior to others insofar as he understands them without being understood by them; this is, moreover, the only possible definition of progress. But to say, as Hegel sometimes seems to, that the philosopher alone represents human reality is really to show a "professional deformation". A footnote adds: man can be "superior" only to man; he is not really superior to the beast or the stone; he is essentially "something else", that is all. The definition of superiority as understanding without being understood repeats the first lecture's definition of progress (p. 281). The charge of "professional deformation" is a mild and precise way of calling Hegel's anthropology a philosopher's self-flattery. The footnote refines it: superiority is a relation among humans; between man and nature there is only difference.

Kojève thinks Hegel is right to say that without philosophy there would have been no history. No history understood, since philosophy is precisely "history understood" (*verstandene Geschichte*), the self-consciousness of human reality in its whole extent. And no real history, since if the historical present is co-determined by the past, it must be by the past understood: as long as man does not become conscious of his new situation in the world by comparing it with the old, he cannot see the contradiction, the negation, it implies; so he cannot negate it by his action, and his action in it will not be truly human or historical. And in fact there has always been a philosophy at the basis of every revolution. History is only a permanent revolution, since it progresses by negations of the social given. The concession is substantial: philosophy is necessary for history, both as its understanding and as a condition of revolutionary action. "History is a permanent revolution" is a phrase with Trotskyist resonance in 1939, used here in a purely structural sense.
