But nothing will prove that there will always be philosophers as long as there are men on earth. History could stop before reaching its truly unsurpassable term. One must therefore make efforts so that it does not. Or again: «il ne suffit pas de se dire qu'un philosophe vient toujours tôt ou tard ; chacun devrait se dire, même sans raisons convaincantes, qu'il est peut-être seul à pouvoir devenir ce philosophe attendu» (it is not enough to tell oneself that a philosopher always comes sooner or later; each should tell himself, even without convincing reasons, that he is perhaps the only one who can become that awaited philosopher) (p. 404). The sentence is the lecture's ethical conclusion and one of the most personal in the book. It turns the contingency of the philosopher into a vocation: since the Sage is not guaranteed, each must act as if it depended on him. It is also the clearest indication that Kojève does not believe history already completed.

And one must not forget that, practically, if history is understood by philosophers, it is created by those who generally are not. Hegel knows this well, since he says that without the Empire created by Napoleon his own philosophy would not be possible. Certainly, speaking of Napoleon, he stresses that this is a case of consciousness, not self-consciousness (Hoffmeister p. 471), and he is right, since Napoleon was not a philosopher. But it is visibly going too far to say that this great man was not a truly human being. The example of Napoleon completes the critique: if only the philosopher is fully human, the man who completed history was not, which is absurd.

Returning to the text of Chapter VIII: for Hegel history reduces in the end to the history of philosophy. So in the passage following the sentence cited, where by that sentence there should be a question of "real history", there is only the history of philosophy. In its first sentence Hegel specifies once more the difference between philosophy and religion, theology; in the second he speaks of the birth, with Descartes, of Christian philosophy after the destruction of Christian theology in the Renaissance; in the sentences ending the passage he summarises the history of Christian, modern philosophy, speaking without naming them of Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, the Enlightenment, Kant, Fichte, and Schelling. Kojève does not translate this passage (Hoffmeister pp. 559–560), since it is almost incomprehensible without commentary, and a satisfactory commentary would take months. The identification of the unnamed philosophers in ¶803–804 is conventional.

He wants only to explain why in this summary Hegel speaks of philosophy in the ordinary sense, of the metaphysical systems of Descartes, Spinoza, and so on, whereas in the text of the *Phenomenology* he did not, evoking only the anthropological doctrines of these philosophers, notably Kant's. Wisdom, absolute knowledge, is a synthesis of consciousness and self-consciousness; philosophy, insofar as it leads to knowledge, is the attempt at such a synthesis. Philosophy therefore has a double aspect. On the one hand it constitutes self-consciousness: through it man knows what he is as opposed to the external world. In this "subjectivist" aspect philosophy is an anthropology, and it is only this philosophical anthropology that was discussed in the first seven chapters, since in them consciousness was still opposed to self-consciousness. So subjectivist philosophical anthropology is completed there by science in the ordinary sense, which reveals the object or natural world, and by religion or theology, which unconsciously and symbolically reveals the social world. A footnote adds that it is in its anthropological aspect that philosophy passes into literature and determines the "culture" of an epoch in general; and in this aspect too it contributes to the realisation of the historical movement, revealing to man the contradictions implied in him and his world and so inciting him to action. But every philosophy worthy of the name aspires to total knowledge, seeks a synthesis of consciousness and self-consciousness, and in this synthetic aspect it is "metaphysics" or philosophy in the proper sense; a footnote adds, in a sense of which literature and "general culture" have not the slightest idea. The distinction between philosophy's anthropological aspect, which enters literature and culture, and its metaphysical aspect, which does not, explains why the *Phenomenology* could be read as anthropology. The footnotes' disdain for "general culture" is characteristic.

The synthesis of consciousness and self-consciousness took place only in Chapter VIII, more exactly in the summary of the seven chapters found there. Only in Chapter VIII, after this summary, can the metaphysics of past philosophers be understood. In the first seven chapters these philosophers appear as representatives of consciousness; here philosophies appear as so many attempts at synthesis of consciousness and self-consciousness. The synthesis succeeds fully only at the end of history, in Hegel's Science. As long as history continues there is real contradiction between man and world, and every philosophical synthesis or "agreement" can only be false, being itself in disagreement with reality. That is why philosophies "abolish" one another, why there is a history of philosophy, whereas there can be no history of wisdom. «Et l'histoire de la philosophie, — c'est l'histoire des tentatives nécessairement avortées pour réaliser une Totalité de la pensée avant d'avoir réalisé la Totalité de l'existence» (and the history of philosophy is the history of the necessarily aborted attempts to realise a totality of thought before having realised the totality of existence) (p. 406). A footnote adds that total existence is, as we know, the existence of the man who has completed his life or history: the man who is dead. The definition of the history of philosophy as premature syntheses is one of Kojève's most elegant. The footnote, total existence is that of the dead man, repeats the ninth lecture's conclusion in a single clause.

It is these premature attempts at metaphysical synthesis that Hegel summarises and criticises in the third and last step. Kojève passes to the third and last section of the second part. Hegel has just said how and why wisdom results from the evolution of philosophy, and why this evolution could stop only with the advent of Hegelian absolute knowledge; he has explained philosophically the why and how of the Sage's advent. Now, in the third section, he will speak of the Sage himself. "Man's true being is his action": to say what the Sage is is to say what he does; and since the Sage does nothing but his Science, to speak of the Sage is to speak of the birth of Science, of the Sage's action that produces Science. A footnote notes that Hegel speaks of this Science itself in the third part of Chapter VIII; he proposed to set out Science in the second part of the System, which was never written. The Sage is the philosopher who has succeeded in explaining himself; to speak of the Sage is to say how he sees himself, and the best way is to show how his correct self-understanding differs from the philosopher's inadequate one. So Hegel sets out his ideas on the Sage's activity by opposing them to the ideas on the philosopher's activity set out by the last two philosophers, Fichte and Schelling. The method makes the text, already much too short, rather difficult. The definition of the Sage as "the philosopher who has succeeded in explaining himself" is the one by which Kojève has just found Hegel wanting.

Kojève translates (Hoffmeister pp. 560–561): Spirit has shown itself to us as neither the mere withdrawal (*Zurückziehen*) of self-consciousness into its pure inwardness, as Fichte thinks, nor the mere sinking (*Versenkung*) of self-consciousness into substance, into natural given being, and the non-being of its differentiation, as Schelling thinks. Spirit is this dialectical movement of the self that alienates itself (*sich seiner selbst entäußert*) and sinks into substance, and equally, as subject, has gone into itself from this substance, making it object and content, as it overcomes this distinction of objectivity and content. The passage (¶804) opposes Hegel to Fichte and Schelling.

To interpret it in detail one would have to set out Fichte's and Schelling's ideas, which would take too long; Kojève gives only a very superficial commentary. It concerns Spirit; but Spirit reveals itself in and through Science, which is the Sage's self-consciousness; so to speak of Spirit is also to speak of the Sage. Hegel says first that the Sage does not take refuge, contrary to Fichte, in his subjective "inwardness"; the Sage's activity has nothing to do with the poet's, who isolates himself from the world and withdraws into himself. But, Hegel says next, it has nothing to do either with the activity of the scholar, in the ordinary sense, who loses himself in the object and forgets his personal I. The Sage, contrary to what is usually thought, is not "disinterested" or "objective"; he continues, contrary to Schelling, to refer the world to himself. But, contrary to Fichte and unlike the poet, it is a real world he refers to himself, not an imaginary "universe". The typology, poet (Fichte) and scholar (Schelling), places the Sage between subjectivism and objectivism.

The Sage in his action is "the dialectical movement of the self", says Hegel. The Sage's I is therefore an I that opposes itself to a world and at the same time abolishes this opposition, that is absorbed by the object and at the same time creates itself as subject. Hegel said exactly the same of historical man in general. No wonder, since Hegel speaks here of Spirit, and the "dialectical movement of Spirit" is for him nothing but history. Insofar as Spirit reveals itself in its "movement" by knowledge, the Sage remakes universal history in his thought. In the last lines of Chapter VIII Hegel will say that the Sage or Science, insofar as they are turned toward the past, toward time, the "movement" of Spirit, are nothing but "comprehended history" (*begriffene Geschichte*). This history is referred to the Sage's self, this self being the final goal and crowning of history; but the self relates to the real historical world, since it is nothing but the understanding of this world. The Sage's attitude is thus at once supremely "subjective" or "interested" and supremely "disinterested" or "objective". The formula "comprehended history" (¶808) is the book's final phrase for absolute knowledge.

Hegel develops the idea in the next passage (Hoffmeister p. 561). Kojève translates, with bracketed names: this first reflection from immediacy (the negativity discovered by Fichte) is the subject's act of differentiating itself from its substance, the concept dividing itself, the going-into-itself and becoming of the pure I. Insofar as this differentiation is the pure activity of the I = I (the identity discovered by Schelling), the concept is the necessity and emergence of empirical existence, whose essence is substance and which maintains itself for itself. But (and this is the totality discovered by Hegel) the maintenance of empirical existence for itself is the concept posited in determinateness, and so equally the dialectical movement of the concept within itself, the movement of descending into simple substance (Schellingian identity), which is subject or Spirit only as this Fichtean negativity and this movement, Hegelian totality. Kojève's brackets map Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel onto negativity, identity, and totality, which is the triad of Appendix I.

This is again a confrontation of Fichte, Schelling, and Hegel, but the text is even more difficult, being a very condensed summary of the ultimate principles of their metaphysics. Retain only that Hegel opposes to Fichte's abstract I and Schelling's substance "negativity" and "the dialectical movement of the self", which is to say action and history. "Substance", given being and the natural world, can become "subject" or "Spirit", can reveal itself to itself by speech, only by realising itself as a temporal historical world, a world that implies acting man. If the Sage wants to realise Spirit fully by revealing the totality of being through his Science, he must first conceive the becoming of Spirit, history. Being that is "substance" is revealed being or "Spirit" only insofar as it implies man; to reveal being in its totality is therefore to reveal man; man is action, and action is "movement", becoming, time, or history. «Par conséquent, pas d'Ontologie (ou de "Logik") sans Phénoménologie ou Anthropologie préalable, qui révèle l'Homme et l'Histoire» (consequently, no ontology, or "Logic", without a prior phenomenology or anthropology that reveals man and history) (p. 409). The priority of phenomenology over ontology is Kojève's methodological thesis, which he shares with Heidegger's fundamental ontology.

A third and last presentation of the same idea ends the third section and the second part (Hoffmeister p. 561, printed as p. 461). Kojève translates: the I, here the Sage's, must not, contrary to Fichte, fix itself in the form of self-consciousness as opposed to substantiality and objectivity, as if it feared its alienation or externalisation (*Entäußerung*). The force of Spirit consists rather in remaining identical with itself in its externalisation and, as being in and for itself, positing being-for-itself only as a moment, just as being-in-itself. Nor is the I, contrary to Schelling, a third thing that casts differences into the abyss of the Absolute and proclaims their identity in it. No, knowledge, incarnate in the Sage, consists rather in this apparent inactivity that only contemplates how what is differentiated moves itself within itself and returns to its unity. The phrase "apparent inactivity" (¶804) is the one Kojève comments last. Hegel's "abyss of the Absolute" alludes to his famous jibe at Schelling's Absolute as "the night in which all cows are black" (Preface, ¶16).

It is always the same thing. To Fichte's isolated self-consciousness and Schelling's Absolute in which self-consciousness is annihilated, Hegel opposes "the dialectical movement of the opposed toward the unifying unity". On the plane of reality this means that the total and homogeneous unity of being is not given, since the unity before the opposition is unknowable, but creates itself in and through the time that opposes man or subject to nature or object. On the plane of revelation by speech it means that ontology, the conceptual revelation of being, to be set out in the *Logic* in the second part of the System, must be the "result" of a prior conceptual revelation of becoming, of history, of man, set out in the first part of the System, the *Phenomenology*. The thesis that the unity of being is made, not given, restates the third lecture's active identification (p. 303).

A few words to conclude. Hegel speaks of the "apparent inactivity" of absolute knowledge, of what constitutes the Sage's very being. "Inactivity", because the Sage, as has always been said, only contemplates what is, changing nothing in it. But inactivity only "apparent", because the Sage contemplates action, and only through the contemplation of action, of "movement", becoming, or history, does he reach the contemplation of being in eternal identity with itself. Science therefore essentially presupposes action. That is why Science is itself, if one likes, an action, in the sense that it is a perpetual circular movement; in other words, it is dialectical. But it is dialectical only because the being it reveals is dialectical; and being is dialectical because it actually implies man, action, and because being that implies man realises and reveals itself in and through time, through historical human action. The Sage's "apparent inactivity" is the contemplation of completed action: contemplation is the last form of action, since its object is action.

The action of the Sage, of Science, detaches itself from man and passes into the Book. The "dialectical movement", ceasing to be the movement of the world or history, becomes the movement of the word-concept, "dialectic" in the ordinary sense. This detachment from man, this passage from "movement" to the word-concept, occurs because, being free of contradictions, the world and man can no longer "move". In other words, the world is dead; it is past, with everything it implies, man included. And being dead, the world and man-in-the-world can no longer serve as material support for the "dialectical" concept that continues to "live" or "move". The material support of the perpetual "movement" of the concept is henceforth the Book called *Logic*: «c'est ce Livre ("Bible") qui est le Logos éternel incarné» (it is this Book, "Bible", that is the eternal *Logos* incarnate) (p. 411). The Sage therefore does not act as a man. But he does not act so only because man can no longer act at the moment when wisdom becomes possible. And conversely, wisdom becomes possible only at the moment when all possible human objectives have already actually been attained. The last paragraph closes the second part with the Book as the eternal Logos incarnate, the secular Bible. The concluding chiasmus, the Sage does not act because man can no longer act; wisdom is possible because all human aims are attained, restates the dependence of wisdom on the end of history, which the lecture has just shown to be contingent on the existence of a philosopher.

### Eleventh Lecture: Interpretation of the Third Part of Chapter VIII (Hoffmeister pp. 561, l. 28 – 564)

The second part of Chapter VIII concerned the Sage, whom Hegel calls "absolute knowledge" or simply "knowledge": the man who produces "Science" (*Wissenschaft*), the complete and perfect revelation of the completed totality of being; or the empirical existence (*Dasein*) of Science in the natural world. The third part will concern Science itself, taken independently of the Sage or man who produces it, of its empirical existence in the world. In all that precedes, the whole *Phenomenology*, Hegel showed the why and the beginning of the appearance (*Erscheinung*) of Science. In this last paragraph he will explain briefly what this Science is, the Science he proposed to develop in full in the second part of the "System of Science", of which we possess only the first part, the *Phenomenology*, which is only an introduction to Science proper, to be set out above all in the *Logic*. The framing places the book's last pages as a sketch of the unwritten second part.

Hegel begins by recalling the result of the *Phenomenology*, which reflects the real evolution of universal history (Hoffmeister p. 561). Kojève translates: in knowledge, the Sage, Spirit has therefore completed the movement of its incarnation in concrete forms, insofar as this incarnation is affected by the unsurmounted difference of consciousness. In knowledge or the Sage, Spirit has reached the pure element of its existence, the concept. Hegel repeats here what we have long known. Knowledge is the Sage, the author of Science and of its introduction, the *Logic* and the *Phenomenology*. In the Sage, Spirit "completes the movement of its concrete formations". Shapes (*Gestalten*), the concrete forms of Spirit, are simply historical man. With the advent of the Sage the series of historical and social phenomena, truly and specifically human, is completed; the Sage's advent is therefore the last historical event. Historical evolution is "the unsurmounted difference of consciousness": man properly speaking, historical man, is opposed to nature, and history lasts as long as man has not managed to "abolish" this opposition by the negating action of fight and labour. When the Sage, and so Science, appears, the opposition is already abolished. Man no longer has Desire; he is perfectly and definitively satisfied by what is, by what he is; he no longer acts, no longer transforms the world, and so no longer changes himself. «Bref, il est devenu... sage, très sage» (in short, he has become ... wise, very wise) (p. 413). And the Sage who reveals what is by speech or concept reveals it definitively, since what then is remains eternally identical with itself, no longer modified by restlessness (*Unruhe*). The Sage's Science is therefore Science simply, true in the proper sense, universally and definitively. The pun on "sage", wise and well-behaved, is one of Kojève's rare jokes: post-historical man has become as tame as a good child. The identification of *Gestalten* with historical man restates the whole reading of the book.

Truth is the coincidence of the real or object (*Gegenstand*) and the concept (*Begriff*). One can therefore say that in and through the Sage the concept has "reached" the real; but also that it is the real that "reaches" its concept in and through the Sage. The being that reveals itself by the concept or discourse (*Logos*) is not only pure and simple being (*Sein*) but spiritual being, real Spirit (*Geist*). One can therefore also say that in and through the Sage, who produces absolute Science revealing the totality of being, Spirit "reaches" the concept. That is what Hegel says in the passage cited. The three formulations, concept reaches real, real reaches concept, Spirit reaches concept, express the same coincidence from three sides.

From this moment, Hegel says, the empirical existence (*Dasein*) of Spirit in the world is the concept. But it is a concept no longer opposed to its object, no longer outside the thing it reveals: a concept that no longer has as material support the existence of historical, acting, negating man; a concept that is no longer time; a concept that no longer changes and remains eternally identical with itself, identical to the identical being it reveals to this being itself. We know that the material support of this "eternal" concept is no longer historical man, nor even the Sage, but the Book that reveals by discourse, materialised in printed words, its own content, the "System of Science", whose first part is the "Science of the Phenomenology of Spirit". The chain of negations defines the post-historical concept by everything it no longer is. The Book returns as the concept's support.

A footnote justifies the role Kojève attributes to the Book, which may seem exaggerated from the text of Chapter VIII alone. He cites the end of the Preface (Hoffmeister p. 58): we must be convinced that truth has the destiny of making its way when its time has come, and appears only when this time has come; that it therefore never appears too early and never finds a public unripe for it; and that the individual needs this effect on the public so that what is still only his solitary cause may prove itself true (*bewähren*) for him by this effect, and so that he may experience that conviction, at first belonging only to particularity, is something universal. This is clear enough: to prove itself true, philosophy must be universally recognised, ultimately by the universal and homogeneous State. The empirical existence of Science is therefore not the Sage's private thought but his universally recognised word; and this "recognition" can in fact be obtained only by publishing a book. Existing as a book, Science actually detaches itself from its author, the Sage or man. A passage in Chapter V, A, c confirms this (Hoffmeister pp. 236–237): when one opposes a man's work (*Werk*) to his inner possibilities, capacities, or intention, only the work must be considered as his true objective reality, even if he is mistaken about it and, returning from his activity into himself, believes he is something other inwardly than he is in the deed (*Tat*). The individuality that entrusts itself to the objective element by becoming a work exposes itself to being changed and perverted; but what makes the character of the action is precisely whether it is an objectively real being that maintains itself or merely an intended work (*Gemeintes*) that vanishes into nothing. Objectivity does not change the action but only shows what it is, whether it is something or nothing. «Il est clair que la Tat (Action) et la Wirklichkeit (réalité-objective) du Sage sont non pas sa pensée, mais son livre» (it is clear that the Sage's deed and objective reality are not his thought but his book) (p. 414). The footnote grounds the Book thesis in Hegel's own texts: the Preface's claim that truth needs a public, and the physiognomy section's claim that a man is his work. The theory of recognition applies to philosophy: truth is recognised truth, and recognition requires publication.

The three sentences after the cited text form a kind of interpolated note. It is a rather obscure text, where Hegel explains what the term "concept" means, or more exactly the fact that the empirical existence of Spirit is henceforth no longer a "shape of consciousness", a human, social, or historical reality, but the concept itself. Kojève translates (Hoffmeister pp. 561–562): considered according to the freedom of its given being, the content is the self that externalises itself, the immediate unity of self-knowing. The pure movement of this externalisation, considered in the content, constitutes the necessity of the content. The differentiated content, as determinate, exists in relation and not in itself; it is its restlessness of overcoming itself, negativity. Necessity, differentiation, is therefore as much the self as free given being; and in this egoistic form, where existence is immediately thought (*Gedanke*), the content is concept. Kojève's rendering "égotiste-et-égoïste" for *selbstisch* keeps Hegel's pun.

The text is rather difficult, one of those "ideogram" texts in which Hegel manages to give in a few lines a summary of the ideas underlying his whole system: a new way of presenting the relations between being, man, and Science, which is the revelation of being by man; or, what is the same, between eternity, time, and concept. Kojève has already spoken at length of all this. To translate the "cabalistic" language of the passage into "normal" language, which would be rather long, he would have to repeat what he has said several times. He will not, since the text brings nothing really new. The "ideogram text" is a good name for Hegel's condensed passages. Kojève's decision to skip it is consistent with his method in these last lectures.

Having written this explanatory note, which could be put in brackets, Hegel returns to the last sentence of the short summary, where he said that in and through the Sage "Spirit has reached the concept" (Hoffmeister p. 562). Kojève translates: having reached the concept, Spirit develops existence and dialectical movement in this ether of its life, the concept, and is thus Science. When in and through knowledge or the Sage Spirit "reaches" its concept, it becomes Science (*Wissenschaft*), of which the third and last part of the last chapter will speak, and which was to be developed in the second part of the System, above all in the *Logic*. "Ether of its life" is Hegel's image for the concept as the medium in which Spirit now moves.

Note first that Science is not a science of Spirit. It is Spirit itself that is Science: "der Geist ist Wissenschaft". Spirit is being revealed by *Logos*, discourse, concept; and *Logos*, discourse, or concept that reveals being is ultimately Science. Spirit is Science and Science is Spirit. Or again: Science is the revelation of being (*Sein*); but being revealed by Science is Spirit, and it is Spirit only insofar as it is actually revealed by Science. Being is actually revealed by Science only insofar as Science itself is real and effective. Science must *be*; it must be part of being, insert itself into being; it must appear in the empirical existence of being, the world, and have a reality there; it must maintain itself in the world. For this the world, and so being, must include man, since man is precisely the concept or *Logos* that reveals being. Man, existing in the world and so in being, reveals being by speaking of being; or better, as human reality, being speaks of itself and so reveals itself to itself. But as long as the revelation of being is not complete, one can distinguish being, which is then only part of the totality, from its revelation; and it is the concept distinguished from the being it reveals that is man properly speaking. The concept tends to unite with being, to encompass the totality of being, and this "movement" of the concept toward totality is man's becoming, time or history. At the end of this movement, being coincides with the concept and the concept with being. Man therefore ceases to exist. The total concept, which detaches itself from man properly speaking (man opposed to the world, man who is only part of total being) and coincides with the totality of being, is Science and exists as Science in the Book. This Science is the revealed totality of being, Spirit. Empirical existence (*Dasein*) and dialectical movement (*Bewegung*) are now no longer outside the concept, in unrevealed being opposed to its revelation by man, but in real Spirit itself, the total concept or Science, which "exists empirically" as a Book. The concept that no longer opposes being no longer modifies being; it is no longer Desire, action, historical or temporal human existence. If there is still "movement", it no longer disturbs eternity: it is a cyclical movement, an eternal return upon itself, and this eternal cyclical movement is Science. Since this "movement" of Spirit is the process of revealing being by discourse, one can say that the "empirical existence" of revealed being, Spirit, is henceforth reduced to the "empirical existence" of the total concept or Science, the Book that materialises it. «Car, même si l'Homme disparaît tout à fait de la surface terrestre, le Livre restera» (for even if man disappears entirely from the face of the earth, the Book will remain) (p. 417). The world, the real totality of existing being, will therefore include a discourse, *Logos* or concept, and will so be the "empirical existence" of Spirit. It is henceforth because of the Book, and no longer because of man (who brings nothing new, but without whom the Book would not be possible), that being is Spirit. The sentence about man's disappearance and the Book's survival is the most extreme statement of the Book thesis. It makes Spirit independent of living humanity once history is over. The parenthesis concedes that the Book requires man, but only as its past condition.

The question now is what Science is: how the existence of Spirit as Book differs from its existence as man; how the eternal revelation of being differs from its temporal revelation; how the final aim of history differs from history itself; or, since temporal reality, history, is described or revealed by the *Phenomenology*, how the latter differs from Science proper, the *Logic*, for which it serves as introduction or way of access, as real history is the road leading to wisdom and Science, which is the result of the Sage's action presupposing the whole of humanity's historical action. The four formulations frame the lecture's central question: the relation of *Phenomenology* and *Logic*.

Hegel speaks of this now (Hoffmeister p. 562). Kojève translates: in Science proper, the *Logic*, the moments of Spirit's dialectical movement no longer present themselves, as in the *Phenomenology*, as determinate shapes of consciousness; on the contrary, the difference of consciousness having returned into the self, they present themselves as determinate concepts and as their movement grounded in itself. The *Phenomenology* describes the "shapes of consciousness", the concrete, plastic, even spatial forms of a consciousness that reveals being while being, and knowing itself to be, something other than the being it reveals. The *Phenomenology* describes man: it is an anthropology. But it describes the *Bewegung*, the "movement" of Spirit in its concrete forms, which means it is a genetic or historical anthropology: it describes man in his becoming, as he creates himself in and through, or better as, universal history. As Hegel will say at the end of the chapter, the *Phenomenology* is "comprehended history" (*begriffene Geschichte*) in its definitively completed whole. The characterisation of the *Phenomenology* as a genetic anthropology is the formula for Kojève's whole reading.

In Science proper, the second part of the System, "the difference has returned into the self", says Hegel. If historical man relates to the world in and through, or as, the negating action that creates a real or objective "distinction" between subject and object, the Sage relates to the object, in producing Science, only in and through his passive thought or contemplation. There is no longer in him a real opposition between the concept that reveals the thing and the thing revealed by the concept. «Et c'est dire que là où il y a le Sage, il n'y a plus d'Homme proprement dit. Il n'y a que le Concept» (and that is to say that where there is the Sage, there is no longer man properly speaking; there is only the concept) (p. 418). The relation between subject and object therefore no longer modifies either. One no longer leaves identity, and the "movement" or development of Science creates nothing new. This "movement" has no future; it is therefore not time, nor history. It is, if one likes, "eternal": the "organic movement" of the concept within itself, the "dialectical" development of the concept, the concept of being, into a "total" discourse returning perpetually upon itself, since, being in its whole its own conclusion, it incites itself to develop again. The claim that the Sage is no longer a man but only the concept extends the ninth lecture's "death of man" to the Sage himself.

Hegel confirms this in the next passage (Hoffmeister p. 562), comparing the *Phenomenology* and the *Logic*, the first and second parts of the System. Kojève translates: if in the *Phenomenology* each moment is the difference of knowledge and truth and the movement in which this difference is overcome, Science, by contrast, contains neither this difference nor its overcoming. The moment of Science, having the form of the concept, unites the objective form of truth and that of the knowing self in immediate unity. It does not present itself as the movement back and forth between consciousness or externalising representation and self-consciousness. The pure form of the moment, freed from its appearance in consciousness, the pure concept, and its progression depend solely on its pure determinateness. The passage (¶805) is Hegel's own statement of the difference between the two parts of the System.

The history of man, time, will last as long as a difference subsists between subjective "knowledge" and objective "truth", reality revealed by knowledge. History will last as long as there is in the world a being that errs and gradually eliminates its errors itself. This being is man and only man. The animal and nature in general do not err. Or, if one likes, nature errs too; but if it errs, its error, a monster for instance, or a living being not adapted to its milieu, is eliminated immediately: it dies or annihilates itself without being able to maintain itself temporarily in existence. «L'Homme seul peut maintenir l'erreur dans le Monde, en l'y faisant durer sous forme d'un Discours erroné» (man alone can maintain error in the world, making it last in the form of an erroneous discourse) (p. 419). And history is the history of man's erroneous discourses, which gradually become truths; not only because they change to conform to given reality, but because man, working and fighting, transforms reality itself to make it conform to his discourses, which at first diverged from it. When the conformity of reality and discourse is perfectly realised, when man can no longer err because he no longer transcends the given real, having no more Desire, history stops. Then subjective knowledge is at the same time objective, true definitively and completely; and this "absolute" knowledge is Science. The account of error is one of Kojève's most original contributions. Nature's errors (monsters, the maladapted) die at once; man's errors survive as discourse and can become truths by the transformation of the world. History is the process by which man's errors become true.

There is "movement" in Science too, since it is a "dialectical" concept or a discourse that develops. But this movement is no longer temporal, historical, human, or active. It is no longer, Hegel says, a matter of passing from subject to object and back: neither of rectifying knowledge by contemplating the real, "doing experiments", nor of "rectifying" the real by fighting against it and transforming it by labour. The subjective "movement" reveals the objective "movement" without modifying it; now, and only now, one can say: *ordo et connexio rerum idem est ac ordo et connexio idearum*. The "movement" takes place in the concept, in the revealed real, in true, even real, revelation. It is the movement of *Logos*, of discourse, which, being free of contradictions, remains identical with itself while developing. This movement is therefore "eternal"; more exactly, it is real eternity revealing itself to itself by itself as the movement of *Logos*. It is no longer the temporal movement of negating action but the "eternal", logical movement of discourse. The quotation of Spinoza's *Ethics* II, 7, the order and connection of things is the same as the order and connection of ideas, marks the point at which Spinozism becomes true: at the end of history. This confirms the seventh lecture's thesis that Hegel's system is a Spinozism made possible by time.

The logical movement of Science therefore reproduces the movement of being. Being "moves" in time, or more exactly as time; time is history; and history is man. So the real movement of universal history corresponds rigorously to the ideal movement of Science. And the "System", to be complete, must represent or contain not only the eternal or logical movement of revealed being, which is concept, but also the real or historical movement of the concept, which is real being or man. So the System necessarily has two parts or two complementary aspects, the *Logic* and the *Phenomenology* (Hoffmeister p. 562). Kojève translates: conversely, to each abstract moment of Science corresponds a concrete shape of appearing Spirit in general, described in the *Phenomenology*. As existing Spirit is no richer than Science, it is no poorer in content. To recognise, as the *Phenomenology* does, the pure concepts of Science in this form of shapes of consciousness constitutes the aspect of the reality of Science according to which its essence, the concept posited in Science in its simple mediation as thought (*Denken*), unfolds the moments of this mediation and presents itself according to its inner opposition. The correspondence between moments of the *Logic* and shapes of the *Phenomenology* (¶805) is the textual basis of Kojève's claim that the two parts have the same content.

History is neither richer nor poorer than being itself. This is evident. One can develop in time only what is; and the eternal totality of being is nothing but everything that has been in time. Being creates itself; but in creating itself it does not go beyond itself, since outside being there is nothing: nothingness. For the same reason there is no longer a future beyond time. The spatio-temporal totality of being is therefore itself neither spatial nor temporal. It is nothing but being itself revealed to itself by the concept; this totality is Spirit. But it is Spirit only insofar as it includes the concept. The concept included in being is man, and the "movement" of the concept in being, the real movement of the concept, is history. The claim that the totality of being is neither spatial nor temporal, though its parts are, is the resolution of the sixth lecture's problem: eternity is the totality of time.

The *Logic* and the *Phenomenology* therefore have one and the same content. Only the eternal "movement" of Science appears in the *Phenomenology* in the form of the temporal "movement" of history. Each stage of the *Phenomenology* corresponds to a stage of the *Logic*, and conversely. One truly understands the anthropology of the *Phenomenology* only by understanding the ontology of the *Logic*, which says what, from all eternity, the Spirit is that appears (*erscheint*) to itself in the temporal, historical, or human form described in the *Phenomenology*. Conversely, one understands the *Logic* only by understanding the *Phenomenology*; without it the eternal "movement" of discourse is empty and meaningless. One understands what Spirit is only by knowing how it appears in its "empirical existence" (*Dasein*), and the "empirical existence" of Spirit is man, history, or time. The thesis of the mutual dependence of *Logic* and *Phenomenology* is Kojève's answer to the old debate about their relation. It concedes that the anthropology needs the ontology, an important qualification of his anthropological reading.

The "System" therefore has meaning only on condition of having two parts: an anthropological phenomenology and an ontological logic. One is incomplete without the other, and only the whole has meaning: the whole in which, as in being itself, the eternity of *Logos* is realised by the temporal "movement" reproduced in the *Phenomenology*. In other words, the "System of Science" is necessarily circular or cyclical. Having read the *Phenomenology*, one is necessarily pushed toward the *Logic*: one understands that whoever could write or read the *Phenomenology* can do nothing but understand what is in eternal identity with itself, being as such, the theme of the *Logic*. And having read the *Logic*, one is just as necessarily sent back to the *Phenomenology*: learning at the end and through the whole of the *Logic* that being is Spirit or Idea, being revealed to itself, one also sees that this revelation is possible only because being is time and becoming; and to understand being as becoming one must read the *Phenomenology*. The System is a cycle between its two parts, which is Kojève's reading of the circularity criterion applied to the whole.

All this Hegel will explain in the two pages ending the *Phenomenology*: first in condensed form in the first paragraph of this final passage, positing the idea of the scientific circle, then commenting on it. Kojève translates the condensed text (Hoffmeister p. 562): Science contains in itself this necessity of externalising (*entäußern*) itself from the form of the pure concept, and the passage of the concept into consciousness. For Spirit knowing itself, precisely because it grasps (*erfasst*) its concept, is the immediate equality (*Gleichheit*) with itself that is, in its difference (*Unterschied*), the certainty of the immediate, sensible consciousness, the beginning from which we started in the *Phenomenology*. This release (*Entlassen*) of itself from the form of its self is the supreme freedom and security of its self-knowledge. The passage (¶806) is the textual locus of the circle from *Logic* back to *Phenomenology*.

On the one hand this text can be referred to the *Phenomenology*, to the *Logic*, or to the System as a whole; in all three cases we are dealing with circular, even cyclical, knowledge. On the other hand one can give it an anthropological interpretation, referring it not only to Science as such but to its "empirical existence", the Book and the man who wrote it, the Sage. The plan of the commentary: first Science, then the *Phenomenology*, then the Sage.

Refer the text first to Science in the narrow sense, the *Logic* or the second part of the System generally. The *Logic*, says Hegel, necessarily implies the passage (*Übergang*) from concept to consciousness. Consciousness is the subject opposed to the object, and the knowing subject that is other than the known object is man, man properly speaking, the historical man described in the *Phenomenology*. The *Logic* therefore necessarily implies a return to the *Phenomenology*, from which it necessarily emerges, as one sees in reading the last chapter. Why this necessary passage? Because, says Hegel, Spirit that "grasps its concept" is "immediate identity or equality with itself". In the *Logic* as in the *Phenomenology*, Spirit "grasps its concept" at the end, since only at the end of the logical development does the "being" (*Sein*) from which one started reveal itself as "Idea", existing concept and conceived existence. What characterises *Sein*, static given being, is precisely its homogeneity and unity, its absolute identity with itself. The "Idea", the absolute identity of concept and being, is therefore nothing but *Sein*. So, reaching the end of the logical development, one is thrown back to its beginning: the *Logic* is circular in itself. The inference that the Idea, as absolute self-identity, is indistinguishable from pure being is Kojève's reading of the end of the *Science of Logic*, where the absolute Idea returns to the immediacy of the beginning.

More exactly, it is cyclical, since having returned to the beginning one must retrace the path already travelled. The *Sein* found at the beginning of the *Logic*, being absolutely identical with itself, absolutely homogeneous and universal, is not revealed being (Idea), since being reveals itself through the concept, and revealed being implies a duality or opposition, a difference (*Unterschied*). *Sein* is identical with itself, homogeneous and universal in its homogeneity; it fills everything itself; there is no room in it for the concept; so as such it is not revealed. But the beginning of the *Logic* is not *Sein* itself but the concept "*Sein*", a meaningful word. There is therefore from the beginning something other (*Anderes*) than *Sein*. But *Sein* is homogeneous and universal (identity = thesis). The other, being what *Sein* is not (negativity = antithesis), can only be pure nothingness (*Nichts*). But *Sein* being absolutely universal, there is nothing outside it. "There is" nothingness only if *Sein* is itself nothingness. And *Sein* that is nothingness, nothingness that is, is necessarily becoming (*Werden*; totality = synthesis). This means *Sein* annihilates itself to the very extent that it is; it is in time, or better, it is time, time that is. Only so is it revealed as *Sein*, can it be, or become, the meaningful word or concept "*Sein*". And so on. Progressing necessarily from stage to stage, one arrives at being fully revealed in its totality by the concept, the "Idea", which, being absolutely homogeneous, universal, and identical with itself, identical with its being and with its own concept, is the same eternal (pre- and post-temporal) *Sein* from which one started. But this *Sein* is revealed; it is the word or concept "*Sein*". Therefore, and so on; and one retraces the circle indefinitely, without ever being able to stop. This is Kojève's reconstruction of the opening triad of the *Science of Logic* (being, nothing, becoming) in terms of his own theory: becoming is time, and being is revealed only as time. The derivation of the need to begin again from the difference between *Sein* and the concept "*Sein*" is precise: the word is already other than being.

The *Logic* is thus cyclical in itself. But the whole System is a perpetual cycle. The beginning of the *Logic* is the word "*Sein*". To speak with Kant, without *Sein* itself this word is empty of meaning; without this word, *Sein* is blind, unrevealed, mute. The *Logic* therefore presupposes a duality or opposition (*Entzweiung*) of *Sein* and concept. In the *Logic* itself this duality is "overcome" in and through the Idea. But for the movement to reach the Idea it must begin, and for it to begin there must already be, and so have been, a dualism of concept and being. The concept of being opposed to being within being is man; more exactly, it is negating Desire engendering duality or rupture (*Entzweiung*) within identical being or the eternal Idea, turning this Idea into *Sein* opposed to *Nichts* and object opposed to subject. This Desire is the origin of the "movement" described in the *Phenomenology*: the origin of history, which finally ends in the production of the *Logic*, after having understood or revealed itself to itself in and through the *Phenomenology*. Reaching the end of the *Logic*, the Idea, one is thrown back to its beginning, *Sein*, and one retraces the cycle. But the cycle of the *Logic* as a whole throws us back to its own origin, the *Phenomenology*; and it is the whole System that is a perpetual cycle. The paraphrase of Kant's "concepts without intuitions are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind" applied to *Sein* is apt. The identification of the *Entzweiung* that starts the *Logic* with anthropogenic Desire is the decisive link: the *Logic* presupposes man as the rupture within being.

It remains to know whether the *Phenomenology*, the first part of the System, is itself cyclical. Referring the text to it, one sees that it is. Real history, and so its revelation in and through the *Phenomenology*, ends in absolute knowledge, the Sage or incarnate Science, the *Logic* existing empirically in the world as a Book. In and through this Book, Spirit has "grasped its concept": being and concept coincide absolutely and perfectly in it; being is entirely revealed by the concept that the Book's meaning develops, and the concept is completely realised in being by the Book's existence. But there remains a difference (*Unterschied*) between the Sage and the Book. Without this "difference" the concept could not have been a Book, could not have been realised in the world, and being, not really being the concept, would not really be revealed; it would not truly be Spirit or Idea. But the Book, the knowledge that differs from the Sage, is a sensible object: it is through sensation, "sense-certainty" (*sinnliche Gewissheit*), that the Sage is in real contact with it; it is through sensations that he writes it and it is read. To understand real Science one must read the Book printed in black on white paper. And to understand the Book's meaning one must understand the possibility for man of writing and understanding it; one understands this possibility only by beginning with the nature and possibility of the sensation the printed Book gives. One must understand what sensation is in general, and to do so one must retrace the cycle of the *Phenomenology*, whose first chapter treats precisely this "sense-certainty", which Hegel here calls "sensible consciousness". The argument that the Book's being a sensible object sends one back to Chapter I is Kojève's most concrete reading of the circularity: absolute knowledge is read with the eyes, and seeing is sense-certainty.

This means that knowledge can never transcend the sensible real. Spirit too is a sensible being, and non-sensible or "supersensible" being is only an idle fantasy. Without sensation and all that follows from it, the *Logic* itself is only a heap of meaningless words, whose origin and existence are moreover incomprehensible. For the word "*Sein*" from which it starts is "filled" with meaning only by pure sensation, which reveals being as *Sein*, absolutely universal in its perfect homogeneity excluding all differences. And sensation reveals *Sein* to the man of Desire (*Begierde*), who alone will one day be able to write the *Logic*, realising the concept by inserting it into empirically existing being, so transforming being that was only *Sein* into Spirit or Idea, and so proving true the final result of the *Logic*, that being is Idea; a result that, if per impossibile it could be reached without passing through the real history created by this man and the revelation of this completed history by the *Phenomenology*, would simply be false, and indeed inconceivable in its very falsity. The claim that "Spirit too is a sensible being" is Kojève's materialism at its most emphatic. The *Logic* without the *Phenomenology* would be false: ontology without history is empty.

The same holds for all the stages of the *Logic*. It has meaning as a whole only because there is an experience (*Erfahrung*) of becoming being, lived by man in the course of his history, of the history that creates conscious and voluntary becoming, which alone makes being accessible to the concept, which itself is born only of the opposition between subject and object, the opposition that constitutes experience and that, taken in itself, is anthropogenic Desire, the Desire that realises and satisfies itself by the negating and creative action of fight and labour, forming in its whole universal history. The *Phenomenology* is therefore as cyclical as the *Logic* and the whole System. The long sentence traces the whole genealogy of the concept back to Desire, as in the eighth lecture.

This cyclical character of the anthropology that is the *Phenomenology* has an immediate anthropological meaning. Hegel's Sage, the perfect man, has nothing to do with Plotinus's "Sage", for example, who in the ecstasy of absolute knowledge rose, according to Porphyry, a few inches above the ground. No, the Hegelian Sage stands firmly on his feet. His very Science has no meaning and becomes empty verbiage as soon as it is detached from sensation and Desire and all that follows. The levitation anecdote does not appear to be in Porphyry's *Life of Plotinus*; the attribution seems loose. The contrast is nonetheless pointed: the Hegelian Sage does not rise above the earth.

Certainly Plotinus's "Sage" eats and drinks too; otherwise he could not have risen above the ground. But as Sage, in his Science, he pretends to forget it, to be uninterested in it, not to need it. Hegel tells us this is absurd. One must hold to and account for the fact that one must eat and drink to write the Book of Science, and that one must do so too for this Book to have a meaning. For if being ceases to be hidden and ineffable, fundamentally unrevealed, purely natural, and so mute or bestial, it is because it has been revealed by man in the course of time, following his historical action, which is impossible without Desire, which Desire, while human, even negating, can arise and subsist only by relying on a natural or animal Desire, which it negates. The remark that the Book needs eating and drinking both to be written and to have meaning is Kojève's reply to every spiritualist reading of Hegel. Human Desire negates animal desire but depends on it: the Introduction's necessary-but-not-sufficient condition (p. 11) returns at the end.

In short, to say that being reveals itself by historical time or as historical time, or, what is the same, that the *Logic* can be written or read and understood only after one has written or read and understood the *Phenomenology*, is also to say that the Sage cannot disown the sensible real in and outside himself. If he himself does not act and desires nothing, it is because for him and around him there is nothing more to do or desire. But Desire and action are as essential to him as to the common man. He must remember them, and it is only this remembrance (*Er-innerung*) of action and Desire, told in the *Phenomenology*, that makes him a Sage, a perfect man, capable of revealing that same homogeneous and universal totality of being that he lives by drinking, eating, and remembering everything that resulted from the desire to drink and eat that was one day repressed "for the first time" by a specifically human, or better anthropogenic, desire for recognition. The image of the Sage drinking, eating, and remembering the first repression of hunger by the desire for recognition closes the book's circle: the end remembers the beginning, the Introduction's Desire (p. 12).

When Hegel says in the last line of the cited passage that this return to sensation is "the supreme freedom and security" of the Sage's self-knowledge, he says it consciously opposing the Sage to the Neoplatonic or Christian ascetic fleeing the world, of whom he spoke in Chapter IV, saying (Hoffmeister p. 168) that he can be only "a personality limited to itself and its own petty actions, brooding over itself, as unhappy as it is impoverished". The reference to the unhappy consciousness's asceticism (¶225) makes the Sage its opposite: freedom lies in returning to the senses, not in fleeing them.

This must be taken into account if one does not want to yield to the temptation of a theological interpretation of the *Phenomenology*. Spirit is *Wissenschaft*, Science; and Science is *absolutes Wissen*, absolute knowledge, a "shape of consciousness", a being living in the natural world. This being is therefore the incarnate *Logos*. But it is not a God who is born and dies, lives, eats, and drinks despite his divinity, but who could do without these things. No: the being Hegel has in view is *Logos* because it drinks and eats, is born, lives, and dies, «et meurt pour de bon, sans ressusciter» (and dies for good, without rising again) (p. 426). Its spiritual reality is the discursive revelation of its sensible reality and cannot be detached from it. Such a detachment would mean for it not an elevation into the luminous heaven but a dissolution into the night of nothingness ("diese Nacht"), simply death. The contrast with the incarnate Christ is precise: the Christian God eats and drinks despite his divinity; the Sage is Logos because he eats and drinks. "Diese Nacht" alludes to the last paragraph of the *Phenomenology* (¶808), where Spirit, withdrawing into itself, is "sunk in the night of its self-consciousness".

That is why one must say that the Hegelian Spirit that is Science and absolute knowledge is not God but man: the Sage who has actually reached perfection, without wanting or being able to disown the temporal imperfection that gave him birth, and who is fully "satisfied" by the mere fact of having understood and explained, and so, if one likes, "justified", this imperfection, showing that without it he could not have understood. The final sentence of the lecture defines the Sage's satisfaction as the justification of the imperfection that produced him. It is Kojève's secular theodicy: the evil of history is justified by the understanding it made possible.

### Twelfth Lecture: Interpretation of the Third Part of Chapter VIII (Continued and Concluded)

In the passage on the circularity of the System, it was said that reaching the end of the *Logic* throws one back to its beginning, and that having completed this circular movement one sees the need to go beyond it, to pass to the *Phenomenology*. To pass from the *Logic* to the *Phenomenology* is to pass from the identity or perfect coincidence of subject and object, concept and reality, consciousness and self-consciousness, to their opposition or "difference" (*Unterschied*). The distinction between consciousness and self-consciousness that characterises the *Phenomenology* presupposes a real difference between consciousness in general and non-conscious reality, a real distinction between man and world. Consequently a System that necessarily falls into two parts, a *Logic* and a *Phenomenology*, must necessarily be "realist", as one says. The inference from the two-part structure to realism is the lecture's thesis: the *Phenomenology* is needed only because being is not simply thought.

This observation is decisive for understanding Hegel. Misled by the Hegelian expression "absolute idealism" (*absoluter Idealismus*), people have often affirmed that Hegel's system is "idealist". In fact Hegelian absolute idealism has nothing to do with what is ordinarily called "idealism"; if one uses the terms in their usual sense, one must say that Hegel's system is "realist". To be convinced it would suffice to cite some texts from the early writing *Difference between Fichte's and Schelling's System of Philosophy* (1801). Kojève translates (vol. I, pp. 47, 48, 77): neither the subjective alone nor the objective alone fills consciousness; the pure subjective is as much an abstraction as the pure objective. It is for the sake of the identity of subject and object that I posit things outside me with as much certainty as I posit myself: things exist as certainly as I exist (*So gewiss Ich bin, sind die Dinge*); Kojève adds that Hegel is thus even more "realist" than Descartes. Both, subject and object, have not only the same right to existence but the same necessity; for if only one were referred to the Absolute and the other not, their essence would be posited unequally, and their union, and so the task of philosophy, to overcome the rupture (*Entzweiung*) of subject and object, would be impossible. The reading of Hegel as a realist is Kojève's most polemical claim against the neo-Kantian and idealist readings of his day. The *Differenzschrift* passage is well chosen: "as certainly as I am, things are" states a realism of equal footing.

This is clear. But the "demonstration" of realism in Chapter VIII reveals little-known but very important aspects of the problem. Hegel posits the principle of metaphysical "realism" in the passage immediately following the one where he demonstrated the necessity of passing from the *Logic* to the *Phenomenology*. Kojève translates (Hoffmeister p. 563): yet this externalisation (*Entäußerung*) is still imperfect. It expresses the relation (*Beziehung*) of self-certainty to the object, which, precisely because it is in relation with the subject, has not yet attained its full freedom (*Freiheit*). It is not enough to pass from the *Logic* to the *Phenomenology*. The *Phenomenology* concerns the relation between consciousness and self-consciousness, thought and reality; the object appears there only insofar as it is related to the subject. For a Reinhold or a Fichte, this relation takes place within the subject, the object being only an aspect of subjective activity. For Hegel, by contrast, the dialectic of subject and object that takes place within the subject and is described in the *Phenomenology* has meaning only if one supposes the existence of an object properly speaking, an object external to the subject and independent of it. As Hegel says, one must give the object "its full freedom". In short, relying here on Schelling, Hegel has just posited, against Fichte, the absolute necessity of a "realist" metaphysics. The object's "full freedom" (¶806) is Kojève's key text for realism: the object must be independent of its relation to the subject.

In the following text (Hoffmeister p. 563) Hegel briefly indicates the nature of this "realist" metaphysics. Kojève translates: knowledge knows (*kennt*) not only itself but also its negative, its limit (*Grenze*). To know its limit means to know how to sacrifice itself. This sacrifice (*Aufopferung*) is the externalisation in which Spirit presents (*darstellt*) its becoming toward Spirit in the form of a free contingent happening (*Geschehens*), intuiting its pure self as time outside itself, and likewise its being (*Sein*) as space. The passage (¶807) is the book's last metaphysical statement, and Kojève reads it word by word.

The passage first contains a kind of "deduction" of realism that can be misunderstood if taken in isolation. It is directed against Fichte, and in speaking to Fichte Hegel speaks Fichte's language (*Grenze*, and so on). So the text seems to speak of an act of the subject positing the object by positing its own limit, which looks like pure Fichte, "idealism". But reading carefully and comparing what Hegel says with what Fichte says elsewhere, one sees a polemic. First, it is not the I or subject (*Ich*) that posits the object or limit, but Spirit (*Geist*); and Hegel never tires of repeating that Spirit is not origin or beginning but end or result. Spirit is revealed being, a synthesis of objective being and its subjective revelation. It is not the subject but Spirit, and so being, that posits itself as space and time, or, as will be seen, as nature (= *Sein*) and history (= man = subject = *Selbst*). Second, Hegel does not say, like Fichte, that knowledge "posits" (*setzt*) its "limit", the object; he says only that it "knows" (*kennt*) it. Hegel simply means that knowledge can understand itself, explain or "deduce" itself, only by supposing the existence of a non-knowledge, a real object external to and independent of the knowledge that reveals it. This is exactly the opposite of what Fichte says. The two textual distinctions, *Geist* not *Ich* and *kennt* not *setzt*, are precise and convincing: Hegel's sentence uses Fichte's vocabulary to reverse Fichte's thesis.

There is therefore no "deduction" of realism in the Fichtean sense, only a "deduction" in the Hegelian sense: an *a posteriori* deduction or conceptual comprehension of what is. It is not a question, as in Fichte, of deducing the object or the real from the subject or the idea. A footnote adds that it is in fact absurd to want to "deduce", to demonstrate, realism: if one could deduce the real from knowledge, idealism would be right and there would be no reality independent of knowledge. Starting from Spirit, a synthesis of the real and the ideal, Hegel renounces deducing one from the other, as he says clearly in the 1801 text. He posits, that is, presupposes, both, and "deduces" them only after the fact, from Spirit, their common result. He tries only to understand their relations, which are the becoming of knowledge, starting from the fact, for him acquired, of absolutely true knowledge in which the real and the ideal coincide. But he says that in possessing the truth, the "Science" or "System", one must not forget their origin, which is not coincidence but the opposition and interaction of an independent real and ideal. One must not believe that if Science is a knowledge, being is knowledge or subject too. Being is Spirit, a synthesis of knowledge and the real. And the System itself is not a game of the subject within itself but the result of an interaction between subject and object; so it is a revelation of the object by the subject and a realisation of the subject in the object. The footnote's argument is elegant: realism cannot be demonstrated, since a demonstration of the real from knowledge would refute it. Realism can only be presupposed and understood after the fact.

Hegel starts from Spirit, which he says is a "result", and wants to understand it as a result, to describe it as resulting from its own becoming (*das Werden des Geistes zum Geiste*). Spirit being the coincidence of subject and object, or, as Hegel says here, of *Selbst* and *Sein*, its becoming is the road leading to this coincidence, along which a difference between the two is therefore maintained, which only metaphysical realism can account for. The becoming toward coincidence presupposes a difference along the way; only realism explains the difference.

Having said this, Hegel gives two extremely important precisions. First, he says that "the becoming of Spirit" has the form of "free, contingent happening" (*freien zufälligen Geschehens*). He repeats what we have long known: "deduction" is possible only after the fact, *a posteriori*. To say that the becoming of Spirit is "contingent and free" is to say that starting from Spirit, the end or result of the becoming, one can reconstruct its course, but one cannot foresee it from its beginning or deduce Spirit from it. Spirit being the identity of being and subject, one can "deduce" from it the prior opposition of the two and the process that abolishes it. But starting from the initial opposition one can deduce neither its final abolition nor the process leading to it. That is why this process, history in particular, is a free sequence (*frei*) of contingent events (*zufällig*). The phrase "free contingent happening" is the textual basis for Kojève's thesis, stated since 1934–35 (p. 73), that transitions are free acts deducible only retrospectively. Necessity is backward-looking.

Second, Hegel says that in its becoming Spirit, the revealed totality of being, is necessarily double: on the one hand self (*Selbst*) or time, on the other static being (*Sein*) or space. This is very important. It is first a new affirmation of realism, since realism is necessarily dualist, and an ontological dualism is always "realist". A footnote adds that the claim that everything is object or "matter" is equivalent to the claim that everything is subject or "spirit"; the materialist and the idealist or spiritualist claims coincide, being equally meaningless. The whole question is how to define the two terms opposed in realism. Hegel says they must be opposed as time and space. In saying so he sums up, as it were, his whole philosophy and indicates what is truly new in it. Taken in isolation the claim seems paradoxical: no one ever thought of dividing the totality of being into space and time. Insofar as Western philosophy has been "realist" or dualist, it has divided the totality of being into subject and object, thought and reality, and so on. But we know that for Hegel time is the concept. At once, instead of paradoxical, Hegel's division seems banal: it is the Cartesian opposition of extension and thought. In fact Hegel made a great discovery in replacing "thought" by "time"; Kojève has tried to show this and will not return to it. The equivalence of materialism and idealism in the footnote is a characteristic Kojèvian dismissal: monisms are all empty. The replacement of Descartes's "thought" by "time" is the lecture's formula for Hegel's originality.

The text is interesting for another reason too. Hegel identifies space and *Sein*, static given being, which is banal and very Cartesian. But the identification of time with the *Selbst*, the personal self, man, is new: it is the Hegelian conception of man = action = negativity, of which there is no need to speak now. Kojève wants to stress that Hegel here opposes the self (= time) to *Sein* (= space). Man is therefore non-being (*Nicht-sein*), nothingness. A footnote adds that in the *Logic* the totality of being, Spirit, is defined at the beginning as being (*Sein*) and nothing (*Nichts*), their synthesis being becoming. To oppose time to being is to say that time is nothingness; and there is no doubt that time must indeed be understood as an annihilation of being or space. But if man is time, he is himself nothingness or the annihilation of spatial being. And we know that for Hegel it is precisely in this annihilation of being that the negativity that is man consists: the action of fight and labour by which man maintains himself in spatial being by destroying it, transforming it by creating unprecedented novelties into a true past, nonexistent and so non-spatial. It is this negativity, nothingness nihilating as time in space, that forms the very basis of specifically human existence, truly active or creative, historical, individual, and free. It is also this nothingness that makes man transient in the spatial world: he is born and dies there as man. There is therefore a nature without man, before man and after man, as Hegel will say presently. The chain man = time = nothingness completes the ontology begun in the Introduction's "revealed nothingness" (p. 12). The inference from man's being nothingness to his transience, and from transience to a nature before and after him, grounds the realism in finitude.

Finally, referring the same text to knowledge, one must say that man properly speaking, man opposed to the one and homogeneous spatial being, the free historical individual Hegel calls "*Selbst*", is necessarily error and not truth. For a thought that does not coincide with being is false. So when specifically human error is finally transformed into the truth of absolute Science, man ceases to exist as man and history ends. The abolition of man, time, action, in favour of static being, space, nature, is therefore the abolition of error in favour of truth. «Et si l'Histoire est certainement l'histoire des erreurs humaines, l'Homme lui-même n'est peut-être qu'une erreur de la Nature qui "par hasard" (liberté ?) n'a pas été immédiatement éliminée» (and if history is certainly the history of human errors, man himself is perhaps only an error of nature that "by chance" (freedom?) was not immediately eliminated) (p. 432). The sentence recalls the eleventh lecture's account of nature's errors, monsters eliminated at once (p. 419), and turns it on man: man is the monster that survived. The parenthesis "(freedom?)" identifies the chance of survival with freedom, a vertiginous suggestion.

In Kojève's view the division of the totality of revealed being, of Spirit, into space and time is neither a paradox nor a banality but a truth discovered by Hegel. If one admits it, one must say that "realism" in philosophy means in the end nothing other than "historicism". Whoever says "realism" says ontological dualism; and in naming the two members of the fundamental opposition "space" and "time", one introduces into philosophy the notion of history, posing not only the problem of an anthropology or phenomenology of historical man but also that of a metaphysics and an ontology of history. To say that philosophy must be "realist" is therefore to say in the last analysis that it must take account of the fact of history. The equation of realism with historicism is Kojève's most compact philosophical thesis. It gives his whole reading a single formula: to be a realist is to take history seriously.

And Kojève believes this very correct. If, per impossibile, there were not what is called ontologically "negativity", metaphysically "time" or "history", and anthropologically "action", idealism, monism, would be right: it would be superfluous to oppose being to thought ontologically, and one would have no need to go beyond Parmenides. Kojève does not believe one can define the real properly speaking otherwise than as Maine de Biran, among others, did: «le Réel, — c'est ce qui résiste» (the real is what resists) (p. 432). But one is quite wrong to believe that the real resists thought. In fact it does not: it does not even resist false thought; and as for true thought, it is precisely a coincidence with the real. A footnote gives the example: if I say I can pass through this wall, the wall does not resist what I say or think at all; I can say it as much as I like. It begins to resist only if I want to realise my thought by action, if I actually bump into the wall. And it is always so. «Le Réel résiste à l'Action, et non à la Pensée» (the real resists action, not thought) (p. 433). So there is truly philosophical "realism" only where philosophy takes account of action, history, time; and philosophical "realism", or "dualism", indeed means "temporalism" or "historicism". The appeal to Maine de Biran's definition of the real as resistance, grounded in the experience of effort, is apt. Kojève's twist, the real resists action and not thought, is decisive: the wall example makes realism a matter of the body in action, which links the ontology to labour and fight.

A long footnote draws the consequences. It makes no sense to oppose, as "realism" usually does, the knowing subject to the known object; once they are opposed, one can no longer understand their union in true knowledge. If one wants to take account of the real, one must not oppose the natural world to a "subject" situated one knows not where, whose sole function is to know the world, to reveal it by discourse or concept. One must not oppose being to thought or the knowing subject; one must oppose natural being to human being. In Hegel's terms: on the phenomenological plane, *Sein* to *Selbst*; on the metaphysical plane, space to time; on the ontological plane, identity to negativity. One must see in man something other than a knowing subject, and oppose man to the natural world precisely insofar as he is this something other (*Anderes*). True knowledge, which is what is usually spoken of, is impersonal (*selbst-los*), inhuman: in it subject coincides with object, and one can say it is the object that reveals itself to itself in and through this knowledge. Suppose a man understood as "knowing subject" reduced himself to the adequate knowledge of a single particular reality, "dog". He would then be nothing but the revelation of this reality: we would be in the presence of revealed dog-reality, a self-conscious dog, not a man knowing a dog; and so of a real dog, a natural being, not a man with canine form. In Hegel's terms there would be only mute self-feeling (*Selbstgefühl*), not speaking self-consciousness (*Selbstbewusstsein*); the concept would be incarnate in the thing it reveals and would not exist outside it as a word. "Realism" would have no meaning, since there would be no separation of subject and object. For there to be realism the concept, knowledge, must oppose itself to the thing, the object; and only human or "subjective" knowledge opposes itself to the object it relates to, materialising itself outside the object in discourse. But this subjective knowledge is by definition a knowledge that does not coincide with its object; it is therefore false. The problem that requires a "realist" solution is therefore the problem of error, not of truth. And positing the fact of error, one must pose the problem of its origin. Evidently it is not passive cognitive contemplation, opening itself to the object and making it accessible, that can explain the origin of error, which slips away from the object and conceals it. If the seat of error is man or the "subject", he must have as support something other than passive contemplation of the given; and this something other is called in Hegel negativity, time, and action (*Tat*, *Tun*, *Handeln*). It is not by chance, then, that man makes errors when he loses his composure, hurries, or does not have enough time, or ... stubbornly says no. "Realism" has meaning only insofar as one opposes, on the one hand, the natural world or given being (*Sein*) revealed by the concept, being with its knowledge, and on the other hand man understood as negating action of given being. Or knowledge, revelation, relates indifferently to natural being and to human being, to space and to time, to identity and to negativity; there is no opposition between being and knowledge; an opposition exists only between natural being (known) or *Sein* and human being (known) or *Tun*; and error and "subjective" knowledge in general presuppose this ontological opposition. This footnote is one of the most important in the book. It relocates the realist opposition from subject/object to nature/man, and grounds it in error rather than truth. The thought experiment of the man reduced to knowing a dog, who would thereby become a self-conscious dog, is Kojève's most vivid argument that pure knowledge is not human. The remark that we err when hurried or "stubbornly saying no" ties error to time and negation with a light touch.

Returning to the text: having opposed given being or space to self or time, Hegel specifies the nature of the two opposed entities, beginning with space (Hoffmeister p. 563). Kojève translates: this last-mentioned becoming of Spirit, nature, is its living immediate becoming.
