Nature, externalised Spirit, is in its existence nothing but the eternal externalisation of its subsistence (*Bestehens*) and the movement that produces the subject. *Sein* or space is nature, the non-conscious natural world; and this world is eternal in the sense of being outside time. Nature is the "eternal externalisation" (*ewige Entäußerung*) of Spirit. Here too there is becoming (*Werden*) or movement, but, as in Descartes, a non-temporal or geometrical movement; natural changes, biological becoming, do not transform the essence of nature, which remains eternally identical with itself. This natural "movement", "evolution", certainly produces the "subject", man, or more exactly the animal that will become man. But man, once constituted in his human specificity, opposes himself to nature and so engenders a new becoming, which essentially transforms given natural being and is the time that annihilates it, the history of negating action. The distinction between nature's geometrical, non-essential movement and history's essential transformation completes the dualism. "The animal that will become man" places anthropogenesis at the boundary.

Hegelian "realism" is therefore not only ontological but metaphysical. Nature is independent of man; being eternal, it subsists before and after him. It is in nature that he is born, and, as will be seen, man who is time also disappears in spatial nature, since nature survives time. A footnote, the most famous of the book, follows. The disappearance of man at the end of history is therefore not a cosmic catastrophe: the natural world remains what it has been from all eternity. Nor is it a biological catastrophe: man remains alive as an animal in accord with nature or given being. What disappears is man properly speaking, negating action of the given and error, or in general the subject opposed to the object. In fact the end of human time or history, the definitive annihilation of man properly speaking or of the free and historical individual, means quite simply the cessation of action in the strong sense. Which means practically: «la disparition des guerres et des révolutions sanglantes» (the disappearance of wars and bloody revolutions) (p. 435). And also the disappearance of philosophy: since man no longer changes essentially, there is no longer reason to change the true principles at the basis of his knowledge of the world and himself. «Mais tout le reste peut se maintenir indéfiniment ; l'art, l'amour, le jeu, etc., etc. ; bref, tout ce qui rend l'Homme heureux» (but everything else can be maintained indefinitely: art, love, play, and so on; in short, everything that makes man happy) (p. 435). This Hegelian theme, among many others, was taken up by Marx. History properly speaking, where men (classes) fight each other for recognition and fight nature by labour, is called by Marx the "realm of necessity" (*Reich der Notwendigkeit*); beyond it lies the "realm of freedom" (*Reich der Freiheit*), where men, recognising each other without reserve, no longer fight and work as little as possible, nature being definitively tamed, harmonised with man (*Capital*, III, ch. 48). The footnote of 1946 states the end of history in its gentlest form: no more wars or revolutions, no more philosophy, but art, love, and play. The link to Marx's realm of freedom is apt. The sentence "everything that makes man happy" will be withdrawn in the second edition's note.

The Note of the Second Edition (pp. 436–437) revises this footnote, and it is among the most discussed pages of twentieth-century philosophy. Kojève writes that the text of the note is ambiguous, not to say contradictory. If one admits "the disappearance of man at the end of history", if one affirms that "man remains alive as animal", specifying that "what disappears is man properly speaking", one cannot say that "everything else can be maintained indefinitely: art, love, play, etc." If man becomes an animal again, his arts, loves, and games must also become purely "natural" again. One would have to admit that after the end of history men would build their edifices and works of art as birds build their nests and spiders spin their webs, would perform musical concerts after the fashion of frogs and cicadas, would play as young animals play, and would indulge in love as adult beasts do. But one cannot then say that all this "makes man happy". One would have to say that the post-historical animals of the species *Homo sapiens*, living in abundance and complete security, will be content as a function of their artistic, erotic, and playful behaviour, since by definition they will be contented with it. Moreover, the definitive annihilation of man properly speaking also means the definitive disappearance of human discourse (*Logos*) in the proper sense. The animals of the species *Homo sapiens* would react by conditioned reflexes to sound or mimic signals, and their so-called discourses would be like the supposed "language" of bees. What would disappear then is not only philosophy or the search for discursive wisdom but that wisdom itself, since there would no longer be, in these post-historical animals, [discursive] knowledge of the world and of themselves. The self-correction is rigorous: if man returns to animality, his activities lose their human character, and "happiness" must be replaced by animal contentment. The bees' language completes the picture: the end of man is the end of *Logos*, and so the end of the Book's readers.

At the time he wrote the note (1946), Kojève continues, the return of man to animality did not seem to him unthinkable as a prospect for the future, more or less near. But he understood soon after (1948) that the Hegelian-Marxist end of history was not yet to come but already present. Observing what was happening around him and reflecting on what had happened in the world after the battle of Jena, he understood that Hegel was right to see in it the end of history properly speaking. In and through this battle the vanguard of humanity virtually reached the term and goal, the end, of man's historical evolution. What has happened since has been only an extension in space of the universal revolutionary force actualised in France by Robespierre–Napoleon. From the authentically historical point of view, the two world wars with their train of small and large revolutions have only had the effect of aligning the backward civilisations of the peripheral provinces with the most advanced European historical positions, real or virtual. If the sovietisation of Russia and the communisation of China are anything more than the democratisation of imperial Germany (by way of Hitlerism) or Togo's accession to independence, or even the self-determination of the Papuans, it is only because the Sino-Soviet actualisation of Robespierrean Bonapartism obliges post-Napoleonic Europe to speed up the elimination of the many more or less anachronistic sequels of its pre-revolutionary past. This process of elimination is already more advanced in the North American extensions of Europe than in Europe itself. One can even say that, from a certain point of view, the United States has already reached the final stage of Marxist "communism", since practically all members of a "classless society" can appropriate whatever seems good to them without working more than their heart tells them. The thesis that history ended at Jena and that everything since is spatial extension is the most radical form of Kojève's historicism. The description of Hitlerism as the democratisation of imperial Germany and of Soviet and Chinese communism as "Robespierrean Bonapartism" is deliberately provocative. The account of America as realised communism anticipates later discussions of consumer society.

Several comparative journeys between 1948 and 1958 to the United States and the USSR gave him the impression that if the Americans look like enriched Sino-Soviets, it is because the Russians and Chinese are only Americans who are still poor, and indeed on the way to rapid enrichment. He was led to conclude that the American way of life was the way of life proper to the post-historical period, the present presence of the United States in the world prefiguring the future "eternal present" of all humanity. So the return of man to animality appeared no longer as a possibility still to come but as a certainty already present. The convergence thesis, Americans are rich Soviets and Soviets poor Americans, is one of the book's most quoted formulas. It turns the Cold War into a difference of wealth within one post-historical form of life.

It was after a recent journey to Japan (1959) that he radically changed his mind on this point. There he could observe a society unique of its kind, the only one to have had an experience of almost three centuries of life in a period of "end of history", in the absence of any civil or external war, following the liquidation of feudalism by the commoner Hideyoshi and the artificial isolation of the country conceived and realised by his noble successor Ieyasu. The existence of the Japanese nobles, who ceased to risk their lives, even in duels, without beginning to work, was anything but animal. "Post-historical" Japanese civilisation went down paths diametrically opposed to the "American way". No doubt there was no longer in Japan religion, morality, or politics in the "European" or "historical" sense. But snobbery in its pure state created disciplines negating the "natural" or "animal" given that far surpassed in efficacy those born, in Japan or elsewhere, of "historical" action, of warlike and revolutionary fights or forced labour. Certainly the peaks, nowhere equalled, of specifically Japanese snobbery, the Noh theatre, the tea ceremony, and the art of flower arrangement, were and remain the exclusive preserve of the noble and rich. But despite persistent economic and social inequalities, all Japanese without exception are now able to live according to totally formalised values, completely emptied of all "human" content in the "historical" sense. So, at the limit, every Japanese is in principle capable of committing, by pure snobbery, a perfectly "gratuitous" suicide (the classic samurai sword can be replaced by an aeroplane or torpedo), which has nothing to do with the risk of life in a fight waged for "historical" values with social or political content. This seems to allow one to believe that the recently begun interaction between Japan and the Western world will in the end lead not to a rebarbarisation of the Japanese but to a "japanisation" of the Westerners, the Russians included. The Japanese section is the book's most famous and most debated passage. Tokugawa Japan (Kojève's "Yiyeasu" is Tokugawa Ieyasu) is presented as a post-historical society that avoided animality through "snobbery", formal disciplines that negate nature without transforming it. The example of the gratuitous suicide, with its allusion to the kamikaze, is disturbing; Kojève offers it as the extreme of formal negation, the risk of life emptied of historical content. The prediction of a "japanisation" of the West has been read as a prophecy of aestheticised consumer culture.

Since no animal can be a snob, every "japanised" post-historical period would be specifically human. There would therefore be no "definitive annihilation of man properly speaking" as long as there are animals of the species *Homo sapiens* able to serve as natural support for what is human in men. But, as he said in the note above, "an animal that is in accord with nature or given being" is a living being that has nothing human about it. To remain human, man must remain "a subject opposed to the object", even if "negating action of the given and error" disappear. Which means that, while henceforth speaking adequately of everything given to him, post-historical man must continue to detach "forms" from their "contents", doing so no longer to transform the latter actively, but in order to oppose himself as a pure "form" to himself and to others, taken as any "contents" whatever. The conclusion defines post-historical humanity as pure formalism: negation persists, but without content, as style. It is the last and most enigmatic form of Kojève's negativity: man survives the end of history as a snob, detaching forms from contents for the sake of the form. The definition preserves the book's central thesis, man is negation of the given, by displacing negation from labour and fight to form.

In the texts that follow and end Chapter VIII and the *Phenomenology*, Hegel specifies his conception of history, which shows that the introduction of history into philosophy is for Hegel his principal and decisive discovery. Hegel first says (Hoffmeister p. 563), in Kojève's translation: this becoming, history, presents a movement and a slow, inert (*träge*) succession of Spirits, a gallery of images, each endowed with the complete wealth of Spirit, which moves so slowly precisely because the self must penetrate and digest this whole wealth of its substance. Since the perfection of Spirit consists in knowing what it is, its substance, this knowledge is its going-into-itself, in which it abandons its existence and hands over its shape to recollection (*Erinnerung*). The gallery of images (¶808) is the last image of the *Phenomenology*.

It is clear, and there is little to add. Each stage of becoming, each historical world, is "endowed with the complete wealth of Spirit": never, at any moment of time, is there Spirit existing outside the human historical world. There is therefore no transcendence; history is the becoming of Spirit, and Spirit is nothing but this historical becoming of man. The goal of history is knowledge (*Wissen*), self-knowledge, philosophy, which finally becomes wisdom. Man creates a historical world only in order to know what this world is and so to know himself in it. Kojève has said that the concept "dog" can detach itself from the real dog and materialise itself in the word "dog", that there can be conceptual or discursive knowledge of the dog, only because the dog dies or becomes past. The same holds, as Hegel has just said, for man and his historical world. One can know a historical world only because it is historical, temporal and so finite or mortal. One truly knows it, conceptually or philosophically, only in "*Erinnerung*": it is the remembrance (*Erinnerung*) of a past real that is the internalisation (*Er-innerung*) of this real, the passage of its "meaning" or "essence" from external reality into the concept that is in me, within the "subject". If the totality of history can be understood, in and through the *Phenomenology*, only at the end OF history, a particular historical world can be understood only after its end or death IN history. The capitalised prepositions, the end OF history and the death IN history, distinguish the absolute and particular cases of the same law: understanding follows death. The dog of the eighth lecture returns to ground the knowledge of historical worlds.

Hegel says so himself in the *Philosophy of Right* (vol. VI, p. 17). Kojève translates: as the thought of the world, philosophy appears in time only after reality has completed its process of formation and made itself ready. When philosophy paints its grey in grey, a form of life has grown old, and it cannot be rejuvenated by grey in grey, only understood: the owl of Minerva begins its flight only with the falling of dusk. This famous passage, written fifteen years after the *Phenomenology*, is the best commentary on the text being interpreted. The owl of Minerva is the proverbial form of the thesis that understanding follows death.

In the following passage Hegel develops the idea (Hoffmeister pp. 563–564). Kojève translates: in its going-into-itself, Spirit is sunk in the night of its self-consciousness; but its vanished existence is preserved in this night; and this overcome existence, past but reborn from knowledge, is the new existence, a new historical world and a new shape of Spirit. In it Spirit must begin again in the immediacy of this form and grow and mature from it anew, as naively as if all that preceded were lost to it and it had learned nothing from the experience of earlier Spirits. But recollection (*Er-innerung*) has preserved this existence, and it is the inner, and in fact a higher form of substance. If this Spirit, seeming to start only from itself, begins its formation (*Bildung*) again from the beginning, it begins it at the same time at a higher level. This is the phenomenological aspect of the dialectic of being, which is history. The rhythm of history is as Kojève indicated: action, becoming conscious, action. Historical progress, which is what is truly historical or human in history, is a "mediation" by knowledge or comprehending remembrance. History is therefore doubly a history of philosophy: on the one hand it exists through and for philosophy; on the other, there is history because there is philosophy and so that there may be philosophy, finally wisdom. It is the comprehension or knowledge of the past, integrated into the present, that transforms this present into a historical present, a present that realises a progress in relation to its past. The rhythm action, becoming conscious, action is the one stated in the tenth lecture (p. 399), where Kojève contested its necessity. Here he presents Hegel's view without renewing the objection.

This dialectic of action and knowledge is essentially temporal; or better, it is time, a non-identical becoming, in which there is truly and really progress and so a "before" and an "after". Hegel says so (Hoffmeister p. 564): the realm of Spirits formed in this way in existence constitutes a succession (*Aufeinanderfolge*) in which one relieved the other and each took over from its predecessor the empire of the world. If this dialectical becoming is time, it has a beginning and an end, and so a goal (*Ziel*) that can no longer be surpassed. The "empire of the world" passing from one Spirit to the next is the Hegelian image of world history as succession of dominant peoples.

Hegel speaks of this goal now (Hoffmeister p. 564). Kojève translates: the goal of this succession, universal history, is the revelation of depth, and this revelation is the absolute concept. This revelation is therefore the overcoming of the depth of Spirit, its extension (*Ausdehnung*); the negating negativity of this abstract I existing within itself, a negativity that is its externalisation, its substance; and it is the time of this I, time consisting in the fact that this externalisation externalises itself in itself and, existing in its extension, exists equally in its depth, the self. The goal of history, its final term, is "the absolute concept", "Science". In this Science, Hegel says, man dialectically overcomes his temporal or "punctual" existence, truly human, as opposed to nature, and becomes himself extension (*Ausdehnung*) or space. For in the *Logic* man limits himself to knowing the world or *Sein*, and his knowledge being true, he coincides with the world, with *Sein*, with eternal or non-temporal space. But, Hegel adds, in and through Science man also overcomes this extension or externalisation and remains "punctual" or temporal, specifically human: he remains a self. But, as Hegel will say at once, he remains so only in and through *Er-innerung*, the comprehending remembrance of his historical past, which forms the first part of the System, the *Phenomenology*. The Sage's double status, spatial as knower of the world, temporal as rememberer of history, resolves the tension between the death of man and the survival of the self: the self survives only as memory.

Here is the final passage (Hoffmeister p. 564). Kojève translates: the goal, absolute knowledge, the Sage author of Science, Spirit knowing itself as Spirit, has as its path the recollection of the historical Spirits as they are in themselves and accomplish the organisation of their realm. Their preservation, in the aspect of their free existence appearing in the form of contingency, is history, vulgar historical science that recounts events; their preservation in the aspect of their conceptually comprehended organisation is the Science of appearing knowledge, the *Phenomenology*. The two together, chronicle-history and the *Phenomenology*, comprehended history, form the recollection and the Golgotha of absolute Spirit, the reality, truth, and certainty of its throne, without which it would be lifeless and solitary. Only from the chalice of this realm of Spirits foams forth for it its infinity. The last sentence (¶808) quotes Schiller, which Kojève comments on below. "Golgotha" (*Schädelstätte*), the place of skulls, is Hegel's image for history as the calvary of absolute Spirit.

Science proper, the *Logic* or second part of the System, which reveals eternal being or real eternity, is necessarily preceded by a first part concerning the becoming of being in time or as time, history. This is on the one hand historical science in the ordinary sense, humanity's "naive" remembrance; and on the other the conceptual or philosophical comprehension of the past preserved in this naive remembrance, which is the *Phenomenology*. It follows that for Hegel the *Phenomenology* cannot be understood without prior knowledge of real history, just as history cannot truly be understood without the *Phenomenology*. «J'ai donc eu raison de parler d'Athènes, de Rome, de Louis XIV... et de Napoléon, en interprétant la PhG» (I was therefore right to speak of Athens, Rome, Louis XIV ... and Napoleon in interpreting the *Phenomenology*) (p. 441). As long as one does not see the historical facts the book refers to, one understands nothing of what it says. But the *Phenomenology* is something other than a "universal history" in the ordinary sense. History recounts events; the *Phenomenology* explains them or makes them comprehensible, revealing their human meaning and necessity. It reconstructs ("deduces") in its humanly essential features the real historical evolution of humanity. It reconstructs it *a priori*, "deducing" it from anthropogenic Desire (*Begierde*) bearing on another Desire (and so desire for recognition) and realising itself by the negating action (*Tat*) of given being (*Sein*). But once more, this *a priori* construction can be carried out only after the fact. Real history must first be completed; then it must be told to man; a footnote adds that there is no real history without historical remembrance, without oral or written memoirs; and only then can the philosopher, becoming a Sage, understand it by reconstructing it *a priori* in the *Phenomenology*. It is this same phenomenological understanding of history that transforms the philosopher into a Sage, since it is what definitively abolishes time and so makes possible the adequate revelation of completed and perfect, eternal and immutable being that takes place in and through the *Logic*. The self-justification of his historical method is the lecture's retrospective conclusion on the six courses. The formula "*a priori*, but only after the fact" is the paradox of Hegelian necessity that Kojève has defended throughout. The footnote, no history without memoirs, makes memory constitutive of history, not merely its record.

A final remark concerns the quotation from Schiller's poem "Die Freundschaft" with which the *Phenomenology* ends. The quotation is not literal, and the modifications Hegel made, consciously or not, are revealing. He does not dwell on the fact that Hegel says "*Geisterreich*" instead of "*Seelenreich*", though this very "modern" substitution is extremely significant. What matters above all is that Hegel says "*dieses Geisterreich*" instead of "*das ganze Seelenreich*". In doing so he wants to exclude the "angels" Schiller speaks of; he wants to stress that eternal and infinite being, absolute Spirit, which in Schiller is God, arises solely from the totality of human or historical existence. The temporal past of eternal being is therefore human, and only human. If one wants to speak of "God" in Hegel, one must not forget that the past of this "God" is man: a man become "God", not a God become man (who, moreover, becomes God again). The third modification has the same sense: Schiller says "*die Unendlichkeit*", Hegel writes "*seine Unendlichkeit*". The *Phenomenology* thus ends with a radical negation of all transcendence. Eternal, infinite revealed being, absolute Spirit, is the infinite or eternal being of the same being that existed as universal history. The infinite in question is man's infinite. And the "Science" that reveals this infinite being is doubly a science of man: on the one hand it is the result of history, a product of man; on the other it speaks of man, of HIS temporal or historical becoming (in the *Phenomenology*) and of HIS eternal being (in the *Logic*). Science is therefore indeed self-consciousness, not consciousness; and the Sage, reaching the end of the *Phenomenology*, can say that the Science proper he is about to develop in the *Logic* is truly his Science or knowledge. The philological analysis of Hegel's alterations to Schiller is one of Kojève's finest close readings. Schiller's lines read "aus dem Kelch des ganzen Seelenreiches / schäumt ihm die Unendlichkeit"; Hegel's "aus dem Kelche dieses Geisterreiches / schäumt ihm seine Unendlichkeit" narrows the realm to this one, human realm, and makes the infinite its own. The conclusion, a man become God rather than a God become man, restates anthropotheism at the book's last word.

But, as Kojève has said several times, the Sage can speak of Science as his Science only to the same extent that he can speak of death as his death. For in passing to the *Logic*, the Sage completely abolishes time, history, his own truly and specifically human reality, which in the *Phenomenology* is already only a past reality: he definitively abandons his reality as free and historical individual, as subject opposed to object, as man essentially other (*Anderes*) than nature. The comparison repeats the ninth lecture's analogy of Book and death (p. 388): the Sage's Science is his only as his death is, in the future tense of its writing.

Hegel knows it well himself, and knew it at least from 1802, since in his writing of that year, *Faith and Knowledge*, there is a passage where he says it clearly, which Kojève cites in ending his commentary on the *Phenomenology*. Kojève translates (vol. I, p. 303): the whole sphere of finitude, of being oneself something, of the sensible, sinks into true faith before the thought and intuition of the eternal, which here become one and the same. All the gnats of subjectivity are burned in this devouring fire, and even the consciousness of this self-surrender (*Hingebens*) and this annihilation (*Vernichtens*) is annihilated. The passage describes the annihilation of subjectivity in the eternal, and Kojève reads it as Hegel's knowledge of the price of wisdom: the Sage's individuality is burned up.

Hegel knows it and says it. But he also says, in one of his letters, that this knowledge cost him dearly. He speaks of a period of total depression he lived through between his twenty-fifth and thirtieth years: a "hypochondria" that went "*bis zur Erlahmung aller Kräfte*", "to the paralysis of all his forces", and that came precisely from the fact that he could not accept the necessary abandonment of individuality, in fact of humanity, that the idea of absolute knowledge requires. But finally he overcame this "hypochondria". And, becoming a Sage through this final acceptance of death, he published a few years later the first part of the "System of Science", entitled "Science of the Phenomenology of Spirit", in which he reconciles himself definitively with everything that is and has been, «en déclarant qu'il n'y aura jamais plus rien de nouveau sur terre» (declaring that there will never again be anything new on earth) (p. 443). The letter is to Windischmann (27 May 1810), where Hegel describes his own years of hypochondria. Kojève's reading, that the crisis was the refusal to give up individuality and its resolution the acceptance of death, makes Hegel's biography the existential proof of the system: wisdom is the acceptance of one's own abolition. The last sentence of the commentary on the *Phenomenology* ends where the course of 1933–34 began its plan (p. 41): "nothing new in the world". The whole book thus closes on the equation of wisdom, death, and the end of history.

## Appendices

### Appendix I: The Dialectic of the Real and the Phenomenological Method in Hegel

The first appendix gives the full text of lectures 6 to 9 of the 1934–35 course, which Queneau recommended as part of the book's core. It is Kojève's most systematic statement of his interpretation of dialectic, and the source of the 1933–34 remark that "dialectical method" is a misunderstanding (p. 38).

What is dialectic according to Hegel? A first answer can be given by recalling a text in the introduction to the first part of the *Encyclopaedia*, the Logic. In § 79 (third edition) Hegel says: the logical has, as to its form, three aspects: the abstract aspect, accessible to the Understanding (*verständige*); the dialectical or negatively rational (*vernünftige*) aspect; and the speculative or positively rational aspect. This well-known text lends itself to a double misunderstanding. On the one hand, one might think that dialectic reduces to the second aspect of the "logical", which could be isolated from the other two. But in the explanatory note Hegel stresses that the three aspects are in reality inseparable; and one knows moreover that it is the simultaneous presence of the three that gives the "logical" its dialectical character in the broad sense. It must be noted at once that the "logical" is dialectical in the broad sense only because it implies a "negative" or negating aspect, called "dialectical" in the narrow sense. Yet dialectical "logic" necessarily implies three complementary and inseparable aspects: the "abstract" aspect, revealed by the Understanding (*Verstand*); the "negative" aspect properly "dialectical"; and the "positive" aspect, the last two being revealed by Reason (*Vernunft*). The distinction between dialectic in the broad sense (the three aspects together) and in the narrow sense (the negative moment) organises the appendix.

On the other hand, one might suppose that dialectic is proper to logical thought, a philosophical method, a procedure of inquiry or exposition. In fact this is not so. Hegel's *Logic* is not a logic in the current sense, nor an epistemology, but an ontology or science of being as being. "The logical" (*das Logische*) in the text cited means not logical thought considered in itself but being (*Sein*) revealed (correctly) in and by thought or discourse (*Logos*). The three "aspects" are therefore above all aspects of being itself: ontological, not logical or epistemological, categories; certainly not artifices of method. Hegel stresses this in the note following the text: these three aspects do not constitute three parts of logic but are moments of every logically real entity (*Logisch-Reellen*), of every concept or of everything true (*jedes Wahren*) in general. The claim that *das Logische* means being as revealed, not thought, is the thesis of the appendix. It turns dialectic from a method into an ontological structure.

The true, *das Wahre*, is a real entity, being itself, insofar as it is correctly and completely revealed by coherent, meaningful discourse (*Logos*). This is what Hegel also calls *Begriff*, concept; a term that in him (unless he says, as in the early writings and sometimes still in the *Phenomenology*, "*nur Begriff*") means not "abstract notion" detached from the real entity it relates to but "reality conceptually understood". The true and the concept are, as Hegel says, a *Logisch-Reelles*, something at once logical and real, a realised concept or a conceived reality. But "logical" thought that is supposed true, the concept supposed adequate, only reveal or describe being as it is or exists, without adding, removing, or modifying anything. The structure of thought is therefore determined by the structure of the being it reveals. If "logical" thought has three aspects, if it is dialectical in the broad sense, it is only because being itself is dialectical in the broad sense, implying a "moment" or "aspect" that is negative or negating ("dialectical" in the narrow and strong sense). Thought is dialectical only insofar as it correctly reveals the dialectic of the being that is and the real that exists. The "*nur Begriff*" qualification returns from the 1933–34 notes (p. 53), where Kojève noted Hegel's pejorative use of "concept". The principle that thought mirrors being is the realism of the twelfth lecture.

Certainly it is not pure and simple being (*Sein*) that has a trinitarian or dialectical structure, but the logical-real, the concept or the true, being revealed by discourse or thought. One might therefore say that being is dialectical only insofar as it is revealed by thought, that it is thought that gives being its dialectical character. But this formula would be incorrect or at least misleading. For Hegel it is in a sense the reverse: being can be revealed by thought, there is thought in being and of being, only because being is dialectical, only because being implies a negative or negating moment. It is the real dialectic of existing being that is, among other things, the revelation of the real and of being by discourse or thought; and these are themselves dialectical only because and insofar as they reveal or describe the dialectic of being and the real. A footnote specifies: the real revealed totality of being is not only being (*Sein*) but also revelation of being or thought (*Denken*), and this revealed totality is Spirit (*Geist*). What is dialectical or trinitarian is *Geist*, not *Sein*; being is only the first moment of Spirit. The reversal, being is not dialectical because revealed; being is revealed because dialectical, is the lecture's key. The footnote's precision, *Geist* not *Sein* is dialectical, anticipates the thesis that nature is not dialectical.

In any case, philosophical or "scientific" thought in the Hegelian sense, rigorously true thought, aims to reveal by the meaning of a coherent discourse (*Logos*) being (*Sein*) as it is and exists in the totality of its objective reality (*Wirklichkeit*). The philosophical or "scientific" METHOD must therefore ensure the adequation of thought and being, thought having to adapt itself to being and the real without modifying them in any way. That is to say, the attitude of the philosopher or "scholar" (Sage) toward being and the real is purely passive contemplation, and philosophical or "scientific" activity reduces to pure and simple description of the real and being. «La méthode hégélienne n'est donc nullement "dialectique" : elle est purement contemplative et descriptive, voire phénoménologique au sens husserlien du terme» (the Hegelian method is therefore in no way "dialectical": it is purely contemplative and descriptive, indeed phenomenological in the Husserlian sense of the term) (p. 449). In the Preface and the Introduction of the *Phenomenology* Hegel insists at length on the passive, contemplative, and descriptive character of the "scientific" method. He stresses that there is a dialectic of "scientific" thought only because there is a dialectic of the being this thought reveals. As long as the revealing description is correct, one can say that *ordo et connexio idearum idem est ac ordo et connexio rerum*, since the order and connection of the real are, according to Hegel, dialectical. The identification of Hegel's method with Husserl's phenomenological description is the appendix's most famous thesis, and the source of its title. The Spinoza formula returns from the eleventh lecture (p. 419), here applied to method.

Kojève translates the Preface (Hoffmeister p. 45): scientific cognition (*Erkennen*) requires on the contrary that one give oneself (*übergeben*) to the life of the object, or, what is the same, that one have before oneself and express in speech its inner necessity. Immersing itself (*sich vertiefend*) in its object, this cognition forgets that overview (*Übersicht*), supposed to be made from outside, which is only the reflection of knowledge into itself away from the content. But immersed (*versenkt*) in the matter and advancing in its movement, scientific cognition returns into itself; not, however, before the fulfilment (*Erfüllung*) or content takes itself back into itself, simplifies itself to determinateness (*Bestimmtheit*), lowers itself to being one aspect of an existence (the other aspect being thought), and passes over into its higher truth. Thereby the simple whole that surveys itself emerges from the richness in which its reflection seemed lost. The passage (¶53) is the classical statement of immersion in the object. Kojève's bracket, "the other aspect being thought", reads *Dasein* as a unity of being and thought.

"Scientific cognition" gives itself without reserve, without preconceptions or ulterior motives, to the "life" and "dialectical movement" of the real. This truly true cognition has nothing to do with the "reflection" of pseudo-philosophy (pre-Hegelian philosophy) and pseudo-science (Newtonian), which reflects on the real by placing itself outside it, one cannot say quite where; a reflection that claims to give an "overview" of the real from a supposedly autonomous knowing subject, independent of the object; a subject that is, according to Hegel, only an artificially isolated aspect of the known or revealed real. Certainly at the end "scientific cognition" returns to itself and reveals itself to itself: its final aim is to describe itself in its nature, genesis, and development; like ordinary philosophical knowledge, it is self-knowledge. But it is complete and adequate self-knowledge, true in the strong sense; and it is true because even in its return to itself it only passively follows the dialectical movement of its "content", the object, the real and being. It is the real itself that organises and concretises itself so as to become a determinate "species" that can be revealed by a "general notion"; the real itself that reveals itself through speaking knowledge and so becomes known object with the knowing subject as necessary complement, so that "empirical existence" doubles into beings that speak and beings spoken of. For it is real being existing as nature that produces the man who reveals this nature, and himself, by speaking of it. It is real being that thus transforms itself into "truth" or reality revealed by speech, and becomes an ever "higher" truth as its discursive revelation becomes more adequate and complete. The formula "beings that speak and beings spoken of" is Kojève's shortest description of the doubling of existence. The claim that nature produces the man who reveals it is his naturalist anchoring of anthropogenesis.

By following this "dialectical movement" of the real, knowledge witnesses its own birth and contemplates its own evolution, finally reaching its term, the adequate and complete understanding of itself, of the progressive revelation of the real and being by discourse, of the being and real that engender in and by their "dialectical movement" the discourse that reveals them. So a total revelation of real being, a totality (an "undivided whole") entirely revealed, is finally constituted: the coherent whole of being realised in the real universe, completely and perfectly described in the "overview" given by the one and unique "Science" or "System" of the Sage, which finally emerges from being that was at first only a natural world of separate and disparate entities, an incoherent "richness" in which there was neither "reflection", nor discursive knowledge, nor speaking self-consciousness. The image of knowledge "witnessing its own birth" is the *Phenomenology* as self-genesis.

Taken separately, subject and object are abstractions that have no objective reality (*Wirklichkeit*) or empirical existence (*Dasein*). What exists in reality, as soon as it is a question of the reality one speaks of, and since we do in fact speak of reality, it can only be a question for us of the reality one speaks of: what exists in reality is the subject-knowing-the-object or, what is the same, the object-known-by-the-subject. This doubled reality, nonetheless one in itself since indifferently real, taken as a whole or totality, is called in Hegel "Spirit" (*Geist*) or, in the Logic, "absolute Idea"; Hegel also says "absolute concept". But the term *Begriff* can also apply to a fragment of total revealed being, to a "moment" of Spirit or the Idea (the latter then definable as the integration of all concepts, of all particular "ideas"). Taken in this sense *Begriff* means a particular real entity or real aspect of being, revealed by the meaning of a word, a "general notion"; or, what is the same, the *Begriff* is a meaning ("idea") that exists empirically not only as a word actually thought, spoken, or written, but also as a "thing". If the universal or "absolute" Idea is the "truth" or reality-revealed-by-discourse of the one unique totality of what exists, a particular "concept" is the "truth" of a particular real entity taken separately but understood as an integral element of the totality. Or again the "concept" is a "true entity" (*das Wahre*), a real entity named or revealed by the meaning of a word, this meaning relating it to all other real entities and so inserting it into the "System" of the integral real revealed by the whole of "scientific" discourse. Or finally the "concept" is the "essential reality" or essence (*Wesen*) of a concrete entity, precisely the reality that corresponds in it to the meaning of the word that designates or reveals it. The argument that we can only ever speak of the reality-spoken-of, so that subject and object are abstractions, is an elegant phenomenological reduction. The concept as "a meaning that exists also as a thing" is the realist counterpart of the eighth lecture's concept as word.

Like Spirit or the Idea, each concept is therefore both double and one, as "subjective" as "objective", real thought of a real entity and real entity really thought. The real aspect of the concept is called "object" (*Gegenstand*), "given being" (*Sein*), "entity existing as given being" (*Seiendes*), "in-itself" (*Ansich*), and so on. The thought aspect is called "knowledge" (*Wissen*), "act of knowing" (*Erkennen*), "cognition" (*Erkenntnis*), "act of thinking" (*Denken*), and so on; and sometimes "concept" (*Begriff*) in the current sense (when Hegel says "*nur Begriff*"). But these two aspects are inseparable and complementary, and it matters little which is called *Wissen* or *Begriff* in the current sense and which *Gegenstand*. What matters is that in truth there is perfect coincidence of *Begriff* and *Gegenstand*, and knowledge is a purely passive adequation to essential reality. That is why the true scholar or Sage must reduce his existence to the simple contemplation (*reines Zusehen*) of the real and being and of their "dialectical movement". He looks at everything that is and describes verbally everything he sees: he has nothing to do, since he modifies nothing, adds nothing, removes nothing. *Reines Zusehen*, pure looking-on, is Hegel's phrase from the Introduction, which Kojève cites next.

At least, that is what Hegel says in the Introduction to the *Phenomenology* (Hoffmeister pp. 71–72). Kojève translates: if we call knowledge (*Wissen*) the concept, and the essence (*Wesen*) or the true (*Wahre*) the being or object (*Gegenstand*), then the testing (*Prüfung*) consists in seeing (*zuzusehen*) whether the concept corresponds to the object. But if we call the essence or in-itself (*Ansich*) of the object the concept, and understand by object the object as object, as it is for another, then the testing consists in seeing whether the object corresponds to its concept. Evidently the two are the same. But what is essential is to keep in mind throughout the inquiry that these two moments, concept and object, being-for-another and being-in-itself, fall within the very knowledge we are studying, and so we need not bring standards (*Maßstäbe*) and apply our own intuitions (*Einfälle*) and thoughts during the inquiry. By omitting these we attain the possibility of considering the thing as it is in and for itself. But a contribution (*Zutat*) from us becomes superfluous not only in that concept and object, the standard and what is to be tested, are present in the consciousness we study as philosophers in the *Phenomenology*; we are also spared the trouble of comparing the two and of the testing proper, so that, the consciousness studied testing itself, all that remains for us, from this side too, is pure looking-on (*Zusehen*). The passage (¶84–85) is Hegel's own statement of the phenomenological method: consciousness tests itself; the philosopher only watches.

In short, the "method" of the Hegelian scholar consists in having no method or mode of thought proper to his Science. The naive man, the vulgar scholar, even the pre-Hegelian philosopher, each in his way opposes himself to the real and deforms it by opposing to it means of action or methods of thought proper to them. The Sage, by contrast, is fully and definitively reconciled with everything that is: he entrusts himself without reserve to being and opens himself entirely to the real without offering it any resistance. «Son rôle est celui d'un miroir parfaitement plan et indéfiniment étendu» (his role is that of a perfectly flat and indefinitely extended mirror) (p. 453): he does not reflect on the real; it is the real that reflects itself on him, is reflected in his consciousness, and reveals itself in its own dialectical structure through the Sage's discourse, which describes it without deforming it. The image of the flat, infinite mirror is the appendix's emblem of the Sage. It connects to the tenth lecture's "apparent inactivity" (p. 411): the Sage resists nothing.

If one likes, the Hegelian "method" is purely "empirical" or "positivist": Hegel looks at the real and describes what he sees, everything he sees and nothing but what he sees. He has the "experience" (*Erfahrung*) of dialectical being and the real, and so makes their "movement" pass into his discourse that describes them. Hegel says this in the Introduction (Hoffmeister p. 73): this dialectical movement that consciousness exercises on itself, both on its knowledge and on its object, insofar as the new true object arises from it for consciousness, is properly what is called experience (*Erfahrung*). Calling Hegel's method "positivist" is deliberately provocative: it means that nothing is added to what appears.

Certainly this experience "properly speaking" is quite different from the experience of vulgar science. The latter is carried out by a subject supposedly independent of the object and is supposed to reveal the object existing independently of the subject. In fact experience is carried out by a man living within nature and indissolubly linked to it, but also opposed to it and wanting to transform it: science is born of the desire to transform the world according to man; its final end is technical application. That is why scientific knowledge is never absolutely passive or purely contemplative and descriptive. Scientific experience perturbs the object because of the subject's active intervention, which applies to the object a method of investigation proper to the subject and to which nothing in the object corresponds. What it reveals is therefore neither the object independent of the subject nor the subject independent of the object, but only the result of their interaction, or, if one likes, this interaction itself. Yet scientific experience and knowledge aim at the object independent of and isolated from the subject. They do not find what they seek or give what they promise, since they do not correctly reveal what is for them the real. In general truth (= revealed reality) is the coincidence of thought or descriptive knowledge with the concrete real. For vulgar science this real is supposed independent of the thought that describes it. But in fact it never reaches this autonomous real, this "thing in itself" of Kant–Newton, since it constantly perturbs it. Scientific thought therefore does not reach its truth; there is no scientific truth in the proper and strong sense. Scientific experience is only a pseudo-experience. And it cannot be otherwise, since vulgar science deals not with the concrete real but with an abstraction. Insofar as the scholar thinks or knows his object, what exists really and concretely is the whole of the object known by the subject or of the subject knowing the object. The isolated object is only an abstraction, which is why it has no fixed and stable subsistence (*Bestehen*) and is constantly deformed or perturbed. It cannot serve as the basis of a truth, by definition universally and eternally valid. The same holds for the "object" of psychology, epistemology, and vulgar philosophy, which is the subject artificially isolated from the object, again an abstraction. The critique of science as interaction mistaken for revelation of the independent object is Kojève's philosophy of science. Its genealogy of science from "the desire to transform the world" and "technical application" returns to the Master–Slave theme: science is the Slave's knowledge.

A long footnote adds that this interpretation of science, on which Hegel insisted greatly, is now admitted by science itself. In quantum physics it is expressed mathematically by Heisenberg's uncertainty relations. These show on the one hand that physical experience is never perfect, since it cannot lead to a description of the physical "real" that is both complete and adequate (precise). On the other hand they entail Bohr's famous principle of "complementary notions": wave and particle, for example. This means that the physical (verbal) description of the real necessarily implies contradictions: the physical real is at once a wave filling all space and a particle localised at a point, and so on. By physics' own admission it can therefore never reach truth in the strong sense. In fact physics does not study or describe the concrete real but only an artificially isolated aspect of it, an abstraction: the aspect of the real given to the "physical subject", this subject being man reduced to his (moreover idealised) eye, again an abstraction. Physics describes the real insofar as it is given to this subject without describing the subject itself; yet it must take account of the act that "gives" the real to this subject, the act of seeing, which presupposes the presence of light in the broad sense. This abstract description is made not by meaningful words (*Logos*) but by algorithms: if concrete man speaks of the real, the abstract physical subject uses a mathematical "language". On the plane of the algorithm there is neither uncertainty nor contradiction; but neither is there truth in the proper sense, since there is no true discourse (*Logos*) revealing the real. As soon as one passes from the algorithm to physical discourse, one introduces contradictions and an element of uncertainty. There is therefore no truth in the domain of physics, or of science in general. Only philosophical discourse can reach it, since it alone relates to the concrete real, the totality of the reality of being. The various sciences always deal with abstractions: on the one hand because they relate the real not to living man but to a more or less simplified, even abstract, knowing subject; on the other because in their descriptions they neglect either the (abstract) subject corresponding to the (abstract) object they describe, or the (abstract) object given to the (abstract) subject they study. That is why they have methods of thought and action proper to themselves. The footnote develops the eighth lecture's note on the "articulated silence of the algorithm" (p. 378) with explicit reference to Heisenberg and Bohr. Kojève's reading of complementarity as the contradiction that arises when algorithm is translated into discourse is original and has been influential. His "physical subject" reduced to an idealised eye is a sharp image of the observer in physics. Kojève's own essay on determinism in classical and modern physics (written 1932) lies behind this footnote.

Hegelian experience is quite different: it reveals concrete reality, and reveals it without modifying or "perturbing" it. That is why, when one describes this experience verbally, it represents a truth in the strong sense; and why it has no specific method proper to it as experience, thought, or verbal description that is not at the same time an "objective" structure of the concrete real itself that it reveals by describing it. The concrete real we speak of is at once real-revealed-by-a-discourse and discourse-revealing-a-real; Hegelian experience relates neither to the real nor to discourse taken separately but to their indissoluble unity. Being itself a revealing discourse, it is itself an aspect of the concrete real it describes. It brings nothing from outside, and the thought or discourse born of it is not a reflection on the real: it is the real itself that reflects itself, or is reflected in discourse or as thought. In particular, if the thought and discourse of the Hegelian scholar or Sage are dialectical, it is only because they faithfully reflect the "dialectical movement" of the real of which they are part, and of which they have adequate experience by giving themselves to it without any preconceived method. The method of Hegel is therefore in no way dialectical, and dialectic is in him something quite other than a method of thought or exposition. «Et on peut même dire qu'en un certain sens Hegel a été le premier à avoir abandonné la Dialectique en tant que méthode philosophique» (and one can even say that in a certain sense Hegel was the first to have abandoned dialectic as a philosophical method) (p. 455); at least he was the first to have done so voluntarily and with full knowledge. The paradox, Hegel the first to abandon dialectic as method, is the appendix's most quoted formula. It reverses the textbook image of Hegel as the inventor of the dialectical method.

The dialectical method was used consciously and systematically for the first time by Socrates–Plato. But in fact it is as old as philosophy itself, since the dialectical method is nothing but the method of dialogue, of discussion. The etymological point, dialectic as the art of dialogue, frames the history that follows.

Everything seems to indicate that science was born in the form of myth. Myth is a theory, a discursive revelation of the real. Certainly it is supposed to agree with the given real; but in fact it always goes beyond its data, and beyond them it suffices for it to be coherent, free of internal contradictions, to pass for truth. The stage of myth is a stage of monologue, and at this stage nothing is demonstrated because nothing is "discussed", since one is not yet faced with a contrary or merely different opinion. That is precisely why there is "myth" or "opinion" (*doxa*), true or false, but not "science" or "truth" properly speaking. Then, by chance, the man who has an opinion, or has created or adopted a myth, comes up against a different myth or a contrary opinion. He will first try to get rid of it: either by stopping his ears, as it were, by internal or external "censorship"; or by suppressing (in the non-dialectical sense) the adverse myth or opinion, by putting its propagators to death or banishing them, for example, or by acts of violence that will force others to say the same thing as he (even if they do not think it). The genealogy of discussion from the encounter of myths recalls the genesis of recognition from the encounter of Desires: the first reaction to the other is violence. Censorship and killing are the non-dialectical ways of resolving disagreement.

But it may happen, and we know it actually happened one day somewhere, that man begins to discuss with his adversary. By an act of freedom he may decide to want to "convince" him, by "refuting" him and "demonstrating" his own point of view. To this end he speaks with the adversary, engages in a dialogue with him: he uses a dialectical method. It is by becoming a dialectician that the man of myth or opinion becomes a scholar or philosopher. The parallel with the Introduction is exact: discussion is to violence as the Master–Slave relation is to killing. Both begin with a free act (p. 15).

In Plato, and probably already in Socrates, all this became conscious. If Plato has Socrates say that it is not trees but only men in the city who can teach him something, it is because he understood that one reaches science and truth, starting from myth and (true or false) opinion, only by passing through discussion, dialogue or dialectic. In short, for Socrates–Plato, it is from the clash of diverse and adverse opinions that the spark of the one and unique truth finally flashes. A "thesis" is opposed by an "antithesis", which it generally provokes. They confront each other, correct each other, that is, destroy each other, but also combine and finally engender a "synthetic" truth. But this is still only one opinion among many; it is a new thesis that will find or provoke a new antithesis, to associate with it by negating it, that is, modifying it, in a new synthesis, in which it will itself be other than it was at first. And so on, until one reaches a "synthesis" that is no longer the thesis of a discussion or a debatable "thesis"; an indisputable "truth" that is no longer a mere "opinion" or one of the possible opinions; or, objectively speaking, the unique One that is not opposed to an Other because it is the whole: the Idea of ideas or the Good. The reference to the *Phaedrus* (230d), where Socrates says the trees will teach him nothing but men in the city will, grounds dialectic in the city. The triad thesis–antithesis–synthesis is here attributed to Plato's dialogue, not to Hegel.

In the philosophy or science born of discussion, in dialectical or synthetic truth, which realises the Good in man by verbally revealing the One-Whole, the intermediate theses, antitheses, and syntheses are *aufgehoben*, as Hegel will later say. They are "suppressed" in the triple sense of the German *Aufheben*, "dialectically suppressed". On the one hand they are suppressed or annulled in what is fragmentary, relative, partial, or partisan in them, in what makes them false when one of them is taken not for an opinion but for the truth. On the other hand they are also preserved or safeguarded in what is essential or universal in them, in what reveals in each one of the many aspects of total and one reality. Finally they are sublimated, raised to a higher level of knowledge and reality, and so of truth; for in completing each other, thesis and antithesis rid themselves of their one-sided and limited, even "subjective", character and reveal as synthesis a more comprehensive and so more comprehensible aspect of the "objective" real. The triple sense of *Aufheben*, annul, preserve, raise, repeats the Introduction's definition (p. 21), now applied to opinions.

But if dialectic finally leads to adequation between discursive thought and reality and being, nothing corresponds to it in these latter. The dialectical movement is a movement of human thought and discourse; the reality itself that is thought and spoken of has nothing dialectical about it. Dialectic is only a method of philosophical research and exposition. And one sees, incidentally, that the method is dialectical only because it implies a negative or negating element: the antithesis that opposes the thesis in a verbal fight and demands an effort of demonstration, which coincides with a refutation. There is truth properly speaking, scientific or philosophical, dialectical or synthetic, only where there has been discussion or dialogue, an antithesis negating a thesis. This describes pre-Hegelian dialectic: a method without ontological counterpart. The "verbal fight" of thesis and antithesis anticipates Hegel's thesis that the real fight is what discourse reflects.

In Plato the dialectical method is still very close to its historical origins, the sophistic discussions. There are real dialogues in which thesis and antithesis are presented by different characters, Socrates generally embodying the antithesis of all the theses affirmed by his interlocutors or put forward successively by one of them. As for the synthesis, it is generally the listener who must make it: the listener who is the philosopher properly speaking, Plato himself and his disciple able to understand him. This listener finally reaches the absolute truth that results from the whole of the dialectic, the coordinated movement of all the dialogues, a truth that reveals the "total" or "synthetic" Good able to satisfy fully and definitively whoever knows it, and which is therefore beyond discussion or dialectic. A footnote adds that in Plato there is moreover a leap, a break in continuity. Dialectic only prepares the vision of the Good but does not necessarily lead to it: this vision is a kind of mystical illumination or ecstasy (compare the Seventh Letter). Perhaps the vision is silent and the Good ineffable, in which case Plato would be a mystic. In any case it is more and other than an integration of the whole dialectical movement of thought: it is an intuition *sui generis*. Objectively speaking, God or the One is something other than the totality of the real: it is beyond being; it is a transcendent God. Plato is certainly a theologian (compare the "Note on Eternity, Time, and the Concept" in the 1938–39 course). The listener as the one who makes the synthesis is a subtle point: Plato's dialogues leave the synthesis to the reader. The footnote on the leap to the Good repeats the sixth lecture's classification of Plato (p. 342).

In Aristotle the dialectical method is less apparent than in Plato, but it continues to be applied. It becomes the aporetic method: the solution of a problem results from a discussion, sometimes a simple juxtaposition, of all possible opinions, those coherent or non-contradictory in themselves. In this "scholastic" form the dialectical method has survived to our day in both the sciences and philosophy. The aporetic method is Aristotle's review of *endoxa* in *Metaphysics* B and elsewhere. Its "scholastic" survival in modern science is an ironic remark.

But in parallel there was something else. Like every opinion, myth arises spontaneously and is accepted (or rejected) likewise. Man creates it in and by his ("poetic") imagination, content to avoid contradictions as he develops his starting idea or "intuition". But when the confrontation with a different opinion or myth engenders the desire for a proof that cannot yet be satisfied by demonstration in the course of a discussion, one feels the need to ground one's opinion or the myth one proposes (both supposed empirically unverifiable, by appeal to common sense experience) on something other than simple personal conviction or "subjective certainty" (*Gewissheit*), which is visibly of the same type and weight as the adversary's. One seeks and finds a ground of superior or "divine" value: the myth is presented as "revealed" by a god, who is supposed to guarantee its truth, its universal and eternal validity. The genealogy of revelation from the need for proof is Kojève's: when discussion is not yet possible, one appeals to a god.

Like dialectical truth, this "revealed" mythical truth could not have been found by an isolated man alone in front of nature: here too "trees teach man nothing". But "men in the city" teach him nothing either. It is a god who reveals the truth to him in a "myth". Unlike dialectical truth, this mythical truth is not the result of a discussion or dialogue: God alone has spoken, man having been content to listen, understand, and transcribe, and this far from the city, on a mountaintop, and so on. The mountaintop is Sinai: revelation is the anti-dialogue, spoken in solitude.

After being a Platonic philosopher, man can sometimes return to the "mythological" stage. Such was the case of Saint Augustine. But this "return" is in reality a "synthesis": the revealing God of myth becomes a quasi-Socratic interlocutor; man engages in a dialogue with his God, even if he does not go as far as a discussion with him ("Abraham, however, discusses with Yahweh!"). But this divine-human "dialogue" is only a hybrid and transitional form of the dialectical method. So it has varied infinitely among the various "mystics", between the extremes of the true dialogue in which "God" is only a title for the human interlocutor one discusses with, and the various "revelations" on mountaintops where the human partner is only a mute listener "convinced" in advance. The reference to Abraham bargaining with God over Sodom (Genesis 18) is apt: a dialogue with God that becomes a negotiation.

In any case, in fact, the divine interlocutor is fictitious. Everything takes place in the "scholar's" own soul. That is why Saint Augustine already had "dialogues" with his "soul". And a distant disciple of this Platonising (or Plotinising) Christian, Descartes, deliberately let God fall, content to dialogue and discuss with himself. So dialectic became "meditation". It is in the form of Cartesian meditation that the dialectical method was used by the authors of the great philosophical "systems" of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, from Descartes to Kant–Fichte–Schelling. At first sight this is a step backward from Socrates–Plato–Aristotle: the great modern "systems" are like so many "myths" juxtaposed without entering into discussion, created from scratch by their authors without resulting from a prior dialogue. But in fact it is not so. On the one hand the author discusses his "theses" himself and demonstrates their truth by refuting possible objections or "antitheses": he applies a dialectical method. On the other hand the Platonic dialogues in fact preceded these systems, which result from them "dialectically" through the aporetic discussions of Aristotle and the scholastic Aristotelians. And just as in a Platonic dialogue, the listener, here a historian-philosopher of philosophy, discovers absolute truth as the result of the implicit or tacit "discussion" among the great systems of history, as the result of their "dialectic". The line from Augustine's *Soliloquies* to Descartes's *Meditations* is Kojève's history of dialectic internalised. The objections and replies appended to Descartes's *Meditations* illustrate the survival of dialogue within meditation.

Hegel was the first of these listener-historian-philosophers, at least the first to be so consciously. That is why he could be the first knowingly to abandon dialectic conceived as a philosophical method. He is content to observe and describe the dialectic that took place in the course of history and no longer needs to make one himself. This dialectic, or the "dialogue" of philosophies, took place before him. He has only to have the "experience" of it and describe in a coherent discourse its final synthetic result: the expression of absolute truth is nothing but the adequate verbal description of the dialectic that engenders it. So Hegel's Science is "dialectical" only insofar as the philosophy that prepared it in the course of history was (implicitly or explicitly) dialectical. Hegel as Plato's listener at the scale of the history of philosophy: the dialogue has been written by history, and he only records its conclusion.

At first sight this attitude of Hegel's is a simple return to Plato. If Plato lets Parmenides, Protagoras, Socrates, and others dialogue, content to record the result of their discussions, Hegel records the result of the discussion he organises between Plato and Descartes, Spinoza and Kant, Fichte and Schelling, and so on. Here too it would be a dialectical method of seeking or expounding truth that affects the real it reveals in no way. And Hegel does say somewhere that he only rediscovers ancient, even Platonic, dialectic. But looking more closely, one sees that it is not so, and that when Hegel speaks of dialectic he means something quite different from his predecessors. A footnote adds that Hegel is nonetheless right to say he rediscovers Plato, since Platonic dialectic, dialectic as method, is indeed one aspect of the dialectic of the real that Hegel discovered. The footnote reconciles: Platonic dialectic is true as the reflection in discourse of the real dialectic.

One can say, if one likes, that the eternal light of absolute Hegelian truth also springs from the clash of all the philosophical opinions that preceded it. Only this ideal dialectic, the dialogue of philosophies, took place, according to Hegel, only because it is a reflection of the real dialectic of being. And it is only because it reflects this real dialectic that it finally ends, in the person of Hegel, in the truth or adequate and complete revelation of the real. Each philosophy correctly reveals or describes a turning point or stopping point, thetic, antithetic, or synthetic, of the real dialectic, of the *Bewegung* of existing being. That is why each philosophy is "true" in a certain sense. But it is so only relatively or temporarily: it remains "true" as long as a new philosophy, "true" as well, does not come to demonstrate its "error". But it is not a philosophy that transforms itself and of itself into another, or engenders this other philosophy in and by an autonomous dialectical movement. It is the real corresponding to a given philosophy that itself becomes really other (thetic, antithetic, or synthetic), and it is this other real that engenders another adequate philosophy, which replaces as "true" the first, become "false". So the dialectical movement of the history of philosophy, which leads to absolute or definitive truth, is only a reflection, a "superstructure", of the dialectical movement of the real history of the real. That is why every philosophy that is "true" is also essentially "false": false insofar as it presents itself not as the reflection or description of a moment of the real but as the revelation of the real in its totality. Yet even in being or becoming "false", every philosophy worthy of the name remains "true", since the total real implies and will always imply the aspect or moment it revealed. The absolute truth or Science of the Sage, of Hegel, the adequate and complete revelation of the real in its totality, is therefore indeed an integral synthesis of all the philosophies presented in the course of history. Only it is neither these philosophies by their discussions nor the historian-philosopher who observes them that effect the synthesis in question: it is real history that does it, at the end of its own dialectical movement; and Hegel merely records it without having to do anything, and so without recourse to a specific mode of operation or a method of his own. The claim that philosophies do not refute each other but are made obsolete by changes in the real is the materialist theory of the history of philosophy, "superstructure" included. The double truth and falsity of each philosophy restates the 1936–37 theory of ideology (p. 117).

"*Weltgeschichte ist Weltgericht*": "universal history is a tribunal that judges the world." It judges men, their actions and opinions, and finally also their philosophical opinions. Certainly history is, if one likes, a long "discussion" among men. But this real historical "discussion" is quite other than a philosophical dialogue or discussion. One "discusses" not with verbal arguments but «à coup de massues et d'épées ou de canons d'une part, et de faucilles et de marteaux ou de machines de l'autre» (with clubs and swords or cannons on the one hand, and sickles and hammers or machines on the other) (p. 461). And if one wants to speak of a "dialectical method" used by history, one must specify that it is a matter of methods of war and labour. It is this real, active historical dialectic that is reflected in the history of philosophy. And if Hegelian Science is dialectical or synthetic, it is only because it describes this real dialectic in its totality, as well as the series of successive philosophies corresponding to this reality. The instruments of the real "discussion", clubs, swords, cannons for the fight; sickles, hammers, machines for labour, give dialectic its body. The sickle and hammer is a pointed image in 1935: the Soviet emblem as the instrument of the dialectic of labour. The Schiller line *Weltgeschichte ist Weltgericht*, which Hegel adopted in the *Philosophy of Right* (§ 340), frames history as the final judge of philosophy.

Reality is dialectical, Kojève adds in passing, only because it implies a negative or negating element: the active negation of the given that underlies every bloody fight and all so-called physical labour. Hegel does not need a God to "reveal" truth to him; to find it he need not dialogue with "men in the city", nor even "discuss" with himself or "meditate" in Descartes's fashion. Moreover, no purely verbal discussion or solitary meditation can lead to truth, since fight and labour are its only "criteria". He can find it alone, sitting quietly in the shade of those "trees" that taught Socrates nothing but teach him a great deal about themselves and about men. But all this is possible only because there have been cities where men discussed against a background of fight and labour, working and fighting for their opinions and according to them (cities surrounded, moreover, by those same trees whose wood served to build them). Hegel no longer discusses because he benefits from the discussion of those who preceded him; and if he has no method of his own, having nothing more to do, it is because he profits from all the actions carried out in the course of history. His thought simply reflects the real; but he can do so only because the real is dialectical, imbued with the negating action of fight and labour, which engenders thought and discourse, moves them, and finally realises their perfect coincidence with the real they are supposed to reveal. In short, Hegel does not need a dialectical method because the truth he embodies is the final result of the real or active dialectic of universal history, which his thought merely reproduces in discourse. The image of Hegel under Socrates's trees is a reply to the *Phaedrus*: the trees now teach, because history has passed through them, as wood for cities. The claim that fight and labour are truth's only criteria is the methodological consequence of the thesis that the real resists action.

From Socrates–Plato to Hegel, dialectic was only a philosophical method without counterpart in the real. In Hegel there is a real dialectic, but the philosophical method is that of pure and simple description, which is dialectical only in the sense that it describes a dialectic of reality. The contrast is the appendix's thesis in one sentence.

To understand the meaning and reason of this truly revolutionary transposition, one must consent to make with Hegel the philosophical experiment he proposes to the reader of the *Phenomenology* in Chapter I. Consult your watch, he says, and note that it is, say, noon. Say so, and you will have stated a truth. Now write this truth on a scrap of paper: "it is now noon". Hegel remarks that a truth cannot cease to be true by being written down. Now consult your watch again and reread the written sentence: the truth has turned into an error, since it is now five past noon. Hegel's own example in Chapter I (¶95) is "now is night"; Kojève's watch and noon modernise it. The experiment shows that temporal reality turns truths into errors.

What can one say, except that real being can turn a human truth into error, at least insofar as the real is temporal, insofar as time has a reality? This observation was made long ago, since Plato, even since Parmenides, perhaps earlier. But one aspect of the question was neglected until Hegel: the fact that by his discourse, especially written discourse, man manages to maintain error within reality itself. If nature commits an error, an animal malformation for example, it eliminates it immediately: the animal dies or at least does not propagate. Only the errors committed by man last indefinitely and spread far through language. «Et on pourrait définir l'homme comme une erreur qui se maintient dans l'existence, qui dure dans la réalité» (and one could define man as an error that maintains itself in existence, that lasts in reality) (p. 463). Since error means disagreement with the real, since what is other than what is is false, one can also say that man who errs is a nothingness nihilating in being, or an "ideal" present in the real. A footnote adds that Parmenides's assertion, "being and thought are the same", can apply strictly only to true thought, certainly not to false thought. The false is certainly something other than being; yet one cannot say the false "is nothing", that "there is no" error. Error "exists" in its way, ideally, so to speak. The definition of man as "an error that lasts" is the source of the twelfth lecture's remark about man as nature's surviving error (p. 432), written four years earlier. The footnote's analysis of the being of error answers Parmenides: error is neither being nor nothing.

Man alone can err without having to disappear on that account: he can go on existing while mistaken about what exists; he can live his error or in error; and error or the false, which are nothing in themselves, become real in him. The experiment shows how, thanks to man, the nothingness of past noon can be really present, in the form of an erroneous sentence, in the real present of five past twelve. The image of past noon present as an erroneous sentence is the clearest illustration of how man is "the presence of the past".

But this maintenance of error in the real is possible only because its transformation into truth is possible. It is because it can be corrected that error is not pure nothingness. Experience shows that human errors are in fact corrected over time and become truths. One can even say that every truth in the proper sense is a corrected error. For truth is more than a reality: it is a revealed reality, reality plus its revelation by discourse. There is therefore within truth a difference between the real and the discourse that reveals it. But a difference actualises itself in the form of an opposition, and a discourse opposed to the real is precisely an error. A difference that had never been actualised would not really be a difference. There is therefore really a truth only where there has been an error. But error really exists only in the form of human discourse. So if man alone can really err and live in error, he alone can also embody truth.
