If being in its totality is not only pure and simple being (*Sein*) but truth, concept, Idea, or Spirit, it is only because it implies in its real existence a human or speaking reality capable of erring and correcting its errors. «Sans l'Homme, l'Être serait muet : il serait là (Dasein), mais il ne serait pas vrai (das Wahre)» (without man, being would be mute: it would be there, but it would not be true) (p. 464). The argument that every truth is a corrected error is one of Kojève's most original. It follows from the definition of truth as revealed reality: revelation implies a difference between real and discourse, and an actualised difference is an error. Truth thus presupposes the history of its errors.

Hegel's example shows how man manages to create and maintain an error in nature. Another example, not in Hegel but illustrating his thought, shows how man manages to turn into truth the error he has maintained in the real as error. Suppose that in the Middle Ages a poet wrote in a poem: "at this moment a man is flying over the ocean". It was without doubt an error, and it remained so for long centuries. But if we reread this sentence now, there is a good chance we read a truth, since it is almost certain that at this moment some aviator is over the Atlantic. The example of the poet and the aviator is Kojève's best-known illustration of labour making a discourse true. It is the counterpart of the watch: nature turns truth into error; man turns error into truth.

We saw earlier that nature, or given being, can make a human truth false, which man nonetheless manages to maintain indefinitely as error. We now see that man can transform his own error into truth. He began by erring, voluntarily or not, it matters little, in speaking of the terrestrial animal of the species *Homo sapiens* as a flying animal; but he ended by stating a truth in speaking of the flight of an animal of this species. And it is not the (erroneous) discourse that was changed to conform to given being (*Sein*); it is being that was transformed to conform to discourse. A footnote adds that one might say that in inventing the aeroplane man corrects the "error" of nature, which created him without wings; but that would only be a metaphor, anthropomorphising nature. There is error, and so truth, only where there is language (*Logos*). The footnote guards against anthropomorphising nature, consistently with the dualism: nature does not err, since it does not speak.

The action that transforms the given real so as to make a human error true, a discourse that disagreed with this given, is called labour: it is by working that man built the aeroplane that turned the poet's (voluntary) error into truth. But labour is a real negation of the given. Being that exists as a world where one works therefore implies a negative or negating element: it has a dialectical structure. And it is because it has it that there is in it a discourse that reveals it, that it is not only given being but revealed being or truth, Idea, Spirit. Truth is an error become true (or "dialectically overcome" as error); and it is the real negation of the given by labour that transforms error into truth. Truth is therefore necessarily dialectical in the sense that it results from the real dialectic of labour. So the truly adequate verbal expression of truth must take account of its dialectical origin, its birth from the labour man performs within nature. The eighth lecture's "the concept is labour" (p. 377) is here grounded in the example: labour makes discourse true.

This applies to truth relating to the natural world, the discourse that reveals the reality and being of nature. But truth relating to man, the discourse that reveals human reality, is also dialectical, in that it results from a real negation of the human (or social, historical) given and must account for it. To see this, one must consider a case where a "moral error" (crime) turns into "truth" or virtue. For every morality is an implicit anthropology, and it is of his very being that man speaks when he judges his actions morally. A footnote adds: conversely, every anthropology is an implicit morality, since the "normal" man it speaks of is always a "norm" for the behaviour or evaluation of empirical man. The reciprocity of morality and anthropology is a significant thesis: descriptions of man are always prescriptions, and moral judgements are always claims about human being.

Suppose then a man assassinates his king for political reasons. He believes he acts rightly. But others treat him as a criminal, arrest him, and put him to death. Under these conditions he is effectively a criminal. So the given social world, like the natural world, can turn a human truth ("subjective", a "certainty") into error. But suppose the assassination triggers a victorious revolution. At once society treats the assassin as a hero. And under these conditions he is effectively a hero, a model of virtue and civic spirit, a human ideal. Man can therefore transform a crime into virtue, a moral or anthropological error into a truth. The regicide example is the moral counterpart of the aeroplane, and the clearest statement of justification by success, which the Introduction (p. 32), the 1935–36 notes (p. 89), and the 1938–39 lectures repeat. Written in 1935, it has the assassination of rulers, and the revolutions they triggered, in view.

As in the example of the aeroplane, there is here again a real transformation of the existing world, an active negation of the given. There it concerned the natural world, here the human, social, historical world. If there the negating action was labour, here it is fight, the fight to the death for recognition (*Anerkennen*). But in both cases there is effective active negation of the given, or, as Hegel says, "dialectical movement" of the real. The two examples correspond exactly to labour and fight, nature and society.

It is this active or real negation of the given, effected in fight and by labour, that constitutes the negative or negating element determining the dialectical structure of the real and of being. It is therefore indeed a dialectical real and a real dialectic. But this dialectic has an ideal "superstructure", a reflection in thought and discourse. In particular, in the course of history a philosophy (in the broad sense) has each time come to account for the state of affairs realised at a decisive turning point of the dialectical evolution of the world. So the history of philosophy and of "culture" in general is itself a "dialectical movement"; but it is a secondary, derived movement. Finally, insofar as Hegel's thought and discourse reveal and describe the totality of the real in its becoming, they too are a "dialectical movement"; but this movement is, as it were, tertiary. Hegelian discourse is dialectical insofar as it describes the real dialectic of fight and labour, as well as the "ideal" reflection of this dialectic in thought generally and philosophical thought in particular. But in itself Hegelian discourse has nothing dialectical about it: it is neither a dialogue nor a discussion; it is a pure and simple "phenomenological" description of the real dialectic of the real and of the verbal discussion that reflected this dialectic over time. So Hegel does not need to "demonstrate" what he says or "refute" what others say. "Demonstration" and "refutation" took place before him, in the course of the history that precedes him, and they were effected not by verbal arguments but, in the last analysis, by the test (*Bewährung*) of fight and labour. Hegel has only to record the final result of this "dialectical" test and describe it correctly. And since by definition the content of this description will never be modified, completed, or refuted, one can say that Hegel's description is the statement of absolute truth, universally and eternally (that is, "necessarily") valid. The three levels, primary (real dialectic), secondary (history of philosophy), tertiary (Hegel's description), are the appendix's most precise structure. *Bewährung*, the test or proving, returns from the Marx epigraph (p. 9).

All this presupposes, of course, the completion of the real dialectic of fight and labour, the definitive halt of history. Only "at the end of times" can a Sage (in this case named Hegel) renounce every dialectical method, every real or ideal negation, transformation, or "critique" of the given, confining himself to describing it, to revealing by discourse the given precisely as it is given. Or more exactly, it is at the moment when man, become a Sage, is fully satisfied by such a pure and simple description that active or real negation of the given no longer takes place, so that the description remains indefinitely valid or true and is no longer ever called into question or engenders polemical dialogues. The correction "or more exactly" is significant: the Sage's satisfaction with description is the end of negation, not its consequence.

As a philosophical method, then, dialectic is abandoned only at the moment when the real dialectic of the active transformation of the given definitively stops. As long as this transformation lasts, a description of the given real can only be partial or provisional: insofar as the real itself changes, its philosophical description must change too, to remain adequate or true. In other words, as long as the real or active dialectic of history lasts, errors and truths are dialectical in the sense that they are all sooner or later "dialectically overcome" (*aufgehoben*), "truth" becoming partially, or in a certain sense, false, and "error" true; and they become so in and through discussion, dialogue, or the dialectical method. Before the end, dialectical method is necessary; after it, description suffices.

To be able to renounce the dialectical method and claim absolute truth by confining oneself to pure description without any "discussion" or "demonstration", one must therefore be sure that the real dialectic of history is truly completed. But how can one know it? This question, raised in 1935, is the question the 1938–39 lectures pursue: how to know that history has ended.

At first sight the answer is easy. History stops when man no longer acts in the strong sense, no longer negates or transforms the natural and social given by bloody fight and creative labour. And man no longer does so when the given real gives him full satisfaction (*Befriedigung*), fully realising his Desire (*Begierde*, which in man is the desire for universal recognition of his personality unique in the world, *Anerkennen* or *Anerkennung*). If man is truly and fully satisfied by what is, he no longer desires anything real and so no longer changes reality, thereby ceasing to change himself really. The only "desire" he can still have, if he is a philosopher, is to understand what is and what he is, and to reveal it by discourse. The adequate description of the real in its totality given by the Sage's Science therefore definitively satisfies man, even as philosopher: he will never again oppose what has been said by the Sage, just as the Sage no longer opposed the real he described. So the Sage's non-dialectical (non-negating) description will be absolute truth that engenders no philosophical "dialectic", that will never be a "thesis" opposed by an antithesis. The philosopher's residual desire, to understand, is the only one satisfied by Science. This anticipates the 1938–39 thesis that philosophy ends because the philosopher is satisfied.

But how can one know whether man is truly and fully satisfied by what is? According to Hegel, man is nothing but desire for recognition ("*der Mensch ist Anerkennen*", vol. XX, p. 206), and history is only the process of the progressive satisfaction of this desire, which is fully satisfied in and through the universal and homogeneous State (for Hegel, Napoleon's Empire). But first, Hegel had to anticipate the historical future (by definition unforeseeable, since free, born of a negation of the present given), since the State he had in view was only in formation; and we know that even today it is far from having "empirical existence" (*Dasein*), being "objective reality" (*Wirklichkeit*), or "real present" (*Gegenwart*). Second, and much more important, how can one know that the satisfaction given in and by this State is truly a definitive satisfaction of man as such, and not only of one of his possible desires? How can one know that the stabilisation of the historical "movement" in the Empire is not a simple pause, the result of passing weariness? By what right can one affirm that this State will not engender in man a new desire, other than that for recognition, and that it will therefore not be negated one day by a negating or creative action (*Tat*) other than fight and labour? The two objections are Kojève's most incisive. The first concedes in 1935 that the universal State does not yet exist. The second asks whether recognition exhausts human desire, which is the deepest question one can put to his anthropology. The phrase "the result of passing weariness" names the possibility that the end of history is only a lull.

One can affirm it only by supposing that the desire for recognition exhausts all human possibilities. But one has the right to make this supposition only if one has complete and perfect knowledge of man, universally and definitively ("necessarily") valid, absolutely true. But by definition absolute truth can be reached only at the end of history, and it is precisely this end of history that was to be determined. «On est donc impliqué dans un cercle vicieux» (one is therefore involved in a vicious circle) (p. 468). And Hegel was perfectly aware of it. But he believed he had found a criterion both of the absolute truth of his description of the real, its correctness and completeness, and of the end of the "movement" of the real, the definitive halt of history. And, curiously, this criterion is precisely the circularity of his description, of the "System of Science". The admission of the vicious circle is the appendix's most candid moment. Kojève's solution, the circularity criterion, turns the vicious circle into a virtuous one: the system proves its completeness by returning to its start. The tenth lecture's doubt and the second lecture's footnote on non-circularity (p. 291) are the later answer to whether the criterion is met.

Hegel starts from a more or less arbitrary description of the real (represented by a philosophy stated in the course of history), choosing however the one that seems simplest, most elementary, reducing for example to a single word: practically a very ancient philosophy, Parmenides's for example, which reduces to saying "being is". The correct presentation of this description shows that it is incomplete, that it reveals only one aspect of being and the real, that it is only a "thesis" that necessarily engenders an "antithesis", with which it will necessarily combine to give a "synthesis", which will be only a new "thesis", and so on. A footnote adds that the philosopher who set out the "thesis" did not know it was only a thesis that must engender an antithesis. In other words, even the aspect of the real he in fact described was not described correctly, since he believed he was describing the totality of the real. Hegel, by contrast, knows it is one aspect of the real, which is why he describes it correctly, so as to show the necessity of the antithesis that describes the complementary aspect. He knows it because he no longer opposes the given real he describes, being satisfied by it and desiring only its correct description, not its transformation; «c'est le désir inopérant de transformer le réel qui engendre l'erreur chez le philosophe» (it is the inoperative desire to transform the real that engenders error in the philosopher) (p. 469). Hegel sees all this because he already knows the final synthesis of all intermediate theses, antitheses, and syntheses, having described the completed, truly total real created by the whole of the real dialectic reflected in the history of philosophy. But it is the presentation of this history (and of history in general) as a series of theses, antitheses, and syntheses that will show him that he has in fact described (correctly and completely) the totality of the real, that his description is a final or total synthesis. The footnote's thesis that "the inoperative desire to transform the real engenders error in the philosopher" is a profound diagnosis: philosophers err because they want to change what they describe but cannot. The Sage, desiring nothing, describes correctly.

Proceeding thus step by step, by simple adequate descriptions, by a correct descriptive repetition of the (derived) dialectic of the history of philosophy, in which each step is as necessary or inevitable as the various elements of the description of a complex real are "necessary" (the description of the trunk, branches, leaves, and so on, in the description of a tree, for example), Hegel finally reaches a point that is nothing other than his starting point: the final synthesis is also the initial thesis. He thus notes that he has travelled or described a circle, and that if he wants to continue he can only go round in circles: his description cannot be extended; it can only be redone as it has already been done once. That is to say, Hegel's discourse exhausts all the possibilities of thought. No discourse can be opposed to it that would not already be part of it, reproduced in a paragraph of the System as a moment of the whole. So Hegel's discourse sets out an absolute truth that no one can deny; and this discourse is not dialectical in the sense of being a "thesis" that can be "dialectically overcome". But if Hegel's thought can no longer be surpassed by thought, and if it does not itself surpass the given real but merely describes it, being and knowing itself satisfied by what is, no ideal or real negation of the given is possible any more. The real will therefore remain eternally identical with itself, and its whole history will belong forever to the past. A complete and correct description of this real will therefore be universally and eternally valid, absolutely true. And the circularity of Hegel's description proves that it is complete and so correct, since an erroneous or incomplete description never returns upon itself, stopping at a gap or ending in an impasse. The comparison of dialectical necessity to the necessity of describing trunk, branches, and leaves is an important deflation: dialectical necessity is the necessity of complete description, not of deduction. The argument that an incomplete description cannot return to its start is the logical basis of the circularity criterion.

So, by demonstrating without "discussion", without "refutation" or "demonstration", the absolute truth of the System, the circularity simply noted by the Sage justifies his purely descriptive or non-dialectical method. Circularity justifies description; description needs no dialectic.

There is no need to insist on the non-dialectical character of Hegel's method. There is not much to say about it, and what one could say has already been said by Edmund Husserl about his own "phenomenological" method, «qu'il a eu grand tort d'opposer à la méthode hégélienne qu'il ne connaissait pas» (which he was very wrong to oppose to the Hegelian method, which he did not know) (p. 470). For in fact Hegel's method is nothing other than the method called today "phenomenological". The judgement on Husserl is pointed: Husserl's polemic against Hegel in *Philosophy as Rigorous Science* (1911) rested on ignorance. Kojève, who studied with Jaspers and knew Husserl's work, here enlists the phenomenological method for Hegel.

By contrast, one must speak at greater length of the DIALECTIC Hegel has in view, the dialectical structure of the real and of being as he conceives and describes it in the *Phenomenology* and the *Encyclopaedia*. First one must see what the trinitarian structure of being itself is, as described in Hegel's ontology, the *Logic* forming the first part of the *Encyclopaedia*. Then one must see what the dialectical triplicity of being means in the "appearance" (*Erscheinung*) of its "empirical existence" (*Dasein*), as described in the *Phenomenology*. Recall the general definition of dialectic in § 79. The "logical" or "logical-real" (*das Logisch-Reelle*), being and the real correctly described by a coherent discourse (*Logos*), necessarily have three "aspects" (*Seiten*) or "moments" (*Momente*). These three moments are constitutive of revealed being, and so they are found again in the discourse that correctly reveals this trinitarian or dialectical being. The plan announces the analysis of § 80–82 that follows: identity, negativity, totality.

The first aspect is defined in § 80 (vol. V, p. 105). Kojève translates: thought (*Denken*) taken as Understanding (*Verstand*) stops at fixed determinateness (*Bestimmtheit*) and its distinctness (*Unterschiedenheit*) from other fixed determinations; such a limited abstraction counts for the Understanding as subsisting (*bestehend*) and existing for itself, independently of the other determinations and of the thought that thinks them. Thought in the mode of the Understanding is man's current thought: naive man's, the vulgar scholar's, the pre-Hegelian philosopher's. It does not reveal being in its totality; it does not reflect the three moments of being and of every being but stops at the first; it describes (in principle correctly) only the "abstract" aspect of being, precisely the moment "accessible to the Understanding". The identification of the Understanding with common thought, vulgar science, and pre-Hegelian philosophy repeats Chapter III's typology.

The thought of the Understanding is exclusively dominated by the primordial ontological (and so "logical") category of identity. Its logical ideal is perfect agreement of thought with itself, the absence of all internal contradiction, the homogeneity, even identity, of its content. Every identity is true by definition, and every truth has a content identical with itself and in itself. And since truth is an adequate revelation of being or the real, being and the real are, for the Understanding, always and everywhere identical with themselves and in themselves. What is true of being and the real taken as a whole must be true of everything that is or exists, of every particular entity that really exists. For the Understanding every real entity always remains identical with itself; it is determined once for all in its specificity (*feste Bestimmtheit*) and is distinguished precisely, fixedly, and stably from all other real entities, equally fixedly determined (*Unterschiedenheit gegen andere*). In short, it is a given entity that one can neither engender nor destroy nor modify in any way. That is why one can say it exists for itself (*für sich*), independently of the rest of existing being, and in particular independently of the Understanding that thinks it. The definition of the Understanding by the category of identity makes it the logic of nature: fixed, given, indestructible entities.

According to Hegel, real being is in fact as the Understanding reveals it. Identity is indeed a fundamental ontological category, applying to being itself and to everything that is. Every thing is in fact identical with itself and different from all others, which precisely allows thought (scientific or "naive") to "define" it or reveal its "specificity", to recognise it as remaining "the same thing" and as being "something other" than what it is not. The thought of the Understanding is therefore true in principle. If there were no identity in and of being, no science of the real would be possible (as the Greeks saw very well), and there would have been no truth, no reality revealed by coherent discourse. But this "coherent" or identical thought is also false if it claims to reveal the totality of being and not only one of its (three) aspects. For in fact being and the real are something more than identity with themselves. The concession that identity is real is important: Kojève is no Heraclitean. Identity is one of three ontological categories, and the one that governs nature.

The thought of the Understanding moreover manifests its own insufficiency. Pursuing its ideal of identity, it finally ends in a universal tautology empty of meaning or content, and its "discourse" finally reduces to the single word "being", or "One", and so on. As soon as it wants to develop this word into true discourse, to say something, it introduces diversity, which contradicts identity and renders it obsolete or false from its own point of view. This insufficiency was shown by Plato (notably in the *Parmenides*); Hegel spoke of it in the *Phenomenology* (notably Chapter III) and elsewhere; and in our day Meyerson has insisted on it at length. There is no need to return to it. What must be stressed is that for Hegel this thought is insufficient because being itself is more and other than identity, and that it is because being is not only identity that thought can go beyond the stage of the Understanding or tautological "discourse". This thought does not reach truth because it cannot develop into discourse revealing real being; and it is not circular, does not return to its starting point, because it does not manage to leave it. But if this thought is not a truth, it is because real being is something more than what it reveals of it. One must therefore go beyond the Understanding to reveal real being in its totality; or more exactly, the thought of the Understanding is surpassed because the discursive self-revelation of being reveals not only its identity with itself but also its other fundamental ontological aspects. A footnote adds: tautology reduces to a single word and so is not true discourse (*Logos*). But it admits an indefinite algorithmic development, and in this form it can be considered a "revelation" of the real or a "truth". But tautology, mathematical or other, can reveal only the identical aspect of being and the real. One could say it reveals correctly and completely given being (*Sein*) or natural reality, the natural world, to the exclusion of man and his social or historical world. «Mais Hegel lui-même ne le dit pas» (but Hegel himself does not say so) (p. 472). The footnote is a precursor of the eighth lecture's note on the algorithm (p. 378): mathematics, the development of tautology, is the adequate knowledge of nature, which is identity. Its last sentence again marks Kojève's divergence from Hegel. The remark that tautological thought "is not circular because it does not manage to leave its starting point" is an elegant contrast with the circularity of Science.

To reach truth, to reveal the totality of real being, thought must therefore go beyond the stage of the Understanding (*Verstand*) and become Reason (*Vernunft*), "rational" (*vernünftig*) thought. This thought reveals the other fundamental aspects of being as such and of everything real. First, as "negative" Reason, it reveals by its discourse the "negatively rational" aspect of what is, the moment of (revealed) being and the real that Hegel calls "dialectical" in the narrow or proper sense, precisely because it is a negative or negating element. The transition to § 81.

This second moment of being (in fact of revealed being) is defined in § 81 (vol. V, p. 105). Kojève translates: the properly dialectical moment is the own self-overcoming (*Sichaufheben*) of these finite determinations and their passage (*Übergehen*) into their opposites (*entgegengesetzte*). It is important first to note that it is not negatively rational thought (or Reason) that introduces the negative element into being and so makes it dialectical: it is the determinate and fixed real entities (revealed by the Understanding) themselves that negate themselves "dialectically" (that is, while preserving themselves) and so actually become other than they are or have been. "Negatively rational" or "dialectical" thought only describes this real negation of the given "accessible to the Understanding" and its fixed "specifying determinations". The emphasis on "own" (*eigene*) self-overcoming is Kojève's: negation belongs to the things, not to thought.

Hegel himself insists on this in the second explanatory note to the paragraph (vol. V, p. 105). Kojève translates: dialectic is generally considered an external art (a "method") ... Often dialectic is indeed no more than a subjective seesaw of reasoning going back and forth (*hin- und herübergehendem Räsonnement*) ... But in its authentic determination dialectic is on the contrary the proper, true nature of the determinations of the Understanding, of things (*Dinge*), and of the finite as such ... Dialectic is this immanent going-beyond (*Hinausgehen*), in which the one-sidedness and limitation (*Beschränktheit*) of the determinations of the Understanding present themselves as what they are, their own negation. «Tout ce qui est fini (alles Endliche) est un acte de se supprimer-dialectiquement soi-même» (everything finite is an act of dialectically overcoming itself) (p. 473). Consequently the dialectical (*das Dialektische*) constitutes the moving soul of scientific progress (*Fortgehens*) and is the only principle through which an immanent connection (*Zusammenhang*) and necessity enter the content of science. So it is the real itself that is dialectical, and it is so because it implies, in addition to identity, a second fundamental moment that Hegel calls negativity. The quotation from § 81 Remark, "alles Endliche ist dies, sich selbst aufzuheben", was cited in the eighth lecture (p. 380) as the ground of human finitude. Here it grounds the reality of dialectic.

Identity and negativity are two primordial and universal ontological categories. A footnote, among the most important in the book, adds: in the *Encyclopaedia* Hegel says that every entity can "overcome" itself and is therefore dialectical. But in the *Phenomenology* he affirms that only human reality is dialectical, nature being determined by identity alone (compare Hoffmeister p. 145 and p. 563). «Personnellement, je partage le point de vue de la PhG et je n'admets pas la dialectique de l'Être-naturel, du Sein» (personally, I share the point of view of the *Phenomenology* and I do not admit the dialectic of natural being, of *Sein*) (p. 474). He cannot discuss the question here, but would say this: the implication of negativity in identical being (*Sein*) is equivalent to the presence of man in reality; man, and he alone, reveals being and reality by discourse; being revealed in its totality therefore necessarily implies negativity; it is indeed a universal onto-logical category; but within total reality one must distinguish, on the one hand, purely identical natural reality, which is therefore not dialectical in itself, does not dialectically overcome itself; and on the other, essentially negating human reality, which dialectically overcomes both itself and the identical natural reality "given" to it. The dialectical overcoming of the given (by fight and labour) necessarily ends in its revelation by discourse; reality revealed by discourse, reality taken in its totality or concrete reality, is therefore indeed dialectical. Example: the acorn, the oak, and the transformation of the acorn into an oak (as well as the evolution of the species "oak") are not dialectical; but the transformation of the oak into an oak table is a dialectical negation of the natural given, the creation of something essentially new. It is because man "works" the oak that he has a "science" of the oak, the acorn, and so on; this science is dialectical, but not insofar as it reveals the acorn and its transformation into an oak, which are not dialectical; it is dialectical insofar as it evolves as a science (of nature) in the course of history; and it evolves so dialectically only because man carries out real dialectical negations of the given by labour and fight. This footnote is the most explicit statement of Kojève's dualism in the book, and its earliest (1935). The acorn, oak, and oak table are its emblem: growth is not dialectical; carpentry is. The distinction between the dialectic of nature, which Kojève denies, and the dialectic of the science of nature, which he affirms, is precise: science evolves because labour changes man's relation to nature. The footnote is the root of later debates about the dialectic of nature in French Marxism, notably Sartre's *Critique of Dialectical Reason* (1960), which takes the same position against Engels.

Thanks to identity, every being remains the same being, eternally identical with itself and different from others; or, as the Greeks said, every being represents by its temporal existence an eternal immutable "idea"; it has a "nature" or "essence" given once for all; it occupies a fixed and stable "place" (*topos*) within a world ordered from all eternity (*cosmos*). But thanks to negativity, an identical being can negate or overcome its identity with itself and become other than it is, even its own opposite. In other words, the negating being, far from necessarily "representing" or "showing" (as "phenomenon") its given identical "idea" or "nature", can negate them itself and become their opposite (become "perverted"). Or again, the negating being can break the rigid bonds of the fixed "differences" that distinguish it from other identical beings, "freeing" itself from these bonds; it can leave the place assigned to it in the cosmos. In short, as Hegel says in the first edition of the *Logic*, the being of negative or negating being, dominated by the category of negativity, consists in «das nicht zu sein, was es ist, und das zu sein, was es nicht ist» (not being what it is and being what it is not) (p. 474). The formula from the first edition of the *Logic* is Sartre's definition of the for-itself in *Being and Nothingness*, "being what it is not and not being what it is", which comes, through Kojève, from Hegel. The image of leaving one's place in the cosmos joins ontology to the Introduction's theme of freedom from nature.

Concrete (revealed) real being is at once identity and negativity. It is therefore not only static given being (*Sein*), space, and nature, but also becoming (*Werden*), time, and history. It is not only identity or equality with itself (*Sichselbstgleichheit*), but also being-other (*Anderssein*), or negation of itself as given and creation of itself as other than this given. In other words, it is not only empirical existence (*Dasein*) and necessity (*Notwendigkeit*), but also action (*Tat*, *Tun*, *Handeln*) and freedom (*Freiheit*). To be other than one is (negativity) while remaining oneself (identity), or to identify oneself with an other while distinguishing oneself from it, is to be, and reveal by discourse, both what one is oneself and what one is not. A footnote illustrates: being that "overcomes" itself as being while remaining itself, being, is the concept "being". To identify with the tree without becoming a tree is to form and have the (adequate) concept of the tree. To become other while remaining oneself is to have and keep the concept of one's I, in and through "memory". To become other than one is is to take a position toward oneself, to exist (as one has been) for oneself (as one is now). The being that dialectically negates the given real also preserves it as negated, as unreal or "ideal": it preserves it as the "meaning" of the discourse by which it reveals it. It is therefore "conscious" of what it negates; and if it negates itself, it is self-conscious. The simply identical being, by contrast, exists only in itself and for others, in its identity with itself and through the relations of difference linking it to the rest of identical beings within the cosmos: it does not exist for itself, and others do not exist for it. The footnote's definitions of the concept, identifying with the tree without becoming a tree, are the clearest in the book and anticipate the eighth lecture's "being minus being" (p. 375). The derivation of consciousness from negativity, to preserve the negated as meaning is to be conscious of it, is Kojève's genealogy of mind.

So the being that is at once identity and negativity is not only homogeneous and immutable being-in-itself (*Ansichsein*) and fixed and stable being-for-another (*Sein für Anderes*), but also being-for-itself (*Fürsichsein*), split into real being and revealing discourse, and being-other (*Anderssein*), in perpetual transformation that frees it from itself as given to itself and others. The identical and negating being is therefore "free" in the sense that it is more than its given being, being also the revelation of this being by discourse. But if this discourse reveals being in its totality, if it is truly true, it reveals not only the identity but also the negativity of being. That is why the discourse is not only that of the Understanding, dominated by the sole onto-logical category of identity, but also a discourse of negative or properly "dialectical" Reason, dominated by the onto-logical category of negativity. But this is not yet enough: the discourse is truly true or revealing of the concrete totality of (revealed) being only on condition of also being a discourse of positive or "speculative" Reason. The hyphenated "onto-logical" marks the identity of ontological and logical categories: being and its discourse share the same structure.

Indeed, the negating being negates itself. It is therefore as the same that it negates itself or becomes and is other: it is negating as identical and identical as negating. One cannot therefore say that being is identity and negativity: being both at once, it is neither taken separately. Concrete real (revealed) being is neither identity (pure, which is being, *Sein*) nor negativity (pure, which is nothingness, *Nichts*), but totality (which is becoming, *Werden*). Totality is therefore the third fundamental and universal onto-logical category: being is real or concrete only in its totality, and every concrete real entity is the totality of its constituent moments, identical or negating. It is in the aspect of totality that being and the real are revealed by "positively rational" thought, which Hegel calls "speculative". But this thought is possible only because there is in being and the real themselves a real "speculative" or "positively rational" moment, which "speculative" thought merely reveals. The mapping of identity, negativity, and totality onto *Sein*, *Nichts*, and *Werden*, the opening of the *Logic*, completes the ontology: becoming is the truth of being and nothing.

Hegel defines this real "speculative" moment in § 82 (vol. V, pp. 105–106). Kojève translates: the speculative or positively rational grasps (*fasst auf*) the unity of the determinations in their opposition (*Entgegensetzung*), the affirmative contained in their dissolution (*Auflösung*) and passage (*Übergehen*). The negating being negates its identity with itself and becomes its own opposite, but it remains the same being. This unity in opposition to itself is its affirmation despite its negation or "dissolution", even "transformation". It is as this self-negating affirmation, as re-affirmation of its first identity with itself, that being is a "speculative" or "positively rational" entity. So being that re-affirms itself as identical with itself after having negated itself as such is neither identity nor negativity but totality. And it is as totality that being is truly and fully dialectical. But it is a dialectical totality and not a tautological identity because it is also negativity. Totality is the unity of identity and negativity: «c'est l'affirmation par la négation» (it is affirmation through negation) (p. 476). In other words, taken as totality, being is neither being-in-itself only nor being-for-itself only, but the integration of the two, being-in-and-for-itself (*An-und-Fürsichsein*). The paragraph is § 82 of the *Encyclopaedia* (Kojève's text says § 83). "Affirmation through negation" is the formula for synthesis, and it names the structure of human action: to affirm oneself by negating the given.

Totality is therefore revealed being or self-conscious being, which Hegel calls "absolute concept", "Idea", or "Spirit": split by negativity into static given being (*Sein*) and its discursive "ideal" opposite, it is or becomes again one and homogeneous in and through this doubling (*Entzweiung*) when the totality of being is correctly revealed by the Sage's "total" or circular discourse. So, despite the negativity it contains and presupposes, the final totality is as one and unique, homogeneous and autonomous, as the first and primordial identity. As the result of negation, totality is as much an affirmation as the identity that was negated in order to become totality. The final totality is a second identity, mediated: the end returns to the self-identity of the beginning, which is the circle in ontological terms.

In the first explanatory note to § 82 Hegel explains why negativity is not nothingness, why it does not lead to the pure and simple destruction of the self-negating being but ends in a new positive determination of this being, which in its totality becomes again absolutely identical with itself ("the synthesis is a new thesis"). Kojève translates (vol. V, p. 106): dialectic has a positive result because it has a determinate (*bestimmten*) content; because its result is truly (*wahrhaft*) not empty abstract nothing (*Nichts*) but the negation of certain determinations (*gewissen Bestimmungen*), which are contained in the result, precisely because it is not an immediate (*unmittelbares*) nothing but a result. The note is the classical statement of determinate negation, which Kojève now formalises.

Dialectical negation is the negation of an identity, of something determinate, specific, corresponding to an eternal "idea" or a fixed and stable "nature". The determinateness (*Bestimmtheit*) of the negated (identical) determines and specifies both the negation itself and its (total) result. The negation of A has a positive or specifically determinate content because it is a negation of A, and not of M or N, for example, or of any indeterminate X. So "A" is preserved in "not-A"; or, if one likes, it is "dialectically overcome" (*aufgehoben*) there. That is why not-A is not pure nothingness but an entity as "positive", determinate or specific, even identical with itself, as the A negated in it. Not-A is all this because it results from the negation of a determinate or specific A; or again, not-A is not nowhere, because A has a fixed and stable place within a well-ordered cosmos. The spatial image, not-A is not nowhere because A has a place, makes determinate negation intuitive: one can leave a place only from somewhere.

If identity is incarnated in "A" identical with itself (A = A), negativity is concretised in and through, or as, the *not* of "not-A". Taken in itself, this *not* is pure and simple nothingness: it is something only thanks to the A it negates. The isolated *not* is absolutely indeterminate: it represents absolute freedom, independence from every given determination, every "nature" fixed once for all, every localisation in an ordered cosmos. It is the presence of the *not* in "not-A" that allows what was "A" to go anywhere from the place "A" occupied in the cosmos, to create for itself any "nature" other than the innate "nature" of "A", to determine itself otherwise than "A" was determined by its fixed differences from what it was not. But the presence of "A" in "not-A" limits the absolute freedom of the *not* and concretises it, determines or specifies it. One can certainly go anywhere, but only from the place "A" occupied; one can certainly create any "nature" for oneself, but only on condition that it be other than "A"'s. In short, if the point of arrival of (dialectical) negation is arbitrary, its point of departure is fixed and stable, determinate and specific, given. So negation is not just any negation but the negation of "A". «Et c'est cet "A" dans le "non-A" qui concrétise ou détermine la liberté absolue du "non", qui en tant qu'absolue n'est que Néant pur, ou mort» (and it is this "A" in "not-A" that concretises or determines the absolute freedom of the "not", which, as absolute, is only pure nothingness, or death) (p. 478). The formalisation of freedom as the *not* of not-A is Kojève's most precise logical rendering of his anthropology. Absolute freedom, the *not* without A, is death, which repeats the Sceptic's isolated negativity (p. 65) and anticipates Sartre's situated freedom: free toward any future, but from a given past.

Moreover, as soon as there is "not-A", the purely negating "not" is as much an abstraction as the purely identical "A". What really exists is the unity of the two, "not-A" as a totality or entity as one and unique, determinate and specific, as "A" itself: the "not-A" that is a "B". The step from not-A to B is the step from negation to a new positive being.

A is preserved in B (= not-A); but the *not* that negates A is also maintained there. A is therefore preserved only in its negation, just as the *not* is maintained only as the *not* of A. More exactly, B is the negation of A, a negation that maintains itself in positive existence (*Bestehen*); more exactly still, B is the (positive) result of the negation of A. So B is an A not only suppressed and at the same time preserved but also sublimated (*aufgehoben*) by this preserving negation. For if A is immediate (*unmittelbar*), B is mediated (*vermittelt*) by negation; if A is pure identity, B is totality implying negativity; if A is purely and simply given, B is the result of a negating action, that is, created; if A exists only in itself (*an sich*) or for others (*für Anderes*), B exists also for itself (*für sich*), since in it A takes a position toward itself, negating itself as given and affirming itself as created by this self-negation. The series of contrasts, immediate/mediated, identity/totality, given/created, in itself/for itself, gives the full content of *Aufhebung*.

But B exists not only for itself; it exists in and for itself (*an und für sich*). For in it A affirms itself as totality, maintaining its identity with itself taken as negated, negating, and resulting from negation: it is A itself that negates itself by the "not" and itself becomes the "not-A" that is B. That is why B is not only totality resulting from negation and so implying negativity, but also identity. And as such B too is given and in itself: it too has a determinate specific "nature" and a fixed place in the cosmos. B's being also an identity is what allows the process to continue: every result is a new given.

That is to say, B can provoke a new "not"; negativity can be concretised in and through a "not-B". This "not-B" will be "C", which may engender a "not-C", and so on indefinitely; or, more exactly, until the negation of some "N" brings us back to the starting point: not-N = A. Then one can only retrace indefinitely the circle just closed by this last creative negation. The series A, B, C … N and the closing equation not-N = A formalise the circle of history.

In fact the real (or active) dialectic stops at the "N" whose "not-N" is "A". This "N" is totality in the proper and strong sense: the integration of everything that has been affirmed, negated, and re-affirmed, and of everything that can be, since to negate "N" is to affirm "A", which has already been affirmed, and so on. "N" is totality, being-in-and-for-itself, real being perfectly self-conscious or completely revealed to itself by a coherent discourse (the Sage's absolute Science). To negate itself really, actively, total real being would have to desire to be other than it is. But being perfectly self-conscious, it knows that in negating itself as it is it can only become as it was (since not-N = A). But as it was, it negated itself and finally became as it is now. To want to negate it as it is now is therefore, in the last analysis, to want to make it as it is now: in other words, it is not really to want to negate. "N" therefore does not really negate itself and never becomes "A" again by becoming "not-N". A footnote adds: we know that the real dialectic (history) progresses by the negation implied in man's fight and labour; total reality (our "N") implies satisfied man, man no longer acting by negation of the given; hence the definitive halt of the real dialectic. The argument for the end of history is here purely formal: negating the totality would only reproduce it, so self-conscious totality cannot want to negate itself. The footnote gives the anthropological content: satisfied man does not negate.

But the will of total being to become again what it is is not absurd. And this will is still, if one likes, negating: it is a will to become again what one is otherwise than one has become it. Every negation transforms the in-itself into the for-itself, the unconscious into the conscious. The will in question is therefore simply the desire of the totality of the real to understand itself in and through a coherent discourse, and to understand itself in its real becoming by reproducing it in discourse or thought. From the real "N" one passes by negation (or the renunciation of life for knowledge) to the ideal "not-N = A", and one retraces in thought the path that led to "N", this final term being here also ideal (the "Idea" of the *Logic*). And this last negating action of real being is incarnated in the Sage's will to produce his Science. The phrase "the renunciation of life for knowledge" defines the Sage's last negation: he negates the real only ideally, by understanding it. This is the formal counterpart of the 1938–39 thesis that the Sage's satisfaction lies in knowledge.

Only the Sage's negation is ideal, not real. It therefore creates no new reality and merely reveals the real in the totality of its becoming. The movement of Science is dialectical only insofar as it reproduces or describes the dialectic of reality. That is why this movement is not only circular but cyclical: reaching the ideal "N", one negates it ideally (this negation being the desire to rethink Science or reread the book that contains it) and so returns to the initial "A", which forces one to go forward again to "N". In other words, the discourse of Science that describes the whole of the real dialectic can be repeated indefinitely, but it cannot be modified in any way. And that is to say that this "dialectical" discourse is absolute truth. The desire to reread the book as the ideal negation that restarts the cycle is the formal version of the ninth lecture's cyclical Science (p. 393).

Concrete real being is totality. It therefore implies identity and negativity, but as "dialectically overcome" in and through totality. Identity and negativity do not really exist in isolation; like totality itself, they are only complementary aspects of one and the same real being. But in the discursive description of this concrete real being, its three aspects must be described separately and one after another. So the correct description of the trinitarian dialectical real is a "dialectical" discourse in three stages: the thesis precedes the antithesis, which is followed by the synthesis; the latter then presents itself as a new thesis; and so on. The triad thesis–antithesis–synthesis is thus justified as a feature of exposition: discourse must say successively what is simultaneous in being.

The thesis describes the real in its aspect of identity. It reveals a being by taking it as given, as a static being that remains what it is without ever truly becoming other. A footnote adds: the identical being can nonetheless *become* what it is; it can represent its eternal given "nature" in the form of a temporal evolution, like the egg that becomes a hen (which lays a new egg). But this evolution is always circular, even cyclical: one can always find a segment of the evolution that remains indefinitely identical with itself (the evolution from egg to new egg, for example). The antithesis, by contrast, describes the aspect of negativity in the real being. It reveals a (dialectical) being by taking it as the act of negating itself as given and becoming other. If the thesis describes the being (*Sein*) of the real, the antithesis describes its action (*Tun*); and also the consciousness it has of itself, which is nothing but the doubling of the real into a real negated in its given being (this being thus becoming "abstract notion" or "meaning") and a real that negates this given being by spontaneous action. Finally, the synthesis describes being as totality: it reveals a (dialectical) being by considering it as resulting from its action, by which it suppressed itself as given being, of which it became conscious in and through this very suppression. If in the thesis being simply is, in itself and for others, in the antithesis it exists also for itself, as a given it is in the process of actively suppressing; and in the synthesis it is in itself and for others as existing for itself (as self-conscious) and as resulting from its own negating action. If one likes, the thesis describes the given material to which action will be applied; the antithesis reveals this action itself and the thought that animates it (the "project"); the synthesis shows the result of this action, the completed and objectively real work (*Werk*). This work is, just like the initial given; only it exists not as given but as created by the negating action of the given. The mapping of thesis, antithesis, synthesis onto material, action (with its project), and work is the clearest demystification of the triad in the book: dialectic is the logic of labour. The footnote's egg and hen repeat the 1935–36 notes' "from egg to egg" (p. 83): natural becoming is cyclical identity.

But the transformation of given being into a work created by negating action does not happen all at once. Certain elements or aspects of the given material are preserved as they are in the work, without active negating or creative transformation. In some of its aspects, some of its elements, the work too is a pure and simple given, liable to be actively negated and to serve as material for a new work. That is why the synthesis must describe being not only as work or result of action but also as a given that can provoke other negating actions, a being to be revealed in a (new) thesis; unless the being described in the synthesis (which will then be the final synthesis) is such that it no longer implies givens transformable into works by negating action. The definition of the final synthesis as a being that contains no more transformable givens is the formal condition of the end of history.

Hegel expresses the difference between "thetic" being and the real (identity) and "synthetic" being and the real (totality) by saying that the former are immediate (*unmittelbar*), while the latter are mediated (*vermittelt*) by the "antithetic" action (negativity) that negates them as "immediate". One can say that the fundamental categories of immediacy (*Unmittelbarkeit*) and mediation (*Vermittlung*) sum up the whole real dialectic Hegel has in view. The immediate (*das Unmittelbare*) is static given being (*Sein*), necessity (*Notwendigkeit*), fixed and stable maintenance (*Bestehen*) without any true action or self-consciousness. The mediated (*das Vermittelte*), by contrast, is action realised in a work, freedom, dialectical movement, and discursive understanding of oneself and one's world. But there are degrees of immediacy and mediation. Each advance in the real dialectic represents a (partial) mediation of a (relative) immediacy, and this dialectic stops when everything immediate (and mediatable) has in fact been mediated by (conscious) negating action. As for the "ideal" dialectic of Science, it only describes this "movement" or process of progressive mediation, from its beginning, absolute immediacy, to its end, the same immediacy completely mediated. Immediacy and mediation are Hegel's own vocabulary; Kojève notes below that the triad thesis–antithesis–synthesis is not.

One can say that the whole Hegelian dialectic is summed up by a single fundamental category, that of dialectical overcoming (*Aufheben*). For what is to be "overcome" is precisely the immediate, and the "overcoming" itself is mediation by the negating action that creates the mediated, this being nothing but the immediate taken or posited as dialectically "overcome". And of course it is real being itself that is finally entirely "overcome": the verbal "overcomings" of Science only describe the real process of active "overcoming" or mediation of given being or the immediate by action. A footnote adds: Hegel often speaks of "negativity" but rarely uses the terms "identity" and "totality". The expressions "thesis", "antithesis", "synthesis" hardly ever appear in him. The current "dialectical" terms are "immediacy", "mediation", "overcoming", and their derivatives. Sometimes Hegel expresses the dialectical structure of being and the real by saying they are a "syllogism" (*Schluss*, or *dialektischer Schluss*), in which the "middle term" (*Mitte*) mediates the two "extremes" (*Extreme*) of the immediate and the mediated. When Hegel wants to speak of the real dialectical process he simply says "movement" (*Bewegung*; very rarely *dialektische Bewegung*). The footnote is philologically exact and important: the triad thesis–antithesis–synthesis comes from Fichte and the textbooks, not Hegel. Kojève uses it while acknowledging that it is not Hegel's language.

In the last analysis one can say that Hegel's philosophy has a dialectical character because it tries to account for the phenomenon of freedom, or, what is the same, of action in the proper sense, conscious and voluntary human action; or, and this is still the same, because it wants to account for history. In short, this philosophy is "dialectical" because it wants to account for the fact of man's existence in the world, by revealing or describing man as he really is, in his irreducible specificity or as essentially different from everything that is only nature. The equation freedom = action = history is the motive of dialectic: it exists to account for man.

If freedom is something other than a dream or a subjective illusion, it must inscribe itself in objective reality (*Wirklichkeit*), and it can do so only by realising itself as action operating in and on the real. But if action is free, it must not be a so-to-speak automatic result of the given real, whatever it is; it must therefore be independent of this given while acting on it and amalgamating with it as it realises itself and so becomes itself a given. Hegel's merit was to have understood that this solidarity in independence and independence in solidarity takes place only where there is negation of the given: freedom = action = negativity. But if action is independent of the given real, since it negates it, it creates in realising itself something essentially new in relation to this given. Freedom maintains itself in the real, really lasts, only by perpetually creating the new from the given. And truly creative evolution, the materialisation of a future that is not a mere prolongation of the past by the present, is called history: freedom = negativity = action = history. But what truly characterises man, what essentially distinguishes him from the animal, is precisely his historicity. To account for history is therefore to account for man understood as a free and historical being; and one can account for man so understood only by taking account of the negativity he implies or realises, by describing the "dialectical movement" of his real existence, which is that of a being that remains itself while not remaining the same. That is why the descriptions of Hegelian Science have a dialectical character. The chain of equations is the appendix's anthropological core. The definition of freedom as "solidarity in independence and independence in solidarity" with the given is precise: freedom is neither indifference to the world nor determination by it, but negation of it.

Certainly it is not only the anthropology (set out in the *Phenomenology*) that is dialectical in content; Hegel's ontology and metaphysics (set out in the *Encyclopaedia*) are too. But to discover the dialectical character of being as such and of the real in general, it sufficed for Hegel to take seriously the notion of the concrete and to remember that philosophy must describe the concrete real instead of forming more or less arbitrary abstractions. For if man and his historical world exist really and concretely, on the same footing as the natural world, concrete reality and being itself, which actually is, imply, in addition to natural reality, a human reality and so negativity. That is to say, as we know, that being and the real are dialectical. Hegel insisted several times that philosophy must deal with concrete reality, notably in the second note to § 82 (vol. V, p. 106). Kojève translates: this (positive or speculative) rational, though it is a thought and abstract rational, is at the same time a concrete (*ein Konkretes*) ... Consequently philosophy has nothing whatever to do with pure abstractions or formal thoughts, but only with concrete thoughts. The argument that dialectic follows from taking the concrete seriously grounds the dialectic of total being in the presence of man within it.

Hegel does not merely say that his philosophy concerns concrete reality. He also affirms that the philosophy that preceded him, as well as vulgar sciences and "naive" man, all deal with abstractions. But the concrete real is dialectical; abstractions are not. That is why Hegelian Science alone reveals or describes the real dialectic. To understand this apparently paradoxical assertion, take a simple example. The claim that all other knowledge deals with abstractions prepares the table example.

Consider a real table. It is neither the table "in general" nor "any" table, but always this concrete table. But when "naive" man or the representative of any science speaks of this table, he isolates it from the rest of the universe: he speaks of this table without speaking of what is not it. But this table does not float in a void. It is on this floor, in this room, in this house, at this place on the earth, which earth is at a determinate distance from the sun, which has a determinate place in the galaxy, and so on. To speak of this table without speaking of the rest is therefore to abstract from this rest, which is in fact as real and concrete as the table itself. To speak of this table without speaking of the whole universe that implies it, as to speak of this universe without speaking of this table implied in it, is to speak of an abstraction and not of a concrete reality. And what is true with regard to space is true also with regard to time. This table has a determinate "history", not another, nor a past "in general". It was made at a given moment with this wood, taken at a given moment from this tree, which was born at a given moment from this seed, and so on. In short, what exists as a concrete reality is the spatio-temporal totality of the natural world: everything one isolates from it is by that very fact only an abstraction, which exists as isolated only in and through the thought of the man who thinks of it. The table example recalls the fourth lecture's table (p. 316) and the Jena table (p. 164). The extension of concreteness to the galaxy and the seed is Spinozist in spirit: only the whole is concrete.

All this is not new; Parmenides already saw it. But there is another aspect of the question that Parmenides and all pre-Hegelian philosophers forgot: that this table (and indeed every table) implies and presupposes the real and concrete something called labour performed. As soon as this table exists, to speak of the concrete real is therefore also to speak of labour. The concrete, total real implies human labour as much as it implies this table, the wood it is made of, and the natural world in general. And the concrete real that implies labour has precisely the trinitarian dialectical structure Hegelian Science describes. For the real labour implied in the real really transforms this real by actively negating it as given and preserving it as negated in the completed work, where the given appears in a "sublimated" or "mediated" form. That is to say, this concrete real is precisely the real dialectic or "dialectical movement" Hegel has in view. And if the naive, the vulgar scholar, or the pre-Hegelian philosopher can ignore this dialectic, it is precisely because they deal not with the concrete real but with abstractions. The table as implying labour is the decisive step: the concrete totality contains labour, so it contains negativity, so it is dialectical. Parmenides saw the totality but not the labour.

To introduce labour into the real is to introduce negativity, and so consciousness and the discourse that reveals the real. In fact this table is the table I am speaking of at this moment, and my words are as much part of this table as its four legs or the room around it. One can certainly abstract from these words and many other things, the so-called "secondary" qualities for example. But one must not forget in doing so that one is then dealing no longer with concrete reality but with an abstraction. The concrete real implies this table, all the sensations it has provoked, all the words spoken about it, and so on. And the abstract table is truly this table, a concrete reality, only in and through its inseparable union with these sensations, words, and so on, and in general with everything that really exists and has really existed. Once more, the concrete real is nothing but the spatio-temporal totality of the real, this totality implying, in addition to nature, the whole of real actions and discourses, history. The claim that "my words are as much part of this table as its four legs" is a striking formula for the inclusion of discourse in the concrete. The reference to secondary qualities targets Descartes and Locke: abstracting from them is legitimate only as abstraction.

In the course of history man speaks of the real and reveals it by the meaning of his discourses. The concrete real is therefore a real revealed by discourse; and that is what Hegel calls "Spirit" (*Geist*). Consequently, when he says (for example in the *Phenomenology*, Hoffmeister p. 24) that nature is only an abstraction and Spirit alone is real or concrete, he states nothing paradoxical. He simply says that the concrete real is the totality of the real from which nothing has been removed by abstraction, and that this totality, as it really exists, implies the something called history. To describe the concrete real is therefore also to describe its historical becoming; and this becoming is precisely what Hegel calls "dialectic" or "movement". To say the concrete real is Spirit is therefore to affirm the dialectical character of the real, to say that it is a real revealed by discourse, or Spirit. The deflationary reading of "nature is only an abstraction" is characteristic: Hegel's apparent idealism means only that nature without man is not the whole.

A long footnote then states Kojève's most explicit critique of Hegel. Hegel's reasoning is certainly correct: if the real totality implies man, and man is dialectical, the totality is dialectical too. «Mais, en partant de là, Hegel commet, à mon avis, une erreur grave» (but, starting from there, Hegel commits, in my view, a serious error) (p. 485). From the dialecticity of the real totality he concludes the dialecticity of its two fundamental constituents, nature and man (= history). In doing so he only follows the tradition of ontological monism going back to the Greeks: everything that is, is in one and the same way. The Greeks, who philosophically discovered nature, extended to man their "naturalist" ontology dominated by the sole category of identity. Hegel, who discovered (continuing the efforts of Descartes, Kant, and Fichte) the "dialectical" ontological categories of negativity and totality by analysing human being (man being understood in accordance with the pre-philosophical Judaeo-Christian tradition), extended his "anthropological" dialectical ontology to nature. But this extension is in no way justified, and it is not even discussed by Hegel. For if the ultimate foundation of nature is identical static given being (*Sein*), nothing in it is comparable to the negating action (*Tun*) that is the basis of specifically human or historical existence. The classical argument, everything that is, is in one and the same way, should not have obliged Hegel to apply one and the same ontology to man and nature, since he himself says in the *Phenomenology* that "man's true being is his action". But action (= negativity) acts otherwise than being (= identity) is. In any case there is an essential difference between nature, which is "revealed" only by man's discourse, by a reality other than itself, and man, who himself reveals the reality he is as well as the (natural) reality he is not. It therefore seems necessary to distinguish, within the dialectical ontology of revealed being or Spirit (dominated by totality), a non-dialectical ontology (of Greek and traditional inspiration) of nature (dominated by identity), and a dialectical ontology (of Hegelian inspiration, but modified accordingly) of man or history (dominated by negativity). The symmetry of the diagnosis is exact: the Greeks extended a natural ontology to man; Hegel extended a human ontology to nature. Both are monisms. The argument from "man's true being is his action" is Kojève's strongest internal objection: Hegel's own formula implies that man is in a different way from things.

Hegel's monist error, the footnote continues, has two grave consequences. On the one hand, basing himself on his single dialectical ontology, he tries to elaborate a dialectical metaphysics and phenomenology of nature, visibly unacceptable, which should according to him replace "vulgar" science (ancient, Newtonian, and so also ours). On the other hand, admitting the dialecticity of everything that exists, Hegel had to see in the circularity of knowledge the sole criterion of truth. But we have seen that the circularity of knowledge relating to man is possible only at the end of history, since as long as man changes radically, creating himself as other than he is, his description, even correct, is only a partial and quite provisional "truth". If then nature is creative or historical in the same way as man, truth and science properly speaking are possible only "at the end of times". Until then there is no true knowledge (*Wissen*), and one has only the choice between scepticism (relativism, historicism, nihilism, and so on) and faith (*Glauben*). The second consequence is decisive for the end-of-history thesis: Hegel needed the end of history for truth about nature only because he made nature historical. Under dualism, truth about nature is available at any time.

But if one admits that the traditional "identical" ontology really applies to nature, a truth relating to nature, and so a science of nature, are in principle possible at any moment of time. And since man is nothing but an active negation of nature, there is also a possible science of man, insofar as he belongs to the past and the present. Only man's future would then be doomed to scepticism or faith («c'est-à-dire à la certitude de l'espérance, pour parler avec saint Paul», that is, to the certainty of hope, to speak with Saint Paul) (p. 486): being a "dialectical" process, creative or free, history is essentially unforeseeable, unlike "identical" nature. The consequence is significant: under dualism, the science of man covers the past and present, while the future remains open, the object of hope (Hebrews 11:1, "faith is the substance of things hoped for"). This revises the end-of-history thesis from within: Kojève's dualism makes absolute knowledge of man possible without closing the future.

It seems moreover that an ontological dualism is indispensable to the explanation of the very phenomenon of history. History implies and presupposes an understanding of past generations by those of the present and future. But if nature changed in the same way as man, discourse would be incommunicable across time. If the stones and trees, as well as the bodies and animal "psyche" of men in Pericles's time, were as different from ours as the citizens of the ancient city are from us, we could understand neither a Greek treatise on agriculture or architecture, nor Thucydides's history, nor Plato's philosophy. In general, if we can understand any language not our own, it is only because it contains words relating to realities everywhere and always identical with themselves: if we can know that "*Hund*" and "*canis*" mean "dog", it is because there is the real dog, which is the same in Germany and France, in Rome in Caesar's time and in contemporary Paris. And these identical realities are precisely natural realities. The argument from translation is the footnote's most original: the possibility of understanding the past depends on the permanence of nature. History needs a non-historical ground. The dog, *Hund*, *canis*, returns from the eighth lecture (p. 373).

An image may show that the enterprise of a dualist ontology is not absurd. Take a gold ring. It has a hole, and this hole is as essential to the ring as the gold: without the gold, the "hole" (which moreover would not exist) would not be a ring; but without the hole, the gold (which would nonetheless exist) would not be a ring either. But if one has found atoms in the gold, it is in no way necessary to look for them in the hole. And nothing says that the gold and the hole *are* in one and the same way (of course it is a matter of the hole as "hole", not of the air "in the hole"). The hole is a nothingness that subsists (as the presence of an absence) only thanks to the gold around it. Likewise man, who is action, could be a nothingness that "nihilates" in being, thanks to the being he "negates". And nothing says that the ultimate principles of the description of the nihilating of nothingness (or of the annihilation of being) must be the same as those of the description of the being of being. The gold ring is Kojève's most famous image, cited in every account of his thought. It makes the dualism intuitive: the hole needs the gold, the gold does not need the hole, and they are not in the same way. The asymmetry, gold would exist without the hole, restates the twelfth lecture's realism: nature before and after man.

The first attempt (very insufficient, moreover) at a dualist ontology (or more exactly metaphysics), "identical" and "dialectical", was made by Kant, and in this lies his unparalleled greatness, comparable to Plato's, who laid down the principles of the (monist) "identical" ontology. Since Kant, Heidegger seems to be the first to have posed the problem of a double ontology. One does not have the impression that he went beyond the dualist phenomenology found in the first volume of *Sein und Zeit* (which is only an introduction to the ontology to be set out in volume II, not yet published). But this suffices to have him recognised as a great philosopher. As for dualist ontology itself, «elle semble être la tâche philosophique principale de l'avenir. Presque rien encore n'a été fait» (it seems to be the principal philosophical task of the future; almost nothing has yet been done) (p. 487). The ranking of Kant with Plato, and the recognition of Heidegger, place Kojève's project in the line of *Being and Time*'s distinction between *Dasein* and the *Vorhandene*. The final sentence states his own philosophical programme, which he pursued in the *Essai d'une histoire raisonnée de la philosophie païenne* and the unfinished *Concept, Temps et Discours*.

Like every true philosophy, Kojève returns to the main text, Hegel's Science develops on three superposed planes. It first describes the totality of real being as it "appears" (*erscheint*) or shows itself to the real man who is part of the real, who lives, acts, thinks, and speaks in it. This description takes place on the "phenomenological" plane: the *Phenomenology* is the "science of the appearances of Spirit", of the totality of real being revealing itself to itself through the discourse of the man this being implies (*Wissenschaft der Erscheinungen des Geistes* is the second title of the *Phenomenology*). But the philosopher is not content with this phenomenological description, which is philosophical because it concerns the concrete, the totality of the real, unlike "vulgar" descriptions relating to abstractions. He also asks what objective reality (*Wirklichkeit*), the real (natural and human) world, must be in order to "appear" as it in fact "appears" as "phenomenon". The answer is given by metaphysics, which Hegel calls philosophy of nature and philosophy of Spirit (*Geist* taken here in the sense of man). Finally, going beyond the metaphysical plane, the philosopher rises to the ontological plane, to answer the question of what being itself, taken as being, must be in order to be realised or exist as the natural and human world described in metaphysics, which appears in the way described in phenomenology. This description of the structure of being as such takes place in ontology, which Hegel calls Logic (and sets out before metaphysics but after phenomenology). A footnote adds: on the dualist hypothesis, ontology would describe separately being, which realises itself as nature, and action, which negates being and realises itself (in nature) as history. The three planes repeat the eighth lecture's division (p. 365). The footnote's dualist ontology, being and action described separately, is the programme in its simplest form.

Hegel described (in the *Phenomenology*) the dialectical character of "phenomenal" empirical existence (*Dasein*), and he can explain it only by supposing a dialectical structure of objective reality and of being as such. Consequently, if the method of Hegelian philosophy is that of simple description, its content is dialectical not only in "phenomenology" but also in "metaphysics" and "ontology". So far Kojève has spoken chiefly of the dialectic of being and the real described in the *Logic* and the *Encyclopaedia*. But he must also speak of the real dialectic of empirical existence, the "phenomena" or "appearances" (*Erscheinungen*) of dialectical being in its reality. For if, objectively speaking, this "phenomenal" dialectic is only the "appearance" of the "metaphysical" and "ontological" dialectics of the real and of being, it is, subjectively speaking, the only dialectical datum that can be described directly, and it is from it or its description that one can describe or reconstruct the other two "basic" dialectics. The priority of phenomenology "subjectively speaking" repeats the tenth lecture's thesis (p. 409): no ontology without prior phenomenology.

Before indicating what the "phenomenological" dialectic is in Hegel, described by the whole *Phenomenology*, Kojève must make a general remark. What is dialectical according to Hegel is the concrete real, totality or total synthesis, Spirit.
