In other words, it is not given being (*Sein*) itself that has a dialectical structure, but revealed being (*Begriff*). Revealed being implies, on the ontological plane, two moments: being as revealed (identity, thesis) and being as revealing (negativity, antithesis). Consequently, on the metaphysical plane, one must distinguish two worlds, inseparable but essentially different: the natural world and the historical or human world. Finally, the phenomenological plane is constituted by the reflection of natural empirical existence in human empirical existence (consciousness of the external, *Bewusstsein*), which is reflected in turn in itself (self-consciousness, *Selbstbewusstsein*). The mapping, identity/negativity, nature/history, consciousness/self-consciousness, aligns the three planes.

Hegel expressly says that negativity is the specifically dialectical moment. Identity has nothing dialectical, and if totality is dialectical, it is only because it implies negativity. Passing from the ontological to the metaphysical plane, one would therefore have to say that the real is dialectical only because the natural world implies a human world, nature not being dialectical at all in itself. As for "phenomena", one would have to say there is phenomenal dialectic because the real "appears" to man: only man's "phenomenal" existence is dialectical in itself, and natural "phenomena" are dialectical only insofar as they are implied in human "phenomenology" (as natural sciences, for example). The consequence of Hegel's own principle, negativity alone is dialectical, is Kojève's dualism.

In the *Phenomenology* Hegel seems to admit this way of seeing things. He repeatedly stresses the essential difference between man and animal, history and nature, always bringing out the dialectical character of the human and the non-dialectical character of the natural. So when he identifies (in Chapter VIII) nature with space and history (man) with time, this means for him that nature is dominated by identity alone, whereas history implies negativity and is therefore dialectical (compare Hoffmeister p. 145 and p. 563). The texts cited are the transition to Chapter IV (¶168–171) and the end of Chapter VIII (¶807).

But even in the *Phenomenology* Hegel's position lacks clarity. On the one hand he opposes specifically human existence (*Bewusstsein* or *Geist* in the sense of "man"), which is dialectical, to animal life (*Leben*), which is not. On the other hand he gives (in Chapter V, A, a) a vitalist "phenomenological" description of nature, presenting it as a dialectical "phenomenon". Certainly this is a description of nature by a certain type of "bourgeois" intellectual represented by Schelling, and Hegel does not entirely identify with Schelling, in that he sees in Schelling's *Naturphilosophie* only a phenomenological description, whereas Schelling believed he had made a metaphysics of nature. But Hegel believes that as a "phenomenon" nature is in fact as it "appears" to Schelling, and he would like to replace the vulgar natural sciences by Schellingian vitalism. And this vitalism takes on, under Hegel's pen, a clearly dialectical character. The ambiguity in the *Phenomenology* is located precisely: Chapter V, A, a's vitalism.

In the *Encyclopaedia* this way of seeing is affirmed without ambiguity. On the one hand Hegel sets out a metaphysics of nature in which nature is described as a frankly dialectical reality, with the same trinitarian structure as human reality described in the metaphysics of man or "Spirit". On the other hand, in the ontology itself, the *Logic*, Hegel takes practically no account of the fact that the total being or "Idea" (= *Geist*) he describes presents, on the one hand, a dialectical aspect, which transmits its dialectical character to the totality of being but which is itself action (*Tun*) and not being (*Sein*), and on the other a fundamentally non-dialectical aspect, which is static given being or natural being. The charge against the *Logic*, that it does not distinguish action from being within the Idea, is the ontological form of the critique.

«Tout ceci est à mon avis une erreur de Hegel» (all this is in my opinion an error of Hegel's) (p. 490). Of course Kojève cannot make here a critique of Hegelian philosophy that would be at all convincing. But he wants to point out that in his view the real (metaphysical) and "phenomenal" dialectic of nature exists only in Hegel's ("Schellingian") imagination. Under these conditions it would be difficult for him to summarise the dialectic of natural "phenomena" found in the *Phenomenology* (Chapter V, A, a), which he confesses he understands very badly. And he does not want to propagate this error of Hegel's, which can only harm his philosophical authority and could cast doubt on the value of dialectic in general and in particular on Hegel's description of the "phenomenal" dialectic of human existence. In his view, this description, contained in the *Phenomenology*, is Hegel's principal title to glory. So it is only of it that he will now speak, setting out the phenomenological transposition of the metaphysical and ontological dialectic. Certainly, to know what the phenomenological dialectic of human empirical existence is according to Hegel, one must read the whole *Phenomenology*, which is entirely devoted to its description. A footnote adds: the (dialectical) phenomenology of nature set out in Chapter V, A, a can be considered an element of the phenomenology of man: the description of the existence of the man who (under certain social and historical conditions) devotes himself entirely to the observation (*Beobachtung*) of nature and interprets it as a vitalist, in Schelling's manner. So understood, the description of Chapter V, A, a remains valid. But one finds in the *Phenomenology* some very short passages that bring out the true meaning of this dialectic and show how the three fundamental dialectical categories of ontology and metaphysics "appear" to man on the phenomenological plane as fundamental categories of the "anthropology" describing human empirical existence. These texts he now cites and interprets. The admission that he "understands very badly" Chapter V, A, a is candid. The decision not to "propagate the error" explains the anthropological selectivity of the whole book: it is a deliberate choice to protect what Kojève considers Hegel's real achievement. The footnote's rescue of Chapter V, A, a, as a description of the vitalist observer rather than of nature, is consistent with the 1935–36 reading (p. 83).

Hegel sets out the fundamental principles of his phenomenological anthropology by criticising Gall's phrenology, in fact every naturalist anthropology that assimilates man to the animal and sees no essential difference between them (Chapter V, A, c). To this static and monist conception of man he opposes his dialectical and "trinitarian" conception. Kojève translates (Hoffmeister p. 227): the (human) individual is in and for himself; he is for himself, that is, a free action (*Tun*); but he is also in himself, that is, he himself has an innate, specifically determined given being (*ursprüngliches bestimmtes Sein*) ... This given being, the body (*Leib*) of the specifically determined individuality, is its innateness (*Ursprünglichkeit*), its not-having-done-it (*Nichtgetanhaben*). But since at the same time the individual is only what he has done (*getan*), his body is also the expression (*Ausdruck*) of himself produced (*hervorgebrachte*) by him; it is at the same time a sign (*Zeichen*), which has not remained an immediate thing (*unmittelbare Sache*) but something through which the individual only makes known what he is, in the sense that he puts his innate nature to work (*ins Werk richtet*). The passage (¶310) defines the body as both given and made: innate and expressive.

To say that man is, exists, and "appears" (*erscheint*) as being and existing "in and for himself" is to say that he is being-in-and-for-himself, totality or synthesis; it is therefore to say that he is a dialectical (or "spiritual") entity, that his real and "phenomenal" existence is a "movement". A footnote adds: admitting that only human being is dialectical in the Hegelian sense, one can say that Hegel's dialectic is an *existential* dialectic in the modern sense of the word; that, in any case, is what the dialectic described in the *Phenomenology* is. But every dialectical totality is also, and above all, identity, being-in-itself or thesis. Ontologically speaking, this identity is *Sein*, given being; metaphysically, it is nature. In "appearing" man the aspect (*Seite*) or moment of identity, of *Sein* or nature, is his "body" (*Leib*) or his "innate nature" (*ursprüngliche Natur*) in general. By this aspect of his body man is a natural being with fixed characters, a "specifically determined" animal living within nature, having his "natural place" (*topos*) there. «Et on voit immédiatement que l'anthropologie dialectique ne laisse pas de place pour une "survie" de l'Homme hors du Monde naturel» (and one sees at once that dialectical anthropology leaves no room for a "survival" of man outside the natural world) (p. 491). Man is truly dialectical, human, only insofar as he is also nature, an "identical" spatial or material entity: he can become and be truly human only by being and remaining at the same time an animal, which, like every animal, annihilates itself in death. The footnote's description of Hegel's dialectic as "existential in the modern sense" places the *Phenomenology* beside Heidegger and Jaspers. The body as identity, the thesis of the human totality, grounds the denial of survival: since man's identity is his animal body, he dies with it. This is the bridge to Appendix II, on death.

In man, however, identity or the in-itself is not only his body in the proper sense: it is his "innateness" in general, his "not-having-done-it". It is first man's "innate nature", everything in him by biological heredity alone: his "character", "talents", "tastes", and so on. It is also the mere fact of being born a "slave" or "free" (*als Freier geboren*). For Hegel this so-called purely innate "freedom", like hereditary nobility and in general membership in a "class", is only a natural or animal character, which has nothing to do with true human freedom, actively acquired by fight or labour: a man is free only when he has made (*getan*) himself free. But this "identical" and "natural" not-having-done-it in man is also everything that penetrates him purely passively, everything he is and does "by habit" or "automatically", by tradition, by imitation, and so on, by mere "inertia". If, per impossibile, man ceased to negate the given and to negate himself as given or innate, to create the new and to create himself as "new man", contenting himself with maintaining himself in identity with himself and keeping the "place" he already occupies in the cosmos; in other words, if he ceased to live according to the future or "project" and let himself be dominated exclusively by the past or "memory", he would cease to be truly human; he would be an animal, "learned" perhaps and very "complicated", very different from all other natural beings, but not essentially "something else" than they; and so he would not be "dialectical". The extension of "identity" from body to habit, tradition, and imitation makes inertia the animal in man. The phrase "born free" (*als Freier geboren*) is Hegel's; Kojève's rejection of innate freedom anticipates the critique of heredity in the final State (p. 146).

A footnote, of great importance, glosses "per impossibile". According to Hegel, man always sooner or later negates the given as long as he has not realised the total synthesis that "appears" as his definitive satisfaction (*Befriedigung*). «Personnellement j'admets la possibilité d'un arrêt en cours de route» (personally I admit the possibility of a halt along the way) (p. 492). But he thinks that in that case man would in fact cease to be human. Hegel admits the final halt of the historical "movement": after the end of history man no longer negates properly speaking, actively. Yet man does not become an animal, since he continues to speak (negation passes into the Sage's "dialectical" thought). But post-historical man, omniscient, all-powerful, and satisfied man (the Sage), is not a man in the proper sense either: «c'est un "dieu" (il est vrai, un dieu mortel)» (he is a "god", a mortal god, it is true) (p. 492). Every education implies a long series of self-negations by the child: parents only incite him to negate certain aspects of his innate animal nature, but it is for him to do so. (It suffices that the puppy no longer does certain things; the child must also be ashamed to do them.) And it is only because of these self-negations ("repressions") that every "educated" child is not only a trained animal (identical with itself and in itself) but a truly human (or "complex") being, though in most cases only to a very small degree, "education" (self-negation) generally stopping too soon. The footnote, written in 1935, is the earliest version of the position Kojève takes in 1938–39: a halt in history short of its end is possible (p. 400), and post-historical man is no longer man but a "mortal god". The contrast between the trained puppy and the ashamed child is a fine illustration of self-negation: shame is the inner form of negation. The remark that education "generally stops too soon" is a mordant aside.

Man is "total", "synthetic", "dialectical"; he exists "for himself", consciously and speaking; he is therefore "spiritual" or truly human only insofar as he implies in his being, existence, and "appearance" the moment of negativity. Taken in itself, negativity is pure nothingness: it is not, does not exist, does not appear. It is only as the negation of identity, as difference. A footnote adds: Parmenides was right to say that being is and nothingness is not; but he forgot to add that there is a "difference" between nothingness and being, which in a certain measure *is* on the same footing as being, since without it, if there were no difference between being and nothingness, being itself would not be. Negativity can therefore exist only as a real negation of nature. But this existence of negativity is precisely specifically human existence, and one sees why man is reduced to nothing when he dies as an animal, when he is, so to speak, outside nature and can no longer really negate it. But as long as negativity exists as real negation of the identical natural given, it also appears, and its "appearance" is nothing other than man's "free action" (*freies Tun*), as Hegel says in the text cited. On the "phenomenal" (human) plane, negativity is therefore real freedom realising and manifesting or revealing itself as action. The footnote on Parmenides is one of Kojève's subtlest: the difference between being and nothing "is" in a sense, and is the ontological place of man. The explanation of death, man reduced to nothing when he can no longer negate nature, follows: negativity needs a body to negate through.

In the text cited, Hegel also says that "the individual is only what he has done". He will say a little further (Hoffmeister p. 236): the true being (*Sein*) of man is rather his deed (*Tat*); in it individuality is objectively real ... Individuality presents itself in action (*Handlung*) as the negative essence that is only insofar as it dialectically overcomes (*aufhebt*) given being. If given being (*Sein*) corresponds on the ontological plane to nature, it is the deed (*Tat*) that represents man as man on this plane. Man as man is not given being but creative action. If the "objective reality" of nature is its real existence, that of man properly speaking is his effective action. The animal only lives; but living man acts, and it is by his effective activity (*Handeln*) that he "manifests" his humanity and "appears" as a truly human being. Certainly man is also given being and nature: he exists also "in himself", as animals and things exist. But it is only in and through action that he is specifically human, and that he exists and appears as such, as being-for-himself or as a being conscious of himself and speaking of himself and of what he is not: "he is for himself, that is, he is a free action". And in acting he realises and manifests negativity or his difference from natural given being. The formula "the animal only lives; living man acts" is the cleanest statement of the distinction. The quotation (¶322) is the one Kojève cites throughout the book.

On the "phenomenological" plane, negativity is therefore nothing but human freedom, that by which man differs from the animal. A footnote cites Rousseau: "it is therefore not so much understanding that makes the specific distinction of man among the animals as his quality of free agent" (*Discourse on the Origin of Inequality*). But if freedom is ontologically negativity, it can be and exist only as negation. To be able to negate, there must be something to negate: an existing given and so an identical given being. That is why man can exist freely, humanly, only by living as an animal in a given natural world; but he lives in it humanly only insofar as he negates this natural or animal given. And negation is realised as action performed, not as thought or mere desire. It is therefore neither in his more or less "elevated" "ideas" (or imagination) nor by his more or less "sublime" or "sublimated" "aspirations" that man is truly free or really human, but only in and through the effective, active negation of the given real. «La liberté ne consiste pas dans un choix entre deux données : elle est la négation du donné» (freedom does not consist in a choice between two givens: it is the negation of the given) (p. 494), both of the given one is oneself (as animal or as "incarnate tradition") and of the given one is not (the natural and social world). Moreover, these two negations are in reality only one. To negate the natural or social world dialectically, negating it while preserving it, is to transform it; and then one must either change oneself to adapt to it or perish. Conversely, to negate oneself while maintaining oneself in existence is to change the aspect of the world, since the world then implies a modified constituent. So man exists humanly only insofar as he really transforms his natural and social world by his negating action and changes himself according to this transformation; or, what is the same, insofar as he transforms the world following an active self-negation of his animal or social "innate nature". The definition of freedom as negation rather than choice is one of Kojève's most important theses. It rejects liberum arbitrium, choosing between given options, in favour of the creation of what was not given. The Rousseau citation places the thesis in the line of the *Second Discourse*, where free agency, not understanding, defines man.

Freedom realising and manifesting itself as dialectical or negating action is thereby essentially a creation. To negate the given without ending in nothingness is to produce something that did not yet exist, which is precisely what one calls "creating". Conversely, one can truly create only by negating the given real. For this real is, as it were, omnipresent and dense in itself, since there is nothing (nothing but nothingness) outside it or other than it; there is, so to speak, no room for the new in the world; emerging from nothingness, the new can penetrate being and exist only by taking the place of given being, by negating it. The image of a dense, full being with no room for novelty, so that the new must displace the given, recalls the 1937–38 theory of sacrifice (p. 245): the new takes the place of the old.

In the dialectical interpretation of man, of freedom or action, the terms "negation" and "creation" must be taken in the strong sense. It is not a matter of replacing one given by another, but of suppressing the given for the sake of what is not (yet), thus realising what has never been given. That is to say, man does not change himself and transform the world in order to realise conformity with a given "ideal" (imposed by God or simply "innate"). He creates and creates himself because he negates and negates himself "without preconceived idea": he becomes other only because he no longer wants to be the same. And it is only because he no longer wants to be what he is that what he will or can be is for him an "ideal", which "justifies" his negating or creative action, his change, by giving it a "meaning". In general, negation, freedom, and action do not arise from thought, nor from consciousness of self and of the external; it is these, on the contrary, that arise from negativity realising itself and "revealing" itself (by thought in consciousness) as effective free action. The thesis that the ideal follows the negation, not the reverse, is radical: man does not negate in order to realise an ideal; the ideal is the meaning he gives to his negation after it has begun. This is the anthropological counterpart of the thesis that the concept follows labour.

In sum, negativity (or freedom) realising and manifesting itself as creative action is man who, living in the natural world, remains himself while not always (or "necessarily") being the same. One can therefore say that dialectical anthropology is the philosophical science of man as he appears in the (pre-philosophical) Judaeo-Christian conception, of man who is supposed to be able to convert in the strong sense, to become essentially and radically other. According to this conception, man created perfect can nonetheless radically pervert this innate or given nature; but essentially perverted man can re-negate the "old Adam", thus becoming the "new Adam", other than the first but still more perfect than him; man can "overcome" his hereditary sin, which nonetheless determines his nature, and so become a saint, who is nonetheless something other than man before the fall; a pagan whose "natural place" is hell can "convert" to Christianity and so gain heaven; and so on. In the Hegelian or dialectical conception of man it is exactly the same: the stages of the dialectic described in the *Phenomenology* are nothing but a series of successive "conversions" that man carries out in the course of history and that are described by the Sage who lives at its end and who also "converts" to absolute truth (incarnated in the Napoleonic Empire). The reading of the *Phenomenology* as a series of conversions secularises Augustinian anthropology. The Sage's own "conversion to absolute truth" is a striking phrase: wisdom is the last conversion.

In agreement with Aristotle, Hegel admits a radical difference between Master and Slave. According to him, man can appear in nature or create himself as man from the animal he was only if a fight to the death for recognition (*Anerkennen*) ends in a relation between a free man and a man enslaved to him. From the start man is therefore necessarily either Master or Slave; and that is what Aristotle said. But according to Aristotle (who did not see the dialecticity of human existence) it will always be so: man is born with a servile or free "nature" and can never suppress or modify it; Masters and Slaves are like two distinct, irreducible, "eternal" animal "species", neither of which can leave its "natural place" in the immutable cosmos. According to Hegel, by contrast, the radical difference between Master and Slave exists only at the beginning and can be suppressed over time. For him mastery and servitude are not given or innate characters. At least at the beginning, man is not born slave or free but creates himself as one or the other by free or voluntary action. The Master is the one who went to the end in the fight, ready to die if not recognised, while the Slave feared death and submitted voluntarily, recognising the Master without being recognised by him. But it is one and the same innate animal nature that was transformed by the free action of the fight into servile or free human "nature": the Master could have created himself as Slave, and the Slave as Master. There was no "reason" for one of the two animals (of the species *Homo sapiens*) to become Master rather than Slave. Mastery and servitude have no "cause"; they are "determined" by no given; they cannot be "deduced" or foreseen from the past that preceded them: they result from a free act (*Tat*). That is why man can "overcome" his servile "nature" and become free, create himself (freely) as free; even born into servitude, he can negate his innate servile "nature". And the whole of history, the whole "movement" of human existence in the natural world, is nothing but the progressive negation of servitude by the Slave, the series of his successive "conversions" to freedom (which will not, however, be the Master's "identical" or "thetic" freedom, free only in itself, but the "total" or "synthetic" freedom, existing also for itself, of the citizen of the universal and homogeneous State). The contrast with Aristotle (*Politics* I) is the clearest in the book: Aristotle described the first moment of history and took it for eternal. The insistence that there was "no reason" for one to become Master restates the Introduction's "irreducible acts of freedom" (p. 15).

A footnote adds: in truth, only the Slave "overcomes" his "nature" and finally becomes citizen. The Master does not change: he dies rather than cease to be Master. The final fight, which transforms the Slave into citizen, suppresses mastery non-dialectically: the Master is simply killed and dies as Master. It is therefore only in its servile aspect that human existence is dialectical or "total": «le Maître ne représente, au fond, que l'Identité (il est vrai : humaine)» (the Master represents, at bottom, only identity, human identity it is true) (p. 497). One can therefore say Aristotle correctly described the Master. He was only mistaken in believing the Master to be man in general, in denying the humanity of the Slave. He was right to say the Slave as Slave is not truly human; but he was wrong to believe he could not become so. The footnote's thesis, the Master is human identity, completes the mapping: Master = thesis, Slave = antithesis, citizen = synthesis. It also makes Aristotle the correct philosopher of mastery, which is a generous historicist reading.

If negativity is freedom realising itself as action negating the given, and if it is man's very humanity, negativity and man can "appear" for the first time in nature only as a being that negates or "overcomes" its innate animal nature: man creates his humanity only by negating himself as animal. That is why the first "appearance" of negativity is described in the *Phenomenology* (Chapter IV) as a fight to the death for recognition, or more exactly as the risk of life (*Wagen des Lebens*) this fight implies. The desire for recognition that provokes the fight is the desire for a desire, for something that does not really exist (desire being the "manifest" presence of the absence of a reality): to want to be "recognised" is to want to be accepted as a positive "value", precisely to make oneself "desired". To want to risk one's life, which is the whole reality of the living being, for something that does not and cannot exist as inert or merely living real things exist, is therefore indeed to negate the given one is oneself, to be free or independent of it. And to negate oneself thus in the strong sense, and nonetheless maintain oneself in existence, is indeed to create oneself as new and so to exist as created by oneself, as free or autonomous. The *Wagen des Lebens*, the risking of life, is Hegel's phrase in ¶187. The definition of recognition as "making oneself desired" restates the Introduction (p. 14).

It is the risk of life, of the life that integrates for the living the totality of the given (and is also the supreme natural or biological "value"), incurred in a fight for pure prestige, absolutely without any biological "reason for being" or "vital interest", that is the negating, creative, or free action that realises and "manifests" negativity or freedom, and so man. Man realises (= creates) and "manifests" his humanity (= freedom) by risking his life, or at least by being able and willing to risk it, solely "for glory" or by virtue of his sole "vanity" (which by this risk ceases to be "vain" or "nonexistent" and becomes the specifically human value of honour, as real as animal "values" but essentially different from them); or, what is the same, by risking his life by virtue of "duty" alone (which is *ought-to-be* precisely because it is not given being, and which therefore exists only as recognised, this recognition presupposing and implying, even demanding, the risk of life). The triad vanity, honour, duty returns from 1936–37 (glory, vanity, dignity, p. 123). Vanity becomes honour by risk: the value is real because someone died for it.

A footnote analyses duty. One acts only by virtue of a duty one recognises. But the duty one recognises oneself is always supposed to have to be recognised by others, who must by definition also recognise the value of the one who acts according to this duty. To want to act by virtue of duty is therefore in fact to want to be "recognised". But one may not realise it; one may think of duty without thinking of "recognition". Often the being supposed to "recognise" the one who acts "out of duty" is God. So one may believe in acting that one wants to be "recognised" by God alone. «Mais en fait "Dieu" n'est que le "milieu social" substantialisé et projeté dans l'au-delà» (but in fact "God" is only the "social milieu" substantialised and projected into the beyond) (p. 498). It sometimes seems one does one's duty only so as not to fall in one's own eyes; but this too is an illusion. In this case there is a doubling of individuality into its two components: the one who acts represents the agent's particularity; the one who judges him "morally" represents his universality, the social aspect of his existence; man judges his own "particular" actions by the "universal" values admitted by the society he belongs to. Certainly one may not recognise "admitted" values. But if one takes one's "nonconformism" seriously, realising it by action, one transforms or wants to transform the given society precisely so as to make it admit the values in whose name one acts. Here again one acts in fact by virtue of the desire for "recognition", but one does not always realise it. The footnote reduces duty to the desire for recognition through three steps: duty implies others' recognition; God is society projected; conscience is society internalised. The Durkheimian formula of p. 72 returns. The analysis of conscience as the universal side of the individual judging the particular side is a sociological reading of Kant's moral law.

No animal can commit suicide out of mere shame or pure vanity (as Kirilov wanted in Dostoevsky's *Demons*); no animal risks its life to take or retake a flag, to win stripes, or to be decorated; animals never wage bloody fights for pure prestige, whose only reward is the resulting glory, and which can be explained neither by the instinct of preservation (defence of life or search for food) nor by that of reproduction; never has an animal fought a duel to wash away an affront that harmed none of its vital interests, just as no female has died "defending her honour" against a male. It is therefore by negating acts of this kind that man realises and manifests his freedom, the humanity that distinguishes him from the animal. The catalogue of uniquely human acts, suicide from shame, the flag, the decoration, the duel, the defence of honour, makes the theory concrete. Kirilov returns from 1934–35 (p. 65).

But fight and risk are not the only "appearance" of negativity or freedom, of humanity, in the natural world. Labour is another. No animal works, properly speaking, since it never transforms the world it lives in according to "projects" not explicable by the given conditions of its real existence in this world. A land animal never builds devices allowing it to live in an element other than its natural one: underwater, for example, or in the air. Man has built by his labour the submarine and the aeroplane. In fact labour essentially transforms the given natural world and dislodges the worker from his "natural place" in this world, so essentially changing himself, only insofar as the action in question is truly negating, insofar as it does not follow from any "instinct" or given or innate tendency but negates a hereditary instinct and suppresses the innate "nature", which then "manifests" itself by opposing it as "laziness". «L'animal en liberté n'est jamais paresseux» (the animal in freedom is never lazy) (p. 499), since it would die of hunger if it were, or would not propagate. Man can be lazy only at work, precisely because work properly speaking corresponds to no vital necessity. The thesis that laziness is the resistance of nature to labour is one of Kojève's most original: only a being whose work negates instinct can be lazy. The submarine and aeroplane, devices for living in a foreign element, are the emblems of labour as leaving one's natural place.

Being a realisation and "manifestation" of negativity, labour is always "forced" labour: man must force himself to work; he must do violence to his "nature". And at least at the beginning, it is another who forces him and so does him violence. In the Bible it is God who imposes labour on fallen man (but this is only a "necessary" consequence of the fall, which was "free"; here too labour is the consequence of a free act, the manifestation of the negating action by which man negated his innate "perfect" nature). In Hegel labour "appears" for the first time in nature as the servile labour imposed by the first Master on his first Slave (who moreover submitted voluntarily, since he could have escaped servitude and labour by accepting death in combat or killing himself after his defeat). The Master makes the Slave work to satisfy by his labour his own desires, which as such are "natural" or animal desires (in satisfying them the Master differs from the animal only in satisfying them without effort, the necessary effort having been supplied by the Slave; so, unlike the animal, the Master can live as a "pleasure-seeker"). But to satisfy the Master's desires the Slave had to repress his own instincts (preparing food he will not eat though he wants to, and so on); he had to do violence to his "nature", to negate or "overcome" himself as given, as animal. Consequently, being a self-negating act, labour is a self-creating act: it realises and manifests freedom, autonomy with regard to the given in general and to the given one is oneself; it creates and manifests the worker's humanity. In and through labour man negates himself as animal, just as in and through the fight. That is why the working Slave can essentially transform the natural world he lives in, creating in it a specifically human world of technique. He works according to a "project" that does not necessarily result from his own innate "nature"; he realises by labour something that does not (yet) exist in him, which is why he can create things that exist nowhere else than in the world produced by his labour: works of craft or works of art, things nature never produces. The parallel with Genesis 3 is precise: labour as the consequence of a free act (the fall). The parenthesis that the Slave "submitted voluntarily", since he could have died or killed himself, makes servitude a choice, which grounds the Slave's capacity to unchoose it.

The "manufactured objects" created by the working Slave's active self-negations insert themselves into the natural world and so really transform it. To maintain himself in the reality of this transformed (= humanised) world, the Slave must change himself. But since it is he who transformed the given world by working in it, the change he seems to undergo by counterblow is in fact a self-creation: it is he who changes himself, who creates himself other than he was given to himself. That is why labour can raise him from servitude to freedom (which will however be other than that of the idle Master). The argument that adaptation to a world one has made is self-creation is the core of the theory of labour.

So, despite appearances, the Slave works (also) for himself. Certainly the Master profits from his labour. Having negated his animal nature by the risk accepted in the fight for recognition, the Master has realised his humanity; unlike the animal, he can therefore assimilate, as man does, the specifically human products of the Slave's labour, though he did not "order" them: he can use works of craft and enjoy works of art, though at first he did not "desire" them. That is why he too changes according to the modifications the Slave's labour brings to the given world. But not working himself, it is not he who produces these changes outside him and so in himself. The Master evolves because he consumes the products of the Slave's labour. But the Slave supplies him with more and other than he desired and ordered, and he consumes this surplus (truly human, not "natural") involuntarily and as if under constraint: he undergoes a kind of training (or education) by the Slave, if he must do violence to his nature to consume what the Slave offers him. «Il subit donc l'Histoire, mais ne la crée pas» (he therefore undergoes history but does not create it) (p. 500): if he "evolves", he evolves only passively, as nature or an animal species evolves. The Slave, by contrast, evolves humanly, voluntarily and consciously, actively or freely (negating himself knowingly). Negating his own given nature by labour, he rises above it and is in (negating) relation with it: that is to say, he becomes conscious of himself, and thereby of what is not himself. The entities he creates by labour, which therefore have no natural reality, are reflected in him as ideal entities, as "ideas", which appear to him as "models" or "projects" of the works he executes. The Master educated by the Slave's products is a striking reversal: the Slave trains the Master's taste. The Master undergoes history passively, like a species, which makes him the human analogue of nature.

A footnote on the origin of ideas: the idea (*Gedanke*) arises from desire, from the not yet realised negation of the given; only the effective action of labour realises this negation. One can therefore say labour is carried out according to a preconceived idea or project: the real is transformed according to the ideal. But the idea is *a priori* only in relation to the effective and completed labour, not in relation to the man who works: it is not an "innate" or "Platonic" idea. Man creates the idea by ideally creating the given (natural or social), and realises it by inserting it effectively into the given through the labour that really transforms this given according to the idea. The evolution of means of transport, for example, did not take place according to the "idea" or "ideal" of the automobile, given in advance and approached by successive efforts. Man began by having himself carried by other men or animals only because he no longer wanted to walk "naturally", on foot. And it is by successively negating the various means of transport first given to him that he finally produced the automobile, which is a true creation not only as material object but also as "idea", which did not "pre-exist from all eternity" in man or elsewhere. The automobile example is one of Kojève's best: technical history proceeds by negating the given, not by approaching an ideal. It is the technological form of the thesis that the ideal follows the negation.

The man who works thinks what he works on and speaks of it (as he thinks and speaks of nature as the "raw material" of his works); and only by thinking and speaking can man truly work. So the working Slave is conscious of what he does and has done: he understands the world he has transformed and realises the need to change himself to adapt to it; he therefore wants to "keep up with the progress" he himself realises and reveals by his discourse. A footnote of great interest follows. If truly self-conscious, the man who has created a technical world knows he can live in it only by living (also) as a worker. That is why man may want to go on working even after ceasing to be a Slave: he can become a free worker. In fact labour arose from the desire for recognition (through the intermediary of the fight), and it maintains itself and evolves according to this same desire. To realise technical progress, humanity must work more or better, supply an extra effort "against nature". There have certainly always been men who knew they worked "for glory". (The mere desire to know the given leads to its scientific "observation", but not to its transformation by labour; not even to "experimental" intervention, as the example of the Greeks shows.) But most people believe they work more to earn more money or to increase their "well-being". Yet it is easy to see that the surplus earned is absorbed by expenditures of pure prestige, and that the so-called "well-being" consists chiefly in living better than one's neighbour or no worse than others. So surplus labour, and so technical progress, are in reality a function of the desire for "recognition". Certainly the "poor" profit from technical progress; but it is not they, nor their needs or desires, that create it. Progress is realised, begun, and stimulated by the "rich" or the "powerful" (even in the socialist State). And these are "materially" satisfied. They act only by virtue of the desire to increase their "prestige" or power, or, if one likes, by duty; duty being quite other than love of neighbour or "charity", which has never engendered technical progress nor, consequently, really suppressed poverty, precisely because it is not a negating action but the instinctive outpouring of an innate "charitable nature", perfectly compatible in fact with the "imperfections" of the given world that nonetheless make it "suffer" (which is why Kant refused to see a "virtue", a specifically human manifestation, in an action resulting from an "instinctive inclination", a *Neigung*). The footnote's economic theory is striking: technical progress is driven by the desire for prestige of the rich and powerful, not by the needs of the poor, "even in the socialist State". The analysis of consumption as positional, living better than one's neighbour, anticipates Veblen's conspicuous consumption, which it resembles, and later sociologies of distinction. The remark on the Greeks, who observed without experimenting because they did not work, restates the genealogy of science from labour. The rejection of charity as non-negating, and the appeal to Kant's refusal to call *Neigung* virtue, repeat the 1937–38 critique of charity (p. 260).

It is therefore labour that is the authentic "appearance" of negativity or freedom, since it is labour that makes man a dialectical being, who does not remain eternally the same but constantly becomes other than he really is in the given and as given. The fight, and the Master who embodies it, are so to speak only the catalysts of history or of the dialectical "movement" of human existence: they engender this movement but are not themselves affected by it. All (true) Masters are equal as Masters, and none has himself "overcome" (insofar as he is Master) his Master's nature to become something other than he is (since he could only have become a Slave); if the Masters have evolved, their evolution has been only external or "material", not truly human, willed; and the human content of the fight, the risk of life, has not changed over the ages, despite the fact that more or less servile workers have supplied the combatants with ever new types of weapons. Only the Slave can want to cease to be what he is (a Slave), and if he "overcomes" himself by labour, which can vary indefinitely, he becomes ever other, until he becomes truly free, fully satisfied by what he is. One can therefore say that negativity "manifests" itself as fight only in order to be able to "appear" as labour (which otherwise could not have been engendered). The catalyst of the Introduction (p. 30) and the axe and machine gun (p. 177) return. "Negativity manifests itself as fight only in order to appear as labour" gives the fight a teleological subordination to labour.

Certainly, at the end, to free himself definitively or become truly other, the Slave or former working Slave must resume the fight for prestige against the Master or former Master: there will always be a remnant of servitude in the worker as long as there is on earth a remnant of idle mastery. But this last transformation or "conversion" of man takes the form of a fight to the death only because the idle Master is uneducable, the peaceful transforming education (*Bildung*) of man taking place only through labour. The Slave is obliged to suppress mastery by a non-dialectical suppression of the Master who persists in his (human) identity with himself, by his annulment or putting to death. And it is this annulment that manifests itself in and through the final fight for recognition, necessarily implying the risk of life on the part of the freed Slave. It is this risk, moreover, that completes his liberation begun by labour, introducing into him the moment of mastery he lacked. It is in and through the final fight, in which the former working Slave acts by fighting for glory alone, that the free citizen of the universal and homogeneous State is created, who, being at once Master and Slave, is no longer either but the unique "synthetic" or "total" man, in whom the thesis of mastery and the antithesis of servitude are dialectically "overcome", annulled in what is one-sided or imperfect in them, preserved in what is essential or truly human, and so sublimated in their essence and being. The phrase "the idle Master is uneducable" justifies the violence of the final fight: the Master cannot be transformed by *Bildung*, only killed. This is Kojève's theory of revolutionary violence in its starkest form, written in 1935.

To say that man is dialectical and "appears" as such is therefore to say that he is a being that remains itself without remaining the same, because by fight and labour he negates himself as given, either as animal or as man born in a certain social or historical milieu and determined by it, but also maintains himself in existence, or, if one likes, in human identity with himself, despite these self-negations. That is to say, man is neither identity nor negativity alone, but totality or synthesis; he "overcomes" himself while preserving and sublimating himself; he "mediates" himself in and through his very existence. And to say so is to say that he is an essentially historical being. The formula "remains itself without remaining the same" is the anthropological definition of the dialectical being.

If identity or being-in-itself "manifests" itself in man as his animality in the broad sense, everything in him that is given, innate, or inherited; if negativity or being-for-itself "appears" in the world as human freedom, realised as the negating action of fight and labour; totality or being-in-and-for-itself "reveals" itself on the human "phenomenal" plane as historicity. Man who fights and works, thus negating himself as animal, is an essentially historical being, and he alone is: nature and the animal have no history properly speaking (a footnote: in the *Phenomenology* Hegel opposes history to nature, Hoffmeister p. 563). The triad animality, freedom, historicity is the phenomenological form of identity, negativity, totality.

For there to be history there must be not only a given reality but also a negation of this reality and at the same time a ("sublimated") preservation of what has been negated. Only then is evolution creative, with true continuity and real progress; and that is precisely what distinguishes human history from mere biological or "natural" evolution. But to preserve oneself as negated is to remember what one has been while having become radically other. It is by historical memory that man's identity maintains itself through history, despite the self-negations carried out in it, so that he can realise himself through it as the integration of his contradictory past, as totality or dialectical entity. History is therefore always a conscious and willed tradition, and every real history also manifests itself as a historiography: there is no history without conscious and lived historical memory. The thesis that history requires historiography, that there is no history without memory of it, repeats the twelfth lecture's footnote (p. 441). It makes tradition the synthesis of history.

It is by memory (*Er-innerung*) that man "internalises" his past, making it truly his own, preserving it in himself, and inserting it really into his present existence, which is at the same time a radical active and effective negation of this preserved past. It is thanks to memory that the man who "converts" can remain "the same" man, whereas an animal species that converts by "mutation" into another has nothing more to do with the one it came from. And it is memory that concretises man's self-negation, making this negation a new reality. For in remembering the given he was and has negated, man remains "specifically determined" (*bestimmt*) by the concrete characters of this given, while being free with regard to it because he has negated it. Only so does man become specifically other by his self-negation and preserve himself as real and so concrete: another man in a new world, but always a man with specific and specifically human characters, living in a human world that is always a specifically organised historical world. It is therefore by history created, lived, and really remembered as "tradition" that man realises himself or "appears" as dialectical totality, instead of annihilating himself and "disappearing" by a "pure" or "abstract" negation of every given whatever, real and thought. The contrast between conversion with memory and mutation without it is precise: memory is what makes self-negation a history rather than a replacement.

A footnote draws the political consequence. It is in the lack of historical memory (or understanding) that lies the mortal danger of nihilism or scepticism, which would negate everything without preserving anything, even as memory. A society that spends its time listening to the radically "nonconformist" intellectual, who amuses himself by negating (verbally!) any given whatever (even the "sublimated" given preserved in historical memory) solely because it is a given, ends by sinking into inactive anarchy and disappearing. Likewise «le Révolutionnaire qui rêve d'une "révolution permanente" niant toute espèce de tradition et ne tenant pas compte du passé concret, sinon pour le supprimer, aboutit nécessairement, soit au néant de l'anarchie sociale, soit à sa propre annulation, physique ou politique» (the revolutionary who dreams of a "permanent revolution" negating every kind of tradition and taking no account of the concrete past except to suppress it necessarily ends either in the nothingness of social anarchy or in his own annulment, physical or political) (p. 504). Only the revolutionary who manages to maintain or re-establish historical tradition, preserving in positive memory the given present he himself relegated to the past by his negation, succeeds in creating a new historical world capable of existing. The footnote's target is hard to miss in 1935: "permanent revolution" is Trotsky's formula, and the revolutionary who ends in "his own annulment, physical or political" fits Trotsky, exiled in 1929; the revolutionary who "re-establishes tradition" is commonly read as Stalin. Kojève's political sympathies are perhaps clearer here than anywhere else in the book. The critique of the nonconformist intellectual returns from 1935–36 (p. 87).

The total or dialectical, real or concrete man is therefore not only negating action: he is a completed creative action, a work (*Werk*), in which the negated given is preserved, as raw material is preserved in the finished product. That is why Hegel said at the end of the passage cited that man exists humanly only insofar as "he puts his innate nature to work (*ins Werk richtet*)". Man "has not remained an immediate thing (*unmittelbare Sache*)", Hegel says, because he "is only what he has done (*getan*)", because he acted by negating himself as given. But he is a concrete reality that "appears" or "makes itself known (*erkennen lässt*)" by a "sign (*Zeichen*)", because he is a work (*Werk*) produced with the given, in which the negated has therefore been preserved. And this preservation of the negated in man takes place in and through the memory of the very one who negated it. That is why man is a dialectical human reality only insofar as he is historical, which he is only by remembering his surpassed past. The return to the phrenology passage closes the analysis: man is a work, and his body is the sign of what he has made of his nature.

In short, to describe man as a dialectical entity is to describe him as a negating action that negates the given within which it was born, and as a work created by this very negation, from the given that has been negated. On the "phenomenological" plane this means that human existence "appears" in the world as a continuous series of fights and labours integrated by memory, as the history in the course of which man freely creates himself. "A continuous series of fights and labours integrated by memory" is the shortest definition of history in the book.

Hegelian dialectic therefore accounts philosophically for two fundamental categories implied in the pre-philosophical Judaeo-Christian anthropology that, in being secularised, became modern anthropology: freedom and historicity. It also lets one understand why these two categories are in fact inseparable. There is history, creative or unforeseeable evolution, only where there are free agents; and freedom is realised only by the creation of a specifically human, historical world. Dialectic shows that negativity (= freedom) differs from nothingness only insofar as it is inserted in totality (= historical synthesis, in which the future is incorporated into the present through the past), and that the real is totality, instead of pure identity, only insofar as it implies its own negation, which frees it precisely from itself taken as given. History is what it is, totality or synthesis, creative evolution or progress, and not a pure and simple tautology or an "eternal return", because it is the unity of essentially different constituents, created by negation of the elements preceding them, and so independent of them, or free. The structure "future incorporated into the present through the past" is the eighth lecture's time (p. 368), stated here in 1935. The rejection of eternal return, Nietzsche's and Aristotle's, follows.

But Judaeo-Christian and modern anthropology implies (more or less explicitly) a third fundamental category, inseparable from the other two: individuality. The man of this anthropology is a free historical individual. And Hegel's philosophical anthropology accepts this conception of man; in the texts cited it was always a question of the individual, of human individuality. Unlike an animal, a plant, or an inanimate thing, a human being is not merely an "exemplar" or any representative of a natural "species", interchangeable with the other representatives. (Hegel often insists that in French the expression "*une espèce de*", applied to a man, has a pejorative sense.) A man is supposed to be "unique of his kind", differing essentially from all other men; and at the same time he is supposed to have, in his irreplaceable uniqueness, a positive value more absolute or more universal than that of a "species" as such. A footnote adds: for example, one sees no harm in killing or destroying any representative of an animal or plant species; but the extermination of a whole species is practically considered a crime. This universal value attributed to something absolutely unique is precisely what characterises individuality, being attributed only to it. The footnote's observation about extermination of species is a fine illustration of the reverse relation: for animals the species has value and the individual none; for men the individual has the value a species has.

In Hegel's terminology the individuality that characterises human existence is a synthesis of particular and universal. Insofar as this existence "manifests" itself on the "phenomenal" plane, individuality "appears" as the active realisation of the specifically human desire for recognition (*Anerkennen*). According to Hegel, man is truly human (free and historical) only insofar as he is recognised as such by others (in the limit by all others), and recognises them himself in return (since one can be truly "recognised" only by one whom one "recognises" oneself). One can say it is social recognition that distinguishes man, as spiritual entity, from the animal and from everything that is only nature. And it is in and through the universal recognition of human particularity that individuality is realised and manifested. Hegel said this very clearly at Jena in 1805–06 (vol. XX, p. 206). Kojève translates: in the act of recognising (*Anerkennen*) the personal I ceases to be this isolated particular (*Einzelne*); it exists juridically (universally, as absolute value) in recognition; that is, it is no longer in its immediate (natural) empirical existence (*Dasein*) ... Man is necessarily recognised and necessarily recognising. This necessity is his own, not that of our thought as opposed to the content. As act of recognising, man is himself the (dialectical) movement, and it is precisely this movement that dialectically overcomes (*hebt auf*) his state of nature: he is (the) act of recognising; the natural entity only is; it is not a spiritual entity (*Geistiges*). The Jena text, "*der Mensch ist Anerkennen*", is the source of Kojève's whole theory: man *is* recognition. Its phrase "the natural only is" restates the distinction between being and action.

Every man insofar as he is human (or "spiritual") would want, on the one hand, to differ from all others and be "unique in the world". A footnote illustrates: Napoleon was deeply vexed and saddened when his Malay gardener took him for a legendary conqueror of the Far East. A society woman is vexed and saddened when she sees on a friend the dress sold to her as "unique of its kind". In general, no one wants to be that "average man" one often speaks of, but always as someone other than oneself. But on the other hand he would want to be recognised, in his very unique particularity, as a positive value, and this by the greatest number, if possible by all. That is to say, in Hegel's terminology, that truly human man, radically different from the animal, always seeks recognition and realises himself only as actually recognised. This means he (actively) desires individuality and can be real only by realising himself (actively) through recognition as individual. The footnote's examples are among Kojève's wittiest: Napoleon mistaken for another conqueror, and the "unique" dress worn by a friend. Both show that the desire for recognition is the desire to be recognised as unique, not as a type. The "average man" no one wants to be is the statistical abstraction that individuality refuses.

Man can therefore be truly human only by living in society. And society (and belonging to a society) is real only in and through the effective interaction of its members, which interaction "manifests" itself among other things as political existence or State. Man is therefore truly human, "individual", only insofar as he lives and acts as a "recognised" citizen of a State (compare vol. VII, p. 475). But at the moment of its appearance, and throughout its historical evolution, the State does not fully satisfy the human desire for recognition and so does not perfectly realise man as individual. For in the real historical conditions of his existence, a man is never only "this particular", recognised by the State as citizen in his unique and irreplaceable particularity. He is always also an interchangeable "representative" of a kind of human "species": of a family, a social class, a nation or race, and so on. And it is only as such a "representative", or as "specific particularity" (*Besonderheit*), that he is universally recognised, being recognised by the State as citizen enjoying all political rights and as "legal person" of civil law. Man is therefore not truly individual, and that is why he is not fully satisfied (*befriedigt*) by his social and political existence. That is also why he actively and freely (by negation) transforms the given social and political reality. The analysis of recognition as always mediated by *Besonderheit*, family, class, nation, race, is the 1936–37 definition of the homogeneous State (p. 146) in its negative form: as long as one is recognised as a member of a group, one is not recognised as an individual. Race appears in the list in 1935, which gives the passage a sharp political edge.

So man transforms the given social and political reality so as to make it such that he can realise his true individuality in it. And this progressive realisation of individuality, through the progressive active and free satisfaction of the desire for recognition, is the "dialectical movement" of history that is man himself. The definition of history as the progressive realisation of individuality unites the categories of the appendix.

In fact individuality can be fully realised, and the desire for recognition completely satisfied, only in and through the universal and homogeneous State. For in the homogeneous State the "specific differences" (*Besonderheiten*) of class, race, and so on are "overcome", and this State relates directly to the particular as such, who is recognised as citizen in his very particularity. And this recognition is truly universal, since by definition the State encompasses the whole human race (even in its past, through the total historical tradition this State perpetuates in the present, and in its future, since the future no longer differs from the present in which man is already fully satisfied). This 1935 text contains the first formulation in the book of the universal and homogeneous State. The extension of universality to the past, through tradition, and to the future, which no longer differs from the present, gives the State a temporal as well as spatial universality.

By fully realising individuality, the universal and homogeneous State completes history, since man satisfied in and by this State will not be tempted to negate it and so create something new in its place. But this State also presupposes the elapsed totality of the historical process and cannot be realised at once by man (since the State, and man himself, are born of the fight, which presupposes a difference and cannot take place in universal homogeneity). In other words, a being can be truly individual (and not merely particular) only on condition of being also historical; and we have seen that it can be so only if it is really free. Conversely, a really free being is necessarily historical, and a historical being is always more or less individual, finally becoming entirely so. A footnote, important for Kojève's later thought, adds: to tell the truth, the Sage is no longer "individual" in the sense of differing essentially from all others. If wisdom consists in possessing the truth, which is one and the same for Hegel and all his readers, one Sage differs in no way from another. That is to say, he is not human in the same sense as historical man (not being free in the same sense either, since he no longer negates anything by action): he is rather "divine" (but mortal). The Sage is nonetheless an individual in the sense that it is in his existential particularity that he possesses universal Science; in this sense he is still human (and so mortal). The footnote completes the earlier one (p. 492): the Sage is a "mortal god", individual only in that he possesses universal truth in a particular body. Its consequence, all Sages are identical, anticipates the 1946 note on the end of individuality after history (p. 435).

The "phenomenological" description of human empirical existence therefore already reveals the three fundamental categories (implicitly discovered by the Judaeo-Christians) that dominate this existence and distinguish it from purely natural existence: individuality, freedom, and historicity. And this same description brings out their indissoluble solidarity, showing that man cannot "appear" as an individual without "manifesting" himself as the free agent of history, that he can "reveal" himself as free only by "appearing" as a historical individual, and that he can "manifest" himself historically only on condition of "appearing" in his individual freedom or free individuality. In revealing this solidarity, the "phenomenological" description presents man as a being that is dialectical in its empirical existence; or rather, it must present him as dialectical in order to account both for the solidarity of the three categories and for each taken separately. The three categories, individuality, freedom, historicity, are the appendix's anthropological triad, which Kojève attributes to Judaeo-Christianity and Hegel's secularisation of it.

We have already seen that a free or historical being is necessarily dialectical, and it is easy to see that the same holds for a being that is an individual in the Hegelian sense. Individuality is a synthesis of particular and universal, the universal being the negation or antithesis of the particular, which is the thetic or self-identical given. In other words, individuality is a totality, and the being that is individual is thereby dialectical. The particularity of an entity, determined by its *hic et nunc* and its "natural place" (*topos*) in the cosmos, not only distinguishes it rigidly from everything that is not it but also fixes it in its identity with itself. And this particularity is a given or "thesis", a given being (*Sein*). For what is at the origin (despite what "creationists" of every kind think, beginning with Plato) is not the universal but the particular: not, for example, the table in general or any animal, but this particular table and this particular animal. Yet (at least in the world one speaks of, the world where man lives) one can negate the particularity of the existing entity by detaching it from its given *hic et nunc* and making it pass from the natural cosmos into the universe of discourse. So this table, which is now here, can become the "general" notion of the table, which is in a sense always and nowhere (except "in thought"), and this animal the "abstract" notion of any animal. But what constitutes concrete reality (of the world inhabited by man) is neither the particular entities alone nor the universal notions corresponding to them, taken separately. Concrete reality is the whole or totality of particular entities revealed by discourse with universal (or true) content, and of general (even generic) concepts realised in the spatio-temporal world by the *hic et nunc* of particularities. And it is only as the particular realisation of a universal concept, or as "representative" of a species or genus, that a given real entity is an "individual". (Likewise the concept would be a pure abstraction, pure nothingness, if it did not correspond to given being; and it is the identifying particularity implied in this being that differentiates general concepts by "individualising" them.) The priority of the particular over the universal, against Platonic "creationism", is Kojève's nominalist premise. The derivation of the concept from the particular by detachment from the *hic et nunc* repeats the eighth lecture's theory (p. 373).

But when it is a matter of purely natural particular entities (animals, plants, or inanimate things), the universalising negation takes place only in and through man's thought or discourse, outside them. That is why one can say the natural entity is, in itself, only particular: it is at the same time universal, and so "individual", only by and for the man who thinks it or speaks of it. So individuality (and dialectic in general) can "appear" only in the human science of nature, not in nature itself. The purely natural entity is not properly speaking an individual: neither in itself, nor by itself, nor for itself. Man, by contrast, is individual (and so dialectical) in himself and by himself, as he is also for himself. He is so for himself because he knows himself not only as "this particular" but also as a "representative" of the human race (and can act as such). He is so by himself, since it is he himself who negates himself in his given animal particularity in order to conceive and manifest himself (by speech and action) in his human universality. And man is finally individual in himself, really or in his very empirical existence, since the universality of his particular being is not only thought by him and others but recognised as a real value, and recognised really or actively by a real or State universal (which he himself creates, moreover), which really universalises him since it makes him a citizen acting (and so existing) by virtue of the "general interest". The triple form of human individuality, for himself (self-knowledge), by himself (self-negation), in himself (State recognition), is a precise analysis. The last makes the State the existential condition of individuality, not merely its acknowledgement.

To say that man is an individual or a (real, even "existential") synthesis of particular and universal is therefore to say that he is himself the preserving (universalising) negation of himself taken as given (particular); and that is to say that an individual is necessarily a dialectical being. We have seen that on the "ontological" plane the dialectical being must be described as at once identity, negativity, and totality; and that negativity "manifests" itself on the "phenomenal" plane as human freedom, while totality "appears" there as historicity. It is therefore natural to say that identity "reveals" itself phenomenologically as individuality, the third fundamental anthropological category. The mapping completes the correspondence: identity–individuality, negativity–freedom, totality–historicity.

Kojève had said, it is true, that identity "manifested" itself on the human "phenomenal" plane as animality; but there is no contradiction. It was a matter not of animality simply, as it "appears" in nature, but of animality in man, his (originally animal) given nature as dialectically overcome or preserved as sublimated in the totality of human existence. The given or innate (animal and social) "nature" of a man is precisely what determines his particularity, his rigid and irreducible difference from everything that is not him. As dialectically overcome, this "nature" appears as negated particularity, as universality. And insofar as this "nature" is preserved and sublimated in its negation, universality in man implies particularity and is thus a manifestation of individuality. One can therefore say that individuality indeed "reveals" identity in man, insofar as his individuality preserves and sublimates the particularity of his innate "nature". If negativity serves as the ontological basis of freedom, and totality of historicity, identity is the ontological foundation of individuality. It is thanks to the identity implied in individuality that a man can remain "the same individual" despite having become "quite other", having changed essentially by negating the given particularities of his "character" and so freeing himself from it. And it is as such an "individual", who remains the same while negating himself, that a man has a personal "history". A footnote adds: nowadays one often speaks of a man's "personality". But "personality" (*Person* in Hegel) means nothing other than "free and historical individuality": it is not a new anthropological category but a word designating the whole (in fact inseparable) of the three fundamental categories of Judaeo-Christian anthropology. The resolution of the apparent contradiction, animality versus individuality as the phenomenal form of identity, is subtle: identity in man is sublated animality. The footnote's reduction of "personality" to the three categories targets the personalism of Mounier and the review *Esprit*, founded 1932.

But this way of speaking is not absolutely correct. What really exists is neither identity nor negativity but the totality that implies both as constituents. It is therefore always totality that "appears" on the human "phenomenal" plane as individuality, freedom, and historicity. These three human "phenomena" are only three aspects, different but complementary, of the "appearance" of one and the same real totality, which is the existence of man's very being. Individuality "reveals" totality insofar as it implies identity; freedom "manifests" this same totality as implying negativity; and historicity is the "appearance" of totality as such, as the synthesis of individual identity and free, or better liberating, negativity. The self-correction is characteristic: the three categories are aspects of one totality, not three separate manifestations.

To say that man is a free and historical individual is to say that he "appears" (*erscheint*) in his empirical existence (*Dasein*) as a dialectical entity, and so that he is dialectical in his objective reality (*Wirklichkeit*) and in his very being (*Sein*). It is therefore to say that man is and exists only insofar as he dialectically overcomes himself, preserving and sublimating himself. In a passage of the *Encyclopaedia* already cited (vol. V, p. 105), Hegel said that it belongs to every finite entity (*alles Endliche*) to overcome itself dialectically. Kojève sets aside the fact that this passage affirms that every finite entity is dialectical, and necessarily so: «c'est là une incorrection de langage ou une erreur extrêmement grave, sur laquelle je ne voudrais pas insister» (that is an incorrectness of language or an extremely serious error, on which I would not want to insist) (p. 512). He retains only that, according to the context, the passage affirms that only a finite entity can be dialectical, that every entity that is (or can be) dialectical is necessarily finite in its very being, objective reality, and "phenomenal" empirical existence. To say that man is dialectical is therefore not only to say that he is individual, free, and historical, but also to affirm that he is essentially finite. And the radical finitude of being and reality "appears" on the human "phenomenal" plane as the something called death. Consequently, to say that man "reveals" himself as a free historical individual (or as "personality") and that he "appears" as essentially mortal in the proper and strong sense is to express differently one and the same thing: a free historical individual is necessarily mortal, and a truly mortal being is always a free historical individual. A footnote refers to Appendix II on death. Kojève's reading of § 81 Remark is a careful inversion: he rejects "every finite thing is dialectical" (which would make nature dialectical) and keeps its converse, "every dialectical thing is finite". The equivalence of the free historical individual and the mortal being is the appendix's final thesis.

To remove the paradoxical aspect of this assertion, one must say at once that for Hegel human death is essentially something other than the finitude of purely natural beings. Death is a dialectical finitude. The dialectical being, man, is alone mortal in the proper sense. The death of a human being differs essentially from the "end" of an animal or plant and from the "disappearance" of a thing by mere "wear". The distinction between death, end, and wear repeats Heidegger's *sterben* and *verenden* (p. 64).

In a fragment of the young Hegel (1795?) on love (Nohl's edition, *Hegels theologische Jugendschriften*, 1907, pp. 379–381) there is a passage on death in which the main themes he will later develop already appear. Kojève translates: since love is a feeling of the living, the lovers can distinguish themselves (from each other) only insofar as they are mortal, insofar as they think this possibility of separation, not insofar as something were really separated ... There is no (raw or given) matter in the lovers (as lovers); they are a living (or spiritual, since at that time Hegel identified life and spirit) whole; that the lovers have independence or autonomy (*Selbständigkeit*), their own vital principle (*eigenes*), means only: they can die. The plant has salts and earthy parts, which carry in themselves their own laws of action; the plant is the reflection of something foreign (*Fremden*), and one can say only: the plant can decay (*verwesen*). But love tends to overcome (*aufzuheben*) even this distinction, this possibility as mere possibility, and to unite the mortal itself, to make it immortal ... And so one has: the united-one (*Einige*), the separated, and the re-united (*Wiedervereinigte*). The re-united separate again, but in the child the union itself has remained unseparated. The fragment on love (1797–98, usually dated later than Kojève's "1795?") is the earliest Hegelian text on death as individuating. Its triad, united, separated, re-united, is the first form of the dialectic.

To understand the full scope of this "romantic" text, one must know that when it was written Hegel believed for a moment that he had found in love the specifically human content of man's existence, and that it was in analysing the love relation that he first described the dialectic of this existence, which distinguishes it from purely natural existence. To describe man as lover was then for Hegel to describe man as specifically human and essentially different from the animal. In the *Phenomenology*, love and the desire for love became desire for recognition and the fight to the death for its satisfaction, with all that follows: history ending in the advent of the satisfied citizen and the Sage. Mutual recognition in love became social and political recognition through action. The "phenomenal" dialectic is described no longer as a love dialectic but as a historical dialectic, in which the objective realisation (*Verwirklichung*) of recognition in the sexual act and the child (mentioned in the last sentence of the text cited) is replaced by its objective realisation in fight, labour, and historical progress ending in the Sage.
