In the *Phenomenology*, the "united-one" of the text cited is man (or more exactly pre-man) before the fight, animated by the desire for recognition, which is (originally) the same in all; "the separated" are the Master and the Slave created in and through the "first" fight, essentially different from each other; and "the re-united" is no longer the sexual act or the child but the satisfied citizen and the Sage, who "synthesise" mastery and servitude and result from the whole historical evolution of humanity, as the integral totality of the "dialectical movement" of fight and labour. In general, the complete and adequate "revelation" of dialectical human reality is no longer love, a "feeling of the living", but wisdom or Science, the discursive or conceptual understanding of the totality of being given to man and created by him. The genealogy of the Master–Slave dialectic from the young Hegel's dialectic of love is a significant philological thesis. The transposition, lovers into combatants, child into citizen, feeling into Science, is precise.

A long footnote on love follows. The "romantic" and "vitalist" origins of the dialectic of recognition and fight appear clearly in the "formal" description of this dialectic in the introduction to Chapter IV of the *Phenomenology* (Hoffmeister pp. 135–138); the close links with the youthful text are evident. Human love too is a desire for recognition: the lover wants to be loved, recognised as absolute or universal value in his very particularity, which distinguishes him from all others. Love therefore realises (to some extent) individuality, and that is why it can procure (to some extent) satisfaction. In any case it is a specifically human phenomenon, since in it one desires another desire (the other's love) and not an empirical reality (as, for example, when one simply "desires" someone). What Hegel (implicitly) reproaches love with in the *Phenomenology* is, on the one hand, its "private" character (one can be loved by very few people, whereas one can be universally recognised), and on the other its "lack of seriousness", given the absence of the risk of life (only this risk is a truly objective realisation of the specifically human content that essentially distinguishes man from the animal). Not presupposing risk, love (= love recognition) does not presuppose action in general. It is therefore not action (*Tun*) or work (*Werk*) that are recognised in it as absolute values, but given being (*Sein*), precisely what is not truly human in man. (As Goethe said: one loves someone not for what he does but for what he is; that is why one can love a dead person, since the man who truly did nothing would already be as if dead; that is also why one can love an animal without being able to "recognise" it: let us recall that there has never been a duel between a man and an animal, or a woman; let us recall too that it is "unworthy of a man" to devote himself entirely to love: legends of Hercules, Samson, and so on.) Consequently even a man "happy in love" is not fully "satisfied" as long as he is not universally "recognised". Accepting the standpoint of the *Phenomenology*, one would have to say that man can truly love (which no animal can) only because he has already created himself beforehand as a human being by the risk incurred in a fight for recognition. That is why only fight and labour (born of the desire for recognition properly speaking) produce a specifically human objective reality (*Wirklichkeit*), a technical and social, even historical, world; the objective reality of love is purely natural (sexual act, birth of the child): its human content always remains purely inner or intimate (*innerlich*). «C'est l'Histoire et non l'Amour qui crée l'Homme» (it is history and not love that creates man) (p. 514); love is only a secondary "manifestation" of man who already exists as human being. The footnote is Kojève's theory of love: recognition of being rather than action, private rather than universal, without risk. The definition repeats the 1937–38 account of the Family's love (p. 188). The remarks about duels with women and Hercules and Samson are dated, and they show the masculinist assumptions of the theory. The thesis "history and not love creates man" places Kojève against the romantic anthropology of love and, implicitly, against Christian agape.

But in both "phenomenological" descriptions of the human dialectic, death plays a primordial role. Already in the youthful writing Hegel affirms that the lovers (who "manifest" the human in man) can distinguish themselves from each other and from everything that is not them only insofar as they are mortal; that is to say, only as mortals do they possess an individuality, since this necessarily implies and presupposes particularity "unique in the world". Likewise, it is only thanks to death that the lovers have an independent or autonomous, even free, existence. Finally, it is again because of the lovers' mortality that love is realised as the dialectical "re-union" of the "separated", as a synthesis or totality unfolding and integrating itself in time, in the form of a series of successive generations or a historical evolution (the "synthesis" of the lovers being the child). In his mature writings Hegel maintains this indissoluble link between death and individuality, freedom, and historicity. The three roles of death in the love fragment, individuating, freeing, and temporalising, are the three categories of the appendix.

But what must above all be stressed is that the "romantic" text radically opposes the death of man (= the lovers) to the mere disappearance or "decomposition" of purely natural entities (everything Hegel says there of the plant applies also to the animal and the inanimate thing). The finitude and actual disappearance of natural entities (the "death" of an animal, for example) are determined, necessarily and univocally, by laws foreign (*Fremdes*) to them, or, if one likes, by the natural place (*topos*) they occupy in the given cosmos. Man's death (= the lovers'), by contrast, is an immanent law, a self-suppression: it is truly his death, something proper to him and belonging properly to him, and which can therefore be known by him, willed or negated by him. The "death" of the natural being exists only "in itself or for us", for the man who becomes conscious of it: the finite natural being knows nothing of its own finitude. Death, by contrast, exists also for man; it is "in and for itself": the lovers "think the possibility of separation" in and through their death. That is why man (= the lovers) alone is capable of willing the infinity and immortality of what is finite and mortal, as he alone can give himself death: in nature death is only a given, but in man and in history it is also (or can always be) a work, the result of a conscious and voluntary action. The thesis that death is "a work" in man, something one can do, is Kojève's most striking formula for human mortality. The "mineness" of death, his death, belonging properly to him, is Heidegger's *Jemeinigkeit* (*Being and Time* §47), read into the young Hegel.

To say all this is to say that the "decomposition" or "corruption" of a natural entity that puts an end to its "empirical existence" is a pure and simple (or "identical") annihilation, whereas human death is a "dialectical overcoming" (or "total"), which annuls while preserving and sublimating. It is to oppose to the "identical" natural world of (Aristotelian) "generation and corruption" the "dialectical" human or historical world of (active or negating) creation and death (always conscious and sometimes willed or voluntary). We will see what this dialectical character of human death means in Hegel. But we already know that the "preservation and sublimation" it implies have nothing to do with survival, since the dialectical being is necessarily finite or mortal in the strong sense. If, according to Hegel, man can be truly human only because he must and can die, he does not die in order to rise again, nor to live in a world other than the natural world where he is born and where he creates his own historical world by action. The insistence that dialectical overcoming in death is not survival is the guard against any spiritualist reading of *Aufhebung*.

In general, the introduction of the notion of death changes nothing in Hegel's description of dialectic as we already know it. To say that man is mortal (in the sense that he is conscious of his death, can give it to himself voluntarily, or "negate" it in a myth of immortality) is to say nothing other or more than what one says in affirming that man is a totality or dialectical entity: totality always appears as a free historical individual who is necessarily mortal, and the truly mortal being is necessarily a free historical individual who is and exists as a totality or dialectical entity. But one must see a little more closely why this is so. The equivalence is restated before its demonstration.

It is first evident that a dialectical or "total" being can only be finite or mortal. There is by definition dialectic and so totality only where there is negativity. And negativity in the isolated state is pure nothingness. Its "synthesis" with identity or given being (*Sein*) can therefore only be a penetration of nothingness into being, an annihilation of being or a nihilating of nothingness in it. But being annihilates itself only in time, and nothingness nihilates in being as time. The dialectical or total being (Spirit in the *Phenomenology*, or Life in the young Hegel's terminology) is therefore necessarily temporal: it is realised or, if one likes, materialised time, a time that lasts (in being or space). And to last is necessarily to have a beginning and an end (in time), which "appear" as birth and death. A dialectical or total being is therefore indeed always mortal, at least in the sense that its empirical existence is finite or limited in and by time. The derivation of mortality from temporality, and temporality from negativity, is the 1938–39 theory of time (p. 368) stated in 1935.

But "dialectical" death is more than a mere end or limit imposed from outside. If death is an "appearance" of negativity, freedom is another, as we know. Death and freedom are therefore only two ("phenomenological") aspects of one and the same thing, so that to say "mortal" is to say "free", and conversely. Hegel affirms this several times, notably in a passage of his writing on "Natural Law" (1802). Kojève translates (vol. VII, p. 370): this negative or negating absolute, pure freedom, is in its appearance (*Erscheinung*) death; and by the faculty (*Fähigkeit*) of death the subject (= man) proves himself (*erweist sich*) free and absolutely raised (*erhaben*) above all constraint (*Zwang*). The *Naturrecht* essay passage is the textual root of the equation of freedom and death.

On the "metaphysical" plane it is easy to see that this is so. If given being is determined as a whole (otherwise there would be no possible science or truth), it determines, by its whole, everything that is part of it. A being that could not escape being could not escape its destiny and would be fixed once for all in and by the place it occupies in the cosmos. In other words, if man lived eternally and could not die, he could not escape God's omnipotence either. But if he can give himself death, he can refuse any imposed destiny, since he will not undergo it by ceasing to exist. And passing to the "phenomenological" plane, one sees that suicide, voluntary death without "vital necessity", is the most evident "manifestation" of negativity or freedom. For to give oneself death to escape a given situation to which one is biologically adapted (since one could go on living in it) is to manifest one's independence from it, one's autonomy or freedom. And since one can kill oneself to escape any given situation whatever, one can say with Hegel that "the faculty of death" is the "appearance" of "pure" or absolute freedom (at least in potency) with regard to every given in general. The argument from suicide is the strongest form of the equation: the possibility of suicide is the proof of freedom from any given situation, including God's will.

A footnote on Kirilov: this Hegelian theme was taken up by Dostoevsky in *Demons*. Kirilov wants to kill himself solely to demonstrate the possibility of doing so "without any necessity", freely. His suicide is to demonstrate man's absolute freedom, his independence from God. Dostoevsky's theist objection consists in saying that man cannot do it, that he necessarily recoils before death: Kirilov kills himself out of shame at not being able to do it. But this objection is not valid, since a suicide "out of shame" is also a free act (no animal commits it). And if, in killing himself, Kirilov annihilates himself, he has, as he wanted, suppressed the omnipotence of the external (the "transcendent") by dying "prematurely", before "it is written", and has limited infinity or God. «Je suis redevable de l'interprétation de l'épisode Kirilov à M. Jacob Klein» (I owe the interpretation of the Kirilov episode to Mr Jacob Klein) (p. 518). The acknowledgement of Jacob Klein, the historian of Greek mathematics and Leo Strauss's friend, is a precious biographical detail. The reply to Dostoevsky, that suicide from shame is still free, is characteristic: any self-chosen death refutes determination.

But if suicide (which evidently distinguishes man from the animal) "manifests" freedom, it does not realise it, since it ends in nothingness and not in a free existence. What reveals and realises freedom, according to Hegel, is the fight for pure prestige, waged without any biological necessity for the sake of recognition alone. But this fight reveals and realises freedom only insofar as it implies the risk of life, the real possibility of dying. A footnote adds that the fight for pure prestige is moreover a suicide (with uncertain outcome), as Hegel says in the Jena lectures of 1805–06 (vol. XX, p. 211): it appears to each adversary, as consciousness of the external, that he goes to the death of another; but he goes to his own; it is a suicide insofar as he exposes himself (voluntarily) to danger. The fact that the adversaries remain alive subjects them to the necessities of existence; but this necessity passes into the Slave (who refused the risk), while the Master (who accepted it) remains free: in his labour the Slave undergoes the laws of the given, but the idle Master, who consumes products already "humanised" by labour, prepared for man, no longer undergoes the constraint of nature (in principle, of course). One could also say that the Master is in fact humanly dead in the fight: he no longer acts properly speaking, since he remains idle; he therefore lives as if he were dead; that is why he no longer evolves in the course of history and is simply annihilated at its end: his existence is a mere "survival" (limited in time) or «une "mort différée"» (a "deferred death") (p. 518). The Slave frees himself progressively by labour, which manifests his freedom; but he must finally resume the fight and accept the risk to realise this freedom by creating through victory the universal and homogeneous State of which he will be the "recognised" citizen. The distinction between suicide, which manifests freedom, and the fight, which realises it, is precise: the fight is a suicide with an uncertain outcome. The Master as "deferred death" is one of Kojève's most memorable phrases: having realised his freedom in the one act of risk, he lives on as a survivor of himself.

Death is therefore only a complementary aspect of freedom. But to what extent is it also a complement of individuality? Individuality is by definition a synthesis of the universal and the particular "unique in the world". Rising to the "ontological" plane, one can show that free particularity (or particular freedom) is incompatible with infinity. Aristotle already saw very well that a "possibility" never actualised or realised (as long as time lasts) would in fact be an absolute impossibility. If then any being, and in particular a human being, were infinite in the sense of lasting eternally (= as long as time lasts), and if it did not realise certain possibilities of being, these possibilities would be impossibilities for it or in relation to it. In other words, it would be rigorously determined by these impossibilities in its being and existence, and in its "appearance": it would not be truly free. Existing eternally, a being will necessarily realise all its possibilities and none of its impossibilities. The given whole of its possibilities, or, what is the same, of its impossibilities, constitutes its immutable "essence", its eternal "nature", its innate "character", its Platonic "idea", and so on, which it can develop in time by realising and "manifesting" it but can neither modify nor annihilate. In the real and "phenomenal" world this being would only be the "representative" (perhaps unique) of a "species" determined in its "essence" by the given structure of the being of which it is part, as it were "before" its temporal realisation and "manifestation". Or, to speak with Calvin, who was implacably logical on this point: the man who existed eternally would be "elect" or "damned" before his "creation", absolutely incapable of modifying in any way his "destiny" or "nature" by his "active" existence in the world. The Aristotelian principle, a possibility never realised in infinite time is impossible (*Metaphysics* Θ 4, *De Caelo* I 12), turns immortality into determinism: an eternal being has realised its essence, so it has no freedom. Calvin's double predestination is the theological form of this consequence.

The infinite or eternal being, and in particular immortal man or man benefiting from a "survival", would be particularised by his restricted possibilities or impossibilities, and could be distinguished from all other beings, having impossibilities the others do not have. He would therefore be a particular being. But this particular would not be free, and so would not be an individuality in the proper sense. Unable to go beyond his "nature", he could not negate, "overcome", or "transcend" his given particularity and so rise to the universal; and having nothing universal in himself, he would be only particular, without being a true individual. So in this conception of man, individuality appears only where human particularity is projected onto divine universality. Calvin's man is an individuality different from mere animal and thing-like particularity only by being "elect" or "damned", "recognised" in his very particularity by a universal God. But this God determines him in "recognising" him, and "recognises" him only by virtue of a predetermination prior, as it were, to the very existence and "appearance" of the determined one to be "recognised". Taken in himself, "immortal" man with limited possibilities is therefore neither free nor individual in the proper sense. As for the infinite being that realises all the possibilities of being, one can say of it, if one likes, that it is "free", at least in the ancient and Spinozist sense of the absence in it of all immanent constraint or constraint from outside. But if every man realises and manifests all the possibilities of being (if only of human being), there will no longer be any true difference between men, and none of them will represent a particularity, without which there is no individuality properly speaking. Aristotle already understood this, and his discovery was taken up by the Arabs and by Spinoza. The infinite or eternal ("immortal") being, "free" in the sense of not being limited by impossibilities realisable elsewhere, is necessarily one and unique: a universal divine "substance" realising and manifesting itself in and through an infinite multitude of particular "attributes" and "modes". If one likes, there is in this infinitist conception freedom and individuality; but the free individual is here God alone, and there is no longer a purely natural world, nor man in the proper sense; and so there is no longer the "movement" called history (a footnote refers to the "Note on Eternity, Time, and the Concept"). The dilemma is elegant: an immortal being either has limited possibilities (and is determined) or all possibilities (and is indistinguishable from others, so God). Either way there is no free individual. The reference to "the Arabs" is to Averroes's unity of the intellect, which makes all minds one.

If man is immortal, if he "survives" his biological death, there is therefore no freedom or individuality in him. Man's freedom is his effective negation of his own given "nature", of the "possibilities" he has already realised, which determine his "impossibilities", everything incompatible with them. And his individuality is a synthesis of his particularity with a universality that is equally his own. Man can therefore be individual and free only insofar as he implies in his being all the possibilities of being but does not have time to realise and manifest them all. Freedom is the realisation of a possibility incompatible (as realised) with the whole of the possibilities realised before (which must therefore be negated); there is therefore freedom only where this whole does not include all possibilities in general, and where what is outside it is not an absolute impossibility. And man is an individual only insofar as the universality of the possibilities of his being associates in him with the particularity, unique of its kind, of their temporal realisations and manifestations. «C'est uniquement parce qu'il est infini en puissance et toujours limité en acte par sa mort, que l'Homme est un Individu libre qui a une histoire» (it is solely because he is infinite in potency and always limited in act by his death that man is a free individual who has a history) (p. 520), and who can freely create a place for himself in history instead of being content, like the animal and the thing, to occupy passively a natural place in the given cosmos determined by its structure. The formula "infinite in potency, limited in act by death" is the appendix's central thesis on finitude. It inverts Aristotle: man's potency exceeds his act because he dies.

A footnote illustrates with the forked road. If an animal, or a man as animal, faces two forking paths, it can go right or left: the two possibilities are compatible as possibilities. But if it actually takes the right path, it is impossible that it took the left, and conversely: the two possibilities are incompatible as realised. The animal that has taken the right path must retrace its steps to take the left; man as animal must do so too. But as man, as historical (or "spiritual", even dialectical) being, he never retraces his steps. History does not turn back, and yet it finds itself on the left path after having taken the right. That is because there was a revolution, because man negated himself as engaged on the right path and, having thus become other than he is, found himself on the left. He negated himself without disappearing completely and without ceasing to be man. But the animal in him that was on the right path could not be on the left: it therefore had to disappear, and the man it incarnated, die. (It would be a miracle if a revolution could succeed without one generation replacing another, naturally or more or less violently.) The forked road is one of Kojève's finest images. History reaches the other path without going back, by revolution, which requires the death of those who took the first. The parenthesis on generational replacement is unsettling in 1935: revolutions succeed only when a generation dies, "naturally or more or less violently".

Man is therefore a (free) individual only insofar as he is mortal, and he can realise and manifest himself as such an individual only by realising and manifesting death too. This is easy to see on the "phenomenological" plane. Hegel saw it in his "romantic" youth, analysing the "manifest" existence of the "lovers", two human beings who transcend their animality and commune completely in one and the same truly human life (where the human value attributed to oneself is a function of that attributed to the other, and conversely). He saw that only death could separate and distinguish these two beings, particularise them, and so individualise them. For if each could live in and through the other, and so to speak in the other's place, each had to die for himself, his death being truly his, and his alone. This observation remains true even taken out of its romantic framework, considering man's historical existence and not his love life. If in the truly homogeneous humanity realised as State at the end of history human existences become really interchangeable, in the sense that the action (and "man's true being is his action", according to Hegel) of each will also be the action of all, and conversely (*Tun Aller und Jeder*), death will necessarily oppose each to all others and particularise him in his empirical existence, so that universal action will always also be particular (or liable to fail where another succeeds), and so individual. A footnote adds: what would remain of the individuality of Christ if Jesus had not been born and died? The application to the final State is decisive: in a homogeneous humanity where actions are interchangeable, death alone individualises. This answers the worry that the end of history abolishes individuality. The footnote on Christ is pointed: the incarnation individualises God by death.

The freedom and individuality of man therefore presuppose his death; and the same holds for his historicity, since it is nothing other, as we have seen, than free individuality or individual or individualised freedom. For Hegel history begins only with the "first" fight for recognition, which would not be what it is, anthropogenic, if it did not imply a real risk of life. And history as a whole is only an evolution of the "contradiction" (*Widerspruch*) arising from the "immediate" (*unmittelbar*) solution of this first social or human conflict, through the opposition (*Entgegensetzung*) of mastery and servitude. According to Hegel, history would therefore have no meaning, no reason or possibility of being, if man were not mortal; and it is easy to see that this is so. The historicity of death completes the triad.

If man lived eternally (as long as time lasts), he could certainly "undergo an evolution", like the animal or plant. But "evolving" in time, he would only "develop" a determinate eternal "nature" given or imposed in advance; and his evolution would be anything but a historical drama whose end is unknown. Seriousness enters a historical situation and transforms a given existential situation into a "historical" one only insofar as man can definitively miss his human destiny, insofar as history can fail to reach its goal; and this is possible only if history is limited in and by time, and so if man, its creator, is mortal. It is solely because of the essential finitude of man and of history that history is something other than a tragedy, if not a comedy, played by human actors for the entertainment of the gods, who are its authors, who therefore know its outcome and so cannot take it seriously, nor truly tragically, any more than the actors themselves if they know they are playing a role given to them. «C'est la finitude de toute action historique, c'est-à-dire la possibilité d'un échec absolu, qui engendre le sérieux» (it is the finitude of every historical action, the possibility of absolute failure, that engenders seriousness) (p. 522) characterising man's effective participation in history: a seriousness that allows man, creating history, to do without any spectator other than himself. The thesis that seriousness depends on the possibility of absolute failure is one of the appendix's deepest. History needs no divine spectator because it can fail. The comedy for the gods returns from the 1936–37 theory of Christian comedy (p. 122).

A footnote addresses the Platonic-Kantian solution. According to Plato–Kant, each man, while eternal or immortal, chooses (outside time) a determinate particular existence that he lives for a certain time. But such a temporal existence has nothing truly historical about it. Seriousness lies at most in the "transcendental choice": its temporal realisation is only a comedy, of which it is hard to say why and for whom it is played, the content and outcome being known in advance. Moreover, if the eternal man plays only one temporal role, something (in fact God) prevents him from playing others (especially if the one he played ends badly): he is therefore not free as eternal. One does not see why the transmundane man chooses one role rather than another, nor why he chooses a "bad" role (unless he chooses "at random", that is, precisely without freedom). So Calvin was right to say that on the Platonic hypothesis the choice of role is necessarily determined by God, not by the one who seems to make it. Finally, if each man can choose any role, and the exclusion of roles other than the one chosen is imposed on him by God, it is God who particularises his universality, and man is an individual only for and by God. The footnote completes the critique of the myth of Er and the intelligible character (p. 347): the transcendental choice is either arbitrary or divinely determined.

In short, human death presents itself as a "manifestation" of man's freedom, individuality, and historicity, of the "total" or dialectical character of his being and existence. More particularly, death is an "appearance" of negativity, the true motor of the dialectical movement. But if death is a manifestation of man's dialecticity, it is because it overcomes him dialectically, preserving and sublimating; and it is as dialectical overcoming that it differs essentially from the mere "end" of a purely natural being. Once more, there can be no question in Hegel of man's "survival" after death; this "survival", which would maintain him eternally in given being, is incompatible with the essential finitude of every dialectical being. In and through his death man annihilates himself completely and definitively; he becomes pure nothingness (*Nichts*), if one can say so, ceasing to be given being (*Sein*). The "dialectical overcoming" by death and of death is therefore something quite other than immortality. The repetition, death as total annihilation, is emphatic.

Negativity in being (identity) assigns it temporality (totality), which exists as the real duration of the world and manifests itself as historical time or history. Negativity is therefore actualised by the negation of being (which sinks into the nothingness of the "past"). But this negation is dialectical in that it does not end in pure nothingness: in going beyond or transcending given being (*Sein*), one creates the concept (*Begriff*), which is being minus the being of being. Negation therefore preserves the "content" of being (as concept: "being"), and sublimates it by making it subsist in "ideal" rather than "real" form. And without negativity, without finitude or temporality, being would never be a conceived (*begriffen*) being. If then death is a manifestation of negativity in man (or more exactly of man), it is a transformation of his real being into ideal concept. It is because he is mortal that man can conceive (*begreifen*) himself as he really is, precisely as mortal: unlike the animal, he thinks himself as mortal, and so thinks his own death. He therefore "transcends" it, if one likes, and places himself in a way beyond it; but he does so in the only way one can "go beyond" given being without sinking into pure nothingness: in and through thought. "Being minus the being of being" is the 1935 form of the eighth lecture's "being minus being" (p. 375). The thesis that death is the transformation of real being into concept makes mortality the condition of self-knowledge: one can conceive oneself only because one can die.

According to Hegel, man rises "for the first time" above mere animal self-feeling (*Selbstgefühl*) and reaches human self-consciousness (*Selbstbewusstsein*), conceptual and discursive consciousness in general, through the risk of life accepted without any necessity, through going to death without being forced to. For it is by the autonomous acceptance of death that he "goes beyond" or "transcends" the given being he himself is, this "going beyond" being precisely the thought that "reveals" this being to himself and others, illuminating it as it were from outside and from a nonexistent beyond. If man were not voluntarily mortal (free, individual, and historical, total or dialectical), he could neither think nor speak: he would differ in nothing from the animal. The image of thought as illumination "from outside and from a nonexistent beyond" is precise: the vantage of death, which does not exist, is what makes self-consciousness possible.

To say that human death, unlike the animal "end", is a "dialectical overcoming" (free, since it can be biologically premature) is therefore first to say that man knows he must die. The animal, the plant, and the thing end "in themselves or for us", only for an external observer. A man's death, by contrast, exists also "for himself", since he is conscious of it himself. It is this end "in and for itself", dialectical or "total", that is death in the proper sense, which takes place only in man; and it is because man is mortal in this sense that he is truly human and essentially different from the animal. A footnote adds: the famous reasoning of Epicurus holds only for the animal, or for non-dialectical being in general, which can only undergo its end without ever going to meet it. This being is as long as it lives and annihilates itself after its death; death therefore does not in fact exist for it, and one cannot say of it "it dies". But man transcends himself in and through his very existence: living, he is also beyond his real existence; his future absence is present in his life, and it is not the Epicurean argument that can erase this presence of absence in his existence. So man is mortal for himself, and that is why he alone can die in the proper sense. For he alone can live knowing he will die. And that is why in certain cases he can live by virtue of the idea of death, subordinating to it everything dictated to him only by his life (asceticism). The reply to Epicurus ("when death is, I am not") is Kojève's most elegant: the argument holds for animals, but in man death is present as "the presence of an absence". The reference to asceticism as life organised by the idea of death recalls the unhappy consciousness (p. 70).

It is by actually risking his life (without necessity) that man rises to the consciousness of his death. And once in possession of this consciousness, he can, unlike the animal, either die consciously or voluntarily, or refuse death in and through his thought and will. On the one hand man can die "without losing consciousness"; he can voluntarily face death in a reflective and calculated risk, or aware of the imminence of the fatal outcome; he can even give himself death for any motives he judges valid. On the other hand he can negate his death, as he can negate (mistakenly) everything actually given to him in and through his consciousness: he can declare himself immortal. But man cannot really become immortal. It is the being of the negated that passes into the negation and realises its result. So by (actively) negating the real natural world, man can create a historical or human ("technical") world, equally, though differently, real. But death is pure nothingness, and it subsists only as the concept of death (= presence of the absence of life). And by negating a concept one can create only another concept. The man who negates his death can therefore only "imagine" himself immortal: he can only believe in his "eternal life" or "resurrection", but he cannot really live his imaginary "survival". But this faith, which has as its counterpart and origin the faculty of freely giving oneself death, also distinguishes man from the animal. Man is not only the only living being that knows it must die and can freely give itself death: he is also the only one that can aspire to immortality and believe in it more or less firmly. The argument that negating death produces only a concept of immortality, since death itself is only a concept, is a precise logical refutation of real immortality. It also explains religion: the belief in immortality is the negation of the concept of death, which only a mortal being can perform.

So to say that man's death, and so his very existence, are dialectical is to say among other things that he "manifests" himself as a being knowing itself mortal and aspiring to immortality, "going beyond" his death in and through his thought. But man's "transcendence" with regard to his death "manifests" itself otherwise than by the erroneous "subjective certainty" (*Gewissheit*) of survival; this transcendence "appears" also as a truth (*Wahrheit*), being the revelation of an "objective reality" (*Wirklichkeit*). To say that man is dialectical or mortal in the proper sense is to say that he can freely go to meet his death, or go beyond his given existence, whatever it is, independently of the proper character of this existence. It is therefore to say that his possibilities exceed all his effective realisations and are not univocally determined by them. But it is also to say that he can effectively realise only a limited number of his infinite (or better indefinite, as every not-A is indefinite) possibilities. In other words, man always dies in a sense prematurely (which "justifies" to some extent his desire for survival), before having exhausted all the possibilities of his being (or better: of his negating or creative action). The animal can annihilate itself after realising everything it was capable of, so that a prolongation of its life would no longer have any meaning: its death is then "natural". «Mais l'Homme meurt toujours, si l'on veut, d'une mort "violente"» (but man always dies, if one likes, a "violent" death) (p. 525), since it is his death that prevents him from doing anything more than he has done. A footnote adds: even the so-called "violent" or "accidental" end of the animal appears "natural" if one considers nature as a whole: it is always determined, even "justified", by the animal's natural place in the cosmos. The fact that the animal's offspring merely reproduce its own existence proves that in procreating it has exhausted all its essential existential possibilities. But the "spiritual son" always goes further than his "father", even if he takes a wrong path; and that is why the "father" had in a sense the "right" (or human possibility) to live longer than he did. The thesis that every human death is "violent", premature, interrupting unexhausted possibilities, is one of Kojève's most humane. The footnote's contrast between the animal's offspring, which repeats it, and the "spiritual son", who goes further, grounds history in the transmission of unfinished work.

Every man who has died could have prolonged his activity or negated it: he has therefore not completely exhausted his human existential possibilities. That is why his human possibilities can be realised humanly, in and through another man, who will take up his work and prolong his action (which was his very being). That is how history is possible, and why it can be realised not despite but rather because of death. For it is in knowing themselves mortal that men educate their children so that they can complete their works, acting by virtue of the memory of departed ancestors. And it is precisely this projection into a future that will never be a present for the one who thinks it, and this prolongation into an existence of a past that is not one's own, that characterise historical existence and distinguish it essentially from the mere evolution observed in nature. The education of children "so that they can complete their works" is the existential basis of tradition: history exists because the dead leave unfinished work.

It is this transcendence of death in and through history that is the truth (= revealed reality) of the subjective certainty of "survival": man "goes beyond" his death insofar as his very being is nothing but his action and this action propagates itself through history (which is itself finite, moreover). But man reaches this truth only very late and always reluctantly. At first he believes (or rather would like to believe) in his own survival after death, and negates, in his imagination, his definitive annihilation. But man is human only by living in a world. So he can think himself living humanly after his death here below only by imagining a transcendent world or "beyond" called "divine" («le divin ou le "sacré" n'étant pas autre chose que le "lieu naturel" des hommes morts», the divine or "sacred" being nothing other than the "natural place" of dead men) (p. 526). But we have seen that where there is eternal life and so God, there is no longer room for human freedom, individuality, or historicity. So the man who affirms himself immortal always ends, if he overcomes the contradiction, by conceiving himself as a purely natural being, determined once for all in his purely particular and in no way creative existence. And if he possesses the idea of free historical individuality, he attributes it to God alone, attributing to him thereby the death he refuses himself. But man can be satisfied only by realising his own individuality and knowing that he does so. Consequently the man who believes himself immortal, or, what is the same, the man who believes in God, never reaches satisfaction (*Befriedigung*) and always lives in contradiction with himself: as Hegel says, he is an "unhappy consciousness" (*unglückliches Bewusstsein*) and lives in "doubling" (*Entzweiung*). The definition of the sacred as "the natural place of dead men" is Kojève's most compressed genealogy of religion. The thesis that the believer attributes to God the death he refuses himself is a striking reading of the crucifixion: the dying God bears the mortality man disowns.

The definitive satisfaction of man, which completes history, necessarily implies the consciousness of realised individuality (through the universal recognition of particularity), and this consciousness necessarily implies the consciousness of death. If then the complete satisfaction of man is the goal and natural term of history, one can say that history is completed by man's perfect understanding of his death. And it is in and through Hegelian Science that man for the first time fully understood the phenomenological, metaphysical, and ontological meaning of his essential finitude. If then this Science, which is wisdom, could appear only at the end of history, it is only through it that history is perfect and definitively completed. For it is only by understanding himself in this Science as mortal, as a free historical individual, that man reaches the fullness of the consciousness of a self that no longer has any reason to negate itself and become other. The equation of the end of history with the understanding of death makes Hegel's Science essentially a philosophy of finitude, which Appendix II develops.

Hegelian Science culminates in the description of man understood as a total or dialectical being. And to say that man is dialectical is to say that he "appears" to himself as mortal (phenomenological plane); or, what is the same, that he exists necessarily in a natural world that has no beyond, where there is no room for a God (metaphysical plane); or, what is the same again, that he is essentially temporal in his very being, which is thus, in truth, action (ontological plane). A footnote adds: God and survival have been denied by certain men since always. But Hegel is the first to have attempted a complete atheist and finitist philosophy with regard to man (at least in the great *Logic* and the earlier writings). He not only gave a correct description of finite human existence on the "phenomenological" plane, which allowed him to use without contradiction the fundamental categories of Judaeo-Christian thought; he also tried (without completely succeeding, it is true) to complete this description by a metaphysical and ontological analysis, radically atheist and finitist too. «Mais très peu de ses lecteurs ont compris que la dialectique signifiait en dernière analyse l'athéisme» (but very few of his readers have understood that dialectic meant in the last analysis atheism) (p. 527). Since Hegel, atheism has never again risen to the metaphysical and ontological level. In our day Heidegger is the first to have undertaken a complete atheist philosophy. But it does not seem that he pushed it beyond the phenomenological anthropology developed in the first volume of *Sein und Zeit* (the only one published). This anthropology (undoubtedly remarkable and authentically philosophical) adds nothing new at bottom to the anthropology of the *Phenomenology* (which, moreover, would probably never have been understood had Heidegger not published his book); but atheism or ontological finitism is implicitly affirmed in it in a perfectly consistent way. Which has not prevented certain otherwise competent readers from speaking of a theology of Heidegger and from finding in his anthropology a notion of survival. The footnote is the book's most explicit statement of its debt to Heidegger: the *Phenomenology* "would probably never have been understood" without *Being and Time*. The claim that *Being and Time* adds nothing new to the *Phenomenology* is a provocation, but it states precisely how Kojève read Hegel: through Heidegger, as a philosophy of finitude and death. The remark about readers finding a "theology of Heidegger" anticipates the later debates about Heidegger's relation to theology.

In summary: Hegelian dialectic is not a method of philosophical research or exposition but the adequate description of the structure of being, and of the realisation and appearance of being. To say that being is dialectical is first to say (on the ontological plane) that it is a totality implying identity and negativity. It is then to say (on the metaphysical plane) that being is realised not only as a natural world but also as a historical (or human) world, these two worlds exhausting the totality of objective reality (there is no divine world). It is finally to say (on the phenomenological plane) that objective reality exists empirically and appears not only as inanimate thing, plant, and animal, but also as essentially temporal or mortal free historical individual (who fights and works). Or again: to say there is totality, or mediation, or dialectical overcoming, is to say that besides given being there is also creative action resulting in a work. The summary closes Appendix I by restating its three theses on three planes and reducing them to one: besides being there is action that makes a work. The parenthesis "there is no divine world" makes the atheism of the metaphysics explicit.

### Appendix II: The Idea of Death in the Philosophy of Hegel

The second appendix gives the full text of the last two lectures of the 1933–34 course. It is the earliest continuous statement of Kojève's reading, and its subject, death, is the one the 1938–39 lectures and Appendix I repeatedly referred forward to. Queneau placed it in the book's short path.

In a capital passage of the Preface to the *Phenomenology* (Hoffmeister pp. 19–24), Hegel traces the main lines of his philosophy and indicates its principal aim; he lists the principles at its basis and the main consequences that follow from them. Understanding this passage gives the key to understanding the Hegelian system as a whole, and the *Phenomenology* in particular; and the passage clearly shows the primordial role the idea of death plays in Hegel's philosophy. Hegel begins by indicating what in his view the essential and new content of his philosophy consists in. Kojève translates (Hoffmeister p. 19): in my view, which can be justified only by the exposition of the System itself, everything depends (*es kommt alles darauf an*) on expressing and understanding (*aufzufassen*) the true (*Wahre*) not (only) as substance but just as much as subject. The thesis that Preface ¶17 is the key to the whole system, and that it shows death's primordial role, frames the appendix. The link from "substance as subject" to death is Kojève's, and the appendix sets out to establish it.

This sentence is directed first of all against Schelling and his conception of the "Absolute" as "Substance". But the Schellingian conception only takes up the Spinozist one, which itself represents a radical form of traditional, Greek or pagan ontology. Hegel therefore opposes his philosophy to all those preceding it (with the sole exception of the philosophies of Kant and Fichte, and to some extent Descartes). Following Thales and Parmenides, pre-Hegelian philosophers attached themselves exclusively to the notion of "substance", forgetting that the notion of "subject" is just as primordial and irreducible. The genealogy Thales, Parmenides, Spinoza, Schelling is the line of substance; Descartes, Kant, Fichte the beginnings of the line of the subject.

Philosophy is not only a truth or a true description; it is also, or should be, a description of the true. If truth (*Wahrheit*) is the correct and complete "revelation" (= description) of being and the real by coherent discourse (*Logos*), the true (*das Wahre*) is being-revealed-by-discourse-in-its-reality. It is therefore not enough for the philosopher to describe being; he must also describe revealed being and account for the fact of the revelation of being by discourse. The philosopher must describe the totality of what is and exists. But this totality in fact implies discourse, and in particular philosophical discourse. The philosopher therefore deals not only with static given being (*Sein*) or substance, the object of discourse, but also with the subject of discourse and of philosophy: it is not enough for him to speak of the being given to him; he must also speak of himself and explain himself to himself as speaking of being and of himself. The distinction between truth (description) and the true (described being as described) makes self-reference a requirement of philosophy: the philosopher must include his own discourse in the totality.

In other words, philosophy must explain how and why being is realised not only as nature and natural world but also as man and historical world. Philosophy must not be content to be a philosophy of nature; it must also be an anthropology: besides the ontological bases of natural reality, it must seek those of human reality, which alone is capable of revealing itself by discourse. The step from "subject" to "anthropology" is Kojève's: the subject of discourse is the human being.

It is in describing the true also as subject, in analysing the specific characters of human reality, that Hegel discovers the dialectical structure of being and the real, and the ontological category of negativity that is at the basis of this dialecticity. And it is in describing the real dialectic that he discovers the circularity of the true and of truth, and so of his philosophy itself. Hegel says so in a passage that closely follows the text cited (Hoffmeister p. 20). Kojève translates: further, living substance (neither static nor given) is the being that is in truth subject, or, what is the same, that is in truth objectively real only insofar as substance is the (dialectical) movement of positing itself (*Sichselbstsetzens*) or the mediation (*Vermittlung*) with itself of becoming other than itself (*Sichanderswerdens*). As subject, substance is pure simple (*einfache*) negativity, and thereby the splitting (*Entzweiung*) of the simple, or the opposing (*entgegensetzende*) doubling (*Verdopplung*), which is again the negation of this indifferent (*gleichgültigen*) diversity and of its opposite (*Gegensatzes*). Only this self-restoring equality, or reflection into itself in otherness (*Anderssein*), is the true, not the original (*ursprüngliche*) unity as such, the immediate (*unmittelbar*) unity as such. The true is the becoming of itself, the circle that presupposes its end (*Ende*) as its aim (*Zweck*) and has it for its beginning, and that is objectively real only through its working-out (*Ausführung*) and its end. The passage (¶18) condenses the dialectic: negativity, splitting, restored equality, circle.

This very condensed passage implies all the fundamental notions of Hegel's "dialectic" and sums up everything essential and truly new in his philosophy. If substance conceived as natural static given being (*Sein*) has as ontological foundation identity (with itself), the subject of discourse revealing this being and itself, man, has as its ultimate basis negativity. And man, dominated in his very being by negativity, is not static given being but action, the act of positing or creating himself. He is objectively real only as a "dialectical movement" whose result is "mediated" by the negation of the given being that serves as its starting point. It is this negativity, associated in being with the identity of being, that splits this being into object and subject, creating man opposed to nature. But it is also this same negativity, realised as human existence within nature, that re-unites subject and object in and through true knowledge, where discourse "coincides" with the being it reveals. The true, or revealed being, is therefore not, as Parmenides and his emulators thought, the first and primordial, even "immediate" or given and natural, identity of being and thought, but the result of a long active process that begins by opposing man to the nature he speaks of and "negates" by his action. The reading of ¶18 as anthropology is Kojève's earliest statement of his thesis: negativity is man, and it both splits being and reunites it in knowledge.

The re-establishment of unity, the final coincidence of "substance" and "subject", takes place in the adequate description of the totality of being and the real by "absolute" philosophy (to whose elaboration the whole human existence of its author, the Sage, is reduced, who therefore ceases to oppose himself actively, as "subject", to nature taken as "substance"). But the totality of the real implies human reality, which exists only as a creative movement. The perfect and definitive adequation of being (= substance) and discourse (= subject) can therefore take place only at the end of times, when man's creative movement is completed. And this completion is revealed by the fact that man no longer advances and is content to retrace (in his philosophical thought) the path already travelled (by his active existence). So "absolute" philosophy, the true in the strong sense, can appear only as a circular description of the real dialectic taken in its totality. This philosophy describes, on the one hand, the path leading from the birth of discourse (= man) within being (= nature) to the advent of the man who will reveal by his discourse the totality of being; and it is, on the other hand, itself this discourse revealing the totality. But this totality implies the discourse that reveals it, as well as the process of the becoming of this discourse. So, reaching the end of the philosophical description, one is thrown back to its beginning, which is the description of its becoming. The "end" of this described becoming is the advent of absolute philosophy. But this advent is also the aim pursued from the beginning, since philosophy is absolute, describes the totality, only insofar as it understands itself in describing its own becoming. But this description can be made only from the standpoint of absolute philosophy, which is therefore the "beginning" or origin of every adequate description. That is to say, like the totality it describes, absolute philosophy too can realise itself objectively only in and through its "development", as the whole of its circular discourse forming an indivisible whole that reproduces the closed dialectic of reality. It is this circularity of philosophical discourse that guarantees its unsurpassable and unmodifiable totality, and so its absolute truth. The 1934 text already contains the whole theory of circularity of the 1938–39 lectures. The definition of the end of history as the moment "when man no longer advances and is content to retrace the path" is its first formulation.

Hegel says this himself (Hoffmeister p. 21), resuming after an explanatory note the idea stated at the end of the passage cited. Kojève translates: the true is the whole. But the whole is only the essential reality (*Wesen*) that completes itself through its development. It must be said of the Absolute that it is essentially result, that only at the end is it what it is in truth; and precisely in this consists its nature of being objectively real (*Wirkliches*), subject or self-becoming (*Sichselbstwerden*). The true, or being-revealed-by-discourse, is a totality, the whole of a creative or dialectical movement that produces discourse within being. The Absolute, or the totality of the real, is not only substance but also subject perfectly revealing the real; only it is so only at the end of its dialectical (= historical) becoming, which ends in its own revelation. And this revealing becoming means that the totality implies human reality, which is not a given eternally identical with itself but an act of progressive temporal self-creation. This self-creation of man takes place through the negation of the (natural and human) given. Human reality, the I, is therefore not a natural or "immediate" reality but a dialectical or "mediated" one. To conceive the Absolute as subject (and that is the essential, according to Hegel) is therefore to conceive it as implying negativity and as realising itself not only as nature but also as I or man, as creative or historical becoming. "The true is the whole" (¶20) and "the Absolute is essentially result" are the Preface's most famous sentences. Kojève's gloss "result = end of historical becoming" gives them his historical sense.

Hegel says this (after a new explanatory note) in the sentence following the passage cited (Hoffmeister p. 21). Kojève translates: mediation is nothing but self-equality (*Sichselbstgleichheit*) in (dialectical) motion; or it is reflection into itself, the moment of the I existing for itself, pure negativity, or, reduced to its pure abstraction, simple becoming. And (after a new note) Hegel continues (Hoffmeister p. 22): what has just been said can also be expressed by saying that Reason (*Vernunft*) is purposive action (*zweckmäßiges Tun*). The sentence "Reason is purposive action" (¶22) is the textual basis of Kojève's anthropology of the project: reason is action toward an end.

To say that the Absolute is not only substance but also subject is to say that the totality implies negativity in addition to identity. It is also to say that being is realised not only as nature but also as man. And it is finally to say that man, who differs essentially from nature only insofar as he is reason (*Logos*) or coherent meaningful discourse revealing being, is himself not given being but creative action (= negating the given). Man is a dialectical or historical (= free) movement revealing being by discourse only because he lives according to the future, which presents itself to him as a project or "aim" (*Zweck*) to be realised by negating action on the given, and because he is himself real as man only insofar as he creates himself by this action as a work (*Werk*). It is from the introduction into ontology of the fundamental category of negativity or action (*Tat* or *Tun*, which is "man's true being") that all the characteristic features of Hegelian ("dialectical") philosophy follow. The chain, Absolute as subject, negativity, man, action, future, project, work, is the 1934 programme of the whole book.

Among other consequences, one we already know, which Hegel formulates as follows (Hoffmeister p. 23): among the various consequences that follow from what has been said, one can single out that knowledge is objectively real and can be presented (*dargestellt*) only as Science or as System. "Science" or "System" mean in Hegel the adequate, and so circular, description of the completed or closed totality of the real dialectical movement. Indeed, as soon as one introduces negativity or creative action into given being, one can claim absolute truth, total and definitive, only by admitting that the creative dialectical process is completed. And a description of the completed dialectical process, the process ending in a term whose negation is no longer the creation of a new term, can indeed only be circular. A footnote adds: according to Hegel, no truth is possible before the completion of the dialectical (= historical) process. But this consequence is necessary only if one admits the dialecticity of the totality of being. Admitting, by contrast, that negativity intervenes only in human reality and that given being is governed only by identity, one can maintain the traditional notion of truth, at least with regard to nature and man's past. The footnote, written in 1934, is the earliest statement of the dualist consequence developed in Appendix I (p. 486): if nature is not dialectical, truth about nature is available at any time.

Finally, ending the passage (Hoffmeister pp. 19–24) in which he briefly sets out the essential features of his whole system, Hegel says that one can sum up everything he states about the dialecticity of being by saying that the Absolute is Spirit (*Geist*). Kojève translates (Hoffmeister p. 24): (the fact) that the true is objectively real only as System, or that substance is essentially subject, is expressed in the representation (*Vorstellung*) that states (*ausspricht*) the Absolute as (being) Spirit, the most sublime concept, which belongs properly to modern times and their (Christian) religion. Only the spiritual (*das Geistige*) is the objectively real (*das Wirkliche*): it is (on the one hand) the essential reality or the in-itself (*Ansichseiende*); (on the other hand) what relates (to itself and to others) (*das sich Verhaltende*) and the specifically determined (*das Bestimmte*), otherness (*Anderssein*) and being-for-itself (*Fürsichsein*); and (finally) what remains in itself (*in sich selbst Bleibende*) in this specific determination or in its being-outside-itself (*Außersichsein*), that is, it is in and for itself ... Spirit that knows itself thus developed as Spirit is Science. It is the objective reality of Spirit and the kingdom it builds for itself in its own element. The passage (¶25) attributes the concept of Spirit to "modern times and their religion", which Kojève will read as Hegel's acknowledgement of the Christian origin of his anthropology.

To say that the Absolute is Spirit is to affirm the dialectical structure of being and the real taken as a whole, as integrated totality. For Spirit is at once being-in-itself (identity, thesis, given being, nature), being-for-itself (negativity, antithesis, action, man), and being-in-and-for-itself (totality, synthesis, work, history = "movement"). Being a dialectical totality, the spiritual is the objectively real, and it alone is. For concrete reality implies everything that is in any way: the natural world as well as the human or historical world and the universe of discourse. Subject and object, thought and being, nature and man, are only abstractions taken separately, just as isolated discourses and particular thing-like entities are abstractions. Only the whole of reality revealed by the whole of discourse is an objective reality; and this whole, with its double aspect, the natural world implying the man who speaks of it, is precisely what Hegel calls "Spirit". The table of correspondences, in-itself/identity/thesis/being/nature, for-itself/negativity/antithesis/action/man, in-and-for-itself/totality/synthesis/work/history, is the most complete in the book.

To study the real philosophically by conceiving it as Spirit is therefore not to confine oneself, as the Greeks and the philosophical tradition did, to the phenomenological, metaphysical, and ontological description of given being and the "eternal" natural cosmos, but to extend this triple description to the creative action that is man and to his historical world. Only then does the real described appear as dialectical or "trinitarian", even as "spiritual". The three planes appear here in 1934, four years before the eighth lecture (p. 365).

But the man Hegel has in view is not the one the Greeks believed they saw and bequeathed to philosophical posterity. This supposed man of the ancient tradition is in fact a purely natural (= identical) being, without freedom (= negativity), history, or individuality properly speaking. Like the animal, he only "represents", in and through his real and active existence, an eternal "idea" or "essence", given once for all and remaining identical with itself. Like the animal's life, his empirical existence is absolutely determined by the natural place (*topos*) he has always occupied within the given immutable cosmos (his possible "deviations" being only the effect of "chance"). And if he differs essentially from the animal, it is solely by his thought or coherent discourse (*Logos*), whose appearance in the cosmos, moreover, could never be explained. But this discourse negates nothing and creates nothing: it is content to reveal the given real (error remaining in fact inexplicable). Discourse, man, is therefore one body with given being. And what there is in the last analysis is this one and unique being that thinks itself eternally in its given totality. Or, as Spinoza will later say, what there is in the last analysis is God, who is substance. The critique of Greek anthropology is sharp: the Greek man is a rational animal, with a *logos* that is inexplicable and does nothing. The observation that error remains "in fact inexplicable" for the Greeks anticipates Appendix I's theory of error (p. 463).

The man Hegel analyses, by contrast, is the man who appears in the pre-philosophical Judaeo-Christian tradition, the only truly anthropological one. This tradition maintained itself during "modern times" in the form of "faith" or "theology", incompatible with ancient and traditional science or philosophy. And it is this tradition that transmitted to Hegel the notion of the free historical individual (or "person"), which he was the first to analyse philosophically, trying to reconcile it with the fundamental notions of the pagan philosophy of nature. A footnote adds: in fact Hegel was preceded on this path by Descartes (the first attempt at a Christian philosophy), Kant and Fichte (Christian philosophers par excellence). But these three attempts at philosophical anthropology failed because their authors did not dare abandon the traditional idea (and in the last analysis "pagan" or "naturalist": identity!) of the immortality of man or the "soul". By his notions of "monad" and "sufficient reason", Leibniz is a precursor of the Hegelian notion of Spirit, totality at once "subjective" and "objective"; but Leibniz did not see the essential difference subsisting between nature and history, and there is in him no anthropology properly speaking (explicit). As for Hegel himself, he did not manage to reconcile his ("dialectical") anthropology with the traditional ("identical") philosophy of nature. Rightly, he refused to apply to man the "naturist" categories of the Greeks and renounced their pseudo-anthropology. But wrongly, he also abandoned their philosophy of nature, trying to apply to the whole of the real (human as well as natural) his own dialectical categories, which are in fact specifically and exclusively anthropological. The footnote is the 1934 root of the dualist critique: Hegel was right to reject Greek anthropology and wrong to reject Greek physics. The diagnosis of Descartes, Kant, and Fichte, that they failed because they kept immortality, which is a pagan category of identity, is striking: the soul's immortality is the Greek remnant in Christian philosophy.

According to this Judaeo-Christian tradition, man differs essentially from nature, and differs not only in his thought but by his very activity. Nature is a "sin" in man and for man: he can and must oppose it and negate it in himself. While living in nature, he does not undergo its laws (miracles!): insofar as he opposes and negates it, he is independent of it; he is autonomous or free. And living in the natural world "as a stranger", opposing it and its laws, he creates in it a new world of his own: a historical world, where man can "convert" and become a being radically other than he is as given natural being (*Anderssein*). In this historical world, and by this free "conversion", man is not any representative of an eternal or immutable given "species": he is created, and creates himself, as an individual unique of his kind. The reading of miracle as the theological form of man's independence from natural law is witty and exact: the miracle is the image of freedom.

When Hegel says that his whole philosophy is nothing but an attempt to conceive substance as subject, he means that the principal aim of this philosophy is to account for the existence of man in the natural world, man conceived as the Judaeo-Christian anthropological tradition conceives him. And that is precisely why, in the text cited, Hegel uses the word "Spirit" to sum up the whole of philosophy. For he takes care to stress the Judaeo-Christian origin of the anthropological notion of *Geist* and to oppose this "modern" notion to the whole ancient or pagan tradition, which is that of "substance" alone or of natural given being (*Sein*). The reading of "belongs to modern times and their religion" as acknowledgement of the Christian origin of *Geist* is Kojève's.

But if, according to the text cited, Hegel detaches himself from the pagan philosophical tradition and accepts the Judaeo-Christian anthropological tradition, he stresses in the same text that he also separates himself from the latter on a point of extreme philosophical importance. The Judaeo-Christian anthropological tradition is essentially religious, even theist (and "theological"). Certainly the Judaeo-Christians discovered the "spirituality" (= dialecticity) of man, his freedom, historicity, and individuality. But for them "spirituality" is realised and manifested fully only in the beyond, and Spirit properly speaking, truly "objectively real" Spirit, is God: an infinite and eternal being. Man himself, made in God's image, is truly "spiritual" only insofar as he is eternal, and he is eternal or "immortal" by the very fact of being Spirit. Man really transcends the natural world in the sense that he also lives in a transcendent world (and not only in a "transcendental" historical world, immanent to nature). This world is beyond nature, which among other things implies man taken in his empirical existence (*Dasein*); but this world is said to be still more "objective" and "real" than the natural world here below. Man enters it after his death, never to leave it; and he participates in it also during his life, having already been there before his birth. To say that man has an "immortal soul" (which is precisely Spirit in him) is to admit the reality of this transcendent world; and to admit this reality is to affirm the immortality or infinity of man. But this world does not depend on man: it is given to him once for all, being "prior" and essentially immutable in itself. On the contrary, it is temporal man who depends absolutely on this transcendent world: the historical world man creates here below is in fact only a reflection, in spatio-temporal nature, of the eternal world beyond. This eternal world is therefore not, properly speaking, human: it is beyond the free historical individual, as it is beyond the animal and the thing. This infinite and eternal world is a divine world, and its one and unique totality, which is Spirit, is not man but God: man accedes to God only after his death, and only then does he fully realise and manifest his "spirituality". The distinction between the "transcendent" world of religion and the "transcendental" historical world immanent to nature is Kojève's key terminological contrast: the historical world is a transcendence within nature.

But according to Hegel the "spiritual" or "dialectical" being is necessarily temporal and finite. The Christian notion of an infinite and eternal Spirit is self-contradictory: the infinite being is necessarily "natural" static given being, eternally identical with itself; and the "dynamic" created or creating, historical or "spiritual" being is necessarily limited in time, essentially mortal. And the Judaeo-Christian tradition did finally realise this. Admitting the immortality of the soul, it admitted the reality of the divine world, the "natural place" of man after his death (this death annulling him as an integral element of the natural and human world here below). And by the logical force of things, Christian thought had to subordinate immortal man to its eternal, infinite, transcendent God. It had to renounce human freedom, and so man's true historicity and individuality. At once the three fundamental (= dialectical) anthropological categories were applied literally only to the true Spirit that is God: for Christian theological thought, Jesus Christ is the only free historical individual properly speaking, the freedom, historicity, and individuality of ordinary man being only effects of divine "grace", of a trans-human action of the trans-mundane God. But even applying these categories to the eternal God-man one meets insurmountable difficulties. Christ is truly autonomous only insofar as he is God. But being God, he can be nothing other than the one and unique being that thinks itself while remaining eternally identical with itself. Instead of a free historical individual, one therefore has the Absolute-Substance that Parmenides already had in view, that Spinoza rediscovered, and that Schelling took up at the very moment Hegel was elaborating his "dialectical" or anthropological philosophy. The argument that an eternal Spirit is self-contradictory, since eternity is identity and spirit is negativity, is Kojève's central objection to theism. Its consequence, Christ as God collapses into Parmenidean substance, makes the incarnation logically unstable.

Hegel wanted from the start to apply to man the Judaeo-Christian notion of free historical individuality, unknown in pagan antiquity. But analysing this "dialectical" notion philosophically, he saw that it implied finitude or temporality. He understood that man could be a free historical individual only on condition of being mortal in the proper and strong sense of the term, finite in time and conscious of his finitude. And having understood this, Hegel denied survival: the man he has in view is real only insofar as he lives and acts within nature; outside the natural world he is pure nothingness. The step from individuality to mortality to the denial of survival is the appendix's thesis about Hegel's development.

But to deny survival is in fact to deny God himself. For to say that man, who effectively transcends nature insofar as he negates (by action), nonetheless annihilates himself as soon as he places himself outside it by dying in it as an animal, is to say that there is nothing beyond the natural world. The so-called "transcendent" or "divine" non-natural world is in reality only the "transcendental" (or speaking) world of human historical existence, which does not exceed the temporal and spatial frameworks of the natural world. There is therefore no Spirit outside the man who lives in the world. And "God" is objectively real only within this natural world, where he exists only in the form of man's theological discourse. The inference from the denial of survival to the denial of God is direct: if man's spirit cannot exist outside nature, no spirit can. "God exists only as man's theological discourse" is the realist definition of God.

So Hegel accepts the Judaeo-Christian anthropological tradition only in a radically secularised or atheist form. The Absolute-Spirit or Substance-Subject Hegel speaks of are not God. The Hegelian Spirit is the spatio-temporal totality of the natural world that implies the human discourse revealing this world and itself. Or, what is the same, Spirit is man-in-the-world: «l'Homme mortel qui vit dans un Monde sans Dieu et qui parle de tout ce qui existe et de tout ce qu'il crée, soi-même y compris» (mortal man who lives in a world without God and speaks of everything that exists and everything he creates, himself included) (p. 539). The definition of Spirit as mortal man in a godless world speaking of everything is the appendix's most compact formula.

And that is what Hegel says implicitly at the end of the passage cited. He says there that "Spirit" is "Science", that it is "Science" that is the only "objective reality" of Spirit. But this "Science" is nothing other than Hegelian philosophy, which appears within the natural world at the end of man's historical becoming. Spirit is therefore nothing other than the spatio-temporal totality of the natural world insofar as it is entirely revealed by the discourse of the perfect (= satisfied) man or Sage, this discourse being itself a simple integration of the true meaning of all the discourses pronounced by men in the course of history. Or again: the Spirit the Judaeo-Christians called "God" is in reality Hegelian philosophy, insofar as it is absolutely true, insofar as it correctly and completely reveals everything that has been, is, and will be. The identification of God with Hegel's philosophy, "the Spirit the Judaeo-Christians called God is in reality Hegelian philosophy", is anthropotheism in its most provocative form, stated in 1934.

But according to Hegel, the discursive revelation of being is possible only if the revealing or speaking being is essentially finite or mortal. The Hegelian Spirit is therefore truly not a "divine" Spirit (since there are no mortal gods): it is human in the sense that it is a discourse immanent to the natural world and having as its "support" a natural being limited in its existence by time and space. The parenthesis "there are no mortal gods" sits uneasily with Appendix I's "mortal god" (p. 492), written a year later: in 1934 Kojève denies the Sage divinity outright; in 1935 he grants it as a metaphor.

When Hegel says that the essential content of his whole philosophy can be summed up by saying that he interprets substance as subject, or conceives the Absolute as Spirit, this means that this philosophy must above all account philosophically for itself as a discourse revealing completely and adequately the totality of being and the real. It does so by explaining how and why man comes to speak coherently of himself and of the world he lives in and creates. And this explanation is a phenomenological, metaphysical, and ontological description of man understood as a free historical individual.
