To describe man as a free historical individual is to describe him: as "finite" in and by himself, on the ontological plane; as "worldly", spatial and temporal, on the metaphysical plane; and as "mortal", on the phenomenological plane. On this last plane man "appears" as a being always conscious of his death, often accepting it freely and, knowingly, sometimes giving it to himself voluntarily. So Hegel's "dialectical" or anthropological philosophy is, in the last analysis, «une philosophie de la mort (ou ce qui est la même chose : de l'athéisme)» (a philosophy of death, or, what is the same, of atheism) (p. 539). The conclusion of the first lecture of the appendix is its thesis: Hegel's philosophy is a philosophy of death, which is the same as atheism. The equation is the book's most radical interpretive claim.

The analysis of the passage of the Preface in which Hegel traces the main lines of his philosophy clearly shows the primordial role the idea of death plays in it. The unreserved acceptance of the fact of death, of human finitude conscious of itself, is the ultimate source of all Hegelian thought, which only draws all the consequences, even the most remote, of the existence of this fact. According to this thought, it is by voluntarily accepting the danger of death in a fight for pure prestige that man appears for the first time in the natural world; and it is by resigning himself to death, revealing it by his discourse, that man finally reaches absolute knowledge or wisdom, thus completing history. For it is starting from the idea of death that Hegel elaborates his Science or "absolute" philosophy, which alone can account philosophically for the existence in the world of a finite being conscious of its finitude and sometimes disposing of it as it pleases. So Hegelian absolute knowledge or wisdom and the conscious acceptance of death, understood as complete and definitive annihilation, are one. Hegel says it himself in so many words in another passage of the Preface (Hoffmeister p. 29 ff.), of absolutely capital importance. Only by reading this truly remarkable passage does one grasp the ultimate motives of Hegelian thought, understand its true meaning, and realise its full scope. The thesis that death frames the whole of history, accepted in the first fight, understood in the last wisdom, gives the book its arc from Introduction to Chapter VIII.

Kojève translates the passage (Hoffmeister pp. 29–30): the activity (*Tätigkeit*) of separating (*Scheidens*) is the force and labour of the Understanding (*Verstand*), of the most astonishing (*verwundersamsten*) and greatest power (*Macht*), or rather of the absolute power. The circle that rests closed in itself and holds its moments as substance does is the immediate relation, and therefore in no way astonishing. But that the accidental as such, separated from its surroundings (*Umfange*), what is bound (*Gebundene*) and objectively real only in its connection (*Zusammenhang*) with something else, should obtain an existence (*Dasein*) of its own and a separate freedom (*abgesonderte Freiheit*), is the tremendous power (*ungeheure Macht*) of the negative; it is the energy of thought (*Denkens*), of the pure abstract I (*Ichs*). Death, if we want to call this unreality (*Unwirklichkeit*) by that name, is what is most terrible (*Furchtbarste*), and to hold fast what is dead is what requires the greatest force. Powerless beauty hates the Understanding, because it demands (*zumutet*) of it what it cannot do. But the life of Spirit is not the life that shrinks (*scheut*) from death and keeps itself pure (*rein bewahrt*) from devastation (*Verwüstung*), but the life that endures death and maintains itself (*erhält*) in it. Spirit obtains its truth only by finding itself in absolute disruption (*Zerrissenheit*). It is not this (tremendous) power by being the positive that turns away (*wegsieht*) from the negative, as when we say of something: this is nothing, or (this is) false, and, having (thus) finished with it (*damit fertig*), pass from there to something else; no, Spirit is this power only insofar as it looks the negative in the face (*ins Angesicht schaut*) and tarries (*verweilt*) with it. This tarrying (*Verweilen*) is the magic force (*Zauberkraft*) that converts (*umkehrt*) the negative into being (*Sein*). This (power of Spirit, this magic force) is the same as what was called above (p. 19) the subject, which, giving in its (own) element an existence to determinateness, dialectically overcomes (*aufhebt*) abstract immediacy (*Unmittelbarkeit*), that which merely is in general (*nur überhaupt seiende*), and (which) is thereby the true substance, being or immediacy that does not have mediation outside itself but is itself this mediation. This is Preface ¶32, the most famous page Hegel wrote, which Kojève has cited throughout as "the key to the whole system" (p. 375). His translation keeps every German term in brackets.

To understand the somewhat enigmatic beginning of this passage, otherwise perfectly clear and univocal, one must bear in mind the following. Philosophy is the pursuit of wisdom, and wisdom is the fullness of self-consciousness. Aspiring and claiming to wisdom, Hegel wants in the last analysis to account for himself, for what he is and what he does. His activity, to which his truly human existence reduces, is that of a philosopher or Sage, who reveals by his discourse the being he is himself and the being he is not. Philosophising, Hegel must therefore above all account for his own philosophical discourse. And observing this discourse, Hegel notes that it is not a passive datum but the result of an "activity" that can be called "labour" and requires very great "force", supplied by what he here calls the "Understanding". He therefore notes that the Understanding is a "power", and says this power is "greater" than all others and truly "astonishing". "Understanding" here evidently means what is truly and specifically human in man, since it is the faculty of discourse, which distinguishes him from the animal and the thing. It is also what is essential in every philosopher whatever, and so in Hegel himself. The whole question is what it is. Hegel tells us that the Understanding (= man) is an "absolute power", manifesting itself in and through "the activity of separating", or better still as "the act of separating" (*Scheiden*). But why does he say so? The reading of *Verstand* in ¶32 as "what is specifically human in man", rather than the inferior faculty of Chapter III, is important: here the Understanding is the power of discourse itself.

He says so because the activity of the Understanding, human thought, is essentially discursive. Man does not reveal instantaneously, as in a flash, the totality of the real: he does not grasp this totality in a single word-concept. He reveals one by one, by isolated words or partial discourses, the constituents of the totality, separating them from it in order to do so, and only the whole of his discourse extended in time can reveal the total reality, even simultaneous. But in fact these elements are inseparable from the whole they constitute, linked by spatial and temporal, even material, indissoluble bonds. Their separation is therefore indeed a "miracle", and the power that performs it deserves to be called "absolute". The argument that discourse must separate because it is successive is the ground of the eighth lecture's thesis that the concept is temporal.

The absolute force or power of the Understanding Hegel has in view is in the last analysis nothing other than the power of abstraction found in man. When one describes any isolated object, one abstracts from the rest of the universe. Speaking of "this table" or "this dog", one speaks of them as if they were alone in the world. But in fact, as real, the dog and the table occupy at a given moment well-determined places in the real world and cannot be separated from what surrounds them. But the man who isolates them in his thought can, in this thought, combine them as he pleases. He can, for example, place this dog under this table, even if in fact they are separated at this moment by a distance of a thousand kilometres. And this power thought has of separating and recombining things is indeed "absolute", since no real force of attraction or repulsion is powerful enough to oppose it. And this power is in no way fictitious or "ideal". For it is by separating and recombining things in and through his discursive thought that man forms his technical projects, which, once realised by labour, really transform the aspect of the given natural world, creating in it a cultural world. The example of putting the dog under the table a thousand kilometres away is Kojève's concrete image of abstraction. The link from abstraction to technical projects to labour makes the power of the Understanding the root of culture.

In general, when one creates the concept of a real entity, one detaches it from its *hic et nunc*. The concept of a thing is this thing itself as detached from its given *hic et nunc*. So the concept "this dog" differs in nothing from the real concrete dog to which it "relates", except that this dog is here and now, whereas its concept is everywhere and nowhere, always and never. But to detach an entity from its *hic et nunc* is to separate it from its "material" support, univocally determined by the rest of the given spatio-temporal universe of which this entity is part. That is why the entity can be reworked or "simplified" at will after it has become a concept. So this real dog is, as concept, not only "this dog" but also "any dog", "the dog in general", "quadruped", "animal", and so on, and even "being" pure and simple. And once more, this power of separation, which is at the origin of the sciences, arts, and crafts, is an "absolute" power to which nature can oppose no effective resistance. The thesis that the concept is the thing itself detached from its *hic et nunc* is the earliest form of the eighth lecture's theory (p. 373). The chain "this dog", "any dog", "animal", "being" shows abstraction as successive detachment.

It is not correct, however, to say that the real entity become concept is situated outside time and space. Aristotle was right to specify that Platonic "ideas" exist only in spatial and temporal, "material" things, of which they are the "essences" or "entelechies". The absolute power of the Understanding manages to separate an "essence" from its natural support: the essence "dog" from this dog that runs and barks here and now. But it cannot transport it into a "hyper-celestial" world, as it were, outside space-time. Once detached from its natural support, the "essence" becomes "meaning" or "idea". But "meaning" does not float in the void; it is necessarily the meaning of a word or discourse: spoken, written, or only thought, but always existing within the spatial and temporal world. The concept is not an "idea" or "meaning" but a word-having-a-meaning, a coherent discourse (*Logos*). So the absolute power of the Understanding separates the idea-essence from its natural support only to attach it, as idea-meaning, to the specific support of a discourse, which too is here and now (since it is a meaningful discourse only insofar as it is understood by a concrete man). The thesis that meaning always needs a material support, the word, is Kojève's anti-Platonism: there is no *topos hyperouranios*, only words in time. The essence moves from the dog to the word "dog", never into heaven.

But the separation of the "essence" from its natural support is nonetheless not an event that takes place spontaneously within nature but the result of an "activity" of the "Understanding", of a "labour" requiring a "force" endowed with "absolute power". One can well say with Hegel that this power is "astonishing" and that the main task of philosophy or Science is to account for it. The "astonishment" (*verwundersam*) echoes the Greek *thaumazein* as the beginning of philosophy; Kojève makes its object the existence of discourse.

But Hegel's philosophical precursors went about it badly in answering the question, in explaining the miracle. They saw and posed the problem badly. They spoke of the "subject" in general or of "thought" as such, asking how and why being is also concept, how and why it can have a meaning; but they forgot to say that there are also the meaningful discourses men pronounce, write, or think in space and time. Simplifying the problem in this way, they certainly reached a result. Parmenides affirms the identity of being and thought; Aristotle speaks of the being that eternally thinks itself in its totality; Spinoza, inspired by Descartes and inspiring Schelling, says that thought is an attribute of substance. Hegel does not contest this result of the philosophy preceding his. He says only that the relation between being and thought this philosophy had in view is nothing very remarkable. To account truly for the relation in question, it would have sufficed to identify, with Hegel, the concept and time, or, what is the same, to affirm the temporality of being itself. For the concept, or more exactly the meaning of being, differs in nothing from being itself except by the absence in the meaning of being of this being. And the same holds for the meaning of any thing that is, since being is the integration of everything that is, so that the meaning "being" is an integration of all meanings in general. The meaning-essence of a thing is, as one says, this thing itself minus its existence. But the "subtraction" that removes being from being is nothing other than time, which makes being pass from the present, where it is, into the past, where it is not (no longer), and where it is therefore only pure meaning (or essence without existence). And since it is not a new being that is in the present but the "old" or past being, one can say that being is an essence that has acquired existence; or, what is the same, that being is not being only but concept; or, what is the same again, that being has a meaning to the very extent that it is (as time). Likewise, since it is the same past being that is in the present and will be in the future (where, not yet being, it is also essence without existence), one can say that being has an aim (this aim, the transformation of future into present or the granting of existence to essence, being moreover nothing other than the transformation of present into past, of being into concept): which can also be expressed by saying that the very being of being has a meaning; or, what is the same, that being has a reason for being (this "reason" being the thought of being by being). So, if being and time are one, one can well say that being coincides with thought, that it thinks itself eternally, and that thought is the attribute of its substance, or, if one likes, its "aim". This dense paragraph, written in 1934, contains the eighth lecture's "being minus being" (p. 375) in full. Its title formula, "if being and time are one", invokes Heidegger's title as the hypothesis under which Parmenides, Aristotle, and Spinoza become true. The derivation of teleology from time, being has an aim because the future grants existence to essence, is one of Kojève's most original speculative moves.

Hegel too agrees to say so. Only, according to him, this relation of being and thought within Parmenides's "sphere", Aristotle's "circle" (which Hegel evokes in the text cited), or the Spinozist and Schellingian "substance" (of which he also speaks), has nothing "miraculous" about it. For this relation is "immediate", says Hegel; and "immediate" means for him "natural" or "given". And indeed this relation presupposes no "activity", "labour", "force", or "power". For here the "essence" is not separated from its "natural" support: the essence of being subsists in being itself and in it alone, just as the essence of the dog subsists only in the dog (and that is why there can be no table in this being, for example, no artefacts). There is here neither action, nor labour, nor power, because the given being remains as it is given, in its immutable identity with itself. The parenthesis "there can be no table in this being, no artefacts" is decisive: a world in which essence never separates from existence is a world without labour, since the artefact requires an essence (project) separated from any existing support.

What is "miraculous", by contrast, is precisely the separation effected by the Understanding. For it is indeed "against nature". Without the intervention of the Understanding, the essence "dog" would exist only in and through real dogs, which would determine it univocally in return by their very existence. And that is why one can say that the relation between the dog and the essence "dog" is "natural" or "immediate". But when, thanks to the absolute power of the Understanding, the essence becomes meaning and is incarnated in a word, there is no longer a "natural" relation between it and its support; otherwise words that have nothing in common with each other as spatio-temporal, phonetic, or graphic realities, and are moreover arbitrary (*chien*, *dog*, *Hund*, and so on), could not serve as support for one and the same essence, all having one and the same meaning. There has therefore been here a negation of the given as given (with its "natural" relations between essence and existence); that is, creation (of concepts or meaningful words, which as words have nothing to do, by themselves, with the meaning incarnated in them); that is, action or labour. The argument from the arbitrariness of the sign, *chien*, *dog*, *Hund*, recalls Saussure's arbitrariness of the sign; it is used here to prove that the concept is a creation, a negation of the natural bond between essence and existence. This is the linguistic form of the thesis that the concept is labour.

If the traditional conception of being-thought accounts for the possibility of discourse revealing the meaning of what is, by explaining how and why being has a meaning, it does not say how and why discourse becomes real, how and why one actually manages to "release the meaning of being" and incarnate it in a set of words that have nothing in common with this meaning and were created out of nothing for this incarnation. But it is precisely the reality of discourse that is the miracle philosophy should explain. What is miraculous, says Hegel, is that something really inseparable from something else nonetheless obtains a separate existence; or again, that a mere attribute or "accident" becomes an autonomous reality. The distinction between the possibility of discourse (explained by the tradition) and its reality (unexplained) locates the problem precisely: why does discourse actually exist?

The essence is a "bound entity" to its support, and it is "objectively real only in its connection with something other" than itself, precisely with its support. Nonetheless the Understanding manages to separate the essence from its natural support and procure for it "an existence of its own" by incarnating it in a spoken, written, or thought word or discourse. And this "existence" of its own of the essence become meaning is also its "separate or isolated freedom". For the meaning incarnated in the word and discourse is no longer subject to the necessity governing essences bound to their respective natural supports, univocally determined by their *hic et nunc*. So, for example, the meaning incarnated in the word "dog" can go on subsisting even after all dogs have disappeared from the earth; it can (transmitted by wireless, for example) cross obstacles insurmountable for a real dog; it can be situated where there would be no room for the latter; and so on. And it is this "separate freedom", and the "absolute power" from which it follows, that condition the possibility of error, of which pre-Hegelian philosophies could never account. For this "freedom" allows meanings incarnated in words to combine otherwise than the corresponding essences bound to their natural supports do. The examples of the meaning's freedom, surviving extinct dogs, crossing by radio, are the first forms of the eighth lecture's extinct species (p. 375). The derivation of error from the freedom of meaning completes Appendix I's theory (p. 463): error is possible because words combine freely.

It is this "activity", capable of releasing the meaning of being, separating essence from existence, and incarnating meaning-essence in discourse, that is the miracle philosophy (or more exactly Science or wisdom) is supposed to account for. And it is in seeking to account for it that Hegel discovered (or specified) the fundamental (ontological) category of negativity, which he here calls "the negative". This negativity is "the energy of thought" that releases the meaning of being by separating essence from existence. It is "the energy of the pure abstract I" engendering "thought", the "Understanding" and its discourse. But, though it has sometimes been said, discourse does not fall from heaven, and it does not float in the void "above the waters". If it expresses a "thought" that belongs properly to an "I", this I necessarily has an empirical existence in the natural spatio-temporal world, being a human I. What is "abstract I" (*Ich*) on the ontological plane (this I being the form in which negativity subsists in identity or given being) is human "personal I" (*Selbst*) on the metaphysical plane: it is man who "appears", on the phenomenological plane, as a speaking free historical individual. The allusion to Genesis 1:2, the Spirit "moving upon the face of the waters", is pointed: discourse does not hover above creation; it is the word of a mortal body. The three planes, *Ich*, *Selbst*, speaking individual, are the triad of Appendix I.

The miracle of the existence of discourse that philosophy must account for is therefore nothing other than the miracle of man's existence in the world. And indeed one can refer to man himself the sentence of Hegel's interpreted by referring it to discourse. For man too is a "bound entity" that is "objectively real only in its connection with something other": he is nothing without the animal that serves as his support, and he is pure nothingness outside the natural world. And nonetheless he separates himself from this world and opposes himself to it. He creates for himself "an existence of his own", essentially different from all purely natural empirical existences. The identification of the miracle of discourse with the miracle of man's existence closes the analysis: man is the accident that became independent of its substance, the essence separated from nature. The next pages will draw from this the role of death.
